Few years ago when I watched the trailer for Tomb Raider reboot I was so amazed that decided to play it right away. But search results on Steam returned many more and so I decided to play those first. Winter sale was just around the corner so I waited a little bit and bought all of them. This is because I'm kind of man who likes to have a good look at the origin story because thinks that almost 20 years from game's release there may be something I could miss if I skipped all the previous ones.
Obviously when we're talking about a game that is this old we're not looking for pretty graphics but rather an atmosphere, story and even feelings that it may bring. Talking about graphics characters are blocky and Lara's breasts could poke your eye out but that's fine by me. What I remember from the game after 2 years since playing it? I remember when I sat in a dark room for better immersion and rushing to the couch to make myself comfortable before any intros begin. It started with a nuclear blast somewhere in a desert and a conversation in some hotel in New Mexico. I was listening very carefully to consume all those story details that I wanted so badly. And that scene wasn't the most exciting thing in the game. But when I stepped into the caves I was hooked that very moment. It felt a bit scary even. It seemed like it was snowing inside my room and I could feel the cold. Thankfully I was able to put myself together and start playing.
And so the game began. I had those famous double pistols I saw in Lara Croft movies. I tried moving around, shooting, figured out controls. But little did I know what was waiting for me in those caves. I liked a lot how the game was actually teaching me to paly. Even though I skipped the training course in the mansion (which I regret by the way). I was so immersed that my first encounter with the wolver scared the hell out of me. And probably it wasn't the wolf but the music that played when it appeared in from of me. But it wasn’t just the music that was adding to the atmosphere the sound effects in general. Howling winds, Lara's jogging, shooting sounds it was all great. But let's get to the gameplay, shall we? At firs it is no problem to progress. But farther I went the harder some puzzles became. I will try as spoiler-free as possible so I'll just focus on how it felt for me rather that what it was. And I think those puzzles actually shaped the game quite a bit. It felt so satisfying to solve some of them and they were quite logical and some of them even required knowledge of Greek mythology. Quite nice if you ask me. And sometimes there were hidden puzzles which would reward you with ammo and/or guns. And you need to be very attentive when you're looking for them. But it was totally worth it because even though you can complete the game with just your pistols having those cool guns makes the game much more interesting and shooting your foes more satisfying and badass. And you'll probably need those guns when you encounter the first boss in the caves.
Bosses to Tomb Raider are awesome. They are not too easy or too hard to beat. All you need to do is some tinkering to find their weak spot or pattern of their attack and movement. So I would describe them as 'fun'. And this what games supposed to be - fun. And I had a lot of fun in general. They are not repetitive and diverse and that's what made me waiting to get to one. And what's great is that you don't always know when you find one. But be prepared anyway. And there's one thing that is keeping you from them are the levels and it's not something to sneeze at because you can get lost in some of them, some levels took me quite a white to find a way out of. Luckily you can save in any place at any time. And I found myself overusing it and sometimes I was saving a lot while being afraid of loosing my progress and instead I was loosing sense of immersion. Checkpoints is something I would totally appreciate but I don't think the concept was even there in 1996. There's wasn't quick save either. There was a button but you still had to select a save slot. Other than that I don't really have any complaints.
Final level was very creepy and I wished I could complete it fast but it wasn't to be because it was quite large too. But I soldiered on and reached the final boss. And boy was it epic. I had big guns and was able to kick♥♥♥♥♥ If I said anything else I would spoil it all for you. Also remember to use your guns on your way to the boss because I found myself having to many unused ammo in some cases and sacrificed some fun while going through the levels before the boss.
So there you have it. I totally recommend playing it especially now when you have it not only on PC but on mobile phones and tablets too. But beware that I recommend it to people who care about solid gameplay more than about graphics.

With Crysis 2, the series finally arrived where it was always meant to be. Crysis 2 is the equivalent of the loud, obnoxious blockbuster movie dazzling the audience with its fancy effects. Hell, they even got Hans Zimmer to do the soundtrack.
That being said, despite cutting down a lot on the open world aspect, Crysis 2 is probably a better game than the original. At least this one has something resembling proper pacing. The game does a far better job alternating between quiet moments, full-on shootouts and everything in-between. It also throws the player into a couple of memorable scenarios instead of making him infiltrate the same military base over and over again. The gunplay is also improved as it finally has some weight to it and the recoil doesn't seem that random anymore.
However, not all areas have been improved upon. The enemy design, for instance, is actually a step back since you're mostly fighting aliens who look like oversized (human) grunts with squishy heads - the predecessor's design definitely looked and felt more 'alien'.
The story is still completely irrelevant and only serves as an excuse to drag the player through different setpieces. And yet, the game feels the need pester you with radio chatter and cutscenes regularly even though it neither cares about the characters it introduces nor the story it was supposed to tell.
Despite some improvements, Crysis 2 is still lackluster. Although I did enjoy some parts of the game and the scenery of a war-torn New York does have a certain draw to it, a first person shooter that features subpar gunplay is simply not that enjoyable. It doesn't help that the opportunities to use various suit powers have been drastically reduced.
Even if it fails at everything else, the game is a competent benchmark to torture your GPU with.

EDIT: Well, seeing as how this review is getting a lot more mileage I'll put some more work into it. For Honor at its core is VERY fun. No game plays like it, the combat is meaty and satisfying, and the character customization is just indepth enough that it's something you want to keep playing towards. Actual seperate armor pieces with their own paint patterns to customize, not just "pick a skin". Unfortunately, everyone unanimously agrees that they wish ANYONE besides Ubisoft had gotten this game. Here is a SMALL list of some of its incompetency.
- The game is plagued by 'defense meta'. Daring to attack first is simply a bad idea because if you get parried from it, you are subject to massive health punishment. Despite ubisofts (extremely slow) efforts, this has yet to be rectified at all.
- What this means is that at high-level play, only characters with extremely fast attack, or very safe physical shoving attacks are viable at all. Which leaves us with a handful of usable characters out of a total of currently sixteen.
- This number is made even smaller by the fact that many of these shove-capable characters cannot GET anything after shoving people, so the actually viable people at higher level come down to about three or four characters. To play a game where you stare at eachother and someone attacks first in the hopes they don't lose. (There's literally only one well designed character in the cast. Gladiator.)
- The "timesnap" system WAS a lag compensation system for network play. But Ubisoft removed it because of supposed "input delay" worries. Without lag compensation, characters attacks are completely inconsistent in timing. Some characters attacks will hit you at exactly the same time they start animating, making them completely unreactable. This has totally broken network play and Ubisoft continues to say they will not reimplement timesnap.
- Ubisoft's "public test" version of the game isn't being used well at all. Almost not at all. In their first iteration, they tried to fix defensive meta with MULTIPLE changes to how the core game operates. That was months ago. To this day they've only really implemented one of those changes.
- When they tried to buff the Raider's running grab, the community noticed during the public test that the Raider could actually grab someone in literally one frame and made it VERY clear to ubisoft that this was a problem. Ubisoft did not listen, and let it go into the live game. Only when a Raider won a ubisoft-hosted tournament by just running around in circles and fishing for run grabs, did Ubisoft finally fix this.
- When implementing certain buffs many people were excited for, for their SECOND Public Test, ubisoft didn't allow players to JUST play duel mode to test it. The only available modes were Tournament, and Dominion. Tournament simply couldn't gather enough players even after hours of matchmaking, and Dominion is 4v4. Not a good place to excrutiatingly test things. So that public test was useless.
- The character Conqueror, started the game at top tier because his shield bash could be chained into a light attack that was too fast to punish him for dodging the shield bash. After they fixed this, he instantly became a bad character because he has NO tricks or good parts of his kit. And then he got nerfed. And then they nerfed him again. And again. And again. And again. Conqueror continues to get nerfed directly or indirectly with almost EVERY patch since his initial fix and he has never been helped. There was a point where, during Revenge Knockdown changes, for whatever reason he was still the only person that could be knocked down by Revenge shoves. Hell, even his emotes got nerfed at some point.
- The character Shinobi had their kick ability nerfed, but ever since then have been given nothing to compensate. Duelyst is a game developed and published by
. A competitive game focused on tactical combat, squad building, and ranked ladder play.
Duelyst is a perfect mix between CCG and chess. The matches are played out on a five-by-nine board that starts with just you and your opponent’s general. Each general has a unique Spell. Like most other CCGs, you draw cards from a custom built deck, play spells, and summon minions until you’ve killed the opposing general.
The card pool is split into six factions, each with their own unique style, along with a large group of neutral cards. Right now, I'm starting to like the playstyle of Vanar and Songhai. All six factions feel unique and expressive, in both their playstyles and their art.
And speaking of art. This is a major high point of Duelyst. Pixel art has become a popular option among indie developers, and is associated by some skeptics with a lack of resources to make something ‘better.’ But Duelyst’s sprites feature some of the greatest pixel art animation I’ve ever seen. Only the units and card effects are pixelated, but the extreme level of detail that goes into each one is stunning. And thanks to Duelyst’s dynamic lighting system, the sprites don’t feel out of place in its non-pixelated battlefields and UI.
Alough the game offers you in-game purchases where you could buy Spirit Orbs—Duelyst's version of pack of cards. It turns out to be really rewarding since you get gold for winning games and completing daily quests.

First I thought like, hmm, this looks nice and the description fits my interest, but those negative reviews.., I dunno man. This seems to be a rather bad game of an interesting concept.
Now, I did buy the game and my final verdict is:
This game looks good, plays okay for an arcade controls helo game and it sure does catch my interest.
So, what is Heliborne all about?
Simply put, you're the helicopter part of the game World in Conflict.
You take out hostile units and emplacements and deploy troops to fortify your own positions.
The basic formula is not hard to grasp, the execution ranges from easy to strategic.
It just depends on how you want to play the game.
Another nice feature is the option to choose with what kind of helicopter you want to fly and how you want to arm it.
Ofcourse, to keep things balanced you aren't allowed to pack twenty machineguns on a Kiowa.
But, the more firepower you pack, the more valuable your ride becomes leaving even less room for errors to minimize respawn. (Which is a nice feature)
Getting shot down doesn't really give you a penalty, besides a respawn timer which is pretty fair and doesn't really hurt your ego, to put it that way. But, as soon as your tax dollar ride goes up in flames you know that your team lost a valuable asset which can't be used for a couple of minutes and that might change the entire scenario.
So, does this game have potential?
Forget that, it's already potent in its current form and the developers aren't done yet.
Buy this game if you like helicopters, don't need simulator realism and if you want to have a nice twist regarding the battlefield franchise.

Heliborne
Multiplayer Helicopter Combat
JetCatGames
JetCatGames
is a multiplayer helicopter combat simulator developed and published by JetCatGames, and it's currently available on Early Access.
The game looks very good, with a far view distance and detailed environments full of plants, trees and buildings. While I am not an expert, the helicopters seem very realistic and similar to the ones in real life, and it shows that a lot of work went into their design. Also, the performance is very smooth, getting a costant +60fps on High settings.
The first thing that you need to do is create a squad: you can pick between multiple choppers for both the US and the Soviet forces ranging from the 1960s to the early 2000s. This will determine which maps you can play (a squad has to be historically accurate, so no modern helis in Vietnam) and which side you will be taking. However, this can lead to some really unbalanced sessions where you are alone against 3 other players.
The main objective is to conquer every control point of the map by bringing the infantry there with your helicopter. You must also destroy the enemy vehicles and troops that are stationed at each control point. This is a very good variation of the age-old Control Point mode, and it does feel very fresh to me. The vehicles control closer to a GTA game rather than a real simulator, and I appreciate that immensly. I can't wait for the developers to add more game modes as well, such as a Capture The Flag or Deathmatch.
As already stated, the game can be very unbalanced. Also, the ground troops have some very heavy artillery that can blow you up in just a few seconds if you aren't careful.
The sound design is very good, but you do miss the presence of an epic soundtrack in the background.
There are currently four maps to choose from (one from each time period) and one game mode to play. It will keep you entertained, but you do feel like we need more content.
Overall, this is a very enjoyable multiplayer game that I do recommend you guys to support: it looks great, it plays well, and it is also very cheap. Highly recommended to fans of arcade flighting games.

The first, and definitely still one of the best. I don't think I need to sing its praises too much. The Steam port runs on DOSBox, so it comes with a few issues that may bother you, but these are easily fixable and the community is super helpful about it. The lack of music can also be fixed with a mod, and the Gold exclusive levels can also be downloaded free and legally from the official site and made to launch from Steam. Overall, DOSBox can be a blessing in disguise if you're willing to work with it, so don't let it discourage you. Read up on some community guides and ask the forumites for help if necessary. Or, if you'd rather not bother, there is also a guide to play it without DOSBox, and there is also a multipatch you can find on the Square-Enix forums that installs the Gold expansion levels and your choice of soundtrack, hassle-free.
Being the first game in a successful series, it shares the same quality as many other great firsts in gaming history, and there's certainly nothing wrong with it, but the sequels did build on it and raise the bar, so anyone who played those first might find the original a bit lacking in some areas. For one thing, TR1 was made to run on the SEGA Saturn, so the performance is a bit slower than TR2-TR5, and Lara's ponytail is missing because the Saturn simply couldn't handle it. The weapon selection is also limited, as 3 of the 4 weapons are clearly tiered upgrades over each other, the shotgun being the odd one out with strategic uses. There is also no dynamic lighting, so the game is mostly brightly lit with a few rare dark areas you can't really do anything about. The sound design is also more basic. There aren't specific sounds for Lara's footsteps on each type of texture. If these all sound like nitpicks, it's because they are. Where this game truly shines is in its level design, and the environments that are fun to just explore, even when you're stuck. Tomb Raider the first is a great game, and you should play it... but if you're new to the series, you definitely shouldn't stop here.

I know this game was praised as a graphical masterpiece when it was released and it still holds up extremely well as a benchmark for your rig.  It's vibrant with tons of effects and well textured throughout even if certain assets are reused over and over again (some of it can be immersion breaking but I thought think you're here for the roleplaying aspect anyway).
It's a solid FPS experience with hours of content unlike the modern day shooters you see with a few hours, the campaign definitely felt lengthy and the storyline present.  The plot isn't something to write to your mother about but it's passable for the genre and even had a few memorable characters (though lots of blank ones too).
The gameplay itself offers lots of variance in tackling objectives while spoonfeeding you certain ones using the "Objective scanner" by pushing B.  While helpful at times so it's clear what you have to do, some of this definitely took a lot of the challenge away and feelings of accomplishment on completing any objective or entire mission.
Some of Prophet's abilities are a bit too strong as well such as Stealthing (which seems to be a common complaint among players) that it takes too much of the challenge away from the game but with the Ceph enemies using EMP pulses and the like - I found just enough variance and challenge to enjoy the experience.  It 'will' get repetitive to an extent but it overall was a pleasant experience with a large enough variance in weapons and secondaries.
The A.I. is one of the few complaitns I have with the game - sometimes the enemies were buggy and multiple times during the playthrough - I found them clipped or stuck on terrain (especially the Heavy Ceph).  While this meant they were exploitable in a game that already felt a bit too easy.  Other times the enemies (especially Ceph) would just randomly patrol/pace back and forth while you were shooting at them - as if they were trying to decide if they should fight back or run away.
Overall I wouldn't say it's a must-play game release but it didn't have enough shortcomings for me to warn people away from the experience if they are a fan of futuristic-tech FPS campaigns.

Sadly it doesn't hold up well, and definately is no longer worth the relatively premium USD10 (September 2017) price tag. Shop around and buy it for cheap so you can at least experience once of the original gems of indie horror games.
What does make this game interesting is the story, but sadly the revelation of the story is ruined by obvious jump scares, chase scenes, deaths, and whole-level reloads. It's frustrating that such a deep story (which allows for a fair amount of interpretation as you try to work out 'what happened?' and is predicated on hints of folklore, generational sacrifice, and community paranoia) is hampered by the mechanism for how the story is told.
I get that this is one of the hallmarks of the gameplay (collecting pages) - but the problem is that you don't feel you really have the luxury, time, or ability to really hunt for and find the pages in order to fully experience the story. Instead you're constantly running away from something, and hoping you didn't miss a key page or note or story item.
On their own, these two methods of horror games are great (slow burn of a complex, psychological story and being chased by scary things), but mixed together in the way it was in this game just makes it annoying and frustrating. I wanted to learn more about the story...but bloody Slender Man and the Chaser and others kept getting in my way, leading me to just enabling god mode so I could least enjoy what parts of the story I was able to piece together.
It looks like Blue Isle learned a lot from this game, and Valley is an example of a great game based on collecting background notes that form a story - obviously it's not a horror game and so they've removed the jump scares and death chases but it's a better example now of the studio's excellence at forming a narrative tied to gameplay in a logical sense.

Duelyst is a game developed and published by
. A competitive game focused on tactical combat, squad building, and ranked ladder play.
Duelyst is a perfect mix between CCG and chess. The matches are played out on a five-by-nine board that starts with just you and your opponent’s general. Each general has a unique Spell. Like most other CCGs, you draw cards from a custom built deck, play spells, and summon minions until you’ve killed the opposing general.
The card pool is split into six factions, each with their own unique style, along with a large group of neutral cards. Right now, I'm starting to like the playstyle of Vanar and Songhai. All six factions feel unique and expressive, in both their playstyles and their art.
And speaking of art. This is a major high point of Duelyst. Pixel art has become a popular option among indie developers, and is associated by some skeptics with a lack of resources to make something ‘better.’ But Duelyst’s sprites feature some of the greatest pixel art animation I’ve ever seen. Only the units and card effects are pixelated, but the extreme level of detail that goes into each one is stunning. And thanks to Duelyst’s dynamic lighting system, the sprites don’t feel out of place in its non-pixelated battlefields and UI.
Alough the game offers you in-game purchases where you could buy Spirit Orbs—Duelyst's version of pack of cards. It turns out to be really rewarding since you get gold for winning games and completing daily quests.

Duelyst is an interesting take on CCGs. It introduces a 9x5 grid, adding a new dimension of complexity onto the standard model. The resulting game is something like a blend of Hearthstone and Final Fantasy Tactics. Fans of both games will find comfort here. Units move across a board to combat other units, making positioning a key element to success. The units themselves have mechanics in accord with the standard CCG. As well as its unique gameplay, Duelyst features a distinctive art style. Hand-drawn portraits and landscapes are put alongside some of the most well-done pixel art I've seen. In terms of gameplay, Duelyst is quite accessible. Players spend in-game currency on card packs to build a deck. The gold acquisition rate is quite generous--players will find it fairly easy to earn a pack a day in about 45 minutes of play. Along with generous gold gain, the packs themselves are very charitable on drops. On average, a player can expect a Legendary (highest card rarity) in 1 of 4 packs. This alleviates the new player's problem of card scarcity, and encourages continuous play.

I have a love-hate relationship with this game. Until recently, I was a PS4 exclusive player of Siege. During Operation Health, support for this game seemed to be dropping each day and many gamers felt betrayed. However, after getting back into it and experiencing it on PC, I have to say that I am back 100% !!
The care and attention that the devs put in this game is the best I've seen. Each year, a clearly defined roadmap is published with specific details on upcoming content. There is no mystery or confusion about Ubisoft's intent or planned direction with this game. They are constantly striving to improve it and while we have had some rough patches in the past, I think the R6 crew at Ubi has really committed to being transparent with their player base and putting out quality content.
Pros:
- Balance. This is evident in the way Siege has been able to offer operators for real money (rather than grinding) without the huge backlash like we saw recently with Battlefront 2. The balance between Operators facilitates an environment where one operator isn't objectively better than any other. The choice of operators is a team-based decision, either chosen to counter an opposing operator or boost the capabilities of another operator. Each player has an opportunity to thrive regardless of their operator and this explains an excellent balance despite their varying abilities and stats.
- Premise. This game truly is one of a kind. While it shares many of the same aspects you would expect in an FPS, it revolutionizes the genre by introducting a whole new level of destructible surfaces. This game truly creates a full spectrum, 3 dimensional shooter where the enemy can approach from any direction in a dymanic environment. The suspense in each game is palpatable and no game is the same. The choices that the environement presents you means that each round, each match presents an entirely unique problemset.
- Optimization. This game runs BEAUTIFULLY on my system. Other games like PUBG, I experience frequent issues with framerate, lag, marshmallow textures, and many other glitches that I have come to expect to out from games considering many are released in alpha. With siege, it is evident that this comes from a AAA developer. I average about 140 frames during a match and even when it drops, it never goes below 60. I have yet to experience a significant graphical or performance issue with this game. and this is at default settings. I couldn't expect any better.
Cons:
- The Players. As with any online game, other players can be very toxic. If you are considering purchasing this for your children, I wouldn't recommend it. Siege doesn't really censor the text chat and with audio as well, it can be very harsh and toxic for young players or those who arent accustomed to that type of behavior or language. There has also been a pretty significant issue with team killing which may not have been adequately addressed by the devs as of yet and of course they do experience players that hack or exploit but I believe Siege has been doing a much better job combatting this than other major games out right now.
-  micro-transactions. While I don't necessarily have an issue with this so long as it is merely cosmetic items and nothing that provides an objective advantage in the game, I do have issue when those items can never be acquired using in-game currency. Even if it is a ridiculous amount of renown, that is fine. But when you only offer certain items with real cash, it comes off greedy and doesn't reallly seem fair to the players who have put in countless hours only to be overshadowed by a new player that was willing to put down 20 real dollars for a headgear or uniform. there should be a choice to earn it.
-  Support. While Ubi does a pretty good job of communicating to their audience about upcoming content . They really suck when troubleshooting problems. The reason I quit during OP Health and didn't come back until recently is because A) their 50% sale got me back into it but also B) I was temporarily banned due to a team kill. Each time I did so in self defense due to toxic players that were either killing the entire team or wounding players in an attempt to bait them into a TK. I contacted Ubi about it with video footage of the player in question. Their response was simply "Even if a player is attempting to kill you, you should let them. If you kill a player, even in self defense, it is in violation of the rules and will result in a ban" Rather than find a solution that fixes the root problem, banning players that abuse the rules. They were content with merely enforcing an automated system that exacerbates the problem and didn't care to hear or see real instances of abuse.
Overall this is a great game. While many times I find myself seething from a death, it is all worth it for those moments you are the one pulling off truly exceptional plays and bringing your team to victory.

Tomb Raider is a game I returned to with eyes glazed with nostalgia. I do this every few years with various things I liked as a tween, Linkin Park, being another prime example, before remembering that my 12 year old self wasn't actually that bright.
That's not to say Tomb Raider is bad. It's just aged pretty badly, early 90's 3D makes Lara look like she's been carved out of wood and she always tends to be trying to merge with the scenery. Environments aren't much better, in the back of your head, you're always vaguely aware that the whole game seems to be built on a grid, (every block the same size, etc). So aesthetically it's crap, but how does it play?
Moderately badly now you mention it. To be fair Lara does control extremely well for running around, making huge leaps, somersaulting and shooting. It's when the game gets into the second act and the fiddly jumps come in that the controls become a problem. If you, like me, played Tomb Raider back before the iPod was invented then you probably remember with fondness the screaming masogynistic curses you would yell at Lara as she dived into a spike pit instead of the desired ledge. It is not actually that fun reliving said experience.
My final gripe is actually hard to describe. (some background) I got all the old Tomb Raiders in a steam sale and binged on them over a weekend off, (this is the best of the lot) and I started to get this nagging feeling. The same feeling I got while playing too much Diablo 2: 'it's all the same.' you are doing the same thing over and over. Theres not much game here really, just a series of levers you have to pull in the correct order. That combined with the ugliness and the frustration drove the final nail into the nostalgia coffin.
Having said all that, it's still a great game and definately worth £4.99. The reason for this is similar to the reason I like similarly hideous game 'Deus Ex'. Because it's ugly as sh*t the designers could make pretty much whatever they wanted. The game is loooooooong, the variety is fantastic and the different locales are great. the game is packed with highlight set pieces, like the T-rex attack, the colosseum fight, the Sphinx, a statue turning Lara into gold, Atlantis city and a certain (very vertical) level in which you must pass the challenges of the gods. That's the reason I kept coming back to the shoddier sequels. For that sense of adventure I shared with a woman with an extremely impractical set of mammary glands.

This is a real gem and I'm surprised I haven't heard about it before fairly recently. It really helps to walk your first steps as a guitar player and improve when you're more advanced. There are theory lessons with examples, games improving your technique, guitar-hero like mode where you can play your favourite songs with your favourite bands, multiplayer part and finally - session mode where you can truly master your improvisation and knowledge of scales. And there are hundreds if not thousands of additional songs you can buy as DLC.
It won't replace a good guitar teacher. It's definitely good to consult your technique and progress with someone more experience every now and then but it made my own practice way more interesting.

There are also things I'd like to see improved - i.e tab view in songs or improved riff-repeater where you can take even just a couple of notes looped and practice endlessly.
Otherwise I think it's the best executed idea in guitar world since Fender Stratocaster.

Regarding Windows 10 Audio issues:
I'm one of those that had the issues. For me the follwing did the trick:
Check that your soundcard is configured with Stereo 16bit 48000Hz.
I've 3 Audio interfaces (Onboard Soundcard is disabled):
1. Display Port Screen
2. Bose USB Speakers
3. Steinberg ASIO Interface
The 2. Interface is stuck at sorround in the Sound settings and I'm not able to change it to Stereo -> Game doesn't work with this one set as standard
The 3. is set to 24 bit and I'm not able to change the settings to 16 bit (altough I'm able to change it to 48khz) -> doesn't work
The 1. Interface is set to the recommended settings -> Works like a charm without any lag issues. So currently I set the display port screen as the default sound interface and connect the screen to either the Steinberg Adio Interface or the Bose speaker -> Works without any lag.
May be a bit bothersome but it did the trick for me.
I tried changing all settings that one can find in the ini file and the forums but nothing appears to work for the other interfaces.

Score: 8.5/10 (+1)
Commentary:
1. You get to move your king and summons like a chess piece(1 turn after they're summoned), and of course you whack your opponent's king hp to 0 to win the game.
2. The game utilises movement of every units' mechanism as a core strategy, with 3 mana orb at the center of the map to be conquered or just left alone.
3. Custom your card deck 40/40, gauntlet arena 30/30
4. Level-unlockable "Kings" with their own natural abilities that just seems OP in their own way, which is fun.
5. Graphic is pixelated, spell effect makes your eye ♥♥♥♥♥♥. But thats a good uniqueness
6. Card Abilities are creative, especially the "Range/Blast", "Flying" and "Air Drop" summons excluding the classic mechanism/abilities from other card games
7. Paywall exists of course, content: card box, emoticons, card covers & specific map access
8. Comparing through the 5 card games i had played so far... this relies on skills in strategy than RNG in drawing your cards. (partially thanks to the Card Replacement ability)
9. An immense amount of experience differences starting rank 15, where lots of uncommon cards are involved and put into battle more frequently than you've ever seen, at rank 10, its all Unique and Legendary cards that will make you hate this game.
10. Fun but limited time events, including puzzle solving and some AI bosses to play againts.
11. Theres lore context and back cultures, more importantly, bgm, go inspire.
12. The community leans more towards [Professionalism] over [Friendliness] term. Not a fan of events are we...

This is my first review ever as I don't usually describe games and just say "This is cool". But this time I just couldn't help writing about this awesome game, because I felt I should try to draw your attention, pals!
So, starting with the fact there are lots of people who compare Duelist to Hearthstone, I should stress that Duelist does resembles Blizzard's child. But, however, I like Duelist much more, because it's not really a card game. It combines some card mechanics with two-dimensional tactics. It's combat system feels a lot like Heroes of Might and Magic and M&M: Clash of Heroes, but it has a lot of it's own features. There is much more in this game than you could judge there is from the first sight! Give it a try and you'll see. There's a special mode called Challenges in this game, which will help you to see the game at it's full potential.
There are combinations you wouldn't believe they would lead you to the win, though they do! They do if you turn on your brains. And it gives you so much joy!
Special thanks to a funny system of quick-chat-emotions and for a possibility to cheer up a loser by giving him 5 gold coins, I think this should build a great community. At least I tend to pay to people I defended.
I wish this game a prospect and long long years of life. Thanks a lot to Counterplay Games team, I wish you all the best.
So, guys, I hope I will manage to attract you to this masterpiece! See you on the battleground!

In Tomb Raider, the player controls the female archaeologist Lara Croft, in search for the three mysterious Scion artefacts across the world. The game is presented in third person perspective. Lara is always visible and the camera follows the action from behind or over her shoulder. The world she inhabits is fully drawn in three dimensions and characterised by its cubic nature. Ledges, walls and ceilings mostly sit at 90 degrees to each other, but sometimes feature sloping planes.
The object of Tomb Raider is to guide Lara through a series of tombs and other locations in search of treasures and artefacts. On the way, she must kill dangerous animals and other creatures, while collecting objects and solving puzzles to gain access to an ultimate prize, usually a powerful artefact. Gunplay is restricted to the killing of various animals that appear throughout each stage, although occasionally Lara may be faced with a human opponent. Instead the emphasis lies on solving puzzles and performing trick jumps to complete each level. As such, Tomb Raider in essence harkens back to the classical form of platform style gameplay.
If anyone likes the new Tomb Raider game, you should give the game that started it all a go! :D

Ive never reviewed a game before, And ive played somewhere around 1000 hours on steam.
Competition, thy name is Duelyst.
Seriously, even as a low-tier player, you and your opponent will be trying their absolute darnest to round off every turn perfectly. Resource for resource, in what I see as a very balanced system, the game flashes before your eyes in a spectrum of 8-bit sparks. You will have your favorite pieces, and this game has a magical way of making it all come alive. Its an artful form of mental arm-wrestling.
Don't believe me? It's stealing Hearthstone's players. Trump and Kibler both got into this one.

I'm not really that much into these card based strategy games but Duelyst is pretty fun.
Here's my first impressions video on the game:

Man this game is so *good.*
I wasn't sure about the sci-fi fantasy thing they've got going on but quickly began to fall in love with it. The animations are excellent and bouncy and the character and unit design are incredibly unique and diverse. The soundtrack does a great job of tying it all together and the sound effects are just icing on the cake. Very visually pleasing game.
THIS GAME IS NOT PAY-TO-WIN. Like all smart people looking at the F2P section of Steam that's probably what you were looking for above everything else. Anyways, to continue:
Turn-based summoning tactics. It feels almost like the table-top game Warmachine but if you took a faction deck and randomly drew spells/units and used whatever you got (But like, really well balanced because of Duelyst's mana system). You get a whole plethora of cards which you can use to populate your own custom decks and tailor them as much as you please.
And talk about tactical depth: The abilities and stats of the units are somehow more diverse than their looks. There are some wild and winning combos (Though no clear meta builds which is good, anything seems to work it's just how smart you are going about combining unit abilities and spells), nothing seems bad. What I really like about playing online or against AI is that when you lose it doesn't feel like you got cheesed with a bad hand or the enemy used some OP combo: Really and truly it just feels like you were outplayed, (Which you were).
The tutorial is incredibly helpful and they have a whole plethora of interesting custom challenges that not only earn you currency for spheres (Which poop out 5 random cards to add to your collection) but also challenge you to play out some more unique strategies which will improve your playing in normal games. I honestly appreciate it a lot, it's helped me grasp the logic this game plays best with.
As it is a free to play game, I figured I should address this as well. Like I said earlier, Duelyst certainly isn't a Pay-2-Win kind of game. Honestly the transactions are almost entirely for asthetic: It's stuff like emoticons for your generals, alternate skins, card-backs, and player icons. You can also use money to purchase spheres which, as I said before, give you random assortments of cards. I myself have not bought any nor felt the temptation too: The challenges and daily challenges reward you with coins upon completion and the spheres aren't terribly expensive. Will I buy some in the future after I've completed the 50 challenges that come with the game? I'll probably end up doing that but in-game purchases definitely are not a difference between winning and losing in this game, which is really fantastic.
So yeah, Duelyst comes highly recommended and if you're a fan of any kind of turn-based game you owe it to yourself to try it out. The fact that it's free and a tiny install also helps. Great, great game.

As a fan of scrolling shooters and "cute-em-ups" in particular you have no idea how much it pains me to slap a negative rating onto this one: in my opinion there are few things the modern, self-serious gaming landscape could use more than a straightforward, arcade-style romp involving an evil, mustachioed piece of broccoli and a bunch of dessert-themed superheroes out to stop his nefarious veggie-centric schemes. Unfortunately, while the developers behind Ice Cream Surfer appear to have had their hearts in the right place, their execution simply does not do justice to Twinbee, Parodius, and the other more illustrious goofball shooters to come before it.
After picking one of five characters to blast off with (be advised that some are much less effective than others), you traverse a handful of side-scrolling worlds, shooting down various cute and/or ridiculous baddies and collecting the shiny gems, power-up popsicles, option helpers, and bonus letters they leave behind, expending a bomb when you need a trump card. This, sadly, is often, since your player sprites (and hitboxes) are so large that maneuvering through gaps is very difficult, and enemy shots are very small and difficult to see. This is especially a shame since the candy-colored visuals are not bad to look at, and it would be nice to have the opportunity to admire the scenery a bit without worrying that a pinprick-sized bullet will steal a life away from you in the meantime. Even discounting that, there's no auto-fire either, which means you have to mash the shot key to keep a steady stream of attacks coming; this would be merely irritating if the fire rate was decent (or if a charge shot was available), but no matter how quickly you tap there's a strict limit to how potent your offense can get, especially when at your default pea-shooter power level...and the fact that you lose everything when you die means that you'll be dealing with that frequently.
Out on the periphery there are numerous additional unfixed issues that are unlikely to ever be addressed: the screen options don't work, controller support is sometimes sketchy, the post-stage roundup screen scrolls by too fast to read, and so forth. I hate to do it, but I must insist, even if you're hungering for a throwback to the good old days when you'd beat up a bunch of ninjas to earn a burger invite from Ronald Reagan and nobody batted an eye, don't let this game lure you in: your fond memories of those times will only end up melting away into an unsightly puddle, like a forgotten bowl of vanilla fudge swirl on a summer evening.

Games that focus almost solely upon comedy for their entertainment value can be difficult to judge, and often don't find themselves garnering critical acclaim. The main reason for this is the numerous varieties there are of comedy, and the equally various tastes people have in comedy. That being said, will you enjoy a game like Jazzpunk? Well, that depends upon what you find funny.
Jazzpunk is an Adult Swim game, and if you're familiar at all with Adult Swim's programming, then you already have an idea as to what varieties of comedy to expect here. Jazzpunk is silly, mildly dark, and more often than not surreal. I can see people comparing this to an acid trip; howeer accurate that may be, I wouldn't know, but it seems like the thing people would say.
That being said, there's still the big question: is it funny?
Yes. Yes it is funny. From the surreal humor to its equally bizzare aesthetic, Jazzpunk is a funny, good time.
But again, that's the kicker. It all depends on what you find humorous. Throwing a jar of spiders at someone? Silly side-mission videogame parodies? Surreal encounters with vagrants? If any of these seem appealing, then Jazzpunk will prove to be a fun time for you. If not, then you have a poor sense of humor. Good day, sir. I said, GOOD DAY SIR!

Hyper Light Drifter is a great, emotional, exploration and skill based combat game that has very incredible pixel graphics and a uniquely told wordless storyline.
Though at first I wasn't really into the game, I was quickly drawn into it and felt like I couldn't stop playing until I reached the very end and defeated the final boss. The game is very diffcult in the way that it you can't rely on getting better gear and health throughout the game. Instead, It's definitely a skill-based game with you having to learn the attack patterns of each and every enemy and boss that you encounter throughout the journey, which means that in the beginning, there could be a ton of deaths involved if you fail to learn many enemies' attack patterns. I learned this the hard way.
The only issues I FELT like I had with this game is for one, how unclear it could be at times. Sometimes I felt lost because I was a moron and needed a little guidance to help me get through some of the parts of the game that didn't seem the most transparent. But I eventually realized that this game doesn't hold your hand in that regard. That's the thing about having a game where you have a story expressed without words, you're essentially on your own (*cough* minus looking up guides to how to find all the modules but I definitely didn't do that *cough cough*). I also feel like it was a bit too short, when I was starting to really enjoy the game to the fullest potential was in the southern zone when things amped up in difficulty a ton. I'm not saying that I didn't like the other zones, as I liked nearly all of it, but that's when my deaths started to go to a sudden minimum because I knew what I was doing finally (minus the bosses of course).
I think this is a game better self experienced instead of just looking up a lets play of it. I saw others uploading videos of this game about a year ago and I decided for once I wanted to go through a game myself without watching a bunch of others playing it first. I'm glad I did this.

This is a bad game all around. Avoid it even if on sale.
The game has nothing to do with loneliness. The title is clearly an afterthought. The game has no emotional connection in any way.
You navigate a bunch of rectangles around obstacles into rectangular ending "doors." There's a narrator but no plot. Fake, pointless love stories are made up between the rectangles. Rectangles randomly get eaten by a "pixel cloud." At the end two rectangles who were made up half way through the game "escape" and you get a five second cut scene.
The music consists of three differnet 45 second loops, sometimes literally just played on top of each other in dissonance which clashes horribly. The quality of the music is good, but the length is inexcusable.
There are levels where you have to move five or more (sometimes ten!) rectangles into little doors, switching between them using only left and right controls. It's hell.
I've never seen a game before that only has rectangular collision but still has buggy physics. The rectangles stick to things, clip through obstacles moving in the level, and can't jump at random times.
The level design is very bad. It's completely uninspired, and you're forced to repeat the same actions over and over for no reason. Often a "zig zag" pattern is thrown in with absolutely no purpose. You'll be forced to climb 10 stairs, instead of 1, the exact same horrible, mind numbing sequence for each stair, because why not?
There are barely any puzzles. 99% of the time you're trying to figure out the least annoying way to make a staircase out of the newest randomly introduced rectangle that you dont' care about. There are no creative puzzles, which is surprising for a game in this genre. Nothing makes you think, most things only make you frustrated.
The only stylistic element in this game is the light source, which is done with almost zero effort. Most levels only have one light, if any.
There's a saying that if all your components are good, your product is great. Today I learned the converse. All of the components of this game are bad, and the product is awful. The quality of the narrator and music are good, but the narrator doesn't say anything meaningful and the music is very short loops.
Do not buy this game.

I've been with for honor since closed beta and feel like I've been with it long enough to have some real insight. For those who don't want a wall of text there'll be a TL:DR at the bottom of the review.
Let's start with some key things that while seemingly unrelated and random come together to paint a core problem with this game for me now as of September 9th 2017.
- I respected this game when it came out for not making assassins the blatant overpowered, whilst good in their own rights really only 1 assassin out of the 3 on release was viable and was still "easy" to beat if you were familiar with her moveset.
- Whilst many people hated the slow grindy style of gameplay on release referred to as "defensive meta" I loved it, made it feel like a seriously rewarding game to get good at and getting solid knowledge of each of the 12 heroes on release was necessary to being good at this game. Getting twitch reactions and having masterful prediction skills of your opponent was a great high level gameplay reward as no true combos in this "fighting game" meant every play was interruptible and had counterplay you were always trying to beat your opponent mentally.
- The playerbase was unfair to this game on release. I boil it down to pure Ubisoft hate, people wanting to vent their frustrations at a company so hard they took it out on a development team working on their own game. Through red tinted goggles they saw this flawed game and touted it as being the worst game of 2017 and used it as a Ubisoft bashing point.
Now then you can read these points and say okay that was what it was like on release, what about now as of season 3 post patches? Well it's become exactly what I was worried about.
- Assassins are honestly just a step too far ahead of everything else now, a good peacekeeper is the top dog in this game, gladiator feels like warlord ramped up beyond beating and centurion (hydrid assassin) Is honestly the reason most people stop playing for weeks at a time with the developers hesitant to nerf his core issues like chain wall splatting and at least 50% health true combos off a semi difficult parry or wall splat.
- Predictions matter less and the game has purely become about aggression. This is why assassins now flourish. It was a rock paper scissors of sort with defense meta; light attacks beat guard breaks, guard breaks beat heavies, heavies beat parry fishers. Heavies no longer beat guard breaks in season 3 so mixing them into combos to try and throw off your opponent and go for something greedier is no longer a thing. Guard breaks only come off parries now since anyone who isn't asleep will counter you everytime. This leaves attacking then feinting into more attacking the only way to play since parry is the only thing you have to worry about from defensive players now.

So let's just do a quick summary
Pros:
+ Micro transactions are not necessary, regular play allows you to buy all heroes and outfit a few choice ones with the cosmetics of your choosing.
+ Still fairly rewarding to get good at the game. High win rate is fairly correlating with skill or ability to abuse unskilled players.
+ There is room for unusual playstyles. Lawbringer is weak to skilled players but the longer you play against him the more he grinds you down and makes you make mistakes. Raider is all about testing your opponents nerves and ability to make spot reactions and has a unique out of locked combat playstyle. Conqueror punishes heavy hitting classes. Shinobi is all about mindgames and plays the "zoner" playstyle very well of annoying your opponent into making mistakes.
+ Lots of exploits patched out.
+ Aggressive meta has sped up the game. No more turtling warlords, conquerors.
- Aggressive meta has sped up the game. Only the fastest characters are viable now, no assassin dodge = weak class.
- That's honestly mostly it on the gameplay cons, it's like they said "we don't need varied playstyles and skills in this fighting game, lets just make the playstyles reminiscient of day 1 buttonmashers."
- Exploits have always been present in one form or another, as fast as they patch one out another one crops up.
- Always online with iffy connectivity at best.
- Fighting games don't have dedicated servers they all have p2p transfer. People didn't understand this and everyone has been mad at it since release but it's still a negative just like in all fighting games when someone has a really bad connection it sucks and makes the match unplayable.
- Ranked Duel mode has been released but if you're salty just quit before the score screen on a guaranteed loss, your opponent doesn't get credit for the win and unless they place first in the tournament then their reward tier (which is based on wins) is knocked down a level. I've gotten second place in tournaments but basic reward tier. (A pattern for my armor instead of the paint scheme I should have gotten)
- You can't own everything in this game, even with microtransactions it just isn't possible for any realistic human being to fully cosmetic out more than maybe 3 characters.
- All DLC characters were leaked slightly before season 2 so no surprise to them. Also season 2 DLC characters were horridly overtuned with 1 of them still being top tier to this day, not by being collectively strong but by abusing uninteractable moves and exploits like chain wall splats you can't react to. Season 3 DLC characters are solid but are a good example of giving them too much, they're fairly balanced once learned but have too many tools compared to base classes so learning to play against them is a very uphill battle.
TL;DR -
Pro; This is an opinion but defensive meta is gone so yay for those who hated it.
Con; The game is pure aggression now, all slower defensive based classes are now very weak due to overdone nerfs.
Con; The connection is meh and I don't like the direction they're taking the game removing how much you get to punish someone for their mistakes. (Guard break, feint and heavy attack interactions now all favor the heavy attack.)
Pro; Season 3 DLC characters are miles better in terms of balance than Season 2.
Con; Has become an extremely simplified fighting game, playstyle is reminiscient of button mashers if you're fighting an assassin.
Con; True combos while not in base game are now in the game (Centurion) and are entirely too oppressive.
Con; While lessened in season 3 it still has an extremely steep learning curve.
Maybe I'm too nostalgic but this game has changed from release in a way I don't care for. Now I honestly cannot recommend this game to new players or to fence sitters.

Qud is a desperately cruel and radiated world full of mutations and factions of hate, but also a beautifully poetic living world, where you truly are a part of it, trying to survive as best you can, with only Darwin's help in understanding the selection pressures and the mutations you can mould yourself into.
The game is almost a work of art, a procedurally crafted world laid on a framework of lore from a world inspired by the tabletop RPG Gamma World (along with others). You can roll truekin humans with cybernetics or mutant humans with all sorts of biomutant properties. You have quests to follow, and lore to explore, and the flora and fauna of the various biomes you encounter to use or abuse at your whim. You'll have factional reputation with all species, and your mutations or cybernetics can be adapted to customise your playstyle.
This game is a survival game in the truest sense coupled with traditional roguelike tactical action, and pushing the envelope in lore, character customisation and tactical options available to you. The writing and generated lore will have you exploring purely for curious enjoyment. You will marvel at the inhabitants and the monster diversity on offer. The game is constantly being updated with more content, both systems and lore. The Freeholdgames guys are dedicated to making this a world to play in, rather than a one off game to enjoy and throw away.
Endless possiblities abounds.
Gather your waterskins and torches and lets get crackin' with this adventure!

This is absolutely one of my favorite fighting games. The learning curve is insane, but it feels so darn rewarding when you finally get it down. No other game has gotten my blood pumping quite like this one. The combat is visceral and at times unforgiving if you make a mistake. The graphics look great, the characters are mostly balanced, and the combat system is insanely fluid.
A lot of the negative reviews for this game mostly have to do with the servers, but once you actually get into the game it's extremely addicting. Sure, sometimes the servers don't quite work and Ubisoft really needs to get working on that,but when that happens I just find something else to do, not the end of the world. This isn't generally a game you would play for long periods of time.
However I feel like the matchmaking system of this game is really where Ubi dropped the ball. I'm not quite sure how it works, because either you get paired with someone who instantly stomps your head in, or with someone who probably doesn't know how to use a controller. Evenly-matched opponents aren't an often occurrence, at least for me.
You don't have to pay to win, no matter what some of these reviews tell you. Currency can be bought, but it's easily earned through completing contracts or just plain winning matches. And even then, most purchases are purely cosmetic. No one is forcing you to pay for a flame effect out of your own wallet. 500 Steel can be spent to scavenge for premium items. I'd say that's a pretty good deal, considering how easy it is to come by. And besides, you don't need all the bells and whistles to be good at the game. It's only a grindfest if you make it one. Just play it at a normal rate, and the money and gear will stack up.
I recommend playing a few custom matches with either friends or bots before finding an online match, as many of the people who play this game already have it down. I've met quite a few players who were nice enough to give advice to either me or my teammates, so always be open to it if someone offers. There are a lot of toxic players that frankly don't give a rat's behind if you suck, and those same people throw fits if you beat them.
Parting advice to keep in mind if you decide to buy: always be respectful to your opponent. For Honor has a lot of unspoken rules about dueling. Here's a small list of things to keep in mind:
1. Actually fight. Don't throw people off the edge or into hazards right off the bat. If it comes to that, then it's fair game, but unless you're backed into a corner, it's generally just a bad move.
2. Don't whine or insult the winner if you lose. You'll just look like a child. Same goes for if you win, don't gloat and call the loser trash. It's a fair game, that you lost. Don't blame it on cheating, improve yourself.
3. Wait your turn in 2v2. Now this isn't necessarily a solid rule, as many people treat it as a deathmatch. Generally during 2v2's, the teams form 2 1v1's, and then the winners of those fights duel. Also reviving your fallen teammate is looked down on as well. But as I said it varies depending on who you play against, so just keep it in mind.
4. No character is broken, you just have to know how to play against them. (Except centurion, screw that guy)
5. Keep it competitive, but friendly. This game is plagued by toxic people, and it would go a long way for new players to stay away from that attitude. If you grow to become skilled at this game, help new players every chance you get. Give them advice. Playing this game with friendly people will go a long way towards keeping your blood pressure levels down, trust me on this one.
I'm not the best at making reviews, but these are just my 2 cents, and I encourage you to buy this game.

Heliborne. This game is clearly unfinished, but those are my opinions about it.
PROS
+An already vast choice of helos to choose from, and all of them are different between the others.
+Very distinct and separated roles, that heavily encourage cooperation between your teammates. Ah, don't try to shoot down an attack helicopter with that Blackhawk, ok?
+Weapons are already simulated pretty well: bullets have their speeds, and no, it's not a hit detection fault that you can't hit anything, it's just that you have to LEAD your enemies. Unguided Rockets are simulated very well for an alpha.
+Friendly devs, open to critics and suggestions. I also became a friend with one of them, so you can guess it yourself.
+Very good balancing between helos of different teams.
+Requires SKILL, and not just LUCK.
+Graphics and effects are nice for such an alpha state.
+Vietnam and Afghanistan.
+Intuitive and easy controls
+Flying is realistic to an extent, but not too much to become a simulator, flight mechanics are simple but most realistic maneuvers can still be used. Physics aren't bad.
+Devs are litterally machinegunning us with updates, Never seen a dev team that fast.
+Perfectly balanced pricetag
Like any game in this universe, Heliborne has it's
CONS
-Team Balance is a bit awkward. Sure, you can win alon vs 2 players if you're good, but it's annoying.
-It still has a young and scarce community, not so much people playing.
-Sounds aren't as good as the graphics
-Some helos are bit overused, even if it's not a developing issue
-Minor bugs.
-No AH64 | Asiimov Factory New (Joking)
________________________________________
Verdict
So, Heliborne is still young and has it's problems. Considering it's current status, it's almost impressive to see such an already fun and enjoyable Alpha. I'm sure all the CONS i've stated will be fixed or worked on, since our devs are really working hard to make this game become a good indie.

I have the original version on the PS3 that I bought for my son as he wanted to learn to play the guitar. Being on console it came with the real tone cable.
2014 version comes out on steam and during the sale I got it. It seems like an improvemnet over the previous version so far (only 4hrs in at the mo). The previous version seemed to restrict you on tracks YOU wanted to play. You could only play certain tracks once you'd mastered the ones it pushed forward.
The 2014 version lets you jump straight into the track YOU want to learn to play! I've found sometimes it'll throw every chord at you from the go then adjusts down till you get comfortable. It'll then assess your play through adding in more or less, it'll even slow the track down, if its too fast and your making mistakes.
Track selection and variance is also improved over the previous version with a larger selection on the DLC options too.
There were two main issues when first playing the game which were:
1: The Real Tone Cable on some machines doesnt automatically connect in the game. You have to go into the system (pc not game) audio settings and you'll see the cable listed under recording devices. By default the pcs microphone is set as priority so you need to change that to the Real Tone Cable.
2: LAG...Like guitar hero etc the lag between the chord and the screen marker during play is or is sometimes out by quite a bit but this can be changed in the ingame settings under options video. there is also an otion under adv settings which requires a restart of the game.
In all its a vast improvement over the previous version. I've not played a guitar in over 25yrs so its a challenge getting back into it.

I can say with certainty that this game makes playing the guitar a lot of fun!
However, this game's useability as a teaching tool is dependent on the type of skill you already possess with the guitar.
If you've learned guitar already, and are looking for something to extend your learning then Rocksmith 2014 will definitely help you in ways you probably wouldn't expect. If you've played chords before, but never bothered to learn hammer-ons and other nuances, this game can teach you those things. If you find that playing the guitar has lost its challenge, prepare to be motivated to improve with dynamic difficulties that can change either manually or automatically (it's in the option menu).

However, if you're coming in never having played a guitar before you might find it less useful. This game doesn't teach you how to read music (or even tabs, which is much simpler than reading sheet music). In real situations, especially in bands, reading music in some shape or form is absolutely necessary to play with other real people. With that said, you can certainly learn how to properly hold a guitar, and learn quickly how to strum and even pull of complicated chords with a little determination. Just don't expect to jump into any real gigs soon without some outside classes or lessons revoling around reading sheet music or tabs.

I got this to use with my Acoustic-Electric planning to use it to practice with to accompany my main book learning, for which I got Leavitt's "A Modern Method for Guitar".  After paying ~$40 (4 times what I paid for the game) for the special cord that you need to buy to use your guitar with this game, I find myself pretty much never playing it.  In terms of improving at guitar, it just seems much rather ineffective for a motivated learner.  I really don't like how it starts with you not playing full chords, and then moves to half chords and such before the full chord, even when the chords are fairly basic (and thus even a beginner would be mechanically able to play them, although not necessarily quickly).  I'd much rather just learn the songs by playing the full chords at a slow speed, then slowly get up to speed.
That said, and it is actually quite fun to play songs along with the vocals and such in the background, and feels like you are playing with a band, so I do expect to come back to this game later just to do that, but only after either learning the song outside of Rocksmith or becoming good enough compared to the song's difficulty that I can pick it up very quickly at the full difficulty.  But then the catalog is not big enough to have that many songs I would really want to learn, and song dlcs are way too expensive.
So basically, I would recommend against getting this unless they make the cord a lot cheaper to match the price of more standard cords so that you can spend maybe $30 on the game and cord together, or they introduce some system of adding some songs for free over time.

I have bought this game in a bundle. Well, I am glad I did, because I didn't really like it. Let me explain you why.
At the beginning, there was this game called GRADIUS by Konami. Konami thought "Let's make a parody of it!" and made created one of the best gaming series ever: PARODIUS!
Memories! I remember playing that game on the SNES and on the very first Playstation console.
Yes, THIS game is similar to Parodius.
Oh, I wish there was an original Parodius port on Steam available!
Unfortunately, there is none. And this game failed me...and I will tell you a few lines later why.
Remember the humour the Parodius series had to offer? Well, I do.
Vegetables, natural food, goofy bosses and angry animals are trying to kill you this time and you have to dodge them and/or their bullets, hearts or whatever they are shooting at you.
I must say the creators did a good job with the character and level designs. Everything is colorful and humorous. Now you might think "wait a minute, seems you like it! Why the thumbs down then?"
K, here is the answer: The controls are the reason!
I started the game after a couple of issues (I will explain that a few lines later), and pushed the down-key after the 1st level started. I don't know if you know this Arcade game called Tapper's, where you move up and down and switch to fixed positions. It felt like my character in this game moved down and stopped at certain position where I thought there are some kind of "lanes" and you move your character up and down to swtich between these.
No, the thing was, there weren't any fixed positions, you can move your character by keeping the direction keys pushed.
Guess what: You can't tell if your character will stop moving after you release the direction key. It might still be moving a little bit more, or stop immediately.
Well, imagine you release the direction key and your character keeps moving to the same direction before it finally stopss...at the wrong position where it catches an enemy bullet! This happened to me.
And then, there is this thing with the control settings in the main menu.
Right after I started the game, I didn't know which key I had to push to enter the selected menu.
Rushing over all key on my keyboard, I made it to the keyboard settings menu.
It didn't show you any list of the keys, but instead it asked me to choose which key shall be used for what (left, right, up, down, attack, super-attack, pause). First it asked me "", then "Press a key for right", etc...
Oh, that "" I just mentioned is true, the words "Press a key for up" are missing, so I saw no text instead.
Right, did I forget to mention anything? I guess not. If they can fix the controls, it'd be great. But with these broken controls, it's not fun.

Hyper Light Drifter is a great, emotional, exploration and skill based combat game that has very incredible pixel graphics and a uniquely told wordless storyline.
Though at first I wasn't really into the game, I was quickly drawn into it and felt like I couldn't stop playing until I reached the very end and defeated the final boss. The game is very diffcult in the way that it you can't rely on getting better gear and health throughout the game. Instead, It's definitely a skill-based game with you having to learn the attack patterns of each and every enemy and boss that you encounter throughout the journey, which means that in the beginning, there could be a ton of deaths involved if you fail to learn many enemies' attack patterns. I learned this the hard way.
The only issues I FELT like I had with this game is for one, how unclear it could be at times. Sometimes I felt lost because I was a moron and needed a little guidance to help me get through some of the parts of the game that didn't seem the most transparent. But I eventually realized that this game doesn't hold your hand in that regard. That's the thing about having a game where you have a story expressed without words, you're essentially on your own (*cough* minus looking up guides to how to find all the modules but I definitely didn't do that *cough cough*). I also feel like it was a bit too short, when I was starting to really enjoy the game to the fullest potential was in the southern zone when things amped up in difficulty a ton. I'm not saying that I didn't like the other zones, as I liked nearly all of it, but that's when my deaths started to go to a sudden minimum because I knew what I was doing finally (minus the bosses of course).
I think this is a game better self experienced instead of just looking up a lets play of it. I saw others uploading videos of this game about a year ago and I decided for once I wanted to go through a game myself without watching a bunch of others playing it first. I'm glad I did this.
Overall, amazing game. Can't praise it enough.

The game has pretty much everything I love: mini-events, some dialogue choices, RPG elements like gaining experience and leveling up skills, Oregon Trail-esque choice of camp leader profession (and chances to lose your survivors horribly), backstories and specialties for all of your survivors, interesting enemy factions, cute flavour text ("I didn't think plants were that effective against zombies..."), trading, Sim City-esque building... it's a great strategy sim with zombies, and I highly recommend it.

Let me start by saying that Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart is a good SRPG. It's not mindblowing, it plays like any SRPG out there, but its loveable characters and art style makes it stand out a little bit.
HOWEVER.
It could've been polished a lot.
- Sound tracks loop BADLY. You can tell whenever the track ends and starts over after a second delay, and that happens for every track.
- The "Cutscenes" animation is better than any of the RE;Birth games, making use of more movement and special effects, but the moving mouths are a pink pixelated mess.

The purpose of this review is to tell absolute beginners what they are going into (hence the review with only a few hours of gameplay).
First things first:
It will still be a struggle, no questions asked. Even callibration felt patronizing because every few times the instructor would say the same few lines. Pretty much every step that you fail will feel very, very repetitive to the point that you would think that this game is ideal for intermediate players. It's interesting how I haven't seen people mention this because this would have been downright unacceptable if this happened for a first-person shooter. I digress.
Second of all:
You will need to do some research and out-of-game practice. I tried practicing shifting (playing adjacent notes in quick succession) and my hand started to hurt. I am almost sure that my finger placement is wrong, but I need to make sure.
Third and lastly:
You need to realize that this is software that is not even close to 1-to-1 training. Rocksmith cannot detect funky things that you are doing with your guitar (e.g. "wobbly/loose" strumming). That said, you especially need to understand that the grind will be much harder until you start getting the hang of things.
Bottom line is that the road to playing guitar well is still very, very rough, but it should pay off if you REALLY want to git gud.

Phenomenal writing.  Truly unique and original setting rich with lore.  Total character customizability and freedom of choice.  Brutal, punishing difficulty that revels in killing you over and over again, so you can start again with a better understanding of what it takes to survive in the harsh, unforgiving world of Qud.
Be a teleporting mind-reader, or a four-armed sword-wielding behemoth with horns.  Hack off your enemies' limbs and bludgeon them to death with them, or slice off their face and wear it as a mask.  Put on mechanical wings and fly above the battlefield, hosing your enemies with a tank-fed flamethrower, or do the same thing as a mutant with your own organic wings and the ability to shoot gouts of fire from your palms.  Chisel through grainy sandstone walls with a pickaxe, or superheat metal with fire until it's reduced to a puddle of molten slag.  Overwhelm your enemies with psionic attacks that render them little more than jabbering, disoriented cretins that stumble and trip over their own feet.  Gather liquids to concoct your own tonics and remedies from ancient texts, or play around with them to see what happens if you mix a little of jar A and jar B.
Get infected by fungal spores and grow glowing tendrils on your back.  Contract a disease that makes your tongue swell and rot away, leaving you only with the dialogue option of "Nnnnnnnnnnn."  Douse yourself with your remaining supply of fresh water to put out your flaming clothes.  Get sucked into a rip in the space-time continuum and ejected at an unknown location miles underground with no light source.  Find yourself hunted by interdimensional psychics hell-bent on ending you at every turn.
This game is not for the faint of heart, but if you have a shred of imagination, do yourself a favor and get this game.  Endure the initial learning curve and accept that you're going to die.  A lot.  Trust me, it's worth it.

I remember that great time when I was playing Tomb Raider I. And you know what? I still have fun. And many many great memories come back. And now, I wanna play Anniversary (I have it). You want to know that time I grew up? Play Tomb Raider. You'll understand why Lara Croft became that icon (it's not only the boobs, guys and girls).
As a girl, having a female main character that is using her brains is very refreshing. Lara Croft has really left her mark on me. Lara Croft is an adventurer/archaeologist, contacted by Jacqueline Natla to retrieve an artifact called the Scion, in Peru. And that's how Lara began her journey through Peru to the lost city of Atlantis.
Tomb Raider is a mix of adventure/shooter. Playing in a third person perspective, you control easily Lara, despite some weirds camera movement. You have weapons to defend yoursef against animals like wolves, bats, lions, gorillas.... and the famous T-Rex. In that first game, Lara doesn't really face humans apart for Natla's men (and they're not in majority).
But generally, you're running, jumping, swimming from a point to another because you have keys to find or levers to use to open doors. And if you're hurt, you can find health kits. As for the weapons, the pistols have infinite ammo.
The soundtrack is good and the ambient sounds are also a huge factor: you hear it when you're in a cavern.
Keep in mind that Tomb Raider I is the 1996 game. Back then, these graphics were really good. Even if Lara's boobs are not...well, round. But you know when you're in Egypt: between a Sphinx and hieroglyphs and sand...
True, Anniversary is taking some liberties and is a remake of Tomb Raider I. True, Anniversary may be better than Tomb Raider I. But while I prefer Anniversary, Tomb Raider I will be forever as one of these games that marked me with Doom II, Colonize, Age of Empires and Half-Life.
I may be not the avid fan of Lara Croft, I grew up too. But she will be forever in my heart. She will be forever that female character that made me finally feel like I was at my place as a girl playing video games.
