I had never heard of Rebuild untill this game. Before I bought this I played the original flash version on a website, and that hooked me. So I got this game in early acess to support the development.
This game is a lot of fun. Managing how many farms you control to keep food supply up, deciding which block to reclaim next. Do you get a new apartment or do you get a hospital?
You start off with 4-5 survivors, usually 1 leader, 2 soldier, 1 builder, 1 scavenger. You also start off with 5 tiles that are yours. When you kill all the zombies in an adjacent tile you have the ability to reclaim that tile. This builds a wall around it and allows you to use that building. This is how you expand. You can also change any building into something else, such as converting a restaurant into a hospital.
After a while hoards of zombies will start arriving and you will have to defend againt them. Did you recruit enough survivors to be able to defend and expand?
I don't write reviews, but this one was good enough to deserve one.
Side Note: At the time of writing, the main bug was a "lack of memory" pop up that forces you to restart the game. Usually just hitting ctrl+enter fixes it by shifting from windowed to full screen and vice versa. If that doesn't work a quick relaunch will start you off at the point where the game crashed.

Don't let my playtime fool you.
I've played this game for a lot of hours before it came to steam.
While this may look like a hearthstone clone, it is actually much, much more.
Duelyst is an incredible, gorgeous, well polished, competitive strategic board game based on card decks.
Mastering this game is a real challenge since unlike other card games, this one requires good planning, positioning, complex strategies and an experienced knowledge of hundreds of difficult game mechanics.
Compared to hearthstone you gain way more good cards from packs which helps you creating a good budget deck pretty early in the game, legendaries  are also way more common than HS, in other words less pay 2 win. You can also put the same card 3 times in the same deck (while in hearthstone you can only put 2 copies) and you can switch a card from your hand to your deck every turn. All of this makes the game waaaay less luck based than hearthstone.
Have fun :)

great game and one of the better balanced games that i have seen in a while, and while the graphics and cards are unique and fun to play with they most certainly have some balancing issues with thier cards and factions. some factions posses cards that let them permanently control any unit. late game this is extreemly frustrating and difficult to manage as you will spend all of your points to summon a powerful monster and next turn the enemy will swoop in with a less powerful card and permanently take your monster. any game that lets a single faction permanently take control of creatures will inherently have balancing issues in my opinion. aside from that, there is a specific faction in the game that has the best starting units and by best they have the highest overal attack and health compared to cost letting them dominate early game and defeting most faction which are designed to last mid to late game. the chess board style as well as the summoning of cards and unique abilities makes the game very strategic and enjoyable. like i said earlier balancing issues certainly get frustrating to deal with but hopefully things will be changed.
Essentially hearthstone with the competitive features for the non-casuals and none of the RNG bs. Unit positioning adds a whole new layer of skill and strategy.

Hi, I am an old player of this game... Having played it for much much longer then my 200 something steam hours would have you believe, I have a few things I would like to share.
This isn't a salty dress down of duelyst where I act like an educated♥♥♥♥♥and think I know best about this game, I am just here to point out why duelyst was amazing beyond my expectations and how the devs let everybody down.
A little about myself and my experience coming into duelyst, I joined late december during the snowchaser promotion in 2015 where everyone got the snowchaser emote (when it was still exclusive) and the game was in the middle stages of open beta, it was a very different game back then.
Back then as you may have heard we had an infamous period of time where you would draw two cards at the end of your turn and start with 3 cards... The game was unbalanced and a total mess to play but god damn it was fun, the game was hitting a huge growth spurt and was just getting attention in gaming media outlets (like kotaku) as I believed it deserved at the time and it was showing unbelievable promise.
Lo and behold what came in this period of time were decks that revolved around one or two cards and always drawing them when you needed to and tempo was everything. Every game was 2 drop spam and things like holy immolation or Killing edge (and old third wish which gave one unit +3/+3 and blast around january/feb), needless to say not many things were good and card plays were completely predictable but what made up for it was the tactical play with the board. It basically brought card games to life as if that is what they were missing and the hair pin strategies that you came up with were awesome every single time. I loved every second and wasted the first part of my year on this game...
What really gave this game some staying power though was that the community was empowered by the devs, people ran community contests and tournaments and people got scouted by counterplay to work for them. They even got into debates with us about lore and art which was ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, the support and love the devs had for the game that they gave back to the community resonated in every aspect... I'll never forget this. Except that ended up working against me as for some reason the devs began to turn their backs on us and it hurt.
It started with a few changes, the first being the sudden change to one draw into pushing for official release far before the game was fleshed out and ready (why on earth would you change half the fundamental mechanics of the game and then release it with only 1 month of live testing?) and they completely stonewalled any communication on that regard simply reffering to it as "release hype". I understand now they wanted to gamble with an explosive release (they had a cinematic and everything lmao) but back then it seemed just plain wrong and it didn't work in the end despite all the buzz it got from critics. Understand initially I just looked askance at this and had total faith in these guys but now it feels gutless considering the slippery slope the game took henceforth.
Once release was out the way, updates were much slower... normally when something was a big problem we could just rely on the mid month patch to fix it but as one dev put it "Since we are out of beta we are going to be much less active in changing the game as there are less things to address". Yet now we have loot crates, boss fights, alternate generals, purchasable emotes (don't even get me started on this) and much more random♥♥♥♥♥♥we didn't need but gives the devs yet another option to make a quick buck (they previously had a very fair payment scheme, where are your values now?). But that also allowed them to put up some smoke and mirrors as to why no significant change had been made in over two months (I understand the maintanence schedule for other card games is much longer but they get away with it due to publicity of the game). Why does all this get me worked up? Well it's pretty simple, the game was getting infuriating and the devs stopped listening to people period.
I didn't want any roundtables where they get to choose what questions to address and interview players kept on a tight leash, I wanted them back in that discord server in open discussion with all the passionate players who were losing faith. Afaik the broken S rank system still hasn't been fixed properly, and the time it took for them to make an initial announcement that there would be a change and they were looking at it was about 5 months at least. Actually I still haven't mentioned the reaction when they announced hero powers lmao, everyone knew it just wasn't faithful to the game but by that point counterplay had their fingers in their ears singing "blah blah blah I can't hear you". Look I could seriously go on all day citing some ridiculous examples but I think you need to hear it from someone else:
This is a game abandoned by it's old warrior backers and community, the devs and pretty much anybody who thought this game was going to go anywhere and it is completely tragic... My name is Topdecked lethal, perhaps you knew of me but probably not these days. I don't want to blow my own horn but I was one of the most passionate and vocal members of this community, I was in literally every community initiative there was but yet this is simply me reading out my speech at duelyst's funeral right now. The game is gone, it was a fun ride but we hit our last stop prematurely. Don't get this game, let it rest.

New players are going to struggle here, but if you can get past that the game is genuinely fun. This game is awesome. If you're a fan of games in the vein of Dwarf Fortress's Adventurer Mode, Angband, or other rougelikes, this could be up your alley.
What separates it from Dwarf Fortress is a much easier to grasp interface - every shortcut can be checked, changes, and easily learned. The graphics itself are also much more readable, as they are tileset based, not ASCII.
Character customization is greatly diverse - you can have 2 heads, more limbs, burning hands, a bird's beak, a turtle shell, a stinger, wings, amnesia, narcolepsia, an evil twin who pursues you across the world untill finally challenging you to duel.
Don't expect Dwarf Fortress here. Don't expect a regular rougelike experience. Caves of Qud brings this lovely taste of something unique - combination of the sci-fi setting straight out of the 80's imagination (my personal impression), the eerie world and encounters, most weird combinations of creatures and their themes, the absolutely OP skills and abilities you may acquire over time, or encounter as used by your enemies (I still remember the first time I was attacked by an enemy Esper, who proceeded to play with my mind and rip me to shreds). A world where currency is fresh water, a world where you fall in love in most unexpected moments...
Expect !FUN!, but most importantly -
Live and drink, my friend!

This game is deep.
The history of the world is a game mechanic. Gather clues about Sultans, legendary weapons, and lost artifacts from books and paintings and statues strewn across the landscape. Pin-point the location of the treasure on the map and go searching for it.
There is a main questline and plenty of story and setting defined to get started but the procedurally generated content weaves itself over these bones and forms a living, moving creature. This is exactly what you want to plant stories in your players' minds. The people, places, and culture create the setting... there's a lot to unearth here but there's no Tolkien-esque world-building: it's generated by a tight relationship between the game and the player.
Gamma World was the PnP RPG that inspired this game. I think after all of these years that Qud has been in development Freehold have managed to surpass is predecessor in terms of mechanics, story-telling and atmosphere. It has a quality all its own.
I cannot recommend this game enough. It really should win GotY.

Resident Evil 6 is not the same as 5 or 4. That is good. Trying new things is great. Unfortunately they made some choices that I do not like.
Pros:
Rolling and sliding are really fun to do if you can find a good key to do it.
There are two classes of enemies, J'avo (which are like the Los Plagas) and zombies. Each class has many different types. For example in the zombie class you have your regular one, one that unloads their gun randomly, a screamer that can attract other zombies and strengthen them, and more. In J'avo you have your normal gunner, grasshoppers (the name is actually in Siberian or something), bee gunners and more. Very nice, very creative too. You can face them in Mercenaries too.
Story is great. Very good if you like action movies. The reasoning behind the attacks is hilarious though.
There are very interesting parts in the game whether it is riding a motorcycle through a BOW infested city, fighting a giant monster in an underwater facility, using a wrecking ball to knock out a giant Mr. X, and more
Mercenaries is just as fun and with the different types of enemies it is a real blast.
Cons
This game does away with the weapon upgrade system of 4 and 5. Instead you can apply 3 different skills to your character (ex. more defense, stronger melee, no crosshair but stronger attacks). It’s so so, most don’t really change the way you play that much.
The default FOV is awful but you can change it. I'm just stating this as a con for console owners and people with weak PCs.
Controlling your character is a bit wonky for the PC. Tank controls are gone but you only strafe when you go in shoot mode. With the keyboard everyday walking takes some getting used to.
When you get down it takes 3000 hours for you to actually be able to shoot to defend yourself. Half the time the enemy will be on your but by the time you get the chance to fight back and you will more than likely die. With the previously mentioned wonky PC controls it's almost impossible to get away.
Agent Hunt is something that Capcom probably saw in L4D2. You join another person's game as an enemy and try to kill them. They forgot to copy some things from L4D2. First off you only join for the level. Once the team reaches their objective you are booted and sent to another game. Even if you kill them you don't feel much satisfaction because you just got there. In VS mode of L4D2 you generally join from the start and continue until the end or you are behind so badly that you rage. You are also generally alone and even if there are others there isn’t much you can do to combine your efforts. In L4D2 if someone is pounced or charged a spitter helps by spitting on them and the boomer gets the other teammates. But attacks on an agent just hurt them for 5 seconds and then you get killed. It would be like if in L4D2 a pounce would only last for 5 seconds. Although Agent Hunt gives you the opportunity to play as a BOW from a large list. You can play as a bird, a Chinese gangster with a sword, a spider man and more.
Conclusion
This game is like a horror movie sequel. The first one, RE 4, was really good and then it slowly gets worse as the sequels go on. Yet enough people like it enough to buy enough copies to warrant the next sequel. Alot of the game is well done but some parts and decisions just feel mediocre.

I enjoyed the hell out of this game.  I will admit, the horror is kind of lacking, but they rectified it with an excellent story.  The story is told from four different points of view and you get to see how they handled it from their own perspectives.  I felt that the story was told very well and it seemed like it was more realistic in the sense that you have Leon who has a lot of puzzles to solve while dealing with Zombies, Chris handles all the heavy action that would come in a bioterror event, Jake is found out to be the key to stopping the virus and he needs to be kept alive so that the world can be saved, and Ada is under her own agenda to expose the mastermind behind all this.  {SPOILER ALERT} I really enjoyed the irony that Jake is the key to saving the world, and his father, Albert Wesker, was hell-bent on destroying it.  In Leon's campaign and Ada's Campaign, I can tell that the makers were trying to have some creepiness in it.  The only reason I liked Chris's campaign the best is because Chris Redfield is my favorite RE character.  I also enjoyed how realistic the weapons and their properties were.  Don't get me wrong; I enjoyed in RE5 having an M92F with a clip that carries 100 shots because that's freaking awesome, but in reality, a handgun clip won't usually go higher than 18 shots.  I just really liked that it felt more real than the previous two.  Overall, I enjoyed this game because of how it hooks the player.  I know this game gets some hate, but it's still fun and I highly reccommend it to any Resident Evil fan.  I think that if you enjoyed RE4 and RE5, you'll enjoy RE6 due to its large amount of content and similar playability.

My god, where to begin.
Hyper Light Drifter is one of those games everyone tells you to play, and you may question them as to why. The only real answer someone can give you is "it's a good game". The many things that make up it being a good game would, honestly, undersell it if explained.
The plot is not up front, the difficulty can be high, and the combat is easy to learn, but hard to master. For most games, this is the opposite of approachable, but for Hyper Light Drifter, this is everything that makes it good.
You play as a Drifter, a sort of hyper fast cyberpunk character with a lightsaber that is tasked with...well, good question. You can see your character is sick, you can sort of see why he becomes sick, but all you know is what something like Zelda would tell you. Find the Modules to unlock the thing in the middle of the town, and then you can discover its secrets. While the game shows you these strange, dark, surreal situations at the start, and these appear as you progress through the game, it never fully explains it to you what these are. Something happened, and it is up to the player to find out what. Perhaps with it, you can find your purpose in this world, should it matter to you at all.
The difficulty of the game is heavily reliant on your ability to adapt strategy against your foes, as well as your observational skills of the many different traps. Every battle can be won, and while many of them will feel difficult and hard to approach, they always ended up feeling fair. As you upgrade your drifter, you realize that approaching certain scenarios seems designed around certain skills, and it makes it feel more valuable to sometimes come back to an area if you feel you can't do it. To this end, HLD does well at allowing people who may not be able to handle the difficulty be able to find a way through everything.
The combat itself is surprisingly complex for a 2D title. As someone who is used to 3 dimensions of movement to crowd control and strategize my combat against my foes, having a top down view restricting my interaction with foes was something I was concerned would limit combat complexity. HLD, however, decided that 2D complexity existed in the diversity of 2D games. What I mean by this is that if you look at bullet hell games, top down shooters, and hack'n'slash games like Gauntlet, there is room to kind of throw them all together and create a momentum that chains it all together. You get three specific tools in all of this: your sword, your guns, and your dash. The sword starts with a generic three hit combo, and you can upgrade to get a dash attack, charge cleave attack, and a stab after a dash. The game contains six guns in total, each of which have varying max clip size, functionality, and damage. Guns do not reload by hitting a reload button, but instead reload by landing melee attacks on your foes, creating a powerful flow of melee and ranged combat that benefits greatly from mastery. The last piece is your dash, and this one is what makes everything fall into a nice place. The dash is your evasive tool, your method of control against the dangers of your foes. With upgrades, your dash can be chained with timed button hits, as well as eat projectiles you collide with. In a game like Devil May Cry, I would control the enemies using knock up and knock back attacks to control the ebb and flow of combat itself, but in HLD, the dash is how you control the combat, and it was a unique perspective to have in how combat is done. Using the dash, you can close a gap with a foe and chain a melee string, or run out of range to shoot them down from relative safety. The enemies focused you and only you, and this allows you to learn how to use their aggro to your control. When this finally clicked, I was finally able to beat one of the hardest parts of the game, the last horde room, and I finally felt like I understood how this game was meant to function for those skilled enough to grasp it. This entire system made the games combat become ranked as one of the best in anything I've probably played, and for a 2D game, that made me have an even more positive view of how combat can be done in all genres of games.
But enough of my euphoric enthusiasm on combat, lets get to the bad. Probably only two bad things there. The entire game was an amazing experience, but the side stuff was not so great. Unlocking everything in the game felt like more of a chore than it did an experience. One instance has you dashing in the same room 800 times, and I just had no interest in that, so thank you Autohotkey for helping me there. The other instance I despised was the RNG nature of the horde rooms that you can find behind a key door. They had a lot of potential to be a great place to practice and learn the combat of the game, but end up being a split between "ok, I can tactically engage these guys" and "oh great, two rocket guys and two machine gun guys, not gonna win this one".
That being said, both of these are completely avoidable and are in no way required to complete the game. They just suck for a completionist like me to deal with, and detracted from the experience.
As for any other bad, well, can't say there was much. I'm not great at aiming with an analog stick, so using guns to hit enemies sometimes felt weird, but it was accurate so it was more me than the game. Bosses all felt fun and intuitive, with one of them feeling like a puzzle alongside being a battle. I can't say there was much of anything I didn't like in this game.
So overall, I give it a 9.8/10.

Thomas Was Alone is what I believe to be the perfect game to start a non-gamer on, or to represent how good platforming games are these days.
You'll start out as Thomas, a curious red rectangle which is meant to represent a rogue bit of AI. As you progress through the levels, a smooth voice will narrate what Thomas' thoughts and surroundings are, giving a relaxing feel of someone just roaming about, guided by a sense of curiosity. Gradually, you'll meet (and be able to play as) many different characters, all personified with names.
It is the interactions of these shapes, told solely through the narrator, that gives this game heart. Who'd have thought that you could be rapt in the interactions of such simple quadrilateral and monochromaric shapes? They all seem to represent a different mental state; Thomas, the optimistic observer; John, the love-struck grump; and Laura, the cautious outsider, to name a few.
It's also pretty funny at times, with humour that sometimes breaks the fourth wall.
Soundtracks are incredibly important to me, as a great one can ensure you're fully immersed in the game, putting in as much emotional investment as you can. Gladly, Thomas Was Alone perfectly captures an environment that ranges from the serene, to the fast-paced. Apt music at every stage.
For the completionist, there's also additional challenges, mostly involving reaching difficult places, that can squeeze a bit of replayability out of you. Unfortunately, once you've had one play-through, there's not much else cause to boot it up again.
That being said, it is a game that must exist in your Library, because what it does, it does extremely well.

Came here for the beautiful pixel art, and stayed for the addictive gameplay and heart-wrenching story. Hands-down one of my favorite games of all time. I grew up with the Diablo franchise, and although I love those games (and they were clearly an influence on this one), I might actually go so far as to say I like Hyper Light more because of its subtlety.
The abstract storytelling might be a drawback for some, but it's definitely a plus for me. It makes the game more solemn and personalized to everyone who plays it, or something like that. It's got punishing gameplay for sure. This is a game that requires you to think about what you're doing rather than just mindlessly hacking and slashing your way through. The lore is like that too-- hardly anything is spoon-fed to you; you need to explore and think about what you're seeing in order to piece together the grim story behind the world of Hyper Light.
Also, the ending definitely made me cry. And thinking about the ending makes me cry. It's thematically appropriate, but oh man, is it depressing. I'd rate this game 11/10 if I could.

Hi, I am an old player of this game... Having played it for much much longer then my 200 something steam hours would have you believe, I have a few things I would like to share.
This isn't a salty dress down of duelyst where I act like an educated♥♥♥♥♥and think I know best about this game, I am just here to point out why duelyst was amazing beyond my expectations and how the devs let everybody down.
A little about myself and my experience coming into duelyst, I joined late december during the snowchaser promotion in 2015 where everyone got the snowchaser emote (when it was still exclusive) and the game was in the middle stages of open beta, it was a very different game back then.
Back then as you may have heard we had an infamous period of time where you would draw two cards at the end of your turn and start with 3 cards... The game was unbalanced and a total mess to play but god damn it was fun, the game was hitting a huge growth spurt and was just getting attention in gaming media outlets (like kotaku) as I believed it deserved at the time and it was showing unbelievable promise.
Lo and behold what came in this period of time were decks that revolved around one or two cards and always drawing them when you needed to and tempo was everything. Every game was 2 drop spam and things like holy immolation or Killing edge (and old third wish which gave one unit +3/+3 and blast around january/feb), needless to say not many things were good and card plays were completely predictable but what made up for it was the tactical play with the board. It basically brought card games to life as if that is what they were missing and the hair pin strategies that you came up with were awesome every single time. I loved every second and wasted the first part of my year on this game...
What really gave this game some staying power though was that the community was empowered by the devs, people ran community contests and tournaments and people got scouted by counterplay to work for them. They even got into debates with us about lore and art which was ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, the support and love the devs had for the game that they gave back to the community resonated in every aspect... I'll never forget this. Except that ended up working against me as for some reason the devs began to turn their backs on us and it hurt.
It started with a few changes, the first being the sudden change to one draw into pushing for official release far before the game was fleshed out and ready (why on earth would you change half the fundamental mechanics of the game and then release it with only 1 month of live testing?) and they completely stonewalled any communication on that regard simply reffering to it as "release hype". I understand now they wanted to gamble with an explosive release (they had a cinematic and everything lmao) but back then it seemed just plain wrong and it didn't work in the end despite all the buzz it got from critics. Understand initially I just looked askance at this and had total faith in these guys but now it feels gutless considering the slippery slope the game took henceforth.
Once release was out the way, updates were much slower... normally when something was a big problem we could just rely on the mid month patch to fix it but as one dev put it "Since we are out of beta we are going to be much less active in changing the game as there are less things to address". Yet now we have loot crates, boss fights, alternate generals, purchasable emotes (don't even get me started on this) and much more random♥♥♥♥♥♥we didn't need but gives the devs yet another option to make a quick buck (they previously had a very fair payment scheme, where are your values now?). But that also allowed them to put up some smoke and mirrors as to why no significant change had been made in over two months (I understand the maintanence schedule for other card games is much longer but they get away with it due to publicity of the game). Why does all this get me worked up? Well it's pretty simple, the game was getting infuriating and the devs stopped listening to people period.
I didn't want any roundtables where they get to choose what questions to address and interview players kept on a tight leash, I wanted them back in that discord server in open discussion with all the passionate players who were losing faith. Afaik the broken S rank system still hasn't been fixed properly, and the time it took for them to make an initial announcement that there would be a change and they were looking at it was about 5 months at least. Actually I still haven't mentioned the reaction when they announced hero powers lmao, everyone knew it just wasn't faithful to the game but by that point counterplay had their fingers in their ears singing "blah blah blah I can't hear you". Look I could seriously go on all day citing some ridiculous examples but I think you need to hear it from someone else:
This is a game abandoned by it's old warrior backers and community, the devs and pretty much anybody who thought this game was going to go anywhere and it is completely tragic... My name is Topdecked lethal, perhaps you knew of me but probably not these days. I don't want to blow my own horn but I was one of the most passionate and vocal members of this community, I was in literally every community initiative there was but yet this is simply me reading out my speech at duelyst's funeral right now. The game is gone, it was a fun ride but we hit our last stop prematurely. Don't get this game, let it rest.

Duelyst is the best digital CCG I have played. It isn't quite perfect, but it makes Hearthstone look like the highly polished turd that it is.
The Good:
+ Pixel art with killer animations!
+ Six very different factions with interesting playstyles. Balance isn't quite there yet, but there isn't just one strategy that outright shatters everything else.
+ Tactics! Having a grid makes strategy all the more important to play efficiently and intelligently. Place one card in the wrong spot or make the wrong move and boom! You're in hot water and either losing tempo or the match.
+ Definitely not P2W. Sorry salt farmers, you can play a reasonable amount every day and amass a good collection. You can easily earn a pack a day, maybe more if you are dedicated. And if you look on Reddit, you can get help building low dust (currency to create cards) cost decks that can totally flex with the expensive ones.
+ If you do start paying, you get rare cards at an elevated rate compared to Hearthstone. Add in a more favorable disenchant rate and lots of high quality staples at common and you won't break the bank on this game by any means.
+ The playerbase and community (I played a ton in February-March approximately, so I'm not as up to date) is very friendly and helpful. I'm pretty sure most of us just want to see Duelyst grow and improve.
+ Finally, replacing. Once per turn you can throw a card back into your deck and draw a new one. It adds that subtle amount of consistency that makes the game less of a variance fest. There are way fewer games where you just don't see your deck's key components.
+ Daily challenges! Little bites of brain-teasing single player. Worst case scenario,
The Meh:
~ Crates are sorta lame. I mean, what is this? TF2?
~ RNG additions lately are a little worriesome, but thus far it's nowhere near as offensive as Hearthstone. Fingers crossed it stays under control.
The Bad:
-Nothing
All in all, if you like CCGs and strategy games you need to give this sucker a shot. After all, what's to lose? Oh, right... your social life.

Excellent game, I do recommend it to all city builders. I have been playing this game for more than a year now, and it largely surpasses Simcity 4 Deluxe and all its counterparts, it does have some elements of theSims and Simutrans. Definitely the greatest rival of EA's city-building series, not only that, it overpowers all current city building simulators.
HOWEVER, please note that as of November 29th 2016 patch, highly popular user-created content such as:
--- 81 tiles by BloodyPenguin (which allows to play on huge maps)
--- Traffic++V2 (which allows for road speed and intersection customization)
--- Netword Extensions (which adds more roads such as bus lanes and pedestrian roads)
--- Daylight Classic (which greatly reduces road reflection and makes the game more colorful and less bland)
--- Precision Engineering (which allows road angular customization)
--- etc...
All of these mods do not work anymore, they are currently incompatible with the new patch.
Personally, I enjoy the idea of cataclysms and careful disaster planning, but I marvel at the blatant lack of disaster planning when releasing this patch. The developers should have done something in order to make sure that, either their update is compatible with mods, or that the mods become compatible with the game. Granted, mods are user-created and they are outside the developers' authority, but the developers could have at least warned the modders beforehand in order to make for a smooth transition.
Now that my game is updated, I am currently unable to play on my favorite maps (big and challenging maps such as Shimanto by Aya and San Marino by freshPopCorn) and all of my saves cannot be loaded properly. Also, the game crashes more often or freezes and I find myself forced to end task on Windows Task Manager. Sadly and unfortunately, I cannot play my favorite game anymore.
The developers have worked 19 months on this patch and the Natural Disasters DLC, but have they perhaps, rushed their coding and planning in order to match up with the Christmas Season? Or perhaps, have they overlooked the importance of community content?
Another concern naturally rises, being a Paradox Interactive game, many players are aware of the current marketing policy of their other best-seller, Europa Universalis IV, being a bare-bone game stripped of its core mechanisms which can only be regained by paying for tons of DLCs (that is why I haven't bought EU4, though I thoroughly enjoyed EU2). Thus, I do pose the following question out of deep concern for this wonderful game:
Are you planning on turning Cities Skylines into a money-monger best-seller?
Are you making money with good games OR are you making games for good money?
That is the question...
When the best elements of the best city-builders boil down to: it's Cities Skylines.

After playing this game for a year and seeing how treyarch have come from release to dlc 4 I would like to say that this game has definitely brought a lot of new ideas into how a player interacts and fights in the game. I really am glad that Treyarch has brought in the idea of taking the level sytem in multiplayer and extending it to zombies and single player campaign. The campaign was pretty good. When it comes to zombies, I have to say the zombies team did an amazing job of getting people hyped for the new content. Shadows of Evil, when first played was an incredible experience. With players, like myself, who have been on the zombie train since World at War in 2008, we found that Black ops 3 took zombies in a completely new and incredible direction. It focused more on the story and less on surviving as long as you can. I found it to be a really good change. It made the player really look at every bit of detail the zombie team has put into creating such premium maps as well as trying the new ideas which the directors of Zombies put into it to see how the community responds and how well it fits into the game. The story line from Origins to Gorod Krovi was incredible and brilliant. It starts from the very beginning and takes us on a crazy journey explaining some missing information which the previous zombie games in world at war, black ops, and black ops 2 did not fully address or make clear. When Revelations was about to be release, the whole zombies community and myself were certainly extremely hyped. We felt like we were finally going to get some closure as to who Division 9 was, or the Ascesion group, or to why group 935 was on this journey to kill their 1.0 versions to save the universe. When the map was released we all were really amazed how all of the previous maps were integrated into Revelations, a fractured and broken universe. However, when the community solved what seemed to be the main easter egg, we were all let down. It just seemed to end. We never got to see about the children, or more about Dr. Monty and his purpose except that he is some sort of limited god-like character. All we got was more unfinished story and more loopholes which I personally didn't find satisfying. Yes, most of us want more content (possibly a DLC 5 or a Season Pass 2 which will close all of these loopholes or maybe reveal more. But for now the whole community is at a point where they want more zombies and more closure to the whole plot but aren't as hyped as we were.

Hay una gran variedad de enemigos, cada uno con nuevas formas de matarte, y bosses enormes, espeluznantes y con bastante tendencia a no morirse aunque les estrelles un helicóptero en la cabeza. Igualmente, disponemos también de un buen arsenal de armas para despacharlos a gusto, desde ♥♥♥♥♥s eléctricas y cuchillos, a las clásicas escopetas y pistolas magnum. Incluso puedes desahogarte a puñetazo limpio y machacar cabezas a pisotones.
El juego contiene cuatro campañas de cinco capítulos cada una, lo que lo convierte en un juego bastante largo si quieres completarlo del todo, y cada una está protagonizada por personajes clásicos de la saga, desde Chris Redfield y Leon Kennedy, hasta Sherry Birkin (si, la niña que tanto daba la murga en el RE2). Cada campaña tiene su propio argumento, aunque todas se entremezclan en algún momento, y aunque al terminarlas te dejan con la sensación de que no te lo han contado todo, puedes ir desbloqueando los secretos del juego para ir revelando información. El nivel de dificultad no es gran cosa, pero puedes modificarlo a tu gusto si buscas un desafío mayor, y puedes probar diferentes personajes para una experiencia nueva. En mi opinión, no es mejor que los clásicos o el 4, pero supera con creces a su predecesor.

TL;DR: Fun game that takes time to beat with an extreme amount of replay value.
It's not scary like Resident Evil 0, 1, 2, 3 or Code Veronica. Like it matters though, because this game has so much content, controls beautifully, looks great, sounds great and has a ton replayability. Hated the fact that you couldn't strafe in Resident Evil 4 or 5? No problem. This game can do it. Like feeling helpless with barely any ammo and no herbs to heal you with? This game will make you feel like that if you choose a high difficulty. Like a game that will take a long time to beat? I've played this game for about 23 hours (On and Offline) and I haven't beaten all four campaigns and haven't even touched the Mercenaries or Agent Hunt. It also has Left 4 Dead 2 content in it. Wanted to kill a Witch with a remote detonating bomb and/or an RPG? You can in this game. However, like every video game that exists, this game has problems. First being the character Piers Nivans. Who the ♥♥♥♥ is Piers Nivans and why do we care about him? He doesn't do♥♥♥♥♥♥besides help kill the final boss in Chris's campaign. Even Helena Harper, a newcomer to the franchise, like Piers has story, development, a likeable personality and everything good that Piers doesn't. He does nothing before that, but ♥♥♥♥♥ and complain about how his childhood hero turned into a vengeful squad leader and that has no effect on the story whatsoever. Next problem is the graphics. While they are beautiful, sometimes during cutscenes there's this transparent higlight that surrounds the characters and the game likes to blur the background if you are taking cover and not aiming. Next is the controls. You have to aim before you're able to take cover. Kind of stupid, but miniscule. Next, we come to the soundtrack. This game has this hybrid soundtrack of beautiful music like the safe room theme in Resident Evil Code Veronica and the rest is powerful testosterone filled gritty action music like something you would hear in Robocop, Last Action Hero or Die Hard. Finally is the game modes. There aren't a lot (Campaign, Mercenaries and Agent Hunt) and if you want 4 more multiplayer game modes that are actually really fun you have to pay $3.99 for each one. All in all, this game is really fun with a ton of content and replayability and the problems with it are nitpicky at best. I highly recommend this game.

Thomas Was Alone had gone on sale for the Holidays, and after reading reviews and friends' recommendations, I'm honestly glad that I bought it.
A brief synopsis, spoiler free. Thomas' story revolves around him and the friends he meets along the way. Some of his friends want nothing to do with Thomas, and others just want to be noticed. Together they discover the digital world they live in, and what lies beyond the portals.
Even though it is a shorter Indie game (~5 hours and all achievements found), this was a rare instance in that even after I completed it, I wanted to keep playing it over and over again. Never has a narrator captured the personality of quadrillaterals so brilliantly, to the point where at times I found myself utterly captivated.
The puzzles are appropriately challenging, without getting to the point where you want to rage quit. Because each geometric shape has it's own unique "power", you have to think logically on how you can get to the end of the level.
Aside from a bit of a lag towards the last levels (a computer restart fixed this), I can't find anything bad or worth fixing in this game. The graphics, mood-setting soundtrack, and platforming environment are all perfect for this world. Sometimes simple is best, since too much going on or too intricate of graphics can draw away from an amazing storyline. This is one of those instances, where simple was key and the brilliance of this decision radiated through the game.
All in all, this has to be one of my favorite Indie games, hands down. Sure, this game was greatly hyped about by many, many people; However this was all for good reason. With an enriching storyline and likable (and cheeky) characters, Indie gamers with an affinity for platforming and excellent storylines will be riveted. For in the end, we are all adventurers seeking a bigger and brighter world, and we (like Thomas) are never alone.

PLEASE NOTE, MY TIME IS BUGGED DUE TO INTERNET PROBLEMS. TIME IS PROBABLY AROUND 4-5 HOURS.
So, games and comedy. Sometimes that is an absolute MESS of a combo. A combo which should never work. But Jazzpunk. Wow, does this game do such an amazing job of it. The comedy in this game is crude and sometimes dark. But the comedy aspect of the game just works!
Alright, so walking away from the comedy side of the game, let's consider the actual gameplay. The gameplay is smooth. I mean, really smooth. This is one of those games that you could honestly just play again and again because of the controls. The turning is responsive, the controls are tight and stiff. Just amazingly well done with how they made the controls work.
As you progress in the game, there are no massive learning curves or any new "gizmos" which can help you. This is no way makes the game boring. The game always has something to keep you on your toes, be it trimming a man's back hair or just putting lipstick on your character to glamourize yourself. Speaking of the game having no "learning curves" I deem it important to tell you all that the game has pretty much ANYTHING you can do. Hell, there's an achievement for just freakin' using a metal detector and finding treasure! And what does the treasure do for you? Nothing, zilch, 0! And is it good? Hell yeah it's good! The ability to do those quirky little things just for the sake of it is totally unique and something that is rarely done in games.
Speaking of that, most games will have you do some grindy-bore-fest task just to get yourself some better gear or loot. This game just allows you to do it for free! You can choose to do it, there's nothing to gain OR lose from it. And that's good. It rewards players with an achievement - which most people don't care about, so they don't have to bother with it. I know this is sounding like a ramble now, so let me sum this one part up.
- Doing things for an achievement is good.
- Making sure that the game isn't grindy is good.
- Not making the player more powerful for something that they can do which others may not want to do.
This game has side missions. And do you get any neat items from it? Nope! Anything at all? Well, yes. A few have achievements which is why I did them, so there's achievements for all you achievement hunters. Speaking of achievements, this game is perfect for all you achievement hunters. The achievements are easy to get, fun to achieve and actually feel rewarding. The game will make you go out of your way for some and others.. Well for others you just gotta play the game!
This game, is just breath-takingly unique. The comedy element is just too well done to the point that you don't get sick of it and you don't feel like you want more. There's a perfect balance of gameplay and comedy. The game doesn't shove the jokes in your face going "LOOK WE MADE A FUNNY, WE EXPECT YOU TO LAUGH," instead they make it so that you know the joke and that it's going to bring a small grin to your face. Be it the cheesiest joke ever, or a woman falling out a window from a bomb♥♥♥♥♥pillow fight!
So, do I recoomend this game? Yes. 100% YES. Honestly, if you're looing for a game to spice up your library and make you giggle like an idiot for a few hours, get this game. Sure, it's short but it has a bunch of replay value and side missions. The achievements are fun to get and easy to get, so yeah. Get this game for a memorable little gem.

Excellent game, I do recommend it to all city builders. I have been playing this game for more than a year now, and it largely surpasses Simcity 4 Deluxe and all its counterparts, it does have some elements of theSims and Simutrans. Definitely the greatest rival of EA's city-building series, not only that, it overpowers all current city building simulators.
HOWEVER, please note that as of November 29th 2016 patch, highly popular user-created content such as:
--- 81 tiles by BloodyPenguin (which allows to play on huge maps)
--- Traffic++V2 (which allows for road speed and intersection customization)
--- Netword Extensions (which adds more roads such as bus lanes and pedestrian roads)
--- Daylight Classic (which greatly reduces road reflection and makes the game more colorful and less bland)
--- Precision Engineering (which allows road angular customization)
--- etc...
All of these mods do not work anymore, they are currently incompatible with the new patch.
Personally, I enjoy the idea of cataclysms and careful disaster planning, but I marvel at the blatant lack of disaster planning when releasing this patch. The developers should have done something in order to make sure that, either their update is compatible with mods, or that the mods become compatible with the game. Granted, mods are user-created and they are outside the developers' authority, but the developers could have at least warned the modders beforehand in order to make for a smooth transition.
Now that my game is updated, I am currently unable to play on my favorite maps (big and challenging maps such as Shimanto by Aya and San Marino by freshPopCorn) and all of my saves cannot be loaded properly. Also, the game crashes more often or freezes and I find myself forced to end task on Windows Task Manager. Sadly and unfortunately, I cannot play my favorite game anymore.
The developers have worked 19 months on this patch and the Natural Disasters DLC, but have they perhaps, rushed their coding and planning in order to match up with the Christmas Season? Or perhaps, have they overlooked the importance of community content?
Another concern naturally rises, being a Paradox Interactive game, many players are aware of the current marketing policy of their other best-seller, Europa Universalis IV, being a bare-bone game stripped of its core mechanisms which can only be regained by paying for tons of DLCs (that is why I haven't bought EU4, though I thoroughly enjoyed EU2). Thus, I do pose the following question out of deep concern for this wonderful game:
Are you planning on turning Cities Skylines into a money-monger best-seller?
Are you making money with good games OR are you making games for good money?
That is the question...
When the best elements of the best city-builders boil down to: it's Cities Skylines.

Didn't like it, despite loving the first game. I found the smaller, more linear stages to be confining in comparison to the sprawling environments of its predecessor. What's the point of being stranded in an urban jungle if you can't explore it and are forced to go from point A to B with no way of approaching a threat from a different direction. They tried to address this by providing you with different objectives that allow you to sneak past enemies by going underground or by finding perch areas where you can snipe the opposition from but it still ended up being overly guided and constraining.
I also found the story to be jarring and non-sensical, espeically since the game begins without a clear transition between the events at the end of the first game and the begining of this one as it begins with New York already half-destroyed with seemingly new types of aliens that weren't in the original game with no explanation as to what transpired in-between. We also don't find out why Prophet suddenly went rogue and was clashing with elements of the military, and the person you end up controlling and playing as has no voice and goes along with whatever he's told to do unlike the oppinionated and more believable characters of Crysis 1.
I also found the sparsity of checkpoints (why remove quicksaves in this type of game) to be frustrating as you could go up against waves of enemies for a period of 10-15min only to be killed by a new, tougher enemy and have to replay the whole thing over again. I think the devs did this to try and 'cover-up' their linear environments and repetitive scenarios by artifically lengthening the game in this manner but it didn't work, I'M ON TO YOU SUCKAS!
On the plus side controlling the updated suit is a blast: the new suit mode changes make more sense and it's fun to customize your suit (and weapons) as you progress through the game as you can do so seamlessly on the fly. However another gripe I had with the game becomes apparent here as you need dropped nano elements from killed alien enemies to upgrade your suit but these disappear if you don't grab them quickly enough. It therefore feels like you're being punished for setting up sniping perches and methodically killing every alien within the immediate vicinity as by the time you're done killing the last alien the nano catalysts drops would have disappeared from the corpses of your first kills. This makes even less sense as the game nudges you towards higher-vantage flanking positions to protect your human allies as they fight aliens but doing so prevents you from nabbing all the catalysts.

Basically a Call of Duty type game.  Blasting your way from inconsequential mission to another.  Not sure what the whole story is about as it didn't seem to matter.  I give it a "Yes" mostly because of the graphics, they were great.  I have good PC system so I like games that are made with really good graphics.
I know lot of gamers say it’s the gameplay not the graphics that count, but I would disagree.  Its the same reason we go to see action movies like Avatar, Batman, Ironman, Spiderman, Captain America etc.  Those are all cartoon stories, with silly plots and even sillier characters if you think about it.  You go to these movies for only one reason; the mind blowing special effects. When you hear that an action movie cost around 150-200 million to make you know that you are in for a visual treat.
Back to the game; another thing I liked about this fairly liner shooter is that you could fight the battles coming at it from different angles.  When you got killed, the approach to enter the battle was always the same, but you could try different tactics, i.e., gun your way through, hit and run, or hide and wait till they came to you.  I found that in most other linear shooters that if you didn't follow the strict "run and shoot" Call of Duty style that there was little other options.  Generally in other game I've played, you have to hit a certain point for the enemy to fight you and if you hide or try stealth, nothing happens till you come of hiding face them full on.  Often the game forces you into the open by one method or another such as lobbing grenades thrown by invisible enemies just to keep you in the open.  In this game I did a lot of hiding forcing them to look for me which actually worked very well and broke up the monotony of the constant skirmishes.  Actually I did a lot of hiding because I was always busy admiring the incredible rendering of buildings and the cityscape.  The detail was phenomenal.  I couldn't get enough of it.
As for the Nano suit gimmick, half the time I forgot to turn it on.  It was nice to have those abilities of armour and stealth, when I remembered to use them.  There were lots of different weapons to choose from, although I generally like to choose a set of weapons and stick with them if I can throughout the game.  As for the shooting mechanics, I find that all FPS suffer from the same limitation; a sometimes inconsistency in weapon damage.   The same weapon can kill an enemy with a few shots or next time you use it need to empty the clip to do the same damage.   Fortunately this incosistancy was no different from any other game.
The plot was confusing and to me didn't really matter.  The only game I ever played a game that had a decent plot was Metro 2033 and that's because it was based on the Russian novel of the same name.   That game followed that novel’s plot reasonably close so the story and game were much closer intertwined.  As for Crysis 2 you are being directed by one character or another and didn't really matter because regardless of the mission by the time you got close there was always one of those "by the way, I forgot to tell you this" scenario that stretched the game out.  For all I cared about the missions they could have been asking me to pick up a quart of milk at the 7-11 while I was on my way to whatever destination I was heading for.  As matter of fact it was kind of like that, sort of like "Hey Alcatraz, before you get here can you picked a quart of milk from 7-11".   Then when you got close it was like "Oh, sorry I forgot to tell there are some bullies hanging around the 7-11 that are going to try and take your money so you're gonna have to fight your way through them to get to the 7-11."
In conclusion, even though the plot was meandering and gun play was getting very repetitious, it still allowed you explore different ways to attack and still get your objective done. You're an unstoppable machine that makes all your enemies blow themselves up because you're too much of a badass.
Obviously this game no longer works for multiplayer, so the only thing this game has worth is its single campaign.
Synopsis
----------------
You play as silent protagonist, Alcatraz, a marine soldier who is sent to extract Nathan Gould, a former employee who has vital information in defeating the aliens that gave everyone the spook in the first installment. However, the situations immediately escalates for the worst and  the aliens kill all of your men. As for you, you barely survive the attack and a man by the name of "Prophet" saves you, and then everything fades to black.
When you come to, you find yourself in the very suit that "Prophet" was in, but "Prophet" is now dead. He says in a recording that he was already infected by a virus, and says that you have to continue where he left off. And now the game begins with you off to save the world.
----------------
If this is your first time playing Crysis, I would suggest watching youtube vids of Crysis 1. It gives you a lot of insight to the story and (personally) makes the game a lot more enjoyable to play.
I went through the game for 2-4 hours completely detached from the storyline only because I didn't know who was "Prophet", what the nanosuit was for and why I should even care that there were a bunch of Squidwards fighting against us. However, when I got to Gould, I finally took time to look at a recap, and the story became more enjoyable because of it.
Granted, the story's not groundbreaking. It doesn't do anything too unique to stand out from most other storytelling games, but it was enjoyable enough for me to care for the characters to a small extent, which was more than enough for me to allow myself to want to play from beginning to end.
As for the gameplay, it has its moments of being entertaining, especially at the beginning.
You're given the option to do things that no normal soldier can do, which is being able to go invisible, have super armor, kicking cars on their side like it was some kid's bike and punching people in the face harder than a heavyweight boxer.
However, this is also the game's weakness.
Due to these features, the game feels too easy regardless of difficulty, and more than half the time, the enemies will make it easy for you, even when you're doing nothing at times.
The AI is...special. They will shoot at you, and if you go into cloaking mode right in front of their eyes, they will immediately forget that you were even there.
Their attention span is equal to that of a hamster. They will see you, and forget that you actually exist until you show up right in front of your face.
Also,  I guarantee you that unless it's a mission where you're forced to fight, you can honestly just cheese through the game in cloaking mode without having to throw a single bullet, which really defeats the purpose of the game even being an FPS.
But despite these flaws, this still doesn't deter from the game being fun at all. If you allow the game to, you can definitely get a nice kick out of the storyline.
So is the game worth its full price at $30?
Wait for a price drop if you really want to try out its single campaign.
And when I say a price drop, I mean a
.
This game is worth no more than $5 to $10 at best, and I wouldn't suggest spending any more than that, especially with the multiplayer gone.
I spent $2 on this, and I say it was more than enough money well spent for my 12 hours of gameplay, especially with my purchase being the equivalence of a small time indie games.
That said, this game gets a thumbs up from me.
But be smart, and buy this game when the time is right.

It's got punishing gameplay for sure. This is a game that requires you to think about what you're doing rather than just mindlessly hacking and slashing your way through. Also, the ending definitely made me cry. And thinking about the ending makes me cry. It's thematically appropriate, but oh man, is it depressing. I'd rate this game 11/10 if I could.

Discussion is based on the Impossible-difficulty.
Rebuild is not a new game in the sense that it is a new idea. Indeed, the developer has produced two earlier Rebuild games that  are floating on the Internet as a free flashgame and as a nominal fee mobile game. Those who have played either one of those games will be very familiar with this incarnation of Rebuild.
However, dismissing this Rebuild because of that would be a mistake. Already in this stage of it's Early Access cycle it has way more to it than those earlier versions.
Graphically, Rebuild is colorful and cartoony but does not venture beyond a pseudo isometric map on which icons relay the bulk of the information, supported by textboxes that in their information provide much of the immersion and feel of trying to survive in a zedpocalypse. Rebuild will not dazzle you with next-gen graphics, or offer you outlandish options and resolutions for which you need two Titans in SLI and several monitors.
Due to this, Rebuild can be enjoyed by most anyone with a computer bought anywhere in the last five years.
The tone of the game is lighthearted, which does hide the fact that the game is actively trying to kill you. The tone of the game and it's graphical presentation makes it easy to underestimate the efficiency it can display in giving the player a false sense of security, leading to the player taking risks which appear to be calculated but will prove to be anything but.
The player has many option to taylor the gameplay. First and foremost there is the map, which comes in a slew of basic dimensions from tiny to gigantic. All of those basic dimension are however procced so no map is ever the same and no specific strategy will play out the same from map to map. In itself, the basic size of the map is somewhat of a difficulty adjuster in and on itself, as the number of zeds on the map increase dramatically the larger the map chosen is.
Then the composition of your team will differ each time, though there will always a soldier, a builder and a scavenger in it. The Soldier, obviously, is your go-to survivor for combat duty. Nothing out of the ordinary with this survivor. The soldier kills zeds...
The builder is quite a talented survivor. Not only can a builder demolish buildings to provide you with the materials resource, the builder is also the survivor to turn to when you need to transform a cityblock into something else.
The scavenger.., well, apart from his/her obvious task of gathering food and resources from blocks not yet reclaimed, he/she is also the survivor to turn to to scout out blocks you haven't been to yet. You have to careful with your scavengers, they're not soldiers, though they can defend themselves if need be.
The scientist is your survivor who can act as a doctor and as a researcher, provided you can present the scientist with the buildings he needs to ply his trade.
The leader is your diplomat. Through him, you can recruit more survivors into your fort and conduct other charismatic things, like preaching in the church (if you build or reclaimed one) to bolster party-morale.
All survivors can do all tasks described, but using the right person for the job will see it done quicker or with more success.
As your survivors do the things they do best, they acquire perks. These perks buff their main talent. As of now, the player is not notified of this and the player has to scan the roster frequently to see if a survivor can activate a perk.
The player starts on the map in a five-block 'Fort'. From the very start, zeds are massing at the gates and the player can set the soldier to work as soon as turn1 is underway. The food-situation is dire and decisions about farming have to be made immedeately. Scavengers will have start risking body and limbs scrounging for food right from the get-go.
This pressure will not relent, yet your survivors will go mental if they can't rest up. So the player will constantly juggle a lot of factors that become increasingly harder to juggle. In order to remain functional, new survivors have to be recruited. More survivors means needing more farms, but also more apartments. That means that the player is forced to expand by reclaiming blocks. Getting bigger means a larger perimeter, which needs soldiers to defend... But next to the constant zed-attacks, the zeds can also mass into a herd which will be harder to defeat, forcing the player to make decisions on where to focus the defence. Next to that... ammunition is finite and needs to be fabricated.
After a few turns the factions surface of which the subtitle of Rebuild hints at. If you thought that defending yourself from the zombies is a handful... prepare to deal with gangs that all have their own agendas which do not necessarily include being nice to you...
But in all this chaos there is you. You, the player, is represented in the game through a customizable avatar (limited customization right now) and you're special. Unlike the survivors who have one talent only, your avatar has all five and can level up in all of them. This versatality means that you can jump in and help out where you're needed the most, though that in itself brings with it a new set of decisions. Will you go and recruit that survivor holed up in the suburbs or will you lend a hand in transforming an officebuilding into a farm?
It's all up to you.
Will you like Rebuild? Rebuild is a x4 RTS. It offers nothing out of the ordinary right down to the tried and tested zedpocalypse trope. Lopsided commentary in-game is there, the zeds are there, gruesome deaths are accounted for and decisions between a rock and hard place are thick as flies. There's even a research function and a tech-tree to explore.
The 'impossible' difficulty on which my review is based is suitably hard, but in my opinion still fair. That is, all my defeats left me with something I feel I can do different the next time.
Should you buy it?
No.
You shouldn't buy Rebuild because it is an Early Access title. You have no guarantee that the developer will ever finish producing Rebuild to release-candidate status. You have no guarantee that the developer will make good on the development-list. There's a good chance that you buy a game that for all you know is abandoned already. The fact the developer is active on the forums means little, as there are examples enough where 'active developers' suddenly fell off the face the earth taking the money with them and leaving the players with an unfinished heap of alpha-code.
Buying Early Access is a gamble I do not wish for people to make on my saying so.
So that leaves me in the weird position that I'm very positive about Rebuild. I like it very much and in it's current state it is most certainly perfectly playable and enjoyable. But I can't recommend it because it is Early Access and therefore is completely devoid of any guarantee to the buyer that Rebuild will ever be developed through and finished.
-Merdakah

Black Ops III is quite a fine instalment in the Call of Duty franchise. Continuing the trend of cybernetic warfare which started with Advanced Warfare, Black Ops III takes it further.
Multiplayer is a blast. Movement is fluid and of very high speed. If you are not used to the fast-paced shooters of the past, it's going to take you some time to get used to Black Ops III. Wallrunning, matling, sliding, you name it. Weapons are varied but a little locked down. You can only unlock certain weapons via the black market which can be a put off for some. Specialists are varied and each one has their own unique style of play. While very fun, can be unbalanced at times. Much to my frustration. Customisation is great too with paint jobs allowing you to decorate your firearms to your heart's content. Though unfortunately, it isn't quite a way to create your own custom camos. Camos and paintjobs are not the same thing here. Furthermore, the paintjobs only allow you to decorate a portion of the gun, not the entire gun. Though to be fair, the paint jobs are quite prominent in first-person view despite the small portion which you are allowed to decorate.
Now for the Singleplayer campaign. I would say the story was a little more convoluted than what I would be comfortable with. As I progressed in the story, I started to lose track as to what is really happening and things just only got more confusing from there. There's just too many "mindblows" going on in the game for me to catch up with. The characters seem less than favorable too. I didn't see myself liking any particular character in story and the linear gameplay limits the player's choice quite a bit which is a stark difference from Black Ops II where the player's choices do have a pretty big effect in the story's progression. Enemies are varied and combat can be fun at times. Although I do feel that the storyline could have been less confusing and perhaps more open toward the player's choices because, the story's progression isn't that much different from sci-fi shooters years ago. Though I did like the co-op campaign which I think is a great addition as it makes playing through the campaign, even after completion solo, very fun with a friend or even a group of friends.
In conclusion, Black Ops III is quite a decent shooter in an aged genre capable of providing many hours of fun in multiplayer and also the co-op singleplayer. The Black Ops series has become one of my favorites and I would recommend it to those looking for a sci-fi shooter. Though I would recommend playing it with a friend for maximum fun.

I reviewed this game more than a year ago and since then it has been updated a ton. Firstly, there is now a "firing range" map to test helicopters which is just awesome. Also, the servers are alot more active and are continuinig to grow. Even if you can't find a server, now you can play single player missions with procedurally generated taks solo or with friends for a total of four players (I think).
In addition to game changes, there is now new maps such as the Afghanistan, Khost Province and Balkans, Kosovo. Creating squadrons is now improved and cosmetics and ranking have been implemented. Cosmetics include; helmets, stickers, medals and ribbons. As well as trading cards for badges.
From what I know there is still no interactive in-game tutorial, however I am sure this will be implemented by the time it is out of early access and you can use the test map to practice anyway.
In conclusion, I believe that this game has come along way since first appearing on Steam and ,for an early access game, it has a lot of content. The developers are very active and should have your full support. I would fully recommend that you buy this game (£11 is pretty good, might go up when it comes out of early access) and if you dislike it, just get a refund! This game will definitely appeal to people interested in helicopter aviation and/or historic wars like Vietnam but everyone should try it. At current I want to give this game at 10/10, but I will give it a 9/10 because they need to try and advertise the game more so that the servers are more active. I fully support this game and it's developers, thanks for reading.

Cannot recommend this game yet. There are not enough people playing it, i counted 1 server in the US with 14 people on and 1 server in EU with 4 people on.
Yep thats right, 1 server for the entire EU continent with only 4 people in total playing, the US server was laggy and randomly closed after 10 minutes of playtime (host probably left the game, more on that later).
The gfx and sfx are quite poor too, there are only 3 maps, games can take forever, and that is before we even start with the controls. They are terrible. Nothing feels fluid and it doesnt feel like any helicopter i have ever flown in any game, ever, it just feels clunky and weird. Real helicopters do not have a forward or reverse control, to go forward you tilt the nose down, to slow or reverse you tilt the nose up. Simple. So why do we have an accelerator and a brake in this game? It doesnt make sense.
The gameplay (when i finally found a server with enough people for a match) feels boring, the combat is seriously lacking and for me it just doesnt feel fun at all. You can clearly see people being killed frequently, but when you look at the scoreboard, you realise that the AI gets 95% of the kills in this game. Usually the seriously OP AA missiles. Kinda defeats the object of a multiplayer team game doesnt it?
Did i mention all the servers are run by the players? There are no dedicated servers at all, meaning the players have to create the games, which in return means any game you manage to join can close down at any time. Neither is there any team balance. It seems to be normal to be in 6v3 or 7v3 matches. This, and never knowing if you are even going to get to finish a match let alone win, becomes old very quickly.
Then there is the hit detection, which is quite broken. You can shoot at players and can clearly see the impact of the munitions, but nothing happens. Then the sound will disappear for no reason...
Requested a refund, will check back later this year and see if anything has changed and improved. I feel there is quite a lot of work to do yet.
Edit: I keep hearing how there are loads of people playing this game with multiple full servers and i am just talking nonsense, but here are the facts.
The peak player count yesterday was 38, that is over the EU, US and Asia servers combined, and the player numbers have been steadily dropping since the games release which is worrying.
It might be a decent game in the future, but for me at the moment, it is just a little bit too early access yet. Keep watching youtube videos, keep up to date with updates, and more importantly track the playercount.
If you have money to spend and really want to support the development, then by all means go ahead and buy it, but if you have a limited budget to buy a game i would suggest you buy something else.

What to say about Jazzpunk? It's a blast in every way possible.
Ok, the world is limited and the graphics are basic. Who cares? The personality and originality of this game surpasses any other. Set during the Cold War, it's a mockery of conspiracy and the fear of new technology that abounded in that era.
You enter each level by taking pills, then you have to solve the puzzles using the craziest interactions possible to discover who the bad guy is. There is plenty to explore in each level that doesn't have to do with the main story.
By the way, this game predicted ebola.
Fun includes: Zapping pigeons, killing pizza, turning on the fire and ice alarms, playing WeddingQuake, putting as much makeup on as you want, catching a robotic pig, racing gravy dishes, killing someone in a pillowfight, and getting eaten by a crocodile  (or is it an alligator?)
Short and sweet. You'll be it in an hour or two but it's an interesting experience.

Caves of Qud can be intimidating to try to engage with. It is unabashedly esoteric, with countless stats and it's quasi-ASCII aesthetics. The world is one of the strangest you will ever encounter, with strange creatures and even stranger humans. The worl is massive, especially for a a permadeath game, with countless screens to walk through to your destinations, and potentially infinite caverns to descend with all kinds of hellish adversaries to fight. It's also blisteringly hard. Death can come in an instant. You might spend hours with a character only to stumble upon an aggressive and impossibly strong enemy and get destroyed instantly. In short, Caves of Qud is a scary game in these ways.
But once you get past that hard exterior, Caves of Qud is an immensely addicting and engrossing game. There are so many ways to build your character, so many directions to explore, and so many ways to die. For those like myself who have never touched a 'true' rogue-like before, Caves of Qud might be that first game that let's into it's dank & deep corridors and drives you up the wall. You might need to read a beginner's guide, and you might need to keep a wiki open, but the sheer depth and beauty of Qud is something that doesn't come very often, and is more than worth your attention. Look past it's complexity and into the nightmare that lies dorman within, simply waiting for you to sink your teeth into it's flesh.

GAMEPLAY:
The platforming is precise and you can tell exactly where you'll end up. This calls for some amazingly designed and frustratingly hard levels, such as level 5.4, the second level with James. Jumping never feels impossible to do, and the different jump heights are ingrained into your mind such that you can tell from a glance "Can Thomas make this jump?" The different characters' abilities are excellently integrated into the level design, and you get a chance to get used to them before they're added into the usual gang. The spikes and water are simple, but add a genuine challenge that makes you legitimately tense, especially when things start moving.
All of the characters that I've played upto this point (Thomas-James) have had unique abilities that are very easy to understand. No complicated "sometimes this, sometimes that", if you can't solve the puzzle it's completely your fault; and The way Thomas and James interact is really cool, with them both being able to essentially float in midair. Gameplay is all-around phenomenal.
STORY:
This is where Thomas Was Alone really fell flat. The personalities of the characters seemed forced and unnecessary, being only there to richen the storyline. After the first few levels of beating the dead horse of a new character's traits, they were never brought up again, a good example of which being Claire being a superhero. The love between Laura and Chris was completely redundant as well. I do like that there's a quote from one of the programmers involved with these AI's, especially talking about it in the past tense as a sort of clever foreshadowing, but it doesn't fix the ultimately pointless story.
ART & AUDIO:
The art is basic and effective. Black squares used for platforming are perfectly fine, and I feel like the game would lose alot of its charm if it changed it to something more complicated or changed the color. I really like the look of the water, and some of the shapes' jump animations are really nice. The sound effects are good, not perfect, but I do like the bitcrunched landing sound. The soundtrack is absolutely incredible, one of the best I've ever heard. It fits the mood of the level, and it's just a great thing to listen to. Usually I watch YouTube videos while playing games, but the soundtrack is just too excellent in Thomas Was Alone.
OVERALL:
Thomas Was Alone is a great platformer, one that doesn't need complicated art to envelop a player. The soundtrack is one of my favorites, but the story is lacking.
