If there is only one thing you get out of this review, it is that this game is a complete rip-off for $60. The sad thing is that this game could have been such a success and such an excellent game; but unfortunately, Ubisoft screwed it up. When you first play the game, it is very fun and entertaining. The graphics are great, has an interesting combat system, lots of customization, and so on. However, after a week or so of playing you will start to notice that this game has more issues than your crazy ex-girlfriend. What are these issues you ask? Well, lets list them:
1). The characters, combat system, and general gameplay is horribly bugged and broken. The combat system, although an excellent concept and is fun when it works or is not abused, was implemented terribly by ubisoft. Again, the sad thing is, if done properly, this game could have been a gem. The Combat system is bugged and things such as blocking does not work half the time. It is too common for strikes not to register as well. Your characters "unblockable" attacks are able to be blocked by those who are able to abuse the bugs while other characters normal attacks seem to be unblockable while they are being spammed. It is bugs like this that make the game extremely frustrating.
2). Another major issue is that the characters are horribly unbalanced. Mix Over-Powered characters with a buggy combat system and you now have a game that is based on who can abuse their characters exploits and general exploits of the game most. Many characters have combos that are virtually unblockable, and can be spammed to eternity. The only real way to combat this is to learn the exploits of your character and abuse them. In essence you have to fight BS with BS and unfortunately, some characters have more BS than others.
3). The match-making system in this game is atrocious. Honsetly, whoever designed For Honor's match making needs to be publicly executed. When you get into a match there is a 50% chance you are going to be thrown into a game already in progress and typically it is just a massacre. If you happen to get into a new game, there is high probability that you will get kicked from the game for some stupid "error" or "anti-cheat error". While playing a match, the game is constantly being paused to (which always seems to happen in a duel that you are winning). These server issues are extremely obnoxious. Also, match-making balancing is virtually non-existent. It is rare that you get into a game that the 2 teams are evenly balanced. There always seems to be a stacked team.
4). Revenge: A mode your character can enter in when you take enough damage and/or block enough attacks. Revenge gives you a health boost, damage boost, and defense boost. This is complete BS. It is very aggravating when you get your oppenent down to a sliver of health and then all of a sudden they go into revenge mode and seem to go into a PCP induced rage giving a huge health boost, and doubles their damage and defense. There is virtually nothing you can do about it. Worst of all, it is stackable. It also seems like with some characters if you so even look in their general direction they get this mode.
5). If you are wondering about the solo campaign, here is a quick overview. It is entertaining and graphic (which is very nice) however, the story really makes no sense, and is VERY corny. Also, you can literally be disconnected from a solo campaign game for server issues (seriously)?
6) Want to know what should never be in a $60+ game? MICROTRANSACTIONS. You pay $60 for a game and the first thing that comes up when you start the game is a sales pitch for you to buy in-game currency or a ridiculous "season pass" which costs $30 or $40. The season pass allows you to play brand new characters (which are absurdly OP) and will also allow you to skip the "grind" of leveling up characters and gaining new equipment. Paying an intial $60 and buying a $30 season pass and/or other microtransactions puts you close to $100 in the hole for a broken game. It's nothing short of a scam.
7). The worst problem this game has is the refusal of Ubisoft to fix these obvious issues with their game. These issues have been around since the game first released and they have yet to fix them as we are approaching a year since its release. With all these issues that this game has, you would think that they would work to fix them. Instead, they would rather create new characters that are absurdly OP that you can only gain access to after purchasing a $30 season pass. Funny how that works huh? Create a few new Obviously OP characters to entice you to spend more money in the store, and if you don't buy this pass to have access to these characters, you are at a major disadvantage. This is BS.
I wish I could recommend this game, but unfortunately it is not nearly worth the $60 price tag. It's not even worth half that price in its broken state. If they have not fixed these issues as of yet, then I doubt that they will ever fix them in the future.
Do yourselves a favor and spend your hard earned money elsewhere.

For Honor is a game that has a lot of potential to be good, but unfortunately does not come nearly close to meeting the price of $60. The game has a cool idea to it with a unique combat system that if built properly could be really fun. Unfortunately though, there are multiple problems in this game that the developers have completely neglected to fix:
1. The biggest problem with this game is the obvious flaws there are in the combat system. Multiple characters have moves that are essentially unblockable. Once they catch you in that move, they can just keep mashing it over and over without you having any way of protecting yourself. Everyone who plays is now aware of this, so everyone does it to try to get the most kills. The melee system will also not register blocks at times, making the system all the more unfair.
2. The second huge problem with this game is the over powered characters. Most of the characters that are overpowered are purchased using the season pass, which is an additional $40 to the already $60 game, in order to get over powered characters. These characters are not only able to abuse the melee system easier, but they are just all and all over powered. The developers could fix the problems with the combat system, but instead they make more OP characters so people will be forced to spend $40 more to get them.
3. The "revenge" system. When a character blocks enough shots (supposedly), they can activate something called revenge which gives the player more health in the fight. However, players have found a way in which to get revenge after they have blocked maybe one shot. It is ridiculous because all some players have to do it block a shot or two and they get a huge health boost, making it nearly impossible to beat them.
4. The price of this game. While this game can be fun at times especially if playing with friends, its not even close to worth the $60 price tag. This game has many flaws that ruin the gameplay and make it very infuriating at times to play it. If you could get this game on sales for $20 I would say to give it a try, but do not spend $60 because you will regret it.

Empire TV Tycoon is an unashamed homage to M.A.D. TV. It plays very similarly with some update to the gameplay and adds some depth to the strategy of planning your tv schedule. Gone is the love story that was the main drive of the 90s game and a pure "best tv in the building" goal is in play.
Real movies are present and part of your potential library, with different genres in place to be juggled as you try to appease different audiences in a push to have the highest audience in each of the 1 hour slots. Different workers add a bit of flavour in the way of bonuses or extra insight into the day and you will have to decide which ones to get based on your strategy, as limited space is available. There are also daily quests and prizes to be won for best in-house productions, which adds diversity to the game without diverting you from the ultimate goal.
The main drawback of the game is that, at least in normal difficulty, once you start pushing ahead consistently it is very difficult for the AI to catch up with you. A snowball effect happens when you start building up your bank account and being able to afford the better programmes. The game rarely, if at all, throws you a curveball, so you can easily rinse and repeat the formula every day until you get to the ultimate goal of 600 audience points. It would be nice to see some random events affecting your plans somehow - banned genres or some limiting factor on your hability to plan your tv listing, for instance.
All in all it's a very solid homage to M.A.D. TV which will easily appeal to old fans and scratch that itch - it surely scratched mine - but newcomers to the game might struggle to enjoy it due to the potential repetitiveness of the game.

"Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare" is a mild horror game wich is fun, has acceptable graphics (considering that it is from 2001) and a nice story.
It has been quite entertaining to play through this title, especially because of its good level design and interesting characters. The graphics are still OK, even by today's standards. Basically, it uses the same mechanics as can be found in the original "Resident Evil", that is, you have pre-rendered backgrounds with animated 3D characters and items in the game world. If you want to play it on Windows 10 and want to have a higher resolution, just check the info on the Steam community. I think it will not work on newer OS if you do not fiddle a bit with it and use the fixes provided in the forum here. The setting is very atmospheric and eerie, and the rather nice-looking lighting effects add to this impression.
In general, both the effects and music are good. Sometimes the disturbing music and some creature sounds are even really terrifying which is of course a good thing in a horror game.
The controls are also good, except for some glitches when auto-aiming. I think the difficulty is medium. It would have been nice if there was an option to change it for those who would like to have more challenge.
Characters and voiceover is also quite decent, only some of the male character's one liners and comments are a bit dull. Some might even like this as it makes the character more unique. You can also choose between the male and the female character. I have only played the man's storyline, but I think there are quite some differences when you choose the woman at the beginning.
The only two real flaws to this game were occassional minor glitches with some enemies or other objects and that there are sometimes the notorious invisible walls or obstacles. So, when you run near the walls you hit an invisible boundary, even though your character is not actually touching any physical object.
All in all, I would give this title a 75 % rating.

Jazzpunk is a dubiously entertaining mishmash of a game.
Chances are, you've heard of this from a youtuber(s) playing it and are thinking of picking it up to try it out. No doubt, the game is pretty odd experience, and from what you've seen it seems like one you cant miss out on. Jazzpunk sports a very cartoon like presentation, which is welcoming with its plot (which is a satire on classic spy movies like james bond). That said, the plot doesn't even really matter, as the main point of the game was to showcase many ludicrous out of place jokes through minigames and tasks you complete. Most of these minigames aren't particularly fun and serve either as punchlines or bizzare humor on their own.(wedding quake was a blast though)  The 3 levels you play in have some explorable areas and characters that you can interact with, but they have very limited responses and are pretty much just one time gags. Controls feel a bit floaty, but I honestly cant complain about that in a game with a length like this one, which leads to another large flaw: Playing and completing the actual game can be as short as 15 MINUTES. Jazzpunk has a shockingly minuscule amount of content for its price, and I felt myself regretting my purchase as the credits rolled in. If a youtube video inspired you to get this game, chances are that video has shown most of what you've already wanted to see in the game. Unless you want to watch the same scripted jokes played out again, its not worth your time or your money.
Pros
-Gives the player freedom in the environment (no forced actions unless to progress the level)
-Is actually quite immersive in a surreal sort of way and lots of things to interact with
-Lots of jokes
-Lots of references
Cons
-Extremely short
-Exploration is essentially just finding more jokes
-The game can potentially be very unfunny if it's humor isnt your type
-The "Game" for the most part is not very entertaining as a game
-no real reason to replay at all
Conclusion:
Unless you want a very short interactive game that may or may not be funny to you, I would not reccomend buying this except if it is on sale for more than 50% of its price. Otherwise, there are plenty more options with a better content to cost ratio than jazzpunk.

I love this game but I thought my review could be more helpful to prevent people from buying the game because they do not realize what kind of game it is. Therefore, I took the time to dispel a few things that people might not realize about the game. I can not say it enough that I absolutely love the game but I want to at first go through some things that I notice get negative reviews and explain them.
This game has old school ASCII art like the nethack game except they use custom tiles and not all ASCII art from what I can tell. If you like something with high quality graphics then this game might be confusing or difficult. I am not saying you will not like it but you should beware. To me the graphics are high quality but they are just not 3D or dense. It requires some imagination to sort of realize a more comprehensive environment. This is expected from this type of game and you can tell by looking at the videos and screenshots; however, beware if your not sure. Steam offers a refund but make sure you stop playing before two hours.
The user interface is actually really easy but at first it will be really hard if you have never played any games like this before. It is all keyboard commands; however, its not too terribly difficult to learn. But, if your not into using the keyboard and learning the commands then its likely going to not be fun. It does have an experimental interface that you can use a mouse on from what I have seen but I never play with it because the keyboard works great for doing everything with minimal movement on my part.
The game is hard but it is not hard like Dark Souls; however, by default, just like other rouge games it has permadeath by default. However, you can turn the permadeath off in options. The key to this game is to farm a while at the beginning at least. You need to gain a few levels. Also, use the L key to look around at NPCs to determine if they are hostile and how powerful they are. Without using the L key you are going to end up walking blind into battles that you can not win. Even if you use the best tactics and have tons of experience you will still eventually die.
It is an RPG but its really a rouge game which means it does not play like a normal RPG where you can load a previous save when you die unless you disable permadeath.  It has all the RPG features but the game's super genre is rouge which is where the permadeath and randomized play through comes from. It is also the reasoning for a significant amount of randomness.
The randomness can make you lose to something that is lower leveled then you if you are already in a weak condition or state; however, being prepared if the key. You have to be really cautious in this game. If you like a fast paced hack and slash game then be careful. This game can be fast paced but its might not be the style of fast paced you like because of the randomness sometimes. You can see some powerful enemies in the beginning area so you have to be prepared by gaining levels and taking it easy.
It is also very open world - to the point where some players can feel lost or aimless. It does have quests but only a few at the beginning since you have to find the others, therefore, sometimes your going to be exploring just to explore and see what is out there. It is also a fairly big world and a large part of the experience is down in the underground areas. These appear as stairs going down.
Some of the books (not sure how many) are randomized and many of the things about the game can be that way too. It can make you feel like there is no story to the game. There is a story but its in the quest line and from some of the static things in the game. The random books and things are just kind of interesting because they make you try to figure out if its something important. If you are not proficient in English then you might find the game a challenge.
I have experienced one bug in my ten hours of play. The game locked up and I guess it did not autosave before I had gained a level and one of my mutations stabilized, therefore, I lost my four arms I had gained. My point being is that there are likely a few bugs and they could cause you to lose your game and progress. Its not as terrible as others games since it is a rouge type game and you will eventually die but be prepared for a few bugs at least. I would generally say the game is almost bug free from my experience but that also comes with early access. Its essentially an almost finished game but just beware.

One of the craziest games I have ever played. A real rouge-like adventure. You can play with four arms, contract fungal spore infections that cause you all sorts of misery and do damage at the same time, get all sorts of crazy abilities I have never seen in a game before, and its all fairly randomized so no play through is the same.
** Novel mechanic: Analgesia - No hitpoint numbers! Only general state! **
There are a lot of games that claim to be random and this one does have static places and events. Its a hard game so you will die a lot and believe me each play through is different. That is something I have never experienced with any other game. It has permadeath enabled - BUT its actually fun. It is also a game where skill and experience helps you to last longer and get further. It has randomness but its not overwhelming or crazy.
Want to gain a mutation to release corrosive gas that eats through walls, have precognition to travel backwards in time to fix a mistake you made before you die, or play with amnesia? This game amazingly brings some of the most novel game mechanics I have ever seen.
I guess the developer was able to spend more time with actual game mechanics and content instead of graphics and it turned out to be a great game.
I recommend playing the weekly and daily challenges. You get a interesting build and you can play it at least a few times before it changes. Also, you get ranked on how high of a score you got. Where the score is computed from various things such as turns survived, experience gained, complexity of items in inventory, and all sorts of things. It is interesting playing a new build and trying to see how well you can place on the leaderboard for the weekly and daily challenge.
This is also one of those games that is cheap to buy and gives you lots of hours of play here and there when you get board. Its not too demanding on the computer either so even a junk box can run it.

A very curious and interesting world set in an old-school rogue-like ascii-esc aesthetic. Based within a post-apocalyptic world of a world that was once thriving from a golden era with unimaginable tech, now has both fallen to rubble and has crept back into life. This world has a wonderful and colourful world to explore, with new things to explore with every run.
Alongside the intriguing backstory surrounding the game, there is of course the gameplay. The game plays like you would expect most old-school rogue-likes to play. The mechanics are somewhat complex and you might have a tough time figuring them out at first, especially because there is a lot of different things you can do. While this is a downside that should be corrected, it can be lived with because it gives you increased capabilities once the controls are learned, with ease of access.
The AIs are more intelligent and diverse than in most games, to the point that the "mobs" will attack each other if they were already in a fight or per chance hate each other more than they hate you. There are civilizations and factions of all kinds of creatures that you can either befriend or attack. This is a refreshing change of pace from any other game I have played recently, and one reason I always return.
Overall, this is a great game for anyone that likes a more complex or in-depth rogue-like (if you have liked games such as: Brogue, Don't Starve, etc). The game is great and there is just so much to be done or that you can do. As great as the game is, I do have a few reservations; I feel they should work on the UI to make it easier for people to start off the game, even though it is playable as current. Also I feel there should be a better way to make a keep or home or some place of residence. Most times I end my runs because I feel I'm continueing on hoping to get somewhere, only to realise that place doesn't exist (end game). Regardless, this is a great game, give it a try. Well Worth.

First of all, I have to say that this is the first time I play a game of the Neptunia series. I always heard great many things about this franchise,
, but also for its rather interesting setting that tends to appeal to gamers and the huge amount of customization and turn-based combat that these games tend to provide and so, because of that, I decided I’d give this one a chance. So far, for someone who had never played a game of this series before, I must say that I’m really enjoying the universe so far and I plan to play the other games as well.
takes place in the world of
, a place where games are released at an unrelenting pace, which is also divided into four different nations, each with its own rulling goddess, or CPU - Console Patron Unit. These nations are constantly at war with each other, seeking to expand their control and convert the faith of the citizens into power in the form of shares.
Thanks to the evil plot of a certain mysterious character, a chain of unfortunate events starts to unfold, which results in the breakdown of the Sharicite, the physical representation of the peoples shares and the CPUs power. This forces the four goddesses to unite themselves in order to save the world of Gamarket. While I assume that this will feel like a very generic storyline to some people, I like it and find it rather interesting and each of the characters is unique and has its own personality.
I think I wouldn’t be mistaken if I said that the game is split 50/50 by two very different genres. It is a
, such as party turn-based combat.
The
is pretty much just dialogue, which is voice acted for the most part. You’ll spend a lot of time interacting with the main protagonist, Noire, the CPU who presides over Lastation, one of the regions of Gamarket. Visually I really like the art design, but I understand some people will find it abhorrent, but those people will most likely not even read this, so yeah. That said, some of the characters are pretty much half naked, and even though I have no problem with that, I’m sure some people won’t find it appealing. The conversations are also full of suggestive themes, puns and sexual jokes.
Once you unlock the Lastation city screen, you’ll be able to do tons of stuff here including, selling, buying and crafting items, you can also talk to various different characters, take on missions or go and talk to Noire on her room. On Noire’s room, there is also some sort of dating/visual novel aspect in the form of customizing her room and answering to requests of the citizens with her, which will eventually unlock some extra scenes. Still, if you don’t want any of that you can completely ignore it. If you go to your Mission HQ, you can play new missions and simulations. Simulations consist on replaying old missions to get more rewards. You can also choose if you want to go straight for the main story missions or take on some side missions which, despite not providing any sort of story, they still give you some nice rewards.
As for the
, it comes in different ways such as customizing your characters with many different weapons and pieces of equipment and loot that you get either by killing enemies or completing missions. The combat is presented in a chibi art style, which contrasts with the visual design of the rest of the game and I find it be rather lovely. Combat itself is turn-based, which means that in each turn your characters can move and attack once, and movement is grid based. Still, you can move before or after performing an offensive action. When choosing an enemy to attack, you’ll be able to see how much damage you’ll do and its accuracy, as well as the enemy’s counter rate and expected damage. By killing enemies you’ll get loot and experience points which will allow you to level up your characters. Combat also rewards you for placing units next to each other when using special abilities, by improving the relationship between the two characters and granting you points to use more powerful skills.
Initially you’ll only control one character, the main protagonist - Noire (Black Heart), but soon enough more will join your cause. Even though I enjoy a lot games with turn-based combat, I do think that this is one of the weakest points of the game, albeit still a good one. Combat can get somewhat repetitive, especially if you plan on playing every single mission and simulation more than once. Some of the levels in which you fight offer some variety such as traps like electrified fences and floor plates, or the addition of height/verticality.
Hyperdevotion Noire lets you experience a visually appealing, charming and funny story that takes place in a
. It has a pretty solid combat system that offers some replay value with different combinations and because of that, I recommend this game to both fans of visual novels and SRPGs. Needless to say that it this is must check for fans of the Neptunia series.

Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart takes the series familiar CPUs in a new direction once again, this time taking the series into the turn-based, tactical role-playing strategy realm.
Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart sets itself apart from the previous Hyperdimention Neptunia games available on Steam in several ways. The number one way is the game is now more about tactics and strategy than it previously had been. Using the terrain to your advantage is one of the strategy elements. Each weapon type in the game has its own hit box. For example, spears can hit two squares away but can’t hit a higher or lower elevation. On the other hand, swords are limited to one square away but can hit one level above or below.  A hit from the side or the back will do more damage than hitting a character from the front and also reduces their chance to counter attack. You need to plan your moves out carefully as all characters have a limited amount of mobility. For instance, you cannot walk through an enemy or go over a wall with a higher level than your jump score will allow you to scale. This means you can easily get yourself trapped in a corner if you don’t plan your route carefully. In addition to having to figure out where you want to end up once you make your single move for that turn, you need to pay attention to the route your character plans to take to get there. Your characters are a bit like Lemmings that will blindly fling themselves over ledges or walk into traps if you tell them to. Changing the direction your character is facing allows you to adjust their route to help avoid those situations. Just because you dodged a trap doesn’t mean it won’t get you though. If you stop next to a trap, an enemy will often use its knockback attack to try to push you into the trap setting it off.  As you can see, there is a lot of planning, strategy and tactics involved in this game but there is even more than that to consider.
Each character in the game has its own abilities. Using these abilities, regardless of the intended target, will cause any characters that are one square away from the user to boost that ability’s effect. This means that if you cluster five of your characters in a plus shape and have the one in the middle cast a buff or long range attack, the other four characters will “peck” the caster enhancing the effect and boosting their Lily Ranks in the process. The higher the Lily Rank, the more effective the boost will be. You may be thinking that a good strategy would be to cluster your units and let the enemy come to you. There is a drawback to that plan though; some abilities can hit multiple targets. Instead of hitting just one of your characters with their strong attack, it’s possible they could hit multiple or all of them. Now you can see the tactics in this game are quite complex and not to be taken lightly. There is one more thing to cover on the tactics side though.
Elements are introduced as a way to play a pseudo rock, paper, scissors game. One element is stronger against another element but in turn is weaker to yet another element. Some chests found in the levels can only be opened using an elementally infused normal attack (skills and abilities usually have no effect on objects). Having characters with each of the elements available will aid you in looting each of the levels effectively assuming the characters have the ability (jump score, etc.) to reach the chest before the rest of your crew either kills off the enemies, or the enemy you were saving alive dies to a counter attack.  There are still more tactical elements to this game, but I will leave those to you to discover.
Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart features a crafting system. As you kill various monsters and complete missions you will aquire drops. These drops allow you to fabricate various things you will need to survive. Better weapons and items can all be crafted. This is where the strategy comes into play. Each piece of equipment has different effects. Sometimes you must make a trade off. To increase your movement range, you may have to reduce your defense a smidge. For the most part, you only need to craft a new item once for it to then appear in the store. This means you don’t have to worry too much about tracking down something you don’t currently have enough of to make another of the same. Buying from the store has its advantages too. Whenever you make a purchase you get Sim Points. Consider them like customer loyalty points of sorts. You will use these points to upgrade Noire’s house. The various things you buy will be added to her home and you can talk to them to get tips or fun conversations. You can also craft and name your own games within the game. Games are an upgrade that allows you to pick and choose what perks you want based on the elements that went into making the game.
Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart isn’t set in Gameindustri like the Hyperdimention Neptunia series, it is set in Gamarket. The four CPU Goddesses are all vying for total control of Gamarket. The series, if you are completely unfamiliar with it, is a satire of the current game market. Each of the CPUs represents one of the major console brands. Noire of Laststation, who as the title suggests is the star of the game much to Neptune’s displeasure, tries to end the fighting by listening to a strangers suggestion. This leads all of the Shares (think of them as likes/upvotes/retweets) in the land to disappear leaving the CPUs powerless and Gamarket in a political power vacuum.  I won’t spoil the story by going further, but it is quite in-depth. Much like previous games in the series, the gameplay is bookended by long expositional scenes. These are often cute, humours and quite enjoyable. It can also be quite fun trying to figure out who the next General pays homage to. For example, one of them named Lid, is a Solid Snake reference. She likes hiding in cardboard boxes and using air ducts to move around.
The art style in this game might be a little off-putting to some at first, but eventually it grows on you even if you had doubts going in. The Anime style characters are now Chibi during game play and resume their usual Anime form when talking to each other between missions. Chibi means they have oversized heads and tiny bodies. The style actually suits the way the battlefield works, and I think that having normal characters would have likely looked a bit weird there. Being Chibi lets you see their face clearly so you know who it is you are controlling just by looking at them. If you are being off put by the Chibi art style and plan on skipping it for solely that reason, you are doing yourself a great disservice.
Overall, Hyperdevotion Noire: Goddess Black Heart is a great turn-based, tactical role-playing strategy game. It is reminiscent of Final Fantasy Tactics so if you enjoyed that take on the Final Fantasy series, you will more than likely enjoy this take on the Hyperdimention Neptunia series. Current fans will not be disappointed either!

Events
The randomly generated events, and the ability to create your own survivors adds a sense of actual connection to the story. You will feel pressured by the logical side of a decision, and the emotional side. Every event has multiple outcomes, good and bad. But each event will also rely on what you have, and how are you prepared.
Relationships
Each character will not like somebody else for one reason or another in the start of the game. This means over time they will start to fight with eachother, and possibly hurt one another. If you dont get it under control, this can mean everybody will start to get upset. But you can fix this with rumors! But be careful, each rumor has sideeffects if your not careful! I have had a group of people perfectly happy with one another, but after one misplaced rumor hated eachother. So be careful! Events, or certain actions may anger one another too.
Replayability
This game is randomized to your will. It can be completely random, or you can add in people/items/locations/jobs if you would like. This means every game will be diffrent, no two maps are the same! It is a game of pure chance to a extent. But you can win it everytime if you are smart about how you play.

Wow!  Cogmind isn't for everyone - read the full description, including the warnings and system requirements, and maybe watch some Let's Plays depending on your spoiler tolerance - but if it's for you it's
and well worth the purchase price.
Cogmind is deliberately crafted for immersion, from the audio feedback on every action and log message to the fully animated and highly customizable GUI.  In my experience, the interface polish doesn't get in my way; it unobtrusively wires the AI's low-level programming up to my intuitions for seamless use.  And it's very solid low-level programming too, automating calculations like "fastest path to this point while avoiding known traps" and "current chance of this enemy hitting me" while providing full and ready access to the absolute precision befitting a machine.  I quickly found myself comfortable inhabiting the little processing core that could, even when using parts that add on new senses entirely.  The atmosphere and immersion is
.
Roguelikes are
by default, and Cogmind is no exception; indeed, the default difficulty is the hardest.  At its simplest, turn down the difficulty, attach the highest-rated parts (each part has an overall rating visible as soon as you find it), and shoot up some robots - or just watch them go about their work, which usually isn't about you.  If you want a challenge beyond the default, multiple endings, an extended endgame, and conducts galore are available.  You can also go spoiler-free without having to write things down yourself; in-game galleries are provided for both found parts and found
(the lore is entirely optional) and are available at any time.  The parts gallery is especially valuable for considering specialized build options - overall part rating is only a starting point, as there are several factors to balance and many possible synergies for the various strategies available.
When I was reading about Cogmind, I saw an old comment made by a single person suggesting that the arrow keys movement scheme could handle diagonal movement by using the modifiers Shift for "up and" and Ctrl for "down and" on an arrow direction.  That's in the game now - the sole developer put it in in response to that one comment.  Indeed, the developer is frequently on the game's forums, subreddit, and Discord server, all of which have systems for spoiler avoidance should you so desire it.  (There are also regular gameplay streams by players of varying experience levels, but it's much harder to avoid spoilers in those.)  Personally I mostly use the Discord, which has conversations several times a day and readily welcomes new players.
If these appeal to you and the warnings don't put you off, you will probably enjoy being a Cogmind.

You can hardly be more minimalist than Thomas Was Alone, and yet those rectangles had a better character design and development than any other game out there. It is literally impossible to not grow attached to Thomas and his friend as they go on their quest for freedom.

The art is good and the puzzles are a reasonable difficulty, but the Frostrune takes itself far too seriously.  I found the mythos to be tiresome and the soundtrack annoying.  In particular, the immature protagonist's inner dialogue, as revealed innocently and unemotionally in text boxes, oddly contrasted with the heavy doom emanating from the ghosts, with their gravitas-laden pronouncements and quasi-religious chants.  The protagonist seems naively unaffected by the heavy atmosphere and thus disjoint from her context within the game.  That'd be fine if the ghosts could have lightened up a bit, but it was all Nordic gloom, all the time.  The game would have been better if the ghosts had almost all been mute, textually and aurally.
Mechanics-wise, the need to click to put away the inventory is annoying:  You can move forward with the inventory open, but backtracking requires closing it.  I'd have preferred a non-fullscreen mode, and once, trying to click through the startup screens, I selected a language I didn't know because a click in a blank area was sent to a screen that hadn't loaded.  These minor annoyances made me feel the game wasn't fully baked.
These criticisms aside, I do recommend the Frostrune, as the core point-and-click gameplay is satisfying, and it is possible to mute one's speakers.  The art is well-done and enjoyable to look at while playing.  Hopefully they can hire a better audio team for the next one.

Something that doesn't seem to be mentioned about this game: this is a horror story. You play a 13 year old Viking girl. Her father and his longship was sunk out from under her, then the settlement she washed ashore at has no living people and many signs of conflict. One of the first things you see is magical ice, the mark of the Norse gods most effective enemies.
If you are primarily interested in a game's mechanics, that's an area where this game may fail. It is designed in the style of current mobile games, with a minimal interface and simple menu. It doesn't even have an internal volume control, and it could use one. There are no save files, you simply continue. Once you get to the core gameplay it becomes fairly linear.
As an experience the game is amazing. It's also not for the faint of heart. You are dealing with dead bodies and ghosts throughout the game. The artwork is fantastic. The soundtrack is good. The language is all in Old Norse with the subtitles of your choice. The level of detail, both in period accuracy and little details like increasing the number of flies around the corpses, is incredible.
If you want a gorgeous, effective horror story to play through, I very highly recommend this.

This game is not perfect yet, but I feel it is worth playing so I'm throwing in a "recommended" review to counteract the  hate train. Also, I waited until it was on sale for half price, so I don't feel as salty as I would have if I dropped $60 on it at launch. But, since I have already bought virtual fun money for some stupid digital Steel, I'm sure Ubi will get the rest of their dough from me soon enough.
Pros: This game is gorgeous, and the combat system is polished and fun. However, there is defnitely a learning curve (morseso if you don't normally play fighting games), so prepare to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked across the battlefield (like I have). This game feels really hard at first, especially when you get cornered by a Centurion and have your stamina beaten out of you in 3 hits. It feels even harder when matchmaking can't find anybody near your level so you get placed with prestige 16 players who mop the ground with you. Even though, with practive I've started blocking more consistently (and actually getting a few parries in), so it doesn't feel as impossible now. And yes, you're still going to sometimes get matched with that one peacekeeper or Shinobi who goes 16 and 2, dunking on your team the whole time.
The biggest beef I have with this game is the P2P multiplayer. Peer to peer matchmaking is a terrible design choice and it screams "we're too cheap to pay for servers, so we'll let Billy host 8 players from his mom's 256 kbps DSL connection in the basement". This has killed other games that I really enjoyed (like Space Marine), and it's just as clunky and frustrating in this game. Someone ragequits? Wait while the host migrates and re-syncs everybody. However, Ubisoft got the hint after hearing the community's backlash (and seeing how much the number of active players plummeted). They are being more transparent now, they are listening to our demands (sorta), and they have said they will EVENTUALLY implement Dedicated Servers.
Based on what I've seen from the game so far, I'm going to put my faith that Ubisoft will eventually fix this and some of the other outstanding complaints from the community. I am a big fan of the melee combat that this game offers, so I will keep playing with the hopes that it keeps improving with time.

I've been looking for a modern version of Mad TV for a long time, so I was quite excited when I stumbled upon Empire TV Tycoon on Steam. I had a lot of fun with it, but there were also some frustrating moments which I will explain in a moment.
How do the game mechanics compare to Mad TV?
The similarities are immediately apparent when looking at the interface. You are a tiny person using an elevator to navigate through a high building which houses your offices, film studios, a movie library, an advertising agency and so on. There are two AI opponents with their own channels.
You are presented with a timetable for each day with 12 slots. In each slot you put a news or marketing clip first, then a film, then an ad. Films (or Shows) come in 1, 2 or three slots. You buy them at the library or produce them in your own studio. Producing your own stuff is a lot more simple than in Mad TV, therefore you can immediately start doing that and add some variety to your daily schedule with your own productions.
Advertisements require a certain amount of viewers and you have 2 or 3 days to air a certain amount of blocks to fulfill the contract and get paid, if you fail, you lose money.
Variety and the advertising system, however, are somewhat flawed in this game by design decisions that make sense at first glance but are implemented in weird ways.
First of all, there is the fame system. At the end of every in-game hour, fame points are distributed. The channel with the most viewers gets 3, the other two get 2 or 1, respectively. What do you do with fame points? You upgrade your movie library for access to better films (which means more viewers) and you buy sattelites to increase your possible viewership.
Since the distribution of fame points is based on absolute numbers, the first channel to receive the upgrades is almost guaranteed to get a lot more fame points, meaning he reaches the next level upgrade earlier, and so on. The result is that you absolutely have to rush towards your first 75 fame points because if the AI gets there with a large enough advantage you'll never catch up and may just as well restart the game. But the opposite is true as well, if you get there first, the game becomes easier and easier over time because you will simply always reach a higher numver of viewers. The movie library upgrades are automatically given to your AI opponents when you buy them, but it doesn't help them too much without the sattelite upgrades, in my experience.
The other annoying thing is how advertisements and viewers are handled. As an addition to the classical Mad TV system, you now have 1, 2 or 3 viewer groups attached to each timeslot. These are, as far as I can tell, randomized. In order to maximize your viewership, you need to air what they like. On the one hand, it's a good system because it adds a new layer of challenge to your daily planning. On the other hand, the randomized nature of it can be quite frustrating if you can't puzzle it together the right way.
These fixed viewer groups are also attached to advertisements. Some of those are general, but most are bound to one specific group, so there must be among the viewership when the clip airs or it fails. During my playtime it happened several times that I needed to air just one more block of an ad, but during the whole day the required audience wouldn't appear a single time, so I could do nothing and lost a big chunk of money.
Finally, in contrast to the fame point distribution, the required viewership for ads is percentage-based. Upgrading your sattelites will not make it easier to fulfill ad contracts. This is also a source of frustration because - I don't know if there is some mechanic at work that I don't understand - most ads offered to me required 80 - 130% of my viewership. It is possible to boost your viewership by a certain percentage with special marketing ads, but still, I don't know how it's possible to reliable reach such high numbers, especially with the weird audience type system in place.
I just rushed to the ad agency at the start of each day and bought the available ads with 40-70% requirements which fortunately give you more than enough money to breeze through the game after a while.
In conclusion, the biggest flaw of the game in my opinion is the randomized audience system. It prevents you from creating a "themed" channel because you have almost no way of influencing it. You have to layout your program based on your randomized audience for each day, which is fun in its own right, but if you want to realize your own vision of a sci-fi / horror channel or whatever, the game doesn't allow it. Every channel will always run just a wild mixture of everything.
What makes the game fun is the challenge of being better at organizing your weird TV station than your opponents and then stomping them into the ground with all your cash. It's great that mods allow for the inclusion of current movies and shows and also real actors which you can use for your own productions. Your scriptwriter will give you a charming description of whatever script he wrote for you, those are usually completely insane, so why not cast Nicolas Cage and Paris Hilton for your horror flick?
Empire TV Tycoon is a solid 7/10 and considering the low price you should definitely support the developer. Maybe they'll make a sequel that's even better.

this wont be my longest review as to put it bluntly there inst really much in the game itself to review but okay here goes ...  so i was a big fan of the first Crysis game, was a ridiculously stunning piece of design with a solid frame work of story, mechanics and gameplay .. a model shooter for its time despite being generations ahead of other shooters of the day. saying this i was always going to be skeptical of a sequel as sequels are usually a bit rubbish. and to a degree this game both exceeded my expectations and at the same time failed to meet them. weird i know but it managed it.
the game is  set years after the Lingshan island incident that saw the deaths of all but two members of Raptor team (Prophet and Psycho) new york is in the grip of a deadly virus infecting its citizens and the CELL corporation has stepped in to take control of the mess that has ensued. you take a step away from raptor squad in this game and play as a strong but silent (and i mean literally silent) marine named Alcatraz. you are sent on a recon mission to rescue a scientist when your submarine is hit by the CEPH aliens and all of your team is wiped out and you are left floating in the river until you are saved by prophet. prophet then places you into the suit to save your life and (SPOILERS) .. in short you must then progress the game as Alcatraz trying to save New York from the grips of the CEPH and CELL alike. now i like the story for this game i think its well written and well paced for a shooter .. its not the most imaginative story in the world but it appeals to me.
the game itself is your standard shooter so don't expect much in terms of adventurous mechanics or gameplay. mechanics are to be expected as pretty solid .. you run jump, sprint,slide and ledge grab same as the last game with solid steel shooting mechanics (you shoot the guys and they die nothing overly adventurous really) some new toys in terms of suit upgrades allowing you to swap out nodes to allow for different approaches in combat which i quite like. you can swap out weapons with various attachments to suit stealth and various other aspects and play styles and with a wide variety of weapons available you can get quite adventurous in how you want to play out the situation. the mechanics for the powers hold nothing new in this game so i wouldn't get  your hopes up about that part. the little bits of tat you can collect throughout the game as well can be a bit annoying to find as Crytek were very imaginative in the hiding places. the energy bar can seem a bit stupid in terms of longevity to start with but you get used to being a bit more tactical with it after the first attempt to Rambo a group of enemies winds up with Alcatraz having more holes in him that a block of Swiss cheese.
the graphics really are the main selling point of this game and they sell it very well. i played on the PC with a reasonably powerful machine and i like to think im quite demanding from my games but this game blew me away. the detail of the environment is not flawless but it is close to being so, the level of detail that Crytek have given this game takes it to a whole new level for the PC gamer especially on ultra settings. the Crytek engine allows for stunning visuals that make the world the player is experiencing all that more immersive. but excellent graphics do not make up for the shortfalls the game has in terms of the average story and the generic shooter gameplay
this is a game where i wish steam would have another recommendation button for i think its decent but not amazing, the story is good the gameplay is solid despite being a tad generic but the graphics do make up for this sin some way .. in the end i would recommend the game to fans of the series and FPS fans but if you are looking for a great sci-fi game with some depth then this inst the game for you.. this game is great ... but flawed ...

In a world of zombie apocalypse games that involve running around bashing zombies in the head with pointy objects or shooting them, Zafehouse: Diaries is a breath of fresh air. Well, not too fresh. Slightly festering and putrid, if I'm being honest. But, what do you expect from a zombie infested town?
I look at Zafehouse: Diaries as a cross between an RTS, in that you have a town to explore, the top down view of the map, the careful exploration; and an RPG in the careful balance you need to accomplish between your team members, the collecting gear, finding food and medication, and praying you don't get too badly injured. Injuries are bad. They severely compromise that character's ability to do tasks, and require proper medical attention and supplies to treat.
There are three modes of gameplay - Survival, escape by road, and escape by air. Each presents a very different type of game. Survival is the easy option. You start off solo, and have to survive for as long as possible, building your team as you go. My longest time is in the weeks. My shortest, in the minutes.
Escape by road is the 'middle difficulty'. You have a team of 5 characters, each with their own priorities, prejudices, likes and dislikes, and have to balance their happiness and health long enough for you to explore the town, find the car, and collect all the parts you need to get it working again. This is the type of game I have completed the most, and I can tell you that there are multiple endings, depending on how you do.
The final game type is the hardest. You have one week to assemble all of the clues and find a radio, and that will allow you to contact a helicopter for rescue. Take too long though, and you miss your opportunity. Move too quickly, and you risk your people being picked off one by one as they split up to search houses, shops, warehouses, factories, churches, schools, and so on.
The last thing I would like to mention is the Mods menu. Built into the game itself is the ability to create new characters to use, and new buildings for the town. Doing so, however, will disable achievements as this can be used to severely unbalance the game.
On the whole, if you are enjoy a good zombie apocalypse, but are looking for something a little different, then this could be the game for you.

Zafehouse Diaries is a zombie survival horror genre type of game that tries hard to please the audience but fails due to certain limitations and unbalanced issues. The game is text based and makes usage of a diary used to read all the events happening every hour, a clock used to advance the time and a map with the locations in game. The game itself seems quite pleasing at the first glance especially if you are a fan of survival games such as State of Decay and This War on Mine but unlike those titles, the game fails to deliver due to the random events that seem to be counter-productive most of the time.
The game has a couple of features that can be accessed from the very beginning, such as improving objects, scouting for zombies, making meals, barricading the building you are in, making traps as well as quite some other features. More of those features unlock depending on the location where you establish yourself. The game also has survivors which come different background, personalities, professions, prejudices and usually perks such as better cooks, better improving items, better at fighting zombies and so on. Through the game you also get random events such as getting extra survivors, people asking for food or raiders attacking your place. Those events are usually pretty limited and the game stalls after a while.
The graphics of the game are pretty average overall however the sound does redeem a game a little.
Unfortunately, the game tends to lack in quite some domains. For instance, the survivors you have never actually level which means that the game will always be hard and they will always be at risk of dying. Some might see it as a challenge but unfortunately the game has even more tedious issues which makes it downright frustrating sometimes. In a specific game I had a house fully equipped with traps and yet four zombies slipped by and killed my two survivors. This is but an example of the frustration you will be dealing with in the game. There is no balance so to speak and even with the best weapons and armors your survivors might die to just a couple of zombies. This scenario was tested on easy, therefore I cannot imagine what is required to survive on hard mode considering how unbalanced the game is right now.
Another big issue is the lack of support in the game. The last patch has been done on 22 October 2013, therefore the game is left by the developers so do not expect any fixes nor any new features or DLC. Overall, I would not recommend the game due to all the limitations and issues.

I've played over a 200 hours of this game (played on two accounts), I evangelize it to friends, family, and strangers alike, but Idk what to say in a review. Should I approach the review from the angle of "this game has the most active devs imaginable and new stuff is added every Friday with development streams on Twitch every Thursday”? Or "Holy f*cking sh*tballs, you can play a psychic turtle gunslinger who has four arms and is bros with Fungi and is not welcome in the holy places of Cats”? I mean the first option seems most appealing on paper, as it is the most measured and most rationally persuasive, but I know that it has usually been the *weird* reviews that get me to buy games.
So I’m going to do both.
In the last two months, a major feature arc was added to the game, The Water Ritual. Fresh drinkable water is scarce in Qud, so much so that the standard unit of currency in the game is about an ounce of water. To gift your life-preserving water to someone is a show of great respect and brotherhood, doing so is so culturally important in Qud that it happens in a form of ceremony that is acknowledged and respected by all of the 40+ factions of Qud. Commencing this ritual boosts your reputation with the faction whose leader you gifted the water, but it also decreases it with the enemies of that person. Each named NPC in Qud has a generated history and reputation with every faction in the game, which is different each time you play. This means, depending on who you encounter in a given game, you can make friends with even the most initially hostile of factions. 
Now lets talk crazy. You know how most games when they do something unbalanced that breaks the game, they usually nerf that power by making it less powerful? Caves of Mud had that problem with its Psychic class of mutant. So did the debs make the Psychics less powerful? No. They created an in-game multiverse and sent extra-dimensional enemy Psychics to hunt you down if your psychic power grew to such prominence that it threatened the stability of the universe. That was a nerf. Adding a multiverse was a nerf. They did that three weeks ago.
I have bought this game for friends and family just so I could be able to talk to them about it. I have offered to buy this game for complete strangers who were on the fence about it. If you aren’t already playing it, you owe it to yourself to give it a try. Don’t let early access tag fool you, this game has more polish and devotion poured into it than Chrome on the Towering Spindle that pierces the skies to the far east. Descend into the Caves of Qud, claim their secrets, tempt fate and survive.

A new favorite time-waster. The game's evocative prose, beautifully understated music, and simple, yet communicative sprite art do an excellent job of inspiring the imagination into weaving a real sense of intrepid wonderment... Plus, any game that, within it's mechanics, allows me to create a four-armed, four-legged barbaric mutant with a penchant for severing limbs, heads, and faces to be worn as trophies alike is a-ok by me.
As a player who had always held an interest in old-style, more traditional roguelikes, but always found them to be overwhelming at first glance, I feel Caves of Qud is an excellent place to start for those like me, looking to finally make that jump. Though a bit overwhelming at the start of my first game, a brief ten minutes spent pouring over the concise hints section helped to keep the game from feeling outright insurmountable, and I developed a decent understanding of the mechanics within an hour or so of play. CoQ does feature permadeath, and can suddenly spike in difficulty at times, but between the quick turnaround time on rolling up a new, interesting character, and the partial randomization of the world every new run, the game is designed to abide by the classic roguelike credo of "death is fun." Even after an untimely death well into one of my luckier, lengthier runs, I'll still often find myself itching to come back again and start a fresh adventure no more than a few hours after the fact, eager to try out some wild, ridiculous new combination of mutations, or hoping to stumble across a back-mounted set of mechanical arms not two minutes out from the starting village.

Excellent Roguelike with a great user experience aesthetic.  Robust keyboard and mouse controls, traditional Rogueish ASCII visual mode with more user friendly tiles for those of us who can't remember our squiggly lines anymore from the days of playing Rogue and Nethack.
What's refreshing is that this isn't yet another swords and sorcery adventure, and instead you're scrapping your way out of a robotics facility after gaining some bit of self control.  There's ton of lore to be found, and the developer is accessible, responsive, and yet not afraid to stick to his vision of what he wants the game to be.  Very respectable and part of why I jumped on this game though I'm super wary of any Early Access title nowadays.
This game is feature rich as-is and completely enjoyable in its current state.
If you're on the fence, I highly recommend jumping on YouTube for playthroughs.  For the developer just search for "Grid Sage Games" and "nuzcraft" is another source for narrated and informative gameplay.  On sale it was a no-brainer, but this is one of the few games I would pay full price too.
It does have a bit of a learning curve, though the exploration of how the world works is part of the fun.  Play it, then check elsewhere for resources.  There's a manual, gameplay examples, and some helpful fans too out there.
NOTES:  Read the warnings at the bottom of the Steam description (expand it).  The developer has been very transparent about certain unforgiving elements both in gameplay and system needs.  The game is wonderfully small at just under 50MB, but you do need a sizable display/monitor to play the game as intended.  It may not be a game for everyone (what game is?), but it's a very rewarding game if you give it a chance.

Cogmind is an easy game to pick up for a roguelike, it has high production quality with tileset graphics (and toggleable ASCII mode), mouse controls (and full keyboard controls too), sound effects and a well designed UI that makes good use of a roguelike style.
Cogmind is an extremely tactical roguelike where every combat encounter has to be started and dealt with caution or avoided completely. A badly thought out fight can turn out sour, leaving you scraping for resources while trying to avoid enemies.
Granted, bottlenecking is mostly the strongest strategy especially in early floors where enemies possess simple weapons incapable of piercing walls and don't have explosives. The reason why combat encounters are so dangerous is because:
You are Cogmind, the little robot that could...
..attach parts to itself, as well as detach them, making you one versatile and dashing metal box. There is no XP, no levels, only parts. And you WILL lose them. And you will replace them.
Parts can be obtained by scavenging them off other robots, which requires destroying them, or lying around the Complex 0b10 in caches. So combat is not all bad, you get some replacement parts back, but they can be damaged or destroyed in the fight, just like yours.
Once you get to know which kinds of robots use what parts you can start hunting for specific robots based on your needs.
You will have to combine both methods of part scavenging, as neither robots nor caches alone are a completely reliable way of obtaining optimal parts. There are also fabricators that can construct parts from schematics that can be obtained by hacking terminals. It's well possible to make specialized specs, but be always ready to change up to a plan B.
The two obvious ways to play are stealth and combat. Playing as a big tank that carries a bunch of weapons is very easy to start off with, but destroying a lot of enemies raises your alarm level high, which makes the central AI of the complex recognize you as a real threat and send harder and more enemies against you. This means you don't want to fight every patrol you come up against, not only will you be risking your valuable utility parts but making future floors even more difficult. You can pick what to fight by using some sensors to feel upcoming areas, don't load your utility slots with only combatitive parts.
Stealth is harder to learn how to play, you will have to pay a lot of attention to how the enemy AI behaves in different situations and come up with strategies to either go unseen or distract enemies. Speed and scanners are essential for spotting enemy patrols and you can then wait them out in a room, but that is boring, goot thing the game allows for more creative stealth strategies. One of my favorite "stealth" strategies is connecting hallways and rooms by carving tunnels using grenades or rockets to avoid going into hazardous areas. This does cause a lot of noise and has to be timed correctly, don't want a passing patrol come investigate the explosions.
There are many other aspects to Cogmind like the floors that grow different and more difficult in many ways as you make your escape from 0b10, branching side areas that lead to new story paths, terminals that can be hacked for various useful things, resource management in the form of energy/matter/heat systems and much more

I got lucky last Sunday and won Frostrune in a giveaway by IGN. I was eager to play the game as I had heard good things about it. I wasn't disappointed. The backgrounds are beautiful and the soundtrack, especially the song of the warriors is of the same high quality as the visuals and I spent some time just listening to them singing.
As I like Scandinavian languages I especially appreciated the narration in Old Norse (with subtitles). One can feel that the developers put a lot of passion and research in their project as is shown by the love to detail in the game e.g. the embroidery in the Town Hall or the rune tablets look authentic.
I took me about four hours to complete the game as I stubbornly wanted to avoid the hints. Alas, I'm too dumb and finally gave in and used the hint system in the last third of the game.
The Frostrune is the most memorable indie title I played in a long time. Even if you don't play point-and-click adventures you should make an exception. The black borders on top and bottom on a 16:9 display due to the image size of the backgrounds are the only things that I could do without.
I hope the game is a success and I'll definitely be on the lookout for other games by Grimnir Media.

-You like minimalistic colorful graphics and clear, well thought-out UI
-You can live with the fact that you probably won't discover all the game's secret hidden areas (my favorite part)
You should not buy this game if:

Having watched the trailers I thought it would be more of a narrated story, and it isn't. However, it is still very well anchored in the old norse religion, as we know it and its legends today. I went back and saw them again after I finished the game, and they made so much sense, and added to the story. I wish they were in the game, like some extra credits, in Norwegian/old norse, too. But regardless, the story that you uncover in the game is in itself very good and I really enjoyed playing it. I particularly love the spirit relm affiliations. Rocksmith 2014 is a brilliant product for those who want to learn to play guitar and have a lot of fun in the process. Not all of your favorite songs are available, but there are a good number of them and they keep adding more for a reasonable price of $3 per song. Learning songs by giving you a small percentage of the notes at first - in time with the music - and adding them little by little as you correctly play them is nothing short of amazing. There's nothing else like it. If a song starts to get to fast or busy for you then you turn on the Riff Repeater function which lets you take a short segment of the song (like the lead or bridge) and repeat it over and over until you learn it note for note.
I've been playing guitar by reading TAB books for 20 years so I have a huge library of books, but this "game" is far more effective because it's so fun to play along with the band that I want to play every day and that's the trick to getting better.
Note to the developers: Any chance of getting some songs by a few more guitar oriented rock bands like Led Zeppelin, AC/DC and Metallica? I'd buy them all. Thank you for creating a killer game!

As someone who loves PS1 horror games like Resident Evil,Silent Hill,Martian Gothic,Dino Crisis,Countdown Vampires and other I also have a special place in my heart for Alone in the Dark series . The New Nightmare is very spooky game with obscure plot,dark atmopshere and traditional horror-survival gameplay with fixed backgrounds .
You may need third party software to use some controlers properly . I was able to assign all buttons to a controler but LT,RT not supported on F310 so I had to utilize Start/Back . (which is fine but not optimal) Free/Look is very hard on controler so be prepared to use mouse for some puzzles and maybe enemies on low elevation . For the most part you do not need to aim at enemies as long as you shoot in general direction .
Some people can't get Part2 of this game to work which is what PS1 copies were known to do . I can only speak for myself and the game works fine for me on win7x64  . According to some folks using this game on Win 10 is a pain in the butt ( although I am not sure why people expect a game this old to work with abomination that is Win10 ) If there is a compatibility mode try that .
Very similar to Resident Evil 1 when it comes to controls and game format .Fixed Backgrounds,Tank controls,puzzles and reloading from inventory - classic .Some enemies are vulnarable to effects of Light so you can sometimes save bullets by using flashLight or turning on lights in room . Also some puzzles will utilize Light effects so keep that in mind .
Some enemies respawn infinitely so if you stack and looking for a puzzle solution you will eventually get hit .Navigating in this game is also a pain in the butt . There are hundreds of god damn doors ,eveything is dark and camera angles sometimes make it worse . I played for hours with no ammo because i just missed a shotgun in the shade :)
There are 2 playable characters which have some unique areas sorta like Resident Evil 2 had with Claire and Leon . One of the bosses even chases you around which reminds me RE3 Nemesis .
You can save the game at any point if you have a medalion ( No save room? I know right )
Among all horror games on PS1 The New Nightmare was the best looking horror game having superior visual effects,textures and 3D models. Sure it looks dated now but back then it was as good as it got .Probably the most important thing for a Horror game is great atmosphere which this game has in spades .In the dark surrounded by shadows you will meet few characters and they won't bring you comfort.
Walking through dark corridors not knowing what is ahead , what you need to do or if you have enough ammo to fight what is coming .The New Nightmare is truly immersive game that makes you feel alone in the worst place you can imagine . The hellish soundtrack is just the cherry on cake .
On a side note I love camera angles in this game that add to gloomy mood ( if you playing as detective watch out for camera angle from the window of the house it is ♥♥♥♥en cool )
. If you like PS1 horror games with tank controls you will feel right at home . This game is somewhat cryptic and can be pretty obscure with puzzles. Most of enviroments are very dark so it is hard to find items and navigate with respawning enemies . Intense settings,fun gameplay and beautiful backgrounds overall make up for the minor problems . A new favorite time-waster. The game's evocative prose, beautifully understated music, and simple, yet communicative sprite art do an excellent job of inspiring the imagination into weaving a real sense of intrepid wonderment... Plus, any game that, within it's mechanics, allows me to create a four-armed, four-legged barbaric mutant with a penchant for severing limbs, heads, and faces to be worn as trophies alike is a-ok by me.
As a player who had always held an interest in old-style, more traditional roguelikes, but always found them to be overwhelming at first glance, I feel Caves of Qud is an excellent place to start for those like me, looking to finally make that jump. Though a bit overwhelming at the start of my first game, a brief ten minutes spent pouring over the concise hints section helped to keep the game from feeling outright insurmountable, and I developed a decent understanding of the mechanics within an hour or so of play. CoQ does feature permadeath, and can suddenly spike in difficulty at times, but between the quick turnaround time on rolling up a new, interesting character, and the partial randomization of the world every new run, the game is designed to abide by the classic roguelike credo of "death is fun." Even after an untimely death well into one of my luckier, lengthier runs, I'll still often find myself itching to come back again and start a fresh adventure no more than a few hours after the fact, eager to try out some wild, ridiculous new combination of mutations, or hoping to stumble across a back-mounted set of mechanical arms not two minutes out from the starting village.

The writing is excellent.
Ultimately, it delivers on every aspect on what it wants to be. And I've been here with this game since day one and holy criminy comparing earlier updates to the current one now is just downright impressive.

I have no idea what to say about RESIDENT EVIL 6, really. Suppose I'll just ramble a bit.
tl;dr at the bottom
The gameplay is fairly solid and the action is exhilarating, for sure. The production values and graphics are impressive, and playing with a buddy in coop is a blast.
However, what really brings this game down for me is the ludicrous story, illogical character actions, and punishing length of the game.
Those sound like strange criticisms for a Resident Evil game, I know, but they truly transform this game into something that's not Resident Evil. The story is divided into four sections, with 3 of them following different sets of characters, and a final epilogue where everything is wrapped up neatly (that's not including the bonus add-on story mission). Though the action is always rising in pitch, it never truly felt like the story was moving along at the same pace; plot progression would be dragged back by long boss encounters and extensive action scenes where nothing is accomplished, aside from the characters receiving a couple extra scars...which is insane, since many of those sequences should have resulted in grisly death, not near-misses.
Again, seems like a strange criticism for a Resident Evil game, a series known for crazy nonsensical plot elements. But much like the film adaptations, RESIDENT EVIL 6 is an adrenaline-pounded sequel to a series that benefitted most on subtlety and horror, with only tiny slivers of its former glory tacked on.
The game is also brutally long. You'd think that more game equals better, right?
That's not the case here, unfortunately. The game is padded by extensive fight scenes, and progressing through the story feels like a drawn out chore rather than an enjoyable gauntlet. Just when you think you've reached the climax of the game, and must be close to the end, you end up playing for 3 more hours. THEN you're close to the end.
In the final chapters I just wanted the game to be over. I was tired of fighting the same boss, who would always "resurrect" himself with some new appendage or mutation. Having bosses continually come back certainly sucks the tension out of the game, when you expect that the abomination you just torched will arrive again in 10 minutes.
RESIDENT EVIL 6 is also punishing to completionists: if you want to finish the game "100%" you'll have to go through the entire game TWICE, once as one character, then again as their partner. The play time I currently have logged is from going through the entire game (and the bonus mission) just once. I don't think I have the patience to go through the game a second time.
Also never expected to find continuity errors in a video game. Before the main game starts you have to play through a tutorial prologue that shows certain characters in peril. However, when you catch up to that point in the story in the main game things are completely different. The game lies to you right at the start, and changes certain events throughout the game as you switch between sets of characters. It's crazy.
Though it has its moments, RESIDENT EVIL 6 isn't a game I want to revisit any time soon. Unless it goes on sale for like 5 bucks or something, I'd recommend avoiding this title.
--------------
tl;dr
+Impressive graphics and production values
+Solid gameplay elements
+Action scenes are intense, though over the top
+Best played with a friend; coop makes the game fun and enjoyable
-Story is a large departure from other Resident Evil titles; nonsensical, illogical, over the top
-Main characters are seemingly immortal
-Game is frustratingly long and slowed down by too many battles
-Bosses are regularly recycled and resurrected, eliminating tension
-Story is plagued with continuity errors and plot holes
-Lacks old Resident Evil charm
