Despite the slightly ominous title, Thomas was anything but alone. This game is one of the greatest games I have ever played, somehow managing to stay in my mind even though I haven't played it in a while.
Thomas was Alone feature a LOT of (in-story) AIs that you must guide through different levels, each one equipped with different abilities than the other making this feel like true "single-player cooperative".
These AIs, though depicted as differently colored and sized quadrelaterals, are some of the most shockingly human characters I've seen (in gaming) yet. These characters are well written to the level of Telltale's The Walking Dead, Bioshock, or even Mass Effect (2).
Along with this, the game's soundtrack is stellar, perfectly fitting the game (maybe not your musical taste, but it fits the atmosphere). The visuals also work with this to create a game that feels very sterile, which actually allows the player to easily understand what's going on and accentuates the aliveness of the characters.
But that would be leaving out two major issues- the user interface, namely switching between characters, can be quite annoying and tedious, which makes some of the levels even more excrutiating. This comes to its apex when you have to control a team of 5 completely identical characters by manually switching between each one. This team is also present in the other issue- the story's ending.
Without giving spoilers, the story goes on longer than it needs to. Granted, I would have loved to stay with the enthusiastic Thomas and the sassy Chris for much longer, but that wasn't what the "extra bit" of story gave me. However, I must give credit where it is due- the extra bit of story, while seeming a bit rushed, provided one of the best endings possible. While I was satisfied with what I thought was the ending, I was much more pleased with the actual end.

The ruins of Manhattan here are how destroyed London should have felt in Mass Effect 3. Sadly, there are no hot alien chicks to flirt with. Or Biotics. Or Garrus. Or manual saving. God damned checkpoints; on hard difficulty I found stealth to be the least frustrating way to play this game. Otherwise you (read: I) die too fast too often and keep refighting the same battles, until it gets too tiring and you just use invisibility to avoid combat altogether and finish it. Strangely, there didn't seem to be the same amount of variety as the first Crysis. Fights became repetitive.
Seeing New York in rabbles is cool, but overall it was a mediocre experience for me. Hard difficulty funnels your play style towards the quiet approach, lack of proper tutorial made me understand most of the mechanics and small touches only around halfway into the game - how to use which weapon and the advantages of your binoculars – and I felt no desire to explore the levels. There are collectibles, yes, but they weren't nearly interesting enough to encourage you to hunt them down. Nothing as engrossing as BioShock's audio logs, for example.
If you want a shooter with a bit of a creative touch in the form of the Nanosuit and its abilities (cloak, speed, armor), it might be enjoyable. Even then, though, you get the gist of it very early on and the game doesn't evolve enough to keep battles exciting. If you're looking for a rich experience with captivating characters and an intriguing storyline, skip this one altogether.
And if you imagine you're playing Shepard in London rather than Alcatraz in Manhattan, it both remedies a bit of the sour taste left in the end of Mass Effect 3 as well as makes Crysis 2's environment more exciting.

The New Nightmare looks and play like most other survival horror games. Those of you familiar with the Resident Evil series of games will instantly know what to expect and how to play/control this game. If you are looking for a Silent hill game on steam I think Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare is your best bet. Unless you have not played RE HD Remaster yet.
You can play as either Edward Carnby, a private detective looking for revenge or Aline Cedrac, a university student specializing in ancient Indian culture. Each character has their own unique adventures on Shadow Island and while they will interact at times, each must rely on their own strengths to solve the puzzles and complete the game.
Edward's game relies on weapons and combat and features more monsters while Aline's game consists of more puzzles that require you to use your wits. You can play either character first although for maximum enjoyment I recommend playing as Edward Carnby. He is the stronger of the two characters, and you will learn the layout of the mansion quicker and easier while playing as him.
P.S : Don't forget to download the 'patch' that let you play in 1920x with High Resolution. It's a must have but when playing the game it won't give you play time on steam.(since you have to start the game with the new launcher.) I have completed the game but my playtime didn't register!

Also, they recently added offline bot matches where you can play as Jason, you also gain XP, which unlocks characters. It's a real win-win. I don't know if they'll add in more offline content, like a story mode or anything, but it's a great new feature.

I've been a fan of the Friday the 13th movies ever since I was a kid back in the 80s. I was super hyped when I heard that this game was being made, and loved that they had such talented folks involved. However, after reading more and more about it, I hesitated buying the game for over six months. See, I'm not much of a multiplayer-game guy. They're okay, and I don't fault those who do enjoy them; they're just not really my thing. Then I saw it on sale during the Christmas sale and figured I'd pick it up for half price, if only to support the team who put so much love (and extra, free content) into it. And now, I was able to check out the game with the addition of offline bots. Yes, the AI for the bots is not the greatest. Even on 'Hard' difficulty, I've never had a counselor escape. It is good for learning maps, and basics about the game though before diving into the online portion. Also, there is the Virtual Cabin 2.0, which I played through to completion. In my opinion, this feature alone is worth the cost I paid for the game; although maybe not the full price. The puzzles were fun, although I did seek help on 2 of them, and it was a great refresher on the series. I hope the team continues to develop the Virtual Cabin for future content. All in all, I really do recommend this game. Yes, there are bugs. Yes, the offline bots are dumb. Yes, there are very toxic members of the community. Still, the team behind the game obviously care about the game, and have put a ton of love into it. Plus, they are constantly putting effort into improving it. You can't ask much more from a developer.

Cogmind is a roguelike game, where you constantly build and rebuild your character. Your capabilities are defined by the items you acquire. There is no experience (no grinding!), you gain 'levels' by climbing to the next floor. This system makes various builds equally viable: combat, speed, stealth, all sorts of hybrids and so on.
Items are not just stats +X. You will balance energy output, heat generation and support with your combat capabilities, speed and information gathering capabilities. There are over a thousand different items: weapons, power sources, cooling, propulsion, sensors, armors, shields, hackware, build and repair utilities and many, many more. Each item has a cost to use it, with more powerful items typically having bigger costs. There are various synergies and you can get some sick combos! But don't get too attached to the components you currently own, because sooner or later they WILL get destroyed. That's why you constantly need to acquire new parts (they are everywhere!) to rebuild yourself, sometimes completely respecializing to a different build type (You were a heavy tank, machine of destruction, but after a particularly tough fight not much is left of you? Time to become an ultra light jet that zips past enemies before they get a chance to act!).
Levels are procedurally generated, parts you find are randomly chosen, encounters are random (reasonably!). Each playthrough will be different and you will never get bored of it. Even veterans find early levels non-trivial and thus replaying the game is interesting, challenging and fun at all times.
There is an exciting backstory which you discover as you play. With each run you find something new and new things just keep coming! It's actually really fun to hunt for these lore pieces as you play.
This game is 'turn based', but you're not waiting for your opponents to move between your turns. Everything happens immediately. If you can click fast enough, you could do a 100 turns per second. Only when you need more time to make a decision (or contemplate your inevitable doom) the game will slow down for you. Think of this 'turn based' system more like an active pause - you get as much time as you want when you want it, but otherwise game moves forward smoothly. Even better - you can fast-forward less exciting parts like exploration (when nothing of interest is found) or waiting for that patrol to pass by.

The game is often pitched as a robot building game, but for me, the level of detail, variety and complexity on offer reminds me more of the design process required when putting together an effective Battle Mech. Subsystems such as locomotion being open to multi-legged, treads, wheels, hover or true flight, multi-slotted weaponry with a deliciously obscene number of options, and an array of utility tech that keeps getting more interesting and tactically useful as you ascend towards your freedom (and possible doom!). These subsystems require careful balancing with your build's limits on weight, heat generation, core protection as well as power and matter resource management. The struggle for survival also takes a toll on the durability of all your components. The machine under your control is not one that takes part in Robot Wars. The machine is more like a sophisticated piece of military hardware such as a MechWarrior or Battletech frame, yet it is built from the ground up, according to your designs or playstyle.
The environments are varied and comprise of procedurally generated zones where a whole ecosystem of hostile and non-hostile bots go about their business whether that be patrolling the area, or cleaning up scrap parts, or fixing the zones infrastructure. There is plenty of diversity on offer in terms of what bots you'll come up against, if you like their kit, you can kill and salvage (or even steal it).
It's a tinkerers paradise. There is always something new to pickup and consider integrating it into your build. There is always something better, somewhere else. And the journey is a battle to out-configure the calamities you will face on the way.
The game delivers a beautiful action framework, lavished with interesting detail and engaging danger, where you can actively take part in an emergent narrative, with surprises galore!
My hopes are that the game will reach an extended audience of not just the diehard roguelike players, but also the tinkering dungeon crawlers and the mech building tactical players who want a deep and interesting challenge.

This game, folks, is a tragic example of the risks of Early Access and the greed of devs.
I was with it since basically the start. It was fun, inventive, and I had a great time. Microtransactions were sparing, and if you were smart there was a glitch to open the gold crates anyhow. The game didn't seem to be P2W and was a legitimate challenge.

Then, as the game deteriorated, so did the community. It's dead. The Nether are interesting creatures, and some are hard, but you learn the tricks fast enough. People are an interesting challenge - and one that no longer exists meaningfully in the game.
Don't buy it. The devs (rightfully so) lost any good faith they earned when they let it turn into garbage - they did reclaim it from the dev team that ruined it, but only after a year or so and the damage had all been done at that point.
I well and truly wish it stayed the course. It had real potential, and it was fun. But now it is dead - a fickle dev team, greed, and a transition to milk it ruined it totally. It's a lesson about early access in general, don't spend money you wouldn't want to waste on Early Access games.

OK, let's see. Why did I say No to this game? Because I don't want Capcom to make the same mistake again.
The game contains 4 campaign, one of which is captivating. I played Leon’s campaign repetitively, like an actual insane person. I can’t say that it has any major issues, expect the game’s general issues, which the entire game has. I know the dialogue is a little more than cheesy, and you won’t really want to listen to the character’s talk, but the rest is fine. The game (I’m speaking exclusively No Hope difficulty, the hardest mode of the game) doesn’t give you much ammo, which makes it much MUCH more survivor than Resident Evil 5, and you’ll have to do a lot of headshots combined with the following melee attack in order to get through chapters. Of course, sometimes it get pretty annoying when killing an enemy is mandatory, you’ve used your bullets judiciously, but the game is refusing to give you bullets and instead keeps showering you with skill points.
This campaign is dark and nostalgic. I actually lived through it. I missed Raccoon city so much; I missed the atmosphere of Resident Evil 3, and this game came so close, which I’m grateful for. Thank you, Capcom.
The bosses, as always, are needy pathetic characters you can’t grow a liking or respect for (which doesn’t count for a flaw.)
Chris’s campaign is where the bugs and issues come to life for the first time, but the campaign still feels like an actual game. Here, you will see enemies actually shooting “through” each other. While you can’t possibly shoot an enemy through another enemy (the first enemy is blocking the other one), enemies can do this. Their bullets fly right through each other and reach you.
It has ridiculous artificial intelligence. When you’re hiding behind a wall and an enemy is using a machine gun from 100 feet away to kill you, the enemy will aim at you even when you’re moving behind the wall. HOW CAN THE ENEMY SEE WHERE I’M MOVING FROM BEHIND THE WALL?
There are these round and explosive enemies who will explode when you get close to them or kick them. Piers, your partner for this session, keeps kicking them all the while, regardless of where you’re standing. If I had a cent for every time Piers killed me, I’d have a dollar.
Then there are the headshots, which is a very crucial thing in the No Hope difficulty of the game. When you do a headshot, then enemy starts crying and pressing the wound, giving you a chance to perform a lethal melee attack. But the thing is, if you do 1000 more headshots, the enemy won’t show reaction again until he’s done crying, meaning you won’t be able to get the enemy to react again until it’s done with his first reaction. Now that’s just a big flaw.
Oh, the Camera, the Camera. Do I even want to tell you about the camera? The heroes are constantly looking around, and the camera follows their looks. When they’re done sightseeing, you’re usually attacked instantly, which is hideously annoying in No Hope difficulty, where you can actually die because of that. Sometimes a bus is following you, and you have to dash in order to escape. The character is looking at his front, but the camera only shows his back, which results in you being blocked by some crate or something, and then dying. In Chris’s campaign, luckily, there isn’t much to block your way. But in Leon’s campaign, you can be sure to die at least once.
There are these cut scenes that you can’t skip, which will annoy you to death for two reasons. One, the enemy has the ability to move during these scene, but you’re not. And when the cut scene is finished, the enemy will attack you instantaneously, giving you null chance of defending yourself.
Now, please pay attention that I got an S (the highest score possible) on every chapter of this game without cheating or using tactics that count as cheating. So I’m not annoyed because I don’t know how to play or anything. The game is seriously flawed.
One time, a truck ran over my partner Helena in chapter one, and she died. I’m only made responsible for my own character in this game. Why the hell does my partner die like that at times?
I don’t have much more to say about Chris’s campaign. I should add that it’s STILL worth playing. Once you get used to the bugs and flaws, you’ll really like this game. It has beautiful bosses. If you know what I mean by beautiful. Really fun to kill.
Don’t even play the third and fourth campaign. I continuously felt like I’m waiting for the game to begin. The chapters were either too short or too long. And they didn’t feel like games, they felt like prologues.
Speaking of prologues, the prologue of the game is most boring thing ever. Helena is dying and you have to save her. The more boring thing is that you have to play that part of the game for a second and third time (as Leon, and then as Ada).
The story was beautiful. This is the only Resident Evil game with an actual storyline, with character development. It’s no longer about saving a certain somebody and escaping a certain town (which happened for five games), this one actually contain some drama. You may even cry. :D Don’t say I didn’t tell ya’. ;)
Verdict:
Do not buy this game if you’re not a Resident Evil fanatic, because you’d only be supporting a failure. You’d be rooting for another game of this type.
There is much more I can say to dissuade you from buying this game, but I’m not gonna. This is becoming longer than I had expected.

UPDATED AS OF 7/16/2017
Initially, this game and me did not get along together well. I believe it reminded me of DOTA 2- I enjoyed aspects of and greatly disliked others, and all too often I found these were things I could not avoid running into. Among my initial complaints, I felt like things quickly became samey and that it was difficult to feel accomplishment or get anything rewarding when your stuff could be quickly erased with a death.
I tried to use the quicksave/quickload feature but I found it didn't really help me. I tried to go about the game slower and be more cautious, and while I still find that at times there's really nothing you could've done other than die, I've found my footing a bit better. Things that got me killed before, I've figured out how to approach or avoid. I've gotten better at not just rushing in, and examining things before I act. The learning curve was steep but now that I'm actually getting into the game it's so much more enjoyable.
Pros:
+ Small, helpful community akin to Dwarf Fortress.
+ Devs are active and responsive, which is unbelievably refreshing for an early access game.
+ There are a lot of different ways to play the game.
+ The world, and pre-generated lore is overall interesting and diverse, and there's still more that the devs are planning on adding.
+ Once you get over the initial difficulty the game gets much more enjoyable.
+ In particular, this new update with espers being watched has added some more interesting stuff to the game for me.
Neutral
= The game requires some creativity to play if you need visuals to enjoy stuff, as the game is ASCII centered.
Cons
- The learning curve is, as I said, very steep. It's not impossible to overcome but most people who are new will probably want to start off with reading a guide or maybe trying a build.
- Some things in the game are repetitive. In the early game, fighting the same, relatively basic enemies is boring (since the cool enemies are harder and kept in the later areas), or you read the same sultan histories over a hundred times.
TL;DR game has a crazy learning curve but it's not insurmountable, use guides and possibly builds to lean on. Community and devs are active and responsive so if you have questions ask them. The game can be a bit boring in the early stages but once you've overcome beginner problems you'll find the game much more enjoyable. Could use some more variety with sultan histories.

"The Frostrune" is a point-and-click game made by the Norwegian game company Grimnir AS, and published by Snow Cannon Games.
The object of the game is to find out why the entire island you washed up on the shore, is completely abandoned, dead and frozen.
The story is interesting, mysterious and intriguing, filled with familiar Norse elements. The puzzles are diverse and neither too hard, nor too easy. Some puzzles left me scratching my head for a while, but I solved them and completed the game in approximately 2 hours.
The art and graphics are indeed beautiful, magnificent and smooth.
The game has different options of texted languages to choose between (Norwegian, English, Italian, Spanish, Arabic, Russian, French and German), which is a great choice from the developers, Grimnir AS.
The only minus point from my side, is that you cannot skip scenes and texting in the game.
I was so lucky to have Grimnir AS visiting my school, Buskerud Folkehøgskole in Norway, some days before the release date of this game. They spoke to us about the development of the game, the art, behind the scenes, the inspiration of the Norse elements, and how they programmed and sourced the game. They also gave my entire class and our teacher free Steam keys for us to beta-test "The Frostrune". We're even mentioned in the credits!
Overall, I would give "The Frostrune" a score of 8/10.

Slender: The Arrival is a survival horror video game developed by Blue Isle Studios. One could say that it is a sequel to the well-known Slender: The Eight Pages. It was released on March 26, 2013 for PC with a PS4 and Xbox One version released in March, 2015. The game is obviously based on the Slender Man.
Unlike The Eight Pages, Slender: The Arrival does have an actual storyline (kind of). You are Lauren, a woman who went to see her friend Kate. Kate's mother passed away just a short time before the events of the game are actually supposed to happen. There's a fallen tree that is blocking her path, but, just like in all other horror games, she, for God knows what reason, decide to continue.
The Arrival is built around the ideas of the original game (Slender: The Eight Pages) but with a basic story divided into 5 chapters, all of which require you to find certain objects hidden throughout the chapter. At first, this doesn't sound like anything bad, but after you get killed all over and get more-less the same goal in every chapter you play, it becomes really annoying.
Eventually, the game will introduce you to a "new" enemy - The Proxy, a creepy kid who blindly follows Slender. Giving you no chance to defend yourself and having both Slender and Proxy awaiting you behind every wall, every door and every corner, you're given almost no chance to defend yourself, much less to escape. This becomes obvious in the 3rd chapter where Slender could camp in a room with the last generator you need to activate.
A really positive thing about the game is the combination of the background music, environment sounds and the atmosphere itself. Every now and then you will experience that great combination of those three which will mostly mean that you're about to run into quite a few problems. However, the moment when you hear and feel all of it, that moment is the one that gives you a dose of excitement and it is something you simply can't describe with words. If possible, try it out using the headphones.
Sadly, no matter how good the claustrophobic feeling works in some areas, the effect of it is often ruined by pretty crappy and stupid controls. Most gamers understand that you usually do particular stuff with one particular key, but what I couldn't stand in this game is opening doors using the MOUSE1 button which you have to hold and move in a certain direction. Theoretically, that might be a good idea, but when you end up trying it out in the game, it will be really annoying.
The game is running on the older version of the Unity engine. The graphics don't really stand up when compared to the games from its period. The models and the textures are a bit blurry and are pretty basic. When the camera, however, is twitching and your flashlight is wobbling while you are running through the woods, the final result does look pretty decent. Other than that, though, the game doesn't have much graphically to offer.
While Slender: The Arrival is a really decent horror game experience in which you spend almost every moment thinking whether Slender himself will be behind this wall or not, it simply relies on the original Eight Pages' game mechanics and goals, be it either the wood with its eight pages or the generators in a mine. It just shows how The Arrival feels simply too repetitive and even though some people will be able to finish the game in around 30 - 35 minutes, it likely will take most people up to a few hours to finish the game. All in all, the game's horror experience is really decent and more-less unique, but due to some of the problems mentioned in the review, the game tells us that even the greatest ideas shouldn't rely on the concept only, but should be expanded and improved where that is possible.

It's the game that makes you feel like you're reading great book and writing it at the same time. It plays with your imagination, it makes you feel things. And it almost certainly sets you up to fail... and you learn a mistake and give it another shot, with new survivors, new city, new relationship grid, but the same aim: survive another day.
Sounds easy, huh? Well, you try to make it in Zafehouse: Diaries, when your destiny hates you, plays jokes with you, and your survivors ain't no Rick Grymeses, but ordinary people with their own prejudices, fears, feelings, weaknesses and exhaustions.

Pros -
The graphics are immersive and bring the story to life.
Random events keep things from getting too monotonous.
The custom content generator lets you personalize the apocalypse. Put together some character from pop culture and you've basically got Total Drama Island with zombies.
Cons -
The audio starts out strong, but gets annoying fast. The audio levels are also unpredictable.
Game mechanics are never explained clearly, so every fight feels like a coin toss.
It's hard to tell how useful high level gear is.
Character relationships don't feel authentic, and consequences for negative relationships feel over the top.
Using custom content disables achievements.
TL;DR: a poor strategy game, but a good story generator. I recommend getting it on sale if you have the patience.

I shall always remember this as a game that scared me the most. The story and the depth of it are most memorable, so for a game of its age, it does incredibly well. Due to change of hands, the title has been milked ever since, making this as the one and only decent game of its series. There are slight compatibility issues which are to be expected for such an old game, however there are several fixes out there. It's a shame that there was never a remake of this.

AiTD is the resurrection of the old games retold in a new fashion (aka a reboot).
The mansion you are at has these demons that are afraid of the light. Light is your best weapon in this game. If there is a shadow, you might as well expect something to be there or waiting for you to get near it. Back in the old school days before Resident evil and Silent Hill, this was the horror game.
Too bad the port and storyline have been utterly mangled. As far as the port is concerned, they did not update the graphics so it looks nowhere near the quality it should. There are no video settings so larger resolution monitors are going to resize this a lot.
As far as gameplay is concerned, they tried too hard to make a fully 3 dimensional game that they forgot to add the mystery to the horror aspects. Everything feels too scripted and not eerie. The voice acting is pretty bad. Sometimes in a funny way.
If you can overcome these setbacks, the game is not that bad. It was a good attempt and welcome attempt to trying to bring back a classic game. If the developer spent a little more time on it, it could have been a great game.

Empire TV Tycoon is a neat management game in the veins of the Mad TV of the old. You buy movies, tv shows, advertisements, etc... and air them according to the viewer categories and try to increase your channel's fame. It is an OK management game. However, what the game offers die out pretty fast. After 3-5 hours it becomes really repetitive. There seems to be a single strategy to win the game, so you learn that strategy and play along with it to victory.
I cannot say it is a bad game, however it is a very limited game compared to the tycoon games of the past.
So, if you want to play a TV themed game, yeah it worths its price tag. Otherwise, my personal recommendation would be try another game.

Friday the 13th The Game was a huge Kickstarter project started from the bottom now all the way to the Steam Marketplace,Xbox and Playstation Stores all around.This is definately a addicting game that I have came back to multiple times compared to Dead By Daylight though thats another story.This game has its pros and cons however lets start with all the pros about this game from the beginning.
PROS:
1.Stays true to the franchise and gives every single Jason from each movie there original designs,even Sackhead Jason comes back to kill a counselor or two.
2.All Counselors are there own Unique Characters with Different Playstyles and abilities and have a Roll A Perk System which you can use to benefit your counselors and make them either more useful to you or against Jason.
3.Every Map was handled with such care as you can see by all map representing each Movie and giving there own unique looks from every movie.Even Jarvis House which everyone Hates has been 100% modeled after the movies.It truely shows appreciation to the movies.Even I have to admit I go exploring every cabin cause its the closest thing to actually being there in those cabins where these movies were made.

At first Endica VII The Dream King gives you the impression of being something it is not. The tag says it is a metroidvania game and in a way It is, but the game hides its mechanics making the experience seem more simple than it is. When you start the game you are faced with a very difficult boss battle that unless you are careful means a one hit kill, after this, you get a very cinematic escape with our hero jumping down pits like Luke Skywalker in Empire to escaping a gigantic boulder like in Indiana Jones. I have to admit, I died a lot during this introduction to the point that I got mad at the game, but like many things in this game, first impressions were really deceptive. Once you reach town that is when the game starts taking shape and we start noticing all the intricate and well arranged gameplay mechanics that are set in place to draw you into this epic open world action rpg.
At first the gameplay reminds you of Mega Man, simple platforming and money collecting. In a way it reminds me of the arcade game Dragon Buster by Namco, even one of the heroes looks like the main character of this game. Platforming is well balanced and the boss fights can be beaten by learning their battle patterns. I was misled to believe that this was a simple game by its first half an hour of gameplay, but the truth is that the game hides its leveling up and complexity and for a long time makes you think there is nothing to collect, but the truth is that the world map is littered with upgrades for the vast cast of characters and if you use a character more than others they start leveling up. It seems that you cant level up your life bar, but in truth, as you play your life bar gets more levels. When you level up you will get a screen telling you of new abilities like double jump, dash and so on. So the game rewards you for sticking with one character. All the characters have different starting attributes and special attacks but by using them more they might become better at what they lack.
Level design is very organic, valleys lead to hills, hills lead to mountains and mountains into caves, this is presented in a very natural way. Sound design is finely tuned to be atmospheric and highly magical, when you enter caves you hear the wind howl, or water dripping and subtle echoes in the distance. Caverns are vast, full of hidden chambers, temples and hundreds of goblin like creatures. The developer even paid attention to having the same race of monsters in different ages, like youngsters, adults and elders. The world is full of details and life, from hanging moss to mushrooms and fruit orchards that you can eat from. There is animal life as well and it comes to play as a game mechanic when using a very interesting female character. The game plays like if Castlevania 2 had a baby with Mega Man and this baby had Skyrim aspirations. The real life backgrounds combined with the sprites somehow reminds me of Bakshi's Lord of the Rings.
The story starts in the middle of a conflict, with the backdrop of a cursed land under the spell of war. The story draws many parallel with the Dragonlance novels and is heavily influenced by anime shows like Slayers [the main character looks like Xellos from slayers], Legend of Crystania and Record of Lodoss War.
The soundtrack is magical, inspired by Secret of Mana, Ys and FF Crystal Chronicles. This soundtrack should be on sale, because it has a lot of replay value by itself.
Negatives -
- Analog joystick doesnt work properly, digital works fine.
- Town design makes no sense for a small rural town [too many stores]
- Initial load takes forever.
- Town exploration needs diferent character models.
- You need a menu to see your stats and a map.
I really recommend this game and I could be talking about its many details for hours, like the hidden town maze, or the underworld under the caverns, or the docens of homages to Castlevania, and other games, but I will leave these for you to find and enjoy. I cant wait to see what is next from this talented developer.

Bro-Force is almost over and I was looking for something. My aim was not as high, but I did read about this starting out as a megaman Fan Game project with 4 players, but the devs decided to switch to pro because they had invested in the project too much. Well ... I understand making a game is not easy and I hope they try again, but this game is not good.
My problems are not with the wonky hitboxes or the low quality graphics. It's more of usability issue
* There's no tutorial
* The intro text is distorted and practically unreadable
* The intro animation could have all that back story, but instead you are thrown into it (instead we get to see a seizure warning sign and a completely unrelated Mandelbrot fractal zoom after many minutes waiting for it to load). Problem is, it's really not that good; not because of the writing (though the style seems more like a draft) but because the animations are lacking, yet showcased as if though they had been fully developed.
* There are very poorly placed spawn points
* Enemies at the begining can already kill you, not in an I wanna be the guy kind of way but more in a this one barely harms you that thing will kill you right off if you touch it. And the only way to tell is by trial and error...
* Pressing Escape closes it, instantly. It will take minutes to play, but can be closed instantly while searching for ways to change character... Yeah, fun
All in all, this game is lacking in design and had far too many loose ends, which must be why it was abandoned (no updates through 2017 is abandoned to me). The sound is bad, the graphics are bad, the gameplay is dull, the characters are uninspiring (level design has already been discussed by many). And the worst part is I really wanted to like it, in fact I rarely ever make a negative review, and I searched the internet like crazy for the Fangame it spawned from and have played many many amateur proyects (poorly made RomHacks? Heck yeah!). But this one just doesn't gel.
It seems like it was partially repurposed, partially patch, parts here, parts there, whole nowhere.
I am sorry, I hope to see a more developed project later, I really do. As for this little guy, it just doesn't cut it.

Quick Review
Let's face it, Resident Evil has lost its step. It isn't the horror juggernaut it used to be. 4 and 5 made it clear that it was transitioning into a more action-esque genre which upset a lot of fans. So where does this put 6?
RE6 is by no means an amazing game, nor is it the best Resident Evil game. However, for what it provides, it's a good game. The action combat feels refined with the ability to move while you aim and shoot. Gone are the days where you had to stand still to fire a gun. This certainly makes for better action gameplay. While the quick time events are more consistent in what they ask the player to press and when, the game unfortunately throws several more at you than 5. What about the narrative?
Resident Evil 6's plot is still that silly B movie narrative that it's always had. It tries so hard to be serious and emotional, but follows so many expected tropes that it never hits the nail hard enough. However, it isn't a complete travesty and shouldn't be shunned completely.
Overall Resident Evil 6 is a decent entry into the Resident Evil franchise. If you at least enjoyed 5, I'd reccommend picking 6 up, but only if it is on sale. This game is worth about $15 USD at most, and that's stretching it. If you didn't enjoy 5, you probably won't enjoy 6.

30+ hours in for 10$? Hard to give that a negative review for certain, and I don't intend to. Qud does a far better job of creating world immersion by having an actual world setting, rather than endless and fairly nameless levels of dungeons like other roguelikes. Although at times charmingly clunky, the pregenerated books and stories of the world add a wonderful touch to the world feeling alive and lived in. Very much takes after Dwarf Fortress adventure mode, but with far more progress and polish.
That said, the game isn't without its flaws. With additional complexity, ontop of the Roguelike genre's brutal approach to "difficulty", this game should not be your first delve into the genre. After cutting my teeth for a couple years of casual play on Stone Soup and getting my first win, Qud is a welcome step up in breadth of features. As to the game itself Inventory management needs some cleanup, autopathing needs a couple travel exclusions added to it, and friendly spore path exclusion needs to be removed at the very least.
It's under active development though, so I have high hopes small issues like this will get smoothed out. Anyway enough writing, Scorpion died at the hands of a Bear God clone on a stroll through the flower patch, it's time for Sub Zero to take his revenge.

I highly, highly recommend Caves of Qud to fans of old-school RPGs, regardless of whether or not you have experience with roguelikes. As soon as I found out what it was and got into it, Qud cemented itself as an immediate classic in my mind. Even in its incomplete state it's won me over completely; definitely in my top 15 favorite games of all time, at least. Don't let the early-access designation and minimal graphics throw you off; it's an absolutely engrossing, deep, gorgeous experience that's worth every penny and more. It is permadeath and is intended to be played that way, though there are ways to disable that. But the difficulty is, for the most part, fair and predictable enough that I never felt the need to do so. My biggest complaint is how monotonous the early-game can be, and it's the part of the game where RNG has the highest chance of getting you killed, which is both a good and bad thing I guess.
It's far from complete, but it's also being very actively developed, with weekly updates and lots of developer communication. What's here already is a substantial, enjoyable and truly unique experience. As far as overall feel, I suppose parallels could be drawn between it and games like Wasteland and Fallout, but the setting is truly unique, bizarre and esoteric, with a quirky and fascinating mix of post-apocalypse and otherworldly fantasy elements. You've got lasers and robots alongside plate armor and talking plants, and while it's often wacky it never feels nonsensical or obnoxiously absurd. The biggest hurdle for most people to overcome would probably be the somewhat convoluted controls, but they're more than tolerable once you get a hang of them and the devs are actively making efforts to make the controls and interface more accessible, which I think is great. This game deserves a huge following and anything that makes it more accessible is wonderful. It's also super easy to mod, if you feel like getting in to that.

First of all, yes, I'd definitely recommend it! I've sunk a lot of hours (and quite a bit of money, with DLC and disc import tools) into both of the RockSmith games. RockSmith 2014 fixes a lot of the problems I had with the previous version, most noticeably the latency. Also - in contrast to the previous game - most of the gear is unlocked from the get-go, so you can spend hours fooling around with different setups, then map your tones to a hotkey to switch to them at any time.
But here's the rub for me - one gets the feeling RockSmith is aimed primarily at guitar players, with bass tacked on as an afterthought. There's a few good challenging songs here and there, but if you want to challenge yourself a bit, you're probably going to have to grab some DLC. I've hoarded some Rush, Iron Maiden and Rick James' "Super Freak" to start with. But some of the bass arrangements for some of the songs are almost borderline insulting to a bass player who's been playing for any length of time. I didn't practise my♥♥♥♥♥off to pedal away at eighth-note roots! That said, even the simple songs (like "Pour Some Sugar On Me") are fun to play.
Also new is Session Mode. Although I would have loved to have seen more options (time signatures, bigger tempo range and maybe some horn/wind instruments, just off the top of my head), it does what it does amazingly well and can be quite the time-sink. One of my guitar player friends had a jam on it for three hours straight, until he broke his high E string =P
All in all, I'd absolutely recommend RockSmith 2014. Even if you didn't like the previous one, I'd definitely recommend giving the new one a go. It fine tunes many of the fundamentals that needed a tweak, has a pretty good set list and a wide range of DLC and most importantly, it can suck you in for hours and make practising FUN! It's been totally worth the price of admission for the wicked callouses I'm developing on my fingers. Here's hoping further installments will continue building on this rock-solid base.

The title went from being 'meh', to being something I can sink the occasional hour or two into thanks to the developers having expanded on the content and game play to include mod support, where I can modify the actors and movies, to include custom images.
Game play wise, it has a few things that I find a little annoying.
1. Your ai opponents aren't restricted to the same measurements that you are, where you can only do certain things once you've reached a certain level of fame, I noticed that the ai was more or less using my fame level to determine what they could obtain and do. Such as placing antennaes for expanding your audience, and the higher quality movie library.
2. Get used to the option to speed up time. Without it, you'll feel like you're watching paint dry.
The first one is a big annoyance, the second one is more a warning to use the buttons to speed things up if it seems like it's mind numbingly slow.
If you're looking for pro's - here's a few.
1. You can make your own tv series or movies. You do it by hiring a script writer. They make a script that has a certain quality, you can give it a title of your choosing, then you can hire two actors (lead and supporting), and then produce it where you assign production points to topics in order to try and influence the movie quality.
2. You've a variety of staff you can hire. Max you can hire four staff members from what I noticed, although there are more than four 'jobs' - so choosing the four types that you hire is a strategy based on your play approach.
3. It's intersting trying to find content that meets certain viewing groups desires, although some groups are defintely easier to please than others. Alone, you can quickly figure out what they like, but when you've 3 groups together, such as kids, elders, and rockers, and suddenly finding something they'll all tune in for gets a bit trickier.
4. It's not rocket science. I'd say it's a step past casual and just short of complex in regards to figuring out what you need to do in order to be semi-successful.

It could have been so much better. (TL; DR at the bottom)
You schedule programs (during the same day people are to be watching them!) based on knowing what type of people (rockers, elders, et cetera) will watch it? Shoulden't it be that you schedule programs weeks in advance, and that you get viewers based on what you air?
Your ads should reach a set percentage of viewers? Shouldn't it be a set amount of viewers? Upgrading your antenna, making you reach more viewers, just makes you have to show the ad to more people without getting a bigger reward. What is the advantage? (EDIT: Simply put,after having played this game for almostr 15 hours, I still don't understand the mechanics involved.)
You play in an environment with two other companies, sharing an elevator, but you can't play multiplayer? (This will be added in later, says a developer)
The formula for which audiece groups likes which shows is not random for each game, meaning it is possible to make a chart and use it to schedule the best shows for the given audience groups. Which means that 1. you learn this eventually and 2. replayability suffers greatly. (EDIT: you can change this in settings, apparently) It would be better if this info was given from the start, in-game, and your job was to try to air shows that will cater to as many audience groups as possible while getting your ads contracts done. Also, you could try to cater more to certain groups, and thus getting acces to special shows and events, while accepting that you have a smaller viewer base and thus get less money from ads.
TL; DR--> this game is totally backwards. I cannot recommend it.

I've been a casual fan of traditional roguelikes for a long time, and it's been fun to see the genre get picked up and taken in new directions, though it's often been through a mashup of genres—e.g.The Binding of Isaac—which results in fun and interesting games which owe a debt of inspiration to rogulikes but ultimately are something quite different. Cogmind, however, is a traditional roguelike that evolves the genre.
It has a terrific UI. As advertised the game takes full advantage of mouse or keyboard modes of input. Both modes are comfortable and it is great to see a roguelike taking advantage of drag-and-drop and right click context menus. My favorite method of input is still the keyboard. I never need to reach for the mouse and I am not missing anything. All of the contextual information and ease of use provided by the mouse has equivalents within the keyboard controls. It is really nicely done.
At its heart, Coglike is a game of exchangeable parts. You build yourself up out of the pieces of your slain enemies. (Or, sometimes the quasi-innocent bystanders that are busy doing their own jobs.) The variety of items feels expansive, and there are numerous item interactions—not the charming but frustratingly opaque interactions of Nethack, but of a more narrowly logical variety; i.e. some items make other items work better. Will there be surprises? Or are the surprises reserved for the story line?
We are not told what the point of the game is. There is no Amulet of Yendor driving the action of Cogmind. We just know we need to get out, to do something, to go somewhere. Discovering what Cogmind is about is one of the mysteries of Cogmind. Who is Cogmind? What is the context and history of this world? Is it Earth? When is it? I frankly do not know whether Cogmind is a freedom fighter or an evil robot. Delicious little bits of data are dropped from time to time, like breadcrumbs leading... somewhere.
There are a couple areas where I could dream of having a little more quality of life customizability, of the kind which I can provide myself in other roguelikes that run within a terminal emulator: fonts and colors.
The Cogmind screen is dense with information. There is a map, and surrounding it are panels containing various textual elements. I prefer ASCII graphics in roguelikes because they remain crisp and clear, and are easily identifiable at much smaller sizes than graphic sprites. Tiles may be pretty, but they are less distinct and require more detail to deliver the equivalent information. At 1920x1080 on a 24" screen I find myself wishing I could make the map font smaller and the text font slightly larger. And while I might kind of wish that I could substitute my own favorite font variants, the game does include a large number of fonts of various sizes and visual characteristics which can be used for the panels of text. The map font currently defaults to a square sci-fi themed font. That it is square is a good thing, as it makes the map tidily grid-like, but I find the letter shapes trade a little bit of clarity for aesthetics.
[Update—See my comments to Kyzrati re: the map font. TL;DR: Give the default map font some time. The glyphs may not have the kind of clarity desirable for reading text, but as isolated entities on a map they are really quite good and they support the aesthetics of the game.]
The other element I would prefer some control over is the color palette. When playing roguelikes in a traditional terminal emulator I typically create a profile with a color palette that has just the right amount of contrast for my monitor and for my eyes. This, again, is due to day-long work sessions staring at a screen that wants to burn my eyes out. With Cogmind I find some of the colors, particularly the lighter green, becomes a little bright and tiring after a while. And though it would probably be aesthetic anathema, I might really prefer not to have to stare at green on black. Aesthetically it is the right choice. It has the right sensibility for the game. But strictly in terms of ease of viewing, a sea of green on black can be a bit much after a long day.
These really are minor complaints however, in a UI that is far superior to any traditional roguelike I’ve ever played. A lot of effort has been invested in making the game as interactive and user friendly as it is, and I do not want to appear unappreciative of this. And I suspect these are things that may be addressed with a future modding API. The developer is incredibly responsive and present in the community.
Cogmind is a lot of fun and I look forward to spending plenty of time with it. Maybe one day I'll escape, or transcend, or destroy the whole damned place. Who knows?

Summary
Cogmind is a traditional turn based rogue like where you manage your robots inventory and components. You can equip your bot to be a fast flying hacker, or a tank treading missile launcher and many more!
This game does not feel like an Early Access or Beta. It is fully playable, fun, with no bugs (as far as I have seen).
It is an amazing traditional Roguelike with modern design and usability.
It is deep, full of theme, great animations and sound.
Pros
- Active and transparent developer.
- User friendly UI
- Deep gameplay mechanics
- Lots of surprises if you can live long enough to find them
- Story and lore to keep you coming back to learn more
- Very challenging
Cons
- Small font might make it inaccessible to some people.
- So far there is not much music (plenty of great sound effects though)
- Very challenging (this could be a pro or con depending on your tastes)
Long review.
I first heard about this game on Steam and quickly starting looking in to Let's Plays and reading about it.
I have had a hard time finding a traditional Roguelike that I enjoyed. Most had bad UI or bad controls or just did not provide enough of something new each time to interest me. I very much enjoy many modern rogueLITES (ftl, dungeon of the endless, steredenn, enter the gungeon etc..) So the ideas of traditional roguelikes are very appealing to me but most have failed to provide the experience I was hoping for.
Cogmind has since changed that. It provides a great focus on usability and player feedback. Animations and sounds all provide the player with the theme and feedback that makes it "feel" polished. Each time I play I find a bit of lore or an npc or surprise event that I have never experienced before. This really encourages that "one more turn/floor" feeling.
Cogmind requires a lot of inventory management and you will be constently making decisions on what to keep and how to "build" your robot. There are many "systems" that interact with each other and learning how everything works is a big part of Cogmind (and roguelikes in general).
Trying new and weird things is encouraged by this game. After each death (and there will be many) I always think of what new "thing" I could try.  New robot build, new tactic, new path through the world, how do I get back to that awesome event that I just found...
The developer has been working for several years and has released a fully playable game. Why it's even early access I don't know. Just know there is more "stuff" to come.
I feel comfortable recommending this game in Early Access at Full Price! It is well worth it. You can also check out the Gridsage game website to provide the dev with more support if you are able.

Что тут можно сказать, товарищи, игра замечательная! Рогалик нашего времени на лицо, не похожий на многие из них, уникальный во всех смыслах этого слова, если вы не играли никогда в рогалики то это ваш шанс вступить в наши ряды, а если же играли, то крепитесь - качаться здесь вы будете совершенно по-другому.
Коротко перечислим плюсы и минусы данного шедевра.
Из плюсов:
-Как игра выглядит внешне. Да, как вы могли заметить по трейлеру (который я очень советую посмотреть, он может освободить вас от моего нудного обзора), игра прямо-таки играет красками и цветами! Красивая анимация, отличное звуковое сопровождение м просто легкое, грубокое и непринужденное погружение в игру (кому-то может показаться в тягость отсутствие музыки, но поверьте, вам и без нее понравится). Есть режим ASCII и тайлов.
-Механика. Это игра совершенно не похожа на классические рогалики как DCSS, ADOM, Nethack и многие другие, кроме разве что пошаговости. Здесь нет ни уровней, ни опыта, ни навыков. Все здесь построено на частях вашего робота, которые в свою очередь разделены на 4 группы: источники энергии, двигательные установки , различные вспомогательные устройства и наконец оружие.
-Пользовательский интерфейс. Здесь все особенно круто, все, что вам нужно вы поймете и получите смотря на экран не читав всякого рода инструкций (которые здесь очень четко описаны и позволяют ответить на все непонятные для вас вопросы). Все необходимые на ваше усмотрение вещи можно вывести на экран, а можно и спрятать; есть специальный продвинутый режим, в котором информация отображается детальнее (например расчет точности выстрела как формула). В начале вам предлагается играть с мышкой, но необязательно ее использовать, здесь есть клавиатурный режим по нажатии клавиши F2, ветеранам пригодится.
-История aka лор. Эта игра далеко не просто стрелялка-бежалка. На фоне всего этого стоит довольно-таки глубокая история, в которой вам придется изрядно покопаться, ведь она здесь не просто для галочки, в ней содержится куча подсказок и получить все за раз вы не сможете, только маленькими кусочками. Вы всегда можете приостановить игру, чтобы посмотреть интересующую вас информацию.
-Контент. Хоть вышла эта игра в Стим относительно недавно, на деле же разрабатывается более четырех лет. За это время здесь накопилась куча контента и перечислять я его могу очень долго. Из наиболее значимых: огромное множество оружия (автоматы, пушки, гранатометы, ракетные установки, магнитные установки, расщепители материи и много-много прочего), такое же количество всяческих утилит, генераторов и двигательных установок; прилично количество уровней (есть главные и есть ответвления). Все это вы можете исследовать сами, здесь есть варианты для неспешной игры и наоборот, для быстрой.
Сам разработчик при этом активно общается с игроками и участвует в сообществе и не думаю, что в скором будущем у него закончатся идеи.
Из минусов:
-Порог вхождения. Хоть игра и имеет достаточно внятный туториал, придется умирать и возможно даже множество раз :( Да, игра сложная (но есть уровни сложности для новичков), думаю те, кто имели опыт в играх с тактической тематикой как XCOM смогут здесь лучше обустроиться. В то же время это может оказаться плюсом, в игру вы будете входить постепенно, не торопясь и анализируя свои предыдущие ошибки.
-Отсутствие локализации. К сожалению для многих этот пункт может оказаться решающим, без минимальных знаний английского вы врятли чего поймете и локализация в не планируется (и в принципе невозможна).
-[НЕ ИГРОВОЕ]Цена для русского покупателя может кусаться, хоть у нас и так в основном все гораздо дешевле в сравнении с USD вариантом.
-[НЕ ИГРОВОЕ]Ранний доступ. Для тех, кто пострадал от подделок в этой области может кольнуть в боку, но я вас уверяю, эту игру можно выпускать в релиз, хоть она и активно дорабатывается.
НЕ ЧИТАЛ ЛИСТАЮ ВНИЗ: покупайте этот шедевр, поддержите разработчика и наслаждайтесь рогаликом 21 века!

It's not often there comes a game that knows how to keep a player coming back for more. Disney Winnie the Pooh however, is one of those games that falls under this criteria. From the rich gameplay, to the charming characters, Disney Winnie the Pooh is an experience that demands to be felt by everyone capable of playing a video game.
To touch brief on the story, the game centers around detective Winnie the Pooh, a former member of the narcotics division of the Hundred Acre Wood Police force, and how he has to piece together why his troubled ex-wife, Christopher Robin, has returned to see him after 25 years of silence. The story goes much deeper beyond that, but for the sake of preventing spoilers, I won't continue on more. As the game progresses, the player is introduced to a wide variety of characters. All booming with personality and each one just as memorable as the last. Pooh's old friend from the force, Piglet, is easily one of my favorites in the game. Piglet, once a former member of the Hundred Acre Wood Police, is now trapped in the dump known as "the vice" where he spends his days dreaming about his glory years. While there, the player encounters two of Piglet's colleagues, Tigger, and Eeyore. And yes, it's that Eeyore. As seen in Disney Metal Gear Solid for the Sega Pico, Disney really had a way of promoting their game huh? Tigger and Eeyore are a dynamic duo that Pooh comes to grow chummy with, and they soon (along with Piglet) become some of his greatest friends. I'm only scraping the barrel with Disney Winnie the Pooh's characters, but I assure you, the pay off for meeting and seeing them yourself is worth it.
Moving on to the gameplay, Disney Winnie the Pooh is a detective game that requires you to be engaged and inqusitive throughout. A mouse cursor is used for pointing at objects and people of interest, and interacting with them. My favorite part is when on the flight to Christopher Robin's house, the player is given the option to allow Pooh to grope the stewardess (sick ♥♥♥♥). When the player isn't interacting with various entities found throughout the game world, there are intense shooting scenes that can be played with the Sega Saturn Virtual gun, Playstation Mouse, Namco Guncon, or 3DO mouse. Of course, the standard controller for your system of preference will work just as well, but aiming will be a tad bit difficult. No matter what input you use, there is no denying that these moments in the game are the most intense and nerve racking. The player simply moves a crosshair across the screen and shoots their gun at their target. It's simple, yet somehow very satisfying. On the screen, Pooh's ammo count is displayed (he has infinite ammo) and above, is his health bar. If Pooh's healthbar is reduced to completely red, then the player gets a gameover and ends. Fortunately, the player's health is restored after each scene. Making the journey much more seamless.
Being that this is a mystery/adventure game, one puzzle in particular where Pooh and Piglet have to open a jar of honey is absolutely nerve racking and defintely will try your patience. The game has many other puzzles through out, but instead of me telling you about them, you should definitely see for yourself.
Though the game's gameplay and story hold up, how do the visuals and music?
Well good news, the graphics and music are absolutely fantastic. The steam version of Disney Winnie the Pooh utilizes the NEC PC-9800's 8086 5MHz processor that allows for fluent animation and cinematics that will make your spine tingle.  From the opening shot of Pooh sitting at his desk eating a jar of honey to Piglet driving a car, Disney Winnie the Pooh's jaw dropping cyber punk noire 80's graphic style is sleek, stylish, and down right sexy. The breathtaking visuals are of course complimented by an allstar soundtrack composed by John Williams, Robin Beanland, and Kevin MacLeod, an ensemble of absolute awe. Some of these tunes are even iPhone worthy, begging to be listened to even when the game is off.
In summation, Disney Winnie the Pooh is hands down one of the best gaming experiences of 2016. From the jaw dropping graphics and music, to the memorable and attractive characters, Disney has really outdone themselves. Once again providing the world with a classic that will be cherished for decades to come.

The pixel art is fine.  The level design is not.  I was hoping to at least find gameplay on par with Actraiser on the SNES, which basically amounted to running and jumping left and right, swinging a sword and maybe a magic spell, so the bar already isn't set that high.  The controls are tight and responsive and feel fair, sure, but the level and enemy design falls so short of my expectations that I almost want my 99 cents back.  The second boss isn't even animated.  The ground so far is just right angles with absolutely nothing interesting going on, and the same couple goblin like guys who inexplicably shoot out bland balls of mediocrity.  Given the state of the rest of the game, I'm actually surprised they managed to include platforms you can jump down from.  The only aspect of this game that I could I feel remotely justified in applauding is how responsive and clean the controls feel.  Everything else just feels like someone's half-finished first attempt at making a game.

Overall I enjoyed my time with this game, the SNES style graphics, and music takes you on a nostalgia trip back to the glory days of gaming!  There are a few technical issues with the game starting with the long load time(takes close to two minutes for me). Toward the end of the game I ran into a few code error messages, but not frequently enough to ruin my experience. The collision is also a bit suspect at times. I could go through a lot of walls that you are not meant to go through, and even suffered a few cheap deaths from falling through the ground. I also had a bit of trouble setting up my controller initially, I had to use JoyToKey to get it to works, since my Sabrent controller was not compatible at all; however that more likely an issue with the engine and not the game itself. These issues aside I really enjoyed the gameplay. There are a ton of secret sprinkled throughout the land, and I had a lot of fun just getting lost and exploring. The combat is also pretty enjoyable too and you are given a nice variety of characters to adventure with!
Pros:
Nice graphics and music.
Many Secrets to Discover.
Good Variety of Characters.

Cons:
Long Load Time.
A bit buggy with suspect collision and a few code error pop ups.
Setting up controller was a bit of a hassle.

So, I've seen a lot of negative reviews on this game, and, seeing it was 99 cents, well...being the sucker for platformers I am, I decided to take a chance on this game, and see how I liked it. It isn't the greatest game ever, but it certainly is fun, and hard to put down when you get into it. The loading time upon starting the game was a little long, but honestly, it was the only time that a loading screen was seen, too--never saw another one while I was playing. I admit that the inability to change controls on the controller is rather annoying, but the layout as it is is just fine, I think, since on a controller, the Dash button was right next to the Jump, and the two attacks were in good reach, too. Now, personally, this game charmed me the minute the cutscene started, since it channels an RPG story fairly well, similarly to one you'd play on the Super Nintendo, and seeing that put into a platformer with some 'vania elements, I couldn't help but fall in love with it. I admit, some of the attacks seem a little clunky at times, such as the sword upper you can do with your blade-wielding characters, as it leave you vulnerable when you come down, but skills have been fairly diverse so far, and I look forward to delving in further to see what else awaits me! owo
Though, on another note, there have been a few little...iffy moments, two of them standing out more so than others. First, why does touching the "tutorial" boss kill you instantly? I know we're supposed to be getting some challenge, but, that seems kinda extreme for so early in the game. Second, there's a nifty secret area in the castle area that resembles, and even sounds like an NES game, but, upon finding the treasure there, and backtracking to the previous area, I discovered that, well...I couldn't leave. Going the way I came was out of the question, since it was like walking into a wall, and the other doorway which LOOKS like it could be an exit doesn't go anywhere, either, so my only option was to get myself killed by the mob of zombies, which, took quite a while since the character I was using had a lot of health. <w<; last of all, the boss of said castle spews lots of projectiles your way, one of which resembling one from a game many of us remember, if you've played Super Mario World on the SNES. Touch that, and it's an instant death, and it can be quite cumbersome to avoid, often leaving you hit, and instantly dead. Earlier before, when you drop underground into a room with two big mushrooms, and a bridge, going off to the left will lead you to plummet to your doom, since it hasn't been blocked off. And, last of all, the text seems to scroll by on its own, and it does so at random speed, or so it seems. Due to this, I missed a bit of text when trying to advance the text myself, being used to doing so in other RPGs and platformers, so...I hope this is changed later, or that you're at least given the option to choose manual, or auto.
Other than these, so far, I'm quite enjoying myself. I hope that you will give the game a chance in some way, it really is quite nice, and I imagine multiplayer would be quite fun! If I can update this, I'll do so after trying it out somehow.
Pros:

Cons:

A few insta-kills here and there

EDIT: In all seriousness though, the writing in this game is some of the best you'll ever hear. This simple story begins with a rectangular block "feeling alone". While silly in the beginning, the writing is like the paint which colors the game's characters. Sooner rather than later, it'll suddenly hit you that these simple blocks might as well be the characters in a triple-A game, because whether you like it or not, video game characters are and will always be simple pixels. The difference is that one is more visually detailed than the other: everything is just dependant if the characters and dialogue are written well or not. Thomas (the block you start out with) develops a personality, and begins an adventure in which along the way he meets other blocks with varying personalities. Just stop reading and play it, because it really is worth playing!
Be warned though: what I didn't like about the game is that through 70% of the game you really care for the characters and what they go through and for the last 30% of the game the main characters are instantly forgotten about and replaced with different blocks you never heard of!

Thomas Was Alone is absolutely a unique game. And it is also one that should be well-appreciated and respected in the games industry. This game is about AI who are trying to escape. "Up and to the right" is something you will hear quite often. These AIs are colorful quadrilaterals, seemingly boring in a physical aspect. However this is not a bad thing, but in fact adds to the impact of the narrative. This game shines in its narration and story which gives character and life to these quadrilaterals which you control. Not only do they have personality, but also physical variations which complement each other. Their combinations of personality and physicality produce interesting relationships which make you care about these... shapes. Yes, I just said that, this game makes you care about shapes. Their lives and goals will entertain you in more than one type of emotion.
Thomas Was Alone's originality does not come only from its story, however. The audible aspect of the game is definitely significant. The narrator of the story has a very fitting voice and the music playing throughout each level and scenario fills you with awe and happiness. On the visual side, the game's very minimalist art style is very pleasing to the eyes and can sometimes surprise you with unexpected beauty.
For a puzzle platformer, Thomas Was Alone is fairly easy, however certain jumps require you to jump off the absolute edge of a block which can occasionally become frustrating. The puzzles make the relationships of the characters work well, too. For example, two lovebirds have complementary abilites which allows one to do a certain task, but only if the other is present.
Buy this game, you won't regret it. 8.7/10

Clocking in at just around 2 hours, The Frostrune is a short and stunning Point & Click adventure game set in the mid-late 900s in Norway, in a time where Viking myth is predomenant. I don't pretend to know a lot about Viking mythology, or even Norway for that matter (though I have an interest in Nordic subjects in general) as an American, if I'm being honest. That said, this little game is a stunning achievment in showing just how well sticking to the archaeological record can enhance the experience of story-telling. It definitely - DEFINITELY has it's fantasy elements, but those fantasy elements are in the story-telling, not the visual aspects, which is where this accuracy shines.
In terms of the actual plot of the game, it was a very interesting mystery to try to solve, and I found myself eager to learn more. I wanted to know more about everything in the game, which perhaps is it's only "failing" - leaving me craving more information. Which, honestly, doesn't feel like a failing to me - I'm sure I'll spend extra time after playing this game doing research on topics relating to the subjects this game presents. Ultimately, I find myself kind of blown away by the rich mythology that the player is presented with, and I'm sure I'll come back to this game many times to experience it all over again.
Game-play wise, the visuals can create a little bit of confusion for what is or is not able to be interacted with, but the puzzles are not too hard (minus, for some reason the wolf rune - that tripped me up hard). Visually the game is stunning. Props to the artists, because I wanted to stare at the different locations for several minutes at a time just to take them in.
I would absolutely recommend this game for people interested in accurate Nordic/Viking representations based on the archaeological record (aka nerds like me), people interested in vikings in general, and people who like mystery and point & click games.
The price tag was a little high to me when I first decided to buy the game, but having finished it I would say that it's worth it.

Caves of Qud is not the face of mercy. If you don't play things smart, you'll die, die again, probably die a third time, and get revived just to get slaughtered again. Just kidding, this game doesn't do reviving.

Again, this game is not the face of mercy. You'll need to be lucky, smart, and lucky again to get anywhere. (Or just have the right mutation at the right time and remember to use it.)

As a longtime fan of NetHack, I have been looking for a roguelike that captivated me as much. Caves of Qud not only satisfies the type of roguelike experience I'm after, but it does it with an astounding amount of artistry. The music and ambient sound effects coupled with the poetic writing and truly immersive world building make this possibly the best roguelike I've played to date. The world is rich with unique plant an animal life (some familiar like crocs and chameleons, some mutated and viscious, sentient plants, exploding mushrooms, humanoids, I don't even know what else is there but I remember the ones that kill me.) If you are a fan of retrofuturism, roguelikes in general, worldbuilding, storytelling, and particularly worlds such as those in the RPG Numenera and the novel Roadside Picnic which spawned the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, you'll absolutely love this game.

Caves of Qud is a really beautiful, deep roguelike.  The mechanics, visuals, writing tone, and sound all complement each other really well.  The procedural generation is super tastefully done, and adds just enough variety to the game without smothering it in bland sameyness.
The devs are friendly and responsive and have been adding a lot of things to the game recently.  The new water ritual, for example, adds a whole new dimension of mechanics that layer on top of everything else and opens up lots of new options for how to play.
It's not perfect -- the UI is kind of clunky and the learning curve is pretty brutal.  If you want a game with an hour of tutorials and quicksaves every 30 seconds you should look somewhere else.  But if you're a fan of things like Nethack, DCSS, Brogue, DF, Rimworld, etc etc, and if you're willing to put in a few hours to get acquainted with the controls and mechanics it'll reward you with TONS of fun.

Many may look at this game and think it doesn't look all that good, all that advanced, all that much fun, and they would be wrong.
I'll admit I bought Zafehouse Diaries on a whim and I am so glad I did, I am really enjoying playing it.  You have three difficulty options ranging from a casual if still deadly walk-through to a complete Walking Dead, doing everything it takes to survive difficulty and accordingly the challenges you will face are more difficult too to match the level.  The game premise itself is fairly simple, you start off in a building and are required to fortify it, while fighting off hoardes of zombies, other survivors, and each other and are required to search other buildings for supplies, and information about an impeding escape or for parts for the car you hope to fix up to escape (depending ont he level you play).  It is a interesting addictive gameplay, one wrong move can mess up you're game and decimate your survivors but then too cautious  and you risk starving to desk.
The ability to customize characters, professions, items (you can find) and some of the in-game pictures is a really great touch too, and while it would be nice to have a few more customizations to add categories of items in it doesn't detract from the variety you have through the customization. Added to this is the is the ability to edit your diary after the game ends which allows you to add a few more details too.
Would recommend this game if you're looking for something different to play and hope. Even though they are going on to bigger, better, and moremore advanced projects I really hope Screwfly Studios continue with this game or make a follow up, i did enjoy it that much!!.

I highly recommend this game, but you should know that it is not for the faint-hearted. This game is only for the "rough and tough," those individuals that would actually survive the days after the "zombocalpse." This game is one that requires thought, planning, and a balancing act between the attitudes, skills, and oftentimes prejudices of survivors. Something interesting to note is that a survivor's personal bias isn't represented by how another character appears. Example: A survivor might be racist, but that isn't related to the randomized picture of the survivor. In one game, I had a solitary character who was distrustful of women. As it happened, a woman showed up who happened to be distrustful of (and not attracted to) men. Whether you'll enjoy this game really depends on whether you're still aboard the Slenderman train. Given that I'm writing this review in 2016, I'm going to assume that you aren't. It's weird to look back and think that a faceless guy in a suit had everyone scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ five years ago, but the entire horror genre was in a rut at the time, so I guess that helps explain it.
I digress. The game itself is almost exactly two hours long, and does nothing that Amnesia or Outlast don't do better. It can, at times, be more frustrating than scary, since the basic mechanic it operates on is "look for something while being chased." In theory, this leads to the player being forced to enter every dark corner, knowing there's a chance what they're looking for might be there. In execution it leads to you running around like a chicken with your head cut off. It doesn't help that Slenderman teleports. A lot of these games rely on spatial awareness, knowing where your enemy is to avoid them, but that's not useful for an enemy that doesn't adhere to time or space. It sometimes feels like the game could kill you at any point if it just felt like it, which, again, is more frustrating.
To be fair, other enemies come in that are suspectible to space-time, but these have their own issues. The initial appearance of mask-guy is fun and creepy. But then the game starts pulling in burnt zombie/ghost children, which there really isn't any precedent for in the Slenderman lore. The most annoying part of all this is that at the end of almost every scene in the game, the monster gets you. Which leaves the player wondering: "Why did I have to retry when it caught me the last five times just so it could catch me in a scripted event?"
I will give the game this: while it's only two hours long, it never does the exact same thing twice. Each scene plays by different rules than the others. Which keeps the player confused, yes, but also on their toes.
If you still have some affection for Slenderman buried somewhere, this is recommended.
