Alone in the Dark (4): The New Nightmare is a 3rd person survival horror game which was released in 2001. Some may say that it's a ripoff (see Resident Evil), but that's not entirely true. AITD4 is a reboot of the series which is placed in modern times. There are two playable characters with different, but interconnected storylines (similar to RE2), both have average playtime of 4-5 hours. The game has unique soundtrack (created by Low Distortion Unit) which is really atmospheric, scary and menacing. The game offers you limited amount of ammo which strengthens the element of survival horror. It also has puzzles which aren't that difficult (if you actually read in-game's files). There are powerful weapons such as double barrel revolver, triple barrel shotgun, plasma cannon, grenade and rocket launchers and other special weapons. I should also mention that the game also utilized a flashlight which is used for seeing dark areas, for puzzle solving and even as a weapon (see Alan Wake). The PlayStation 2 and PC ports have better FMVs, models and backgrounds, runs at 60FPS, however, the music is badly ported and sounds barely like the original (PlayStation 1). The Steam version of the game has a broken launcher and that's why I suggest getting the GoG version instead (or have them both?). With the proper launcher you can select any rendering resolution, but only 4:3 resolutions are recommended.
AITD is a truly scary game. The mixture of good soundtrack, atmosphere (including rain and thunder), flashes, sudden screams, supernatural monsters does it's job. Be sure to play at night and/or with headphones. Generally underrated game.

Cogmind is a creative and well executed roguelike with some great animations and art.

The items you need to put in the slots tend to be fairly common or easy enough to find. For these and other reasons, there's no reason to grind. This means that every move you make is a tactical or strategic choice, never a chore you have to get out of the way before the real game begins.
It's slightly easy and short compared to other roguelikes, but I think that's a very good thing considering that I've never actually beat any roguelike games (and I've only come close to beating Cogmind, so far). There are also alternate endings, a scoring system and online leaderboards, and secret things you can do to extend replayability, so don't let the potentially short length scare you off.

Cogmind is one of the most innovative roguelikes to come out in recent years.  Despite nominally being in Early Access, the amount of content and level of polish is high.  You play a lone robot trying to escape from hostile territory one floor at a time.  The gameplay blends traditional roguelike elements (turn-based combat on a grid, procedural generation, permadeath) with a unique equipment and build system.
Your capabilities are basically entirely determined by the items you have equipped.  You need to balance concerns such as mobility, vulnerability of systems to damage, and heat accumulation.  Almost every item is obtained by random stockpiles or scavenged from fallen enemies, and your equipped parts inevitably get damaged and destroyed in combat.  This means that you often have to improvise your loadout based on what is on hand.  As you ascend you choose which types of equipment slots (power, propulsion, utility, or weapons) to add.
Like a number of games in the genre, Cogmind is quite difficult.  There are two easier difficulty settings if you are just starting out or wanting a more casual experience, but the standard game mode is quite unforgiving.  The complex is essentially a simulated ecosystem, filled with both noncombatant and security robots.  The more disruptive you are, the more the general alert level rises, leading to more and more dangerous enemies hunting you down.  Thus, even combat-focused builds are incentivized to avoid unnecessary encounters.  Staying on any given level for longer than absolutely necessary (for example, if you're looking to enter or avoid a particular branch) is a deliberate risk.
The game is a traditional roguelike in its presentation, which is to say that the graphics options are 'ASCII characters only' and '2d tiles'.  Note that the game is fixed around displaying a certain grid size, so the game can look compressed on small displays.  My experience with a small screen is that the ASCII mode is quite readable, but if this is a potential concern you should examine full-resolution screenshots to evaluate this issue for yourself.  While the graphics aren't fancy, the green terminal aesthetic is immersive, especially combined with the excellent sound design.
The controls have two modes.  The mouse mode is intuitive and good for anyone starting out with this game or roguelikes in general, and the traditional roguelike keyboard mode is well-optimized for veterans, albeit more complex.  Customizing keybinds is an option, although it's a little arcane.
Due to its unique mechanics, I recommend Cogmind wholeheartedly for anyone interested in roguelikes.  Anyone interested in a system for customizing their own robot a la Battletech should take a look as well.  The game has a large amount of content (much of it in optional branches outside of the main path of levels) and also has superb replayability due to both procedural generation and strategic depth.
Note: My 'Hours Played' statistic on Steam does not account for the fact that I play the game with the Steam client inactive.  I run the game on a Mac using a Wineskin (which works well), and have over 30 hours of playtime (which is admittedly only enough to scratch the surface of the game).

SNAPSHOT
An unfinished middle school class project, at best.
OVERALL - 1.5 / 10
PROS
+ satisfying combat / movement mechanics
CONS
- extremely buggy, frustrating, and unfinished
- horrible interface / options
- art was ripped from every classic SNES game you can think of
DETAILS
I have to be honest, I have no idea how some people are saying this is the "best game they've ever played", unless they've never played any other games or they're acquainted with the developer somehow. Atrocious does not even begin to describe how terrible it is. This game looks and feels like a pre-alpha build, and plays like an unfinished project for a class of middle schoolers. One of the dialogues, for instance, says an NPC has a pet eagle named Cheeseburger, and the art feels like it was taken directly from default stock content, placed somewhere in the game, and then forgotten about. Actually, most of the art and animations look like they were ripped straight out of other games and "repurposed" for this one. Whether this is meant to be an homage to oldschool games or just a lack of any other ideas to the contrary remains unclear.
Overall the game is a just an unpolished, buggy pile of crap, that should be labeled "Early Access" at best. Players will constantly die from getting hit by a single enemy and falling into the multitude of pits or traps the game has that kills them instantly, or fall through terrain for no reason, or even just die from absolutely nothing due to one of the plethora of bugs.
There are no instructions as to what buttons do anything, which often times vary depending on the context. Some dialogues can be advanced by hitting one of the attack buttons, while others inexplicably only accept the jump button. "Cutscenes" happen out of nowhere, and will completely skip sections of the game when they are activated. Every shop for seems to only sell 2 items, but there's about a dozen different shops instead of just 2 shops selling a dozen items.
Level layouts are confusing and downright terrible. Often there are rooms with no visible exits or a random boss in the middle of nowhere. Some doors are locked, but when opened provide absolutely nothing except an extra set of rooms that serve no purpose. Sometimes the only way to progress is to save and then fall down every hole until you find one that doesn't kill you, assuming you don't randomly fall through terrain and die beforehand anyway.
Despite all of this, though, combat isn't terrible, and there are a number of characters that can be unlocked. When you're not dying because you got hit once and your character hitstunned backwards 10 feet off a ledge or into spikes, it is still fun to kill a multitude of enemies.That being said, it is still not enjoyable enough to overlook the complete lack of anything else good in the game.
I'm not sure if the "Casual" tag is meant to indicate that it is meant to be played casually, or if it is just being developed that way, but all in all I would not recommend picking this game up without a major set of updates and fixes. The story and dialogue are god awful, the music and art are probably infringing on a number of copyrights, and the lack of any coherent direction in the game make this nigh unplayable.

Endica VII The Dream King is a game we all deserved growing up and are now gifted to be able to play now.
Gameplay: Let's start with difficulty. If you are person who grew up playing side scrollers and love a challenge, go for hard. It rewards players with bullet hell and difficult bosses. I have also played a bit of normal through the start, but choosing certain characters will let you breeze on by.
With a plethora of characters and distinctions between each, the game has a rich choice of gameplay types. I personally am a rush down type, so Valos and Dash are great for starters. Mages like Emily area amzing as well. The only issue I am having is finding a player 2 to have amage as well.
The mechanics are what define this game. A well polished medroidvania for it first hitting the market, with great platforming, enemies, bosses and more. The game also features skills for all characters, making a personal experience for each and giving different play styles and a sense of completionism. I  pesonally will go back and grab all the coins I can to unlock more to the game. The fast-paced mechanics and quick reactions make this game a phenomenal blend of what I have always wanted in a side scroller I never really got in Megaman, Castlevania, Metroid, Contra, Metal Slug, Legend of Mana, etc. It blends all the wants and needs of a Metroidvania into one.
Story: I know the story may seem childish compared to games of today, but almost all 16 bit fantasy side scorllers usually had a lighter side to them. A close compariosn to me is Secret of Mana, which one of the original composers helped with the soundtrack for the game as well (Disclaimer: The soundtrack is fantastic and holds true to the backdrop of the story and type of game). I am not far into as I wished to write this review, but reading the dialogue is a quick indication.
In closing, the game is a fantasic piece that should not be overlooked! It offers amazing gameplay, a stunning soundtrack, a nostalgic story and boasts so much more. I would recommend playing the game with a few friends for probably one of the best couch co-ops in the last few years or enjoy playing the solo. Either way, this game is simply awesome.

Edit: Steam has a character limit for reviews and comments! I've pasted the current text along with my afterthoughts into a pastebin. You can get the full review here:
Where to begin? Well, lets start by adressing what actually worked for this game:
The music in the game is actually really nice, though there are some issues with volume (such as overworld to town stuff or other places suddenly gets much louder) and some repetition in the music. Wish there were some more actual songs in the game, but what's there already is pretty nice.
There's an attempt at storytelling, and there's quite a bit of dialog. Unfortunately, this comes coupled with the inability to push a button to advance text and as such you're stuck waiting for the game to show you the next line of text. A button press to make the dialog was desperately needed. Another blemish is the coupling of character details inside of storytelling (Such as when you meet a new character the game tells you how to play them, but doesn't actually let you do it while it's telling you that. Show, don't tell.) The game also does not allow you to try playing the character when you get them, instead you must walk to a waypoint to be able to change characters.
Now, let's get to the bad stuff.
HOLY CRAP that load time. I don't have the best computer in the world, but it's certainly not a toaster. The game takes on average a minute to load. That's bad, but not too terrible, until you take that into consideration with the staggering amount of game-crashing glitches you can run into, but more on that in a minute.
A really, really trivial complaint is the title card for the Dream Within logo, it just looks silly, flashing it's name skewed-screen several times before finally coming to a stop. It's not really a problem but I thought it looked strange. On occasion, the game failed to even display that and chose to just give me a retina-burning white glaring screen.
Now, getting into more serious concerns, one of the main selling points is a "Four-Player" cooperative game. While the game does allow you to do this, it feels like cooperative gameplay was an afterthought in the end. The character choices are wide and diverse but unfortunately there are real stinkers in the selection. One such character is Valos. A fast character, capable of dispatching foes with ease and traversing the terrain quickly. Unfortunately getting hit causes a lot of knockback, noticeably more than other characters. The lack of acceleration in the character means you're going from zero to sixty right when you hit the button and whoever's playing that character will be slamming into everything, or flying out into pits. Another character that's not fun to play as is Cenendra. She comes with an invisibility cloak that allows her to avoid getting hit, but unfortunately she is unable to really contribute in any meaningful way during her invisibility. So, using her puts the player at a disadvantage of having an ability that makes you useless to a team contribution when it's in effect.
Now, I understand that there are upgrades coming to the characters but for out-of-the-box, these characters are not fun to play and are detrimental to the game's cooperative gameplay experience. In the co-op game I had with my friends they opted to avoiding the noted above characters because of how bad they are in comparison to the others. It would have been nice to be able to play "Thomas Clones" of pallet swaps, allowing everyone to have the basic character.
On the subject of character selection, you're stuck playing one character between waypoints, having to go back to a checkpoint to save and check characters (and to change game options too, you cannot just pause and change settings which is really strange.) With so many characters available and them supposedly remaining with you during your travel, it's disappointing that you cannot just pause the game and switch characters ala Little Samson. This would have presented some interesting gameplay mechanics of being able to use certain characters to handle specific situations. A missed opportunity there.
One of the core issues with the game though are the game-breaking or game-crashing glitches. On several occasions I and my friends had been thrown back to the desktop with an error message, forcing us to lose our progress (and before you go "You should have saved more often" the crashes happen between waypoints so there's no way you can save between them) and start from square one again. Not fun. Add that into the long load time and everyone's got plenty of time to get a drink or use the bathroom, waiting for the game to turn back on. Some more interesting glitches occur that do not crash the game, but enter into soft locking. I entered into a small building with Reize and Lily standing near a counter of some kind and accidentally paused the game. When I unpaused, everyone had left and I couldn't do anything! I couldn't pause, couldn't unpause or even close the game. Everyone got up and left and I had to Ctrl+Alt+Del to close the game (And yet again, wait through a long load time.) Another crash occured during a dream-sequence with a space-shooting game, crashing back to the desktop.
Going onto trivial stuff, the graphics are just... bad. I understand it's supposed to be retro, but when the sprites look like they're ripped and edited from different source material, the backgrounds look like low quality photograph jpegs taken with a cellphone and the character/enemy sprites look like MS Paint they clash heavily with one another and it detracts from the overall appeal. Enemy sprites are lazy, and enemies themselves look like barely recognizable green blobs. The silouhettes for them don't work making fights with actually dangerous enemies (like the bomb throwers) a cluster♥♥♥♥ because you can't immediately spot them. Larger enemies are hilariously bad, they jiggle and pulsate adding more to that "blob" look, and the big green guys don't even look like they were actually finished (the sprite below the head just goes to darkness/blackness, it looks like he's wearing a body suit.) One of the bosses was a common enemy just stretched to be huge, but it looked like a pixelated mess. Graphics are a minor issue but it hurts the "retro" appeal when the graphics are so inconsistent and boring.
All in all, I can see that there's some effort in the game but it seems like there should have been some feedback from outsiders allowed into the game during it's development cycle. A single dev can make a game but playtesting and feedback from a community does nothing but help. It *might* be worth around as much as an apple or android app (roughly two to three dollars) but the fifteen dollar price tag (even with the 33% discount at the time of writing) is simply too high for the quality of this game. Keep an eye on it, avoid buying it until it goes on sale, and even then only if the dev actually makes an attempt to fix some of the major issues with the game. That being said, I do intend to finish the game with Co-op as best we're able, and feedback and whatnot will most likely be provided in the community hub discussion pages for this game.

Resident Evil 6 is one of the latest of Capcom's Resident Evil installments. Released back in 2012, Resident Evil 6 contains Chris Redfield, Leon Kennedy, Piers Nivans, and Jake's story in 2013, still pursuing Ada Wong, and of course, the zombies. If this game was taking a hit at horror, it definitely missed. As an action game, it is pretty fun, looking at some of the game modes, like mercenary mode featured in Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5, respectively. But as a whole, I wouldn't suggest buying it, unless you're brainless.
-     4 / 10

Despite it being terrible, I had a lot of fun in co-op. Most of our time was spent laughing at the story and poor game design. The gunplay system should have been in another game, but it really is fun to play around with. Mercenary mode is also fun to jump into every now and then.
RE6 tries to do many things, and mostly falls on its face. Grab a friend, jump into co-op, and have a good laugh.

I can't even jump into a random co-op campaign because of all those issues. It's just so boring. It's too bad because the gameplay mechanics are the absolute best in the series. So I strongly recommend Mercenaries and checking out its other game modes.
Overall, it's a fun game best played with a friend so it's easily worth $10 or $20.

Well, if the amount of time I've spent playing this game is any indication, I simply cannot recommend
...enough. This is, hands down, my favorite
, and I proudly say I own every single one they've released for the PC, including the (as of this writing) new ports of
and
, not one but *two* copies of
, as well as both
titles; I even have original copies of both
and
in their original boxes. So trust me, I've devoted a lot of effort to this series.
Up until I finally got around to playing Re6, Re2 and Re4 had the honor of being my favorite games in the series to date (and we're talking about the original, terrible Ubisoft port of the latter, let's not forget). However, in this title, Capcom managed to somehow do just about everything right, in ways few developers can match. While it isn't the quantom leap-forward in genre mechanics Re4 was (and that game is honestly one of the most influential action games of all time and probably won't be topped any time soon), it still manages to take most of the things that worked in that title and improve them for a real-time setting...in short, everything Capcom failed to do in
. We can now move and shoot, and while we're still sadlled with real-time controls, we have a, for the most part, more streamlined inventory with hotkeys for things like grenades; there's even a designated "Combine Herbs and Put them In Your Pocket" and "Heal Yourself" button, not mapped with anything else, the former of which is exclusive to the PC and makes the mouse/keyboard controls the preferred method of play. For once, Capcom gave PC players the port we deserve.
Plot wise, the game itself is one of the better stories in the series. As most reviews will tell you, Leon's story is hands-down the best (and honestly the most relevant to the overall plot), with Jake's a close second, and Chris and Ada's unfortunately bogged down by poor writing and irritating mechanics, respectively.
Leon's story is the closest to the older games. Yes, it does feature zombies, but it's still faster paced than older games, with the exception perhaps of
. Still, I was a little unsure how Capcom would implement free-aim and move-and-shoot with zombies, but they pulled it off beautifully. The zombies themselves are a lot of fun to fight, especially in Mercenaries, and there's some nice variety to their designs. The highlight of Leon's game is the final chapter, which begins with he and his partner fighting their way through a city being overrun by zombies and ends with the game's final boss fights, which are themselves a nice call-back to William Birkin from Leon's debut game.
Chris's story is more action centric, and overall feels more like his last headline game, though fortuantely there's only five chapters we're saddled with him and overall the experience is improved by the game's superior controls. No more standing in the open casually shooting it out with five guys with AKs; despite what a lot of people say, that cover system is
useful in his scenario. The highlight of Chris's game is the second chapter, which shows us what modern warfare looks like in a world full of bio-organic weapons.
Jake Mueller, a series newcomer, has a story more closely reminscent of
in overall tone; Jake and Sherry spend most of it snarking at each other and generally not taking things very seriously, and for the most part it works very well. Their scenario is honestly the direction I wish the previous title had taken, since it never forgets it's a video game and never stops being fun. Unfortunately, there isn't a stand-out chapter for Jake, though the first mission (which parallels part of Chris's second chapter) is a good candidate; however, Jake's signature hand-to-hand attacks make playing as him a blast all its own.
Ada's scenario is probably the most spotty, since it's very similar to "Seperate Ways" from Re4; it's the only one to feature both zombies and the J'Avo Chris and Jake fight. Overall, I felt Ada's was the most uneven, especially due to a poorly implemented stealth mechanic (which is still extremely fun if you can get it to work) and immersion breaking co-op. While no part of Ada's scenario stood out, the opening of her first chapter is solid, as is her last chapter, esepecially her fight with the series' trademark chainsaw lunatic and her second bout with the game's final boss; unfortunately, between these two there's a horrifically broken helicopter segment that puts the HiND portion of
to shame.
It wouldn't be right to ignore the game's extra modes, of course.
"Agent Hunt" is pretty much a Capcom take on "Versus" from
. Playing solo gets frustrating very quickly, and I honestly didn't enjoy it much.
I won't say much about Mercenaries, other than that's where most of my time spent playing this game was, and it alone makes the game worth the $60 USD I preordered it at.
There are also a few paid DLCs, which I also own.
"Survivors" returns from
and is honestly not much fun. Either the game crashes whenever I kill another player or it turns into shotgun spam very quickly, neither of which is an enjoyable experience.
"Predator" is basically "Juggernaut" from Halo, but with Ustanak. This can be a lot of fun, provided you have a full lobby.
"Onslaught" is similar to "Slayers" from the previous game. This gets intense in a hurry, but again, is fun.
Overall,

As a big fan of point & click adventure games, I've already played some very decent ones the past couple of months and It's safe to say that The Frostrune is competent enough to make my "golden collection" list of the genre. It's one of those games that I know what to expect and have faith that it won't let me down after seeing the screenshots and description (well, it's just a hunch basically).
The Frostrune has a beautiful artstyle and it kinda reminds me of Tormentum - Dark Sorrow, which is an amazingly well-crafted game (visually in particular). Apparently, the devs had worked hard to constrcut the environment and build up the atmosphere, laying the foundation for an immersive gaming experience. The majestic soundtrack and voice acting fit in perfectly with the cultural settings of the game as well.
As it is pointed out in the description, the story of TF is inspired by Viking myth and is based on historically accurate Norse culture and environments, which reminds me of Year Walk, a similar game based on Swedish mythological lores. However, when it comes to the depth of the story, TF kinda falls short in my opinion. Although it does deliver a Norse epic vibe, I feel that it could have been done better. I'm not saying that the story of the game is dull or lack of effort, what I mean is that I would be happier to see a more dramatic and elaborated one considering that it's completely linear.
The puzzles in TF are quite straightforward as they all have their own clues either written or depicted elsewhere, not to mention that there's a hint system in the game at your disposal. I believe you can beat the game without many obstacles by your own wit and be rewarded a specific achievement for your heroic undertaking. Well, I'm not a hero because I usually get lazy and undetermined when there's a walkthrough within reach.
To be honest, I was a little hesitant about whether to buy this game or not upon seeing the playtime of a couple of reviewers even it was 10% off at the time. A 2~3 hour experience for almost 10 bucks maybe a little steep if you ask me (considering that Year Walk is about the same length but about half the price), and if you're not a fan of the genre, you'll probably think that it asks for a little too much either. However, after finishing the game, I'm not regret my choice because the effort put in by the devs lives up to the price and I truly had a great time playing it.
Overall, The Frostrune is beautiful, intriguing, and enjoyable, highly recommended to those who have an appetite for point & click adventure games.

Ahh.. Ghost Online.. The infamous Maplestory alternative back in the day with the original four classes (Not even Pirates were a class yet). SoulSaverOnline, formerly known as Ghost Online, is a 2D Side-scrolling MMORPG that seemed to have popped up during a time when Maplestory Private servers were running rampant; It had a business model as draconian as Maplestory, and at least from what I could gather from its population, pretty evenly split between the higher end and lower end. But enough about the past.
It's 2017, and I found this game through serendipic search. I played about an hour and a half on the game. What's changed?
Well I'm glad to say for the first part that
It makes things a lot more convenient. The initial story seems to have been revamped a bit, with a chibi-comic style beginning, and a bit more emphasis on the tutorialization on a 2D side-scroller, Of course, if you already know how to play the game, you won't have to go through that intro again and again.
Some things that do get lost in translation in playing this game however, is
. I don't recall it being this poor in the original version, but it's somewhat strange to see the current version take a step back with some retrograde problems.
An issue I faced in the beginning was a lack of sound or music playing in the main menu, as well as being in-game. By default, this was muted for me, which gives me the impression that the game is meant to play without it. Another problem I came across was the controls. Funnily enough, they teach you a lot about movement and combat in the beginning. If you're a beginner and you're trying to get that epic gear on the ground, there was not much indication over how to do that. I was looking through the publisher's documentation, the controls in-game, and tried speaking to another player. Turns out my leap of faith was that "Air Walk" or by default, [Ctrl] is how you pick things up. It is also how you maneuver across different platforms, so be wary for your control key.
than before. I got to level 15 throughout my current playtime (100min), and it was literally from training on the monsters from spawning into the universe. Item drops seem to be wicked high, considering getting an equipment drop from a monster was a miracle back then, compared to now where you get it every fifth of a monster. It is also just as likely that this is due to an event, but I can't really tell.
It's safe to say that the
It felt kinda strange to either be the only one who spoke English in the channel, or to be the only one not understanding the conversation meta in the game. Lots of the players in-game appear to be super high-level, from their epic attacks and different mounts.
Overall, I see this game as more of a nostalgic value. If you've played this game in the past as Ghost Online, check the game out. You'll be surprised to see what changes they've made. If you're completely new to the game, try to take it with a grain of salt. I can't say for certain myself whether it's a "P2W' game, but it did say from the cash shop that they were not allowed to access it until they were Level 80, so if that's not any indication over whether it inherently gets players to get a direct advantage over new players, I'm not sure what is.

A very different kind of zombie-survival in the most positive way. Simple and satisfying, although a bit hard from time to time.

A different way of portraying a zombie apocalypse. In this game you control 1-5 survivors, by giving them different tasks, in order to survive.
The course of the adventure is displayed in the pages of a diary. Every looted item, every killed zombie, every breached building, all the things happening emerge in the form of letters. I thought this must be boring as hell, but its not.
Theres certain amount of excitement when you anticipate next moves of your survivors, who are most certaintly annoyed of one another, and they will fight each other. You can release the tensions in your group by spreading rumours of certain persons charity work or affiliation in crime or you can have bottle of spirits, maybe even a chess board or guitar in inventory.
The gameplay area is randomly generated, with several different buildings. There are also rare random events, with positive and/or negative side effects.
There are 3 different game modes, easy being the "easiest", where you start with only one survivor, so you could die in the first building you venture into, if not properly geared up. But you have infinite number of other survivors finding their way to you, and your only objective is to survive, with no timelimit. Some buildings also generate resources.
In normal mode you start with 5 survivors, and your task is to find a vehicle, and then find several parts to repair it. There is no time limit, but there are more and more zombies spawning in the town when time passes. You cant replace survivors.
Hard mode also starts with 5 survivors, who cannot be replaced, and must find an evacuation point. Time limit is set to 1 week.
As a fan of zombie games, this 1 is a fresh breeze and welcomed addition, in the evergrowing line of zombie games. But... its very difficult to handle, has several balance issues and the survivors are not from the sharpest end of the pencil.
This is just an all-around fun and fairly in-depth game. Highly reccomended.

Personal Rating: Good Ideas, Not So Fine Implementation
Classic Rating: ★★★☆☆
EDIT: After spending a while more time playing Zafehouse, I'm loving it!
First of all I liked "Zafehouse: Diaries" so far (I haven't played so much) but it surely could be improved in several aspects:
● Random characters generation can get you 5 people almost all without any skill: in my second playthrough 2 women couldn't even prepare a meal, let's not talk about making traps..
● Relations are the weakest point in the game, IMHO. After 8 (ingame) hours gameplay (basically 8 turns) all the survivors got angry at each other and the "spreading rumors" feature which should be used to consolidate those relations was pretty much useless: can be used one time every 24hrs and it's not really effective.
● This is a text adventure game, I would expect some translations, also considering that most of the messages repeat themselves as soon as in 2 hours gameplay.
● Lack of a proper resolution.
● Price is too high: 10€ at the time of this writing.
I do not want to penalize Zafehouse's developers (rating down their game) because it is original and enjoyable but I would not recommend buying it at full price; trade it with somebody (like I did) or wait for a bundle.

I'm recommending this because it works. It's a functionable shooter, nicely optimized, looks very good(even in 2014) with some very obvious AAA features.
That being said it's a really dumbed down game. Way back when in the confusing times of 2009-1012, a lot of games jumped ship to adopt a Call of Duty style gameplay, development and whatnot because of the cash cow Activision had turned that into. This is a perfect example of such a crime. Levels are heavily linear, "go here" objective markers, suit powers are streamlined into 2 seperate catagories with a "3rd" that's just there to have an excuse for sprint and higher jumping, a very superficial sci-fi story with memorable characters but no substance. Again, this isn't bad against the game, none of these features are actually detrimental to the game in any form and they all work as they should. But the creativity is long gone. Your approach to levels comes down to if you want to stealth or not. What comes out is a corridor shooter set in the streets of New York, with 2 sections that open up and make you wish the whole game was set in levels of the like.
So in short, it works. The game is fine in that sense. As a sequel to Crysis? No, it's pretty inferior. But if you can get it cheap, get it.
P.S. There have been some funky resolution issues with AMD users. For some reason this game tries to cap out at 24hz. It won't go into actual fullscreen. You can either force it borderless windowed mode, change your settings on your monitor to 50hz, or download some 3rd party fixes like RadeonPro.

It can easily be argued that Alone in the Dark is the series that created the survival
horror genre. The first game was released in 1992 for the MS-DOS and laid the groundwork
for the genre. After a couple sequels the series fizzed away, until Resident Evil came
around and recreated survival horror. So obviously the original had to come back to the field
and compete, and what it came back with was Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare.
game starts with Edward Carnby, a private detective, finding out that his partner is
dead off the coast of Shadow Island. Edward soon learns of some ancient tablets that can
unlock a secret power. Edward teams up with Aline to find the tablets and avenge his friend's
death. Their plane is attacked by some mysterious creature, forcing them to parachute, become
separated, and become stuck on Shadow Island.
Here the game makes you decide which character you want to be, either Edward or Aline. Each
has their own storyline and adventure, which intersects at certain points. The gameplay
is what you would expect from a survival horror game. Your character controls like in Resident
Evil, where up moves forward and you pivot. The game also uses pre-rendered backgrounds,
that are in fact very detailed and dark. The game has a great atmosphere that is mostly
focused on darkness. You will grow to fear the darkness and the nightmare creatures that
lurk within it.
And like most survival horror games, the game has a heavy emphasis on combat and puzzle
solving. What is different is, while both characters will see their fair share of both,
one is more prevalent in each character’s campaign. Edward has his trusty double barreled
revolver and will always have it in hand. His story involves mostly fighting the nightmare
creatures. The enemies are very tough and ammo is scarce, making you have to know when
to stand up and fight, and when to run away. Aline starts off in a huge mansion and must
solve the puzzles littered through mansion to advance. It is interesting how they separated
these two gameplay mechanics, allowing you to play the game the way you want. But whether
you are solving puzzles or fighting monsters, the darkness will always be there.
This is a great return of the original of the genre. With the separate campaigns and
the beautiful but dark graphics, the game is full of tricky puzzles and terrifying enemies.
his is another strong reason why you should be afraid to be alone in the dark.

Excellent game that was developed with great care. When I first read the informative, thorough blog posts of the author about the development process, I immediately knew the result will be awesome.
Others wrote long descriptive reviews, I'll just stick with some bullet points that I think makes the game stand out from others:
- great atmosphere, from the GUI to the audio-visual effects
- gameplay mechanics offer various styles of play
- deep lore that is revealed slowly through multiple walkthroughs (but not enforced on the player)
- input (keyboard and/or mouse) and graphics options (ascii or tileset) both satisfy old-school players and the ones who are new to the genre

Everything about this game is pretty much amazing. The setting, sparse lore (somewhat like Dark Souls the plot is revealed in small snippets and item or environmental clues, very little is forced on you), and mechanics are all master classes in design and implementation.
The game is hard, you will die a lot. When you're first beginning and are still learning the mechanics it will often seem completely random when you perish. Fret not, as soon as the mechanics start to make sense and you figure out how the gear works you'll realize that there are a plethora of resources available. If you've played Don't Starve it mirrors that beginner's experience in a lot of ways. At first it seems almost impossible to scrape through winter, or the first 3 levels of Cogmind, but after a little experience you'll see resources everywhere. Unlike the traditional rogue-likes, games like Nethack or Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, Cogmind has much better balance and there's not really any filler gear that isn't very useful. Moreover, the awesome mechanics of the game allow an insane amount of characer customization without using experince points or needing any grinding. Its a hard mechanic to describe and you'll have more fun figuring it out yourself so I'll leave it at that.
The interface makes you feel like an operator in the Matrix, the whole aesthetic is simply awesome. While the game has no music at the moment the sound effects and visual animations are excellent while still adhereing to the ASCII asthetic that the game is a clear homage to.
All in all this is a fantastic title that has managed to be the best RPG and strategy/tactics game I've played this year, the story is gripping and gives me a good reason to dive back in even if all I manage to do is unlock a couple extra lore pieces. There are also a lot of factions with different agendas in this game and ambient robot ecosystems going on that give the world a deeply immersive feel.
Fun game with an interesting interface design that becomes better as you play.

Cogmind is a tasty, quick roguelike (turn-based, permadeath) with a futuristic flavor and savory text-mode (with tileset) graphics (awesome explosions!) based not on leveling abilities but combining scavenged items to construct a winning character.   Procedural levels with a huge array of loot make for high replayability.   Very easy to get into and pick up whenever (lunch-mode, save/resume anytime).   Fully configured for keyboard and/or mouse control.  Still in Early Access but polished and well supported by the developer and community.
One more run!

"Jazzpunk is a comedy adventure set in an alternate reality Cold War World, plagued with corporate espionage, CyberCrime, and sentient martinis. Gameplay is inspired by spoof comedy films and cartoons of yesteryear, with a focus on weird gadgets, exotic locales, and open-world style exploration." -Please read the entirety of the review for all considerations-
The Cold War era and corporate-espionage themes are nice and not common in games. There is, mixed in, a world where technological integration and a feeling of publicity in every action taken is felt. The locations visited in the game, especially if they are actually named their alternative national names (in a 'mission' where you fly to your location) are a nice variety.
That being said, for the gameplay; there is a good amount to see on each level and a nice artistic style. While the levels are decent, they tend to be relatively short considering how many levels there are in the game. With a dozen or so levels (there I told you how many there are): some can be completed in a manner of minutes- even one that can be completed in seconds (the 'mission' where you fly to your location). This game relies on the side-missions or exploring the locations to add gameplay, as doing the objective straight-forward results in a even-moreso short game.
The game story is spy-ish and that's nice and all, but with little context as to what you are actually doing and an ending that says "this could be explained later" but, as of September 2015, has no additional missions or follow-up.

I bought this while it was on sale for about $3, and IMHO, it's a gem of a game.
The game feels immersive and keeps you constantly on your toes. At times, it even throws a curveball at you when you think you have things under control. Sure, it can be punishing in the beginning when you are unsure on what to do, but once you have become a "seasoned survivor" (i.e. you get used to the game), it really isn't all that difficult, and most of it, is common sense. For example, before trying to breach into a building with unknown zombie population, it would make more sense to investigate / assault it first, to make sure your whole party don't end up dead. No, having a full party with good weapons does not guarantee that your party would survive a breach when you are surrounded by an entire horde of zombies. Makes perfect sense.
As for the complaints on relationship management, keep doing the right things and the relationship statuses would eventually improve. The rumour feature is just to help out if relationships become really bad. Also, as with real life, if two people don't get along, it's best not to get them to do same activity together, especially in stressful situations and when they are tired (and cranky).
If you are like zombie themed games, as well as text-based games, this comes highly recommended. A solid 7/10.

It would be hard to find any video game genre more pointlessly over-saturated than the first person shooter.  Crysis belongs to a particularly obnoxious brand of first person shooter: the engine seller.  The engine seller exists for no other reason than to show off how amazing the underlying engine is an hopefully sucker some development house into buying it and building a real game off of it.
So Crysis doesn't have a single original idea anywhere in its DNA.  You can hide behind cover, shoot at the two or three enemies that are nearby, and admire the pretty graphics.  At first glance you'd think the map layout is less linear than usual, but that's just an illusion.  The open areas are like lakes on a river.  Sure, you can go anywhere you like on the lake, but to make any progress you have to go to the next narrow river portion.
So it's unoriginal and linear, is it at least fun?  Eh...maybe if you've never played a good fps before.  And no, Call of Duty is not a good fps.  Compare this to something like Serious Sam, and it falls completely flat.  No surprises, no challenge, and no thought required.

If I had to pick a single word to capture my thoughts about Thomas Was Alone I think that word would be “marvel”. It’s a word that is not used all that much when discussing games and I think that suits this game just fine.
Thomas Was Alone is a puzzle platformer that focuses - to a masterful degree - on game narrative and character development. Now you most likely have seen screen shots of Thomas and find that statement rather out of place, and you would be absolutely justified in that assumption. However, each shape that you control on your journey has their own personality, their own emotions and desires, their own flaws. Every time I load up a level I’m blown away by how much more I connect with a square and a rectangle than I do with every other off the shelf action game hero combined. It is impossible to believe until you play for yourself, but trust me that the writing and character development alone is worth every penny you pay for Thomas Was Alone.

Where do I begin...

Set during what I suppose is the Cold War, in what I THOUGHT was Japan, this is one trippy journey into a sweet♥♥♥♥♥world. I've always had a thing for the Eisenhower/JFK era: late 50s early 60s. I also had the pleasure to live in Japan, but my Pops, he had the pleasure to live in Japan during the Cold War. I play games not to get away, but to explore worlds I could never go in real life. This is the closest to 1960s Japan I'll probably ever get.

Jazzpunk is a first person exploration game. There's no real firm location except for one chapter.  The story is not very cut and dry. You play the role of a freelance "Spy" operative. It's never really stated who you ultimately work for, but know The Director is your boss. Really, the story is not it's strength. It's more of a visual adventure into someone's trippy mind. You interact with the world and watch the results. Gags, and jokes galore. Oh the gags! It's hard to categorize the game, the fun is in your curiosity. Walk around each location, and EXPLORE. It's a visual piece of art in my opinion, and the art design is superb. A "retro-futuristic" (think The Jetsons) Japanese aesthetic all thrown into a blender and somehow not coming out as sloppy as you would think. The music has it's strength. It works VERY well with the world. I can't even categorize the music...Latin, Bassnova, Jazz, 1950s shopping music???
The few cons I have is the price tag. Its a very short game, and the content may not justify the price for some. I also noticed other reviewers reporting motion sickness. For me, this was true. The camera is very sensitive to controls and I found myself getting sick. POV movement is quick and fast. Changing sensitivity might help.
This is one my favorite games ever, and I wish there was more to it. I never thought I'd see the day Quake, Street Fighter; It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World and Johnny "Cache" all get referenced in one piece of artwork! Luis Hernandez is definitley on another world. Glad he chose to share it with us. If you have an open mind, if you have an interest in the culture of the 50s and 60s; or if you just want to try something different, this game is for you. One last thing: did Japan win the war in this universe?
Thanks for the trip Mr. Hernandez. I'll raise my bottle of Sake to you.

Gameplay is pretty traditional as far as roguelikes go, although a world map and lots of exploration make things interesting. You always have options regarding what you can do. Want to delve through caverns? The world has a "basement" where you can fight lower and lower. It's so large that I cannot fathom anyone ever exploring the entire thing. Want to become a diplomat and friend of the sentient ape-people? Go for it, the game has factions and reputation systems based on your actions and how you've made your character.
There is so much to do in this game that it honestly never gets old. I heavily recommend it.

A weird little game with super lo-fi graphics. It plays a bit like a tabletop game, both in the way things are calculated, and the way you perceive it. You'll have mutations and stats like 'multile arms' or 'horns' but aside from the label you don't see any of these elements on screen. Functionally they make a difference, but you kinda need to imagine what's going on.
Before even starting, note that you're expected to use a numpad to move, allowing you to move diagonally or use the 5 key to even wait. And if you're not up for a hardcore experience, there's a lot of debug options, and one lets you turn off permadeath. While permadeath is a great way to play, it's not mandatory to enjoy the game. The game does encourage you to make multiple characters and try different things.
The biggest strength in the game is how many different character builds you can construct. There's a lot of skills that affect combat ability in a really satisfying way, or if you want to go more of an esper, a ton of psychic mutations to use. And of course there are physical mutations as well which can give you attacks such as going a target with horns (apparently robots can bleed as well?), or multiple limbs to fight with.
Almost any encounter can be approached differently. Some may have an easier time than others, but I've successfully played a psychic, a knife-wielding rogue, and an axe-wielding barbarian. (All mutant, you can play as a non-mutant as well which a lot of people say is easier for beginning characters.)
The encounters and trials you face are super diverse. Robots, trolls, sentient bears, hordes of worms, etc.
The biggest frustration I ran into (as with any RPG) was inventory management, specifically weight. Water is your currency, and it also has weight, as does food. There's a pretty nice sorting system that allows you to navigate menus entirely via key inputs, however. Since there's no despawn time on items, you can also drop your excess equipment in the starting town or put it in a chest of your own for safekeeping.
It's also not complete yet--later elements of the story are currently missing, and major updates result in your prior saves becoming unusable. You can roll back an update to play old versions, however. Luckily losing a character isn't TOO major a concern normally, just because of how the game is built around being a hardcore experience.
All in all it's a very strange game that appeals to very specific tastes. Chances are if it looks interesting to you, or if you like character sheets and DnD, you'll be more likely to like it. If it looks dull or too strange, or you're not partial to more text-based adventures, you might not.

Just looking at this game for the first time? Thought it looked like Maplestory and wanted to check it out but weren't too sure? Then this is the Discussion/Review for you. I'm going to lay it out for you, no sugar-coating.
After playing this game since 2006 and its multiple various versions (Global/US, Japanese, Korean, Indonesian, Thai, etc.) the one phrase that describes this game is wasted potential.
I started out with Maplestory as my first-ever MMORPG and migrated to SoulSaver Online (back then known as Ghost Online). It was a faster-paced game that allowed for more 'control' over your character and made it feel like you were immersed into the game. If you liked Maplestory's 2-D side-scrolling platforming, you will tolerate if not enjoy this game better.
Here are the PROS:
1)Free-to-Play. This cannot be stressed enough. Unlike other MMO's that tout the free-to-play aspect but really make it so you need to buy various cash items to have any chance at being successful with higher-end content, SoulSaver is one of those games where you really do not need to re-load your wallet every month. There are maybe three to four vital cash items any character quote-on-quote "needs" but everything is purchase-able through a Market system where cash items are buy-able in the games gold. What this means is that any dedicated gamer can develop their account by simply living off of the land and earning gold to buy what you need. Not to mention, a mileage system that is in place to get more bang for your buck.
2) The Soundtrack. Probably the most alluring thing about SoulSaver Online, what the game possibly lacks in art, it makes up for tenfold in its music compositions. Each different section of the games map has a dedicated OST in-tune with the games fast-paced action them and can capture any gamers' attention. Without a doubt, you will have a favorite theme and find yourself wishing to stay there as long as possible either to pass the time when training or doing an activity in real-time. Highly recommended. You can even find many of the Soundtracks on Youtube for your leisure.
3) The Skill System. If you are the type of gamer that likes to feel a part of the job advancement you choose in a game, SoulSaver Online does this perfectly through the skills conveyed. Each class' skills are tailored to fit the general archetype of that specific class. With high artistic value and a plethora of skills to choose from for personalization for each individual, you will always find yourself wanting to get to a higher level to gain access to the skills of that skill tree. Furthermore, skills are divided into two different weapons per class for even more flexibility.
4) The PvP System. SoulSaver Online's coup de grace, this is what separates SoulSaver from Maplestory and the tons other 2-D side scrollers. However this is a double-edged sword but since this is the Pro's section I'll detail the good parts.
-You can fight any other player within 10 levels of your own in every town area and a dedicated PvP Zone
-There is a large-learning curve to understand the mechanics of what your character can do to another character and what other characters can do to you, but the game play is exhilarating in that it invites you to come back and learn the craft.
-Being skilled at PvP will reward you with many different benefits that can aid your character
Truly, this is an entire second half to the game and no review can cover the scope of the ability required to compete. There are multiple different events and features that revolve completely around the PvP System. It is highly recommended to try out for any newcomer.
Now, unfortunately, here are the CONS:
1) Lack of attention to detail. Playing SoulSaver Online feels like it was not polished like other games such as Maplestory. Reading a few NPC Quest Line text and you will get the gist of this. Obviously the creators first-language is not English, but you can tell that they weren't even trying or just slapping on Google Translate renditions of phrases by the just awful and sometimes nonsensical things you'll see when reading. The UI has sections of text that don't fit into their allotted space, several signs, posts, and notifications are either unread-able or in Korean. Anyone taking this game to review as a first-timer will be immediately put off by this obvious lack of attention to detail, point blank period. Just read the Description of this game on its Steam page and you'll know exactly what I'm talking about.
2) The overall difficulty of finding information on the game: If you can get past the lack of attention to detail, this is most likely the REAL killer of this game. There is just too little official bases of information about the game. If you have a question on how to complete a quest, advance, or DO just about anything and you missed it from an NPC's text, you can get confused and lost for HOURS! This I cannot stress enough. You have to rely on unofficial blogs and websites and/or veteran players within the game for various tidbits of information because the website is no help at all. There is an encyclopedia built in, but it hasn't been touched upon since the opening of SoulSaver Online. If you want to play this game, you'll just have to brave through these first two issues.
3) Dead Forums: This ties into the previous point. Just an ugly consolidation of topics on the main website. No pinned topics for real help, no active moderators, it's just a funky mess with several links that don't work and are 'Comming Soon'
4) Lack of activities to do: In theory, this game would be cluttered with activities to keep any gamer occupied for the duration of your time online, but this is not the case. Most of the time, as in any MMORPG, you'll want to level your character. After doing this for an hour or two, you'll naturally get bored and look for something else to do. With a surplus of recreational diversions for your boredom such as PvP, Party Quests, Tag Events, Monster Puzzles, Omok, etc. you'd think it would be fun. However, the problem ties into Issue 2. Many of these activities require other players to start and since there's such little information on everything, most players don't even know how to get started. Thus, no one signs up for anything and the game functions never get to start. This really limits you to nothing but training all the time, boring a majority of prospective players. Plus, leveling gets difficult around level 100, around the time this issue becomes glaringly annoying.
5) Weak English Community: As a global game, SoulSaverOnline does quite well with the Eastern Hemisphere communities (Thai, Korea, Viet, Indo, etc.), but the Western communities are still primordial in nature. You'll struggle to find players that speak fluent English and often be ostracized from being included as you most likely will not understand the language a majority of players are speaking. This is a problem for players from the U.S.A, Canada, Mexico, South America, etc. You will most likely find yourself playing alone, something HIGHLY discouraging to any new player. However, there is a small community of dedicated Western players. Can be found at
. This problem was most likely the reason the game was introduced to Steam and is a good platform to tackle it.
Overall, I have to rate this game 5.5/10
If you find yourself interested and hooked on its fast-paced gameplay and soundtrack, you'll find yourself saying the same thing: 'wasted potential' and braving through all the flaws of the game. I wouldn't say its a Maplestory clone as it is so much more than that, but why torture yourself by having to research so much on a game when you could play something else with less effort.
My advice: Wait for a couple of updates to see if the developers will update and tackle these huge problems before trying it out. This IS a very good game if the management focuses on what needs to be focused on.

Comparing with the first installment in the Crysis franchise, this entry is really lacking in substance and enjoyable playability. Excellent graphics aren't enough to compensate for the appalling story, the claustrophobic confinement of the script and the terrible AI.
Crysis 2 is a game in the Modern Warfare, modern Call of Duties mould. As a standalone game, Crysis 2 is mediocre, or if the mindless modern action is your cup of tea, then you'll appreciate more of the same. Otherwise, I recommend Crysis 1, because that one is a classic, which merits a spot in the "shooter hall of fame" along side Doom and Half-Life.
The Good:
- Graphics
- Some (very limited) choices in approach (stealth or Rambo. I went for stealth, where the AI's weakness becomes the most obvious. For example a soldier calling on the radio "All clear, no target" after one of his buddies was shot down right in front of him, but he couldn't see me since I went back to "cloak enabled")
The  Bad:
- Story / Plot - didn't feel for one moment that my character actually counts for something or that my actions matter. You are just along for the ride, wherever the script takes you. Maybe Crysis 1 was kind of the same, but it offered much more freedom.
- AI is terrible in most ocasions.
- Very strict borders on the environment (it's true that it is a city and all, but a much better feeling of roaming through one was implemented in Batman - Arkham City)
- The modern shooters flavor (which might be a minus only for some)
The Neutral:
- Limited weaponry - once you choose a style, you only use one or two weapons throughout most of the game.
Bottom line: I never felt involved in this game, never felt a need to know how it ends.

I've been following the development process of this game for quite a while, which inevitably led to a fair amount of hype on my end, and after actually getting to play Cogmind I can say the following: it's spectacular on so many levels, it's not even funny.
Gameplay? Check. Combat is very satisfying, with positioning and tactics being very important if you wish to get rid of your enemies as quickly and painlessly as humanly (or, well,
in our case) possible, and believe me: ideally you want to be operating at top efficiency. Winning a skirmish or ten isn't going to do you much good when you have a war to win, with attrition being a very real and sizable threat, so you have to think ahead, and in order to be able to do so you'll need a very solid understanding of the way the game works, and combat mechanics are just one piece of the puzzle.
Graphics? Check. Classic ASCII mode is available (and toggleable with a single keystroke) if that's your thing. Otherwise there's a very solid tileset at your disposal, as well as fancy animations, juicy explosions, and whatnot.
Accessibility? Check. Tutorial and in-game manual are there to guide you, covering just about everything you need to do. You can play the game relying strictly on your keyboard and nothing else, but mouse support is there as well, and it's extremely smooth. The UI feels just right: it works perfectly well right out of the box without any tweaks whatsoever, but if you need more/different info, that can be arranged. Combine all this with I've said about the graphics, and you get something that can appease both the veteran of the genre and the newcomer alike. Finally, there's a number of difficulty settings, so if Cogmind is tormenting you a bit too mercilessly on the default difficulty, there is a way out.
Setting/plot? Check. Can't say I'm fully familiar with both at this point, but I believe I've seen enough to say that whatever is going on here, it's pretty damn intriguing. Let's just say that if an NPC appeared before me, offering me either a local equivalent of BFG or a piece of lore I haven't encountered yet, it'd be a tough call to make.
Long story short, Cogmind is a fantastic roguelike. It stays true to the genre's roots, but at the same time it's undeniably a modern game, and what we have in the end is an immensely satisfying experience.

A deep, tactical and attractive sci-fi roguelike.
Your robot wakes up in a scrapheap and must escape, needing to constantly redesign itself along the way.   Only played for a few hours and I've already encountered over a hundred different modules.  The dev says there's almost a thousand and I believe him. There's a huge variety to the parts which allows for a lot of different play styles.
The presentation is also appealing; the sound effects are superb and so are the flashy ascii effects.  Mostly everything can be mouse-driven but there's also a lot of default keyboard shortcuts that help with the micromanagement you'll need for your modules and exploration.  The amount of information on the screen can seem overwhelming at first but the interface is competently designed and easy to navigate.
Judging by what I've played so far (as well as other reviews) this game is already a complete experience that can only get better from here.  An early access scrapheap this is not.  The dev seems quite passionate and the game is already quite polished.

Though difficult the game hooks you from the beginning with a simple guided tutorial - from then on you have to make your own way and discover the games many secrets.  The games environment is well realised and the graphics and sparse sound effects really help to make the game immersive.  Highly recommended for both roguelike fans and newcomers to the genre.
Sometimes I have to switch builds entirely after making a run for it and it's an interesting experience to scavenge for replacement parts.

Oh bother, where to begin? Think, think, think. I bought this game because I felt like hearing Winnie the Pooh's voice. And it delivered tremendously! It also delivered in a chock full of Poohey atmospheric plot goodness. The narrator was also excellent and is as addictive as listening to G-man from Half-Life.
Although this game is most likely designed for kindergarten, prep aged kids and probably TotalBiscuit, I am most impressed with the approach of ideas to the point where I’d even tell off a few game developers that make mindless FPS mechanics to learn a thing or two about basic gameplay concepts with Winnie the Pooh.
It’s mostly a game where you have to click and find things on the screen. These things are mainly mini (memory recall) games, finding hidden honey pots and interactive hotspots to aid in the progression of the story (which cleverly sneaks in complex words). This is good, because it’s educational to the target audience.
The story is presented as a pop-up book. Where each page is a level that unfolds before your very eyes. The unfolding animation is a cool concept. I know this cause when I was a kid, I use to love pop-up books to the point where I’d even make my own. Why can’t there be anything artistically similar that drives the gameplay of an FPS game?
You can even go backwards and forwards through pages you have completed. There is also a home page which displays a map of your entire journey. I like this very much! It’s not stated what game engine was used, but that it’s a custom designed one from Avalanche Software.
Some things that weren’t a big problem was the 1280x800 screen resolution. However it would have been nice to have at least 1920x1080. There was also a part in the game (page 13) for me where I clicked everywhere furiously trying to find something, but it crashed. The only fix was to start again from page 12, because going directly to 13 would end up crashing the game immediately.
For an adult, it’s a short game, about 90 minutes long. Those are quality minutes! I definitely recommend this game. Also how often do you get to own a game called Winnie the Pooh. Pooh! POOH! POOH! … POOOOOOOOOOOOOOOH! Pooh-Pooh.

This is a quirky and fun adventure-type game.  I say adventure-type because while you are trying to solve puzzles, they are, thus far in my admittedly short play-time, quite easy.  The pull of this game is the stylized 60's spy-thriller setting.  Basically you are given a set-piece environment that you explore and try to "solve" to make it to the next level.  There are opportunities to interact with a number of objects in the game, including "characters" that rather look like they belong on public washroom doors to identify "men's" and "women's", with some terrible-but-in-a-good-way puns and jokes.
One caution I would give is that this is a first person game.  Your character "runs" smoothly across the environment with no bobbing or jumping.  As the environments are very busy and colourful, I found myself feeling a little motion sickness at times.  Admittedly I am succeptable to this phenomenon, and by simply moving more slowly and in more straight lines I was able to continue.  I would also like to suggest there be an EPILEPSY warning for this game.  The intro scene in particular was intense with flashing lights and crazy sounds.
My 9 year old daughter saw this and immediately wanted to play it.  There are some risque jokes, but really it's pretty PG.  Additionally, many of the jokes went right over her head, particularly the non-sequiturs and those referencing old computer terminology.  She was mainly attracted to the blocky and colourful artwork and the physical jokes, of which there are plenty.
The music and sound are particularly mentionable.  The "Jazzpunk" music is a blend of jazz and... I'm not sure punk exactly.  Imagine Miles Davis improvising with modern jazz while tripping on acid.  It can get a little much - but then again I'm old so what do I know?
I was able to get this game on sale, and at under $5 I can whole-heartedly recommend it.  If you are sitting on the fence about this one, I'd probably wait until it went on sale.  If you want to experience something unusual and trippy, then go for it.
If you like games with avant-garde humor or just want to have an odd gaming experience, Jazzpunk will do just fine.

At first, it is easy to feel overwhelmed by this game. Agressor dilemmas are perhaps a little more regular than you'd like, and its easy for your group to fall apart as a result of arguments and disputes. However, when you actually get into this game and develop a strategy, the majority of these things are either avoidable or fixable with a little effort.
Whilst there are plenty of FPS zombie games around (dear lord, someone make it stop), survival and reclaiming games such as this or Rebuild 3 are rarer. This game is very clever in forcing you to depend on not just your supplies but also the status of the members in your group to stay alive, providing a much more realistic post-apocalypse survival experience.
Of course, your group is varied every time in terms of background, age, gender, sexual preference, fitness and abailities, and with a randomly genereated map each game, no playing experience is like the one before.  This variability gives the game an epic amount of replayability and - should you complete the three main campaigns - the game has an easy to use in-game  custom content creator. Want to survive the apocalypse with your friends or the characters from your favourite TV show? Go ahead! Add pictures, careers, skills and personal abilities to your custom characters, playable in an endless sandbox game or on the campaigns.
Many reviews on here will complain that the group argues too much which causes everything to fall apart - cook a large meal and everyone will get along. Don't have enough food for a large meal? Break into a store. Dont have the weaponry to break into a store? Modify your weapons to create spiked bats and double barreled hand guns so that you CAN breach the store. Create a stronghold at the police station, steal medical supplies from the hospital. THIS. IS. A . STRATEGY. GAME. You can't just expect everything to go dandy,
This game is a challenge, and I love that. It has a stand out format with a fresh new style and thoughtful gameplay. I couldn't recommend it more.

Thomas Was Alone. Was. But not for long.
This short tale is a heart-warming story of equality, acceptance, sacrifice, and above all, friendship. You may think that the characters in this game are simple rectangles, but they are so much more. Each of them forms a strong character as they strive, as one, to their goal.
They quickly learn to accept their differences; nay, to embrace their differences, using each other’s strengths in order to overcome obstacles and complications which they would never be able to do by themselves, due to their own individual weaknesses and flaws.
Helping them to accomplish their destination, you will be challenged at times, but every time they get one step closer to their collective target will reward you and leave you feeling enthralled.
The game seems simplistic but it flows fluidly and artistically, accompanied with a charming, witty narrative and a beautiful soundtrack. The result: a game that comes together perfectly, filled with emotion and verve.
When I finished the game I found myself wanting to play more of it. Not because it is too short, but because I felt like I had personally connected with each of the characters and I wanted to spend more time getting to know them.
You will laugh, you will cry, but at the finale you will be captivated by this truly magical experience.

Firstly this game has the potential to be an incredible experience for both competetive and casual players. It has all of the trappings necessary to not only be an increadibly aesthetically appealing game, but also an enjoyable combat system - limited only by the skill of the player. However it is not, and here are the reasons I feel that the game is currently a poor excuse for a blockbuster title.
Primarily, there is the issue with balancing. As is Ubisoft's MO, if their game isn't instantly a hit, they drop it as a project. The game is rife with issues concerning the balancing of certain heroes. One example is classical heroes such as the orochi are inexplicably overpowered through a combination of both unreasonable speed and quick recovery makes him/her incredibly unbalanced. Others such as the Warlord and the Lawbringer are brutally underpowered by being impossibly slow, while also lacking the necessary abilities (in terms of combinations)  leaving them unable to defend themselves in duels, let alone double< ganks. Finally, heroes such as the Valkyrie are left completely dependent on certain combos - such as the leg sweep - to deal with multiple enemies, a combo that can be easily blocked by a counter stun, leaving her effectively useless.
Secondly, there is the game issue with Matchmaking. To deal with the critical lack of active players, Ubisoft artificially reduces wait times by often pairing you with enemies that have up to 10 to 30 times as many hours as you, or forcing you to fight against full clans. If the first issue of balancing was adressed, this issue would not exist as it would probably have more active players, however the "fix" of pairing with extended skill levels is a pitiful one.
Finally there is the issue of NAT types to contend with. This is an age old issue with Ubisoft games, and is also present in Rainbow 6: Siege. Basically to feed into the development of the console port of the game, Ubisoft decided that the cost to adapt the online behaviour of both For Honor and R6:S, they decided to just leave a critically flawed system of connection selection. For example, a person with a Strict NAT type will not be able to join other players of Unstable or Strict NAT type, even though the players Ping may consistently be low. All it really does is stop friends from easily being able to join each other, and is purely caused by laziness in the game developing process, and a desire to save more money on construction.
I love this game, and as i said before, it has the potential to be an incredible and challenging experience for all kinds of players to enjoy. However due to the lack of love put into the games development by Ubisoft, it will forever have its reputation tainted by bugs, poor balancing, and incredibly poor match making. While it is true that I have not spent long on the game (and that there will invariably be people shouting the "git gud" warcry) i played both the closed and open beta. These issues have always existed and it is embarrassing that they were not corrected.
do not pay full price for this game, get it on 50%< sale. It is worth playing, but until these issues are adressed, it is not worth the hefty price tag.
