EDIT: I have updated my review of the game because the developers have been extremely helpful and communicative, and fixed all the memory errors that were giving me problems. While the game isn't fully complete yet, it already has a special place in my heart next to ADOM. In the hierarchy of great roguelikes, this one is destined to be at or near the top, depending on how much they keep adding content and flesing out their world.
Pros:  Like ADOM, this is an open questing roguelike world, but turned up to 11.  There's a main story quest and various branching sub-quests, but you can literally just start exploring and keep going down until you encounter something that eventually kills you. The game is effectively infinite since every square on the world map correponds to a large overland area tons of random and not-random content, and underneath each of these screens are even more randomly generated linking caves, so you can effectively explore in any direction (except up) until you die from old age or your computer eventually runs out of memory. (which is going to take a long time since my biggest savegame is currently 43MB)
Gameplay is very like ADOM, ...but in a post-apocalyptic setting with lazer weapons and robots, crafting (if you have the Tinkering skill), and the ability to replace your own bodyparts with cybernetic implants! Plus, water as a currency and a consumable is a nice touch. Also, instead of corruption, you can catch various diseases and fungal infections that can make your life miserable until you find the correct cure (Hint: There's a book in the game that tells you how)
It's moddable! And even this early access version has some great workshop content.
There's lots of character customization and fun mutant powers to be had, though this early access version could use some tweaking in terms of balance and starting points. Since it's all XML, I ended up modding my version to add additional mutant points per level so it felt a little more like my character was actually growing and getting something more than a few extra hitpoints with each level.
Meet friends and make enemies. Through the miracle of the water ritual you can even sometimes persuade them to join you. My best game had a sidekick flying serpent who was essentially Trogdor the Burninator, but unfortuately, while he was great at carrying supplied, he sucked when it came to randomly letting fly with jets of flame and acid gas attacks that inevitalby damaged me and destroyed valuable items on the floor.
You can sever body parts. And if you sever a creature's face off, you can then wear that body part on your own face as a mask. Yes, this even includes your own face if you happen to have the two heads mutation and can survive having one of your faces chopped off.
Cons:  The variety of Monsters in early access is currently extremely limited. This area needs to be massively expanded, as it gets boring fighting the exact same crabs, spiders, and slime blobs, but I'm sure it will be.
Monsters that create pools of liquid (especially slime and acid) needs to be scaled back big-time. Default puddles size should be maybe 1, 2, or 3 tiles, not 9. Considering how many slime blobs are in a dungeon, any given floor can quickly degenerate into a slippery mess, where everybody just careens around blindly, and lots of good loot (and water) gets ruined.
It is currenly possible to get key NPCs killed, especially during the attack on Grit Gate, which effectively kills the primary quest dead in it's tracks. It's not that big a deal yet, though since the game isn't complete yet so you can't "win" it anyways.

Short review: It's going to make you want to learn guitar and you might pick some good techniques up, but it wont fully make you learn. It's not a teacher, but if you're really motivated, you'll learn a lot yourself by trial and error. The Learn a Song feature is the main thing and it let's you play whatever song they offer or any of the dlc you can buy, and it let's you play it in your pace, starting with one note after another. The sad thing is that most songs go from really easy to extremely hard (for me as a beginner that is) with one chord after another and depending on what song you picked, you're gonna get power chords and bar chords, that last one is impossible to nail down as a beginner. So to get better there are minigames that are truly wonderful in how they make practice fun and motivating, as they are kind of arcadish and makes you want to beat your own high score.
There is also the lessons mode which doesnt always work on my guitar because some of the electrical stuff is broken but even when the guitar does want to work, it doesnt always pick up that I'm hitting the right tone even though I am. But I guess I'm biased because of my broken guitar, I'd say that the guitarcade and learn a song mode is a lot more motivating and actually learns you stuff by playing your favorite songs over and over and progressively hit more notes. Besides the lessons mode gets sort of annoying because of how it makes you repeat every practice track because of one single little mistake that might not even be relevant to the thing you're learning.
The session mode is... Well, as someone who doesnt know a whole lot of scales and what chords to play, it's fun for a while at least, the other instruments pick up on your playstyle and scale, thus backing you up. I havent tried it with a bass guitar yet, would be fun if everything started circle around the bass. It has a lot of options and instruments you can choose so I'd definitely recommend it to someone more experienced with their instrument or if you just want to play around, the scales pretty much tells you what notes that fits so just play those.
There is also the tune creator where you can customize what kind of amp, effects etc you want on your guitar. Since my guitar yet again is really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everything sounds like a hardstyle album gone wrong except the acoustic ones so Im still sort of biased on it, but try it out. It also has authentic tones which are the ones that are played in the learn a song mode, so if you ever wanted to have the same sound as  your favorite guitarist or bassist you can!
All in all, a wellmade product that is going to make you want to learn guitar and will make you learn it but by learning your favorite songs than practicing scales, although you can do that as awell. It wont really make you learn how to play tabs, notes or any really technical stuff that well, but you'll have fun and you'll get one step further to forming your own band. I'd recommend a teacher so you actually learn to play songs on notes and learning you valuable techniques.

Love the interface - it's functional, clean, sticks to the ASCII terminal hacker aethetic without actually limiting functionality to 90's style terminals that we are stuck with at work. Entirely possible to play the game with just the mouse, but using keyboard hotkeys or just straight keyboard mode is very natural. It's sort like of a perfected version of gVIM - powerful hotkeys at your disposable married with the versitility of the mouse.
Never before have I been so satisfied at ASCII explosions and EM waves put together out of tile graphics. In this respect, Cogmind is top of its class. Graphical developers everywhere should take cues from how Cogmind renders game events in a way that gives both visercal satisfaction at seeing your enemies torn to shreds, as well as concisely communicating information to the keen player.
The game itself is fun, and the concept of "put yourself back together with parts scavenged from dead enemies" is very well applied. In fact, the entire game is balanced around part availibility from finding them in random rooms and killing your enemies, which is something quick players will adapt to easily. Your first win might be out of sheer luck after at least several failed runs where you learn more and more, but experienced players can win reliably (although going for high scores does take some luck and playing the same seed multiple times for optimal moves).
Multiple branches already in the game, with more on the way. Experienced players will be able to plan out what branches they want to take, determining a large part of their build and victory method.
Plenty of lore for the nerds to dig deep into. It will take many runs to discover the various events, dialogue options, and general gameplay options availible to the player.
Well worth the price, in fact I wouldn't mind paying double for all the polish and content that has clearly gone into the game. Satisfying games like this one are rarer than they ought to be.

It's about time I write a review, my first ever actually, on a game and most importantly a developer that truly deserves it.

There is lots of roguelikes out there nowadays and the definition of such varies about as much as plain opinions do. To me, Cogmind is a true roguelike in a modern style. While you can play in ASCII and keyboard mode, the game offers a tileset that feels and stays true to its initial look along with a very well done mouse control, which can be played mouse-only or hybrid with keyboard. It takes a lot of work to implement both this well, especially by only one person creating it and I consider this a big freaking plus, because we, the players, have the option and can choose whichever we prefer. Along with a clean UI that provides all necessary information at most a press of a button away, you will rarely find this amount of polish in an EA game.

As for the gameplay, it's got the basic roguelike features of being turn-based and randomly generated maps (along with many handcrafted parts). Since it's placed in a futuristic setting, it introduces a new type of equipping yourself besides the standard head, torso, four limbs etc. gear which I found is a very refreshing idea. This also opens up the possibility for very different builds and such different approaches of playing the game. The "true" roguelike part however definitely comes from its hidden mechanics - Cogmind is brutally hard, many struggle just getting through the early game, but this is by design. You are supposed to learn and improve slowly until you get a feeling for what's happening, influencing it to your advantage and thus increasing the chance of survival. There is no handholding, nor will you find precise answers on how these mechanics work, you'll get hints at most. Now I do understand that this may throw people off, the main reason why I'm mentioning it and you can trust me, I have also raged at the game, many times... but that's sort of the point of a roguelike, because once you get better, it provides a rewarding experience not many games are capable off.

I have around 200 hrs into the game and can (somewhat) reliably win a run, but true roguelike also means, I am merely increasing my chances, things can and will go wrong. Then again, this is not where Cogmind ends, there is a ton of optional areas available with lots of lore to be found, some of which will lead to different endings. You could consider them an extra challenge, while they do provide benefits, getting there is usually way harder than just advancing on the main path and I have yet to see them all. While every world seed has all of the optional stuff in it, they are not always on the same level, so even if you aim for something specific, you may end up somewhere completely different, which makes for quite unique runs overall. Also, if you're the completionist type, bring a lot of time, because you will need way more than what I've invested so far.

If you are concerned about the EA label, don't be. Cogmind is a complete game already, along with lots of content and a polish I'd wish some finished products would have. Yet, the developer is still improving on the game, even though being hindered by a severe injury currently, he invests a lot of time and is very responsive on the forums. Only if you're new to the roguelike genre, especially the turn-based variant (real-time is just, well... different), I'd say start with something "lighter". For the rest of you, I do not see a single reason why you would not get you're money's worth out of this great game. I, for my part, am really not satisfied easily, but Cogmind has provided me with so many different and fun-filled runs so far that I'm inclined to call it the best roguelike experience I have had, ever.

There are three things I look for when choosing games to play: a game world where the choices I make as a player feel meaningful and interesting, a character that I can personalize, and finally satisfaction and fullfilment brought about by overcoming challenges.
Cogmind has these things in spades.
The world feels alive and doesn't just respond to you; it interacts with itself. Sometimes it's a pleasure to just sit and watch as the environment moves along without you moving an inch. Everything has a place in the world, a goal or mission independent of simply hunting you down and destroying you.
For character development, how you can play the game is directly related to how you
the game. One of the few games I've ever seen where stealth play is a legitimate option, as opposed to something ineffective/useless or the only way to actually win. Stealth play can take you through the game just as successfully as mowing down hordes of enemies will. And I appreciate that.
And for those of you in the know, it's a roguelike. As far as satisfaction and fulfillment from challenges go, enough said.
This game is a gem, and I strongly recommend it to anyone who appreciates a game with endless replayability, meaningful choices, and a fascinating, expansive world to explore and discover.

This game turned out to be exactly what I needed.
It's turn based, so there's never any rush to play it - if I need to go do something, I simply get up and do it, the game will wait.
It can be played exclusively with the mouse/one hand. For those who are interested, it appears to be possible to play it exclusively with keyboard as well. Or - of course - a combination.
The interface is superbly polished and the attention to detail is outstanding. The whole thing is made to look like it's rendered in a terminal which enhances the experience greatly. It even has an ASCII mode that transforms the map into a fully functional ASCII rendered game world (which I prefer). The animations are unobtrusive but very sleek.
It is however - like most roguelikes - not very beginner friendly. It's not outright hostile, but you need to be prepared to put in some time to learn the game. To me, that is a plus, your mileage may vary. Somewhat related to this point: The amount of information that is relayed to the user can be pretty daunting at first viewing. But as I mentioned, this will make sense as you learn the game.
The game is a labor of love and it shows.

I've been following Cogmind for a while now, since one of the betas a few years ago. Watching a game grow bigger as time goes on; perfecting its meta and expanding its content and personality is a really exhilerating experience. Cogmind has really mastered something that a lot of games take for granted: True difficulty.
In Cogmind you are released in the lowest levels, basically a garbage dump, with the scattered remains of failures before you being the only thing that can help you rise from perdition. The concept of building yourself up on the pieces of others is  nothing new, but Cogmind really takes that idea home. Not only do you strengthen yourself with the remains of castaways long dead, but even their pieces are expendable and tossed to the floor often before you bother thinking about where it came from.
It carries through well in a rogue-like. Perma death is a frustrating, belittling experience and repeating the "same" content (RNG and seeded levels make sure you never really repeat anything) can be tiresome. But you're never left feeling like the game is insurmountable. Each enemy is unique and identifiable; your particular playstyle is reinforced with each run; and skill and technique win the day more often than brute force. Cogmind is a tactical game, and if you play it with the idea of  improvement in mind (Picking up the pieces of your failures and using them to succeed) you progress more and more with each playthrough.
The graphics are stunning for such a simple game. There is no music to speak of, and I hope none ever comes since the atmospheric drawl of machines, weaponry and robots is more than enough to draw a player into the world they are playing in. Complexity abounds, and the huge number of weapons, components and computer systems make sure you would be hard pressed to say a particular build is "the best." Cogmind is a game where your choices matter no matter how experienced you are, and each time I pick it up I don't think "Here we go again," I think "This time I'm gonna make it."
Its a complicated game to review, but one I would recommend to anyone who asks. A+, 10/10, a hundred tomatoes. Keep it up Kyzrati.

So, yeah, recruit mode in Crysis 2 is too difficult for me.  I want to see the game world, to enjoy, and not be frustrated by, getting there.  I find little enjoyment in not being able to save the game when I want to save it, instead of relying on checkpoints that assure when I die to have to go through again what I was already sweating to go through the first time with 3 meleeing aliens on me at once, only to die to another one later due to their extended melee range compared to mine (to keep that blood and gore challenge assumption thing going).
So I dedicate this review to all the silent gamers who spend money on games they uninstall a couple days later (as I am going to do with Crysis 2) and have resigned themselves to not being able to change the gaming industry and its assumptions about players that defines "fun" as one type of game play to the exclusion of all others.

This way I can play the game with the level of challenge that keeps it fun for me, the player, the person who paid for the game, the person the game is supposed to be designed for, instead of resenting every penny I spent on this due to the frustration of trying to reach the next area and failling over and over.  If this happened by my own error, that's fine, but instead it's by a legitimized form of bullying, where game designers cater to that aspect of the game and its players but no other.
As I am sure Crysis 2, nor any iteration above it, will ever have what I've suggested so we who want to pay to buy a story (like buying a book) can enjoy the game, I urge anyone else who loves the graphics, loves the stories of games, and wants to give those who went to the trouble to design them, to code them, to produce them, their due, not to buy Crysis 2.
I'm hoping to get Crysis 1 working and that maybe its balance is different, however, I can see that in Crysis 2 I won't be getting passed the part where I have to escort the Marines.  Too many enemy aliens that take 5 shots each to take down (and often more than one head shot with a sniper rifle).  Too much shaking ground when using a sniper rifle.  Too much "they know when you put the crosshairs on em" when my suit doesn't have that innate feature and the aliens didn't have to kill me to earn being able to do that.  Though it is good to see that if I kill a boatload of them, and get to their bodies while fresh kills, I can enable that feature on my suit.  Yet my suit with its entirely inferior armor barely gets me through the first volley of 3 meleeing aliens.  Again, I am playing for the story, not harassment and to become intimately familiar with what it is like to be the scrawny new guy in the prison shower who dropped the soap.
I've played computer games a long time (since the first mainfame text based Star Trek game that was coded in Fortran on punch cards), and have since picked games for the story not the elitism of epeenhood that appears to be the only thing game developers care about today (and mostly because it's cheap).
To be sure Crysis 2 has great graphics, human AI could be better, story isn't too bad as far along as I am in it, but I'll never get to know the rest of the story due to being unable to go any further in the game.

The simple good and bad...
The good:
* This is Resident Evil, in all its cheesy glory with nasty creatures, nastier bosses, and even some of your basic zombies.
* The game is quite long and it's actually a 4-in-1 as you get 4 different campaigns with Leon's one being the closest to classic RE (and the rest being closer to GoW or generic tpp shooters).
* When everything is working correctly it can be a fun experience with running, shooting, dodging and blowing heads clean off (does not sound like your normal RE game, does it).
* You can walk and shoot, it is still a big deal :)
* The gfx, when it's bright enough for you to actually see something.
The bad:
* Respawning enemies. I hate respawning enemies.
* Difficulty. I started on Normal and after finishing the first chapter wanted to throw my PC out of the window. That's how frustrating it was. Constantly respawning enemies, dodging bullets like Neo in The Matrix when I had at most 20 ammo. Not to mention healing herbs are scarce. I switched to Amateur to avoid frustration and everything was dropping left and right after I sneezed in the general direction... Sigh... And don't even let me start on the QTEs. Some of them require not reflex but precognition.
* The gfx, it's dark and dark and dark and you can't see sh*t because it's that dark. Other than that it's quite nice.
* Unskippable animations.
* Bad menus with no in-game pause.
If you like the RE universe and/or shooting mutated zombie monsters in the head then you might want to grab this when it's 75% off, otherwise I would not bother.

This game is actually pretty good.
Graphics and audio are solid, and do a good job of making the game feel gritty and weighty.
Balance is mostly where it should be; there are a couple outliers on both the extremes of weak and strong, such as Centurion being overtuned and Shugoki being undertuned, but that won't be forever; steps are already being taken to improve character balance on the test server.
With regards to the peer-to-peer connection, they have already announced their intent to migrate to dedicated servers, which should mean that one bad connection doesn't spoil the experience for 8 people. Yes, the game should've been on dedicated servers from the start,
Matchmaking isn't great. But it's much better than it was at launch; I can see that 4v4 matches tend to be much closer in outcome, with fewer landslide victories on an average night. Matchmaking will improve with more players.
I'm not asking anyone to buy this game at full price. Wait for a sale, or a free weekend, or try it at a friend's house. But the game, despite all its faults, is really good. If you like fighting games and ARPGs, just give it a chance to hook you. You won't be disappointed.

Seriously, it was early one of the best looking ASCII games in existence, and that coupled with an utterly massive far future setting with a lot of Gene Wolfe styling in it.  Seriously, the otherworldliness of the original was great.  The only thing that the original was only average in was in UI, but that was because there are games like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup in existence.  It combines some pretty good mouse controls with very intuitive menus and a very good looking tileset.   The way controls work was and continues to be one of the few roguelikes I feel comfortable playing with a TKL keyboard (QWE, ASD, ZXC as movement with Ctrl + Movement as basic hotkeys, and 1234 as abilities is my go to, if anyone wants to play with one hand for keyboard and one for mouse)
As for this new version, I'm glad to say that it (I hate to call it just a graphical version) is easily on course to be one of the must play games for gamers in general.  Their included graphic set is the only one I've seen that fits the TONE.  Instead of being just good enough to not hurt the game, I can already tell just by exploring for 10 hours that this will be the best way to play Caves of Qud.  And it's not just a regular tileset, the UI has been so fully integrated that both mouse controls and keyboard feel more natural.
As for the game being Early Access, don't worry.  This team had been with this game since about 2010 I believe, and are very dedicated to the game.  I've checked up on their updates now and then, and they are consistently beneficial to the worldbuilding as a whole.  Simply put please support these people, they're great and a representation of how to release a quality product.

Pros:
This is a proper classic turn-based roguelike, and it's one of the most polished ones you'll ever find. It's worth buying for that reason alone. The ambient sound track is great, and so are the graphical tiles which look lovely while still hinting at the text-based roots of the game.
Cons:
One of the main reasons a roguelike is fun is that there's a lot of variety in the beginning of the game.  Sure, you need to restart every time you die, but the most interesting content is always right at the start of the game and it's different every time. Caves of QuD starts off in the same town every time, with the same few quests. This makes the start of the game feel like a grind after the first few restarts so it lacks the addictive hook that make you want to dive back into games like Brogue and Zangband immediately.

Pushing my way through salt-marshes, reeds obscuring anything more than a step ahead, I fall into a briny wallow, soaking my cloak with foetid water. It is my ill luck that this tiny pond is home to a madpole.
Immediately it latches onto me and rips into my flesh with it's horrific jaws. My blood sends it into a frenzy, and before I can break free, the fish-thing scissors off both my legs and one of my arms. Losing blood, I drag my torso away from the gore-painted puddle. I act quickly, knowing that only the incredible medicines of the ancients can save me now. I fumble an ubernostrum injector from my belt pouch, and apply the rare potion directly to my quickly emptying veins.
I awaken a few minutes later as the potion begins losing effect and the pain returns. I pull myself up into a sitting position and stretch my new leg, it's skin untouched by salt burns and feet without callous.

Caves of Qud is a CHARMING roguelike that even in it's EA state offers a huge amount of options without feeling totally overwhelming. The setting and system are so LOVINGLY intertwined that I find myself gleefully describing it's bizarre adventures and occurrences to anyone who will listen. There are so many wonderful discoveries to make!
For those that have not spent a lot of time with roguelikes the initial difficulty curve is much smoother than many other games in the genre and overall it is a very welcoming experience. It is possible right from the beginning to see how dangerous the various creatures will be. The control scheme is also very user friendly in that you can get by with a mouse or making selections using the movement keys. I currently play using an Xbox One controller and XPadder.
If you are on the fence about this game JUST BUY IT! Development seems to be very active and I can only see this title growing more and more.

I waited for a sale to buy this game because I wasn't sure if I would be into it. I shouldn't have waited.
You play as Jason and try to kill the  counselors or prevent their escape, or you play as a counselor and try to not die and escape. Simple.
I played the new offline mode a few times to get a feel for being Jason (there is no offline counselor mode). I am glad I did because I seem to be Jason in 90% of the matches I play. Not sure why when I don't have a preference set (you can tell the game if you prefer to kill or be killed).
The game has a few bugs, but the worst I have seen so far is a body falling as I did a kill animation and it showed me crushing a head that was not there.
The online community still plays, I have not had any issues starting and joining matches.
I like that you can pick different Jasons from different movies, and they all look and have abilities like in that movie. Jason 2 has a bag over his head, and a few Jasons can't run.
You can buy perks for your counselers, they are random bonuses with randomized stats. One might be to have higher stamina, with a 10% bonus and a -5% speed decrease, but that could have rolled different and been +15% and -2% or some other such pecentages.
You get points to spend on these perks after each level, as well as experience points depending on how you did. Environment kills will net you bones experience, as will cutting power to cabins and killing everyone. Escaping or killing Jason also nets some good experience.
There are also outfits you can buy (dlc) and unlocks for reaching higher levels. Unlocks include different Jasons and counselors to choose from as well as new outfit skins.
I am having fun with the game and recommend it. The more people that have it and play, the more fun it will continue to be.

Anyway, best of luck!

Excellent Rougelike, one of the most polished I've played. While Early Access the game is feature-complete at this stage and can be fully played/beaten.
The game caters to both hardcore and more casual rougelike fans through it's options and settings.
The game's default settings are more of a 'lite' experience that lets casual or new plays focus on higher-level strategies, but hard-core players have opitions for surfacing more information of systems so you can really get into the nitty-gritty if that is what you prefer.
The game has a very nice tileset design, but full ASCII is supported as well. There are sfx and eventually music will be added.
The gameplay is excellent. It scratches that pure rougelike itch of getting thrust into a world and learning its systems to get better through subsequent playthroughs.
There is a ton of lore to the gameworld as well- every system makes ingame sense. This helps fill out the world and really gets me into the game. Thankfully, the lore/story does not get in the way of the gameplay and can actually be ignored if you wish.
If the pricepoint bothers you for a rougelike I will just say that this is HEAVILY POLISHED. With the pricepoint you get the security of knowing that the devolper is devoting full-time to adding features and fixing bugs.
This game in particular has one of the most active inde-devs I've seen and they are very transparent with their devolpment process and where their development hours are spent. Incredibly active on social media platforms as well. If you have a particular problem with the game I would not doubt you could get direct-developer assistance via the forums.

This game fixes my biggest dislike within traditional roguelikes: user friendliness. The tutorial is useful, but not pushy. The learning curve ramps up very pleasantly and
The in-game manual is easy to search through and rather helpful. There are also quick references for keybindings.
I'll be honest, I first bought this game because it looked very pretty (for a traditional roguelike) but 20 hours in and I'm just in love with the core mechanic! Not only is it thematically appropriate, but it creates what many games are lacking these days:
. It gives you the option of changing playstyles mid-way through a run and, after a particularly nasty battle, it enables you to quickly get yourself to a functional level.
The game tells its story through entries you can unlock while playing by hacking terminals. They are written in-universe and, although reading them is completely optional (alongside the entire story) I found them to be very rewarding.
If you've ever been on the fence about traditional roguelikes, this game is perfect for you. The level of polish and care this game has is astounding. Its user-friendliness and accessibility are really pushing the boundries of the genre.

This is probably the most gorgeous roguelike yet in terms of visual and audio design I've ever played, while also having a simple and intuitive control scheme. Each level is strongly themed. Not every robot you meet is hostile - most robots are just there to do their job, and there's no combat XP or currency system to encourage tedious gameplay - all loot has a use, and your robot's capabilities are entirely based on how you choose to equip yourself.
Your goal is not to kill all enemies, or steal a particular item - just to escape. Loading up your robot with guns and tank treads and fighting your way to the surface is perhaps the most obvious option (and an intensely satisfying one, with both the audio and visual feedback being top-notch), but loading up with light and fast parts and sneaking/running your way past encounters is a perfectly valid tactic as well - and you may find yourself switching back and forth depending on what parts you have available to you (and what parts you lose in the process!).

EDITED 2 YEARS AFTER INITIAL REVIEW @ BOTTOM!!!
Well.  It's an incredibly well made game.  The length is great as there is 4 campaigns to play through, each taking about as long as RE5 (only slightly exaggerrating).  The graphics are great, the story is interesting because each campaign ties into the other campaigns and often you're playing with the other characters for a small section of the story lines.
But that's about where the good stuff ends.  What happened to the RE games?  RE4 was the last really great one.  5 was fun but it was....different.  And now RE6.
Secondly:  why does RE6 *NOT* want me to have fun playing it?  Almost every step of the way the player is continuously being punished.  The "running" scenes allow absolutely zero room for error and the constantly shifting camera angles make it impossible to anticipate where to go next, and of course there's no prompts.  Maybe by the 8th death you'll have figured it out.  Some of the boss battles are completely unfair, and they continue to go on and on and on.  These ♥♥♥♥ers never actually die.  Your AI sidekick is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as all hell.  Even on the lowest difficulty, the game is relentless.  I'm an avid gamer, I have quick reflexes, and I usually don't play games on less than the hardest difficulty, but this one is really pressing my patience.  Again, you have zero prompts as to what to do next, where to go, or how to fight the current enemy/boss.  Most of the time in an arena I just run around like a moron running out of ammo trying to figure out how to progress.
Third:  The 'upgrade' system.  I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, by the end of the third campaign, I still have not been able to upgrade my first 3 perks to max level.  It just costs far too much, enemies don't drop enough points (or ammo, or health, or anything).
Fourth:  The boss battles.  I touched on it a little above:  they're relentless.  They have no prompts, there is zero tolerance for error, they're mostly 1-hit kills, and they go on for HOURS.  These punks just never die.  There was only two times in the whole game where I actually had full health *AND* a couple tablets left over.  But then one hit later I'm on the ground crawling for my life, bleeding out and after my parter revives me, I pop the leftover pills only to have it happen again...
I'm tired of typing for now.  The bottom line is this:  the game was fun at first because I played RE4-RE5 so many times I lost count.  But after being punished time and time again for trying to have fun I will not be making a second play through.  Honestly, RE: Revelations was much more entertaining than this.  <-  That's embarassing

"Thomas Was Alone", on it's own, would be a mediocre puzzle game at best. Something you'd see on your App Store or Market for 99p and would distract you for half an hour before you moved on, completely forgetting about it.
BUT (and it's a big BUT), the developer had two brilliant ideas. Firstly, give the game a wonderfully deep and evocative story (which may or may not be relevant as in the end you are still controlling little quadrilaterals). Secondly, get Danny Wallace to perform the narration.
Sure, it seems a little odd and trite the first time you hear it, but after a few levels it grows on you. Suddenly you find yourself desperate to move onto the next level, just to hear what the little blocks are thinking of at the time, and what they plan to do next. It really is that good. Wallace won a BAFTA for his work, and quite rightly so. "Thomas Was Alone" simply wouldn't be half as good without it. And on that strength, it's worth a playthrough at least once, just for the experience.

This game is a great time waster! Play as a mouse, racing against other players to get the cheese and unlock cool items! Each level has something different about it, and as the mice, it is your job to figure out how to get to the cheese, and back into the hole without dying!
On most levels, the player with the highest score will become the Shaman! The shaman's job is to summon different items, and create a path for the regular mice to the cheese. As you level up by getting cheese, or helping other mice, you can unlock new shaman abilities from being able to revive dead mice to being able to fly. You can even make other mice blow you a kiss! The possibilities are nearly endless with 5 different skill trees and about 20 skills each! You'll be playing a long time before you unlock everything.
It isn't just shaman skills that are unlockable, you can also use the cheese you collected to buy items in the shop! The amount of items that are available is insane, and the different ways to customize your mouse is amazing! However, these items come with a pretty heavy price of cheese, most items being well over 100 cheese, and when you can only get 1 cheese per round (At most 2 minutes per round) it takes quite a while to build up what you need.
With a room-wide chatbox, you can interact and communicate with tons of your mouse brethren. You can whisper to specific mice, or just yell something out to the entire room. If you need help with something, ask around and the friendly mice in the room will surely help you out!
Making things even better, if you save up 500 cheese, you can create a tribe! A tribe is basically a clan that you can invite people into, hang out with your friends, and you even get an awesome customizable room! Team up with your tribe, and dominate the scoreboards in a specific room, or try to compete in some shaman battles or bootcamp!
Talking not really your strong suit? You can still display your emotions with varying emotes ranging from blowing a kiss to crying or even to celebrating!
All in all, this game is pretty fun, so come play it! This game makes me go woah dude

Friday the 13th is an asymmetrical third person horror game that challenges 8 players to survive against iconic slasher villian Jason Vorhees, who is of course, a playable character. The game plays very different depending if you're a camp counselor or Jason. As a counselor, you must work together with others to complete several different objectives that will ultimately allow you to escape the camp. While these objectives can be completed alone, if you play against a competent Jason, teamwork is required to survive. Playing as Jason grants you four unique abilities which allow you to teleport across the map and take down counselors one by one. There are multiple counselors and Jasons to play as, each with their own set of abilities and stats to cater to many different playstyles. The devs are working on expanding the game and are continually adding new Jasons and counselors as well as an entirely new gamemode which is coming out soon. Overall this is a very enjoyable game, but like any other multiplayer focused game, it can only reach its full potential if you're playing with good people. 4.5/5

If you're like me, you played guitar WAY before even the original Rocksmith came out. I started playing 9 years ago and still love it to this day. However, at some point I stopped playing for a few reasons. Guitar is an instrument that suffers from feeling kind of lame if you aren't jamming with other people. Playing alone to a song is cool, for around an hour or two, but then you start wishing you had a drummer, or a singer, or a bass. Hence the reason why lots of people form bands and showcase their talent, put it to good use. I was like many who didn't have the opportunity growing up to join or form a band, I just simply didn't have enough friends that played instruments that would sound good together. That's when Rocksmith came around. I'm sure you understand the basic premise of Rocksmith. Simply put it's real life guitar hero. Notes come on the screen in vibrant colors to actual rock songs and you play along, except the catch is you play on a real guitar and are actually learning to play the songs. Great concept!
Here's the deal. Rocksmith will NOT teach the average Joe how to play guitar. The thing Rocksmith succeeds at is making guitar fun for people who already play guitar. I'm sure if you gave it your all you could learn to play guitar with Rocksmith, but it doesn't teach you how to read sheet music or tabs which are rather key in playing guitar outside of Rocksmith. Nevertheless, Rocksmith is awesome for people that play, and it also took me down a peg, realising that playing guitar is NOT like riding a bike. You don't just set it down for a couple years, then come back to it and start jamming to Holy Diver. You have to rebuild lost calluses, regain flexibility in your fingers, all that great stuff.
If you have never touched a guitar before and think you can learn how to play guitar from Rocksmith, that all depends on your determination but like I said before it doesn't teach you to read music. If you're a guitarist like me and are looking for something to bring back that initial spark in your marriage to your guitar then this is the preverbial sexy weekend getaway. With some drinks, a few half broken guitar picks, a spare pack of strings, and a whole lot of 80's hair metal.

I've played a number of roguelikes over the years, with ADOM being my most played game ever (over the past decade).  Caves of Qud has been on my following list for ~2 years and after seeing consistent weekly updates from the developer and a recently released roadmap of future features planned I decided to pick this up.
I've played ~26 hours at this point trying out a variety of characters and haven't had this much fun playing a game in a long time.  I think the difficulty in this game is just right - I am given more leniency to try things out without being killed immediately as in some of the more hardcore roguelikes, but I am still punished with YASD for acting foolishly - but learning from deaths is part of every roguelike.
You start the game deciding to play a mutated human or a True Kin/non-mutated human.  Mutants can be made into physical monstrosities (paralyzing scorpion stinger, burrowing claws, regeneration, body full of quills, etc)  psychic beings (teleporting, charming, shooting concentrated light/lasers, conjuring fire, etc) with you being able to improve each mutation upon leveling up, or spend a few mutation points to choose between 3 random ones.  With a wide variety of mutations you can make some really unique builds.   True Kins don't have access to mutations, but generally start with better gear and attributes, and gain skills at a much faster rate - sills like dismembering (cut of someone's face or legs... and eat them!), charging strike, meditation, tinkering/crafting, etc. As with mutants, you can choose to play a strong dumb oaf, an agile gunslinger, an artifact collector slinging grenades or freezing his enemies.
The world itself has a few set static locations but for the most part is procedurally generated (including procedurally generated quests that lead you to interesting locations) that keeps things fresh and interesting.  You may stumble upon a ruins, a legendary creature's lair, or simply get lost when wandering on the overland map.  Instead of traveling on the overland map, you can choose to travel on the local map where every few screens/zones is considered passing one tile on the overland map.  side from the overland map, there is also an underground biome that spans the entire game world, filled with treasures and monsters.
As nice bonus for players who aren't used to traditional roguelikes and memorizing 50 keys, CoQ streamlined actions into a single key that will perform the most logical action in the square you are targeting, such as looting and chatting to NPCs.  The game is easy to get into, and if you prefer to have less clutter in the UI you have the option you can change around the overlay to a few different options.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes roguelikes - for early access it is an extremely well fleshed out game with tons of content and AMAZING lore.  I think the reviews speak for themselves with a 98% overall thumbs up.

This game is what a true roguelike should be, a procedurally generated adventure that is only limited by your creativity. This starts with character creation, you can choose to be a True Kin, a pure human with advanced skills, or a mutant with the ability to modify their genes and attain obsurd powers and abilities. These mutations can manifest as physical traits, such as multiple arms to use more weapons, Nightvision to see in the dark, Regeneration to restore lost limbs and hitpoints. Mutations also add supernatural/psychic powers such as creating portals in space-time to banish enemies to a random location in the world(Or yourself) Pyromancy/Cryomancy, creating barriers or even cloning yourself to assist in combat. Both mental and physical mutations can be negatives to increase your creation points (Or challenge yourself). You may also choose a background that will buff your stats and start you off with random gear and some skills.
After character creation the game opens up to you. The world of Qud is a retro-future, post-human apocalyptic Tophet, the denizens here struggle everyday and the running currency is precious clean, drinkable water. The landscape is rife with tunnels, wells, caves , ruins, towns,  holy sites and fallen cities, quest specific areas (caves are procedural) are always the same but the land is dotted with randomized locations so each playthrough offers new exploration. Every creature belongs to a faction that exists in the world, flaura and fauna, and you can♥♥♥♥♥♥them all off, or try and befriend them, or instigate war between them.
You can choose to follow the main questline, or just wander the world in search of treasure/glory/scrap/artifacts or forbidden knowledge. The first few levels can be difficult, the first major quest you can recieve sends you to a low level dungeon to kill a creature and bring its corpse back to town, but this can prove difficult when a shotgun weilding,upright walking canine beast shoots a hole through your chest. I recommend killing creatures outside the starting town to gain a few levels. Whn you're ready, head out into the rust and find yourself, and die in increasingly hilarious ways. The game offers much more than I have experienced at this point and thats the beauty of it.
Caves of Qud is a masterwork Roguelike up there with Dungeoncrawl and Dwarf Fortress, winning isn't always possible but you'll always have a story after each playthrough.
All in all, for $10 bucks theres no reason this game shouldn't be in your library if you're looking for an endlessly fun Roguelike/RPG title.
TL:DR
If you combine Fallout, Dwarf fortress and Dungeoncrawl into a single game you get CoQ. Play it.

I got this game in a bundle and was very excited to try it because I've played countless zombie games on gaming websites like Kongregate and Newgrounds. I was very satisfied with my experience.
If you like text-based games, the zombie post-apocalypse theme, and crafting/strategy-based gameplay, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good, there are pictures of items you find and the delivery of the gameplay is very nice - given in the form of a journal with text/picture entries. The game is solely text-based, so do not play this if you do not like reading (or this genre). There are 3 game modes, one of which is endless (easy). The randomized character backgrounds and random events are well-done, however, one complaint I have is the very (seemingly) arbitrary way the character relationships is determined. More on this later.
The controls are simple and there is a brief tutorial to show you how to play. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with survival strategy games. The most challenging aspect of the game is balancing your actions (scout, search, fortify, etc) properly to maximize your chances for survival. You can modify a few elements like how often resource-generating buildings appear and  whether or not characters can get injured from in-group fighting.
The gameplay consists of performing specific actions every hour (equivalent of one turn). Actions include fortifying the building you are in, searching for items, building traps, etc. You can further specify the actions by clicking on keywords that are highlighted in green - for example, you can specify an order to build "traps," "experimental traps" (indoor), or outdoor traps. Certain actions generate noise that will draw in progressively larger groups of zombies. You can counteract this by sending survivors out to patrol, or by sniping surrounding zombies (trade-off is your use of ammo and potentially drawing in more zombies). If the building you are in gets completely surrounded, your characters will be severely restricted in the actions they can do. During the night, visibility is lowered and overall danger is increased.
You can either start with 1 survivor (easy mode) or 5, however, you can only gain new members in easy mode (which is also endless mode). The survivors will have randomized stats - these are given no numerical value. Stats include social economic status (poor, middle-class, rich), job, overall personality traits, and proficiency in actions (better at cooking, scouting, etc). All characters will also have a negative attribute, such as racism or distrust of the opposite sex. You can try to mitigate this by spreading rumors - one each day, and only one of each type. Rumors can be things like a cousin relationship between two characters or a charitable act for certain people. Rumors act as a double-edged sword - it will usually increase the relationship between the associated characters, however, it can also polarize survivors that do not like the associated characters (causing them to like each other even less). The relationship mechanic is crucial to survival because characters in conflict will argue and fight - dropping the overall morale of the group and potentially injuring people. Actions are also completed significantly slower when characters in conflict are near each other, so a good idea is to send polarized characters to different areas (or even sacrificing problem survivors). You can increase relationships by having feasts, but this requires a lot of food and will draw in zombies.
There is a randomized map with different structures in the city to explore. Special buildings yield bonuses like increased security (banks) and better loot/modifying (warehouses). Once you fully secure a building, you can further fortify it - eventually adding things like watchtowers, fences, and sniper posts. Fortifying takes a significant amount of time and will most likely attract larger groups of zombies. A downside of securing/fortifying a building is going back inside it - you will always need a survivor inside to let others in. If you leave a secured/fortified building with no one inside, you will have to break back in, however, there will never be zombies within. A good idea is to at least secure a few safehouses before proceeding to fortify.
There are different approaches you can take when playing this game, adding a decent amount of replayability. Overall, if you enjoy this genre, then you should really give Zafehouse a try.
Definitely recommend!

Almost three years ago I discovered the 7DRL version of Cogmind while skimming through the Devlog posts on IndieDB.  What caught my attention was a post from Kyzrati detailing the development of a full version of his Sci-Fi Roguelike prototype, the very clear expectations he had set for himself, and the passion he had for the project.  Jump to today and his passion has not abated.  The added features through community discussion are numerous, yet he has managed to remain true to his vision for the game.  I played regularly during the Alpha (up to Alpha 4) and played occasionally up to the Steam release to see how things were progressing.  Seeing the game progress hugely over the years has been impressive and the current result is, in my opinion, the best Roguelike available on Steam.
Cogmind is an ambitious game and succeeds in updating the Roguelike genre.  While the gameplay is turn-based it is not your typical Roguelike if you are used to playing Caves of Qud or Tales of Maj’Eyal.  There is no levelling in the traditional sense as there are no skill trees or initial customisation for your character.  Instead, levelling is strongly tied to the equipment you find/salvage/steal and will drastically change how you play the game.  As you ascend you increase the number of pieces of equipment you can equip and your base health.  Equipment can be damaged and destroyed so you will need to adapt and upgrade as you ascend through the levels.  Mechanically similar Roguelikes would include Brogue or The Ground Gives Way.  I personally prefer this system because as soon as you open the game you are in the world, making progress, and making tangible decisions.
This is a cliché, but expect to die…
.  Regularly dying early might give you the impression that there is not much to this game.  This is not the case.  The initial levels only give you access to a limited selection of what is on offer.  There are branching paths, wild variation in a vast range weapons and utilities, a large selection of hostile/neutral/allied robots, and an extensive, well-written lore.  After only a few hours of play you will find that you can progress through the early levels in about 10-15 minutes after which the game really opens up.  I have never successfully completed a run (
), but there are players that regularly beat the game with a variety of builds and the developer has created the game with the intention that every run has the potential to win.  Check out
YouTube channel if you want to see how it’s done.
You have a choice between using the traditional ASCII tiles or a graphical tile-set and by hitting F3 you can toggle between the two depending on preference.  No matter what you choose the visuals are beautiful and destructive with accompanying sound effects that really help to immerse you in the game’s world.  I use the ASCII tiles simply because I find it easier to parse the information on-screen due to the time spent with the 7DRL version.  The ASCII tile-set has a wide variation of fonts so you should be able to find one you prefer.  At this stage there is only one, official graphical tile-set, but player-made tile-sets are possible.
The lone developer has and continues to release regular improvements and additions to the game.  What is there is a complete and enjoyable gaming experience.  If you like following detailed, well-written progress updates I highly recommend checking out the

I'm really mixed on the recommendation. On the one hand I certainly did have fun, but on the other hand it really gets dull and the ending was cut stupidly short.
This is a puzzle platformer using multiple different colored rectangles that have different "abilities". Some jump higher than others, some float in water, some can fit into tight spaces. What makes this game cool is the good writing that gives names and character to the rectangles as if they were people. This makes the game a bit interesting and you'll push through the puzzles just to hear the next bit of narration. They did a good job of making the characters "interact". Note that it is all narration and no dialogue.
There are a lot of levels in this game and some of them are a lot of fun. However, some are overly simple and there seemed to be even more of them toward the end. About 3/4 of the way through the game, the mechanics will change slightly, which was a welcome thing, but it also takes away your "characters" and gives you new ones.  There is an "ending" and I will give them credit for the story leading to it properly, but all you get is a 5 second cutscene. They should have put a little more work into it.
Like I said, I had some fun, but so many of the levels are simple to the point of boring. I was ready for it to be over by the last chapter. If you're curious, I'd say pick it up on sale unless you treat games like movies where you spend $10 for 2.5 hours of entertainment. Then you might be ok paying full price, but I wouldn't be. I finished this in 3.5 hours.

- Great heavy metal music and dubstep music.

Steam users will need to buy the correct USB cord and (obviously!) a guitar, but guess what??? At least you can use that guitar sans-Rocksmith to play an actual instrument.  Take that, rinky-dink GH/RB peripherals.
A few noticeable downsides:
- You can't download certain songs from the previous generation of Rocksmith without buying the older version and THEN the accompanying DLC.  In other words...
- Game has a hard time recognizing certain notes, bends, harmonics, tuning-styles, etc.  For instance, you progress through a song based on your performance, starting with a basic "rendition" of the song to playing the whole thing note-for-note, but if the game refuses to recognize that you're in-fact playing the corresponding notes, it'll keep you at the same difficulty until you get it "right".  I've noticed that any song with E-flat tuning - on both my Strat and Les Paul -  will never yield consistent results.  Prepare to spend a lot of time tuning, dialiing in different combinations of tone and pick-up usage.
Lots of fun, works great on Windows 10 too. Very user friendly yet challenging. Don`t forget to buy the cable!

It's not perfect.  Far from it - but it's got some of what I want in a zombie game... none of them ever seem to pull it all together though so I can't complain... too much.  This one's got barricading locations, scavenging for loot that you NEED to survive, tension between the survivors, and permadeath.  It's kind of a tense game, even though it's mostly text based.  I breached a buildiing before scouting it - that was one big mistake.  One final, big mistake.  I sent three in to breach with what I thought were decent weapons and a good chance to make it back out.  Wrong.  So I send in the cavalry with upgraded guns and lot of ammo.  The three from the first group had fallen as the two remaining, wounded (why I didn't send them initially), survivors made it inside.  Then they quickly became - well... not survivors that's for sure.  Oooops.
So, negatives.  Yes, the above "story" isn't a negative.  Far from it.  My fault for not scouting first.  With "improved' binoculars... bringing me to a negative.  Modifying normal items to be "better" at what they're built to do in the first place.  It's stupid.  I can "upgrade" a butter knife.  You mean sharpen it I hope 'cause anything else is going to make it less good at ... buttering.  You can upgrade binoculars.  In a zombie apocalypse.  You can upgrade... binoculars.  Who the fudge has extra powerful lenses laying around for binoculars?  You "upgrade" firearms by making them "steady", or some other adjective... yeah, think the manufacturers did that already... so yeah, I hate the upgrade system.  Can't pick an item directly either, just upgrade a category of items and you get random bonuses.  Stupidest one I saw so far was upgrading, and get this, weights.  Yup... weights.  How the heck do you upgrade weights in the middle of a zombocaplypse? (that means a zombie apocalypse... it's obvious)  Food consumption and resting are random, as are playing chess, solitaire, drinking, etc.  Not much self control there people, plus they never get along, and I find the relationships to be rather cryptic - plus the "rumour" system could be useful to some degree - but I find it clunky.
I recommend this for what it is, just make sure you know what this game is before you buy it - and try to get in on sale for crying out loud.  Steam ALWAYS has sales.  Heck, it's 50% off right meow.
p.s. I wish I could combine several parts of this game in a blender with DayZ, 7 Days to Die, Rust, Rebuild 1 and 2 (if you haven't tried these, check out Sarah Northway's brainchildren.. and Rebuild 3 on the way), Dead State and State of Decay and have the perfect zombocalypse (I know, not a word - but I like it) game pop out.

Such a simple concept of zombie survival games, Survive and escape. Zafehouse: Diaries expands this, adding survivor skills, qualities, and the horror of a group collapsing in on each other. The greatest qualities are the randomization of your map, the three successful difficulty variations, and the personal customizations you can add to each time you play. Customizations like creating your own survivors and their occupations, locations on the map, weapons and tools to assist in your survival.
Now the few issues in this game. The inability to assign equipment can be an issue when defending or going on patrol, slightly annoying but it is best to stay quiet and hidden from zombies anyway. Another problem is the unrelenting force of zombies that'll attack after accidentally using unsilenced fire-arms, forcing you to relocate and wait until the coast is clear before returning for left behind supplies.
Beyond those two issues involving equipment usage; I can't see any other issues with the gameplay. The game runs very smoothly and I haven't had any issues between my computer and the game itself. Easily one of my favorite games out there, I recommend it to anyone whose looking for a strategy game with a simple goal and challenges to test your resolve to achieve that goal.

This is another game where I felt the concept was a good idea and I wanted it to be fun and challenging, but more often than not I just ended up being frustrated. The fact that every single character in the game has a violent outburst every few days if they hang out with someone they kinda don't get along with is a lazy way to show conflict and character interaction. Not to say the game is without merits; some of the customization options are fun to fiddle around with, but overall it's just another game to add to the pile of 'meh' zombie survival simulation games.

A survival/strategy game that feels a bit like a tabletop game. I enjoyed (and progressed) more when I changed the options to make it a bit easier and turn off in-fighting injuries. It's very easy for your survivors to hate each other - doing anything together except for killing zombies (like assaults) and feasts usually lowers relationships. The game can be a bit overwhelming at first, but once you learn how your options work you can find a strategy that works in clearing out the buildings with an acceptable amount of risk. In the easier modes you can pretty safely clear houses and go through every building (assuming you don't run out of ammo) but in the mode with a time limit you'll have to take on some risk and push forwards to get the objectives in time. RNG can often end the game, so if you don't like to constantly restart you may need to manually copy save files (the game deletes them when your party wipes).

If there was a middle option between recommending and not recommending the game, I would gladly take it.
On the one hand I did enjoy building bridges, finding solution to specific locations and requirements.
But on the other hand, I felt a little bit cheated and lied to, thinking as I did that I would have to build sensible bridges for sensible situations, using proper planning and logic. But then I found myself building not just bridges, but also ridiculous ramps and swings, building death-defying contraptions to get a bus across as if it were a non valuable crate that could risk being destroyed, building Rube Goldberg machines of getting motorized vehicles from point A to point B that made no engineering sense but just fit the materials and budget I was allowed.
The most infuriating was that it often felt like moving a connecting point a single pixel to the side could be the difference between utter failure and glorious success. As a consequence I ended up just moving pixels about until it finally worked, which is not how I normally like to proceed.
Writing all of this, I do wonder why I'm even pressing the recommend button instead of the other one, but I still had some fun building some of the less ludicrous bridges in the less implausible situations. When all is said and done I guess this is a game to enjoy not any longer than it is actually enjoyable.

This is, hands down, the absolute best example of an EA game to date on the Steam platform.
You only need visit the community hub and check out the update topic to see how much care and attention they pour into CoQ every single week. They've also done lots of interviews about the game and engage with their community regularly. If you're looking for your first EA game to see a game grow and what developers put into a project, please consider supporting the development of CoQ. If there's any team that deserves your support, it's this one.
As for the game, I've put in a hand full of hours into CoQ, but the game is so vast and deep that I'd be remiss to say I can provide anyone with a worth while review on the game itself. What I can say is that the character creation process is very, very deep and the world you can explore is extremely open and full of unique situations you will not find in other games. The game is also very challenging depending on how you apporach it and the potential for RP (if you're into it) is there in spades.
Overall, Freehold Games is creating a very fun world to explore full of sentient doors, mutant heroes, and off the wall creatures that will kill you many, many times. It's well worth picking up in its current state, as even just a few minutes with the game will show you its depth and amount of customization, and a few hours will show you the size of the world you'll be exploring. Try it out!

Excellent game. I hate early access titles, but roguelikes are inherently suited to be early access titles because you will be replaying the same content whether it is finished or not. I can tell that CoQ has always been a labor of love; it was a great game before the graphics and sounds were added, but their addition has only reinforced the quality of the game.
CoQ stands out among other roguelikes for it's unique setting, simulation, and adventures; sharing many of the things that make Dwarf Fortress great, but without the tediously detailed simulation found in adventure mode. The closest comparison I can provide would be the differences between D&D Basic/Expert/Companion/Master/Immortal and AD&D 1e. Both are essentially the same game, but in practical execution one is bogged down by procedures and rules [AD&D], and the other is free to circumvent simulation when it aids the flow of gameplay.
I could easily find myself buying this again on other platforms.

Today we’re bringing you Cogmind, a fairly decent Rouge Like game but god damn it’s hard to get into it.
When I say Rouge Like game I actually mean Rouge Like, not rouge LITE which most people get wrong. A Rouge LITE would be The Binding of Isaac or Magicide, a Rouge Like would be for example Sword Of The Stars: The Pit. and Cogmind fits in the Rouge Like genre, it’s a turn based, RPG type, adventure game, that is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥to get into.
The game starts without launching to a menu, it doesn’t send you into a tutorial on your first start up it just tosses you in, tells you to go ♥♥♥♥ yourself, and leaves. That’s basically the first 30 seconds of the game. After your first crushing defeat, having no idea what the hell is going on, you start picking up on small things. Now you know how to attach your wheels, how to shoot your guns, which mind you is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing annoying, and what some of the modules do.
While starting your first game you’ll probably be overwhelmed by the UI, it’s a little bit spooky and has a lot of information on it. Don’t worry about it for now, it’s best to just play through a couple times and slowly learn about the data and what it means instead of sitting down building a spreadsheet with all the info you have. The game isn’t an entrance exam to university, the best way to learn is multiple attempts.
It’s an incredibly difficult game to just jump into, but once you get past that initial hour you start figuring things out and can enjoy the story of this game, and jesus there’s a lot of story content in this game. In a single play through you won’t be able to learn about the entire world, only sections written in Terminals that you must hack to gain access to. Cogmind has an incredibly in-depth well written world.
The game has a pretty neat art aesthetic as well, it can be a little daunting again trying to figure out what everything looks like but you can change whether you want the ASCII art style, or basic textures. personally I’d recommend playing in the ASCII version, I find the Textures to be a little lacking and not very interesting compared to something like Sword of The Stars.
There’s a lot of interesting ways you can play the game as well, you could build yourself to be a massive tank with huge weapons shooting rockets, lobbing grenades, blowing up walls. You could also be a stealthy cheeky beaver burrowing through walls, avoiding your targets. There are plenty options for you to experiment with, you can even try being a Robot Samurai with the Katana’s, though I think you’ll die pretty damn quick
One problem I had was the lack of music in the game. Hopefully this is something the dev is looking at as this game is in Early Access.
I do find this game to not be as in depth as Sword Of The Stars: The Pit but it is still something worth checking out. Personally I’d wait for there to be a sale to purchase this game right now if you’re not really into Rouge Likes, but if you are a fan of this genre you need to pick this game up now.

This is the first time I have ever left a review/recommendation for any game on Steam, but I think if there was ever a game to deserve a positive review it is this one.
First of all, no hyperbole, but the developer is involved with the community in such a huge way, more so than any other game out there. I've never seen someone take the time to respond not only to criticism at large, but to each and every detail of any criticism posted on any site, anywhere.
I got involved towards the end of the alpha cycle for this game and played a decent amount before the beta release and Steam release. I'm not very good, but getting better! And each play-through is fun, no matter what.
This is by design, but the first bit of each play-through often feels more like survival than anything else. It can be slower and the range of experiences diverge less, but once you make it out of the first few levels (and unlock a healthy number of slots to equip modules, weapons, etc.) the game definitely opens up much more. There are tons and tons of opportunities for all kinds of strategies, though those end up being sort of dependent on what types of items/weapons you find lying around. Nevertheless, the depth is there. There are so many interconnected systems at play: you can be a massively power-producing hover-bot with tons of lasers, matching battery banks, and cooling systems... or you can be a stealthy, ice-cold (literally cryogenic), katana-wielding, sneak on wheels... or a hacker who can send out drones to scout the map for you... or a huge armored tank that levels entire rooms with rocket barrages... and the list goes on. Once you begin to understand how all the systems work, you really start to see the huge opportunities for all different types of builds.
However, my absolute favorite experiences with the game (so far) have been in some of the scripted events you can come across. One time, I stumbled onto a few friendly robots about to perform a heist, only to find myself ambushed and in the middle of a huge firefight once the heist went awry - though they had just opened up a vault full of super powerful propulsion systems and missiles, allowing me to basically become a fighter jet. Or recently, I found and booted up a group of robots that pledged their allegiance to me and helped me out of an impossible situation.
There is a lot to love about this game and the developer is very transparent and active about what is happening with the game. I definitely recommend it!

This game is by no means perfect - it  still has poor hit registration, countless amounts of both infuriating and hilarious glitches, and more. This would normally be a deal breaker for a lot of people - especially considering these problems were much, much worse on launch. But Ubisoft listened - they, since almost Day 1, have been listening to community feedback along with interacting with the community to fix the game and turn it around. While they have not turned it around completely (Like I said, there are still issues), they have turned it around to a state where these bugs and irritating moments can ultimately be casted away because of the extraordinarily tense, action-packed, fun gameplay this game has. Be it trying to win a ranked match to finally ascend to Diamond by defending the bomb site against 4 enemies, or just the sheer thrill of placing a breaching mat onto a barricade to explode into pieces as you rappel inside, this game is extremely fun - there's honestly no fancy way to put it, the gameplay itself is simply addictive, rewarding, and fun. It really checks all the boxes.
But then there's how Ubisoft treated the DLC. First off, everyone is given everything for free - Season Pass holders get the stuff (Each Season normally has 1 map and two Operators) early, but ultimately everyone can play that without spending an extra dime on some premium subscription. Normally, you would expect there to be a catch - perhaps insidious microtransactions that offer gameplay upgrades to players who spend their money on RNG crates, for instance. But no - Ubisoft has shown their dedication to the players by basing their primary revenue off each Year's Season Pass (Mentioned earlier) and the mind-numbing amount of cosmetics offered to each and every single weapon and Operator. The loot crates, called Alpha Packs, only contain cosmetics. There are no P2W mechanics whatsoever - this, combined with free content every 3 or so months for all, is just simply fantastic and shows their dedication to the players.
TL;DR: Does it have it's flaws? Yes - I'm not going to hide that fact. It can be a frustrating glitchy experience at times, or maybe you were sure you blasted a 5.56 round into someone's skull yet the game didn't register it. But that is completely overshadowed by the exhilrating gameplay and fantastic post-launch treatment Ubi has delivered to the players. Totally worth it.

Jazzpunk is fun and clever with it's dry humor and pop culture references. There are fun little mini-games throughout the story to encourage the player to exploring each passing level. This should be a $10 game at most.  Get this game when it's on sale. It's a 7/10 for me.
