I want to like this game, I really do. It has a great 'board game' feel to it and it has all the components for a good game. Unfortunately, it breaks down pretty quickly once you start playing.
First off, you can't assign people equipment unless they're moving to a location. I can have the greatest gear in the world, loaded up with a fire axe, motorcycle clothing, and even guns, but my patrolling people will still go outside naked with a pocket knife and then complain about getting mauled. The gear they will use seems to be pretty random too, as survivors just grab whatever they feel like when they need it. Did a zombie break in? Well, let's just shoot it with the irreplaceable crossbow bolts instead of using the silenced pistol with a million rounds of ammo, or the perfectly good fire axe. The will use armor on defense, but only against zombies.
"Who else might attack them", you might wonder. Well, how about your psychopathic survivors? Every. Single. One. Is a psychopath, one bad mood away from murdering someone in cold blood. I don't know if it's a bug or if this game is in KKK central, but murderously racist characters are the most common characters around. There's also a lot of class division, and any and all quarrels are solved by violence. They'll even interrupt important jobs just so that they can wound each other, and then have the gall to be upset when the corpse pile they were supposed to dump came back to life to attack them. And this isn't because they're cooped up too long in one place, they'll start up this garbage the second they're left in the same building. Maybe it's social commentary about what the makers think would happen if you could murder people without police involvement, but given that even the former police officers in this game are cold blooded killers, I really can't say.
With all this hostility to work around, your best bet is to separate your characters into two or three groups. This would work great, if it weren't for the fact that the zombies are psychically drawn to your survivors. If you barricade fast you can fight a losing battle to keep them out, but having to juggle two or three groups will result in stupid injuries (due to refusal to use logical equipment) and inevitable break-ins (since you rarely have two survivors in the same place to watch each other's backs).
With all of these negatives noted however, if you can get a pair or more of survivors in the same place without anyone killing one another, you can actually see some of the potential shine through. There was some serious promise in this game, and if you could assign equipment to people then I would actually recommend this game. Because you can't, you'll get buried underneath the inevitable endless horde of psychic zombies who will wear your stupid naked survivors down until you lose, as you can't really expand or explore when you're having to constantly stay on the defensive. If they ever patch out the insane, murderous survivors so that you could have a proper party together, I'd recommend this game. Since they seem to have abandoned the title though, I'd recommend you play something else. This is definitely not worth $10.
Too long, didn't read: Insane survivors who kill each other at the drop of a hat combined with a lack of an inventory system make this a bust. There's better games out there for $10.

I really enjoy this game. It's simple in theory, but very hard to execute and survive, as it should be. There's a reason you hardly see anyone around in zombie apocalypses.
The customizable features are Survivors, Occupations (which is where all of the characteristics go into), location photos, and items. The only real problems I see here are the following:
Characters always seem to have a problem with a certain type of people, whether it be race or status, and that itself doesn't seem to be customizable, which is a shame, as it seems to have a big effect on how a character feels towards another.
Ages are 21-65. Sucks when you want to create kids (and have them be pretty much useless of course), or elderly. I faced this problem when creating Walking Dead survivors, where a few are kids, and Hershel is older than 65.
The game itself is interesting. Start with either one survivior, and meet more along the way (perhaps), or start with 5 and try to escape. When personalities battle against eachother, it is largely detrimental to the group's morale and makes it much harder to survive. Every now and then, a randon event will occur, whether it be a group of survivors demanding that your hand over your priest, or a super zombie shows up. Managing the group's resources is challenging, and not gathering new resources will quickly destroy your group.
If a survivior is on watch, they will mention the noise level of the group, and that seems to have a huge effect on whether or not zombies will attack. It's a nice realistic feature, and it appears to work. When my group died and the last survivor was a useless woman who couldn't do a thing right, she still survived for many hours in a futile effort to build awful traps. That is, until I ran out of food and sent her out to scavenge more, followed promptly by her death at the hands of zombies.
It's not perfect, but it's at a state where it's fun, challenging, and time consuming. I've yet to survive, unfortunately.
Two major concerns I see when reading other reviews or posts about this game is about the unrealistic...ness of the personalities and the lack of updates. The personalities aren't perfect, yes, but whoever complains about this seems to think that, in a zombie apocalypse, survivors will immediately band together and work together perfectly, in unison, because of the zombie threat. Definitely sounds like a false premise. As for the updates, they're completely done with the game, but they supplied updates for as long (perhaps even longer) as games normally do, and the product is great as is. If you want a new update, wait for their new game, which pretty much has the same exact premise as this, but in a new scenario.

Empire TV Tycoon is an easy to learn fun simulation where you run a tv channel.
As you increase viewership and make those important decisions on what to play and what ads to show, you can climb the ranks from a simple local channel to the world of satellite broadcasting.
Part of the game is programming your day's viewing - which sounds more tedious or daunting than it actually is.
You will recognise some movie titles, and the spoofs of well-known award shows and film festivals. This adds to the immersive side of Empire, and it can be quite fun (if not diabolical) to plan a day's tv viewing based on your favourite films... or least favourites...
You can hire staff, including a scriptwriter which is pretty key if you intend to do the optional portion of entering the aforementioned film festivals and award shows. The scripts themselves don't really make sense, which is a bit of a shame overall, and you end up just looking at the script rating before deciding to tear it up (with the rather satisfying sound effect) or keeping it to make the film.
Making films is pretty straight forward, as you have a studio floor where you hire stars (spoofs of actual stars or iconic movie characters) and decide on the format for your script - tv movie, tv series, feature big budget, etc. You can enter these films in the festivals and then sell them later on after you've screened them on your channel.
You can fill the world with John Waters tributes, or cringe-worthy game shows. Or Meryl Streep performances - the world is your oyster. You call the shots.
Overall gameplay is simple - after my second play through I had already "won" the default game, and had moved onto custom and setting up harder win options. Some people have complained about the AI getting upgrades when you do, but there is a way to uncheck that in the custom options. Others don't like having to take the elevator all the time, but given this isn't Tower Sim or Hotel Sim, using the elevator doesn't really take away that much from time or game play. In fact, it probably adds to the immersion... running a TV station involves a lot of running about.

Let me give you a rundown on a situation you may run into in Cogmind.
You've just finished sneaking around a busy factory, waiting as scout and informer units pass by. You spot an engineer trudging along, rebuilding delapidated walls. You sneak up to it and attack it with a Datajack, a makeshift hacking device only usable at short range. Miraculously, you succeed in accessing the engineers inner systems - of which you have the option to gather information about the droid, attempt to overload its systems, or link it with your own, allowing you to see what it sees. You decide to try and link with it, but it fails, and the engineer quickly runs off down the corridor. You are unable to catch up to it as you are equipped with aluminium legs you acquired from dismantling a combat drone earlier, and they arent fast enough to catch the engineer before it alerts an Informer, who then alerts the combat units in the area. Positioning yourself, you wait for the drones to reach your location so you can tear the parts from their burnt, metal carcasses and use them for yourself. Seeing them approach, you open fire with your weapons - a grenade launcher, beam gun, and particle cannon. All three miss, with the grenade hitting an adjacent wall, blowing it open. Another droid emerges from the debris, and begins firing at you. Its missiles destroy two of your weapons and reduces the integrity of one of your power cores. The battle rages on, and you manage to destroy one of the three combat bots, but not before your power cores give way to the fire. You begin to run. Passing through a door, you look for an empty room to hide in, but before you can progress any further, your aluminium legs are severed by a blade trap. Unable to move much faster than a tile a turn, you decide you will wait. The room you are in has two large machines that you know from past experience are very, very volatile, and you still have your grenade launcher handy, albeit in its disrepair.
A few turns later, after lying in a pile of broken parts and your own dispair, 5 combat droids enter the room.
You press F to target, aim at the machines, and fire.
Based on a true story - this was my very first run.

I've been playing roguelikes since 2002 (ADOM, TOME, Crawl, Angband, etc), so I know a thing or two about roguelikes.  I've been playing Cogmind since 2015 when it was still in Alpha, so I know a thing or two about Cogmind.  This allows me to make the following statement with 100% accuracy and confidence:
Cogmind is an amazing roguelike.
It's really one of the best games I've ever played and I can't recommend it enough.  It's first and foremost a game of tactics and strategy like DCSS and it allows for a wide variety of playstyles and ways to overcome (or outright avoid) foes.  Unlike crawl, and like ADOM, it features a deep world full of NPCs with a rich storyline.  I won't spoil the plot, but it's so much more interesting than your standard let's save the world schlock.
The UI puts the game in a league of its own.  It's polished, its intuitive, its convenient, there's no other roguelike out there that's simultaneously this rich and this easy to get into.  If you've been holding off on playing roguelikes out of a fear that they're all convulted ASCII messes like Dwarf Fortress, this a great roguelike to be your first.  The gorgeous tiles don't hurt either.
Your average winning run lasts about 4-5 hours, so it's longer than DoomRL, but perhaps shorter than ADOM or TOME.  One thing that's great about the game is that unlike most roguelikes, the end game isn't the easiest part.  In Crawl or ADOM once you've gotten your character off the ground, you'll usually die only due to fatigue or sloppiness.  In Cogmind, conversely, the challenge doesn't nose dive towards the end.  Quite the opposite.  It takes a lot of concentration to win, and you'll feel like you've accomplished something when you do beat this wonderful game.
This game is worth the asking price.  You owe it to yourself to pick this one up.  Trust me.

I've been closely following the development of Cogmind for almost four years (almost since the start, really). Don' be scared by the fact that it is early access: it already was an awesome game to play from the first alpha, and is has only gotten better since! And it is more polished and bug-free than many big-budget games are on their official release.
Cogmind can probably best be described as a turn-based scifi stealth-action modernised traditional roguelike. And no, "modernised traditional" is not an oxymoron in this context.
"Roguelike as in Spelunky?" Well... no... that's what the "traditional" signifies. Explaining what a traditional roguelike would take too long - search "Nethack" and do a wikipedia dive. The important bit is that the focus in these games is weaving intricate, interconnected game systems together. Gameplay consists of meaningful choices, where the world built out of these systems responds to us poking and prodding it, to create a rich experience in the process. Graphics often take a backseat to that, and you need to use your imagination to immerse yourself. The richness of the game system usually makes that quite easy!
The downside of all the complexity usually is that the interface also suffers, with I-don't-know how many special commands for input (imagine a fantasy game, like NetHack. In them, you can usually use, zap, drop, throw, break, give, and even (try to) eat a wand.
, and that's just the tip of the iceberg). But not with Cogmind! The interface of this game is streamlined and user-friendly - I am an interface designer by profession and training, and I
this game's interface so incredibly much: it can be completely mouse-controlled, completely keyboard-controlled, or both, and everything about it is incredibly polished.
Same with the gameplay: from the player's perspective, this game is as complex as you want it to be. Instead of requiring you to read a huge manual before you can even get started, you can just start to move around, pick up some gear and equip it, and start shooting your way out, without knowing anything about the intricate systems that make the game tick.
However, to enjoy it to the most, you should be the type to like diving into the various game systems. But her too, Cogmind makes this as easy and frictionless as possible. The whole thing is set up to give elegant, in-game access to learning how the systems work. Hovering over anything gives you information pop-ups, right-clicking gives bigger pop-ups with EVEN MORE detailed information. Want to compare two items? Right click on one, then another, and it will also show the difference in stats for easier comparison! So pick apart the stats decide when to use wheels and when to use robo-legs. Or play it like a mindless coffee-break game, pick up the first weapons you see and shoot every hostile bot that comes your way, and see how far you get until you're inevitably overwhelmed, pew pew!
And that's just the interface! Cogmind pushes traditional roguelikes into new ground on so many different fronts: the UI, the ASCII art animations, the sound design, the game mechanics themselves. I could go on for hours praising this game!
This is all the brain-child of one man: Josh Ge, a.k.a. Kyzrati. He is very reliable and open to user-feedback. When I replied to one of his blog-entries that I am color-blind and had some trouble with the colour scheme at times, he immediately started working on ways to avoid that: adding other non-color ways of communicating status, a mod-friendly system for the color palette, and so on. How amazing is that?
Carl Sagan once said "If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe." I think he was making a philosophical point, but Josh must have mistaken it for a dare. Cogmind is the product of a person who loves a genre of games so much that he broke it down, obsessively deconstructing
about it: evaluating, re-evaluating and re-re-evaluating every design decision, every convention, basically every aspect you can think of, again and again, to get to the essence of what a roguelike
. And in the process, from the ground up, he meticulously crafted this game.
If you have read his (highly recommended) devlog, I'm sure you agree with me that he has worked on this with an almost disturbing level of devotion for four years. This is a Herculean labour of love. And for what purpose? To drag traditional roguelikes kicking and screaming into modernity, so that everyone else will see what it is that he loves so much about them. In my opinion, that makes it a work of art. And luckily for of us, a damn good game.

So, what can I say about this game? It's a modern Resident Evil title. It took a few good things from Revelations 1, one nice thing from the old titles and a lot of bad stuff from a lot of other Resi titles. But I'm getting ahead of myself.
If you want to skip the lengthy part of my review, you can find the pros and cons list below.
First things first: the story.
The story is a bit bigger this time around. For one thing, it's because of the fact that it features five campaigns. On the other hand it's because this time the story centers around the fate of the world - AGAIN! Well. But it doesn't feel as insignificant as Revelations 1 since you'll be fighting against a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥in the USA, China, Edonia and other places. An organization by the name of Neo Umbrella has risen and is terrorizing the world with... well... bioterrorism. Like in all the other games. But the game looks better than its predessecors. So that's a plus. Anyway. The main character cast centers around Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Sherry Birkin, Ada Wong along with their respective sidekicks. Also there's Albert Wesker's son but I won't spoiler anything. These people are trying to save the day by defeating Neo Umbrella. That's more or less the gist of it.
Fans of the old games will be pleased to hear that you'll be fighting classic zombies from time to time. When you first start the game with Leon you'll be watching limping half-corpses around a city in the USA and when you're in China you'll be seeing them there, too. On enemy variety the devs were pretty creative again. But nothing too new tbh. You got the classic zombies, you got the J'avo. The J'avo are somewhat like the Majini and Ganados, only more extreme and instead of a parasite there's a virus responsible for their mutations. The J'avo have some surprises up their sleeve when it comes to mutations so that's not all too bad. These are the main enemy types. But the bosses are where it's really at. Remember El Gignte? You'll be fighting a couple of those in this game (not like the farce of an El Gigante in RE 5). Then there's a bunch of hulking creatures of plates and muscle with are ♥♥♥♥ing annyoing to defeat because they're bullet sponges. And some other boss battles with a giant, invisible snake, crazy people who thought injecting a dose of the virus into themselves was a good idea (didn't see THAT one coming *chuckles*) and some other♥♥♥♥♥♥I don't wanna spoiler.
But wherever there's an enemy, there oughtta be a weapon to defeat it, right? Yes! Weapons wise there's a lot. In every campaign you'll be getting different weapons and every character you play as has a different set of starting weapons to begin with. Over the course of each campaign you'll acquire new weapons and you will find a lot of uses for each of them. And yes, there's an elephant killer magnum gun again. But as always, it's ♥♥♥♥ing hard to find any ammo for this thing so hear my advice and use it in boss battles or if absolutely nessecary. Like when you'll be fighting against those chainsaw ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (that are EVEN harder to kill this time around). Aside from that there's a bunch of stationary weapons and some are one time use only.
But the best part about this is: in theory you don't even need weapons most of the time because they finally improved the melee combat. meaning that you can now punch and kick your way through  hordes of enemies. Given that they don't shoot you down. Warning: not recommended on harder difficulties because it's generally a dumb idea to only do melee fighting in any Resi game. Well, usually if you have to do that you're bsaically screwed and might as well start over. In this one you can deal considerable damage to your enemies with melee combat. Which is a plus. Also the animation set for melee combat is quite nice to look at.
On the technical side of things the game runs fine on highest setting, no FPS drops, no crashes. Only one time it didn't recognize my save file but that problem was quickly sorted out so fear not, you won't have any technical issues with this one. At least I didn't have any.
Game mechanics wise there's a lot of stuff I didn't like and some stuff I was really fond of. As I mentioned earlier, there's half-decent melee combat now, which is a plus. Then you may move while aiming and shooting. First Resi game that brought that one to us was Revelations 1, I believe. Which is a great plus. They finally noticed just how useful this feature is. Knife fighting is no more, you instead screw 'em with your guns in melee combat. Also a good idea. What else? Well, you can walk, run, shoot, hit, die, survive, climb, jump down (a lot of these actions may require you to stand at specific positions however. Resi style) and, when playing with Ada, use your grappling hook.
Oh and there's skills now. Like, you collect skill points and after each chapter or so you can buy and upgrade skills with them. The idea's nice but ultimately useless as I didn't use them all that often. Only scenario where I could imagine them being useful would be on the really high difficulties that aren't even fun anymore.
Also the partner mechanic is back but it isn't annyoing anymore. Now enemies target your partner too (not like RER) and you almost never have to worry about them dying (unlike RE5).
Aside from that it's standard 3rd Person Shooter. Oh, but wait!
They are back. More gloriously than ever before. They Q to the T to the E. QTE sections en masse with this game. I mean, I can understand it having a few QTEs in the game. But in Resi 6 they are pretty much used excessively. Not as bad as most of the reception is putting it but it's not like they had any QTEs left after this one. There are a lot of scenes where you just have to smash a few buttons to come forward and avoid death. At least some of the QTEs are creative in the sense that they require you to click at a specific time. But yeah, they're still QTEs.
What else?
I got a few gripes with this game QTE wise, yeah. But the worst part is that the credits are unskippable. That wouldn't be so bad if:
The credits weren't so long because a trillion people worked on this game and
you wouldn't have to watch them five times.
Why five times? Well, there are five campaigns and after completing each campaign you are required to watch those unskippable, long♥♥♥♥♥credits.
And the final piece of information will be the subtle humour in the game which is most prevalent in Jake's campaign because Jake is just the badass guy who doesn't give a ♥♥♥♥ about most of it and just does his thing along with his audible drek. It's funny, really. Mostly anyway.
So, to wrap this up, pros and cons!
Pros:
+ Improved graphics
+ The story isn't too bad (and feels WAY more significant than RER's)
+ Most of the mechanics in the game are improved
+ Different animation sets for a lot of enemies (not unlike some OTHER games. Yeah RE5, I'm lookin' at you)
+ Oldschool zombie slashing action in the first few hours of the game bringing back good memories
+ Awesome death scenes. Seriously, to die in this game can look pretty cool. There's even an achievement for that
+ Fairly good melee combat and gunplay
+ Ludicrous bosses that are even more crazy than before (I like that stuff)
+ Good enemy variety
+ NO QTEs IN CUTSCENES
+ Replayability because you can choose between two characters playing a campaign and each of them is a different approach
+ And more
Cons!
- A thousand QTEs
- Unskippable credits
- Linear gameplay and story (as always)
- Horror? Lol, no
- Boring "puzzles"
- You'll die frequently because of some QTEs
- I got nothing more honestly
Would I recommend this game? Yeah, it's good for what it does.
At 20 bucks? Maybe think about it. If you're a hardcore Resi fan then yes, if you just like 3rd person shooters wait for a sale.

Poly Bridge is a puzzle game structured in a way that is pretty similar to Zachtronics's puzzle games (SpaceChem, Infinifactory, etc). Most individual puzzles present the player with a discrete challenge - for example, build a bridge at an incline, or use ramps to jump a gap. Poly Bridge does a pretty good job at teaching the player new building techniques through these puzzles, as opposed to elongated tutorials you might see in other games.
Your solution is evaluated in three ways: how much it costs, how much stress it endures, and how much space it occupies. Optimizing these three gives this game an insane amount of replayability. The leaderboards are pretty useful for giving you a feel for how much room for improvement you have, although the top of the leaderboards is predictably filled with hackers. This part of the game could definitely be improved. Filtering out hackers would be nice. Being able to see other players' designs would be a huge improvement as well, similar to Dustforce. This would probably be locked behind some completion gate so players can't ruin the experience for themselves, or you could opt out of sharing your solutions.
Poly Bridge's least fun mechanic is the occaisional inconsistency of bridges. It doesn't come up often, but there are times where you can test a bridge, delete a segment, re-make that same segment, and then run the bridge again with different results. I've never noticed this problem outside of optimizing after solving a puzzle, but it's very frustrating when it happens.
Poly Bridge's second least fun mechanic is gif exporting. There are no export options to speak of, and the presets are awful. Gifs export at about 500x300 (unnecessarily small), play at 15 frames per second (unnecessarily slow), and cannot exceed about 10 seconds (unnecessarily short). These limitations would make sense in 2002; they're ridiculous in 2017.

This is hands down one of the most fun ways to learn how to play Electric Guitar or Bass. When you plug the RealTone USB cable into your computer or console, it simulates all the amps, pedals, and effects you would use for the songs in the game. Also, owning the previous version of the game gets you access to a much larger song library. I've been learning how to play bass since about April of 2015, and I LOVE my Rocksmith 2014! Want to learn to play guitar? Get this game!

Rocksmith 2014 allows teaches you to play guitar or bass, well kinda.
Rocksmith 2014 is the updated version of rocksmith, There is so many improvments that these should be considered seperate games instead of an update. The menu is more user friendly, Instruments react and register better, around 60 new songs. I forgot to mention, this game helps you learn guitar, real guitar not the plastic axe from rockband or guitar hero. To play this you need a real guitar, It does not matter which guitar as long as it works and is a decent guitar. You can get something playable for around the $100 dollar mark, if you are new you might want to get a squire or epiphone guitar. People who already play guitar just need the USB cable, It has to be the Ubisoft Real tone cable, There is a no cable patch but you really need to get the real tone cable to actually make any progress. It should be $30 MSRP.
This game has guitar lessons and minigames that should get you on your self taught way to learning guitar, They are decent and provide enough explanation to learn, however it will take time for newbies to get used to thier intstruments. I was an experienced guitarist before this game came out and played the previous rocksmith, Experienced guitarists will want to learn the songs that the game has. The game comes with around 60 songs, most of them are songs that are well known and are fun to play, Not including the base game, there is over 500 songs to learn so there is something for everyone. Blues, Metal, Rock, Chances are this game has music you like.
There is a learning curve for learning the game interface, but to be honest, if you want to learn guitar or bass then there will be a huge learning curve, guitar is a great hobby and this game is amazing for newbies or experienced guitarists wanting to learn songs without having to worry about playing it wrong. The mechanics are well executed and allow you to practice sections of songs.
You will have to invest in a good guitar and the realtone cable, but rocksmith gives you the basics of guitar. Those who really want to learn the instrument instead of just playing it will seek further guidence but rocksmith is an amazing way to start off. I wish i had this when i started playing.
Should you buy this, if you can afford a guitar, the cable, and the DLC songs you like, then yes. Don't go in expecting to be instantly good, like any hobby practice makes perfect.

If you make mistakes you can hear them clearly, much better to learn the songs to eventually play outside of Rock Smith

is rare not just for the unusual creation that it is (a mostly-text, indie, turn-based strategy survival simulator set in the zombpocalypse) but also for the fact that it makes generous allowance for the player's imagination to engage and enhance the experience.  That imagination factor is a feat which the majority of videogames - in striving for linear, accessible stories and/or impressive visuals & audio - leave little or no room for.

's work here is admirable considering it was a startup with only two guys.  Their next planned project,
is a similar game set in space.  If they do carry over and improve upon the mechanics from Zafehouse, I am definitely picking it up.  For context, I got Zafehouse on Good Old Games a while back, but over time it's been patched into better shape.  My 11 or so hours played as of this writing reflect the time it took me to replay every game mode, grab the achievements for a perfect game and fiddle with the custom content a bit.
Zafehouse has three modes that scale in difficulty from easy to hard:
The game randomly generates your survivors and the town map, then you direct them to essential tasks while progressing one hour at a time.  The story is as barebones as zombie apocalypse gets but there's decent replayability thanks to the gameplay, at least until such time as you've mastered the mechanics on the standard modes and played out custom scenarios to your satisfaction.  Gameplay is a finely tuned balancing act involving staying alive and safe, keeping survivors happy (or at least not at each others' throats) and finding/managing scarce resources while accomplishing objectives within the mission parameters.  The relationship system really does add flavor to the experience and I would love to see more along these lines in gaming.
Perhaps it's not so finely tuned as we would like, but as far as I know this game is one of a kind and the formula can only be improved upon over time.  I'm willing to overlook some design and balance issues as well as lack of depth & complexity in mechanics.  What visual and audio does exist is also limited - serviceable, but not awe inspiring.  There are no technical issues or bugs whatsoever and the game is very low resource, which is unsurprising given that it's a small game.  What you see in the screenshots on the Steam store page really is what you get.
One thing that I had tons of fun with was the custom content manager which I used to create a group of survivors based on my family & friends.  Dropped them into a town with locations based on my own favorite hangouts, and imported pics for all of it.  As I said initially, this is a game that encourages the imagination, and that is all the more true when you get to play out the apocalypse scenario with familiar people and places.
I recommend
if, as in my case, this game immediately caught your eye as something different in the genre and potentially fun.  Normally I make no comment about price or promotions, but I would probably pick this up while it's on sale.  The biggest red flag to be aware of however is that the
.  The journal provides 90% of the information you need to play the game.  I realize that's not for everyone, but for those who aren't revved up at the prospect of reading a wall of text, I will just say by the time you're familiar with the mechanics, you'll be skimming through it very quickly and painlessly.  In closing my reviews I usually provide a few tips but I'll keep that light here, since the fun of Zafehouse includes learning and mastering aforementioned mechanics.

Zafehouse: Diaries isn't well known for it's moving pictures, but does keep you on your toes with it's survivor management gameplay! In-game, you're typically placed inside a set map filled with typical city buildings of importance; Hospitals, Bars, Houses, Police Stations, ect. You decide where you hold up base, and survive the onslaught of zombie "X"'s on the map. But they aren't the only one's you'll be fighting out there... The game comes in three different modes, an easy mode which gives you one survivor, and no objective. You're able to signal for others to join your cause and live as a small little group for as long as you can. The medium and hard mode add objectives, as well as a time limit that you need to keep track of - among other problems. The biggest key feature in this is that you can add just about anyone you know into the game - slap in a picture and a persona and you're set! All you need to do after that is spend hours creating your own weapons and armor in the creator menu. Good luck my friend! You're going to need it!

It is a decent game compared to the horde of other zombie games.
I have not won a game yet but eventually I'm sure I will.
Tips I can give.
1. Save frequently. One thing I've also done is moved the Zafehouse Diaries folder in My Documents to Dropbox. Making a NTFS junction from the original location to the dropbox location means I can technically restore back to any point as long as I have been saving frequently.
2. Events can be cruel, hence tip #1. I've found that sometimes an event is unwinnable but if I reload it enough, sometimes the event doesn't happen or can be mitigated.
3. Your survivors will eat way too fast. Searching for more supplies quickly and efficently is a must.
4. Assault a location before trying to breach it. Assaulting lets you kill more zombies than patrolling does.
5. Having more than two safehouses is useless in my opinion. The time required to secure a location is long enough when done quickly and noisily. Going slowly and quietly can take forever. Hence, I tend to secure two locations on opposite sides of the town right away. If I find the zombies getting too thick nearby, I can move.
6. Guns are useless. They just make alot of noise and draw the zombies.
7. Move your survivors as a group. More people during the assault makes it safer, during the breach too. After a successful breach, you'll want one person patrolling (to thin the herd outside attracted by noise), one person watching (to ensure that the zombies breaking in don't surprise the group), and one person searching (for food, medicine and vehicle parts) at a minimum. If you're in a factory, have one person improving gear (defense, breach/assault, searching). There is always jobs that can be done.

As the (terrible) name suggests, this is a game about stories.
It's about the moments where you send a survivor on a suicide mission to retrieve some snacks for her starving comrades, or finding that one precious item in an innocuous house, or sending someone to aid a survivor besieged by a zombie horde.
It resembles the browser/mobile classic Rebuild, but offers plenty more options in actions and equipment.
It's punishingly hard, and made rather more frustrating by being somewhat arbitrary, or at least obscure. Having well-equipped and skilled survivors wiped out by a motley group of zombies is bad enough, but having the survivors seriously injuring each other over a dispute over who gets to use the shower first is just annoying.
Still, the great moments are well worth the frustrations.

I saw this game during the Wintersale on Steam and it caught my attention, looking like the old Mad-TV, a game that i play even today sometimes.
During the years, there were a lot of bad clones, none of them ever reached the playability of the original.
After playing it around 14 hours, i can say that this is the best clone of MTV to date, and it is not just a clone, it has some ideas on its own.
It is not perfect, but if you liked the old MTV, you should give it a try.
So what is the difference?
You have to plan you Movies based on a specific group of viewers. Women like Romance Movies, Kids like Fantasy and so on. Showing movies to the wrong audience results in lesser viewers and a bad reputation.
It is not realistic, that you have to plan your Movie Schedule based on the Viewers at a specific time. But nonethenless, it gives the game a nice twist. In the old MTV, you simply put the best movies you could get in your Schedule, and the viewers watch whatever you show. Now you have to think hard how you can satisfy Elders, Women and Kids at the same time. I like that.
Here are some things, i dont like:
Betty Botterblum is gone. Ok, i always ignored her until i had enough money to buy the gifts. But without her, something is missing. Also, the hoaxes you could play the other opponents are gone. No elevator signs you can change.
No Boss, no office.
Overall,this wasnt so important, but it added some atmosphere.
No antennas. You upgrade directly to satellite. (Will be changed in future update)
The Animations are bad also, the original is far better.
No Live Footage, like superbowl. Ok, sometimes you can send a small live newsreport, but getting big sport events on my channel were always a highlight in MTV.
Good:
Movie Production and Rating for the competition. Having points that you can distribute around the movie production is cool. That make you really feel a little like a producer. Would be cool it this feature will be enhanced.
Advertising and employees.
The gameflow is good and you can custumize the game.
Quests. But instead of rewarding with money which is unrealistic (why does my mother pay 400K that i show a movie??), you should have other advantages (or avoid disadvantages).
I could write more, but i prefer to play it now ;-)
So, if you like Mad-TV, give Empire-TV a chance.

Wow- when I first saw this game pop up on steam I thought to myself "huh, a MAD TV clone". How very very...right I was. This is exactly what I expected but so much more. Empire TV recreates the game and updates UI without taking away the charm which players would have came to expect. In Empire players fight against AI opponents to make their channel #1. Everything works very much as you would imagine- players plan their days, negotiate advertising contracts, research new tech, buy/steal/create new TV shows and movies to run on their channel... It has three difficulty modes and three gameplay modes. The best mode seems to be the custom mode- which allows you to have a longer competitive game where you decide just how easy or hard it is. With promised mod support down the line and so many different options I really can't wait to see where this game goes.
But what really gets me is the apparent dedication of the devs to this title. This is not just some quick cash in on player's nostalgia, the devs really seem to give a damn about their game. When this title first popped up on steam it did not have any gameplay after the base mode is finished, it completely ended at the end of the game. This turned me away at first and I did not check back until just recently. What do I come back to when I notice the game on sale this time round? Endless mode... lots of changes and additions in content... and even a custom game mode. The forums even have a transparent plan for what they hope to acheive patch wise in 2016. These developers care about their game and it shines through.

Bought this Game on Day 1 at Steam and it already received several Updates (f.e. new game modes,  german translation etc.). The Devs are very responsive and listen so suggestions (take a look at the Discussionforum).

Review might contain minor spoiler of a game mechanic that you'll encounter very early in the game. I've hidden them behind the spoiler tag.
What a great game. I love the Matrix-inspired UI and effects. While the game is as minimalistic as roguelikes usually are, the dev really used all the potential from the ASCII-style graphics.
Usually I have a hard time to get into roguelikes. I've tried Caves of Qud, Nethack, Tales of Maj'Eyal and Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead (among a few others I can't recall), but none of them have really grasped me like Cogmind did. Usually I want to get better at those games, but it seems like a chore. Cogmind on the other hand feels contained, solid, easy to grasp and really immersive. A lot of it has to do with the excellent UI and thought-out shortcut keys. And it has the best setting / lore that I've seen.
The best part about Cogmind is that it rewards stealth and tactical combat. Careful planning and learning how the A.I. works really pays off, and my best runs have been those where I've avoided combat as much as possible. And in the later levels (I've only got to probably -7) I love how flexible the game is build-wise. I can start playing as a flying super fast stealthbot and switch to a terminatorbot on treads because I found a bunch of kinetic guns and managed to get surrounded by enemies.
While the combat seems repetitive and boring on the outside, the best part of it is under the hood. There are so many variables to consider and it's a fresh approach after the "get better armor and weapons to kill higher level mobs" -kind of games. Every time I'm about to engage or consider engaging an enemy I check the stats of my parts and try to get to a safer location to avoid getting ganged up. Do I have enough coverage on my shielding parts or will my guns be the first to go after a few volleys? Will I run out of matter or will I have enough to switch my loadout after my assault rifles get destroyed? Should I just throw away a few less important items so I could unequip my heavy storage unit, equip my flight propulsion and get away quickly from a flight I might lose? Which robot should I kill first? These are only a few examples and it only gets trickier and more complex in the later levels.
I bought the game during the Alpha phase (I think..?) and got the key in an email after the launch on Steam, so I might have played a few dozen hours more than what it shows here. But I know I've only scratched the surface.
Before purchasing I'd suggest you research a bit into Cogmind and realize it's a niche game for a niche crowd. It's a game where you can never get too attached (heh, a robot pun) to gear because it might get either blown off in a few minutes or you might find something way better later. There are no classes, skill trees or masteries of any kind (I think) but your builds are determined by the parts you equip. You can, however, kind of level up by
but that's about it. These choices hardly ever feel irrecoverable, unless you
. But I don't know why you would do that if you pay any attention to the game :D
Only con I can think of is that the game forces the US keyboard layout (I use the finnish one) and I have a hard time finding the right keys for stuff unless I keep the layout's image on the second monitor. So far I haven't tried to rebind the keys, but it's sometimes jarring to try and find the right keys if I don't have the layout open.

I've been playing Cogmind since earlier this year, so my Steam played time doesn't reflect the 100+ hours I've pumped into this game. I'm beyond impressed with this developer and with this game. This dev took an absolutely incredible amount of time truly examining what makes a modern Roguelike work, and how to improve the experience while still staying true to the soul of Nethack, etc. The UI is a crowning achievement in the genre, and works just as well with keyboard as with mouse. The tiles are freaking scalable, and the graphics stick out heads and shoulders above others in the genre while still keeping the old school feel. If you like roguelikes, or turn-based games in general, you NEED to check this game out.

I'm mixed in a lot of ways about this game. It feels like the Binding of Isaac sometimes for me - that is, unsuccessful runs tend to be a slog, while lore-filled or successful runs are far more enjoyable.
I originally wrote a negative review here (preserved below). Combat felt tedious at best and each run seemed nigh-identical to the last, but response from multiple people including the developer and some community members prompted me to continue playing to see if the game held more.
- it had a lot I'd yet to see.
Continued playing revealed not only more areas to explore and parts to utilize that I still hadn't seen, but random encounters I had uncovered an aspect of the game I had yet to even scratch the surface of, making interactions with various machines far more interesting and variable. Not to mention how fun the encounters themselves were - I've found two so far and both were incredibly interesting to me, largely in part because I love good lore and both events were densely packed with it.
Even so, I still have issues with this game that have yet to see resolution, and while further playing may yet have them solved (and if so I will update this), they are still worth mentioning regardless. Before I dig in, however, be aware that:
I have reached -3 (presumably 3rd-to-last level) at the farthest.
Plenty of which could mean a number of changes to this review.
The only build I can successfuly construct thus far is a combat one - I am still trying to create other suitable configurations, and until then any comments from me about their existance or potential should be taken with a grain of salt.
That all said...
I'm a sucker for a quality story, and this game has plenty to offer. Everything from dialogue to stories dug up from terminals is well-written and fun to read, and I constantly find myself excited whenever I find more.
While ambient noise is uncommon, the sound as a whole is well crafted wherever present and never becomes annoying. Additionally, the graphical style - whether you use the ASCII variant or the default - fits together nicely at all times, and I've yet to spot a single thing out-of-place with it.
When the game mentions its part diversity, it isn't exaggerating at any point. I am constantly finding new things to attach or try out, and even amongst those I'm already aware of I still find new uses or even entirely new builds to take a shot at.
It certainly depends a lot on your build as to whether or not you can stick around, but more often than not it's wiser to simply leave for the next level. If you're looking to explore a lot, you need to be careful - even if you've outfitted yourself specifically to do it.
This is another one of the issues that applies moreso depending on what kind of run/build you have. If you're more combat-oriented, odds are almost no fight will truly last unless it is a particularly tough enemy. If you run something less armed, however, you could find yourself embroiled in potentially troublesome lasting skirmishes if you aren't careful.
As I stated earlier, I'm still in the process of designing a working setup of another type, so it's hard to tell just yet.
This has gotten easier as I've learned more things that I can do, but can still be occasionally overwhelming. When I mentioned I got to level -3, I did so on Easier difficulty; even when toned-down, the game can sometimes be quite difficult. This used to be a negative, as easier modes used to lock some areas out, but as of Beta 3.1 this is no longer the case.
A subset of the difficulty, but still separate enough to warrant its own point. System Corruption is rarely a straight-up killing factor for me, but I still find it rather annoying to deal with, as even 1% corruption seems to cause something to screw up unusually frequently. Combine this with the fact that (as far as I know) any level of corruption can cause any manner of negative side-effect, and you get problems like a weapon-misfire from 1% corruption causing a nuclear reactor to get shot and blow up in your face.
Some games can pull off no music just fine, but they usually do so by making up for it with ambient sound - generators humming, steam leaks hissing, etc. While Cogmind
have this sort of thing, they feel somewhat rare to encounter and few machines actually seem to produce any noise. Put this together with other sounds only occuring on a per-turn basis and you can get long periods of silence taking away from the overall experience.
While Cogmind definitely has a lot of effort put in, and is certainly a well-made game, whether or not you should get it varies; I personally didn't enjoy it until I'd put in tens of hours. Hence, I'd recommend it - but only if you think it likely that you'd like it, too.
I'll say it straight up: I don't like this game. While I respect the effort that clearly went in to it (a lot!), the gameplay comes across as very lacking. I find myself suspecting I'm missing something that brings the charm, seeing all the positive reviews, but after four hours of play I still can't find the entertainment.
The lore is good and the sound effects hold as much variety as was promised (and then some), but this is strongly offset by repetitive gameplay. Exploring can be nice, and combat is interesting at first, but both become dull as you go on. Exploring lasts far longer however, as new items and areas show up at a good pace.
Combat is another story; I quickly found myself exasperated with constant streams of enemies and every time new ones appeared I ended up sighing with frustration at the slog I'd now have to deal with. With combat almost entirely consisting of 'Press F to begin targeting, then shoot them, repeat until someone dies.', things get boring extremely fast. Worse yet, even after learning not to push things too far with terminals, enemies still seemed to pour out of every nook and cranny regardless of what I did.
In the end, while I still respect this game and its developer for all the work involved in this product, and while it still has a number of very good elements, I found this game far too grindy to personally be worth $18 (or $20 - I got it on sale). I can't say ignore this game - it has too much potential for that - but unless a good sale comes around or combat gets improved, I'd suggest holding off just yet and seeing what happens first.

"I've journeyed farther than i've ever made it before. Across Moghra'yi, The Great Salt Desert, through teeming forests and dense jungles, past ancient ruins and foreboding caverns. Qud is full of exotic dangers, and i've had my fair share of close calls and narrow escapes along the way. I don't know that i would have made it through my last few encounter if not for my trusty new Vibroblade, which i recently bought off of a merchant who happened to be a sentient potted plant living in a city of talking albino gorillas.  The additional health provided by my mutant second heart also proved to be very useful. But now I'm in trouble. I'm surrounded by snapjaws, a sort of mutant human-hyena hybrid that i've encountered numerous times before with little problem. This time, however, their ranks are joined by an imposing figure named Fungus-Ridden Oofooflowuf. He appears to be some kind of snapjaw leader or hero, and a quick examination reveals that he inspires any other snapjaws in his vicinity to fight more effectively. He also happens to be infected by a parasitic fungus which allows him to emit deadly toxic spores from his body at will, and he is hated by The Wardens for having previously burned one of their leaders in effigy. All in all, not the most pleasant individual to come across. I try to beat a hasty retreat, but there's a wall blocking my path. If only i had the Burrowing Claws mutation i had chosen in a previous life so i could dig my way through the wall, or perhaps the wings so i could attempt to simply fly over my enemies and escape. I do have one ace up my sleeve, though. I haven't used it yet, as i feared what would happen, but now i seemingly have no choice; i activate the mental mutation that allows me to create a portal in the space/time continuum and stumble through it, near death. I step out into a completely unfamiliar landscape, lost but alive. A few yards away a unicorn appears to be fighting some kind of large dragonfly. I set out once again, trying to find my bearings.
Just another day in Qud.
...
Above all else, Qud is an absolute wonder of emergent storytelling. Every playthrough is completely different, and each one will ultimately form a completely unique story. Some of my favorite video game moments and stories of all time have emerged from Qud. Every character in the world has a detailed history, and you never know who you will encounter or how it will play out. There are a wealth of factors at play in every aspect of the game, and each one influences how your story will ultimately unfold, from the mutations at your disposal to the way your build affects your relationships and standing to the personal histories of each NPC and so on. I could tell you dozens of stories of my various journeys in Qud, because each one was completely unique and highly memorable."

Long time RE fan here (RE1 on PSX )! It was very hard for me to hit the recommend button for this game, and there are basically only three reasons why I am recommending it.
1: It does offer a lot of content. This has four normal sized campaigns, even if some of them have a couple of interlapping scenes, it will offer you plenty of hours of playing.
2: With a good co-op friend this game can be extremely fun. People give these modern RE's a hard time because of the less survival horror, or the fact that they are co-op, but I think co-op is actually one of the series biggests strenghts now. In a world with very few co-op games, this game is a fun time if you have some good friends to play it with. I highly recommend playing on the higher difficulties.
3: It's the Resident Evil universe. It's more of an already cool universe with enjoyable monsters and enjoyable characters. Yeah it's not perfect but it's still more RE.
Now what do I not like about this game? The controls take awhile to get used to, I don't know why, but they just feel more awkward than even the older titles. I think pair that with the extremely tight corridors in some of the campaigns and it just makes it feel extremely sloppy.
While the stories aren't bad, I felt there wasn't a good protagonist on the level of Wesker. I did like Chris's target for the first half, but although there was build up it did not end the way you would expect.
Leon's story I felt had the most boring / easy monsters, as well as the least inspired easy boss fights. I feel like Chris's campaign was just better over all.
Then you have some minor nit-picks on things that they took steps backwards from RE5. No DirectX10 support, no LAN support, and over all I'd say RE5 even looked better. The share system for swapping items is gone, and unless someone tells you picking the setting as the host doesn't actually change the other persons difficulty setting.
I think what disappointed me the most is that RE5 was basically a better game in every way. The only thing RE6 had going for it was length, but length is not important when RE5 just has more replay value. I think because I enjoyed RE5 so much more as a co-op game I will always just feel RE6 was one of the biggest let downs in the series. Don't get me wrong I still enjoyed it enough to recommend it, but barely.

Crysis left on a cliff-hanger, a storytelling technique that has irked me in video games since Halo 2. What if they don’t make a sequel?
Story
Well, here is the sequel and they didn’t answer anything.  So, we’re in a new setting of New York, the alien Ceph have somehow turned up there and we’re playing a new character (or old character, I’m really not sure anymore). Would’ve helped if our protagonist, Alcatraz, had something to say about himself but he was blown to bits in the opening alien invasion and dragged to relative safety by our man, Prophet. Prophet is a real mystery, at the end of the first Crysis, he was returning to fight the Ceph head on with Helena and Nomad on Lingshan Island but now he’s in New York and we never find out what happened to Nomad and Helena.
But anyway Alcatraz finds himself in a Nanosuit with a simple goal to find Nathan Gould, a ‘Mr. Scientist’ type who by smashing keys on a laptop can find the answer and stop the alien threat. The story is very thin with the dialogue mostly resting on acronyms with cutscenes being no more than wireframe maps, ala Call of Duty, of where you are and where you should be going. All in all the campaign should last you about 10-12hrs of a story that just about takes you on a path of entertaining set pieces.
Gameplay
And boy, are there some set pieces. Times Square is hit by a tsunami, Grand Central is blown up, Central Park is raised and Lady Liberty is missing her head. Crysis 2 uses it’s setting well but I long for the open island and nonlinear paths of Crysis that required more thinking and exploration to move to each goal.
The Nanosuit that characterised the original Crysis returns in a more simplified, Nanosuit 2.0, form. Instead of selecting individual abilities, each ability is activated when a certain action is prompted. For instance, sprinting will drain suit power instead of selecting the sprint option. Strength will be activated when holding down the key to throw or jump. The abilities that are not automatically selected are stealth and amour, though armour is selected when stealth drains all the suit power. It’s a little more streamlined with the potential to combine suit powers but not having a sprint power means Alcatraz cannot move as quickly without draining power. This might be an offshoot of ‘consolisation’, to slow down movement, but the layout of the map and setting didn’t require the same sort of movement as the original Crysis. In fact, verticality has become a more tactical combat option in the concrete jungle of New York’s skyscrapers. Moving to a highpoint, using the binoculars, picking out enemy positions and assessing tactical options is how most sequences are played out.
But when the option for battle is made, its time to enjoy the incredible gun fights with varied armoury and aggressive AI. The guns feel powerful with recoil and impact and attachments can be added such as silencers and scopes to change the equipment and match the style of approach. First-person shooters just seem like Crytek’s forte, everything down to the movement, FOV, gun recoil, bullet impact and sense of precision is fantastically realised. It’s this sense of solidness with the gunplay in Crysis that you don’t get in the Call of Duty and Medal of Honor games that put me off those franchises.
I played through Crysis 2 twice, once on normal then once on Post-human Warrior, the highest difficulty. The first playthrough offered a decent challenge, due to the decreased effectiveness of the suit’s powers, and I was implored to vary my tactics. However, the second playthrough was slightly disappointing as my character had earned all suit upgrades and therefore most sections of the game were me strolling past enemies in stealth, occasionally hiding behind cover to regenerate suit power but then carrying on towards my goal. It was far too easy to use this method and let me down when it came to increasing the challenge for a second run.
The alien Ceph AI was also a let down as they don’t offer as much variation as they did in the original because they’ve inexplicably sprouted legs. Far removed from the floating, squid-like aliens from Crysis 1 they behave more like the human AI. The C.E.L.L. forces, never really explained who they are, replace the Korean soldiers but don’t seem to have the variety in design or behaviour the Korean soldiers portrayed. Also moving from section to section, the allies are constantly badgering you through the comms to move on even if you just want some time explore, reflect or just observe the world you’re in. It’s as if the game designers treated the design as a conveyor belt, occasionally shooting, with some plot, maybe a set piece but an absolute imperative to stay on track and not stop. I really didn’t enjoy this departure from the open-world freedom that was in Crysis.
Technical
This is Crysis so let’s talk graphics. With the latest updates including DX11, HD packs and advanced graphics options, Crysis 2 is stunning. Lighting was perfect, textures were detailed but the level design lets it down with a mostly wet rubble look and shiny skyscrapers. There isn’t as much variety as the original and it soon gets repetitive. Also, the 3D options were there but lacked the real 3D feel that games like Metro 2033 managed so well. The sound is incredible with guns that are punchy and echo through the deserted streets. The sounds are so finely detailed that it becomes very intuitive to pinpoint a targets location from your surroundings.
Verdict
Crysis 2 is a superb shooter with a poor story, repetitive level design and restrictive gameplay compared to the original.

When Slender: The Eight Pages was released in the summer of 2012, horror fans praised its short, experimental, and completely free take on the genre. Manically dashing through the forest and trying to snag all eight pieces of paper before the creepy Slender Man finds you remains a surprisingly unnerving experience. Cut to spring of 2013, and we now have Slender: The Arrival on PC. This paid-for sequel attempts to pump up the horror experiment into a bigger (though still quite short) game, but it quickly becomes apparent that the simple mechanics of the original Slender crumble under the weight.
Most importantly, The Arrival remembers that the core of any good horror lies in its boogeyman. The Slender Man himself still stalks you with the same terrifying persistence he has in the original, exuding a menacing presence that evolves throughout the story in some unexpected ways. Though his iconic design may be simple, I still got freaked out every time I spotted his silhouette in the distance. You can't fight him, only run from him, and that in of itself makes him more frightening than most game monsters.
The world he haunts is larger and denser, as well. Instead of a dark forest, you’ll wander through abandoned homes, creepy mines, and sunbaked hillsides. Some of the better-lit areas look genuinely great. Trekking through autumnal forests and rummaging through homes that actually feel lived in make the world of Slender an interesting environment.
Some impressive sound design surrounds you with an ambient soundtrack and jarring noises, and it really adds to the already creepy atmosphere. Boards creak, children whisper, and there are some truly terrifying moments that wouldn’t exist without the impeccable use of audio. Like all great horror games, Slender is best served in a dark room with a pair of headphones.
These parts, at least, are done pretty well... but it's simply not enough. While I appreciate the lengths that developer Blue Isle went to flesh things out, The Arrival relies far too heavily on the rudimentary game mechanics of the original, which was only ever meant to last for a few minutes. Like its predecessor, the vast majority of The Arrival essentially boils down to finding a certain number of objects while an increasingly dangerous enemy stalks you. Whether it’s pieces of paper in a forest or generators in a mine, you’re repeating the exact same actions in every part of The Arrival. It feels like being asked to finish a Where’s Waldo book while your house burns down around you.
The fact that I got tired of it during a game this short shows just how repetitive The Arrival is. While a lucky player can dash through in about 20 minutes, it’ll probably take most people a few hours thanks to the unfair nature of the enemies. Slender Man and his minions don’t mind warping directly behind you and causing instant game over. The worst offender of this comes once you reach the abandoned mine and are introduced to a second enemy type. The Proxy, a creepy knife-wielding kid, stalks you throughout the level as you (yup, you guessed it) once again attempt to find a series of objects. He continually killed me with no warning whatsoever, which as you might imagine, gets pretty frustrating.
Although the mine level was genuinely spooky at first, it and many other areas quickly lose their terrifying charm once you’re forced to replay them dozens of times. I appreciate games that are tough yet fair, but those that arbitrarily punish their players sabotage their own fun. This problem persists throughout Slender: The Arrival. The horrifying atmosphere that Blue Isle manages to create is consistently squandered by dull mechanics and unfair difficulty spikes.
Slender: The Arrival manages to deliver some truly impressive scares, but you’ll have to wade through the muck of repetitive tasks and unfair enemies in order to experience them. I found more enjoyment in playing the free original installment, which delivers a powerful horror experience without the annoyances and filler. By trying to stretch the initial concept over five separate scenarios, Slender only succeeds in proving that some ideas are better left in the experimental phase.

Zafehouse: Diaries is a rather unique take on the survival/strategy genre. There are 3 different modes with different difficulties, that ultimately have the same goal, survival. Towns, events, items and survivors are all randomly generated. You can customise a survivor with your own story and backgrounds, which will then be randomly generated from a pool.
You interact with a diary that displays all the events that are happening during each hour.  When I first played the game I was alittle put off by the fact that you interact with a diary. However as I played I fully understood why the interface is how it is and it is surprisingly informative. You can assign tasks for each survivor that they will try to acomplish to the best of their ability depending if they are any good at it (i.e. scavenging, barricading, cooking, etc.).
The game has quite alot of depth to it and some deep mechanics. A good example is that it might be wise to get one of your survivors to scout that motel a few doors down to see if there's any zombies, so that your group have somewhere nice to rest. Or maybe that hospital crawling with walkers has that bandage you so desperately need.
It also runs pretty well, even on them old toasters that are years old.

It is difficult to purchase Rocksmith 2014 without reflecting upon a plethora of unanswered questions:
"Will I be able to play guitar after playing this game?" Well not necessarily, but it helps.
"Will I be able to play the songs outside the game?" With a bit of persistence, you will.
"Should I buy a guitar?" Well yes of course!
Coming from a world of bass, I did not know what to expect from a 'guitar game'. I knew it was possible to play bass on a variety of tracks, but I didn't expect the songs in Rocksmith to be picked due to its groovin' basslines. I was wrong.
For a time I stuck with guitar and happily jacked in my trusty telecaster to learn the classic guitar rock songs and had great fun, whilst getting motivated to improve my guitar skills every day. Then it happened, the game broke, the real tone cable could not track my notes properly. I figured it would be my guitars intonation and started adjusting it, but to no avail.
Alas, and overcome with grief I tried plugging in my bass to at least get SOME worth out of the game, and I couldn't believe what I found. I wasn't stuck with playing root notes following the guitars every move, I had options such as mastering the tapping solo in 'Knights of Cydonia', joining in with The Who in 'My Generation' and even playing as Geddy Lee in Rush! And this was all without acquiring any DLC! Be advised that playing with the emulated bass is not the same as properly playing bass. Get a bass.
Generally I am quite thrilled with my purchase and would gladly recommend it to everyone whether they're musicians or not. The only thing I miss is the ability to view the tabs in the game without actually having the play the track in the game, and no, riff repeater isn't the solution.
Oh, by the way, if your game doesn't track properly, try changing the guitar strings. It worked for me.

(I've had a masterpiece from a level 3 in drama but crap with level 8 in sci-fi. There is just no rhythm to it.)
My biggest complaint is that the audience demographic will completely change right in the middle of a "blockbuster" movie. One minute you're trying to get that last advertising block completed for the genre the movie was made/purchased for and the next you're struggling to find an advert to place in the slot. Why?  Because mid-movie, instead of "women" watching your major league romance production, it's a bunch of old men.  That's not how the demographic works.
This was a very poor design decision imho and given the whole game revolves around what is shown and when, so that you can get the advertising revenue you need to expand, you end up losing 10's of thousands of dollars because you can't complete an advertising block.
If it's cheap, it's a good bit of fun but if you're looking for a half decent, replayable sim, sorry, this is just not going to cut it.

Empire TV Tycoon was developed and published by Dreamsite Games. It was released on October 20th, 2015 for $12.99. A press review copy was provided for The Hidden Levels.
Empire TV Tycoon is a unique member of the tycoon family style of games. It is inspired by Mad TV and Game Dev tycoon according to it’s development team and I agree with that statement wholeheartedly. The first session I played after knowing the full scope of the game was extremely addictive and fun. The aspect of managing the marketing and advertising for best viewership is challenging and though provoking. My station produced many movies and TV shows, and won awards for them. You do this all by hiring writers, actors, and production assistants to help your cause.
What I enjoyed:
Management time – My first completed game for 300 fame felt like it took an hour and a half or so. I was streaming live at the time and as it happens it was closer to four hours of non-stop TV station management. It’s always a good sign when I can lose myself in a game, clicking and planning was more pleasant than I initially expected. The option to speed the game up only gives you a slight push as you’ll need to stop and film new movies or shows, deal with viewer requests, and update your library. Each day adds new challenges that cause the player to adapt their strategy often.
Culture shock – The amount of cultural references (mostly pop culture) in Empire Tv Tycoon is borderline obscene, which is perfect. You buy your movies from one of two iconic characters, Walter white from Breaking Bad is the legal seller, and Silent Bob from Jay and Silent Bob sells the bootleg goods. You buy your ads from Mad Men’s Don Draper, your tech upgrades from Back to the Future’s Doc Brown.. The level of detail to mainstream television is absolutely perfect, this aspect helped sell the entire theme very well.
Reruns – The replay value here is astronomical, you can play an arcade mode to a set number of fame, or play endless mode and see just how far you can take your station over lengthy campaigns. There are a number of various events which give each replay a fresh feel. Producing movies and TV shows to compete in various awards shows also changes from game to game so you never know what you’ll be producing next.
What I disliked:
Information request – The biggest flaw with my experience was that certain genres seem to miss certain viewers that aren’t always logical. I programmed the Sopranos for a one hour block with male viewers to complete a male targeted car advertisement and they not only didn’t hit the numbers but turned their TV to another station. I did fins that fantasy movies were good for kids, and sci-fi good for nerds, but there should be some way to track what genres are working with certain viewers.
See it to believe it – The portion of the game where you have scripts written, hire actors, and film productions is fantastic. The problem I have with it is that you get a numerical rating afterwards and little else. It would be an amazing addition to see some scenes from that movie or show, or see your product in a form other than a numerical rating. This is more of a wishful addition than a complaint, but I often felt that my station worked hard to make the movie, we should get to see at least a funny scene from it or something of that nature.
This was a surprising review for me because at first glance I was somewhat apprehensive to play Empire TV Tycoon. The tycoon style of game often feels bland or boring for my taste but this game really is quite enjoyable. The pop culture references made me giggle often through my game, and certain film or TV shows displayed in the game are childhood favorites. Theme is important and this game delivers it in droves, you’ll really feel engaged and challenged while trying to run your station. For me this was a clear reminder not to judge a game by it’s cover, as this game is an instant favorite in my library.
Score: Buy it now

I was so excited for this game. Genuinely thought it'd be my favourite game ever.
And you know what?
It's a good game. Or rather, it has the makings of a good game. Had it been made by any other company instead of the world's cheapest, heartless corporation it'd easily be one of the best games released in the past few years in my eyes.
But, no.
Instead, they decided that peer-to-peer networking was a much better idea than dedicated servers for what is essentially a multiplayer only game; (the campaign is a few hours at most, and really had no substance.) Peer-to-peer does not work in multiplayer games with more than two people at a time, especially when one requires perfect timing to actually play. Not only this, but you basically roll a dice any time you play a game. Chances are, you'll get; "Cannot join, game full." or my current favourite; "Matchmaking failed." Not only this, but most of the time you'll just lose connection to the game anyway and gain literally no reward for your efforts.
The game itself is quite good, I feel. The characters are fairly balanced, to a degree. I don't see any as particularly broken in comparison to the others, but it's quite clear that resorting to cheap spamming/stunlocking tactics far outweighs any attempt at skillful fighting.
Personally I feel rather cheated. Unwisely, I've spent a total of roughly £100 on this game. I paid for versions on the Xbox and PC, and I paid for the season pass for the PC version. What I paid for is a buggy, broken mess filled plagued by networking errors and a horrifically salty community. But I've drawn a lesson from this. From now on, I'll never purchase a Ubisoft title before waiting for proper reviews to come out regarding it.
My advice would be, wait until they release dedicated servers and fix more of the bugs and exploits.
They might be able to salvage this game, but I can say pretty confidently that people won't forget the state they released this in for a long, long time.

I've only put in 2.6 hours so far but I can already tell this game is a gem.  The creator of this game has put so much thought, time, and love into this game and it shows from how slick the menus are, the cool transition from tiles to ASCII and back again, the AI behaviors, etc.  The manual is very lengthy and takes a bit to get through, but reading that gives you even more of an appreciation for the game as you realize each tile is really a 9x9 grid to accomodate robots of various sizes (smaller robots are obviously harder to hit, but you also have a chance of shooting past a smaller robot to hit a more dangerous opponent behind it) and you realize how the game is a very neat amalgamation of turn based and time based (the game operates on turns, but each action takes a certain amount of time and there is 100 "time" per turn, so if you shoot six weapons it takes several turns worth of time so if you miss your opponent could flee).  I can't wait to put more time in this game.
