So...where to begin? For every game, it will have its pros and cons. For every player, it's up to them to decide what a game's pros and cons are. This review was made to (hopefully) make you decide whether you should buy this game or not. So without anymore delays, long and interesting sentences, long agonizing vocabulary words, and delays...  Let's start with the pros of the game!
Overall, this game is astounding, repetive, and challenging. This game is based on strategy and randomly generated scenarios (mostly RNG).  Every desision you make can and will affect the situation your survivors have in any way possible. Whether choosing to inject yourself with a zombie "cure" (if you find it) or not, to let a little girl inside your safe house or not, or to kill one of your infected surviors or let them live in hopes of finding that cure (RNG could just straight out kill them if it wanted to). One of the best things about this game are the customization options. This game allows you to create your own survivors. Not only that, you can also customize and create your own occupations, locations, even gear! In my opinion, the best thing about this game is the idea of reading your survivors' story/diary. Whether they became trapped and met their awesome demise, or became one of the lucky ones who made it out of that dreaded city alive to tell the story. Now, I believe this game has the capabilities of being a best seller, however like every game, when there are pros, there are also cons.
First of all, you must be accustomed to the fact that you will lose... a lot. It is a tendency to lose in almost every game you will play. No matter how "good" your group is well armed or skilled, you WILL lose. I, myself, have played this game hundreds of times... HUNDREDS! And out of those dreadful hours of losing and preparation, I only beat it fairly... ONCE. And by fairly, I meant getting the achievements I earned so far in this game by using the characters the game gave me, and abusing the save system like a ♥♥♥♥♥. Even if I would use my generated characters and their OP skills, my group would somehow end up being mauled by zombies, shot to death by crazed survivor groups, or being infected and dying from the virus. Survivor relations are also an issue because of the constant stress, arguements, and paranoia that will diminish one of your group member's relations with the rest of your group into hating each other instead of the zombies.
Every so often, I check the statistics of this game (which I will put the link below) to see what the average win/ losses are worldwide. Some days I read that +40% of people killed an old lady that offered to trade supplies with them. Other days, +30% players had their group ditch one of their members in a room full of zombies to save the rest. These statistics show the amount of frustation, determination, and willingness to survive and complete their objective, even if it means to screw other people if it risks killing the rest of the group. Personally, I would have quit my current game or reverted to a previous save if a survivor died because it would just seem wise to do so (also because I'm a perfectionist)
Overall, this game has pros and cons in terms of game play and survival. If I would rate this game, I would rate it an 7/10 because of the interesting factors and potenial. However, success in each game is heavily weighed on RNG.

So this one was an unexpected, yet, pleasant surprise. I got it as part of the blink bundle, which before a week ago I'd never even heard of. When I saw screenshots of the gameplay, I was very skeptical of the rather simplistic diary view, and the whole concept of a game being based entirely on diary entries was a little odd to me. However, as soon as I started playing, I began to see just how fun and engaging it really is. Even without fancy graphics, this game manages to engross you in a zombie infested world, and you'll find yourself being easily absorbed into the addictive gameplay. The easy addition of custom content is just the icing on this deliciously zombie infested cake, and allows you to effortlessly add you and your friends into the game. You can even add your own location photos to take it one step further, allowing you to truly act out the apocalypse in your own home town.

I was on the fence about this as I haven't tended to like text-based games in the past but purchased this on a whim and am so happy I did. I took a bit of time to create a few customized places, survivors, and professions before starting the sandbox mode, and if you have any interest in that I'd highly recommend it. It was extremely easy and, at least for me, added immensely to the game.
It did take me a few tries to get the hang of surviving (on my first start I ended up with a giant horde of zombies around me within the first 24 hours, second start I wandered into a hospital trying to get medicine and learned the importance of scouting), but I had infinite patience once I saw how frequently the survivors I'd created appeared. It added quite a bit more motivation to keep things running smoothly! Imagine my surprise and delight in one game when the starting character (who happened to be the one based off me) came upon the next survivor who turned out to be the character I'd made for my favorite celebrity! We were quickly surrounded by a giant horde of zombies with no weapons, no barriers, and very little food, but I got such a kick out of finding us together that I had to find a way to make it work.
One gripe would be it takes so long to build the barriers (certainly longer than would be realistic, although to be fair they do give you many more supplies inside to build barriers than is realistic) and sometimes even when you're being slow & quiet the lookout will say you're making so much noise you're a beacon for zombies. Haven't quite figured that out yet. Traps haven't seemed to really have a benefit yet either.
But I think that's it. I intended to play for only a little but I found that, even though it paused every turn, I found that I couldn't step away. I completely missed dinner and stayed up way too late, definitely worth every penny.

An interesting, in depth, and addicting game. This game looks at an interesting balance between control and simulation. You can give tasks to your survivors according to their ability and relationships, but there is little control over how they perform, or even what supplies they use. To an extent, this removal of control acts against the game, but it gives the game a layer of complexity, depth, and free form that isn't present in most simulations. It's difficult to see this game as anything other than a simulation, and anybody longing for more control over their characters (such as in XCOM) will find this game lacking.
What I've said is bad about the game, mostly. Describing the game's qualities is difficult to interpret in words. It possesses a dynamic feel, where everything connects to everything else, and challenges players to focus on the intricacies that aren't specified. The game is unforgiving and extremely challenging, which I feel accurately represents a zombie survival situation more effectively than most other games.
Some ideas for updates would make this game really awesome. One idea is to present the player with a floor plan of each building, showing which rooms have been searched, as well as the locations of doors and windows. This will allow players to think much more strategically. Another idea is to provide some form of gameplay, maybe even minigames, which would allow players to have more control over the outcomes of certain events, such as assault, barricade construction, or defense. While the simulation feel of characters doing these tasks on their own is fine, without some form of control in these areas the majority of the gameplay revolves around text.
Overall, a very good game, and I definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a realistic simulation of a zombie survival.

I personally really love Friday the 13th because of all the things to do in it. It's an awesome game to play with friends, I promise you you'll love it with friends. It's not bad to play it solo but make sure you have friends to play this with before you buy it because it can get a little boring if you don't. If your an achievement hunter this is also a game to add to your collection, there's plenty of long lasting achievements to earn along with ingame badges too to make sure you always have something to do. Another thing I love about this game is how everyone from all over the world plays this, and of course I wouldn't forget to mention all the female gamers that played this. I've played video games for at least 9 or 8 years now and man I've never seen so many female gamers before, Friday the 13th has got you covered. In short you'll meet a lot of people here, maybe even make a couple online buddies too.
Now, I'll talk about all the negative things you've heard about this game. Glitches, the bugs, the price, and the servers.
For the glitches and bugs, yeah I'll admit there's a lot of them. In the most recent update I feel like they even added some more! I'll tell you now from my experiences, half of the bugs I've seen are just down right funny, whenever there screwing with your chances of winning or not. Funny enough I was able to forgive them, but it would still be nice if they could patch those. The other half are more of a pessence, fairly hateful. Those kind of bugs I'm just dying to see those go away. However as we all know, the games still pretty new. I'd say just give the developers some time and patience, they'll get rid of them. In the mean time you'll live don't worry.
Now for that price of theirs, as of today it's normally 40 dollars, and with its current state it's not worth it in my opinion. To counter that though, I suggest buying it when it's on sale, as far as I've witnessed whenever it's on sale it will always be 50% of meaning it will be 20$ dollars. So far I've seen it on sale around Halloween and Christmas time.
There are 3 different servers in this game, and unfortunately you may lag depending on what country you live in. For example the closest servers for south American users are the north American ones. So you might want to do some research before you buy the game, I assume there's a forum about this but I don't know for sure, apologies.
In conclusion, I think the games a lot of fun, with badges to earn, people to meet, and friends to help you troll other people, you'll have a blast. If you want to wait until the games more developed though, great idea. If you want to get it now I recommend waiting for sales.

What can I say - I'm a lazy man. Even though back in the day I spent quite a bit of time pillaging the rooms and narrow corridors of Rogue, the glorious days of action-packed simplicity quickly faded away, only to be replaced with more and more complex games that pushed the genre forward. While obviously a great trend for those who love their games deep, this also proved to be an intimidating factor for people like me - as studying a myriad of hotkeys before even considering a successful run of ADOM or NetHack became a must. However, as time went on, some modern roguelikes managed to find a middle-ground between streamlining the interface and simplifying the gameplay, and Cogmind is the prime example of this commendable approach.
The game is extremely easy to delve into - in fact, a blind play is not only suggested, but encouraged in the game's manual. Thanks to the ease of use and clear-cut UI, the exploration of the dungeon becomes a pleasure, not a chore. The most necessary functions are always at the tip of your fingers, the intuitive drag&drop interface takes care of the bulk of your management needs, and you're left with the most important aspect of any true roguelike - strategising. And oh boy does Cogmind shine in this area.
Most of the individual enemies or even enemy groups don't pose an immediate threat to you. In fact, you are quite capable of disposing of hostiles almost right off the bat. However, the mastermind behind the facility that you found yourself in thinks on a global scale - as such, your primary concern is not about immediately destroying whatever you find in front of you, but surviving the long battle of attrition as you navigate your way out of the underground complex. The alarm systems, robot patrols, enemy informers and traps are all connected on a global level. Disturb them too much - and a full-scale army invasion is imminent, in which case no amount of battle prowess will ever save you. However, should you choose to play the system, carefully manipulating the current alarm level, disposing of lone guardbots and avoiding detection, you will most definitely uncover the secrets surrounding this fantastic place - and escape with your core still ticking.
If you're tired of memorising all the possible combinations of Ctrl+, Shift+ and Alt+, can't be bothered to regulate food and water consumption for basic survival and don't care about intricate differences between picking up items comfortably, quickly or normally (which falls under "basic" commands in some old-school roguelike titles), then Cogmind might just be the game to try. An extremely smooth learning curve combined with a novel approach to equipment and an unusual setting set this game apart as a truly outstanding title.
If you like roguelikes at all, you will like this game

***SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW!!!!!***
While I can say that the Resident Evil series makes me feel very warm and bubbly inside, I am sad to say that even though Resident Evil 6 is a very well created and beautiful title, I would not recommend it to long-time fans of the series.
From the zombie-infested streets of Tall Oaks to the war ridden mountains of Edonia, Resident Evil 6 takes you through 4 different storylines, each containing two important characters (excluding Ada Wong's co-op partner, ingeniusly dubbed "Agent.") These four campaigns follow Leon S. Kennedy and his partner Helena Harper, Jake Wesker and his partner Sherry Birkin, Chris Redfield and his partner Piers Ivans, and Ada Wong, and progressively shows how their stories collide in China.
Combat in Resident Evil 6 is unlike any other resident evil game, consisting of a stamina bar, more melee attacks, and a special coup de grace for each character (the latter is featured in Resident Evil 5). Each campaign has it's own arsenal that you will obtain throughout your playing, ranging from Auto-shotguns to Lightning Hawks, the Bear Commander assault rifle to the Semi-Automatic Sniper Rifle.  Quick-Shot and melee attacks take up one sliver from your stamina bar, and once said bar is depleted, your melee attacks are powered down to a weak, fatigued kick. The combo system is very well done, allowing you to quickly stun an enemy and go in for the kill rather easily.
Mercenaries mode makes it's return in this title, as well as a special derivative named "Mercenaries NO MERCY". NO MERCY may sound familiar to fans of one of Valve's most successful series, Left 4 Dead, and you are right to feel such nostalgia. Mercenaries NO MERCY is a version of NO MERCY in which you can play as the iconic survivor cast of Left 4 Dead 2 (Coach, Rochelle, Ellis, and Nick, respectively.) In NO MERCY, music is replaced with songs by the game's fictional greasy rock band, the Midnight Riders, and it is also optional to apply a Left 4 Dead enemy pack which makes Witches, Tanks, and Hunters (from what I've experienced) available for your violent enjoyment.
A new addition to the Biohazard series is titled "Agent Hunt", in which campaign players can set their games to allow such mode to allow other players to join in as zombies or J'avo. This mode is /very/ addicting, but quite difficult if you are playing as the C-virus infected enemies. You control different versions of the zombies and J'avo, and can also control your J'avo after its Chrysalis mutation, allowing you the destructive power to wreak havoc in any way you choose.
All in all, in a review that sounds very positive, I must wrap this up with the negatives.
- Rather low replay value
- Decent graphics, some texturing looks unfinished
- Chock-full of cutscenes, long and short, many uneeded
- Clunky control system
- No pausing the game, at all (unless you're in co-op)
- Very limited array of weaponry
- Difficult to find ammo (but I suppose that is what you'd expect in an apocalypse)
TL;DR it's kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. QTE. Don't buy it unless you want to experience vivid imagery of low-quality scares and body horror.

Might be the best roguelike I've played. I really love the setting, mechanics, and even the look of the game. While I think there could be some better diversity in equipment, the unique skills and mutations really make combat feel satisfying no matter what you're using. It reminds me quite a bit of Cataclysm: DDA, but with less focus on survival and more on combat and exploration. There aren't very many quests to do currently, but I hope there will be more to come because the ones already implemented are engaging with interesting locations and enemies. Also, this game got me to read A Canticle for Leibowitz, one of the inspirations for the game's setting, which was a great read- and it made me appreciate the game even more in turn.
This game has two huge successes which make it special in my eyes. The first is the combat system, which manages to be fairly deep with plenty of moments where you really have to think smart and plan ahead to survive, while also being simple to pick up. There isn't an overabundance of tools at your disposal like in some other roguelikes, just a good number of useful and flexible skills and items, which helps combat keep its flow. The second strength is the setting, which is a bit harder to explain. It's a type of post-apocalyptic environment which is not normally seen in games, where humanity has regressed so severely thousands of years after the initial disaster that even simple batteries are artifacts of an ancient time that an average person might not even recognize. Like I said, it's a bit hard to put it into writing, but it's such an interesting concept that is so clearly present everywhere in the game that it elevates the entire experience.
I give this game a 10. Yes, it's a 10 while it's in early access, and I hope it gets even better in the future.

Zafehouse Diaries tries to create a survial text based rpg game that requires tactics and strategy but ultimately fails at it. The concept itself is really great and somewhat different from the usual zombie games but unique doesn't always mean great.
The basic premise is to lead a group of randomly generated survivors through various gamemodes and reach the rescue vehicle in order to surive the apocalypse. In order to fulfill your goal you have to overcome various challenges. You need ressources, materials, weapons and supplies. Taking care of your group is a vital aspect because each one of them has their own motivations, political views and character traits which sometimes can cause major trouble in your group. The player has to scavenge various buildings and fight off zombies. Everything is an text based form accompanied by a great interface that feels nice and polished.
What makes this game bad is that it's outright boring, the lack of any visual presentation is a really disapointing. The sound assets are weak and there is no real music and just some generic sound effects. There is no atmosphere to speak of or anything exciting. Furthermore the game is outright frustrating, it's really hard to actually complete a campaign. Your strategies and choices always lead to death and it's hard to win even with a group of very good survivors.
Overall this game is really boring and doesn't offer anything special. It might be a more realistic approach to the zombie genre but it doesn't deliver. Despite having some customization options, it's not that amazing. Perhaps if you're really into text based rpgs or adventures.

This game is pretty faithful reimagining of Mad TV (the classic underappreciated DOS game) with a lot of fun improvements and a modern interface.
As opposed to a couple of the negative reviews I've read here, I quite enjoyed the element of having to cater to a varying audience throughout the day. It adds a bit of a puzzle and fast-thinking element to the game, and I feel if you could just choose one particular audience type the game would be far too easy, since you'd only have to worry about one type of show and ignore everything else. The whole point is to build a library of shows and movies for a diverse audience and try to grab the largest market share possible away from the competition.
If you're wondering why the competing stations are in the same building as you, it's because that's exactly how Mad TV worked. It creates some interesting and frantic situations where they can block you from getting to a destination in time, buy a movie or take an ad contract before you, or you can do the same to them. You can see the competing program directors scrambling around just like you, and it's helps foster a little bit of rivalry feeling as you pass them in the halls. I believe, also, that the developer has said something about sabotage in a future update (which was also in Mad TV), so you'd need to be able to visit competitors' offices and such to do so.
The tutorial could probably use a little work, but because I had played Mad TV before, and the game works basically the same way, I'm not exactly sure if I am the best judge of that. The game has a few rough edges here and there, such as a couple of typos in movie descriptions, but overall the polish is pretty solid for a small indie team of 2 people.
Overall, I'd say this game is easily worth its modest price, especially if there are a few more add-ons in the plans.

I enjoyed this although it's not as "Tycoony" as some games with that name - for starters, you're in a race with two other channel programmers to gain "fame" points, so there's no sandbox mode where you can just Netflix and chill.
This race aspect combined with the tech upgrades keep you on your toes, on top of juggling your schedule to keep both your audiences and your advertisers happy. (Fortunately, these two aims usually coincide.)
I have to say I ragequit a couple of times after botching a few ad contracts which left me deep in the red from the penalty clauses. This is what happens when you show gory splatter movies in the early morning to "Children" and "Lovers".
So it's not always easy to get the audiences you need to fulfill your advertising contracts (your main source of cash), as you have to take care to match the program genres to the audiences. You can buy movies and shows (including many real titles) from the library in the basement (or alternatively from the guy selling pirated shows outside, which carries its own risks).
As well, you can hire writers and actors to produce your own productions - you can also enter this original programming to contest awards, which can provide a nice amount of cash and fame as well. If the show you've just produced is just too terrible to air, at least you can hock it off for some spare change. Another source of income are the optional special requests to show a particular style at a certain time - you have to judge whether these conflict with your advertising priorities.
The art is low-bit and low-rez but adept enough to give you the feel of running your own TV station, whilst the UI is generally well polished with the occasional quirk.

Thomas Was Alone is a simplistic platformer with an entertaining narrational
story.  The music sets the atmosphere perfectly, and leads you into really caring
for the blocks that constitute your characters.
The platforming mechanic is basic, but fair, with many savepoints so you
are not drawn out of immersion.  There is a sense of satisfaction as you defeat
each challenge, and a sense of adventure as you progress.  The narration is well
done, and succeeds wonderfully in having you connect on an emotional level with
the characters.
The combination of well written narrative, beautiful music, and simple
yet challenging platforming all weave together to make an entertaining game
that is easy to recommend.

Tremendously disappointing.
Everything in this game's structure screams "Lazy". They even give you an optional infinite ammo cheat right from the start. The expansions to the combat system seem to carry a glimmer of effort, but the contextual commands to do them are so imbalanced and poorly timed as to suggest a lack of playtesting.
You get to carry far too many weapons at once, and it is far too cumbersome to select which specific one you want to use at any one time.  These guns have zero customization, and despite different appearances, many of them are even used the same way.
There are no real puzzles, and no exploration-- everything is totally linear to the point of being boring.
Even the combat difficulty has been toned down, with the only real bit of challenge being your need to adapt to the crappy UI aiming.
The skillpoint system for leveling up is anemic; you get the ability to freely switch between 8 sets of skill combinations, but only a few of them are really relevant. And since you can't swith what is IN those combinations mid-game, the barely-useful skill system becomes obtuse and irrelevant.
And the overuse of Quick-Time Events ( something I despise to begin with) causes death to be nothing more than a constant annoyance-- there is no challenge in this game, and it is not scary.  As a personal gripe, the plot has gone totally off the rails as well. It is so disjointed and filled with plotholes and logic flaws that it is genuinely boring.
The online functions all sound like they should be fun;  but they all fall flat for obvious technical reasons:
Connecting to another player's game requires far too many circumstancial factors to be in alingment. Being able to play as a monster in another player's game might be more fun of the UI and controls for playing as a monster actually worked-- they don't. And even the overlapping portions of the character chapters fail to really present a gameplay environment where interaction  (cooperative/competitive, or even just knowing you are playing with another human being) are really utilized.
This is a game made by lazy developers for lazy people.

Are you too afraid to play Slender: The Arrival, sequel to the PC horror hit that taught us to associate evening-wear with fatal outbreaks of screen static? Well, here’s how to overcome your terror: imagine that Slender Man himself is that awkward person you don’t want to talk to at any given party. As with any social space invader, the guy's core tactic is to materialise silently in front of you, perhaps peeking shyly from behind an object, in hopes of catching your eye. The trick is to let your gaze slide over him to something else in the environment - hey, isn’t that so-and-so from Marketing in the corner? - while stepping casually but firmly to one side.
OK, so it’s not quite that simple. For starters, whenever Slender Man appears the screen goes nuts, stretching and splintering as though in the presence of an undersized black hole. Throw in all but perpetual nocturnal conditions and landscapes that are cluttered with loose objects, and you’ll often struggle to pinpoint your adversary’s precise location.
More troublingly, Slender Man’s the pushy type. The longer you succeed in escaping his clutches, and the more mission-critical items you collect, the more frequently he’ll show up and the closer he’ll get. And have we mentioned the context-sensitive score and audio effects? Because if that spidery, faceless guy in the suit doesn’t give you the willies, the cacophonous, grating report that sometimes accompanies his entrance certainly will.
But what if you’ve butted heads with Slender Man before? Well, The Arrival’s, er, arrival on Xbox One may struggle to impress. It’s largely the same game as on Xbox 360 with negligible visual enhancements and the same problem of diminishing returns. The jewel in the crown is the second level, a re-imagining of Slender: The Eight Pages in which you hunt for notes scattered around a forested area.
There are eight notes in total but 10 locations to investigate, some of which swap places between playthroughs, plus a selection of possible starting points, so no two sessions are alike. Prioritising areas in accordance with Slender Man’s aggressiveness is critical: when he’s at his most annoying, the last place you want to be is the Visitor’s Centre, with its plethora of single-exit rooms. There’s a run button to help you out of a jam, but it’s tied to an invisible stamina bar that’s easy to exhaust when the pressure is on.
Sadly, the scenarios (some accessed by collecting or interacting with certain objects) that make up the remaining hour or two of playtime consist of slightly limp variations on a gambit that isn’t nearly substantial enough to stand comparison with, say, fellow indie offering Outlast. The third level introduces a second foe who can be kept at bay with the beam of a flashlight; the echo of her footsteps through the depths of an abandoned mine is unnerving, but the basic explore-avoid-collect pattern is the same.
A later, more intriguing chapter takes place on a farm estate with some catacombs at one end and a deceptively picturesque cornfield in the middle. It’s relatively elaborate, but it won’t keep you busy for long.
If you like horror, but you’ve yet to have the pleasure of Slender Man’s company, his Xbox One incarnation is absolutely worth its budget price tag. The Eight Page template loses its bite with repeat exposure, but the game’s volatility remains invigorating given the genre's continued reliance on scripted scares and sheer grotesqueness. If you’re a veteran of Slender, however, it’s probably best to avoid eye contact. There’s not enough meat on these bones.
This review is based on the Xbox One, Xbox 360 and PC versions of the game.

I really love this game, but I haven't mastered it yet. I got in early alpha, before it was on Steam, so I have many more hours logged.
It plays like a traditional Rogue-like, but the robot theme gives it a very different feel, and there are some key differences with other games of the genre. You don't have a 'build' or 'class' as such, you have to scavange parts and weld them onto yourself, and whatever you find dictates your playstyle, and as parts get destroyed it creates a tense, dynamic game where you're taking each encounter seriously because a few wrong moves and it could end your game. That means there aren't any trash fights, each and every move around the levels is meaningful and can have a big impact on your game, and that also makes it hard as hell. It is equal parts exciting and frustrating to have your cool toys taken away by a rough fight, only to roll into another room and find something even cooler, or a big pile of something you didn't need. And boy, the weapons in this game are cool, with beautiful visual effects for the various weapon types. There's great variety in weapons each with their own tactical advantages, as well as a ton of utility parts that mix up your playstyle as you go.
The difficulty comes from mastering the tactics and learning AI behaviours and so on, with the UI being polished and informative and the full mouse controls are intuitive and slick. I normally play Rogue-likes with the numpad, but I've played this extensively with the mouse and the keyboard and they both work great.
The graphics are beautiful in my opinion, with a lovely minimalist tileset and really great ASCII art for part schematics, and you can play the game in full ASCII if you want.
Definitely check it out if you like Rogue-likes, and give it a shot if you don't because it's different enough that it might surprise you.

Cogmind is a fascinating game in a very interesting world and so far I am having an insane amount of fun with it.
The biggest difference aside from the looks is that there is no XP grind, levels and classes. Everything is done with parts that you constantly pick up, upgrade and switch to adapt. Your lifeblood is your core that is partially protected by these parts. Resource management exists in form of energy, matter and heat.
The control scheme is very intuitive and works with only mouse, keyboard or both and can be switched via a single button press.
What I like in particular (aside from general gameplay and feel) is the UI that really supports the games ideas and its design core. This has to be one of the most interesting, functional (drag&drop and a compare-item function in a roguelike) and satisfying UIs I have seen so far. Its usage reminds a bit of tiling window managers with a tabbing function.
The aesthetics are a nice blend of ASCII and tiles with some graphical effects (cool explosions, fade-ins, graphical glitches if you are corrupted, etc.). You can switch between ASCII and Cogmind-style on the fly. The interface does an awesome job of explaining everything directly or via popups so that the (spoiler free) ingame manual is not really needed. Still, if you want some formulas and examples, feel free to read up.
Cogmind features an extensive hacking system that even has a manual option where you can type the commmands. To complete the hacking experience, the commands are cAsE sEnSiTiVe and the console has an auto-complete function.
The robot world is alive! Destroy something and robots will come to pick items up, clear debris, investigate, rebuild walls, dig tunnels, etc.
The entire game breathes old meets new.
Cogmind now resides along with
on my "survival thumb drive" for the deserted island / rogue ai / robot revolt scenario.

Cogmind is a roguelike in its own class - withOUT classes, or levels, or skills.  As you progress, you gain slots into which you install a vast array of parts, of four categories: power, propulsion, utility, and of course weapons.  This provides both an incredible amount of customization (since you choose what type of slots you gain) and a demand for careful balancing and planning: depending on your preferred means of propulsion (until it all gets blown off), you can only support so much weight before slowing down.  This means you can't fly around bristling with eleventy billion cannons unless you want to go very slow.  Slap on treatds, though...  you must also weigh the energy demands of your various gadgets - scanners, ECM, etc all take energy, as does moving, and firing weapons.  You need enough power for all that.
So, my experience thus far: scavengers are little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Rocket launchers and grenade launchers make me cackle maniacally, followed shortly by mass devastation.  Watching the ensuing flurry of robots rebuilding in the aftermath is both adorable and engrossing (also tempting if the launcher hasn't gotten blown off). So far I've tried going rambo-mode, flying around sneaky-like, a short lived hacking setup, and now to CRUSH EVERYTHING LIKE A BOSS.
So yeah, buy it.

I was planning on writing a longer review, but zxc's review is already really good, so give that one a read, please.

I've played alot of roguelikes of various sorts, whether they be turn-based, or real-time (no, I dont care about the term "rogueLITE").  The turn-based ones though, are often things I dont get along with.  Such as Nethack for example, which I've never liked (blasphemy!) with it's irritating "your character is dumber than a stump, so every item ever is unidentified, and may explode, HAHA SCREW YOU" sort of mechanics.  Not to mention that they're usually filled with really strange, obscure, and nearly hidden mechanics that are almost impossible to find and understand on your own.  Everything is always hidden, nothing is explained, and just... you get the idea.  Oh, and the UI is typically horrible.  HORRIBLE.  I always wanted a good turn-based roguelike that went AWAY from these concepts instead of just trying to be the 396734th Nethack clone.
Enter Cogmind:  Exactly the game I've been wanting for who knows how long.  A game which keeps the very high complexity and depth of the "core" roguelikes, yet removes all of the problems I've always hated, and replaces them with very well thought-out mechanics of it's own that really make it stand out, and that ooze with quality.
Cogmind's concept is that you're this... floaty robot thing.  You start out as just a core, and you'll then assemble yourself from parts scattered nearby. Legs, treads, guns, reactors, whatever.  These items are all-important, as they define the entirity of your build as well as your abilities.  No EXP or anything here.  But while it's your core's HP that keeps you alive, much of the incoming damage will hit the parts you have equipped.  Before long, some of them will shatter, and you'll have to get new ones.  Good thing this works the other way around as well.  Wreck your robotic foes, and take THEIR parts for yourself.  Unlike you, enemy bots have extremely low amounts of core HP, so destroying them doesnt mean that most of their parts will shatter first.  Still, sometimes you might get a part that's mostly undamaged, and other times you may be stuck with a pile of gizmos that are missing some pieces.  But they'll just have to do.  Rolling with the punches is a huge part of the gameplay, and you'll need to adapt to the situation as well as what items are accessible to you.
Fortunately, there's alot more to it than that.  This is not a game where the RNG alone will kill you.  Finding parts isnt exactly an uncommon occurance. They are everywhere, and there's about a bazillion different types.  Weapons, power sources, utilities... all sorts of awesome stuff.  And they dont just come from shattered bots.  The facility that you're crawling through is filled with all sorts of parts lying around for you to find.  You are given many, many options, very frequently, allowing you to make choices in just how you want to build yourself up.  What's more, these parts are actually INTERESTING.  Deathrays and missile launchers and other crazy weapons are fun and all, but there's more to it than just those.  Utilities in particular can do all sorts of different things.  You might find a targeting processor, giving you more accuracy.  Or you might find a terrain scanner, capable of finding hidden maintenance doors, allowing new avenues of escape.  Or perhaps units to help you hack things, signal jammers, and many others, each more creative than the last.  All of these constantly changing parts make sure that your character and setup never grow stale over the course of the run.
Speaking of hacking, that's another major aspect.  You'll find all sorts of terminals as you explore.  Terminals have boatloads of different functions, but you're not a normal user... you're a rogue bot, and needless to say, you dont exactly have security clearance.  If you want to use these many, many functions... and you do... you'll have to risk hacking these things.  Hacks may fail, they may be detected, they may start a trace routine, leading investigation squads to your location.  But the info and services you can get from hacking is invaluable.  You may get schematics for crafting, or perhaps the chance to see the status and location of security patrols, or many other things.  You have TONS of options here, and the hacking mechanic adds alot to the game overall.
Even with all of those options though, this is one DIFFICULT game.  It's not going to murder you outright.  This isnt one of those roguelikes where some monster can come around the corner and tear you in half with one hit.  It's specifically designed so that DOESNT happen.  If you lose, it's in a non-frustrating way, and there's always a chance to examine where you went wrong, rather than going "What the heck, how was I supposed to deal with that?".  And that's good, because you WILL lose.  Alot.  Your enemies are extremely numerous, and the more trouble you cause, the more concerned and aggressive the central AI will become, sending out larger and more powerful squads after you.  In addition you have to deal with all sorts of traps, each more insidious than the last.  But as with everything else, you have things you can do to counter all of this.  But it's up to you to figure out how to use the tools available.
Oh, and I also want to mention the UI:  It is amazing.  Usually... okay, pretty much always... roguelikes get this horribly wrong, with confusing, broken interfaces that dont make much sense and are hard to even use.  But not this one.  This game goes out of it's way to make everything accessible, and to give you information in a way that's nice and easy to understand.  It's the best interface I've ever seen in one of these.  Not to mention that the game is just gorgeous.  Not just the default tileset, but... everything.  The animated explosions and energy blasts, or even the interface itself, it all fits the game and really emphasizes everything that is going on.  It also makes it easier to see just what's happening.  If a bullet you fire hits it's target, you will SEE it hit it's target, and you'll also see if you did core damage.  You dont have to stare at the combat log the whole time just to see what is going on.  I normally never bring up things like graphics when I review a game, but this one deserves a special mention... it's just that good.
Overall, the game is fantastic.  I honestly cant really think of anything I dislike about it.  It's accessible yet incredibly complicated and deep.  It has an insane amount of content.  There's tons of things to do.  The combat system is fantastic.  The game world is detailed, with tons to see and lore behind all of it.  The challenge is extremely high, but you're given so many options to deal with it... the possibilities are endless, and you're not restricted to any specific playstyle.  Whether you prefer stealth, or want to crash through situations and blow up entire rooms (did I mention EVERYTHING is destructible?), you have that choice, and it's viable.
There's so very, very much more I could talk about here, all of it positive.  But Steam only allows me so much room.  An incredible game that will pull you in and not let go.  You'll die alot, but you'll love every moment of it, and you'll always learn more.  One of the most satisfying roguelikes I've seen, and very highly recommended.

I've had Rocksmith for over a year now and its on sale for the holidays so I thought I'd chime in.
Rocksmith is an excellent learning tool for beginners. It has an intuitive interface for notes which should be familiar to any Guitar Hero/Rockband fans. It has a plethora of lessons, songs, and minigames that are all focused on making you a better guitar player in some aspect. The game touts a 60 day challenge (Play 60 days straight, you know guitar!) while I have some quibbles with that I think this game will bring you up to speed quite quickly.
Rocksmith really shines when you are a beginner and when it is paired with another tool, usually online lessons are recomended. Decent guitars are cheap, and the audio cable needed for the game can be had for cheap (with the game too). If you have had the passing interest, have the time (1 hour a day really),  and have the money (~$200) it is well worth exploring. Furthermore, the game allows you to explore rhythm, lead, and bass guitar at your leisure. And if you own a normal guitar you can "emulate" the bass guitar. So it offfers a lot in what to teach you.
I have two issues with Rocksmith that I think anyone purchasing it should know about:
1) The tutorials, minigames, and other things are quickly outgrown as you progress as a guitarist. This is obviously intentional, but then all you are left with is Session Mode (which lets you just jam) and Learning a Song. This is alot of content, and if you have trouble reading tabs or lack the intitiative to learn then it is a great way to make some music (your own or someone elses)
2) Learn a Song doesn't really teach you a song. The songs in the game have a dynamic difficulty but depending upon your current skill level or knowledge of the song you could memorize or get it in your muscle memory a very simplified part of the song. The dynamic difficulty will up, and then your memory is uselss. Also restarting and focusing on a part of a song is possible but a bit cumbersome. The Riff Repeater allows you to slow down and focus on a specific part of the track. However only certain sections of the song are repeatable. You may have to trudge through a good 20 seconds of the song to get to the 3 second riff that is tying knots in your fingers. Furthermore, I may have sunk a small number of hours into the game but atleast 60 of it has been towards learning a song. There are very few songs I've learnt using Learn a Song or have memorized. The note track really doesn't teach you to memorize it, especially if you are good at sight reading it. Another thing is that Learn a Song is really focused on the rote version of their song. It doesn't care itself with different phrasing or styles. As you learn more with guitar you'll notice the possibilities for exploring and augmenting a song are endless and easy. Learn a Song doesn't give you a nice place to switch the tempo, alter the beat, change the key, or throw in some chord variations. Its a good primer to a song, but if you really really want to get proficient remember that you have a guitar and that it can be played outside the game.
TL:DR Want to learn guitar? This is a great first step, but once you get good at it don't be afraid to start learning outside the game.

The store page's description says pretty much anything I could about what kind of game Caves of Qud is, though I will add in that if you know (or are willing to Google) what Gamma World is, then this is basically
Gamma World: The Video Game. I played this game a few years back when it was free and much less complete thanks to a YouTuber called Plumphelmetpunk's videos on it. Loved it then, love it now, and with all of the frequent updates, it keeps getting better every time I play it.
On to gameplay. Although Caves of Qud is extremely well-made, at it's heart it's still a fairly normal roguelike. You make, you die, you learn. You make better, you live longer, you die anyway, you learn some more. Repeat until tired of game, either due to frustration or total mastery. There's a lot of different options and a ton of fun and viable builds to play with, so you'll have a hard time running out of ways to die horribly. The main thing that sets it apart is the world, which is apparently retrofuturist, but most people will just call it post-apocalyptic and call it a day. There's a lot to do and see out there, but unfortunately most of it is obsfucated behind a pile of purposefully obscure words. Mostly QoC just does it in an attempt to make the world sound as exotic as possible, but there's only so many $5 words one person can handle before you just start glazing over the descriptions.
tl;dr - It's an amazingly good roguelike if you like roguelikes. The world is unique and interesting. Bring a dictionary unless you tend to use words like "tumescent" in everyday conversations.

The game is set in what can be seen as a post-apocalyptic wasteland with mutants, espers, ancient ruins, and a persistent scarcity of water—so scarce, in fact, that it's the default form of currency in the pseudo-barter economy that the whole world has adopted. Honestly speaking, CoQ is better enjoyed when you have time to sit down and immerse yourself, as opposed to favoring the pick-up-and-play nature of many other roguelikes and roguelites. If that sounds like your cup of tea, definitely give this a shot.
Caves of Qud is a roguelike that brings something fresh to the genre, not in its entirety, but in enough ways that I feel it's worth highlighting if you're tired of the same-old Nethack and ADOM experiences. Your direction is not given through narrative exposition, but rather by talking to people and forming your own understanding of what's going on in the world, with the choice of how best to proceed being left entirely up to you. This particular aspect of the gameplay isn't original, but the setting and lore behind the realm you're thrust into definitely is.
The style of the game aside, the controls deserve being commented on due to how much they affect the enjoyability of the game. They're a mix of old and new that most RL veterans will appreciate. It's not quite as modernized as something like Tales of Maj'Eyal, but has enough improvements over the retro fare to be appreciable and praise-worthy. The controls may take some getting used to for those new to the genre, but are otherwise standard fare, with some level of customizability allowing for streamlining use of abilities and talents. It's even possible (using Joy2Key) to map most standard actions to a controller and play the game almost entirely through that, which is something that very few true roguelikes allow for. This is just a quality-of-life thing, but it's a huge one, and one that makes CoQ a perfect intermediary even for people looking to dip their toes in the waters of more complex RL titles. In short, the controls are varied enough to require some minor memorization, but simple and intuitive enough that picking up the many controls doesn't take much time at all.
Last, but definitely not least, is the gameplay itself. God damn does this thing deliver on what makes a great roguelike great: options. This may be best expressed by recounting my initial experiences with the game, as compared to my current one:
My first character was a multi-legged, winged chimera Gunslinger who I intended to be the fastest gunner the game world had ever seen. I took traits to make him faster than almost anything I could run into, gave him the ability to see in the dark, and specced to prep myself for sniping my foes with impunity. He lost his life to thirst, as I had no idea that you could harvest any one of the thousands of vines surrounding the common salt-water pools in the world for an abundant source of fresh water. I made the mistake of using my sole fresh water container to scoop up salt water, intending to attempt to purify it using fire. Not only did that prove not possible (to my knowledge), but I was soon parched and without water to afford... well... water.
Lesson learned: Harvest water from watervines, and treat the liquid as an emergency reserve.
My second character, along with the three or so after him, were all re-attempts of the same initial Gunslinger. This time, I made it to the end of the first 'dungeon', accomplished my mission, and as I was preparing to leave, noticed a massive sleeping mutant Bearling in a corner. I was careful, inspecting it from a distance and assessing that it was far too risky to attempt to wake it. As my luck would have it, a bat in the same room as the Bearling—friendly towards me due to my wings improving my reputation with winged creatures—decided to 'help' me by attacking and waking the hibernating beast. Within the span of two turns, the bat was eviscerated and the bear had charged directly to me, its lunging bite taking me from full life to the game-over screen all at once.
Lesson learned: Pay attention not only to Hostile threats, but even to the supposed allies that might cause me trouble indirectly.
In his next life, my Gunslinger made it much farther along than before, making it to the fourth in-game story location which had me searching an underground complex full of hostile mechs for an important NPC. I noticed an armed turret through a doorway. As I had faced two at once before and survived, I made the mistake of being cocky, thinking I could just walk up to it and melee it to death, as I was low on ammo but too stubborn to retreat to restock. The instant I stepped in the room, I got flashbacks to that one room in Dark Souls 2 with all the ballistas being aimed at the sole entrance; no less than four turrets beeped as they locked onto me. I did the only thing I could, taking a step back to break line of sight, but it was already too late.
Lesson learned: Approach all situations with caution unless completely equipped to handle their potential outcomes.
After a few games like the ones described above, in most cases involving me resorting to killing things with melee weapons as a range-specialized wandered due the combined factors of a scarcity of ammo and my own terrible aim, I decided to try a psychic character instead. This went much smoother early on, as I was able to blast my enemies away using lasers without worry for ammo or missing my targets. However, I was much more fragile in return for my power. This character did not die to thirst, bear, or turret. He died at the end of the first dungeon, 5XP away from his next level, having attempted to gain this experience by attacking a thorny vine on the wall, becoming stuck on said thorns, and subsequently bleeding to death as he tried in vain to pull himself away while the plant lashed out at him in self-defense. If I had simply used my laser on the plant instead of trying to melee it to death, this particularly humiliating but well-deserved death would never have taken place.
Lesson learned: Don't panic. When in danger, stop to consider what tools are available and how best to apply them.
As it stands, I've learned from my many mistakes, and my current character is doing quite well. This learning experience is a huge part of the game though, as the world will not hesitate to beat the player down at every opportunity presented. My advice to those of you who read about these experiences and were enticed by the prospect of a difficult and punishing game would be to read up on the game before-hand, learn what messages mean what, and equip themselves with the knowledge to see themselves towards a successful completion of CoQ. Avoid spoilers where possible when doing so, but absolutely attempt to find logs of other players' mistakes and their consequences so that you can avoid making them yourself. In my case, this kind of involving experience is exactly what I look for in my roguelike titles, and I whole-heartedly recommend this game for it.
Not for everyone but very fun once you figure out how to stop dying.

Caves of Qud is an old school 80's throwback to ASCII permadeath dungeon crawling rogue-likes of yore. It oozes that retro vibe, but in a 80's Apple 2e roguelike way.  Everything about the presentation is phenominal. The style, the sound design, the music, all the way through to the actual game itself.  Caves of Qud is a rogue-like fan's dream come true.
Pros:
- Style. It feels old school in all the right ways. I absolutley love the aesthetic.
- World building. The writing is thoughtfully crafted provides a sense of immersion and detail.
- An open world. In most rogue likes, you are left in a single dungeon and tasked with reaching the bottom. Not here. This game throws you into a complex open world with a variety of locations, settlements, and of course caves.  It really helps build a story and a sense of place.
- OPTIONS - the big one. A TON of ways to build your character and then so many ways to level them up.  Practically endless possibilities. So much to play with here.
- Saving. You have to enable it in the menu, but you can play this game with saving. I would advise new players do so as to understand the expectations of the game and get used to it's systems.
- Steam workshop.
Cons:
- If you dont like ASCII like rogue-likes then this isnt going to help you I dont imagine.
All in all an EASY recommendation for anyone who likes rogue-like games. It is fantastic.

A mysterious roguelike with fun elements such as a variety of physical and mental mutations that you can get, like having wings to fly, a beak, claws for digging, etc. If you're a fan of Nethack or other such roguelikes, I highly recommend this.

Caves of Qud is in Early Access, but don't let that stop you; new features are being added (almost) every Friday.  As of the writing of this review, the most recent updates have revamped Long Blades and Axe skill trees, which had drawn the community's ire for being underpowered.  But enough about that, let's get to the game itself.
Qud is a post-apocalyptic world rife with technology from the old days just waiting to be discovered.  The game is a good old-fashioned roguelike set in this world, offering tons of character customization.  As in most roguelikes, the action takes place on a grid of tiles, operating by turn-based rules, so the enemy only acts when you do, offering unlimited time to plan your approach.  Many sights and interactions are conveyed entirely through text, thankfully very well-written in Caves of Qud's case.  In fact, it's this writing, the setting itself, that makes CoQ stand apart from the rest of the roguelikes.
For example, due to the massive amounts of salt covering the planet, fresh water is such a scarcity that it is actually the game's currency!  As in most roguelikes, your character has hunger and thirst to manage, but water weighs quite a lot, and merchants will take it from you if you can't pony up valuable enough goods for a trade.  Do you hoard water to stay healthy, trade it away for that sweet dagger, or get yourself a gold nugget that weighs very little and (unlike other items) always sells for 100% of its value?  It's a balance of risk and reward unlike anything I've ever seen.
Also, the game's "faction" system can ensure even more variability than most roguelikes.  Nearly every sentient race keeps track of your actioins and allies, and responds accordingly.  One notable instance of this is the Machinimists, who revere the ancient artifacts as holy relics, even the lowly folding metal chair.  One quest in the main story involves entering one of their most revered holy grounds.  Most characters will have to fight their way in, but those closely allied with the Machinimists can simply walk in.  And again, it's not just the Machinimists...you may find yourself allied with birds, the Putus Templar, fungi...and your allies will not attack you, or may even help if they see you fighting someone.
There is a main quest line in the game even in this version, but it's relatively short.  Fortunately, the "Sultans of Qud" update added randomly generated history to the game.  With this history of Qud's ancient rulers comes ruins of shrines, arenas, and more dedicated to them.  By studying engravings and statues around the world, you may gain a lead that points you to a historic site, within which a powerful item lies in wait, one wielded by the sultan themselves.  The explorable world is huge, stretching far and wide as well as deep underground.  Even in the game's current state, there's plenty to do.
But the star of the show here is the customization.  Tons of mutations, powers, skill trees, and equipment ensure that you can play this game however you want.  Be a four-armed porcupine and wield four pistols!  Shoot fire from your mind and electricity from your hands!  Chop off your enemy's face with an axe, then wear it!  Psychically beguile a goat, then proselytize to a lowly farmer, thus traveling with a party of three (who themselves can level up and develop mutations)!  Learn to build and modify machinery, to arm yourself with a stun rod and grenades!  Pull off some sweet angel cosplay with a flaming sword and beautiful wings!  If mutations aren't your thing, staying "pure" grants you access to cybernetic implants, including a railgun!  Or attach robotic arms to yourself and put shields on them, and whip out your best Sundowner impersonation!
Overall, Caves of Qud is a fantastic roguelike that compares favorably to even some of the greats of the genre, and this is in its current Early Access form.  Once more quests are added and the game is released proper, be prepared to see this on a lot of people's best-of lists.

I'd like to preface my review with a disclaimer; my reviews are typically written and intended for older gamers like myself. If you are looking for a competitive management sim with defined objectives, it is a game you will want to try. If you are looking for more freeform play as with previous tycoon titles, you may want to wait until a more suitable mode is included. Having tried and failed as a programmer myself, I respect anyone who can complete a project and follow through.
I've added suggestions as an update to provide a more constructive form of criticism as I had previously stated: There are many things I like about this game. Just because I don't recommend it doesn't mean you wouldn't like it.
"Not really what I'd consider a "Tycoon" namesake, far too linear and defined. The game is very rigid and instead of allowing you to mold a channel for a specific audience, it forces you to cater to a random viewer-type each hour. About the only thing I was actually able to customize about my channel was it's name, and which of 3 avatars I wanted running it.
The economics seem well designed, and progression was available; however, after a few days I realized my MTV-Squared channel was only playing romance and anime to cater to the women and children that were tuning in. If I had been able to pick my content, and draw an ever-increasing target audience, I'd still be playing it... but the way it's delivered is far too unrealistic (afterall, how often does lifetime cater to frat boys?)
The graphics, music and character movement were all enjoyable, and I really appreciated the programmers sense of humor and references to movies."
I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a management simulation with strict defined goals... but a tycoon? Imagine Dino-Park tycoon with a pre-built park, and you need to add the dinos the current guests want to see. An actual tycoon game allows for a lot more freedom, typically does not have a hard ending in which you win or lose, and is less competitive in game (more about staying in the black, and ever-expanding your business/park/etc.)
UPDATE: I would like to point out that I didn't dislike the current game mode; quite the contrary. Multiplayer in this style game is actually a very cool concept. I'd also like to expound a bit on what I think would make this a better tycoon.
1.) Dynamic Crowds/Custom Stations Example: A player buys the game wanting to make a specific-style network (ie. TNT, Nickelodeon, Lifetime, Sci-fi Channel, Comedy Central) but is immediately burdened with the fact they cannot legally purchase several titles within that genre. The player goes to set programming, but the audience is random throughout the day (great for the initial arcade style mode, not so great for cultivating an audience in your personal sandbox.). The player starts airing only one Genre, over and over, and eventually the audience adapts (people stop tuning in when they hate the channel, and make more of an effort to find time when they love it.)
*Granted... the math behind this one may be a challenge with the current system.
2.) Custom Touches, The Little Things: Minor aesthetics go a long way, the ability to set your office decor (maybe a handful of movie posters for the wall, or genre-styled pieces for display). Anything to make the office seem more the players creation and less a defined element.
3.) Office Design/Building: While not entirely necessary to feel more like a tycoon, it would be highly liberating to be able to design your TV Station building to some degree. If a single play/endless style mode were introduced, it would be beneficial to have a smaller overall building to ease navigation and
be less overwhleming for a player to decorate.
4.) More defined identity: Add some additional content for stations that pursue a specific style. (ie. Bonuses/Perks for players who specialize in ads, directing their own films, or broadcasting pirated material.) Reward players for adhering to a specifc discipline or for balanced approaches.
More to come.

Slender: The Arrival was developed by Blue Isle Studios in collaboration with Mark J Hadley, the developer of the original Slender the Eight Pages in 2012. The Arrival is an excellent psychological and atmospheric, story driven horror game in which the player takes on the role of Lauren, who is investigating the disappearance of her friend. As well as facing new enemies such as Slender Man's Proxy, the player can immerse themselves in an all-new, unique and innovative storyline. Players are introduced to a 'scrapbook' feature in which they can view the collectibles that they are able to find throughout the game. The Arrival is a truly interactive and immersive experience. Players will also be rewarded with longer gameplay, stunning visuals and a soundtrack equally as beautiful as it is terrifying and tense. Fans of the original Slender game are presented with a remake of The Eight Pages. Chapter 9 'Genesis' contains all the original landmarks and page locations from the 2012 game, the only difference is that of much improved graphics and lighting for a greater gameplay experience. I recommend this game to all fans of horror whether they be new or familiar with the genre. A must have; 10/10

As you'd expect from the Z in the title, Zafehouse Diaries is a game about zombies. The game is similar to a rogue-like in its random nature; the town is randomized, your survivors are randomized, loot is randomized, etc. so that no two playthroughs are exactly the same. Or so it should be.
You'll find yourself in the usual boring, dreary town with a bunch of useless, racist, janitor survivors that will break each others arms and legs for refusing to play a game of chess (Not kidding). Even worse, you can even end up with Survivors that aren't good at anything at all, and you're stuck with them. If a Survivor dies, they are dead, and you wont be getting another. Expect to be given the short end of the straw many times, and to see the same stock photos for your survivors over and over.
The game is too randomized. Everything you do feels like a roll of the dice in the zombies favor. Trying to fight a number of zombies above ten, even with all your survivors armed to the teeth, is certain suicide. Chances are slim you'll be able to clear the hospital or police station, with the horde's numbers varying from 10 to 20, and even higher. Even then, trying to clear out locations is a hassle. First, you must send out a scout to check out how many zombies are outside and how many zombies are inside. You'll have to go by what they say, because even though they may have seen eight zombies inside, there are actually twenty-three. Now that you have the place scouted out, you'll need to Assault it. This consists of your survivors trekking over to the location through the city, and the murdering every zombie outside and shooting through the windows inside. More than likely, you wont get all the zombies inside. Finally, you'll need to Breach. Your survivors will go back to the location for the third time and make their way inside, where they will proceed to most definitely die - Or kill the zombies if you are immensely lucky.
Overall, the game just feels unfinished and unfair. There isn't much to do besides explore buildings, clear out buildings, try to escape, and survive. Weapon variety is dismal, with most melee weapons being absolute garbage and ranged weapons being entirely too risky to use, lest more than ten zombies surround your 'base' and you have no way to get out. Zafehouse Diaries is a good idea, but it  still feels like an alpha game and not a complete product.
The only thing I really, really enjoy about the game is the journal, although it's severely flawed as you will see the same messages over and over again. When it rains, the journal pages get wet and the sound of rain on the roof fills your ears. When it thunders, light flashes on the screen as it storms outside. When you fight, blood splatters the pages.
Good ideas but with poor implementation. I strongly advise you to buy this at a largely reduced price, at least 4.99.

This is the sort of game that redefines a genre and shows how much flexibility exists in the space. Beautiful, inventive and holds a weath of options under the hood, all wrapped up in a fantastic scifi setting. You should buy Cogmind, hack terminals, and punch robots in the face.

I remember playing a game on my old C64 called Paradroid.  The game was a lot of fun because as you explored each level, you took control of other robots and assumed their powers.  The game always played differently because there was a huge variance of robots and powers to obtain.  Cogmind reminds me of Paradroid in that your build is dependent on which enemies cross your path and how you wish to mix and match the technology that drops from the smoking wrecks.
The game is hard at first (as any proper roguelike ought to be) but once you start experimenting with different playstyles, you'll get a bit farther and farther.  There are a lot of aspects of Cogmind that you won't find in other roguelikes, such as the ability to alter the landscape and the behavior of your enemies by manipulating traps, turrets and using enemies to kill other enemies.
Although I don't look for good graphics in a roguelike, the graphical style of Cogmind is very well done in the Matrix style.  Immersion is very high - you really feel like a roving AI with hacking and shooting abilities.  This game joins the ranks of Caves of Qud and Ivan as a unique roguelike which doesn't sacrifice traditional rougelike mechanics for gimmicks or stale gameplay.

One of the crown jewels of the roguelike genre is now on Steam!
This is a game where you control a robot and you must find the exit to each level while navigating through randomly-generated levels. The main feature here is that you have to pick up and equip weapons and parts so you can properly navigate the enviroments and survive encounters with hostile machines.
If you are not experienced with roguelikes: Not the best entry point to the genre but if any of the words/sentences Grid-Based, Randomly Generated RPG with permadeath, pretty art, i have nothing to do this entire month and masochism say anything to you then keep this one in mind.
If you are a roguelike adept then I really recommend you pick this one as the part scavenging,  and overall spectacular attention to detail make this one of the most unique additions to the genre.
As a beginner on this game (may be like this because I'm a noob :P), the only thing I don't like about the game is that I was expecting more freedom in robot customization but due to the parts taking a lot of damage during combat, I found myself holding on to anything I could just so I wouldn't be left "naked" as soon as I came across an enemy squad.

Cogmind's setting pulled me in almost immediately, the sound quickly sets the imagination ablaze, the "robot-like" ASCII/tile graphics get your imagination going when you get into them, and the exploration, character building, combat, and other systems are fun and deep enough to keep me playing Cogmind for a long time.
The world of Cogmind is a captivating bit of science fiction and mystery. The sprawling facility is dotted with terminals that you can hack for, among other things, interesting lore. Some information is very heavily guarded, like the entry on "Humans." All of the information you find is added to a log that persists between runs, so you can eventually fit all of the pieces together and understand the world of Cogmind.
The game has an ASCII mode and a tile mode, which you can switch between at any time with the F3 key. All objects are labelled when they come into view. Everything is also color-coded; for example, all hostile robots are yellow. The sound in Cogmind also really helps paint a picture of the facility in your mind: my favorite is listening to the ceiling crumble after blowing some things up with the grenade launcher.
The combat creates a lot of interesting and fun decisions. You might start shutting off systems to save energy, or run away for a little bit for your systems to cool down. Sometimes parts will get destroyed and you'll have to fight without a leg, or swap in your backup power source, or run over to some destroyed robot while under fire and attach their weapons to yourself to fire back.
Finally, this is a roguelike, so every run is different. There are tons of parts to experiment with, and there are a lot of different ways to put parts on a robot brain and then use those parts to explore a sprawling complex with lots of interesting floors, machines, and enemies ;) If you like science fiction or are looking for an entry point into "classic" roguelikes, look no further.

I've been playing this game since I was about fifteen, and I'm twenty-two now. I always seem to end up coming back to it. It has that early internet flash game era those of us around my age will appreciate - all those years in school playing Club Penguin (pre-disney) and Neopets... it's that sort of feeling. Fun, cartoony, more than a little silly, with a strong population of twelve year olds that just adore to swear at you.
But this game has come on leaps and bounds since I first played it. Introduction of various game modes (including your basic Vanilla, for us old schoolers, bootcamp for those who have something to prove, and all sorts of other fun.), holiday events, and a never-ending parade of collectibles. The in-game currency is entirely free, though you can buy money, it's definitely not necessary!
Transformice is a classic. It's a bit tricky to get to grips with at first, there's definitely a bit of skill involved - but that's to it's merit. You don't feel like you can win it by just slapping the keys a few times, but it's definitely not impossible! If you can find good rooms with good people, then it's a really fun game to play. A lot of the time I'd say just ignore the chat box, read a few online Shaman guides, and you'll be good to go.
tl;dr - a fun little platformer with a slightly immature playerbase and a learning curve. If you can deal with random swearing in the chat, you're gonna have a great time.

While the game itself is a wonderful learning tool and fantastically fun for beginners and experienced guitarists, I cannot recommend the pc version of this game due to the windows drivers issues that many people including myself have.
The USB cord for the guitar should a simple process of plugging it in to a USB port and once the drivers are downloaded, they will be saved and remembered the next time you plug and play. Rocksmith 2014 is not only a fantastic game but a fantastic tool for learning music.
This game has a lot of great guides and is really a fun way to play along to a lot of songs. Some you will like more than others. The interesting thing is you will find some songs/music you didn't like but are super fun to play.
So I'm a bass player and I've been playing for about 5 years. I came into this being interested in the jam mode, the sound/pedal customization, and just curious to the accuracy of this game. I have to say I came away from this thing very impressed. Will it teach you to play guitar or bass? No. It won't do that for you. This game/tool will give back to you what you put in to it.
Getting good at this game means getting better at your instrument. Getting better at your instrument takes work. If you're willing to put in that work then what you will get out of it is amazing. This provides so many tools at your disposal to learn the songs it has to offer (through the main game, import old rocksmith stuff, or dlc) that it really is amazing. Struggling with a part? Use the mode to break down certain sections and hit it at 20% speed. Oh you nailed that with 100% accuracy? Speed it up a bit more.... Then a bit more... Then a bit more... You can truely nail hard sections of songs and it provides the feedback to help you understand what you're doing wrong.
If you want to learn any of the music in this game and you want to know that the music you're playing is 100% accurate rather than playing tabs you find or trying to get it by ear and it doesn't sound 100% right then this is for you for sure.
All of the tones/pedals/effects options that are available to tinker with are fantastic as well. Interested in the sound/effects provided by a pedal like delay and etc? Hey just tinker with it in this thing and that will help you wrap your mind around it and see if you would actually want to drop the money down on something like that.
As I mentioned though. To get better at playing music it takes work. If you don't like putting in that work to learn/get better at bass/guitar then you probably should go look at rock band or guitar hero. If you're willing to put in the work though then this is a fantastic tool.
