I'm going to be reviewing 2 different versions of this game, as I got it in a bundle which came with both PC and Mobile versions.  If you're only interested in a specific version, skip to that.
OVERALL:
This is one of those games that kinda makes you think and relax at the same time.  It's almost like a soothing trip through the mind of the blocks you play.  Emphasizing this is the naration, which I think is the highlight of the game.  Seems every level there is new commentary that adds to the overall "story" behind Thomas and his friends.
The graphics are wonderfully done for being so miniscule.  I mean, how much rendering can you really do to an untextured square?  But that doesn't stop this game from being a wonderful experience visually.  It seems like all objects have a shadow from a background light source, and that source moves with the player's locaton on the puzzle.  It's an absolutely wonderful experience.
I'd have to give sound in this game a medium score.  While there is plenty of audio to keep your ears entertained, there are a few musical tracks that get a little annoying after hearing them for 10 levels.  Depending on your skills, and which device you're playing the games on, those 10 levels can either be wonderfully fast or painstakingly slow.
ANDROID SPECIFIC:
For the Android devices I used both a Galaxy Tab 10.1 and a HCT One S...  You can tell almost immediately that this game was designed to be multi-platform due to it's minimalistic controls.  It's not really clear which platform was first, I'll assume mobile since it seems better laid out on a touch-screen.  That said, using a touch-screen interface isn't without it's problems.
Thomas Was Alone is one of those platformer games that requires you to have perfect timing on a lot of it's puzzles.  With a touch screen you can be left with delays, or missed taps all together, leaving you to fail the level.  This gets increasingly frustrating as the problem isn't due with your skills, but with the hardware you're playing the game on.  You keep thinking to yourself, "I would have made that stupid jump if the dam touch screen picked up my tap".  Overall I found the portable version of this game fairly annoying, simply due to this control issue.
PC SPECIFIC:
I found the controls on the PC to be a little worse in their default layout, having to reach to some pretty odd positions to swap your characters.  Regular movement is done with the left and right arrow, while jumping is done with the spacebar.  That said, your character swaps are all over the keyboard ranging from Q to L making it awkward to perform fast swaps.  While you can just tap a single key, like Q, to scroll through your characters it is a little slower than if you were to have your characters all lined up, like using Q, W and E for example.
The controls on the PC were, of course, much more responsive.  This led to the early levels being almost too easy, while many deaths were suffered in the portable version during the same levels.  Thankfully the naration was there to draw your mind away from the simplicity of those early levels.
Conclusion:
Control issues aside, Thomas Was Alone is one of those games that simply cries out to be great.  It's got all the aspects of a wonderful platformer mixed in with story naration that's above par.  The game is a wonderful experience and I highly recommend it to not only platformer fans, but anyone who might be on the fence about buying this game.  You won't regret it.

Right out of the gate, Resident Evil 6 is -not- the horror experience you would expect if you are coming from the first few games. Reviewing it would be quite difficult, and a recommendation would only be up for grabs for those who haven't played the original surival-horror RE games. I myself haven't played any of the RE games besides 5 and 6, and I honestly found them both to be great games despite their action-centric gameplay and bucket-loads of quick-time events. I'll make it as short as possible.
RE6 features several campaign runs with different characters and co-op focus(solo is available and not as difficult as RE5). The gameplay is, as most point out, very action-oriented with fancy dodges and organic movement that I found very enjoyable and is a massive step-up from RE5's movement and combat. There are loads of QTE's during cutscenes(as well as dynamic QTE's in combat to dodge attacks), although there is an option to disable the majority of them, or more specifically, the QTE's that result in game overs.
The big negatives are the boss-fights, being frequently reoccuring and never really stay dead. They also have a theme of being quite large and overblown, making most of them rather one-dimensional to fight. Some scenes in the campaign are beyond dreadful to get through(Jakes snowmobile for one), as well as some qte cutscenes like forementioned. The other elephant in the room is how little it lives up as a Resident Evil game, being quite the opposite definition of subtle. It never really builds suspense, you never feel vulnurable and you are often stocked up on supplies.
I won't blame anyone disliking the game for "not being a resident evil game", as I surely would dislike it as well had I been into the earlier games in the series, but for all its flaws, it's still bloody fun. Mercenaries is where it's at for me, with its unprecedented combat and movement shining the brightest! It takes some time getting used to for sure, but it's very rewarding once fully grasped!
All in all, it comes down to what you're after. It won't really live up to building an intriguing story, it won't scare you with psychological horror, and it will most certainly infuriate you in some campaign and QTE segments, but holy christ will it shine with the fun, dynamic combat and movement system! If you want action, get this or RE5. If you're more for horror, get RE7!

A love letter to the roguelike genre, Cogmind fundamentally examines each of the mechanics behind that type of game and turns them into games of their own.
What's a @ do?  Well, they move.  So what if we make your character a robot that you can swap in varous types of mobility, from legs to wheels to hovercraft.  A @ attacks, so how about your character can attach weapons to itself and fires them all per turn.  A @ restores energy per turn to do things, lets look at that somewhat literally, energy in the form of power generators and batteries.  A @ does all sorts of interesting utility things,  lets stick those in utility slots.  Your inventory becomes your character, and the entirety of your character becomes this sort of evolving classless microcosm with lovely, lovely stat numbers.
What about the map?  Well, the map should be generated with a high degree of variety and excellent procedural generation mechanics.  Done.  But what if we want to make the map a living thing?  What if it's inhabited by robots which actually move around the level, expanding the map, rebuilding lost bits, picking up and moving scrap?  Lets give everyone and everything on the map a reason to be there.  Now *this* is a roguelike map with some significance!
How about the lore?  Given that all the robots on the map have a reason to be there, you emerge as a strange robot looking to understand a strange world.  Scattered throughout the level are many terminals which are very miserly with their function, but with multiple runs and lucky rolls, you can pry the story of the world out of them.  Each failed hack risks bringing down the guards upon you, but what can be more precious than secrets to an amnesiac starving for answers?  A certain satisfactory dynamic narrative emerges, not only a greater understanding of this robot-run world, but your character's place in it.
Do you think roguelikes require difficulty?  Cogmind is difficult.  In fact, for the most part I would say you would be better rewarded with stealth, because the setting is one of a hostile world where you are hopelessly outnumbered if you attract too much attention.  I have played more difficult roguelikes, but I have to say I really like the balance I see here.  You will die, of course, with tradtional permadeath.  But each time, you will have learned something new, and have an interesting new strategy to consider going at it.  Like any good roguelike, being brutally returned to rock bottom is an exciting starting point.
Do you think roguelikes require ASCII graphics?  Cogmind has you covered.  In fact, whether you run in ASCII mode or not, you're in for a treat of some of the finest tile-based animations to grace a parser.
It all ties together expertly, with a craftman's attention to nailing the fundamentals and implementation.  All this, well worth your $20, rock solid and playable, and he calls it an Early Access game.
On top of that, I have to say the developer's a real nice guy.  He practically runs the roguelikedev reddit and stoicly puts up with my blathering about the things I do in Unity which can hardly even hold a candle to the magnum opus that is Cogmind.  I like to dream, but I lack focus.  But this game is a lovely reality, and an inspiration to what I might do if I can get my act together.  So yeah, maybe I'm a little biased, but that doesn't change that I have been playing games for decades and I hardly ever see them as ambitious and well-built as Cogmind.

Review:
Cogmind is a roguelike that has been in development since it's birth as a 7DRL challenge. It's very different from 'similar' games in the genre, such as Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup.
You play as a little robot that has to escape a facility. Along the way you will find lots of parts that you can weld to your body, such as threads, weels, legs, shotguns, hammers, scythes, hacking tools, fight units, drone bays, shielding units, collectors, energy cores, gauss rifles, laser weapons, grenade launchers, missile launchers, better missile launchers, amazing missile launchers...and the list goes on (there's a serious amount of different equipment).
You can use all of these items to lay waste upon your enemies...HOWEVER...the more stuff you kill, the more the overarching AI will notice your presence and will send stronger enemies towards you. So maybe being stealthy might be a good thing! There's plenty of terminals to hack, which can give you information about the current security level, but also allows you to learn more lore, new schematics, repair parts, learn where the door to the next level is etc.
It's a very deep game, and it has a very extensive manual. That said, this game does NOT hold your hand and you will be confused for a fair while not really knowing what to do (except dying over and over again). However, if you persist it will reward you!

Friday the 13th: The Game borrows many fan favorite elements from the film series. There’s a camp site, a group of young camp counselors running for their lives, and a terrifying killer named Jason Voorhees killing people who gets in his way. It has all the makings of an 80s teen slasher flick. Though, the setting and story is kept generic enough that it fits into an easy cookie cutter format for each new match. In fact, Friday the 13th doesn’t even have a solo standalone story – it’s just teens trying to survive as Jason is coming to kill them. That’s it! There’s nothing more complex than that.
The game itself is set up as a semi-open world survival horror multiplayer game where (up to) seven players take on the roles of camp counselors. Their job is to explore the camp and find a way out alive. This could be in the form of fixing the camp car/boat and driving off, calling in the police, or even killing Jason himself. The additional eighth player becomes Jason Voorhees. Their job is simple enough: kill everyone. Jason has extra abilities and a wide variety of killing methods that he can use to snuff out any camp counselor he gets in contact with. It’s a tougher battle for the teens to survive, but if they work together, everyone could survive. It can happen! (I’ve played matches where I’ve survived as a counselor, got picked off early on, and as Jason who has killed all seven counselors.)
During actual gameplay, counselors have the ability to explore cabins and search for key items. You can either arm yourself with weapons like machetes and bats or survival items like firecrackers. The best discoveries were the ones that offered a chance at escape. I loved the feeling of walking into a cabin and FINALLY locating a missing part to the camp car/boat that helped me escape. I get so excited finding car keys! Jason, on the other hand, has four abilities that progressively get unlocked as the match goes on. The longer he plays, the deadlier he becomes. And with each new power, it helps him achieve his kills in a quicker and bloodier fashion.
The real treat to the game is the design and personalities of the characters. Each available Jason (after being unlocked) has their own personal strengths, weaknesses and looks. Some can run, others are better throwers, and each has their special abilities that can be used to kill the campers. The counselors, on the other hand, fit the archetype of the typical counselors who Jason would go after. You have the jock, the goth, the geek, the prep, the coed, and the list goes on. Each type is balanced with their own pre-set stats that show off the benefits, or in some cases disadvantages, to use for the player. For instance, certain players have high luck to finding objects in cabins, but they may have low composure and will be instantly terrified whenever Jason appears.
The best way to counteract this is the perk system. For a sum of accumulated points, the player can turn the odds and receive a random perk that will help and hinder them in matches. Perks can affect fighting, stats, escaping or even offer rewards. I’m on the fence with this feature. In certain aspects it’s not advantageous to equip a perk because the consequence does too much damage against the player. And the perk is completely random, so you’re not guaranteed to get something you’ll like, or even need. On the other hand, when you’re awarded a great perk, it can change the course of the game.
Friday the 13th is an ambitious and fun survival horror game that brings the film series to life. If you ever wondered if you could survive an attack from the machete-wielding, hockey mask-wearing killer, this is the game for you. As a horror fan, I got a taste of the campy 80s slasher flair and quite liked it. While it’s not exactly groundbreaking in the PvP field, its momentum is fueled by novelty and the Jason name. The technical issues, however, have affected the experience – even with all the patches, it’s expected that a lag, a drop or a glitch will occur. Many issues have been fixed with patches, but it’s still a long way to go before perfection. Stick with the game; you’ll never be afraid as if you were watching a horror movie – this isn’t that type of survivor horror video game. However, it’s addictive, campy, and it’ll bring out the Final Girl (or Guy) in you.

My First Impression thoughts

Bob is cute, casual and surprisingly challenging. Gameplay is solid, and despite the occasional challenge levels don't feel unfair. is a top-down rogue-lite crawler very similar to

- It seemed like you can only shoot in 4 directions, but after a bit of research you actually can shoot diagonally but it's not explained anywhere in the game on how to do this. (You shoot with A, B, X, Y on a gamepad to shoot diagonally you have to hold say A to shoot down, and then press B to shoot diagonally downright)

Poor Bob is allergic to everything, but one day he decides to step outside and overcome his affliction by travelling the World and blasting anything that moves with his Inhagun 2000, so he can develop inoculations. Immunity won't develop during the course of gameplay however, so everything that moves is a threat. Unfortunately, this backstory is only available by reading the product description. I'd love to see a short intro sequence with some artwork and text. Instead, you are abruptly dumped into Bob's living room without any intro or explanation.
Graphics are cute, chunky, cartoony and bright, kind of like a more colorful Gunheimm. A good deal of attention has clearly been given to the characters and animations, which are quite detailed. Some levels feature extra little pieces of detail like hidden creatures and the lighthouse's rotating rays casting a warm light over the level.
Hypersensitive Bob is easy to pick up instantly and just have some fun with.
Bob travels between one tiny arena-like level after another in his rocket. The journey is complete when you beat them all (approximately 20) and there is no saving in between. Mid-level, you will be given the opportunity to purchase 1 of 3 random bonuses, which boost or change your abilities for the duration of the journey. Bonuses range from common types, to rare to epic to legendary. They really help to add variety and make each adventure a bit different.
Enemies are all based around some type of animal or creature e.g bees, skunks, turkeys and snails. Each one has it's own attack pattern that you'll need to learn. Touching an enemy or getting hit by a projectile docks you 1 life. Lose them all and you're back to the start of the whole adventure, unless you've collected enough points (from defeated enemies, loot, treasure chests or rare "vaccine machines") to respawn at the start of the level.
I was surprised at the level of challenge, but I found that pacing yourself and not trying to get too many shots in at once was key. I also found that I progressed much farther when I got lucky with +HP and +damage bonuses popping up between levels.
Movement is in 4 diections and so is shooting. You can fire in one direction while moving in another, but this will slow you down as Bob has to do a little turn before each shot. Keyboard users can press spacebar to fire in the direction they are facing, but that's not as useful. You have to line your shots up and judge the distance too.
The controls may be a sticking point for some people. Movement is sort of slow (Bob waddles rather than walks) and shooting leaves you stationary for a moment that really leaves you open to getting hit (there is a random bonus that reduces this movement penalty though), so timing your shots and knowing how many times to fire before retreating is crucial.
Judging by the comments in the discussion area, smoothing out the controls seems to be the #1 priority the develoeprs are working on right now.

The game has very simple, minimalist graphics, which makes it easy to run on toasters. The narrator, though he does have some limp moments, is effective at telling a funny and dramatic tale. You'll have to use Thomas and many other shapes to reach the end goal. Some shapes, (like John, a vertical and yellow rectangle) can leap their way through most levels on their own. However, shapes like John are needed in order for the weaker, inferior shapes like Chris to get to the end. Gameplay is like this throughout most of the game, with only a few level in which a single shape is commanded.
I admit that I was initially disappointed with Thomas Was Alone. This disappointment was spurred by narrator. This initial disappointment end after about 3 minutes. At that point, I found myself charmed by this simplistic game. Here's why:
The most distinguishing features of Thomas Was Alone are pretty simple. You play as various shapes. Initially you play as red rectangle named Thomas. You jumped about and at a certain point, the narrator will divulge the shape's thought to you. Then you reach an outline, each shapes with his or her own. Yes, the shapes have genders. You then begin another level, and the narrator continues advancing plot and announcing what the shape's are thinking.
Initially this put me off. The idea that I was supposed to identify and amuse myself with the adventures of a rectangle through the readings of the narrator annoyed me. It seemed like a transparent shroud of "complexity" to hide an otherwise crude game. I was wrong the moment a new shape showed up, something I wasn't expecting. This new shape was Chris, and he didn't want to be Thomas' friend. The fun started there.
From that point, a plethora of shapes are introduced over time. Sometimes they are lost. You'll find yourself playing this puzzle platformer thinking, "Did I seriously just identify with a rectangle?" And, yes, that will happen.

The gameplay and story took a while to get interesting, but it did get very interesting.  Unfortunately, the ending was pretty disappointing for the expected payoff, and there were technical problems like music overlapping between levels and messy graphics on high resolutions.  Still, it's a great game and story.

Literally the worst game I have ever played that I expected to like.  I couldn't justify spending time finishing it.  Contains every bad design decision ever made packed into one game.  The game stands of an example of what not to do when making a game for every possible game-play design decision.  It would be a much better use of your time to just watch the game on YouTube if you're desperate to experience this train-wreck.
If you buy this game you will experience:
Quick Time Events.  Thousands of Quick Time Events.
So much repetition.  Sparse checkpoints in areas riddled with instant deaths.
Forced stealth segments in a non stealth game.
Enemy invincibility frames for common enemies
Failure to save in coop on D/C, which will occur regardless of internet quality (I was on LAN).
Camera grabs during critical game play moments, many times killing you.  Movement during critical sequences is often trial and error.
Coop being unplayable due to said camera grabs focusing on the other character.
Clunky UI.  A combination of mouse and keyboard input is often required even for simple things.
Inventory management hell, in an otherwise action oriented game.
Shaky mouse cross-hair with mouse aiming.
This game is more frustrating than fun.  If you must play it, do yourself a favor and turn off quick time events. You will find enough other "content" to sate your masochism.

The action in this game doesn't get enough credit. The fluid way you can dodge, roll around on the ground, fall backwards away from a grab, all add up to depth. Combat becomes involved because now you're processing how to handle not only the enemy in front of you, but the series of them in the rear.
It's definitely true the sheer amount of QTE (quicktime events) come across as unnecessary, but you manage through them and they don't break the game. I also think the cover-mechanic could use some work, and it's needed heavily in the Chris Redfield campaign.
This is a incredibly enjoyable co-op experience. I play this game couch co-op, split screen. The "No Mercy" Mercenaries Mode is definitely the highlight after the campaign is over, and the reason I keep coming back to this game.

+ Somewhat novel, functional, and aesthetically pleasing UI that changes with each campaign
+ QTE is actually quite fun (I used mouse/keyboard setup)
+ Very easy and fun to mod
+ Very, very short load times
+ EXP is represented as tangible items that must be acquired manually; this adds to the feeling of risk and reward when levelling up
+ The four different campaigns all follow somewhat divergent paths, and intertwine at various intervals; interesting way to tell a story, and the other playable characters feel like cameos
+ Skill system is simple to grasp; upgrade with EXP, spend additional EXP to take skills to next level for added bonuses, rinse and repeat
+ Co-op gameplay is one of this game's greatest strengths, and can be immensely entertaining
- Poor lighting effects
- Absurd, campy, borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue; virtually every spoken line in the game is horrible
- While the way it is told is a refreshing turn from the norm, the plot itself has no merit whatsoever; it is poorly introduced, terribly-written throughout the entire length of the game, and very little is explained or follows any kind of cohesive narrative (I have no idea what this franchise is about, anymore)
- No weapon customization (something I remember enjoying in RE4)
- Absolutely horrendous environmental textures; 90% of the work went into textures for (playable) character models, presumably to dress up the cut-scenes
- Boss fights are terrible; all of the bosses are poorly-designed bullet-sponges with no redeeming moments, no novel mechanics, an no replay value (they also take an inordinately long time to beat, being constantly dragged out with cut-scenes)
- The creature designs are seemingly the product of one guy doodling on a napkin while the oxygen is slowly being sucked out of the room
- Pausing the game does not actually pause the game; your character crouches and you are vulnerable the entire time (I suffered a number of deaths while trying to refresh my drink)
- NPCs are lifeless, cookie-cutter shells with no personality
- Unimaginative, dull and often unintuitive 'puzzles'
- The guy drawing on the napkin also wrote the endings; they are awful
- While the QTE is marginally entertaining in this installment, any enjoyment is eclipsed by the inordinate reliance this game has on QTE in general; the game really shoves it down your throat
- The little things: This game has no charm, no fear element (except poor attempts at cheap jump scares), and no attention to detail; more than I enjoyed the game, I would notice little things that make no sense - the game feels like a cheap imitation of a bad RE fanfiction that nobody liked... with explosions
- The game plays like a rail-shooter; it has more in common with the House of the Dead arcade machines than the earlier installments of this franchise

Designed to offer its user hours of entertainment, Empire TV Tycoon is a game that tells the player to get people in front of their screens, while the game has that very same effect on the player. It’s hard to know when it’s time to stop.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Empire TV Tycoon.
The game gives the player a simple goal: to be the best channel.
As you learn the basics, you’ll soon discover that being the best doesn’t always mean having the best programs, or the best comercials deals, or the most cashflow. Sometimes, it doesn’t even mean having the highest audience.
To be the best - and to win the game - the player needs to achieve a certain number of points, “Fame” as they’re called. These points are obtained each time block, depending on the game mode, as well as your channel’s position when compared to the rival channels. Simply put, the channel with the highest audience wins the most points. However, points can also be obtained by winning some awards, with cerimonies happening every two days, and the player can choose to participate by submitting a movie, self-produced, of a certain genre. Not only are these awards a good source of Fame points, they’re also a good revenue source.
Now, here’s where the real fun, and management starts. There are eight kinds of audience, and twelve program genres - thirteen if you count “Live Events”, so, as you can easily guess, not everyone likes the same programs.
However, you must also consider the overall picture when you have more than one kind of audience in a time block, which means you’ll have to find the best suitable program for all of them to like, or at least have a positive likeability average.
Once you’ve used a program - there are four different types - it loses its freshness, meaning you won’t be able to use it, at least not efficiently, anytime soon. This is where the actual managament comes in to play, as you’ll have to juggle between what is available to you, what the vendor has and what your scriptwriters/production office can put out. Let’s not forget the pirate copies, but piracy is wrong, right?
To help you get more viewers, you can use some marketing features, of which there’s a total of five available to you. This will help you to get that tiny, tiny number of extra viewers you need to finish that one ugly commercial contract you need to comply with, unless you want the penalty hammer to come down on you.
Producing your own programs can be very good, or very bad. Some can be quite expensive, and unless the resources are properly distributed, you might end up with a poor program, while a better one could have, most likely, been obtained for a much cheaper price at the vendor.
As the player’s Fame points increase, new upgrades for the channel will be made available, from an improved movie library, to a wider broadcast, and even better actors, they’re all very good, and important to get that extra edge.
Running a TV channel is a hard thing, and doing it alone is even harder, and that’s exactly why you can hire up to four workers to help you. This sounds extremely sweet, until you’re faced with the available options, all of which have their advantages. As the Rolling Stones have said many, many times, “You can’t always get what you want.”
Who would have thought that something that looks so simple could, in fact, be so complex?
I almost forgot. References! There’s a bucketload of references in the game. From movies to series and even music. I found myself giggling a couple times due to them.
True to its description, Empire TV Tycoon allows the player to manage their own channel, competing with other channels in order to be the one with the highest audience.
From setting the correct program genre to the correct audience, or by choosing the best available, taking into consideration the blocks available, as well as the freshness of the program, it’s up to the player to run a successful channel.
I’d also like to mention that the development team was, and still is, very interested in improving the game, and making sure it’s what everyone expects it to be, and more, while quickly fixing some errors.
Unless you misread the description, or someone gave you the wrong idea, do not expect the game allow you to build your own office, or set up your own studio or set special contracts with actors.
. With a couple changes and a few additions, the Empire TV Tycoon has all it takes to be the best within the sub-genre, for years to come. Don’t be surprised to see my verdict change as new features are added.
For those that want some sort of comparison, imagine Mad TV with a much more appealing look, as well as an extremely engaging atmosphere.
.

I always love me a good Tycoon game. Especially one that has a real "Code Monkeys" type vibe. The concept is simple, you own your own studio in the Empire TV building where you schedule tv shows and movies with varying "freshness" and "quality" ratings (generally the highest) in an attempt to become the most successful channel on cable. You have the ability to buy new movies/tv shows (or pirate them) while also selling old stock to keep an influx of fresh content rolling on your channel. You're also able to schedule ad blocks to supplement your income and you can even purchase advertisement which will boost viewer numbers. There are an assortment of other features in the game from Award Shows, Studio upgrades, making your own movies/tv shows based on a point system and so on. You will be doing all of this while competing against 2 other players (AI). Be sure to move fast though, the AI players are incredibly efficient and will not make your rise on the Silver Screen, easy.
So what do I think of the game?
Well, it's simple, addicting and all about managing time and money in an efficient manner. Despite it's simplicity, Dreamsite managed to include a pretty decent amount of depth and things to do in the game, so you will never be "waiting" around for something to happen. The TV business is constantly rolling and if you even think about slowing down, you will be left behind. It would've been nice if the dev could've gotten more music, it seems like there are only about 2-3 songs in the game that play on loop but honestly, that's just a minor issue. Aesthetically, it's your usual pixel based game... personally, I love it because it makes me think of G4's Code Monkeys! What it does, it does well and it even has time to throw in a lot of Pop Culture references such as actual movie titles; Star Wars, Back to the Future etc and even features TV/Movie characters like Don Draper, Silent Bob and "Doc" Brown. So, I think it's pretty clear that I very much enjoy the game.

First of all, this game is heavily story driven.  If your into games with great visuals, this is not for you.  The game revolves around a cast five randomly generated characters, each with their own characteristics and prejudices.  Depending on your game mode, you have various objectives each playthrough, but overall you have to run around the town searching for items while keeping the zombie hoard and other encounters at bay.  There's no guarantee whats in each building, but typically police stations are full of guns while hospitals have medicine.  There are many other types of buildings from banks to motels.
You do this by assigning roles to each survivors every hour.  They can scavenge the building, barricade openings, patrol outside, cook food, set traps, investigate nearby houses, build improvements for current tools, and many other tasks, but only one action per hour per person and people need to rest every now and then.  Each person has different character traits that effect how well they perform certain tasks.
You are very limited in what you can do.  Your job is to direct the survivors, but there is no guarantee that they follow your instructions.  If you pair up the wrong people for a certain task they may work slower than if either one did it alone.  Even worse they could get in a fight and injure each other.  Events throughout the story can easily change character dispositions towards one another.  If someone gets bitten your group may be divided between what to do with them.  Keeping your group happy effects how well they work and fight together and is key to surviving.
The difficulty is brutal even on the easiest campaigns.  I often find myself regretting past decisions, whether it be breaking into a house without investigating thoroughly enough, making too much noise barricading the current building, discovering a drug addict in our group and having to deal with his withdrawal symptoms instead of letting him have his way, or letting a survivor live who eventually turns and bites someone else.  Every decision has an impact on whether you make it to the end.  Each play through is a unique experience, highly recommended.

If I'm honest, although this game has a lot of potential and I'd still recommend it to those willing to put the necessary time into it, I found Zafehouse: Diaries to be a bit more needlessly complicated than it had to be. Some people like that sort of thing, I'm not among them. A lot of actions I felt could have been simplified, and it took me a good couple hours studying all the mechanics of the game to work out everything I needed to do in order to actually play. I had trouble figuring out how to do anything with equipment but scrap it for the first few rounds playing! Once I was in, the concept reminded me a lot of Rebuild 2 on Newgrounds, which, although there's less detail and customization involved, is easy to get right into.
Okay, so I've complained enough, let's talk about some high points in this game. The fact that you can create a completely custom character with uploaded photos and customized stats puts a smile on my face. It's not every day you can make a group of zombie apocalypse survivors that includes yourself, the Egyptian god Set and Captain Picard. Another thing that caught my fancy was the fact that the characters had their own prejudices and insecurities, causing them to quarrel amongst themselves, a concept I feel isn't touched on enough in similar games. Just like in real times of crisis, the greatest danger can be the person sitting right next to you.
So, in conclusion, this game definitely needs a bit of work to simplify things a little. I really hope it gets that work as time goes on, because it'd be a shame if a game with this much potential ends up overlooked by many because they were frustrated before they even got into the game itself.

A week ago, I didn't even know how to properly hold a guitar pick, and had no idea how to tune a guitar.  Since then, I've put about an hour or so a night into this.  Today, I went online, figured out I was able to read Tabs, and was able to play Saria's Song from scratch in about 30 minutes of practice.  I've still got a long way to go, but this is huge to me.
If you're wondering if this game can teach you how to play the guitar, the answer is a resounding YES.  You will get as much out of it as you put into it.
That said, the game isn't without its flaws.  It has a hard time reading certain notes, especially on my cheapo guitar, so you might have to play with the tuning to get it just right.  It also has a really hard time reading bends, making you feel like you almost have to snap the strings just to get it to read right.
If you've always wanted to learn how to play guitar, but thought it looked too hard or were too afraid to try, get yourself a cheap guitar, the cable, and this game, and you'll get over your fear really quickly.

Without sounding like a true fanboy of the Rocksmith crew (and of Ubisoft I'm definitely not) this is one of the single most revolutionary games/pieces of software I've used to improve my guitar playing, and to learn songs.
Using Rocksmith, Rocksmith 2014, and CustomForge CDLC this is a goldmine of material and practice aids to keep any beginner, novice or even expert guitarist making progress.
After clocking approx 250+ hours on the original Rockmith (XB360), then 20+ hours on Rocksmith 2014 (XB360) before moving to the PC (for access to the CustomForge CDLC which I recommend all users look up) for another 330+ hours I'm still using this every singla day for a minimum of 30 minutes and it's an integral part of my daily guitar routine.
TL;DR If you want to improve with guitar or bass GET THIS GAME!
Edit: 705+ hours in and it's still 50% of my daily practice routine!!!

I am a huge mark for Friday the 13th, to the point where I'll defend the NES game as a misunderstood gem. When this game got announced, the amount of hype I had for it was astronomical. When the game launched, with all its warts and steep asking price, my hype deflated akin to the Hindenberg. It took a while for me to purchase this title, but a 50% discount was too good to pass up. Here's a list of what's good about the game and what's bad:
Pros:
+You can tell that the devs had a lot of love for the franchise. Almost every Jason is represented here, with more on the way. Each map is filled with Easter eggs and references to the films, and these play areas are as close to their movie counterparts as possible.
+Jason is a legitimate threat in the hands of a good player, and never feels too disadvantaged. Likewise, counselors are only as good as their players and teammates. This is a game that is best played with a mic, whether you're serious or not.
+The gameplay is varied enough to stay fresh, and the dev support continues to add on to the framework.
Cons:
-This game is buggy. Oftentimes, its just a visual glitch that takes you out of the moment. Those occasions where you get stuck or things don't work is what really ruins the experience.
-The asking price outside of a sale is a bit too steep. I love Gun Media and appreciate the work they put in. It's their right to charge 40 USD for their product, and their updates are pushing the game closer to being worth that price tag. Still, it can turn some people away.
-The control is a bit clunky. I realize this is done to ensure both Jason and the counselors don't have too large of an advantage over the other, but it really does suck when your actions feel "off" more often than not.
I have enjoyed the time that I've put into this game so far, and I will continue to spread the word about it and support the devs as long as they continue to improve the experience. As I said, I'm a huge Friday the 13th fan so my review is going to be dripping with bias. There are legitimate flaws with this game, but I can't help but appreciate work of the devs and the experiences I've had playing this with strangers over the Internet. Bottom line: you should grab this on sale if you're a die-hard Friday the 13th fan and wanted to play some fun (if flawed) asymmetrical mulitplayer.

I bought this game when it first came out. I love horror games so this seemed right up my alley. The game has had plenty of time to work out bugs and balancing issues but it's still a mess.
The game has a lot of charm early on as you hear the iconic sounds and get that nice 80's killer vibe. You'll get a nice sense of immersion and fun if you play with friends. Playing Jason is what everyone really wants but only 1 person at random gets to be the killer. Unfortunately, the game loses steam quick as its gameplay mechanics will become predictable and boring.
As a Counselor, you'll spend most matches trying not to get killed by your team. If you try to be stealthy, your team will lure Jason to you almost every time. If you try to be fast and loud, Jason will find you first and pursue you until death (or until lured into that stealthy person).
Jason can teleport directly to you or simply "Morph" into a fast-moving ghost and kill you immediately. While most Jason-players will try to pick you up and perform an execution, the unskilled players will simply hack you to death with Mouse1. This means that once found, you will be hard pressed to escape Jason, let alone hide from him. Hiding isnt really an option as "Fear" will build quickly in every Counselor. Jason uses this Fear level to track you so once he engages, your Counselor will be terrifed and very easy to find.
These gameplay elements dont offer a wide range of tactics so your matches will be very similar. Lets not forgot one of the most god awful drawbacks to this game, the end-game wait. Whether you escape early or die quickly, you will have to wait for THE ENTIRE MATCH TO END before getting your rewards (Profile exp and Character points). This means that after a frustrating defeat or swift escape, you will have the pleasure of watching Jason slowly hunt down your AFK teammates. The idea is that if you wait long enough, you might get to come back into the game as "Tommy Jarvis", the strongest character. The issue here is that Tommy has to be called in and even then, only one person can come back to play him.
Long story short: If you're not playing Jason, don't play the game (many people do just that and leave the match immediately if they dont get Jason, thus severely hindering your chances of survival)
In the end, after the nostalgia wears off and the immersion is broken, you're left with a very uninsiping horror game with little to offer players in the future. Sure they can add maps, characters and even new Jasons but the core gameplay will always be terrible. If none of this seems like a deal breaker for you, feel free to give it a shot; there really arent a lot of games out there like this one right now. I would, however, only recommend doing so for $15 or less.

Awesome roguelike, looks amazing as well. Looking forward to many hours playing Cogmind, happy to support it's development and it's devs.
---------------------------------------------
Some first impressions:
Controls: I found the controls for Cogmind, whether you're using keyboard only or using the mouse as well, work very well and smoothly, not like Dwarf Fortess or Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, whos controls take a bit of time learning and are slightly clunky (not to hate on DF or cdda, love both games!). The controls for Cogmind are very easy for newcomers to learn quickly and are well explained. UI works and looks great, and really gives you the feel of being some sort of robot-thing. Reminds me alot of the UI that Duskers has.
Graphics: The default tileset for Cogmind looks good, clean, and crisp for a roguelike, but where the graphics for Cogmind really shines is it's UI (like I said earlier, beautiful and very atmospheric) and the graphical effects of weapons, items (such as scanners), explosions etc... are perfect and impressive while still remaining true to its 2D roguelike roots. Really pushing the bar for roguelikes everywhere.
Gameplay: Fast-paced battles while trying to stay alive and figure out what's going on, unsure if you'll even make it out of this fight. Try to stay alive, be it by fighting, sneaking and avoiding, run-and-gunning, searching for more loot to better equip yourself with weapons and items, all the while looking for answers to the many, many questions that lurk within Cogminds' setting.

So far, I did not have that much time for more playthroughs. But here is the end of my second run, which may give you some idea about the game.
I was following an approach that was purely about going to the next floor, with no fight if possible. I had two treads carrying me, one hammer, one grenade launcher and one prototype energy weapon. Some commando robots saw me, and I tried to escape. I escaped into a deadend though. The enemy was approaching. I tried to hold the chokepoint and cludge the robots one by one as in usual roguelike fashion. It worked, kinda. Since in this game damage is not just a number, and it is distributed to your parts actually, after a while I lost all of my weapons except grenade launcher, my engine and my treads. So my body was consuming more energy than I produced which was zero. Some of the enemies had already died though, and while the others still shooting at me like I am a cyborg duck, I tried to scavange their fellow brethren so that I will have an engine. I even scavenged an armor, which helps me to protect my heart, I mean the core. I decided to use the grenade launcher at the end, but I was in melee range, so I tried to escape, except I had less and less energy. Then I decided to say YOLO and fired the grenade. That did not end well.
Pros
-------
+ ASCII(like) with justification, you are a robot, of course you will be seeing things differently.
+ Already fleshed out and will not have the curse of EA.
+ The game works on its own engine, so no performance issues at all.
+ Combat feels fluid even when played with mouse.
+ Pure roguelike with no metagame nonsense.
+ Scavenging as the main gameplay feature works surprisingly well.
Cons
-----
+ Steam overlay is not fully working (yet).
+ Does not use any feature of steam like friends leaderboards and such (yet).
+ Tutorial is not that well developed.

First impressions of Hypersensitive Bob
Hypersensitive Bob really caught my attention with its very cool and beautiful cartoony artstyle. After first opening the game I was a bit suprised that there was no menu. This confused me a bit and made me think the first playthrough was maybe a tutorial or something. The game throws you straight into the action which is kind of nice however on your first run you will most likely not get too far as you try to work out what is going on.
After your initial run you will probably have a good idea of how the game works. You purchase upgrades, kill plants/animals to collect vials which allow you to progress to the next level and purchase more upgrades. While it does seem a bit repetitive every run feels different and unique due to the different upgrades and levels you get during that run.  This allows for a lot of replay value that makes the $5 price point seem worth it if your a person that likes to drop hundreds of hours playing games like Binding of Isaac.
While I do recommend the game, there are also many things which could be improved to make the starter and the experience overall better for the player. I would like to see more upgrades that modify your weapon instead of locking them behind progression. The upgrades to the weapon are the most interesting upgrades in this game and I think it would be a significant improvement to add some of those early on to show the full potential of the game instead of hiding it behind a progression wall were you have to unlock some of these upgrades. I think It might also be cool to add maybe a little intro or something to give the player a Idea of what the story of the game is without having to look outside of the game. I would also recommend a option to remove the end cutscene as it can get a bit repetitive after your 100th playthrough.
Overall the game isn't perfect. There isn't as much depth as similar games such as Binding of Isaac however for $5 you get a game with a nice music track and cartoony artstyle which you can keep coming back too in your free time. In conclusion I would recommend the game if you interested in a casual rogue-lite however if you are looking for some more hardcore rogue-lite action maybe other games like Binding of Isaac would be more suited to your taste

Hypersensitive Bob is about a poor chap who has the misfortune of having allergies towards EVERYTHING. He isn't letting that get the best of him, oh no, Bob is going to defy his life of isolation and step out into the world, step into his rocket ship and blast off to explore cartoony floating islands...using his modified asthma pipe he must fend off anything that threatens to ruin his day as he collects vaccines from his surroundings...Bob has an odd life...
The gameplay would be immediately familiar to those who have played the likes of Binding of Isaac but with less of a (excuse the language) f*cked up back story.
The control scheme Using WASD to move with the directional buttons (or spacebar) used to fire projectiles, the game does boast controller support but my NVIDIA Shield Tablet Controller wouldn't work (I have heard another reviewer state that he uses an Xbox360 controller so it may just be an incompatibility with this particular model).
There is a handy item system at the end of each level, presenting you with bonuses (or sometimes detriments) to ensure that Bob completes his journey in one piece. The items can be purchased by spending the vaccines that you gather throughout the levels, but be careful, there is a high-cost if you happen to be defeated.
Sound design of the game fit well with the style and feel, however there were no ambient sounds, if Bob stopped moving or no monsters were spawning the world fell into an eerily silent state which caused me a couple times when I first launched the game to restart it thinking that sound wasn't working. (EDIT: Ambient sound and music has been added before release)
Monsters and bosses are varied with their own unique abilities or movement patterns which really help keep the game fresh throughout the levels.
Overall the game achieves a replayability factor with it's unique enemies and random item chance and a nice little addition to the Steam library, something I will definitely check back on as more content is added.

Poor Bob.  He’s allergic to everything!  Trees, flowers, bumblebees… they are all a death trap waiting to happen.  What’s a cute snowman-lookalike to do?  Luckily, Bob is a very rich snowman.  Armed with a modified asthma inhaler, which is now a gun, he takes off in his very own spaceship to explore floating worlds and take on Mother Nature.
Snowman.  Allergy gun. Spaceship.  Sounds pretty cute, right?  It is!  This game has many lighthearted aspects.  The graphics are cartoony and bright.  The enemies are pudgy and adorable.   The whole atmosphere of the game is cheerful and sunny.
As a casual player of platformers, the controls did give me some trouble.  On a keyboard, the game offers two ways of using your allergy gun – spacebar and arrow keys.  Using WASD to move and spacebar to shoot was the standard way of many games, and the option I was more comfortable with.  The arrow keys turn Bob in the direction of the arrow and fires immediately, kinda like a James Bond spin move.  But moving with my left hand on WASD and shooting the arrow keys with my right hand was a bit too backwards for me.  I kept trying to move with the arrow keys and ended up wasting my ammo (which wasn’t a big deal because it automatically replenishes), or I was slow lining up to a target using WASD then hitting the wrong arrow key and firing in the opposite direction.  But any gamer with more experience than me will have no trouble with the key bindings.
After Bob faces off with his allergic symptoms and destroys them, he’s rewarded with orange vials of vaccine. These can be spent on a reward system that’s available between levels.  While Bob is enjoying downtime in his private spaceship (who wouldn’t?), you can spend these vaccines on items to help Bob in the next level.  Increased health, speed boost, ammo…all can be bought to boost Bob’s performance in the next round.  Most of these upgrades are inexpensive, but you can choose to save your vaccine points to revive Bob, in the event of his death, and redo the level instead of restarting the entire game.  This is a more expensive option, but one that definitely comes in handy as you progress through the game.
At the time of playing, I was unable to unlock Bob’s friends, who are chilling in my hideout in big comfy chairs in front of the fireplace.  But I look forward to seeing what these guys do.  Maybe they’ll give me bonus upgrades?  Maybe I’ll play co-op with them on certain levels?  Maybe they’ll just stay at my house and eat all my food?  Who knows!
Overall, Hypersensitive Bob is a cute indie game.  The lighthearted atmosphere makes this a great casual game for gamers of all ages.

This game provides an interesting "choose your own adventure" setting to the zombie world. The game plays out in three different modes ("Sandbox", Goal with no time limit, strict time limit) and puts you in charge of a group of survivors. You'll need to give these survivors orders and plan carefully to win. All the action is communicated through diary entries which makes the game most of a create your own story.
I especially like how the game pushes the relationships as a key element as most zombie games miss this. However, sometimes they seem to hate eachother just because but it's an interesting element.
This game isn't going to appeal to everyone but anyone that doesn't mind using their imagination and loves the Zombie genre will definitely like this game. It's very challenging but be warned there's a lot of randomness to it and you may lose just because the game decides it.
Genre Lovers: Must Buy
Non-Genre Lovers: Skip it
Time to Beat: Each game takes about 1-2 hours but there's tons of replay value as every game plays out differently.
Oh and you can import your own survivors which makes it more fun.

Sometimes, the zombies will kill you. Sometimes, it'll be the mobs. And sometimes, it's your own group. You're going to die. A lot. But it's fun to see how long your survivors can last, and how well they stick together.

I've been playing Empire TV Tycoon for my YouTube channel since yesterday. So far I'm loving the game. The graphics are very unique and beautiful. I love tycoon games in general but this game is right up my alley because it allows you to micro management everything about a TV channel! The game has well made tutorials running you through the learning curve very easily. The game has a lot of depth. You can hire people, buy movies or even make your own productions. I especially enjoy the scheduling screen where you decide what people watch.

I was lucky enough to get a code from the developer to test out the game a few days before launch. That night I stayed up until 3am playing it.  It's definitely one of THOSE kinds of games.
It plays a lot like a cross between Game Dev Tycoon, The Movies, Sim Tower and few other classic tycoon games. It's got a very charming art style and sound design to go with it. Lots of brillaint audio and visual cues play out to keep you constantly aware of what's going on as the game progresses.
A playthrough roughly lasts about 3-4 hours and there's easily a lot of re-playability here with a few different difficulty options available and a competing AI to keep you on your feet.
I really like a lot of what this game has to offer and was incredibly impressed with it from the get go, there's an interesting level of challenge in place as you try to figure out the best show/blocking combination based on the audience that's watching and what your best opportunity is to make money from advertisements at the end of each block. I was constantly trying to figure out if I shoul aim my ads at a specific group that's currently watching, or save that slot for later when I might get more views. Games like this really excel from learning curves, it's what makes them great. I failed my first game, I knew fairly early on that I wasn't doing amazingly but I wanted to continue to get to grips of all the systems.  There's a good amount of information delivered to you in tutorials, but the game doesn't hold your hand too much and encourages you to experiment with it and I really respect that in games like this.
I think the only real problem is that the game could benefit from a continue option once the game is over. (Though I think that's coming in a later update). There's something about just trying to fill and programme your schedule that's addictive enough, I didn't really mind that I'd lost and wanted to continue doing that. So just be aware that at the minute once it's game over, you have to start again.
It's games like this that make you realise just how brilliant the indie scene can be when a developer really loves their product and tries to make something fun and interesting, it really shows. So if you're like me and love tycoon games or any of the games mentioned above I'm sure it's something you'll also enjoy and I'd highly recommend picking it up.

What lured me to try this game were sci-fi theme, visual esthetics and a promise of very interesting game mechanics of robot building from hundreds of various parts and testing its efficiency on the battlefield. The game fulfills these perfectly and it captured me from the beginning. And it turned out to be fun and deep enough to keep me playing for almost a year now.
It really is fun to play. And it is fun from the start to the end. There are no boring parts. The game respects your time. It does not waste your time with time consuming mechanics (like xp-ing or grinding). You do not need to reserve long hours to play. You can play as much as you like, and even just a few minutes are enough to both enjoy the game and make a noteworthy progress in game. A few hours are usually enough to complete a full run. It has an excellent replayability which comes from a bunch of factors: a lot of unique parts you build your robot from, a lot of game mechanics you can incorporate to your playstyle or ignore (combat, stealth, hacking, allies to name a few), branched world, evolution points you distribute every level and story related decisions you make. There are additional challenge modes which turns some mechanics upside-down on top of that.
Cogmind is fun, plays smooth due to extraordinary UI, and has a unique game mechanics which make for interesting gameplay. This is generally what I was hoping for. What I did not expect was the story part of the game. There is a comprehensive world and a lore you slowly uncover with your subsequent runs. At the beginning I considered it a pleasant, climatic addition to the core mechanics - a garnish which is nice to have but definitely not necessarily needed to enjoy this game. The appreciation for the story was gradually growing. It is bigger than it seems. It is perfectly integrated into mechanics. It has a lot of "wow, just wow" moments, and is nonlinear enough and full of flavors and secrets to be enjoyable after hundreds of runs. I am constantly impressed with the attention to details and general thought-out put into every aspect of the game.

Simply put, this is a janky game that requires you to obsess over where you put every last poly of the bridge.  There's no real puzzle element to it where you go, "of course, that makes sense." No your solution will probably make sense from the start, it's simply that you aren't putting the polys in the exact right position to support your bridges.
Furthermore, there's never a tutorial that tells you, "you should use a suspension bridge in this situation or an arch in this other situation".  It's just, "give it a try and figure it out yourself."
The tutorial boils down to an instruction manual.  It tells you a few odd techniques you wouldn't think of on your own and how all the tools work.  However, what I want is a little more depth there.  Give me some more detailed information.  For example, when should I use ropes instead of steel?  Is there an iron-clad rule about their use?
There are even a few tricks I had to learn on youtube which weren't included in the manual at all.  The ability to tie supports together with rope instead of wood/steel for one.
It would be nice for example if you told us what supports to improve first and under which circumstances.  For example, let's say that road section B is breaking and it currently has wood supports.  Should I upgrade them to steel first? Reinforce the road? Change to ropes?
Finally, for anyone else having trouble with the hydraulics.  When you seperate a poly for a hydraulic bridge, the side indicated on the split is not indicative of which side of the split you are dealing with.  It's really confusing as all hell and I spent a full hour figuring out that the red square side of the split is ALWAYS the land mass, even when it's on the opposite side of the land mass.

The inventory system was truly horrid.  And a battlefield unit like Chris's should have a supply system to bring them ammo, I mean, if common sense prevailed, but it doesn't in RE6.  That's ok. I did like the Ada adventure mostly because it filled in some story gaps (but my daughter and I did a pretty good job at surmising what happened).  Ada's cockiness does get a little annoying; it was good to see Leon save her highness' hash.  But upright Leon's fascination for her seems to get more confusing the more he and we learn about her.
I'm getting off track.  This isn't a bad game, but it isn't a good one either.  I gave it a down simply to give fellow gamers fair warning.
Good gaming, everyone!

Caves of Qud is a brilliant game, and is the title that finally hooked me into actual turn-based roguelikes as a genre. Up to now, I've loved rogueLITES (things like Nuclear Throne, Binding of Isaac, and Enter the Gungeon) but rogueLIKES themselves haven't ever been something I could stick with, for whatever reason.
Enter Caves of Qud - a game with a fantastically unique setting, surprisingly easy to learn UI, and some of the best character creation/customization I've ever encountered. Seriously - I'm a guy who loves tinkering with builds, and the mutation system is CoQ is second to none in terms of offering unique and varied playstyles and various options to try out.
True, it's still not the MOST accessible game (you'll almost definitely need Google open on another screen to cross-reference how mechanics work) but you can learn the game in short order, and the Guides section here on Steam has some phenomenal work. I can also speak to the developer and the community's credit - every time I've had a question, it's been answered very promptly on the Discussions board. The game also offers a host of (completely optional, off by default) debug options, including the ability to disable perma-death if you'd like. This is great for people new to roguelikes in general, and who want to get a stronger grasp on Qud's mechanics and learn its ins-and-outs with some training wheels on.
I generally have a rule with any early access game - to justify a purchase, it has to be worth it if the devs stop updating it as soon as it's added to my cart. Qud absolutely qualifies - the game is wonderful in its current state, and seems to be getting regular updates, which is phenomenal. The dev has also promised to release a road map this year on what we can expect leading up to release, which is a level of transparency I very much appreciate.
All in all, I can't recommend this title enough, ESPECIALLY with it still being early access. Live and drink, friends.

Easily more than worth the money.  This is the sort of dollar value you rarely get.  With all the content, customization, randomness, and the steep learning curve, if you're a fan of the over-complex nature of Dungeons and Dragons, you'll be a fan of this.
Honestly, the freedom of mechanics that the lack of graphics gives the game is really, really unique.  Not many games will be confident enough to let you play as a mutated beetle-man who can teleport, or a treant centaur with hands that shoot fire.  Or an agile, dual-wielding rogue.  Perhaps you just want to go for the magic side, and play a magic-laser firing, force-explosion summoning, space-time-vortex creating psychic with an endless series of evil twins that want to kill him.  You can be just about anything you want, clearly.
I spent the first five hours dying without understanding how to get more water, or that quests were worth it.  Instead, I was having a blast slowly dessicating myself while slaying crocodiles and leveling up.

If Caves of Qud was merely a standout roguelike dungeon crawler with clockwork-tight mechanics and a refreshingly accessible UI, it would be deserving of perhaps 20 of the hours I've put into it. It is the writing, the prose within the description of seemingly ordinary items, that has me returning for the additional 200+ hours I have logged.
Qud is an alien world that flourishes with life among the ruins of the old, technologically advanced world, evoking images of towering chrome skyscrapers choked with vines and vast caverns echoing with the sounds of dripping water. The skill system combined with a vast array of mutation options means that no two characters play the same way, and the recent Sultans of Qud update adds procedurally-generated histories (with corresponding ruins and artifacts) to a world already packed to the secondary gills with lore and treasures to uncover.
Caves of Qud is a masterclass in worldbuilding, and in it's best moments evokes the strange beauty of a Frazetta or Brom painting without feeling derivative. I cannot recommend this game enough.

But Caves of Qud is different for one reason or another. It's just a real joy to play, the world is varied and intricate and I want to be in it's universe. I don't particularily mind if I get my limbs torn off my a dozen snapjaws as long as they get torn off in the Caves of Qud.
There are also many unique styles of play based on the interesting mutations system. You want to be a clairvoyant pyromancer with hook hands? You can do it! What about a laser shooting desert nomad? That too! It's endlessly entertaining.

Cogmind is an amazing game. I've been playing it since Alpha 1, way back in mid-2015. Hundreds of hours. Now it's finally hit Steam Early Access, but it's fair to call it one of the most complete games to ever go through EA.
You are the Cogmind, a strange kind of robot. In your bid to reach the surface of a mysterious underground complex, you attach parts to yourself, building yourself into a stealthy flight bot fitted out with sensors, or you know, a walking death machine. It's up to you and what you find. You'll encounter many neutral robots going about their business, as well as quite a few hostile ones who seem to want nothing more than to tear your robot core apart. The combat is tactically rich, and there are definitely more reviews which go into more detail there, but I want to focus on stealth, which is really my jam in games. The stealth experience in Cogmind is raw, and gets to the heart of what I love about stealth in games: gathering information you can use to avoid enemies. If you find and attach a sensor array, you can observe the movement of nearby enemy patrols and take evasive action. Perhaps you attach a terrain scanner and spot that a nearby wall is thin enough to dig through to the other side, bypassing a corridor crawling with enemies. You can use transmission jammers to silence distress calls, optics to increase your LOS range, ECM suites to lose your pursuers quickly, cloaks to reduce the range at which enemies spot you, structural scanners to detect hidden passages... I've had some intense moments where I've been cornered, hiding behind a machine, hoping that the hunters searching for me aren't too thorough with my room. It's such a unique experience for a roguelike, and really brings stealth to a new level. I haven't even mentioned the diverse hostile robot types, terminal hacks, or some of the absolutely crazy unique items you can sometimes find, which may completely alter your strategy. Also, you can reach movement speeds so fast that sentries won't even know you've flown right past them.
Before we dig further into the game, I want to make some brief points on the difficulty and learning curve. This game is a traditional roguelike (despite the modern ideas and polish), and it has all the difficulty you'd expect of one. You're going to get brutally butchered in this game, and rightfully so. It's going to take a lot to get good at Cogmind, but the pleasure from mastering difficult games is one of the main reasons we play them (and especially roguelikes). The game starts off simply, and holds back the coolest areas, lore, and items for later. This is to avoid overwhelming the player at the start, and makes a lot of sense within the context of the game. But you'll probably still get wrecked early on if you don't apply good tactics and positioning. As the game goes on, it gets harder, and the items become more diverse and build-enabling. Cogmind has a much wider set of strategic variables to consider than other roguelikes I've played, and pure tactical ingenuity won't be enough to save you if you make grave strategic misplays down the road. If it's too hot to handle, or if you just want a more chilled game, Cogmind has two easier difficulty modes in the options. There is also a mix of challenge modes in case you really want to be stretched to breaking point. ;)
Story isn't a major component in most roguelikes, and it's been a while since I've played a game with a story I've connected with, regardless of genre. Somehow, against all the expectations I had, Cogmind tells a stellar story, one that has kept me absorbed and thinking about the implications away from my computer just like the best sci-fi films do. You learn bits and pieces about the world and its inhabitants through terminal records scattered throughout the game, but the real gems of lore and story come from exploring the hard-to-reach places in the game. The story is so tightly and expertly woven into the gameplay that you can't help but get drawn into it as you play. Your choices have a large impact on the story and its resolution, and the story has a large impact on your choices. It's kind of hard to explain, so I'll leave you to discover it yourself. On a related note: Cogmind is filled with secrets, and some of them have a
impact on gameplay and also how the pieces of the world and story fit together in your mind, so I
recommend you play this game as unspoiled as you can. You have to do some proper detective work to figure everything out, and it's all the more rewarding when you do.
Now let me tell you about the production values, which are immense, starting with sound. I normally keep sound disabled when playing roguelikes. Not so, with Cogmind. Playing this game without sound is unimaginable. There are sounds for
, and they're so authentic. They really ramp up the atmosphere and draw you into the world. The satisfying sounds of dying robots and the deep rumble of a chain of nuclear reactors exploding just take the cake for sound design in a game. It's the little things, too, like the subtle audio cues when interacting with the interface, and the forbidding ambience of the caves.
Next: the visuals. You have two ways to view the world: the tile set, and ASCII. I myself use the ASCII, which is beautiful and clear. Both options are highly expressive. The animations are grand as well. Most of the combat in the game is ranged, but between the sounds and animations, you can tell pretty much all of the weaponry apart. The explosions are glorious. Even in their aftermath, the walls have collapsed, rubble is strewn everywhere, and the floor is burnt to a black crisp. Every single item has special ASCII art associated with it, and it's phenomenal. There's even a gallery to view all the items you've ever equipped in all their ASCII art splendour, complete with item stats. Gotta equip 'em all! (there's a lore-dex for the lore you've found too)
Now, for the user interface. UI in this genre is too frequently a barrier to players rather than a welcoming conduit between you and the awesome gameplay you know is there somewhere. Fortunately, Cogmind knocks this one out of the park, I mean, seriously, AAA game studios could learn a lot right here. In a game largely about items and information, the UI is vital to get right. Mouse users and keyboard users alike are first-class citizens here. I play exclusively with the keyboard, and all the controls are efficient and polished. The HUD is aesthetically pleasing too, fitting right in with the sci-fi setting of the game. All of this must've been a nightmare of work for the developer, but it's paid off dearly for the players. Lucky us!
This game is a work of art. It's remarkable that one person made all of this (apart from the tile set). You've got to check this out.

An amazing game from an amazing genre by an amazing developer, Cogmind really has it all. I started playing Cogmind back in Alpha 12, and over the course of about a year the game has quickly become one of my favorite games of all time. There are just so many things Cogmind does right that it's hard to name them all in one place, but I'll do my best to touch on some of the best aspects of the game:
UI:
Cogmind has the best UI of any roguelike in existence. It's entirely mouse friendly (though can be played with only a keyboard as well), displays TONS of data transparently (so much that many people are overwhelmed at the sheer amount, though this can be turned off), and has popups for everything (if you have any questions about a UI element, simply hover your mouse over it and a popup will tell you all about it). The UI is so fantastic and innovative that it's hard to play other roguelikes after playing Cogmind.
Art Style / Animation:
10/10. Whether you play in ASCII or Tiles you will not be disappointed with the look of the game. Cogmind makes excellent use of colors to help the player clearly identify friend from foe, and even distinguish difficult enemies from easy ones. The animations are also out of this world... pick up any explosive launcher and fire it to see a spectacular explosion of vibrant color, making large scale battles really amazing to see. Some animations even affect the UI, which I think looks absolutely awesome.
Sound Effects:
10/10. No other roguelike comes close to matching the quality of sound in Cogmind. Every weapon has a unique sound, most explosions have unique sounds, there are unique ambient sounds throught the levels... even the stationary machines make sounds! The sound effects really bring the game world alive, and add a level of immersion that I didn't realize I was missing with traditional roguelikes.
Story:
10/10. I really don't want to say much here (as cogmind is very spoilery and I'd hate to ruin that for anyone), but *wow* is the story good. There are secrets *everywhere*, so much lore to find, and all kinds of things that make you rethink what you think you know about the game. There's even a *huge* twist that most people will never know about... Only the truly dedicated will figure out who's pulling all the strings ;) I've already said too much, so please do yourself a favor and discover this stuff yourself.
Gameplay:
The last category, but also the most important category, is gameplay... and Cogmind excels here as well. There are so many different ways to play through Cogmind, mostly differentiated (but not entirely) by the different propulsion available to you throughout the game. Flight often means stealth (real stealth, btw, no fake mechanics... you stealth by actively avoiding enemies and staying out of their sight), whereas legs or treads often mean combat (guns and explosions, hurray!) Due to Cogmind's extensive use of item destruction, you are not stuck to any type of build throughout the game... rather, you'll find that your builds will evolve as you find things / lose parts. Item attrition is a major component of whether a run will be succesful or not, so it very important to plan carefully. "Do I enter a midgame branch and risk my current parts for the possibility of reward, or do I quickly run through main levels and risk becoming underpowered?" These are the types of questions you will ask yourself as you play. Without giving too much away, I can assure you that the game is exactly as challenging as you want it to be; play it safe and a normal Access win shouldn't be too difficult, but take on some branches / extended and the difficulty will ramp up fast.
I also want to mention that one of my favorite aspects of Cogmind is the ability to "comeback". Since you're characters power is largely determined by the items equipped, should you lose all those items it may seem like all hope is lost... but it's not! Cogmind can very easily run from most situations and rebuild from parts found around the complex, leading to some really spectacular comebacks. Just earlier on stream today I lost all of my flight propulsion to EM traps, and managed to rebuild just a bit later w/ some hover units I found, saving the day! This mechanic really makes for some dramatic and tense moments, which I find exhilarating.
Overall:
11/10. Cogmind is a Masterpiece. If all of that isn't enough to convince you to buy the game, then the final thing I will say is this... Kyzrati, the Developer, is an amazing person who has done wondeful things for the Roguelike community. Check out his blog
or the subreddit's he moderates
and
to see just how much of an impact he makes. The gaming industry needs more dev's like him, and that alone is worth supporting this amazing game in my book.
BUY THIS GAME. You will not regret it.
