I have been playing this game for about a year now and am happy it has finally come to Steam! If you like rogue-likes then you will most likely enjoy COGMIND.
"ASCII evolved: Most advanced terminal interface ever" & "Thousands of particle effects and SFX"
I love the UI for this game. Everything is very nicely done, and I love the ascii art in the item descriptions. I have never had any crashes or issues  running/playing this game. Not only is the UI nice in-game, but Options are well thought out. I prefer to play with the ascii display and only use my keyboard, but you can play with any combination of keyboard and/or mouse. There is a graphic tile set available in the Options (and is the default selection, I believe). There are like 30 combinations of size/font for playing in ascii.
"Dynamic character development without XP/grinding"
When the store page says you can be a slow well-armed tank, or a fast-moving flier, or a stealthy assassin/hacker, or whatever else; you will probably be at least two or three of those options per playthrough if you live long enough. Because you scavenge all your parts to upgrade youself with, you have to adjust based on what you find available. You will die a lot, so you'll get to try a bunch of options. :)
"Dozens of robot classes, each with unique behavior within the ecosystem"
Yup. Obviously many will outright attack you, but some will hinder you in other ways that you might not notice at first, some are just going about their business and will leave you alone if you leave them alone, some will like you and travel with you, and some will frickin' steal your loot too. Since they are all robots, they are all also hackable to some degree. :)
You can do a lot of hacking of Terminals and other machinery as well. Hacking has so many uses in this game (simply opening a vault door, acquiring lore and schematics, crafting, sabotage, etc.) The Complex has a mind of its own and it is tracing and tracking you down too while you do it. Fortunately although you can to a lot with it, it is also not required to make progress in the game, at least in the early levels.
"Procedurally generated world combined with hand-crafted content" & "Fully destructible environment"
Yes, everything can be destroyed, if your weapon if powerful enough. You can dig your own tunnels if you want, either via explosives or mining lasers. You can beat that power generator with your sword until it blows up and kills you if you like. There's only one thing in COGMIND that I think you can't destroy and that's the stairs to the next level, but I could be wrong.
I like that there is an overall story to what's going on in this world too. Thankfully progress in the area of world lore saves and as you find bits of lore and discover new items and such they become available for viewing in the Gallery. Many items have ascii art, but some things are your usual little text snippets of information.
"Seven different animated endings to uncover"
Of which I have found none yet. After a year of playing I can still only make it like 10 levels into the Complex before getting killed, and that's just the tip of the iceberg. I'm always happy for more content, but if the developer decided to release the game as is I would still consider it worth getting at the $20 I got it for.

I've sunk a decent amount of time into both Crysis and Crysis 2, and I have to say I like them both equally, but for very different reasons.  Crysis was an amazing shooter, pure and simple, with it's huge open world and multiple, distinct combat modes.  Coming into Crysis 2, I expected more of the same.  Instead, I got something different, but not necessarily in a bad way.  The combat's been streamlined in this game, and what I mean by that is, the nanosuit's different modes are more integrated.  The only dedicated modes are Armor and Stealth, while Strength and Speed only activate while spriting, jumping, and using melee attacks.  The result is a much different feel that Crysis.  Rather than switching between specific combat modes, it feels more . . . more like a traditional shooter, I guess, with some special tricks thrown in.  Basically, your only two options when confronted with an enemy are A) use armor and try to tough out his attacks or B) use stealth and ambush him.  The level design is also more linear than Crysis, usually confined to a street, block, or square in NYC.  But while I didn't like combat as much as Crysis, I immensly enjoyed the story.  Can't say quite what intrigued me so much about it, but I'm a longtime fan of sci-fi and this really scratched that itch for me.
So, long story short, if you only play games for the combat experience you may not like this game as much as Crysis, but if you're like me and you enjoy a good story as much as the game itself you'll probably find Crysis 2 worth your while.

***I'd like to preface this by saying I'm a HUGE old-school RE fan with a particular affinity to the REmake and RE: Code Veronica. I am about 12 hours into RE6 and havn't finished it yet***
I skipped RE6 when it came out because of how crushingly disappointed I was with RE5. After seeing the review scores, I pretty much figured I knew exactly the kind of terrible the game would be.
Fast forward to a couple days ago, it pops up on the Steam sale for $10, I pulled the trigger just to suffer through the game to see how batshit crazy the story has gotten. What I actually got was one of the most refreshingly playable Japanese-style shooters since Vanquish and Binary Domain. Let's put all the hub-bub aside, as a game with no strings attached; this game has great, tight mechanics and gives you a variety of tough enemies to dispose of.
I think this game is a victim of awkward pacing and unrealistic fan expectations.
The pacing is much better and the story flows much more naturally when you play the first couple chapters of Chris and Jake's campaigns before starting Leon's. IMO the game should have just been one long campaign to better control the pacing of it.
As for unrealistic fan expectations, I honestly think a big chunk of the people complaining either never played RE2/RE3/RE:CV, or they just love those games too much and have trouble seeing that those games were criticized for the same things back in the day. A lot of the complaints about RE6 can be made about the classic Resident Evil games.
- Campy/Ridiculous/over-the-top story
- Bad voice acting
- Not very scary, cheap jump-scares
- Non-conventional controller layout
- Too action-oriented (read some complaints about RE2/RE3/RE4)
There are plenty other complaints that are totally valid. Too many QTEs, too linear, not enough puzzles (early on in the game), almost no exploring of environments, so on. It's far from a perfect game, but I do think it's a very fun game, and I havn't even touched Mercenaries yet.
If you decide to get this game, a few tips:
- Increase the FOV for god's sake! Standard FOV is unplayable IMO. 15/10/10 is perfect.
- Play the game in the suggested campaign order found in various forums
- Play on a difficulty higher than normal to actually give yourself a challenge, make you fear enemies and make ammo more coveted
- Have fun with the campiness of it all! Stop taking RE so seriously!

This game is absolutely fantastic. I've been following it since the ASCII days and it's absolutely incredible how much has been added. In the interest of transparency, I did receive this game for free to help with beta testing way back, but I've spent more than a few dollars buying this game for friends.
It plays like a traditional roguelike but instead of a single dungeon, you're given an procedural open world with static quests and towns. The gameplay is hugely varied and tactical from character to character, mostly due to one of the best mutation systems I've ever played. Every type of weapon has it's own pros and cons with a skill tree for each one. The tinkering system lets you craft any technological knickknack you could ever need. From a laser slinging esper who can create temporary, also laser slinging, clones at will, to a four armed turtle swinging four different axes while spewing corrosive gas, to a non mutated true man outfitted with cybernetics tinkering up various deadly energy weapons, you can build just about anything you're in the mood for.
The aesthetic is one of the best I've seen in any roguelike. There's a CRT screen effect overlayed on the fantastic yet minimal tiles. The writing, believe it or not, is actually one of the games strong suits with vivid descriptions for the various items and enemies you come across and some pretty great dialogue with the npc's you come across. It also has music now, which is generally ambient droning music that does a lot to draw you into the world.
There's still some jank here and there and some unfinished areas, so it's not perfect, but it gets patched weekly and is regularly receiving massive content updates. I can't recommend this game enough though. If you're a roguelike fan, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

If you had asked me about a year ago, I hated anything with the "roguelike" tag. I foolishly assumed them to be lazy. Supply the the resources, give them some procedural rules, and woosh, you have game. I was an idiot, and Freehold Games showed me what I needed to see to change my mind.
Caves of Qud is so rich with narrative and deep in mechanics that this game feels alive, and the struggle to keep a character from becoming another tombstone file can be very suddenly real. You get into a rhythm with the flow of the game, things are going along nicely, you get into a particularly thorny scrap only to survive with little health and a gang of irritable tortoises on your heals. You get distracted piecing together lore that seems more extensive than real world history books, if not infinitely more interesting and bizarre. You can mutate night vision or flaming hands, bring a knife to a gun fight, or become a tinkering archaeologist with penchant for grenades. Caves of Qud is not asking "what kind of game do you want me to be?" instead "what kind of player do you want to be this time?" with its breadth of choice.

I could swear I've seen this exact game as a Facebook app title a few years back... Anyway, in Zafehouse: Diaries, you are tasked with guiding a band of sniveling, hateful survivors into scavenging and sneaking their way through a zombie-infested town in search of supplies, ammunition, and scrap with which to barricade out the onslaught of hungry dead. Hide too long without taking up arms and you'll have an undead army on your hands, but make too much noise blasting the dead and you'll just draw the entire town population right on you. Unfortunately, your survivors are pretty small-minded; each comes with a particular sort of person they just really cannot abide, be it a racial group, sexual orientation, or gender. Keep the party together too long and the petty annoyances will eventually erupt into inter-party combat; split the party too thin and you'll fall prey to Zed in short order. Although you get only a general management degree of control over your team (go search this building, hunt zombies around this area, whip up some vittles, etc.), there is a healthy variety of tasks you can set your party to, and careful decision-making will go a long way toward keeping your merry band together.
Along with the basic sandbox style of gameplay in which you must gather survivors up and avoid death for as long as possible, there are also two more difficult challenge modes available. In one, you must restore a car to working order and hightail it out of town, and in the other you must simply survive for a week. Both of these modes crank up the difficulty tremendously, and once you've learned how to eke a modicum of survival out of your hateful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, they're fun (in a horribly aggravating sort of way).
Unfortunately, the game falls apart a bit in the area it seems most proud of. The eponymous "DIARIES" it shouts about are the prosey bits of horror the game uses to let you know how your team is doing. This is written in the first-person from the perspective of... someone? Some unportrayed member of the team no one else seems able to observe? Who contributes no labor toward the survival of the group? I guess this explains how the writer manages to find the time to scribble it all out and scrap-book in grim polaroids in discrete hourly doses.
While there are some nice touches here (injury reports result in splashes of blood covering the page, and as night falls, it becomes more and more difficult to see the page), the text gets repetitive fast, especially considering how easy it is to lose the game repeatedly and fly through half a dozen false starts. Once you manage to survive for a while, you start encountering special unique events that spice things up, but it's a bit of a trek getting past the early difficulty curve.
Zafehouse: Diaries is not without its charms, and it can be a solidly addictive time sink for a couple afternoons, but don't expect Z:D to make your list of favorites. When everything's added up, I'd be tempted to cautiously recommend it, but the Z in the title just cannot be overlooked or forgiven.

Amongst the uncountable zombie shoot-em-ups surrounding the zombie survival genre, Zafehouse: Diaries provides a refreshing character based angle akin to "The Walking Dead" with a solid squeeze of RTS
Players manage a team of one to five survivors with randomly generated skills, personalities and prejudices attempting to survive against hostile elements, unending zombie hordes, limited resources and at times; even each other
While Zafehouse: Diaries does provide at times a compelling experience, the immersion is often times strained by the lack of feedback, control and strange bugs leading to jarring experiences, like a fight between survivors resulting in a broken leg, every single time, or the inability to avoid turning the last shower into a barricade
Beyond that, it provides a character based survival experience that feels like a genuine struggle to survive that's unique everytime; if a little aloof
and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for such

I bought this game before it came available on steam and it is quite fun. Trying to manage the people however, I find is very difficulty and quite often they ended up at people's throats, but that could be just me failing at this game and I'm tempted to re-visit it.
The idea is you and a group of other survivors try to survive and find out where the helecopter will be landing in town to rescue survivors. It's certainly not a easy game as you have to watch out for food, barricading off buildings your survivors are living in, managing your ammo, making life-or-death decisions that can either end up with losing no-one, one or two or even the entire group as what happened with me in one playthrough.
As you can imagine there is a time limit in days as to what the helecopter is arriving so you need to get all the clues, get to that location, clear out any undead there, board up the place and make sure you have enough food to survive, but one realistic mechanic, which I personally found irritating, was how peoplee have prejudices and hate to other people. Some will have things like "Mr. X claims he isn't racist, but he doesn't like the look of Mr. Y and Miss. F" and others have hatred against rich, poor, middle-class, educated, uneducated and so on. A few times my group fell apart because even if you have the groups doing seporate things, sometimes there will be events where someone two people are laughing, the guy who dislikes them thinks it's about him, they get into a argument and nothing is done on either side.
However there are ways to try and stop this. You can spread Rumours to improve someone's relations by comparing to other people's backstories. For instance, if you have someone who has difficulty getting along with two people because the hatred comes from them you can say "Mr. X worked in a ___" and you put Charity as one of them used to do charity work and then for the next part the other likes the poor, so you choose poor and the sentance turns into something like "Mr. X worked in a Soup Kitchen where he fed the poor." at people's attitues will start to change, however you will get conflicting personalities that might land him in the neutral zone with two people, but have another one hate him so you need to do a lot of balancing.
Not a  easy game by any strech of the imagination, but certainly rewarding if you can get to the end. I havn't yet, but who knows.

Hana is a badly drawn anime figure - whose sole purpose is to give out a handful of supposedly cute but quite meaningless sentences if you figure out and put in various command words. She cannot actually chat, and she'll keep answering even the simplest of your questions with a "what did you say?". See, she is not even polite in her dumbness. She only responds to a handful of words by crafting sentences out of them; but if you were to type in actual sentences yourself, she'll just stand there, dumbfounded. She has two modes: a talk mode, which will respond to various command words only - with various unimaginative ways; and an oracle mode, to which you can ask "yes" or "no" questions to get randomly generated answers. There are a couple built in games that you can play with Hana too, again, if you can figure out proper command words; but they are not interesting or even fun to play. Some might think typing every English word and some abbreviations, one after the other to try and make an anime girl respond can be funny; but obviously I am not one of them.
So... there really, really is no reason to engage with this sadly built excuse of a placeholder game. Instead, please go ahead and spend your dollar on an actual game or an experience which can present you with something to do in a certain quality... Even if you feel terribly lonely, try calling a friend, going out for a walk – I don’t know, seek proper human interaction, for god’s sake! Here, I got my lesson - anime visuals do not always indicate something interesting. Hell, no. This one is a moe bait. Nothing to do. Please carry on.

Purchased during Alpha, before Steam release. I've got many hours in this game unlisted as a result.
Cogmind is one of those beautiful gems you didn't think you'd ever find. Appearing at first to be a regular ascii roguelike, where you have to learn VIM or use unintuitive numpad controls, memorizing a bunch of keyboard shortcuts, it soon becomes apparent that it's much more than that. I'm new to the turn-based roguelike genre, but if you're looking to get into them, or are bored of playing every "shooter roguelike" that releases, THIS IS THE PLACE TO START.
Cogmind is beautifully complex, but presented simply. It's easy for a newcomer to the genre to understand (like myself), but from my understanding, it's complex and difficult enough for even veterans to enjoy. You can use mouse controls, keybaord controls, or a combination of the two to control the game, so it is instantly playable by anyone. There is barely any tutorial, but akin to games of old, encourages you to explore the interface and world, discovering the different ways you can interact with your equipment, the environment, and other robots, as well as with different playstyles.
To someone new to the turn based roguelike genre, it feels much more like an open world RPG that has permadeath than any other roguelike I've dabbled with. If you enjoy games like Skyrim or Fallout due to their many gameplay styles, I would wager you'll enjoy this game.
Throughout the time I've owned the game in Alpha, I've seen the game updated a dizzying number of times, with many features added to the game. Don't let the Early Access tag dissuade you, this game is like Rimworld or Factorio, where "Early Access" simply means "Yeah, we're gonna keep updating this game, like, a lot, but if Early Access didn't exist, it'd be pretty much finished."
TLDR; If you're new or old to the roguelike genre, I can't recommend this game enough. $20 is a steal.

I initially bought this game back in Alpha 13 due to some favorable comparisons to Brogue. Brogue appealed to me as a game with great tactical depth and meaningful decision-making, where every run was vastly different and you had to actually focus to make it out alive, couldn't just set up the same-ish thing in every seed once you'd learned the game a bit.
I have now played Cogmind for some hundreds of hours. While the game is less demanding than Brogue (from the perspective of simply winning, which is still quite challenging), with less seed variance (an approach with pros and cons), the game has effectively managed to appeal to me in a similar manner, in consistently providing decisions with satisfying amounts of complexity that can lead to some very interesting results. There is little in gaming that has been more fun to me than designing various killer-robots consisting of over 20 salvaged/found/fabricated parts in the lategame, with a similar amount of items in inventory, constantly modifying the specific layout based on finding better parts or simply replacements/alternatives to damaged ones, getting some actual pusback from the Complex such that even the best bots still have to think about their actions.
I would recommend the game to anyone with an appreciation for challenging and complex game mechanics, and Cogmind gets a lot of bonus points for presenting that complexity in a way that is viscerally satisfying, this is the one clear advantage Cogmind has over Brogue and similar games: it's rare to get such strategic depth
astonishing sound effects, beautiful ASCII art for over 800 items, lore entries that add a lot of flavor to exploring the world, and an actual interesting story to discover, even if it is difficult to fully discover, being sort of in the background and featuring challenges beyond simply making it out of the Complex alive.

As of this writing I have less than an hour of in-game time listed for Cogmind – though I have quite a bit more with previous versions of the game. And though I desperately want to jump back in and see what the Steam update has to offer, I’m nevertheless taking the time to write a review.
Why? Because it’s worth it.
This is an amazing rogue-like: a blend of old and new, carefully, cleverly, and lovingly crafted. It’s an intelligent game that rewards intelligent thinking. It’s difficult, deep, sometimes infuriating, always rewarding.
Cogmind is quality. Simple as that. It’s a fine single malt, on a shelf of thin bland beers.

I've waited quite a while to write this review. I've been playing since launch (and the beta). I've been trying to give the devs a fair amount of time to improve the game before I left a review. But at this point, I think I've seen enough patterns to make my conclusion.
I'll start off by saying that I do recommend the game. It offers moments that very few (if any) games can match. Thrills, scares, laughs, teamwork, back stabbing, etc...When you have good rounds in this game, you just want to keep playing for more of those moments.
Unfortunately, the game has a lot of bugs, and the developers can be quite slow with patching. Every patch has also managed to introduce new bugs into the game. It seems to be a "1 step forward, 2 steps back" kinda thing. Sometimes (like today) they encounter issues with releasing the patch itself. This has happened several times since launch...and that's the pattern I'm noticing: The developers are incapable of releasing ANYTHING without several new issues, if they manage to release it at all (Xbox once skipped a patch entirely because it took them too long to get it right).
As of today, we're waiting for a patch that includes new content (Virtual Cabin 2.0 and Offline Bots) and some bug fixes. The problem is, none of the bug fixes included in this upcoming patch address the more major issues the game is currently enduring. In fact, we're going on 2 months with the game in a fairly broken state. Since this upcoming patch doesn't address the glaring issues, it means we're waiting AT LEAST another month for a patch that might. It remains to be seen. For these reasons, I wouldn't recommend the game. It's in a rough state. It's essentially a glorified early access title that bypassed early access due to holding the Friday the 13th license. Summer Camp Vol. 1 (what the game was pre-license) would still be in early access today, or dead in the water from lack of funding. That's the simple truth.
I love this game. I really do. But there are so many shortcomings that I simply can't defend anymore. I recommend the game so people can experience the good moments it has to offer. But just keep in mind, it's a buggy mess.
[I'll revisit this review in 4-6 months. Or I'll revise at the 1 year mark. But as of now, the game isn't receiving the support it deserves.]

Friday the 13th The Game is incredibly fun and addictive. Its an online-multiplayer third-person survival game in which all but one player takes the role of camp counselors trying to escape whilst the remaining player takes the role of the iconic movie slasher Jason Voorhees and must kill all other players within the 20 minute game session.
Jason is all but invincible and very powerful, with several abilities that give him supernatural advantages over the counselors. This means that unless highly experienced the most efficient strategy for the counselors is basic survival, raiding the campsite buildings for helpful items and weapons to repel Jason whilst trying to keep as low a profile as possible.
Players can escape via either repairing one of the level's vehicles and driving out or phoning the police and fleeing to the police line once they've arrived. This is easier said then done though- repairs require counselor coordination, finding the correct components and completing repair mini games whilst Jason breathes down your neck!
If caught a counselor can be murdered in seconds, meaning an unlucky start or mistake can lead to a quick demise. Running from Jason is an adrenaline rush, with the hiding and sneaking about before hand filled with dread and foreboding as you know there's always an unpredictable and intelligent human mind behind the killer.
Friday the 13th captures the flavour and tone of the movie franchise perfectly. The visual style is spot on, Jason's kills suitably spectacular and gory, and its clear that the devs not only did their research during game design but have a passion for the movies and the universe they created. Its so good in fact that I have actively sought the movies and delved deeper into the lore when I had no interest prior. Even a Part III Jason Hockey Mask now adorns a shelf in my front room!
Several free updates have expanded on the original product, adding more maps, extra counselors, nearly all the various incarnations of Jason and a rolling effort to tweak and balance the game. There's also a few cheap DLCs that add alternate counselor skins and fun (but extraneous) fluff.
The game's balance has been regularly tweaked, continuing to try and improve the game as time goes on. Probably the most unfortunate effect of the changes is that much of the counselors free choice has been taken away. The original game was like a sand box of choices, where you could block other players paths, injure and even kill each other if you wanted. Now you can do none of those things, extracting a fascinating social aspect that really made cooperative interaction exhilarating (Jason used to be the least of your worries).
At over 80 hours of playing its limited gameplay scope and maps have not got boring, and its 20 minute max sessions are a perfect convenience for my busy life, allowing me to fit a couple of games in very casually as a wind down before bed.
It seems very overpriced at face value, but if it sounds like your kind of thing then I heartily recommend you pick it up. 80 hours of gameplay and still looking forwards to more is about as good as it gets.
Its worth noting on top of this that the 80+ hours clocked have been done so on a minimum spec computer! Even suffering extreme lag and difficulty playing I've still enjoyed the game that much!

I actually really enjoyed this game, but I like puzzle platformers.
When I first saw it, I was dubious how a game with such low-tech graphics (five colored blocks, really?) could actually be fun, but the narration sells it. Each block has a back-story, as told by the narrator, and it's a strange feeling to actually care about the welfare of your colored blocks that each have names (Thomas, Chris, Claire, Paul, etc.) and skills / attributes. The melancholic soundtrack really underpins that sense, as well; a really nice blend of squelchy chiptune/SID with a piano melody.
Puzzle-challenge-wise, the puzzles are typically exploiting the interactions among the characters, and most of the puzzles require switching back and forth between the characters.
A fun game that you can pop into occasionally.

I actually passed on this game many times, until a friend recommended it to me. After actually looking into the game a bit more, I realized it was something that would really interest me. When I finally played it, I was pleasantly surprised.
If you like an interesting storyline following unique "characters," puzzle platforming requiring lots of planning, and witty narration, then you will like this game.
1The aesthetics are good - although the characters are simple shapes, the coloring and effects in the background are well-done. The music and sound effects are very nice, adding appropriate vibes to complement the pacing and atmosphere of each level. The narration is very good, and offers the backstory for the characters. If you like storytelling, you may be surprised by how attached you get to simple shapes. The story is also well-written, and each level adds a piece to the puzzle that is the main plot.
The controls are simple and easy to learn, however, mastering the game mechanics can take a while. As you progress through the story, you will meet new shapes - each with their own special ability - and you will have to use each specialty of each shape propely in order to advance to the next level. The learning curve is mostly minimal to moderate - the main difficulty being in how to solve the later puzzles in the game. Later, there are some timing-based puzzles involved. There are usually checkpoints to help you continue on if death in parts of a level is a possibility. I am currently stuck on a level that requires both timing and careful planning =
For achievement hunters, this game has fairly easy achievements (most are progression-based), the hardest ones to acquire being the jump count ones; however, you will most likely get all of them through progression in the game.
The puzzles are challenging and increase in difficulty at a reasonable, fair pace. You are also (usually) shown basic concepts for what to do in easier levels before you encounter them again in subsequent levels (with more difficult puzzles). So long as you pay attention to how you are solving each puzzle, you should have little trouble solving each stage. Trial and error also helps a great deal.
Overall, the game adds a nice flavor to puzzle platforming, and projects a minimalist, serene feeling while you play. Puzzle enthusiasts should definitely give this one a try.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,

OK, just got 100% on this game and I'll review on five criteria. Gameplay, Plot, Sound, Graphics, and Content.
Gameplay: This game plays like a standard 2D platformer. There are 7 characters you'll be playing as, and they each have different ability. Everyone has a different jump height (The jump in this game is excellent,) and some have special powers such as double jumping or being stuck upside down. However, there are few levels where you play as one character. Almost every level has multiple squares at a time, and you must use the different jumps and powers of each character to get across to the portal which takes you to the next level.
However, these puzzles are cool, but after you figure them out, it takes a long time to physically complete them. The gameplay really suffers from this, as it often has you wishing the squares would move faster. That isn't to say the gameplay isn't good, but this hurts the pace in a lot of ways.
7/10.
Plot: I'll try to make this as spoiler free as possible, but here goes. Thomas is spontaniously generated, and gradually learns how to navigate his environment. He learns how to fall and jump. Eventually, he meets Chris. Chris is smaller, orange and has a weaker jump compared to Thomas. He despises Thomas at first, but they have to work together to get through the place.
Eventually more and more characters are added to the mix, each and every one having tons of backstory, and character. Another thing this game does amazingly is character development. You grow bonds to each character, and the ending was enough to make me cry over these squares jumping from space to space. All because the development of each one is fantastic. Plot is definitely the biggest strength of this game.
10/10
Sound: The whole game has music from David Housden playing in the background. This music is fantastic, but it gets better in the second half of the game. In the first half, the music is rather repetitive. The best part of the whole game though, in my opinion, is the narration. Narrated by Danny Wallace, the narration will make you cry, laugh, and everything in between. It also helps that his voice is amazing.
9/10
Graphics: The graphics are remarkable. Not because they're amazing, but because they push this game to something totally different. While the characters are just squares, and the terrain is black, the background is full of neat colors and always has motion in it. If this game had flat, boring backgrounds, I can safely say I'd like it a lot less. Also, I feel the characters being blocks was the best way to go. As proved by games like Minecraft and Terraria, low graphics are sometimes beautiful.
8/10
Content: This isn't a long game. There are about 100 levels in the main story, but I still completed it in 4 hours. However, there is another, much smaller story arc that tells the tale of a square named Benjamin. This takes place long before the events of the main story.
The achievements don't provide much either. With an even slightly keen eye, you'll get them all in one playthrough like myself. Half of them are even unmissable if you beat the game.
7/10
Overall score: 41/50. This game isn't perfect. The gameplay has some slight annoyances and it isn't very long, but the charm is the prime factor here. The plot is the best I've ever seen in a video game, and the overall feel of the game is GORGEOUS. This game is well worth the 10 dollar price tag, and I recommend it to everybody.
LOVE IT!

This is the best bridge building game ever created. It perfectly captures the spirit of the good old Bridge Builder from the year 2000 and runs away with it by running simulations in beautiful but rather simplistic 3D and by adding different materials, hydraulics, complex scenarios and even ships and planes that run perpendiculary to your building and must not touch it.
The puzzles begin pretty easy and then gradually become harder and harder until they become insanely hard. When the going gets tough and you think you are stuck, you can check how other players solved (or failed to solve) the problematic puzzles in the gallery, which is full of wonderful solutions and epic fails and everything in between. An additional challenge comes in the form of optimizing your solution to fit inside the budget and not to exceed the stress level and break down. There are 105 puzzles in the game with incredible variety, each one feels very unique. And if that's not enough, you can make your own puzzles or play what other players made, via Steam workshop. Automatic saving of your best and last solutions and the ability to save any solution by name make it much easier to experiment with different designs without risking losing your previous work.
There are some negative sides to this game, but nothing major: The building controls are pretty wonky, but are worth getting used to and can be gotten used to too. The physics is not always consistent (the same bridge can sometimes be perfect on one run, but collapse on another), but this usually won't give you too much of a headache.

Caves of Qud is a roguelike that combines traditional elements of the genre with a fully realized post-post-apocalyptic world in the most wonderful ways. You'll find artifacts of the previous civilization hinting at the world they lived in while fighting off mutant hyenamen, cultists who worship the sultans of yore, and horrific wildlife. Each tile of the world map is explorable and contains a nearly infinite dungeon as well as numerous ruins of historical significance potentially containing great treasures.
The as yet unfinished main storyline will take you from the humble caverns of Red Rock to the cesspits of Golgotha, and eventually to the freezing depths of Bethesda Susa, which is as far as I've been able to survive so far. Even unfinished Qud paints vivid imagery in your mind as you begin to understand how the world functions. The technology of the world stretches from simple swords and shields to powerful cybernetics and energy weapons.
As far as character building goes, you can choose to be a mutant with a variety of mutations and defects or a true human from one of the last surviving eco-domes. Humans learn skills faster and start with some gear, but mutants grow in power and number of mutations as you level. The mutations you have range from the physical, like extra limbs or a tough carapace, to the purely mental like conjuring forcefields or directly attacking enemies' minds with your own. There's an innumerous variety of builds once you factor in mutations, caste, and background.
Caves of Qud is like if you put ADOM, D___RL, Dwarf Fortress, and Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup in a blender and let the densest juices from each fill your glass. If you know what any of these games are, Qud is definitely for you.

As of this writing I have less than an hour of in-game time listed for Cogmind – though I have quite a bit more with previous versions of the game. And though I desperately want to jump back in and see what the Steam update has to offer, I’m nevertheless taking the time to write a review.
Why? Because it’s worth it.
This is an amazing rogue-like: a blend of old and new, carefully, cleverly, and lovingly crafted. It’s an intelligent game that rewards intelligent thinking. It’s difficult, deep, sometimes infuriating, always rewarding.
Cogmind is quality. Simple as that. It’s a fine single malt, on a shelf of thin bland beers.

This is a superbly executed game in the traditional roguelike style. Permadeath. Procedurally generated content. Easy to learn, difficult to master but rewarding every step of the way. I've gotten in early here with a review on Steam but I strongly suspect you're going to see a huge mountain of Positive reviews as people start catching on to just how good this is. Been playing this one for about 6 months in Beta and I have to say... IT'S ABSOLUTELY AWESOME!
Firstly there's a lot to be said about how tight the design is: I'm learning to make games at the moment and this one has been on my list of "must examine this because it's brilliant" for a good six months.
Here's some of my thoughts:
1. This is easily one of the most gorgeous looking roguelike games out there. The glowing graphics and animated effects (yes, even in ASCII) are bright, colourful and evocative of the machine-run sci-fi world the game so beautifully represents. The sound effects are solid yet unintrusive, and add a huge amount to the feeling of being drawn into the world around you. This is why we play games with ASCII or simplistic tilesets right? To let the imagination take hold too. The graphical ingenuity in this game never detracts from that imaginative immersion. You can seamlessly flick between the great tileset graphics and the ASCII mode, and this effect is used to great effect in transitions between levels, amongst others.
2. The story is introduced subtly and revealed through exploration. I gather you can play through the game and happily ignore it, although I've found that a combat mechanics focused game like this is only vastly improved with fluff. The fact the lore comes in pieces only adds to the atmosphere. There's a cool story there if you look for it. Just when you feel overwhelmed by the mammoth task ahead of you, you'll suddenly find an oasis in the desert... moments like these are wonderful when they come.
3. The combat mechanics are complex but so well hidden that you don't have to stare at mountains of data in order to perform well. This game will delight stat nerds and people who fear numbers in equal measure I think. There's a game of monsterous complexity under the hood, but the extent to which you interface with that is largely up to you. Everything is tool-tipped, which leads to the...
4. ...superb User Interface: roguelike developers the world over need to look at how good the UI is on Cogmind. It's almost perfect. Menus and game critical information is easily accessed (or, very importantly,  hidden from view) with a single key-press. The game can be played perfectly well with just the keyboard, with just the mouse, or a combination of both. The menus are animated to look like what a Unix operator tripping on acid in the 70's probably thought Unix would look like in the year 2000!
5. Anybody with an appetite for monsterously large amounts of gear to blow up, assimilate and use are going to be in 7th heaven. There's a seemingly endless amount of different guns, legs, reactors, scanners, data hackers... you name it, there's probably about twenty of whatever you named in there. And yet the game doesn't seem to suffer any loss in design elegance for all this "stuff". It never feels bloaty and everything in the game (that I've come across so far) has a use in one of the many custom builds you'll find yourself exploring.
6: There are so many ways to play though. Stealthy airborn data analyser who spots threats way before they spot you then hacks their way past danger? Check. Massive firepower tanky bulk-lord who can literally roll over your foes, guns blazing? Check! Burrow your way through walls to avoid trouble? Check! I could go on...
7: Still reading? Go buy this game and play it!
Negative points? Hmm... as with a lot of roguelikes, it can be very difficult, but the learning curve is actually quite well balanced. Like all good games, when you do die, you know why, and it's always your fault. That being said, you can sometimes feel overwhelmed by the sheer amount of enemies that the game throws at you, even at the start. This might put of casual players, but you very quickly learn how to avoid trouble until you're ready to deal with it.
It's worth stating that you do need to know what you're getting yourself in for with this game. It's tough, and it's big. It requires repeated efforts to learn, but that never feels like a chore.
This is a CLASSIC dungeon crawl roguelike game updated for the 21st Century. Kyzrati has nailed every aspect of this game and raised the bar for the innovation you can get into a genre that has a tendancy to stagnate through dogmatic adherence to outdated ideas: Cogmind is infused with a superb reinvention and execution of the all those classical roguelike features that kept people playing those games in the first place. Cogmind is futuristic in every sense, it's immersive,  technically brilliant, tactically engaging, endlessly replayable and great fun! Buy!
Edit: just to add, how many developers do you know who would think of something as helpful as making a page for potential buyers showing off how the game will look in a range of popular screen resolutions? Seriously man, Josh Ge is a dude, he's thought of everything. One wonders what Nethack would be like if he'd been the lead designer on it? (playable, probably) :)

I have never played a roguelike before, but when I discovered Cogmind, it BLEW ME AWAY.
Coming from the background of playing roguelite, strategy, and RPG games, Cogmind can be described as an adventure, turn-based tactical, RPG-ish game. It can take a bit of time to get used to, but it is rich with secrets and replayability. It rewards players who are willing to mix and match for their characters hundreds of items that can be found. It is enjoyed by those who are willing to adapt to different playstyles on the fly. And it is especially loved by players who are willing to seek huge yet optional challenges to uncover the many mysteries about the world.
As you progress in your adventure, you’ll find NPC’s who can help you, characters you can betray, allies you can recruit, robots who can annihilate you. Slice and dice with your katanas, blow ‘em up with your rockets, sneak your way using sensor array, or mind-control your enemies with your hacking suites.
However, despite all the cool things you can find, Cogmind is not for everyone. The game does not reward grinding. It has no skill trees, no permanent items, no XP, no easy way to win. You need to develop strategy and tactical skills through time, experience, and persistence, but it is well worth it!
There is also a hidden gem in its well-told storyline. I feel an immense satisfaction in not only beating the game but also in discovering plotlines from undertaking challenging maps. These lores are hard to collect, they are what makes this game a true sci-fi epic!
So if you’re willing to take up the challenge, is Cogmind worth buying? Is it really that good? Will you enjoy it? Yes, Yes, and Yes.

Resident Evil 6, is an action-adventure third-person shooter video game and the ninth installment in the Resident Evil series, developed and published by Capcom. It was released for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on October 2, 2012 and for Microsoft Windows on March 22, 2013.
RE6's story is told thru the viewpoints of 7 characters, split between 4 scenarios which follows one of four main protagonists - Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Jake Muller and Ada Wong and each one has its own unique flavour. (Eg: Leon's Scenario tries to recreate the original RE survival horror feel, Chris's scenario felt more gung-ho military styled.)
Prior knowledge of previous Resident Evil games while recommended, is not required to enjoy this game. I would personally recommend playing RE5 first though as this game's has a pretty similar feel to it, both controls and gameplay-wise. Story-wise, one of the main characters also has an important plot-connection with a character in RE5.
The story is interesting, if extremely over-dramatic hollywoodish at times. Expect to see gratuitous explosions, story bosses that just won't die unless the plot requires it, and stupidly cool but unnecessary action sequences.
Like RE5, this game's appeal is in its campaign co-op mode.
The player characters from each scenario will have their own partners which are controlled by either the computer AI or another human player via online multiplayer. Co-op controls are pretty much the same as it was in RE5, but I didn't like that they removed the ability to trade a weapon / item to your co-op partner. Everyone now have their own loot drop.
Graphically, while the environments and lighting are good looking, I don't see much difference compared to RE5 and i'm assuming its using the same engine. While RE5 puts you in a mostly wilderness environment, RE6 has a more urban feel to it. Sound effects are crisp and sharp, and the english voice-over work is still very good with each character voices fitting their role well.
The controls, while certainly reeks of "consolitis" feels alot more fluid then RE5. This time, you can move while aiming down your sights. It still doesn't exactly feel like a FPS though so don't expect it to feel as such.
RE6 now adds the ability to drive vehicles. You can expect to be driving cars in some scenarios,  or piloting a helicopter in some others. Controls are arcadey and simplistic of course, so don't expect much depth in vehicle controls. Still, it was a nice addition.
The best improvement is surprisingly the now classic Quick Time Events (QTEs). People who HATE QTEs, will be happy to know that there is now an option setting to actually skip them! If you are the sort that likes QTEs however, you will be happy to know that the keys to press them are now logically placed and isn't as silly as how RE5 did them.
Overall Rating: 7.0 / 10
Overall feels like a slight improvement to RE5's mechanics, using the exact same engine. As always, it is much more interesting to co-op the campaign with a friend. Definitely no longer a survival horror like the original Resident Evil, and it is basically a 30 hours rollercoaster hollywood action film all the way till the end.
I'm giving it a slightly lower score then RE5 because for me at least, it gave me a "Been There, Done That" feel as I have played RE5 before. That said, if you enjoyed RE5, you will like this one.

I tried really hard to like this game and I know dedicated servers are coming but there are major issues with the game after SIX MONTHS that have nothing to do with the networking.
1. Terrible menus for PC
The game has lots of them and doesn't do you any favors in navigating them. This is obviously due to the menus being designed for a controller and not a mouse + kb.
2. Hero Balancing
There's lots of threads on hero balance on reddit. I'm not a pro fighting game player but some characters have been considered over powered for quite a while. There's also some bugs or "tech" that experienced players will exploit as much as possible. Players from the fighting game community seems to embrace these bugs but since it is not an advertised mechanic in the game it's really obnoxious Ubisoft hasn't patched them out yet or make them a santioned part of the game.
3. Poor Controller Support
If you want to remap buttons you only hope is to use Steam's Big Screen controller feature and you'll lose some functionality with that. Guard break on a face button is really stupid if you ask me. I spent a lot of time trying to get a good controller configuration but it was like trying to flatten out a carpet in a room that's too small.
4. Poor Matchmaking
Low player base means you'll get matched with people who are not your skill level. Add the gear level to the mix and some games are just hopeless from the start. I guess this isn't Ubisoft's fault but at this point the game seems to be bifurated between a trickel of newer players and holdout of very experienced ones.
5. Broken Itemization
Item stats were probably the worst idea for the game. Some game modes do not use item stats but the flagship mode Dominion does. This means that new players are mostly boned in Dominion as the item stats are quite powerful. A Nobushi farm build is going to wreck low geared players at point B because the sustain is just too much. Just the fact that gear can increase revenge damage gives players an edge with such a passive reaction based metagame.
All in all, I played this game as much as I could. It was pretty fun at launch but the flaws in the game quickly overtook the experience to keep my attention. The single player is also entirely unnote worthy.
If you're a fan of medieval action games like Chivalry or fighting games I'd watch for this to go on sale for $20 but with the current $60 price tag on Steam and the current player numbers I fear the multiplayer will be so dead at that point it won't even be worth the time it would take to download.

In terms of balance, I'd say it's a fair difficulty for a roguelike.
It's difficult at first to get a feel for the combat system, the accuracy and speed of a character seems to outweigh other stats, specialty weapons such as grenades I tend to either sell or scrap as they are often more dangerous than useful.
Mutated characters are generally a lot squishier earlier on, but have powerful bonuses later in the game.
Unmutated characters have higher starting stats and various other bonuses, such as better skills or better faction relationships depending on how you go about generating your character.
One could easily sink a couple hundred hours into this, I certainly intend to.

A love letter to the fans of the legendary Friday the 13th series, Friday the 13th: The Game puts you in the hot pants of a hapless counselor or, if you're lucky, behind the hockey mask of the big man himself. It goes without saying that fans of the film series will probably get more enjoyment out of this game--IllFonic ripped out the series' still-beating heart and plugged it into the computer with lovingly-crafted maps, the familiar stings and screeches of the original composer Harry Manfredini, and gut-wrenching mo-cap performances by Thom Matthews (Tommy in Part 6) and of course Kane Hodder. Thankfully, the gameplay stands on its own as an 'asymmetrical multiplayer video game' and offers a tense and deceptively simple challenge: escape or die. Playing as a counselor (each based on several characters from the series), players seek to work together to escape Jason's stalking grounds. By utilizing strategy and their respective skill sets, counselors can either survive long enough to see the next day or, if they're lucky, kill Jason. Good luck with that. Speaking of, Jason's goals are even simpler--kill everyone. With a vast repertoire of moves and tools at his disposal, and a penchant for being pretty difficult to kill, the player truly feels like 'The Man Behind the Mask'. The game is not without its hiccups, of course--cars getting stuck, buggy ragdolls, it's all there. Are these bugs as terrible as they say? Not really. The biggest issue Friday the 13th: The Game suffers from is the playerbase itself--though friendly fire has all but been eliminated, you'll often find your lobby shrinking from 8 players to 2, especially if xXShadowHokage420Xx didn't get picked to play Jason. The game rewards players who stick around until the end of the match, even going so far as to let recently-butchered players come back as Tommy Jarvis, but quitting is still very much a slap on the wrist. It comes with the territory when you have a game based on survival, but I'm hoping things change down the line. In terms of content, the developers are constantly adding new things to the game, albiet somewhat slowly. Slow and steady wins the race, however, and the devs are always happy to talk about an issue and work on the latest hotfix. Add a few non-pay-to-win DLCs and gamemodes into the mix and you've got the best pot of Video Game Development Stew there is. In conclusion, grab this game if you're into multiplayer survival horror, preferably on sale. If you're a fan of Friday, however, you'd be crazy not to pick it up right now!

This game is based on the phenomenon called Slender Man which was born in 2009 as a result of a photo contest announced in a forum. The name perfectly sums up who the antagonist is in these games - a slim, tall man wearing a black suit. Moreover, the creature in question is completely faceless just to add an even more terrifying look to it. Its author claims he was influenced by H.P. Lovecraft, Stephen King and even by the Tall Man from the Phantasm horror films when making Slender Man.
Now, the first game was titled The Eight Pages and was released in 2012. Parsec Productions developed and released it on Windows completely independently from Steam. Blue Isle Studios, a Canadian developer company saw even more opportunity in the concept and released it under the name The Arrival. This now has a backstory to the game and, of course, includes the levels found in The Eight Pages. This "sequel" was released in 2013 and since have become available on PS4 and Xbox One, too.
Now, the gameplay is very simple in Slender The Arrival: we move around in abandoned places (houses, caves, mines, churches) trying to find a way out. In certain levels the objective is to collect something (see The Eight Pages)  - in such cases we have a limited time to complete our goal. Although the game does not give us a time limit the sound of the closing enemies becomes more and more frequent. Not doing anything for a long time or simply getting closer to the completion of our task provokes Slender Man.
Our flashlight and the ability to run both remain our best buddies. Greater difficulty levels allow the flashlight batteries to completely run out and our stamina also depletes much faster. While the game has around 10 levels these do not provide us with increasing difficulty levels. In fact, I believe The Eight Pages remains the most difficult level, plus, it is the one that perfectly captures the phenomenon of this Internet-created antagonist.
The game has decent graphics thanks to the good-old Unity engine. Nowadays more and more Steam games appear utilising the same technology (e.g. Forest). Still, its atmosphere is where The Arrival shines. Its sound design and the constant threat of Slender Man appearing behind us can easily drive any player crazy. There's no blood / gore in this game unlike in Outlast - once Slender Man is in our perspective the screen gets distorted. The closer he gets the more distortion is applied.
The only downside for me was the added levels / backstory. The story did not make Slender Man more interesting. I felt it was unnecessary to include the characters as well as the many collectibles that are scattered throughout the levels and serve as the backbone of the game's story. Additionally, level number 2 (The Eight Pages) is simply so good that the rest of the game can't even come close to it.
Still, The Arrival is a superb horror game with a great soundtrack and some pretty neat jumpscares. If you liked Amnesia, Forest, Outlast or similar survival horror games then you should give this a chance.

Let me put it in a layman term: Let say you are doing an exam about algebra and each question 1 & 2 are link together ( meaning if you cant answer 1, you cant answer 2). You then open your book to read and understand algebra but you dont get it. You then just trial and error question 1&2, knowing you will fail. It's like that.
It's frustrating because I just want to enjoy the game and finish the levels fast but I keep getting stuck and keep going online to get the guide. It's not hard because the game design is hard. It's hard because of the lack of the understanding of the tutorial. AND NO, I can watch videos / guide online doesnt cut it. You watch those videos because you are stuck at a particular level, not the whole game because of its bad hydraulic tutorial.
Lastly, some people might say that it's "my" fault for not understanding it. I can agree with that but here's the thing, if a game has a jump button and tells you that thats the jump button but never teaches you the advance move ( let say double jump or running jump ) and the game introduce you to those mechanic, is that fair? That's what the problem is.
I'll change my review if there is a proper introduction of the hydraulic in the tutorial but knowing that it will take a long time or maybe a huge amount of coding to do ( that will be troublesome ), I doubt the dev will change it.

Original Review:
I've been having a blast with this game. It takes the addictive elements of guitar hero and rock band, and teaches you real guitar techniques.
There are lots of fun songs across all genres to learn, and the game does a good job of letting you ramp up until you are playing every note. It also has a cool "riff repeater" mode that lets you slow down and repeat sections of the song in order to practice. I've played about 50 hours of the game and I can actually play a few songs on my own already.
There is also has a mini game mode that turns practicing scales, chords and other drills into games, which is more fun than just practicing those things over and over.
My only complaint with this game is that it doesn't have very good tools for calibrating audio/visual input lag. I wish it had more robust tools like Rock Band does, because there's not much you can do to correct it. Overall, I'd recommend this to anyone who has had fun with Guitar Hero and wants to actually learn guitar.

Resident Evil 6 is just one of those games you hate to love, and love to hate. While the RE4-6 series is a departure from the series' roots, it is still an enjoyable experience from a run-n-gun point of view, RE6 being the strongest entry in the game series' current evolution. That being said, there are many flaws which can turn an otherwise great experience into a practice of frustration and tedium.
RE6 makes for a solid third person shooter game. While the weapons do not have a realistic feel (nor do they attempt to give that impression), they behave in a way where it really doesn't matter. The gunplay is solid, with everything behaving as it should (with the exception of the hydra, being a 10ga sawn off, I'd expect a LOT more power than it actually offers). Knives and melee attacks do not make for insta-kills, introducing a dynamic of risk vs conservation.
Content in RE6 is FAR from lacking. The game has possibly hundreds of hours of gameplay with the MANY gamemodes offered (most of which I haven't even tried yet, admittedly), and fun side stuff to explore such as notes, figures, and backstory for down time between play throughs. Said content is also well thought out and very polished, making for a very eenjoyable experience throughout.
Models and lighting (especially the wet-look shine) are superb, though the textures are a bit lacking in the resolution department. Then again, what can you expect from a console port?
That being said, this IS a console port, and it shows. Some of the controls (especially for the much loathed QTEs, or Quick Time Events) are finnicky at best, and maddening at worst, and the default binding layout is borderline insane and will frustrate any PC veteran. Then again, the developers did try to bridge the gap, and offer a lot of features that PC vets will love such as FOV settings and some control over the graphic settings.
On the note of the QTEs... Yes, they are possibly THE most annoying things in gaming besides BSODs and CTDs. For me, they ruin the experience and many players will agree. That being said, there IS an option where the game completes them for you, eliminating a lot of the frustrating nonsense that ruins an otherwise awesome experience. Unfortunately, I have noticed that if a player joins your game who does not have the feature activated, it will force you to complete the QTEs as if you had the feature turned off as well. While I suppose this makes sense as it will prevent players from having an unfair advantage over others, it's frustrating as you cannot control who can and cannot join your game.
Players joining, both as friendlies and enemies, can make the game even more fun, however it can also be the one thing, besides QTEs, that ruins the experience entirely. You can either make your game public, limit it to friends, or go solo, and thats it. You cannot set any preference for Mic or no Mic, QTEs, skill level, etc. Furthermore, there is no kick option, forcing you to leave your own game if you're stuck with an incompetent/trollish teammate, or enemies that would rather use exploits to get their kills. This issue is further exacerbated by the huge distance between hard-save points (there is a soft-save system of checkpoints which are lost as soon as you end a session) which can cause you to lose up to an hour of gameplay when you leave the game. Furthermore, the lack of a mute option when dealing with Hot Mic (never turning their mic off, or players who play in absurdly noisey environments, or players who are eight-year-olds) players can be just as maddening.
When it comes down to it, Resident Evil 6 is a great game. I would strongly advise playing with people you know and work well with though, as this game is strongly geared towards a cooperative playstyle, and bad players can ruin the experience. Grab it while its on sale, and you won't be sorry.

The developers are steadily adding more content, including a new historical sites system recently.

I really, really enjoyed this game. It doesn't matter how high a budget is for a game or how large the development team is, so long as you have a good idea in your head an amazing product is possible, Thomas Was Alone proves that.
Thomas Was Alone (in a nutshell) is an Indie platformer where you have to use the unique abilities of each colored shape to overcome obstacles and puzzles. For a game that has such a simple graphics style and very basic gameplay, it has a very compelling and wonderful storyline and atmosphere, and yet even though I don't quite understand the story completely, this game is powerful, it makes you feel for the characters since they go through a ton of character development, even though they're only quadrilaterals... I know, I know, but trust me, this game is worth your time.
The narration voice acting is very well done and so full of character, this game probably has the best narrative I've ever heard in any game, and not just in the Indie genre. The voiceover tells the story of Thomas Was Alone in a witty, charismatic manner as you play and overcome the obstacles ahead leaving you hungry for more of the dialog as you play through the game.
There is very little to fault about this game, I do however think that £6.99 is somewhat of a steep price considering there isn't much length to the game, but I still say that this is worth your time and money. If you are an Indie game collector, enjoy platformers or a compelling story/narrative, this is the game for you.

Caves of Qud is a bit of a mess, mechanically; it's very much like playing a tabletop RPG from the early 90's, with all the jank, imbalance, and game-breaking ability combinations that implies. It constantly frustrates me with its incomplete documentation and over-reliance on randomness.
It makes up for this with personality, some of the most unique level design I've ever seen in a roguelike (Golgotha, in particular, makes brilliant use of environmental hazards) and an impressive (if haphazard) character creation system. It's more of a game to explore and ultimately break over your knee than a game to master, but if you were the kind of person who preferred ADOM and Nethack to DCSS and Angband, this is their successor in the current generation of roguelikes.

This is a really great roguelike. If you are looking for something a little different, that isn't pure sci-fi or fantasy Caves may be for you. Caves is set in the distant future, after the fall of civilisation and humanity. With deserts of salt, horrific mutations, terrifying robots emerging from beneath the rusted ruins that scatter the land and the only currency is fresh water.  Qud has a story, and a persistent world map. Some locations may be in the same place in each playthrough, but when you arrive it is still all randomised.
Travel across a bleak and blasted post apocalyptic wasteland. Battle mutated creatures, make friends with ape people. Kick down the door to an ancient ruin and get blasted apart by a chaingun turret as your chainmail armour fails to stop the incoming fire. Break the laws of time and space by summoning your time clones, encounter you evil twin from another dimension who summons his own time clones. Have a crazy mind laser rave as you all try to crush each other with your psychic brain powers. Panic and tear a hole in the fabric of the universe as an escape route. Spew fire from your hands. Set things on fire with your mind. Have a hardened carapace instead of skin. Play as a 4 armed, double muscled, quad axe wielding barbarian called Krud with a poisonous stinger on your tail. Play as a duster wearing, dual pistol wielding gunslinger. Be a True Kin and strike out from your arcology to explore the secrets of Qud and the Spire.

Ubisoft's "For Honor" is an interesting enigma. The game works like this: you play as part of one of three factions based from real-life warriors ranging from samurai straight out of feudal Japan, vikings or the medieval knights. Each three factions have more or less the same range of playable characters who all bring something different to the field in terms of what they can or cannot do, what they themselves are weak to along with old-fashioned combinations that yeild a variety of different results that can make or break any given duel if used at the right (Or wrong) times. In combat you'll be forced to block, parry and attack in order to survive against any enemies you may be faced with. This is done by moving the mouse to the left, right so on and so forth to block attacks or likewise cast an attack in that direction which can then be strung with the aforementioned combo moves to great effect. This is in many ways what makes the game's concept great, but it's also one of the largest contributers to what damned this game so direly in my own eyes.
Like with most games of this nature the system can be exploited, but in For Honor it's to the point where you can't do anything to actually win against an opponet who has knowledge of such issues. There's bugs in the game that allow other players to just rip into you without a single thing you can do to block, parry or even break away from the relentless slaughter that you'll find yourself victim to. It's what takes away so much of this game's enjoyment, yes, there is a skill window here and you WILL need to learn the game's mechanics in order to have even the faintest chance of survival, but even with such skills players with a knowledge of these exploits will absolutely rip you to pieces. That's not very fun, is it? I know I wasn't enjoying it, neither were any of my friends who also had the misfortune of being caught in the war path.
To make matters even worse there was a heavy dependency on peer to peer connections, as Ubisoft themselves didn't host any sort of official server. This led to instances of players outright disappearing and reappearing randomly about the map, sometimes just walking up to you and killing you instantly thanks to the instability of the matches. Add to this the aforementioned problems of exploits left unchecked, outright unbalanced characters and a complete disregard for anything short of Ubisoft just milking the game through microtransactions leaves me a bit sour on this entire endeavor. The map designs are fine, the graphics and music are all passable but the core game is much too broken for me to feel even remotely confident in recommending to anyone but a die-hard fan of such a setting with the patience of a saint.

After playing the Eight Pages, I was unbelievably stoked for this game, expecting dynamic gameplay through twists and turns of psychological horror and atmosphere. And to be honest, the game didn't FAIL, but it's not worth $10.
First off, the game is disappointingly short, with a total of 5 levels with actual interactive content, if that. Even though the first "level" does a good job of introducing the uncertain atmosphere of what you're entering into, it's still just a prologue. The second level is the age-old Eight Pages level that's been improved on. I can honestly say that they did an excellent job of making you feel completely lost and helpless in the woods even more so than the freeware version did, so props to the developers on that level. The third level is basically a more aggravating variation of the second, and the fourth level is essentially you walking down a linear path set by the game. The fifth level is pretty fun, too, but I won't spoil what happens it that one.
The second thing I disliked about this game is the ungodly difficulty. I enjoyed the atmosphere of the second level, but it was still balls-hard for me to complete. I felt like I had to get lucky enough to a.) actually find the page in the place I was looking and b.) not turn around to see Slender Man standing right next to me. I heard somewhere that the Eight Pages level in The Arrival was supposed to be easier than the freeware version, but I found it just as hard.
The third level is where is gets unbearable. You're trapped in an underground site of sorts with an unknown creature chasing you around, and you have to activate 6 power modules (or something like that) to get the elevator working and escape. Consider this an
more frustrating version of the Eight Pages; by this time, the atmosphere is replaced by unbridled rage as you have to cross your fingers and hope that this time, when you roll the dice, you'll HAPPEN to find the generator and have enough time to make it back before the Chaser pops out from around the corner and beats the tar outta you. Practice did jack-squat for me; one run I'll get 5 activated, the next run I'll get one activated. And it's not like I died prematurely either; I'll be running around for half an hour unable to get more than 3 generators before the Chaser finally finishes me off. In fact, I'm pretty sure the run where I won was one of my shortest runs. Words cannot express my emotion when I beat that level. The fifth level wasn't as much as tough as just completely confusing as what you were supposed to do to survive. That level was fun once I got the hang of it, but before then I was basically flailing angrily.
Bottom line: The Arrival is a small, one-and-done game. The experience is very real, but it's also very short-lived and can quickly be replaced by frustration (which really isn't the point of a horror game). If this was $5 or less, I would say it
be worth a shot if you had the money to throw around. For $10, however, you're definitely better off getting something better like Amnesia.

I really, really enjoyed this game. It doesn't matter how high a budget is for a game or how large the development team is, so long as you have a good idea in your head an amazing product is possible, Thomas Was Alone proves that.
Thomas Was Alone (in a nutshell) is an Indie platformer where you have to use the unique abilities of each colored shape to overcome obstacles and puzzles. For a game that has such a simple graphics style and very basic gameplay, it has a very compelling and wonderful storyline and atmosphere, and yet even though I don't quite understand the story completely, this game is powerful, it makes you feel for the characters since they go through a ton of character development, even though they're only quadrilaterals... I know, I know, but trust me, this game is worth your time.
The narration voice acting is very well done and so full of character, this game probably has the best narrative I've ever heard in any game, and not just in the Indie genre. The voiceover tells the story of Thomas Was Alone in a witty, charismatic manner as you play and overcome the obstacles ahead leaving you hungry for more of the dialog as you play through the game.
There is very little to fault about this game, I do however think that £6.99 is somewhat of a steep price considering there isn't much length to the game, but I still say that this is worth your time and money. If you are an Indie game collector, enjoy platformers or a compelling story/narrative, this is the game for you.

Thomas was alone is about rectangles (squares are rectangles so♥♥♥♥♥♥off). Despite this, I don't think I've seen characterization like this in most other video games. You understand the characters, their motives, their desires, and their fears. They are so clearly distnct that I actually felt sad for Thomas. Let me say that again.
. It's almost funny how videogames spend millions on "complex characters" and they are outdone by a rectangle. Their inner thoughts and stories are told by a narrator who emotes amazingly well and who I want to read me bed time stories.
The music is wonderful with all kinds of different sounds playing together that create an amazingly relaxed and intense atmosphere. Seriously. It's fantastic.
One major "flaw" (I guess?") is the story and the story progression. It starts out simple enough with Thomas. Then they add more characters each of which gets an entire section to emote and display their feelings. However, the story was about them. The characters interacting. The world around them was just a way to bridge the narrative but then later it goes off the rails into this whole mess (not spoiling). It's still an amazing story that is very welll put together but it shifts from the characters to the surroundings a bit too fast. Same with the ending. We don't end on Thomas. We end on some other bloke who isn't characterized much and the extra levels don't really resolve that stream and neither do the resolve Thomas' situation.
Some other minor nitpicks:
Blocks seem to stick on to the sides of moving blocks which might be intentitonal but it seems like a glitch. There a few too many characters introducted at the end and I just didn't care about them because they have motivation but not a character.
However, I would still play this again. You might remember the story but the characters will live with you. A fantastic game.

Blueprint Tycoon is a resource management simulator developed by {Endless Loop Studios}, while sometimes the game can be a bit frustrating (usually by the means of demand not being reached even though you have plenty of resources to go around) the game is quite fun to play, assuming you are into simulator type games. It provides a bit of complexity though not as much as factorio but it does make you think in terms of how to get object B to appear from object A, for example, in order to make milk you need to have a cattle ranch as well as research it which means you need a red vials, lab and researcher house.
My only complaint is that some of the senarios like the jewelery senario has too a certain too high of a demand for something (in my case that was researchers not having enough meat) those need to be tweaked like have a couple of testers test the premade senarios that way you don't have to go in and edit that. Unless your game is community driven (more than likely this is.) then you have done something wrong. There is one thing that bothers me and that is sandbox mode. It gives you literally almost everything right off the bat and I would very much love sandbox more if everything besides a few options (worker house, vegetable harvester, etc) are avaliable then sandbox mode would be more enjoyable. That's just me anyways what everybody else thinks is a completely different story.
Overall, the game is a solid B. I love the way how the game functions and that you have to distribute resources to proceed, a sandbox mode is a great addition, and the music is quite nice though not a whole lot of variation, a few tweaks here and there then it's even greater than ever thought of. I would totally recommend this game to anybody that is into simulation games.
