You could do a lot worse than drop a buck (or whatever) for this sweet little gem of a game.
It's a fun, very more-ish shmup that uses weapons fire to oppose gravity -- but with no fuel constraint or worry about hitting the ground, just the enemies and their shots.  The challenge is in keeping control of your ship while using the various upgrades to its engine to blast away at the enemies and other things that try to bring your lander down.   I like the difficulty progression -- every run starts out easy, and the difficulty increases by the player passing scoring milestones within the run.  So far, I haven't seen any huge, ridiculous jump between one step of difficulty and the next.
A nice variety of randomly-provided weapon power-ups and new ships earned through various high scores and collection of coins  help you go farther, though some are much better at this than others!
When I originally wrote this review, I had only played a bit -- now that I've played more, I have to say I enjoy the variety of music I hadn't experienced yet.   The controls are solid, the gameplay mechanics are well thought out... there really aren't any minuses I can see!

Caves of Qud is a roguelike that brings something fresh to the genre, not in its entirety, but in enough ways that I feel it's worth highlighting if you're tired of the same-old Nethack and ADOM experiences. Your direction is not given through narrative exposition, but rather by talking to people and forming your own understanding of what's going on in the world, with the choice of how best to proceed being left entirely up to you. This particular aspect of the gameplay isn't original, but the setting and lore behind the realm you're thrust into definitely is.
The game is set in what can be seen as a post-apocalyptic wasteland with mutants, espers, ancient ruins, and a persistent scarcity of water—so scarce, in fact, that it's the default form of currency in the pseudo-barter economy that the whole world has adopted. Honestly speaking, CoQ is better enjoyed when you have time to sit down and immerse yourself, as opposed to favoring the pick-up-and-play nature of many other roguelikes and roguelites. If that sounds like your cup of tea, definitely give this a shot.
The style of the game aside, the controls deserve being commented on due to how much they affect the enjoyability of the game. They're a mix of old and new that most RL veterans will appreciate. It's not quite as modernized as something like Tales of Maj'Eyal, but has enough improvements over the retro fare to be appreciable and praise-worthy. The controls may take some getting used to for those new to the genre, but are otherwise standard fare, with some level of customizability allowing for streamlining use of abilities and talents. It's even possible (using Joy2Key) to map most standard actions to a controller and play the game almost entirely through that, which is something that very few true roguelikes allow for. This is just a quality-of-life thing, but it's a huge one, and one that makes CoQ a perfect intermediary even for people looking to dip their toes in the waters of more complex RL titles. In short, the controls are varied enough to require some minor memorization, but simple and intuitive enough that picking up the many controls doesn't take much time at all.
Last, but definitely not least, is the gameplay itself. God damn does this thing deliver on what makes a great roguelike great: options. This may be best expressed by recounting my initial experiences with the game, as compared to my current one:
As it stands, I've learned from my many mistakes, and my current character is doing quite well. This learning experience is a huge part of the game though, as the world will not hesitate to beat the player down at every opportunity presented. My advice to those of you who read about these experiences and were enticed by the prospect of a difficult and punishing game would be to read up on the game before-hand, learn what messages mean what, and equip themselves with the knowledge to see themselves towards a successful completion of CoQ. Avoid spoilers where possible when doing so, but absolutely attempt to find logs of other players' mistakes and their consequences so that you can avoid making them yourself. In my case, this kind of involving experience is exactly what I look for in my roguelike titles, and I whole-heartedly recommend this game for it.

Remember that chaotic little game you played back in 2010?  The one with mice and cheese and cannonballs?
Well, it's back... in
form!
The objective of this game is simple: Get the cheese, bring it back to the mouse hole.  However, that's only the beginning.  To get to the cheese, you might need to use purple trampolines, climb chocolate bars, avoid (or even
) hot lava, or even contend with jealous shaman bent on keeping you from your goal!  All this while playing with a handful of other players, live!
Since 2010, this game gained a cult following, keeping fans of old and gaining fans anew.  These days, it's much the same as it always was... but with far more game modes, such as Race, Survival, and Defilante (Scrolling)!  It also has much more user-created content than it used to, such as maps and even wearable items for your mouse!  That's right: You can customize your mouse with items to set them apart from the rest of the crowd!  But you've gotta earn 'em by getting the cheese, first!  Or, ya know... buying fraises (strawberries), the microtransaction currency of the game, with real-world money. (The prices are actually pretty good, too!)
If you like side-scrolling action/puzzle games with an adorable twist and some amount of customization, or are just an occasional fan of absolute chaos, this is definitely the game for you!

I'm aware how late this review is, but I just wanted to warn any potential buyers to turn and run from this dogs breakfast that ubisoft dares to call a video game.
I've been playing since launch, and I mostly stuck around because the game is, in some places, really damn fun. And at launch the biggest issue the game faced was it's terrible issues with online play (ie being disconnected midgame 1/3rd of the time). But that was pretty much it.

Boy oh boy was I wrong.
Not only are there more issues with the game, but most of the initial problems with the game are STILL there.
First of all constant disconnecting from online play is still just as bad as it was. on top of that the hero's aren't anymore balanced than they were at launch, as most new updates just make 1-2 hero/s insanely op for a brief period of time, before they get nerfed into uselessness.
Next to that, of the 5 game modes you can play online (that were really popular at launch), only 2 of them have more than 50 players in regular circulation at any time. This being due to the introduction of EXTREMELY overpowered DLC hero's that make it impossible to win against in the other 3 modes.
Either way, don't get this game, it looks fun and often is, but it only looks like it's going to get worse and worse as time goes on.

Friday the 13th: The Game borrows many fan favorite elements from the film series. There’s a camp site, a group of young camp counselors running for their lives, and a terrifying killer named Jason Voorhees killing people who gets in his way. It has all the makings of an 80s teen slasher flick. Though, the setting and story is kept generic enough that it fits into an easy cookie cutter format for each new match. In fact, Friday the 13th doesn’t even have a solo standalone story – it’s just teens trying to survive as Jason is coming to kill them. That’s it! There’s nothing more complex than that.
The game itself is set up as a semi-open world survival horror multiplayer game where (up to) seven players take on the roles of camp counselors. Their job is to explore the camp and find a way out alive. This could be in the form of fixing the camp car/boat and driving off, calling in the police, or even killing Jason himself. The additional eighth player becomes Jason Voorhees. Their job is simple enough: kill everyone. Jason has extra abilities and a wide variety of killing methods that he can use to snuff out any camp counselor he gets in contact with. It’s a tougher battle for the teens to survive, but if they work together, everyone could survive. It can happen! (I’ve played matches where I’ve survived as a counselor, got picked off early on, and as Jason who has killed all seven counselors.)
During actual gameplay, counselors have the ability to explore cabins and search for key items. You can either arm yourself with weapons like machetes and bats or survival items like firecrackers. The best discoveries were the ones that offered a chance at escape. I loved the feeling of walking into a cabin and FINALLY locating a missing part to the camp car/boat that helped me escape. I get so excited finding car keys! Jason, on the other hand, has four abilities that progressively get unlocked as the match goes on. The longer he plays, the deadlier he becomes. And with each new power, it helps him achieve his kills in a quicker and bloodier fashion.
The real treat to the game is the design and personalities of the characters. Each available Jason (after being unlocked) has their own personal strengths, weaknesses and looks. Some can run, others are better throwers, and each has their special abilities that can be used to kill the campers. The counselors, on the other hand, fit the archetype of the typical counselors who Jason would go after. You have the jock, the goth, the geek, the prep, the coed, and the list goes on. Each type is balanced with their own pre-set stats that show off the benefits, or in some cases disadvantages, to use for the player. For instance, certain players have high luck to finding objects in cabins, but they may have low composure and will be instantly terrified whenever Jason appears.
The best way to counteract this is the perk system. For a sum of accumulated points, the player can turn the odds and receive a random perk that will help and hinder them in matches. Perks can affect fighting, stats, escaping or even offer rewards. I’m on the fence with this feature. In certain aspects it’s not advantageous to equip a perk because the consequence does too much damage against the player. And the perk is completely random, so you’re not guaranteed to get something you’ll like, or even need. On the other hand, when you’re awarded a great perk, it can change the course of the game.
Friday the 13th is an ambitious and fun survival horror game that brings the film series to life. If you ever wondered if you could survive an attack from the machete-wielding, hockey mask-wearing killer, this is the game for you. As a horror fan, I got a taste of the campy 80s slasher flair and quite liked it. While it’s not exactly groundbreaking in the PvP field, its momentum is fueled by novelty and the Jason name. The technical issues, however, have affected the experience – even with all the patches, it’s expected that a lag, a drop or a glitch will occur. Many issues have been fixed with patches, but it’s still a long way to go before perfection. Stick with the game; you’ll never be afraid as if you were watching a horror movie – this isn’t that type of survivor horror video game. However, it’s addictive, campy, and it’ll bring out the Final Girl (or Guy) in you.

Resident Evil 6 by no means achieves any sort of medium-pushing greatness at any point, but there its set of mechanics is capable of coming together to create a perfectly serviceable and sometimes-compelling action game. However, RE6 does completely fall flat as a survival-horror game, and its multiple campaigns are mostly awkwardly-paced and poorly-written, and the game tends to generally lack a consistent atmosphere or mood that made the earlier entries in the franchise famous. The game tends to achieve its highest points in its bonus and periphery modes (Mercenaries, specifically), where the player is afforded a lot more freedom to use all of the action mechanics at once. The interplay between shooting and melee, dodging and spacing, performing counterattacks, and utilizing environmental familiarity all gels together to be a pretty dang fun action game from time to time. None of these particular mechanics are best-in-genre or even the greatest available in the larger medium of contemporary videogames, but the combination available to the player feels pretty unique to RE6. However, it feels as if the vast majority of content in the game doesn't ever demand the player to utilize the full array of RE6's mechanics at any time. The 4 campaigns feel like they attempt to highlight different distinctive moods and playstyles, and it comes with the cost of sacrificing that interesting and unique interplay of mechanics that RE6 houses under its hood in order to match whatever arbitrary "feel" each campaign strives to achieve. In setting up its separate campaigns this way, it also feels like the game fails to communicate clearly the amount of options the player has during combat sequences, and its unfortunate, because it took me a long time to even realize some of the options I had when it came to evading certain attacks, performing counterattacks, and the variety of movement and spacing options available. It feels like the game barely just tries to set itself up as RE5 with move-and-shoot, but it actually contains a lot more nuance than that.
With that said, RE6 is far from perfect, but it sometimes shines during a few moments sprinkled throughout its huge campaign offerings, and Mercenaries is a nice highlight of the game's distinctive action game feel that can be revisited either casually or hardcore. For anyone that's looking to experience a somewhat unique action title, I personally recommend it, but I understand that it won't carry universal appeal due to its largely incohesive design. If you're an action fan and have played all of the action game darlings (Devil May Cry 4, DmC: Devil May Cry, and Metal Gear Rising get my nods), you might not be too bad off grabbing RE6 on sale and approaching it as an action game. Even more power to you if you can convince a buddy to play cooperative with you.
SCORE: 6/10

An interesting rogue-like set in a Gamma World-esque universe with new content being added on a steady, weekly basis. As with other rogue-likes the death is permanent, but half the fun is experimenting with new builds, which Caves of Qud has in spades. I have played other games in this type of genre, however, none have really scratched that post-apocalyptic itch that Caves of Qud has. The tile art is very fitting (with more being expanded upon it seems) and the musical touches that have been added in the latest patches have created a really nice ambience and immersion into the world. The lore and creatures that are being built into this game are rather unique and the procedural nature of the game allows for some spectacular moments to occur (i.e., a particular Sultan's history revealed that he had killed an enemy with "existential despair"). If you are looking for a game to not invest a lot of time in and only looking for a quick thrill with all the latest bells and whistles that AAA titles bring, then you probably would not enjoy this game. If you enjoy the rogue-like genre, are looking for an interesting and deep world or just want a thoughtful experience, I would recommend you try Caves of Qud.

There seem to be a lot of technical complaints about this game, many claiming that the game doesn't run properly on newer systems, that framerate issues pop up, that it crashes or freezes, or that the authentication code won't work.
I'm running it on Windows 10, and the game works perfectly for me. It never once crashed for me, never froze, the authentication code worked right out of the gate, and I never once experienced any framerate issues. Different systems experience different problems I suppose, but that's the same for many, many games on Steam. So if the game looks interesting at all to you, don't let the possibility of a hiccup or two dissuade you.
All of those subjects aside, I'm personally a big fan of this game, and have been since I first played it on PS3 about seven years ago. It was poorly-received by critics back then, and in some ways I totally understand why that might be. Getting the negative out of the way first, I will say there's a big imbalance between the game's three basic gameplay styles (third-person shooting, jetpack aerial combat, and the unique vertical cover system). The vertical cover system disappears entirely about halfway through, and since those were obviously the scenes that would take the most effort to construct for a level designer, it makes it pretty clear that the game was rushed for release. Likewise, the story, as mediocre as it may have been, ends VERY abruptly, with almost no legitimate buildup to the climax. It feels like it ends right in the middle, and I can totally understand how that would leave a bad taste in the mouths of reviewers back in 2010.
However, if you simply take the game as it is, as a series of battles with some really unique mechanics, it's a total blast to play regardless of its faults. The third-person shooting is, at its core, just your same-old shooting we've seen in a hundred games elsewhere... until you get the jetpack. Once that happens, you're suddenly free to boost and hover around the environments, turning mechanics that tend to take place on a flat plane in other games into a much more vertically-focused affair, hovering over enemies and raining down on them from above, or firing at others above you.
Separate from that is the actual vertical cover system, which only appears at certain designated points, but makes for a really interesting sidestep here and there. Basically, it allows you to cling to the underside of a platform and fire upward at other enemies (or to take cover on top of a platform while shooting downward). It's difficult to describe in words, but makes total sense once you see it, and is especially well-implemented early on, in a sequence aboard a wrecked freighter ship hanging over a cliff.
And, best thing saved for last, we have the aerial jetpack combat. Many reviews claimed back in 2010 that the mechanics for this were confusing, and that it was difficult to get your bearings when the environment might turn upside-down at a moment's notice... but that all feels, to me, like the complaints of people that simply refused to understand how it all works. There's a designated button that can automatically turn you right-side-up again, so complaining of confusion seems silly to me. Replaying it recently, I had absolutely no trouble understanding where I was at any given time, or where the enemies were. There's a button to immediately shift the view to the nearest enemy; simply press that, then turn in its direction. Not hard at all. Ignoring those complaints, there's really nothing else out there that feels quite like the aerial combat in this game. Sure, it may essentially be an extension of the arcade-esque mechanics used in some of the developers' previous effort on the Xbox, Crimson Skies, but there's a completely different feel to it. Never, anywhere else, have I ever gotten to play as simply a guy with a jetpack strapped to his back, dashing through the air, legs dangling behind him realistically, swaying with every movement and evasive maneuver. It's incredibly visceral and exciting and, having been a MASSIVE fan of the Rocketeer movie when I was a kid (actually saw that in the theater), it fulfills a little bit of fantasy that I've always had. I tend to be a sucker for games that involve jetpack mechanics in some form... or rather, I love the
of them. Usually those mechanics begin and end with simply hovering between gaps.
The mechanics here, however, actually take everything into full-on man-versus-aircraft dogfighting. There is
that checks this box for me in such a fun, interesting way.
So, regardless of its obvious faults, Dark Void retains a very special place in my heart.
Just a tip: it's a lot of fun to play with a gampad in your lap and your mouse and keyboard at the ready. I found that mouse and keyboard works best for the third-person shooting (better aiming control, obviously) while a good gamepad works better for the aerial combat (and the occasional QTE). The game allows you to switch between them seemlessly, so for the best experience, I recommend using both.

It's good fun. As long as you end up in a lobby where people communicate, you can have an absolute blast. Great with friends, and great with talkative randoms. For a brief synopsis, for the uninitiated: It's an 8-player game where 7 players get to be Counselors and the 8th player is Jason Voorhees, out to kill them all. Jason's goal is, obviously, to kill the other players, while the Counselors must either survive the night (which in itself is already monumentally hard), or use one of multiple escape methods (fixing a car, a boat, or just calling the cops and running for it). And just to make it interesting, not only are there multiple player characters to choose from (with their own differing stats and niches), but there's multiple different versions of Jason, each with some slight differences
Overall getting into mechanics and subjectives, I have this to say:
+ Actually playing as Jason Voorhees is amazing and a very real (and exciting) power trip, especially with SEVEN (or eight if you backed the game) versions to play with (Part 6 Jason being my personal favorite)
+ Slightly randomized maps, spawn locations, and the like, for a different experience each time
+ Surviving against Jason or better yet, escaping, feels awesome
+ With a good team there's all kinds of potential for humor, excitement, drama, etc. Communication makes everything better
+ The horror atmosphere is real. I've played a small chunk of "survival horror" games but really, aside from STALKER, none of them nailed the feel of being defenseless, powerless, and probably doomed to die. This game DOES
+ As long as it can take to level up, you can earn points to buy new perks for the Counselors and new kill animations for all the Jasons, plus you can change everyone's outfits to your liking as you level up
+ Free updates! I mean it's sad I have to say that's a full-blown positive in this day and age but, it's still worth noting
- If everyone's scattered and unlucky the game can end unfavorably rather... quickly
- It's a lot harder if you're not communicating well
- It's honestly a little bit on the glitchy side and it can be a bit difficult to run properly (I can't honestly complain, my fault for having a laptop). Hey, it's not Payday 2 though
- Some bits of balance seem just a little... off to me. I mean it's all subjective and a good player can get a wipe if they know what they're doing, but Jason Part 7 seems disproportionately worse compared to the rest
- Bit of a learning curve. Ideally, you're gonna want a friend to help you get into it and understand it, and probably also check the Guides section. There's a decent chunk of info that's not spelled out in the game itself
- It's pricey. This obviously isn't a problem for everybody but, unless you play it a TON, it might take a while to justify the whole $40 price tag. The fun lies in just... playing. I mean yeah it might be a bit lacking in overall content but it's the experience that matters here and if you're on the fence about the game, I'd really recommend getting it on a sale. It's DEFINITELY worth it then. Plus hey, free updates!
Overall, it depends on if you think you'd like the experience or not. Personally, it's a lot of fun to me. As mentioned, I would recommend waiting on a sale unless you think you're gonna play it all the time, in which case go for it right away. But if it DOES go on sale, get it asap and you'll probably be glad you did

Let’s state right away that if you are not interested in Slender Man’s particular brand of horror this is not the game for you. Not much about the mythology is ever properly explained, and without prior knowledge of it you only get half of the experience out of the game.
Sure, it’s a slow moving walking sim with some repetitive item hunts and cheap jump scares. But the real horror here comes from the atmosphere, you can never shake the feeling that whatever you do is empty gestures - the Slender Man is already planted in the mind of the protagonist and escape according to the mythos will be impossible. That underlying desperation and hopelessness is what makes the real horror here, not the jump scares.
This is something that the game does very well in presenting with its empty and desolate yet beautiful settings, some fantastic lightning effects and of course the nail biting soundtrack. It’s not often you get a horror game where walking in a beautiful sunset feels like an unavoidable death sentence.
There are some tedious parts though, especially the second chapter that is a remake of the original freeware title, due to the large size of the map and randomization of the item locations it can take forever to complete. There are only two of these big maps though and when you are past them some of the truly great chapters await.
It’s an experience very much recommended for anyone crying from anxiety when watching the Marble Hornets series.
Others may not be as forgiving to the uneven quality of the chapters or the cheap way the story is presented through scattered notes, but as a fan of the mythos it's one of the best walking sim horrors you can find.

I can only tentatively recommend this game, and it's with sadness that I say I borderline do not recommend it at all.
This is possibly the best game within the bridge building genre that I've played, with a very nice art style, intuitive controls, and the useful ability to copy and paste pieces. For the first two worlds of this game it really feels like you're allowed to unleash your creative potential and engineering skills as you make increasingly more complicated bridges.
Then you get to world 3. It's at this point that you'll notice staying under your budget is exponentially more difficult than it was in the previous two worlds, and solutions start to become more obtuse. It gets very frustrating and it starts to feel less like creating your own design and more like guessing at what particular design the developer tested the level with, and this is only compounded by the fact that a bridge can succeed or fail based entirely on whether a single joint is one grid space off where it should be. I'm all for an increased challenge, but it's not fun when you have a design that should be working, and the only thing stopping you from proceeding is fiddling around with the joints to figure out the exact optimal positions for them. There's no in-game hint system either, and even if you resort to walkthroughs you still won't always be able to get past a tough level, as like I said earlier, if you don't have the joints in the exact right spots, your version of the bridge might fail where others succeeded.
The difficulty of world 3 is slightly inconsistent as well, it seems, as on 3-3 Looper, I was able to complete the level under budget with my first design attempt and minimal tweaking. This was odd after 3-1 required many redesigns before I had to rely on a walkthrough, and even had to tweak the walkthrough solution several times before it worked, and 3-2 required several redesigns and tweaking of my own (no walkthrough) before it worked.
It seems that at some point the physics system was changed as well, as I resorted to a guide for 3-4 Hydraulic Jump after my design failed and failed again. Much to my dismay I found that the guide I looked up was using the exact design I had come up with myself, as if it were in fact the intended design, only mine was just not working. A quick look in the comments section revealed that this design does not work on the current version of the game, and it gives me the feeling that the developers changed up the physics engine without going back to test levels to make sure they work.
TL;DR This game is fun, but the difficulty curve spikes abruptly at World 3 and some levels are incredibly frustrating, especially if you try to stay within the budget constraints. World 1 and 2 are possibly worth the price alone if you pick it up on sale.

For a minimialist logic game it seems to have a lot of UI and logic problems. E.g.
- In the tutorial, it tells me to make milk. How? I've built all the buildings available in the UI, and none of them produce milk. Ok, I quit out of the tutorial at that point since it seems deadlocked.
- I try a sandbox game.  It has 3 items involved in making Iron; there is coal, iron ore, and iron ingots. These all show up in the UI as tiny little gray-black asteroids. But wait, there's more!  In the trade route UI all the icons are even smaller, so they are these little 16x16 blackish-icons that are completely indistinguishable. Oh, and if you don't have the needed resource, it then puts a red "X" over its tiny icon to make it even more impossible to read. I try mousing over the thing, but there are no tooltips.
- The interface is inconsistent; I'm never sure when right clicking will get me out of a menu or trigger a new menu.  Multiple small frustrations like that.
- I try a sandbox game. I'd like to build an airship, but to do that I need to get iron stuff into the Main building. How? It doesn't have inputs or outputs. Can I send the resources to my Construction building? No, it doesn't take them either.  Who knows.
- I try a sandbox game. I'd like a ship to iron ore to one island and then take back iron ingots. After fiddling for a while and then going to the forums, it turns out you can't have 2-way trade routes. Your ships can only haul goods one way.  :(

Blueprint Tycoon has everything you could want in a management and tycoon game. The tutorials are very welcoming and help you immediately acclimate to the game's fundamentals. Once completed, the difficulty slowly ramps up in a short “campaign” mode which expands the building and research options. From there, it's all up to you and how you want to build your supply chain empire.
The graphical style really plays a part in this game. It's as if someone literally rolled out a set of blueprints on a table and said “have fun”! Watching your workforce carrying products from one building to another can become mesmerizing especially considering you can continue to add more buildings and more workers.
Players can toggle “route mode” with a hotkey showing where the product is coming from and where it is moving to. This can be daunting at first but Blueprint Tycoon makes it easy to get a grasp on this concept fairly quickly. Successfully setting up the perfect supply chain left me with a sense of accomplishment and only made me want to play more. The game also has islands you can colonize to produce different products. For example, sometimes your main island won't be fertile enough to grow wheat – time to expand! The island system adds another level of complexity because you have to ensure your main island receives the goods it needs for industrial buildings.
Overall, I love Blueprint Tycoon. It is challenging enough to keep you engaged while also not making you feel at all frustrated. If you enjoy complex supply chains, worker management and fun, Blueprint Tycoon may be for you.

If you're expecting a hand-holding first quest to gently bop five harmless creatures and collect their fur, put on a solid helmet and buckle its chinstrap.  Caves of Qud throws you right into the deep end of a mutant sci-fi/fantasy mashup with barbarians, manimals, swordsmen, and a dizzying variety of flora & fauna.
The steep, almost punishing learning curve is par for the course in good rogue-likes, and so arriving in Joppa with NO IDEA of what button to press is a sign -- to veterans of Nethack and Dwarf Fortress -- that a great deal of fun is imminent.  Statting out your character seems easy enough, but the massive variety of options (mutations, backgrounds, tribes) seem to offer hundreds of ways to try to impose your will on the world.  There are excellent help menus, very good context UI, and warnings when you're about to do something stupid (like steal) to help get you up that first vertical surface, though.  Patience, attentive reading, and good note-taking can speed you along.
The graphics have recently improved from colorful ASCII to lo-res sprites. The aesthetic resembles some of the tilesets ou might see in Dwarf Fortress.
The questing & reputation systems are more complete than DF Adventurer Mode, with Mehmet and Argyve giving you quests that skip right over "kill ten toothless rats" and jump straight into "suicidal raid on a nearby hostile zone".  If you can put in the effort to learn the systems and survive the first quests you'll be well on your way toward leveling up a powerful adventurer.
Great for fans of procedural roguelikes, but expect to work hard for the rewards it offers.

Now THIS is a rogue-like. You ever find yourself going through the tag, looking at all the crazy stuff people throw the name rogue-like onto? Have you ever PLAYED the original Rogue? If you haven't, I recomend you do that, its a fun little game for the most part. Once you've done that, you probably have a pretty good idea of what Caves of Qud has to offer. At least, in its most basic form.
Now imagine if Adventure Mode of Dwarf Fortress had a baby with a post-apocalyptic fiction author's imagination. Combine that with the original concept of the original Rogue, and you more or less have Caves of Qud.
Now, my first experience with Qud wasn't that great. I couldn't figure out how to do anything. Turns out, I wasn't really trying hard enough. The key mapping is right there in the Esc menu.
So, Caves of Qud. It's a hard game. Extremely hard? Well, maybe, but definitely hard. It takes a little while to get used to, a little thinking to understand, and a lot of patience and perseverance to really get into the game. It's difficulty will be both a turn on and a turn off, it just depends on who you are as a "gamer", and you should know by now what type of games you enjoy, especially if you're looking at a review for a bona fide rogue-like made with ASCII graphics.
The atmosphere is amazing. The setting is amazing. The gameplay is fun and satisfying. The story it tells is interesting. The character creation is detailed and full of interesting ideas.
In the end, what it all comes down to is this; Do you want a real rogue-like? Do you want to recapture that feeling of exploration and wonder that so many games these days are missing? Do you want to die? A lot? Do you want to be rewarded for your hard work? If the answer to any of these questions was yes, then this is the game for you. If you answered no to any but the second question, you probably shouldnt buy this game. Personally, though, I definitely recommend it.

- It is ridiculously expensive for a game with so little to offer.

Activated in February 2017, the activation server works fine, so those of you who are worried about activation can stop worrying. With that said, the game was... not that big of a deal. Basically, this game was Rocketeer turned into a game with a bit about Bermuda Triangle thrown in where our hero fights a bunch of weird aliens machines after being sucked through "The Void".  The third-person view can be problematic or not depending on your tolerance level, but I agree with others that a controller is definitely needed due to a lot of combo moves, like left stick and jump to shift platforms, and so on.
My problem is with some of the checkpoints. Only a few chapters in, I was supposed to take out two generators to allow the ship to escape. The idea is drop on the platform, kill everybody, open the bottom shield (savepoint) then fly down there, land, the climb my way up, kill everybody, then somehow trigger self-destruct AND get out before the whole thing blows up. It was explained that just drop off edge of the platform and drop straight down. Except... If you were off and hit a cross beam, or you did not shift in time into flight mode, you get to repeat the attack (!) as you would have died and get to resume from the savepoint (!).  When you finally get this right, you get to do the other generator, except the direction is flipped... Fight to open the top, fight your way down, then escape by going up.
And it can only get even MORE complicated.
There is a minor weapon upgrade system, but the currency was in very short supply, and there are quite a few weapons.
If you like semi-Retro aesthetics and gameplay, I guess this ain't that bad.

There's something evergreen about Transformice's brand of online warfare. The combination of breakneck infantry fighting and explosive vehicular warfare breeds conflicts that are exciting, tense, and, perhaps most importantly, diverse. With weapons, gadgets, and upgrades tailored to create a wealth of combat roles, it can often seem like there's no end to the gratifying ways you can contribute to the war effort. This variety has enticed players into Mice games for years, and in Transformice, it's alive and well. The online multiplayer is an absolute blast.
But Transformice is about more than just multiplayer these days, and the single-player campaign in TFM also has some exciting moments. These are sequences that channel the freedom and variety of multiplayer; the levels spent mostly in corridors and in close-quarters combat are more frequent, however, and not nearly as enjoyable. The characters that drive the story show flashes of appealing personality, but these are drowned out by cliche relationships and boilerplate dialogue. Though TFM outdoes its predecessor, the series has a long way to go before the campaign is more than a sideshow diversion.
Fortunately, the online stage is expertly set for some exhilarating moments. One of the best new things about TFM is Obliteration mode, in which two teams fight to gain control of a bomb and use it to blow up three enemy positions. Unlike returning standby Conquest mode, in which the battle ebbs and flows between a handful of set positions, Obliteration boasts conflict zones that can change in a flash with the timely use of land, air, and sea vehicles. Motorized transport has always been a pillar of combat in the Transformice series, and Obliteration mode makes mobility more important than ever. (Thank goodness for the new test range that allows you to practice piloting every vehicle!) A skilled helicopter pilot can swoop in to pick up the bomb carrier and then zip off to an objective point, leaving enemy infantry in the dust. Escaping the chaos to grab a personal watercraft can turn the tide, but perhaps it's better to blow it up so your enemies don't grab it for themselves. Plotting your own dramatic maneuvers while defending against the enemies' is a lively challenge that takes on new urgency in Obliteration.
Matches without vehicles, however, have a different pace. Victory comes from solid squad support and sharp shooting. Battling for bomb possession in winding prison tunnels is a brutal close-quarters affair, and well-balanced matches run the risk of devolving into lengthy scrums in which neither team can make headway. Keeping your squad alive is crucial here, not just as mobile spawn points but also to preserve your field upgrades. These are new attribute bonuses that you gain through squad-related actions, bestowing you with resistance to suppressing fire or better flak protection, for example.
Being able to shoot a little straighter or survive a nearby grenade blast can make a difference in these fast-paced, infantry-heavy matches of Obliteration, as well as in small, speedy matches of Domination (small-scale Conquest) and Team Deathmatch. The other new mode also involves bomb-carrying, but because it has bite-size maps and no respawning, Defuse demands a more careful kind of infantry combat. Weapon choice and enemy detection are key in these short, fraught encounters, and while the heightened tension can result in some very satisfying wins, smaller arenas are not where Transformice is at its best.
The standout action comes in large-scale conflicts that take advantage of the 10 large, well-designed maps. Richer color saturation makes them a pleasure to look at, from the lush alpine fields surrounding a massive satellite dish to the sparkling neon lights of a coastal city. Buildings frequently have stairs or elevators that allow access to upper stories, giving snipers long sight lines and providing parachutists with jumping-off points to better traverse the map. This increased verticality adds some strategic options, but the bigger change is the greater prevalence of water. Marine combat is a much bigger factor in Transformice, whether you're zipping down the narrow canals of a seaside resort while your passenger mows down infantry or patrolling the lanes of a small archipelago and shooting helicopters out of the sky with a fully crewed attack boat.
Naval dominance can help you control a match, but water-based mobility is another huge consideration, as anyone who has trudged across a large empty field instead of hitching a ride knows. Swimming leaves you vulnerable, though you can at least pull out your sidearm, so it's best to secure transport when you can. This much is obvious when fighting in a stormy island chain, but until someone blows the levee on the slightly waterlogged urban map, you can do just fine scurrying around on foot. When the water does rush in, the whole place gets submerged beneath ten feet of water and things change significantly. If you don't stick to the rooftops or hop in one of the newly spawned boats, you're in trouble.
This deluge is the most drastic of the marquee environmental events that you can trigger on each map. Some of these occurrences bring significant change, like the destruction of a skyscraper, while others are more subtle, like closing jail doors to shut off a hallway or raising bollards to block a road. These special events are complemented by the wide range of destructible structures and deformable terrain. Blown-out walls and collapsed buildings have a hard time hiding enemies, and roads pitted by bomb craters are more difficult to navigate smoothly. Destructibility has been amped up from Transformice 2, and being able to blast your way through certain obstructions is a liberating and empowering experience.
In most cases, you must supply the ordnance to take advantage of this destructibility (some maps have large triggered bombs that do the job on their own). Among the weapons and gadgets for each class are a number of explosive options tailored to take down threats on land, at sea, and in the sky. There are also items that support your allies in a variety of ways, from keeping them alive to alerting them to nearby enemies. Thanks to some loadout shuffling and the presence of weapon classes that unlock for every soldier type, there are more ways than ever to customize the four basic archetypes to fill a multitude of combat roles. Of particular note is the new ability to zero your scope, a trick that lets you quickly set the distance at which your bullet will hit the center of your sight, providing a valuable aid for long-range sniping.
Between vehicle and soldier customization, there are a ton of ways to be effective on the battlefield and rack up the points that increase your rank and unlock new stuff. You can intermittently earn battlepacks that provide small rewards, and new map-specific battle pickups like sniper rifles, automatic shotguns, and grenade launchers give you powerful ways to adapt your strategy on the fly. If you prefer to take a broader strategic view, you can join a match as a commander once you hit the requisite level. With a bird's-eye view and a chat line to every squad leader, this mode lets you set objectives for troops, scan for enemies, and reinforce your team in a few other ways. Vehicle and supply drops can conceivably be a great boon to your grunts, but the tools that become available to you depend largely on how well those grunts accept and follow your orders. Oblivious players can make Commander mode drag, so it's a hit-or-miss experience.

So, I felt like I have to write a review to compensate a bit the negativity this games got. The negativity mainly came from an issue with not the game, but its sh|tty, unnecessary and annoying drm, securom. Yeah, there is that, you cant do anything about it, but the point is, the issue with securom has been fixed. A long time ago. So, if youre planning to grab this thing and browsing the reviews just ignore those complaining about "friggin serial not activating...", its history.
The other source of complains is the controls. Well, I play my games with a generic 3-button mouse and a generic keyboard, but I couldnt find any wrong with it, set my sensitivities and I was ready to go (saying this I dont dig games involving flying at all, apart from this one ofcourse). Idk about gamepad controls though, but I dont rly care, were pc gamers, gamepads are for consoles, kids, and maybe sport games anyway.
About the game, yeah, it needs some love, but if you can get through the hiccups (Im detailing them below), its serious fun. Jetpax, man! With guns! And with flying, hoovering and jet-jumping along comes an interesting vertical cover system, flanking, b|tchslapping enemies from behind, from above... Fun times. While there are only 6 weapons in the game (besides your trusty jetpack artillery, what will be your main armament anyway) they are fun and unique, you can also upgrade them as you progress.
Now about the afromentioned hiccups:
- No full screen option: Alt+Enter when the game fired up ONCE, it will start in full screen every time thereafter
- Cant skip intro vids: rename, move or delete the contents of "\Dark Void\nativePC\SkyGame\Movies" folder
- Crash on falling rocks when first time picking up a weapon/at the falling boat after picking up the spare parts (both in chapter 1): this is an issue with ATI cards bc of the forced Physx driver usage afaik, locking the framerate to 30 for these two events helped me to pass them easily (you have to restart the game to take effect!)
Played the game on both XP and Win7, but I didnt run into any other problems. These looks a lot? Maybe, for some. If you find these too much to tinker with, skip this piece. Or play it on consoles. But in the end we play our games on pc, were familiar with this kind of stuff, and at least we have the opportunity to tinker around.
TL;DR:
Fun game if you dont get cold of some tinkering, and since the securom issue fixed, defo worths the €2 this thing goes down to during almost every sale. Get it if youre into jetpacks, guns, or jetpacks with guns!

As you heal people and come across chests you unlock hearts and power-ups to make Princess Remedy stronger and unlock various zones by doing so. One of the most interesting and fun parts of this game for me
is the secrets you can unlock and find along the way. A favorite game series of mine is The Legend of Zelda and finding those hidden chests and pathways always ignites a feeling of happiness from me. You cannot have the timer reach the top nor can you push the button in each level.
Going deeper into gameplay, there are several options of levels to play after finishing the first introductory one. You can choose to proceed to work on the two factors you should worry about, that change between levels based on the one you've selected, as well as your performance. First there is Tiredness, which worsens the "Stress" gained in each level, and Stress, which gradually goes higher, can make managing tasks controllable. Tiredness can have major changes by several optional levels. And then there is Integrity which is the respect you have to the state. This can be tweaked if doing tasks correctly or incorrectly. And just like Tiredness, it can be changed significanly through optional levels. As you progress through the story, you unlock more objects and tasks to use later on.
Now for my experience playing the game, it was a bit hard to control and getting to know the mouse controls at first. You can pick up objects with the left button, drop with the middle, and right-click to change hands. The game also has controller support but I don't recommend it. As for main gameplay, it was an interesting experience playing through and surviving for a small period of time. But it was also a bit stressful for me considering all the micromanagement you have to do in the later levels. But I love how the music tends to fit the mood of panic. This game's structuring reminds me of others like Five Nights at Freddy's for the element of survival.
However, the game can be buggy at times. For example, when you try shooting targets or stamping papers, sometimes it won't confirm the event or I just suck at targets that it's precise. Also sometimes thrown objects can hit the button causing me to reset. The game tries its best to make sure objects don't trigger the button that it doesn't register as a push of it when it lightly touches it, but in unfortunate situations of me playing the final level, I had a few objects get tossed and hit the button. I even had one being tossed high off the screen, and falling directly on the button :C
Anyway, aside from Tetris, this is my other favorite Russian-style game. Quite the thrill playing it. Again, sometimes stressful, but it's still a good game if you like political satire. I give Calm Down, Stalin a 7/10

To be honest, I never liked Crysis. I always looked at it as a techdemo. It was one of those games that had numerous glitches - BSODs and audio glitches were frequent and I do not remember any other games with which I was having similar issues at the time. Also, my rig surpassed the system requirements for the game so I never understood what could have caused these issues. But the various websites and forums on the internet confirmed the same.
In any case, the jungle environment was already familiar following Crytek's Far Cry. So, when the news came that the sequel to Crysis would take place in New York (now an "urban jungle"), I looked forward to seeing and playing it. The game delivered: the destroyed cityscape of Manhattan looks superb thanks to CryEngine 3. We are to navigate between the floors of destroyed buildings and combat on the city streets is common. Finally, the aliens appear in the form of regular soldiers, too - it's not just the big monsters that you need to fight like in the first part.
As for gameplay, the protagonist's nano suit has been streamlined. Strength and speed modes are now combined. We can now perform silent takedowns so following a stealthy playing mode is more rewarding. Upgrading the suit's features is a possibility based on the alien kills we perform - this is an unnecessary role playing section of the game but it does not represent any issues.
Overall, I was satisfied with the sequel. Single player campaign lasts for 12-13 hours which is quite long these days. Cutscenes are frequent and Hans Zimmer's excellent score helps us with the immersion into the world of Crysis. Too bad that starting from June multiplayer mode will be unavailable for good (following the announcement of GameSpy), so, should it be discounted, it should be purchased with only the single player experience in mind.

Game name: Slender: The Arrival
Reviewed by: Wolf
Slender: The Arrival is a superb horror game made in succession to the popular indie game Slender: The Eight Pages by Mark J. Hadley in 2012. The story follows Lauren, who is investigating a disappearance of her friend Kate, after arriving at her home late one evening to find her missing. Racing through the levels uncovering more clues via pages, the story begins to unravel and you will soon learn Kate's fate. With 8 chapters and a secret level, this game delivers a horrifyingly stunning grasp on the tale of the Slender man.
WASD - move character.
Mouse - look around.
Left click - interact with objects.
Escape - pause.
Slender: The Arrival is filled with horrifying sounds. If you've played the orginal title, you'll know when Slenderman gets near or is pursuing you, the screen becomes distorted and sharp noises peirce your ears. This can be especially jump-scare worthy in high-pressure moments, such as collecting the pages in Chapter 2, or turning on the generators in Chapter 3. Not only in addition to Slenderman, new characters are added in pursual of Lauren, meaning it's literally twice as scary! (bad pun intended)
Substantial. If you have the time, feel free to check out the screenshots I've made with this game, they're absolutely phenomenal. I do, however; wish the graphics were supported to double the resolution such as the option in games like The Vanishing of Ethan Carter have.
It is very easy to win this game. I have played multiple times through, so I've learned which paths to take and how to avoid Slenderman and others in a proficient way. Newcomers may find it more difficult, and if playing on hardcore mode, adds a little bit more of a challenge to the game. Still hoping for a mode beyond hardcore though, preferably a veteran mode of some sorts with more appearances, no lighting, and no sprinting.
Fix achievements please. Currently there's a bug with the cloud saving, where if you resetstats in console, the game does not reset scrapbook nor steps, and deletes all achievements. This causes you to not be able to obtain the 10k steps achievement or the collector achievements. Easy fix = disable cloud saving. There's literally no need for a single player game like this.
8/10
Absolutely a must have for any horror fan or veteran. This game offers a much more enticing tale and rivveting experience than the predecessor, The Eight Pages, as well as a much more stunning visual experience.

Slender: The Arrival is Parsec Productions' ramped-up successor to their definitive Slender: The Eight Pages. Pairing everyone's favorite scary meme man with some fresh gameplay and writing from the crew behind the Marble Hornets series on YouTube, The Arrival provides the Slender Man with a fresh coat of paint that, in all honesty, it may not have needed.
Instead of the somewhat-randomized page-grabbing romp through a dark and mysterious park that encapsulated the original Slender game, Slender: The Arrival offers much more of a narrative strung through several environments. From a suburban home to a construction (or logging? I'm not sure) site in the woods and an ever-beckoning radio tower, you're thrust into a quest to gather information on a child's disappearance and the Slender Man himself while avoiding him and several other menacing creatures along the way.
I'm gonna be honest: I was never entirely sure just what I was looking for or why I was supposed to care about what was going on, save for self-preservation. Despite the Marble Hornets people penning the plot, Arrival lacked a lot of the subtle hints and well-hidden clues characteristic of their YouTube work and the expanded material around it. Or, if there was such context, most of it was easy to overlook while trying to avoid whatever was chasing me on a given level. The narrative could have been much more well-established, to say the least.
It was, however, nice to stretch my legs in some new areas with Slendy riding my behind, and the last level or two before the finale did some things I thought were neat. It's also nice to know the "bonus" level, which supposedly offers a little extra backstory but mostly just lets you putz around a bit more, actually works in the PC version rather than being completely broken like the console ports.
Slender: The Arrival isn't fantastic, but it isn't completely awful, either. If anything, I'd say get it on sale.

Initially, and superficially, a very enjoyable game. Feels great to play moment-to-moment, cool characters and cosmetics. Unfortunately, it took me and a friend about 150 hours to realize the gameplay is intrinsically broken. Sure, character balance is a mess, but that's not the even the worst thing about it:
Basically, thanks to its parry system, For Honor punishes you for attacking your opponent.
If your attack is parried in For Honor, your opponent doesn't just get to negate your attack and sieze the initiative; they also get to nail you, immediately, with a *guaranteed* attack or throw.
There are also essentially zero "safe" attacks in For Honor (unless, I believe, you're one of the DLC characters). If your heavy attack is parried, there's a small chance you *could* block the new attack, if the opponent doesn't know their optimal follow-up. If your light attack is parried, there's nothing you can do.
This is an ACTION game, a FIGHTING game, where you are PUNISHED for ATTACKING. Not even recklessly; just for any attack. It's completely baffling. And, for their part, all your opponent did was perform *one* timed button press, and they're not even difficult to pull off.
Furthermore, when a duel isn't a game of chicken, it's a game of "who can exploit their character's cheese the best." You will find essentially NO fights in For Honor that look like the cool promotional material and trailers. I stopped playing a while ago, and as I understand it some balance changes have been decent, but it's a case of one step forward, one giant leap back.
In short, once you start fighting players who know how this garbage works, For Honor's combat is grueling, absurd, and just about the most anti-fun *thing* I've experienced in games this year.
More than anything, though, it's a shame. I got a lot of enjoyment out of this game before everyone figured out how to exploit the system, and there's no real reason for parries to work this way... buuut, as long as they do, I believe For Honor is intrinsically broken and not worth anyone's time or money, no matter how cheap they make it.

As a person who has played guitar for a couple of years. I personally can't really recommend this game and here is why:
1. You need to spend extra money on the USB cable. I understand that Ubisoft didn't want to deal with compatibility issues, but at least let me use my 200€ USB audio interface. If it doesn't work properly I can still buy your cable. There is however, probably not a completely legal way to make it work without the original cable and it works just fine.
2. The dynamic difficulty. The problem for me is, that you start learning a song and learn the note positions. Then when the game difficulty increases, the game adds notes and you have to switch fingers to play on the new difficulty. You often can't build on the positions you already learned.
3. There are no seperate tracks for each instrument. Maybe I want to listen just to the guitar or bass track alone, to better hear what the instrument is playing. If you had sepearate tracks you could also probably slow down the tracks and they wouldn't sound like a friggin disgrace.
4. The interface itself is a problem. You probably can't do a better job if you're using a guitar hero style interface. The problem is however that unlike guitar hero, you have 6 strings and 22/24 frets instead of five buttons. I can't really imagine that a beginner could find the right positions without looking at the fretboard.
5. Asking fo a connection to ubisoft, every time you start the game...No I don't want to make an extra account especially not for Uplay. (╯°□°）╯︵ ┻━┻)
If this game works for other people, that is great. However I find the whole concept to clunky too learn things efficiently. My advice is, if you already know the basics for playing guitar you should probably invest the money in a software like guitar pro. There are tons of files that let you learn the songs. sure they may be not 100% correct but they are free. And being able to play a song is its own reward for me.

If you spend money on just one roguelike, make it Caves of Qud.

The awesome tiles and ASCII actually serve to help you fill gaps in your imagination. Why would you need imagination for a PC game? That's what graphics are for, right?
I hear you, so hear me out. The presentation of roguelikes, Caves of Qud included, is largely a factor of a genre older than most people reading this (myself included), but it still holds a function today in that it's not nearly as limiting to the roleplaying experience as modern graphics are.

Despite being a short game, I do have a little to talk about this game. Which is surprising since it’s really short. Like less than an hour short. It’s still going to be a short review but still.
Story:
You are Princess Remedy and you must travel across Hurtland to heal the Prince who is suffering from something terrible. And along you can heal people suffering from illness, confusion, stubbed toes, questioning their identity, loneliness and death to name a few.
Gameplay:
The game is top down and you have to explore areas for people who are not well. Simply talk to one of them and you have to battle what’s bothering them. You are constantly shooting you healing tool and heal when your not being hit.  In terms of the enemies, like any good game they are simple to identify and know what to do against. At first you fight simple boulders that chase you and breadcrumb mine but soon you fight bats who randomly at high speeds and slime balls that fire a volley in short burst.
Since you only have the one attack, the only strategy is to know who can do what. One tip I can give is to explore every area you have access to before you talk to anyone as you can find chests which contain upgrades like Multi which increase the number of shots fired or Flasks which increases the number of grenades you can use per fight.
I also think I should mention the hard setting, cause it’s not just faster enemies. All of them are replaced with harder version of themselves like the breadcrumbs can charge up three shots at once and many foes that didn’t fire bullets do now. And Master(Which I didn’t do) is everything being fast.
Presentation:
The music is pretty enjoyable. Nothing that can get into your head but its some nice 8-bit tracks. I also like the simple outline graphics but that’s because I like cute stuff. I think the style they were going with was Gameboy cause it not NES and Atari graphic would be an insult to this game.
Verdict:
Although it’s so short I beat the game twice in less than two hours, I see very little, or anything wrong with it.

This little platformer is endearing from the start. Despite what the title might lead you to believe, there is a lovable cast of characters in Thomas Was Alone. Characters might be a strong word, and they are lovable only insofar as one can love a quadrilateral whose thoughts are relayed by a pleasantly voiced narration.
The game's puzzles aren't too difficult, and the platforming isn't rage-inducing. It is a pleasant game with an interesting story.
A few times I felt like the story was dragging on, though. I would feel like the game was coming to an end only to find another chapter to the story. I also found myself frustrated by the character switching mechanic on levels where the character count was high.
All-in-all, Thomas Was Alone is a great, moderately difficult puzzle-platformer

Very mediocre. There's a good game in here somewhere, but it's obscured by a few flaws:
The UI seems to show random information
The tech tree seems to hold you back more often than resource constraints do, especially with the time it takes to finish
Art that seems cutesy at a first glance and then lazy at a second
Unnecessarily complicated production lines
Space optimization without ability to move or rotate buildings after placing
There is a neat feature in that you can try to optimize the way goods are produced within buildings- except there isn't much optimization to be done, and in any case the real issue is getting goods from one place to another, which is extremely inefficient; it's usually the bottleneck in every scenario. You can help along production with upgrades, but those upgrades will require you to pull teeth for a while with the slow transport speed until you can get the infrastructure up to research it.
All in all, not worth the time. Some interesting innovations that I hope the developer will put into their next, better game.

I got 40 minutes into the never-ending "click here, click here, now click here" tutorial and I don't think I'm even halfway through with it. I gave up before it even got to the game part, assuming there is a game part.

The thing that separates Blueprint Tycoon from other resource management/business simulation games is the ability to optimize how your factories work with "blueprints".  It's an interesting concept but unfortunately, the optimizing is just not fun.  You can control what a preset number of workers do with a preset selection of tools in preset stations. I keep asking myself why I can't add another worker to this factory, or why the heck the iron ore bin is so far away from the smelter. This part of the game plays more like a puzzle game than the management sim I thought I was buying.  If you are looking to solve puzzles go for it; otherwise you are better off playing Capitalism Lab.
I really enjoy this little game.  If you like upgrade trees and resource management simulations, in a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, this is for you.

I give this VN 5 stars out of 5.
This is a good VN, recommended. It was made without any budget, and it's really nicely done. I like how the general mood progressively mutates day after day.
-Graphics: BGs, CGs, sprites: they are nice, although the CGs are very few, some are good and some bad (I didn't like the Elizabeth CG), same goes for the sprites (I liked all the Airi sprites, but I didn't like one or two sprites about Rui and Akira)
-Music: it's very good and it fits well in the scenes and characters
-Length: it's not a long VN, but I think it's balanced (there will be more episodes anyway). It's a bit slow at the beginning, and more intense at the end.
-Characters: they're interesting, to me they didn't look stereotyped. My heroines character ranking is, from favourite: Airi, Rui, Elizabeth, Misaki, Akira
PROs:
+It's a free VN
+Interesting story and mysteries that develop throughout the days
+There are puzzles that you must solve by thinking
+Interesting non-stereotyped characters, you'll end up suspecting anyone
+There will be a sequel
CONs:
-There are actually no routes for the characters, most of the choices don't seem to affect the outcome (except for the final ones of course, but some of those seem to to be a randomly "hit or miss"). But I've read somewhere that they'll add routes in the next episodes, so this CON is temporary.
-Getting a non-bad end is difficult (although I don't know if this is actually a CON), i tried many times and failing was frustrating, given the
of the bad ends.
I mostly like and play the "amateur" non-commercial VNs, I've played about 20 of them, and I put this at #3 in my list (the other two are Katawa Shoujo and Everlasting Summer). I will definately play the sequel of Lucid9.

I'm not the biggest roguelike player I know. Sure, I enjoy randomization, I enjoy permadeath (a lot!), and overall, I appreciate the types of games they are. Before I played Caves of Qud, my favourite roguelike was probably Dungeons of Dredmor. I still love it, but that's mostly for the writing, as I loved how goofy it all was.
At first, Caves of Qud didn't really grab me. I didn't play many ASCII games growing up, aside from a really great one called 'Sleuth'. I was among the many that looked at a game's graphics and judged it solely on that. My my, how times have changed.
If you can look past the simple-yet-complex visuals that you're faced with in Qud, and if you get a hang of the fairly easy controls, there is a very, VERY deep game here. One that allows you to opt-in for a character defect that will cause to you spontaneously combust, all so that you can balance that out with something better. What kind of better? Well, how about having hands so cold that you literally freeze your enemies from touching them? Or a way to see 5 moves into the future?
How about the ability to clone yourself to make your own follower? Or give yourself better night vision and hearing abilities, so enemies are easier to detect? Or what if you just wanted the mental ability to 'hate' something to death? All of these options are fairly viable in your character creation process. That's why I love this game, and I've barely scratched the surface.
Play a gunslinger with extra limbs who survives by photosynthesis. Play a water farmer who is constantly hunted by your evil twin. Play a character who has a beak. The possibilities are endless, and endlessly weird.
This game is so much damn fun.

Qud is an amazingly deep and unique world which will constantly surprise you. I've never really gotten far but each playthrough teaches me something new and gives me a better idea of just how much left there is to the game. The recent work on a mouse-driven UI opens up the game more to people who aren't fans of roguelikes or simply don't want to learn yet another control scheme; I'm in the latter group.

The store trailer for this game is
misleading.  The video shows some amazing moving bridges that you'll almost certainly never be able to build, unless you dedicate hundreds of hours to mastering some incredibly fiddly physics.  My biggest complaint is that getting the joints for moving bridges to actually line up seems to be impossible.  This game gives you a lot of tools to make bridges, but it fails to give you all the tools you need to learn to be successful.  There's a short tutorial and mini-guide in game that give hints for success, but actually learning to implement them is unbearably difficult.  Next biggest issue is that most of the time I don't even understand why my bridges fail, which makes it incredibly difficult to learn from mistakes.  Often you can move a joint by the tiniest bit and a successful bridge will turn into a crumbling mess of wood and steel.  The physics just don't make sense!  Occasionally I even notice that the physics engine results in inconsistent results, which is downright unacceptable for a physics-based puzzle game.
Many of the campaign levels seem to have a specific design in mind, but I can't for the life of me envision what the developers were thinking for the ideal bridge.  Rather than allowing for a slew of creativity, the levels seem to force you into a very specific design, which transforms the game from creative sandbox to a figure-out-what-was-intended-here mess.  There's also a lot of really poor level designs here which primarily involve limiting the resources you can use or the points on the ground where you can anchor your bridge.  There's no reason for forcing you to build half a bridge and hope the car is moving fast enough to crash into the finish flag at the end.
I expected a bridge-building game that used sound (or at least repeatable) engineering principles, increasing the difficulty in each level by setting budgets and locations of increasing difficulty while still allowing the player to come up with functional and creative bridges.  Instead, Poly Bridge gives players nearly impossible obstacles to overcome through unrealistic budgets, random material restrictions, and absurd bridge anchor points.  If you want an enjoyable bridge-building experience, look somewhere else.

Well, this was rather an adorable little surprise with the potential for a real game with both charm and challenge for the price of nothing—only the amount of smiles it’ll bring to you. As an avid fan of Ittle Dew, this was a lovely return to the childlike simplicity and challenge from Ludosity.
As someone who grew up in the N64/GameCube era of videogames, it’s rare for a game that harkens back to NES era graphical fidelity and gameplay simplicity to captivate me with so much nostalgia. Immediately as the game launches, the main theme puts you under its spell much like launching StarTropics with the feeling of wanting to go explore the world. What follows is a harmless adventure as you rid the land of its ills by blasting away all the suffering across the land with the healing magic of Princess Remedy. The kind of magic that involves shooting lasers, explosive flasks and dodging projectiles while your cure the ironic symptoms out of your patients.
The gameplay is sort of a mix-up of various classic NES games; it’s a 2D shooter/bullet-hell adventure that uses the original Star Fox controls for combat of movement guiding your automated attacks with Dr. Mario’s enemy designs in battle sequences and a simplified Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest/Star Tropics overworld to explore. Each encounter feels tailored to the situation plaguing the patient with a scaling level of challenge that gets only more complicated the higher you go on the difficulty scale to Master. Eventually, it ends in a gauntlet of a final boss with multiple forms that requires you to be at your very best to beat the game. (And then you can choose who to marry from anyone you’ve met throughout the entire game to be your king/queen.)
Like its roots, Princess Remedy is a rather short game that has NES-Level Difficulty if you raise the challenge up to Master Rating as a Normal run will probably last you over three-quarters of an hour of a quality time. Whether you crave something entertainingly simple, challenging or charming, there’s something for everyone to enjoy within this offering to interest you in buying the prequel.
As a free game any issues I have with the gameplay itself is something I feel is mitigated by how short and to the point is Princess Remedy, and I figured any complaints I would have would better be used in the prequel as that costs money to purchase as well as being a more full experience.
However, there are a few technical/gameplay issues that are the result of Game Maker. For starters, the game has a weird one-button limitation with various buttons to choose that can bring up the menu when you want to run or interact with someone as everything is mapped to one button. The game also has a weird technical issue where if you launch it not in safe-mode the game takes a lot longer to close as it doesn’t appear on the task manager, so you should try relaunching the game in safe-launch until it shows your Steam profile is not in a game. The screenshots are also bewilderingly screwed up to ruin any memento snapshots you’d want to savor for later, which is fine as the Print Screen Button + Paste still works with nothing lost. All of these issues are addressed in the sequel, so I feel it’s fine to mention them here in case they dissuade others from purchasing these gems.
Like the potions from Ittle Dew’s companion, there’s something magically addicting about Princess Remedy from its concoction of simplicity, goodwill and its kick that will have you hankering for more. And unlike reality, there are no hangovers from having too much of a good thing.
Once it’s over and the magic vanishes from the realization that it’s at the end you’ll be discarded for someone else to supply his endless desire for more. Sadly, it’s the natural order and no one can sate Tip—I mean, Princess Remedy the game forever.

The 1960's were a strange time, atomic paranoia fueled the cold war as the space race allowed mankind to make monumental leaps forward technologically. Global espionage was the tool with which the cold war was fought as agents from both of the world's super powers battled for information and technology. Amidst all of this, counter culture exploded and use of psychedelics became a new past time. Jazzpunk uses this period of time as an aesthetic springboard for it's comedic hijinx and in doing so plays out like an episode of Saturday Night Live with an overarching theme to it's skits.

It would probably be most appropriate to categorize Jazzpunk as an adventure game, as players are placed in the role of Polyblank, a secret agent who is dispatched from an abandoned subway station on various missions by a character known as The Director and each one of these misadventures is kicked off by swallowing a pill. The narrative is flimsy, and each mission plays out almost like a skit. An antagonist is introduced in the later missions and helps provide some closure to the game's events. Jazzpunk focuses more on humor than plot and it makes this the kind of experience that you turn on, tune in and drop out of. It assaults players with non sequiturs and irreverent easter eggs. Players can expect to stumble across a frogger style mini game, wander around in an Evil Dead inspired setting made out of pizza, play mini golf with a James Bond style villain and beat up a passenger car Street Fighter II style. It's a tribute to all things nerdy with plenty of tech based humor and refrences to other games. The Adult Swim style humor, a style that makes it seem like being in an altered state of consciousness is a prerequisite to enjoy, is likely to put off many.

Also potentially off putting is just how easy the puzzles are in Jazzpunk. Most players will find themselves progressing unopposed since most levels are as simple as following the instructions laid out in the objectives screen. There are a handful of side quests but they have no bearing on the proceedings and generally exist to provoke a few laughs. Some of the diversions like Wedding Quake, a wedding themed spoof of the classic arena shooter may hold players attention for a decent amount of time but the whole of Jazzpunk lasts a few hours at most and offers little replayability. Think of Jazzpunk as more of an alternative to watching a comedy film than a game poised to occupy a dozen hours of your life. It could be argued that Jazzpunk is most rewarding when you are avoiding the critical path since interacting with random objects and poking your nose around generally uncovers the best easter eggs and gags.

The aesthetics of Jazzpunk leave a favorable impression. Seemingly modeled after Thirty Flights of Loving, it employs blocky characters with simple animations and cell shaded styling. The funky soundtrack adds to the unique flavor of the game making it feel like nothing else as well as helping sell the off beat humor. The aestetics, soundtrack and gameplay click together like legos, delivering a unique experience that in spite of the fact that it borrows liberally from other works.
Jazzpunk is kind of a nightmare game for reviewers... To describe it in terms of the quality of it's gameplay, visuals and the amount of time players can wring out of it simply misses the point of the game. Potential Jazzpunk players should think of it instead as an interactive comedy experiment. An off beat experiment. While it may not stand out as a great game it is a little experimental indie gem that may have an impact on the humor and style of other titles. Turn on, tune in and drop out.
Update: The director's cut only makes this game more worthwhile. Give it a shot.
