This is one of those rare games that will stick with you long after your done playing it for many reasons. It is minimalist in its art and fairly simple in its gameplay and yet that never seems like a detriment, quite the opposite actually. It goes to the very heart of what we (or at least I) appreciate in games. More and more there has been a general trend towards mounds of money going to advanced graphics engine to achieve 'hyper-realism', innovation for the sake of innovation, and multiplatform monoliths that must cram as much game modes and as possible to give the illusion of getting your money's worth. Thomas was Alone proves that none of that nonsense is needed to make a truly great game. There is elegance in its art and environments as we get a fantastic platformer with an engaging story. Through excellent narration by Danny Wallace (Shaun Hastings in AC series) they somehow add human elements to boxes. Humor, love, sadness, self-consciousness, heroism. It acheived the impossible and made  me invested in characters as basic as a little red rectangle. The ambient music is fantastic, among the best of any platformer or indie game.
Thomas is Alone is sublime, got all the heart in the world, and has more personality than most games we see these days. It should be held up as an example of not only what a game should be but how a game can transcend itself and become art. 10/10

TLDR: Currently at 30$ For Honor is a great purchase and worth sticking around if you enjoy deep fighting games, or perhaps played a lot of Dark Souls PVP. With continued support theres always hope everything can be ironed out. However at 60$ I WOULD NOT recommend this game at all, as the story mode is an absolute waste of time unless it's in Co-op with a friend.
I want to start with the good about this game. The combat is deep and fulfilling, the game looks fantastic, sound design is great, and with regular updates this game has the potential to really bring itself back into the limelight. As someone who tends to prefer complex multiplayer games you can spend hours on to get better I was naturally drawn to For Honor from the moment I saw the combat system. The defence system is very unique, and every character has defnined strengths and weaknesses. I seriously enjoyed moments in 2v2s where I finished off my opponent early and got to watch my teammate fight his opponent to the death (that is if you have honor!). It reminded me heavily of "fight clubs" in Dark Souls 3 and the feeling of being a spectator until you are next up. Stand up, pick up your weapon, and fight the foe who has just killed your friend! He is counting on you to win the round and redeem his honor! I live for moments like that and It's something very special about this game. It was like an unspoken rule that people just followed, well or not if thats your thing which just comes with the territory. You could just gang up on the last opponent if you want to and thats understandable, even if it does feel underhanded/cowardly. Thats the only thing that kept me playing this game for as long as I did and should have been the focal point in it's development.
Now onto the bad, and unfortunatley theres a lot. With no dedicated servers (however this may soon change) the beauty of the combat system can't fully shine if the process of experiencing it is so unreliable. In game purchases are rampant, and some would argue necessary in order to quickly gear up your character and be on equal footing with those who are already fully geared. With more game modes as well as options to configure what you want to play (no environmental hazards would be greatly appreciated) as well as dedicated servers at launch this game would have been an absolute slam dunk. The main draw of the game was the combat system in my eyes, why not double down on that and just focus on the multiplayer aspect?
The story mode is absolutely awful and incredibly linear as well as down right boring. Killing waves of piddly little enemies that die in a single hit until you get to the predictable CPU that is usually just another playable character in the game. It's like a watered down, linear Dynasty Warriors and I personally felt like I had seen everything after the first few missions. The collectables feel like such an after thought and are only there to feel like there is more to do than what I mentioned earlier, basically just fluff. I never felt invested in any of the main characters, although I did enjoy seeing their interactions with other main characters when playing through the different faction's story lines. Co-op is the only way to play story mode if you want to experience it as at least it feels like you are accomplishing super strait forward tasks with a friend, but doesn't distract from the overall half baked feel of the story mode regardless. The story mode is this games ball and chain, resourses would have been much better spent elsewhere.
Hope this helps!

Lucid9 is an underrated original English visual novel (OEVN) which appeals brilliantly to both new and seasoned visual novel players. Its characters, story and music are all top notch, and for the very low price of £0.00 you should really give it a go.
This review will not contain spoilers - as a result, some truths may be slightly bent to inform you without giving too much away.
TL;DR:
Story: 10/10
Characters: 9/10
Visuals: 9/10
Music & Sound: 10/10
Verdict: It's free and only 15 hours long, go play it already!
In Lucid9 you play Yama, a high school student enrolled in a private Japanese academy for wealthy kids. At the beginning of the new school year, students start to go missing. Meanwhile a freelance detective approaches you in the hope of solving what the police cannot - how and why these disappearances are taking place.
The game is around 15 hours long, and mainly focuses on the mystery at hand while also fleshing out each character (especially Yama and his past). The story is executed very well, building suspense while keeping the identity of the perpetrator hidden until the very end, but there are definitely enough clues to figure it out yourself if you pay attention. Yama's shaky past and his psycholigical problems that arise from it make the story much more interesting later on. There is also a fair amount of time spent on the daily life of Yama and his friends, but no scene is superflous - they all help build the character of the main cast and their relationship to Yama and each other.
There is one good ending, with many bad endings depending on your choices in the final stages of the game. Although you can gain favour with four characters, Lucid9 isn't a dating sim - Rui is always the 'main girl' of the story and the other characters acknowledge this very early on. This helps focus the spotlight on her, which I think works in the game's favour. The deduction sequences are also fun and don't feel forced at all. Overall the story and how it was presented was fantastic.
Despite there being loads of characters to cram into a very short story, Lucid9 pulls it off perfectly. Firstly, Yama's character is not that of a generic protagonist - he can be lazy and harsh but this makes his character much more interesting. His development is timed well and progresses steadily throughout. His psychological problems and his past are relevant and didn't feel like a gimmick to liven up the story. The other four non-romance characters - Masato, Yukari, Ryouta and Shigure - are also developed, albeit much less. I found Yukari's development to be one of the most interesting in any story, and each character definitely has their own unique charm and story (even if they can sometimes be a bit annoying).
The four girls are also very unique, and you will definitely be enjoying the scenes with at least one of them. I especially liked the developing relationships with Airi and Elizabeth - they felt natural and well written. Akira's scenes are full of energy, Misaki's are sensible and relaxing, Lizzie's are sharp-witted and funny, and Airi's are very calming. Each character's theme was also very well crafted. Finally, Rui's character didn't have that much development and was pretty generic, but she did not bring the rest down at all. I personally found Rui and Misaki to have the weakest characterisation and development - hopefully this is remedied in the upcoming sequel, which should have separate routes per character.
Side note: As someone who has participated in several student drama groups before, I was very happy to see how accurate they made the drama club at the academy! I really got into the two scenes set there and Akira, while slightly over the top, was someone whose escapism I could somewhat relate to.
The visuals in this game are amazing. There was clearly a lot of effort put into the character sprites, backgrounds and CGs. The style is distinct, but not enough to  be jarring. The happy scenes were bright and cheerful and the violent scenes were gory in all their glory. There was a perfect mix of light and heavy - they definitely didn't keep it PG when it came to the violence. However, I felt that in a few CGs the faces were strangely proportioned and some backgrounds seemed to be intentionally blurred.
Note also that there is no sexual content, although due to the graphic nature of some scenes and some disturbing scenes and themes I would recommend not giving this game to someone under 12 years old (also, the deduction sequences would go right over their head).
The music in this game is absolutely exceptional. The generic happy/sad/emotional/mystery themes were great, but what really stood out for me was the character themes. Each character's theme is perfectly suited from them, from Airi's music box and Elizabeth's piano to Shigure's mysterious theme with sirens in the background and Akira's upbeat and energetic melody. The other two outstanding tracks were the title theme, and one other theme called 'Depths' that plays during certain scenes. Depths in particular is a real emotion inducer in context, and it works amazingly.
Lucid9 has no voice acting, although an English voice pack is in the works. Also, the soundtrack can be downloaded for free from Steam (it will appear as a .zip in the game directory).

As Lucid9 is a visual novel, any old potato can run it. You should have no problems no matter what you're running it on. I myself played it on a laptop with integrated graphics and it was perfectly smooth.
If you're still reading, then scroll to the stop of this page and download the game already! It's free, short and has so much effort and love put into it. Also look out for the sequel and voice pack!

For many, the graphical powerhouse Crysis is more notorious for its tendency to bring even cutting edge PCs to their knees, than for its gameplay. While it offered tons of eye candy for those that could run it, the fact remained that most were forced to watch from the sidelines as it was simply impossible to play on anything but the best hardware. But all that changes with Crysis 2, a ruthlessly optimized machine that finally lets all those wondering about the series a chance to see what it’s all about. Unfortunately, it never lives up to its reputation in any way than being a pretty face, and once you look past the visuals quickly evaporates into a game I couldn’t wait to leave.
Everything in Crysis 2 revolves around the Nanosuit, a secret military project which grants the user superhuman powers and provides both tactical and medical support. Armor, invisibility, super strength, and Nanovision (a combination of solar and night vision) round out the list of your abilities, and for the most part you are given free range over how you use them on the battlefield.
This is what sets Crysis apart from other shooters. While still linear in progression, there is a lot more freedom in how you tackle situations than you are typically allowed in a modern FPS. Maybe you’ll choose to go in guns blazing, armor at its max as bullets ricochet off like water drops, or perhaps opt for a stealthier solution and sneak through the water ducks behind enemy lines. Experimentation is encouraged by way of a helpful visor reminiscent of Metroid Prime, which highlights enemies, weapons, and different points to begin your assault. When everything is working right Crysis 2 can be an incredibly rewarding and exhilarating experience where each fight becomes its own puzzle for you to unravel. The real problem though is that these moments are few and far between.
One of the main reasons for this is every feature of the suit is tied into an energy gauge. When you use one, the meter depletes leaving you completely exposed and unable to cloak or use armor. While clearly designed to keep the game from becoming too easy, it also does a fantastic job of taking away from the feeling of being a super soldier developer
tries so hard to create. Getting stuck in a firefight without the suit’s abilities is a common occurrence that almost always results in a near instant death, and even passive abilities such as meleeing enemies and sprinting are tied into the bar, which leaves you essentially helpless once it runs out. Using the energy bar to regulate abilities isn’t a bad idea in theory, but the execution is constantly working against the player to create a frustrating experience constantly stifling its own potential.
The other big issue are the enormous amount of bugs, most of which revolve around the comically bad enemy AI. Cloaking highlights this most, as enemies are entirely oblivious to you when you are cloaked, going so far as to ignore you taking out their comrades mere inches away (I can only assume they are used to seeing their partners suddenly fall to the ground for impromptu naps). Fall into an enemy’s line of sight however and all of a sudden every living being knows where you are. Cloaking then acts as something of an on/off switch for enemy fire which comes grinding to a halt the second you cloke, a useful if entirely unrealistic way to exit a firefight that is equally unsatisfying.
Finally you have the moments when the enemy AI simply breaks, getting stuck on geometry, running in endless circles, and all around being complete fools that are almost more fun to watch than to shoot, because truth be told shooting them just isn’t very fun. When everyone acts like a broken robot it’s hard to feel as if you’ve accomplished anything when you outsmart them, and for as intelligent as Crysis 2’s mechanics may be, every enemy you come up against seems to have drawn the short straw for brains.
The narrative also left me wanting, hitting every cliche in the book and topping things off with some of the most abysmal writing and voice acting I’ve had to endure in a very long time. The interesting premise and opening scene where you, a soldier on his deathbed, are given the nanosuit and along with it the memories of its previous owner, is quickly swept aside in an endless stream of betrayals, convoluted twists, and an inability to ever explain what is really going on. I lost count of the number of times you lose consciousness, only to awake with your allies once again swapped and your motives changed. The writing is overly simplistic and juvenile, turning a lackluster plot into a cringe worthy affair. Rounding out the package is the flat voice acting that never could hit the right emotional tone nor bring any life to the script, but I suppose you can only do so much when given so little.
But if there is one thing everyone is wanting and expecting from Crysis 2 it’s another benchmark graphical showcase, and in that regard it does not disappoint. The level of detail in each scene is astounding, with the lighting effects in particular standing even higher above the rest. Seeing the sun breaking through the dilapidated buildings of New York is awe inspiring, and although I won’t spoil them, the later half of the game is filled with some of the most impressive set pieces I have ever seen. Few games can match the visuals found in Crysis 2 even years after its release, and the amount of optimization wizardry done to ensure it runs well even on lower end machines is nothing short of impressive. Sound design is equally well done, with deafening explosions and gunfire which threaten to blow your subs and does more than anything else to provide a much needed wow-factor to the proceedings. The great score grabbed me right from the opening menu, setting the tone for the game and adding to the overall epic feel of the game.
Undeniably beautiful, Crysis 2 has a lot of good ideas but does a poor job bringing them together. The bevy of bugs and glitches, most notably the terrible enemy AI, took almost all possible enjoyment out of firefights, and the few instances where the game actually worked as intended only further displayed just how much wasted potential was left on the table. What we are left with is a below average shooter wrapped in an extremely pretty package, but one that can’t hide the dull and lifeless game underneath. It’s hard to dislike something that throws so much eye candy at you, but in this case beauty is only skin deep.
: If you are curious why my gametime is so low, it's for the fact I originally played Crysis 2 on the Xbox 360. However my time with the PC version has confirmed that it is very much the same game, aside from the obvious graphical upgrade. I will start this review by stating that I am not a die-hard "Roguelike" player. I haven't played any of the classics except for Tales of Maj'eyal and wouldnt consider myself particularly knoweldgeable about the genre history and so on. With that said I consider Caves of Qud to be one of the, if not, the best game I have purchased and played in 2016.
The first time I heard about this game was on a forum where it was described as retrofuturistic and inspired by post-post apocalyptic fiction. I was intrigued by talk of sentient plants and also a procedurally generated game with more of a focus on a narrative. My expectations were not only met, but were blown away when I finally decided to play the game.
Caves of Qud is hard to describe. Its often comically stupid, full of crazy situations and at the same time solumn and steeped with a history that is intruging and suprisingly deep. Its a world where not much is explained because to explain it would be convoluted, why does a machingun turret worship a god or why are there mutant hyena people living in something called the rust wells? It is a testament to the vision and world the developers have created that something as absurd as a techno-cyborg-bear can not only exist , but actually feels coherant within the setting.
The asthetic choices made in the game also really resonated with me and the ascii / pixel art is superb and full of character, helped by an excellent choice of colour pallet. There are also stylistic flourishes that one wouldn't expect in a game with such simple graphics such as floating text highlighting things happening around you and clever ways of giving items in your inventory more character, despite the text based nature (one that comes to mind is discovering a jewel encrusted item with all the characters in its name coloured differently to represent gems). I would say the sound is quite bare-bones at the moment, but the music and sound effects that are present are good, the music in particular is very evocative and used to excellent effect at special locations (specifically the 6th Day Stilt).
As a game to play CoQ is full of variety, it has a really robust character building system. Essentially you pick between a mutant or a pure-blooded "True-kin". The mutants get to pick between 20 or so "powers" which could be something like shooting flames from your hands or a physical abberation like having two heads. The true-kin can subdue robots and have slightly better base attributes. Mutants pick a background such as marauder or nomad and then True-kin pick which Arcology they hail from. These serve to augment your stats and give different equipment to begin. Both then pick from many skill trees thoughout the game as they level up. Each game you start in the same village, Joppa, and begin the quest anew. You will die and die often, each time you reincarnate to do it again. The world is static, but aside from some plot critical locations each area is randomly generated each time. Each game is familiar, but always different, every character I have created has been memorable in his own way.
The game can feel punishingly hard and unforgiving. Deaths can feel cheap and unfair. Sometimes they are, but it is still in early access.  There are some character builds that work incredibly well, some feel like you are just hindering yourself. Some stats feel useless (willpower) and others too strong (Agility). I personally like the unbalanced aspects, but I can imagine somepeople being upset over the death of a long lived character. I have never made it to the end of the game, in fact I have no idea if there is an end as yet. I can't get enough of it regardless. The developers are very communicative and updates happen frequently. I wouldn't have been dissapointed if I had bought this product as a fully released title, its that good. I have no doubt this game will go from stregnth to stregnth as its development continues. I cannot reccommend it enough.

Form the miljeu of the game I have only to say that its a medievalish society set aeons after an end of the advanced civilizations. Were bronze sword wielding barbarians are gunned down by rustcovered walking missile platforms and floating indestructible laser pyramids. Most of the inhabitants of qud care or know of the ancient world as much as you care or know about the history of pre summerian tribes. The world has moved on.
Apart of the world map obiviously showing the ruins of an overgrown city on a coast of a long since tried sea, the postapocalyptic elemenst of this world are often unobivious. The remains of old world lurk in the details as an almost sinster force. The call of adventure is carried on ever transmitting signal captured by an weird inventor in the marshlands. The chaotic disase ridden dungeon is filled with coveyor belts, burners and haywire waste mangement robots.  The ice dungeon an cryogenic medical facilty. Magical talking stones hyper advanced computers.  The ancient fortresses remains of once urban constructions, the greates of kings lives in a tower that elevates to the very orbit.
Soon after the tables turn, instead of what you can recognise under all the ther salt, rust and slime it's the unrecogizable that turns eerie. Out on the saltbeds church has been build on gigantic skeleton of what excatly? One of the oldest factions on Qud are conglomerate of sentient plants? Who were the Eaters of the Earth? Why most of the books read as weird streams of consioucness? Nightmarish space demons and chrome angels or degenerate bioweapons and malfuctioning robots? Holy artifact or ray gun?
What occured naturaly and what was once made?
Next to Nethack and IVAN this is the roguelike I have played most and to other games in the genere and especialy compared to the Nethack this is much more pleasant to play.
First of all: there is option to disable premadeath as well as an option to enable free saving and loading of the game!
Menus operate as you would expect from a proper computer RPG and while they are sometimes when you need to use letters to pick items you want, for most of the time every thing can be handled with numpad, space and enter.
As writing of this mouse based interface is being implemented and is already working for the game it self, but not yet for all menu screens.  Personaly I prefer the keyboard controls, here is why:
The controls are nothing like the usual RL "command for every leter on the keyboard both lower and upper case".
There is one contex sensitive action key (defaults to space) that automaticly does what ever is most appropriate to do to the cell you stand in or the ones nearby, from talking to opening/closing doors and picking up items or filling your water skin. Spesific keys for all those actions do exists for the rare cases that the contex sensitive action gets confused, but I for example have no clue what the spesific key to start a conversation is and I doubt that I never need to learn that.
Another quality of life feature is automatic exploration to quickly map out screens. Related to that is the fact when pressing + or - to go up or down stairs the character atuomaticly heads to closest seen stairs, while this doesn't work if the stairs are not on the same screen it still makes returning form your deep earth spelunking trough already cleared out cave levels much faster.
Moving on from controls to gameplay itself, the CoQ has a shortage of Nethacks trademark "Yet Another Stupid Deaths".
The command look will always tell you how dangerous the creature you are looking at is compared to you and wether or not is aggressive. You can also always see what said creature is equipped with. Even though you might not know what item you are excatly looking at, in a world where "Unknow artifacts" wielded by hostile mutants are at best grenades and rocket launchers at worst, you know to be cautious.
Corpses do not rot and very few have any effects other than their varying nutritional value.
Like wise there are no 'cursed' items even when items have negative efffects they are told on the items description.
Fidling with an unknow artifact with an character who has a low inteligence will at worst break the said item, meaning that you have to pay for tinker to get it repaired and identified.
There are diseases and infections you can catch and neither are trivial to get rid off. The cures are randomly genereated per character and may cause you some trouble. Though you never know, you may actualy be better off with your new spreading mushroom symbiote infection pals than you were alone.
There are two ways to gain followers one reguires a spesific mental beguiling mutation and other an ability to proselytize, both also need a character with a high ego score. Both methods are limited to one follower so two at max (barring some strange later game occurences like clones). So team based rpg this is not.
Combat is straight forward and rather simple.
Use melee, abilities, fire arms, mutations, throwing weapons and sprint away if your opponent hits harder than you. Effects like stun, bleed and dismemberment of limbs are spesific skills and often limited to certain types of weapons (short blades, long blades, axes and cudgels). Weapons differ with their armor piercing and damage roll numbers, bonus changes to said bleed and dismemberment chances and rarely with extra damage as burning, freezing or electrocuting.
So fancy damage simulations and injury systems this game doesn't have either.
Unusualy for RLs Caves of Qud models temperatures much better than you would even notice at first glance. Any ongoing fires rise the ambient temperature and spamming pyrokinesis and or spraying all over with flamethrower you will son find out that everything in game has an iginition temperature and in worst case scenario an accidently ignited pond of asphalt will skyrocket the ambient temperature causing everything on screen to burst in flames. Hot steam from boiling water has to be one of the most humilating ways to die in this game.
Having a go playing with a mutant build with both cryokinesis and pyrokinesis mutations allows you to get most out of this simulation.
Typical for roguelike games, there is much to do in game and trying out different character builds and mutations will keep you interested for a long time.
That said the game is still a work in progress. Main quest isn't finished yet and side quests are rather few.
The updates have been weekly ever since from the steam release. If you are interested at it's very much good to buy in it's current state with no gratingly missing features or bugs.

TL;DR - This game is absolutely fantastic.  Great sci-fi story, twisted with some mythology, built through found journals and cut-screens at the beginning of each level; excellent weapon selection and upgrade system;  very smooth gameplay (with a few scattered, mildly annoying Quicktime events.)  All-around excellent game and well worth the asking price, though the summer sale is a nice bonus, which makes it a total no-brainer.  DEFINITELY BUY IT!!!
------------------------------
Anyway, I'm not sure why so many negative reviews (at the time of writing, only 41% of 327 reviews are positive) but I feel this game is criminally underrated here.  It current holds a 57 at Metacritic and 60.8% at GameRankings (I did not check the ratings of the console versions), which I still feel are too low.  Perhaps I'm just really easy to please but this is one of the best games I've played in the past year or so.  I will not try to make the grandiose claim that it's one of the best games ever or anything like that but I will say that it is certainly one of my favorites.
Some people may be turned off by the presence of Quicktime events but, honestly, they are few and far between.  There are some brilliant cover mechanics, and the more standard run-n-gun shooter gameplay is supplemented by armed jetpack combat.  There isn't a large variety of enemies but varied environments coupled with a nice weapon selection/upgrades and very fun cover and flight mechanics ensure that the gameplay never gets stale.  There is some amount of replay value to find all of the journals and collect hidden "tech point" caches for weapon upgrades.
If you're interested in more detail of what people like or dislike about the game, there are plenty of reviews here that have already covered it all - no need for me to rehash what others have said (likely far more eloquently than myself as well.)  If you get nothing else from my review, however, the takeaway should be that Dark Void deserves much more attention and praise than it has received.  I believe it's an excellent $10 game.  Even better if you can grab it at 80% off during the summer sale.  Believe me, you could do a lot worse with $2 on Steam.

I stumbled onto this through a Humble Bundle, and as I had read great things about it - I had to try it.
The games is a puzzle platformer done in a very minimalistic style and is about the red rectangle, Thomas. What immediately stands out is the narration of the game (done brilliantly by Danny Wallace) - this is the one key element that I found the most important and enjoyable. Although the score by David Housden is fantastic as well and sets a great mood for the game.
The story is told solely through the narration and a few lines of text between each chapter and is fairly simple, but quite enjoyable. What works so well for this game is that it manages to give these simple rectangular shapes a personality and a role in the story, that makes them very likeable - and even relatable.
Each map has a puzzle sort of layout where you have to use each "character's" unique ability or skill (e.g. high jump, float on water, etc.) and the puzzles increase in difficulty the further you get (more spikes, bigger gaps over boiling water(?), etc.). Ultimately, the puzzles are not that difficult even if you do not normally play the games, so it's not a game to pick up for a serious challenge and it's not a long game either (took me 6 hours to get all achivements and I didn't rush anything).
That said, it's often on sale and even for its normal €8 price, it's an enjoyable game with a compelling story and fantastic narration.
And as a bonus you now get the Benjamin's Flight DLC for free with the game, that adds to extra chapters about the adventurous Benjamin. The principles of the puzzles are more or less the same, but it adds a short story and some new abilities to the new characters.

Played the beta. Came back on the free weekend. Finished the campaign on Realistic and got all the collectibles on it. The campaign was enjoyable but has okay voice-acting and character development at best. What interested me most about the campaign was the plot of the conflict between the three factions, but that was really it. Kept me going though. Being a new player and beating the final boss on the hardest difficulty was satsifying.
The connection quality really isn't bad at all, given you don't live in a bungalow. I've only had one instance where the connection failed after a ton of multiplayer matches. However, the queue times are longer than I would like but it's not too much of an issue. The game can also be really buggy at times, for example I joined a game where the screen was stuck on some sort of stretched texture and everybody on the server was just frozen on that screen while blue team was racking in points.
It also appears that Domination PvP has the most activity. Kind of sucks because the other game modes are cool too, and if you don't like being insta-killed by a rep 20 1 million gear score Shinobi you could queue into PvE or a gamemode without the gear. But, either nobody's playing it or only a handful of people are playing it, because for all the times I tried to queue up into PvE Domination or Elimination in general I haven't found a game for the long time I waited.
A big problem for me is the balance and the ganking of the game. How do you expect to have fun when there's a whole team of Samurais spamming unblockables and uninterruptibles on you, a single guy standing on the point? In most situations they were all decked out with legendary gear or whatever, which brings me to conclude that the gear thing should have an option to be disabled or even removed and replaced for just cosmetic reasons.
Overall, it's a fun game for a time. The extremely interesting combat system is what attracted me. I understand the learning curve, but constant ganks that I'm not pro enough to constantly dodge and block to gain revenge can get annoying. And getting one, two, three shotted from a geared out guy feels like I'm getting cheesed. It's very dissapointing for the game to still feel the exact same from the beta. Hopefully this will turn out like Rainbow Six Siege and come back to glory, but for now I can't reccomend this game because of the stage it's currently in.
Honestly, just buy the game if you like it. Just keep in mind with what you have to work with. I'm tempted to buy it because I like the fluidity and the fighting game style it has going on, but I'm very hesitant at the moment so I'll wait for news of future updates or improvements to invest my time and money in good potential.

It's not bad. It's good fast paced multiplayer of the Counter-Strike style, but it's elevated by a few unique systems, like the destruction physics.
Character models are quite bad, but that's a minor nitpick. Depending on the edition you buy you may also get subjected to a massive increase in grind, which is kind of dodgy.

What can I say? After playing this game for nearly 1000 hours in barely a year, I can affirm with certainty that this is THE best competitive FPS shooter there is. The game has its flaws (it's a Ubisoft title after all), some of which were addressed and solved in previous patches, and some of which are being neglected/not looked into enough. Siege has improved quite a lot since it's release in december 2015 and looks like it's gonna keep on getting better and better. The fact that you don't have to pay real money to buy operators is great (ehrm ehrm, EA), you can buy in game credits to buy them, but you can also farm enough money to buy a new operator (25K credits) in just a couple of days. I still wish there was some kind of campaign, and that they improved on the PVE part of the game, which is basically the same as it was when the game first came out. PVP can be frustrating, both in casual and ranked, especially if you consider the fact that the community (especially in EU servers) can be very toxic and mean. R6S needs a better reporting system, right now you can only report someone for "Suspicious behaviour" which means nothing. We need to say why we are reporting someone, whether it's cheating, poor teamwork, griefing or toxicity, the community definitely needs a "flush".
With that said, the game is fun and rewarding. No two games are ever going to be the same. The game kinda forces you to be creative and find your own way to win. There are no rules (kinda), you can play however you want.

First of all this is kind of a pointless to review such a game which is critically acclaimed by everyone (literally) and secondly, I have completed the game pretty late - considering the time of release of the game.
But these being said, I feel that I should put my thoughts for this awe-inspiring game at least once.
So, I have broken down my thought or review(so to speak) in sections -
Story: The plot is very thick - though it may not have the emotional content that we can find in the popular CoD series of games. But still the plot compels  the player to stick to the game and hear out the different chatters between the NPCs. The link up with the 1st installment of this series is very smooth and "now it all make sense". Still I would have loved to have at-least a couple of side missions / sub-plots in the game (specially when these days when FPS leverage some of the RPG elements).
Gameplay: Very smooth indeed; the keyboard configuration is very nice and also be dragged to the multiplayer games without changing much -  in fact I played the multiplayer with default keyboard and mouse config. The movements are very nice and the transitions between nano suit modes are seamless. You could just put on some strength just before shooting your sniper rifle and then just after the shot switch to cloak without any difficulty. Cut Scenes are very nicely played and well placed
Graphics : well when you are talking about a game that uses Cry Engine 3 "Graphics" is the most spectacular feature that you wish to review. in words - STUNNING!! I have made a few in game snaps that I wish to keep forever. the horizon and the urban landscapes are too good and the NY city is realistically portrayed here. I've spent a lot of my time redesigning bridges to go for a high score (tweaking them until I make them simpler and simpler), and I'm only like 20 levels in out of 100+, and that doesn't even count the community made stuff!
Anyway, if you really love the android bride builders or flash games, this is totally worth the price.

A recent college graduate, Barry B. Benson wants more out of life than the inevitable career that awaits him and every other worker in New Hive City--a job at Honex making honey. Barry jumps at the chance to venture out of the hive, and soon encounters a world beyond his wildest dreams. When Barry inadvertently meets a quirky florist named Vanessa, he breaks one of the cardinal rules of beedom--he talks to her. A friendship soon develops, and Barry gets a guided crash course in the ways of the human race. When he shockingly discovers that anyone can purchase honey right off the grocery store shelf, he realizes that his true calling is to stop this injustice and set the world right by suing the human race for stealing the bees' precious honey.

Thomas Was Alone Review
If you at least have a passing interest in indie games, chances are that you have at least heard of Thomas Was Alone, maybe have already played it.  If you've ever come across any topics of the "are games art" subject, chances are Thomas Was Alone was mentioned.
The main draw here is the polished presentation and music contrasted with the simple graphics and mostly simple gameplay.  The music is modern "feel-good" toned stuff mixed with minor techno bleeps and bips.  There is a narrator that basically is the bulk of the story, explaining what the characters are feeling and what they're thinking.  You'll go from characters that are perky and lively to the ones that lack self-confidence, all the way to the bashful youth types and the double-crossers.
Of course, the characters here are the Atari / Tetris type blocks.  Each character controls differently, some are quick and able to leap anywhere, others are slow and bulky, others can double jump or act as platforms over dangerous water.  The puzzles are built on these mechanics and gameplay elements, and the further you progress through the game the more it expects you to master it.  One good thing is that if you don't play for a long time, the next time you do it won't be too difficult to get the hang of it again.
There were moments where it felt like one level is very hard, and the next chunk of the game is just easy, extremely basic puzzles.  There was one level that I felt stood out as way too hard, took about a half hour alone to complete, and then the rest of the game wasn't nearly as difficult.  I'd prefer a steady rise in difficulty when playing games but everyone is different, and I don't think it's too much of an issue overall.  Again, the narration and story are the main attraction here.
Don't go into this game looking for hardcore platforming and twitch-reflex gameplay.  Just remember that story and presentation are what you pay for.  If you have not played Thomas Was Alone, it is worth a look.

I played Doki Doki Literature Club and I was honestly disappointed with it. Everyone was hyped about it showing itself as a cutesy dating sim that turns sour at the end, but obviously they haven't seen Lucid 9.
This game is a thrill to play. Like DDLC, the beginning is a bit mundane, with adorkable characters, except the protag already has some pessimistic views about the world and obvious trust issues, etc, etc. *But*. That doesn't mean all the twists were any less surprising. *This* is what I call Psychological Horror. I seriously doubted myself with the choices presented at the end, because no choice was good and I know it. It's a VN and I have save files, I know, but if a game makes you suspend that belief and makes you actually sit and think about this the way the protag would, you just *know* it's good writing.
And it is *incredibly* good writing. The characters' personalities show in their use of vocabulary and it's amusing to see how the same character (the protag) could change his tones to fit with the people he's talking with. You know, like real people do. And it didn't come out as if the protag is a stupid one-dimensional character.
Overall, I loved Lucid 9. To anyone who enjoyed DDLC because of that "twist", give this one a try and see something way more.

What can I say? This was my very first visual novel that I was determined to read from the start. The poor male protagonist has his work cut out for him, if he wasnt heading for a nuthouse already, he surly will be in one by the end of this story. I finished this visual novel ages ago however never wrote a review for it, so here we go. I'll try not to spoil the story too much!
My pros, cons and overall review.
- Storyline. It has so many twists and turns that it even gets you as the reader thinking what's gonna happen next, who is it? It gets you on the edge of your seat, you're right there with the group of friends solving the mystery together. It's spectacular!
- Character Development. The charaters were definitely well written along with some sort of backstory but it's just enough to understand the suspicions of the protagonist as well as his friendships with the other characters.
- Music. the music is done well, it really sets the mood. Happy, sad, sinister, you name it and it's there making you feel the same dread as the protagonist.
- Art Design. Magnificently drawn, characters, backgrounds and pictures. They're nicely done for such a dark story.
- Routes/Story Length. The story is nice and long, a good amount of hours will go into reading and there aren't any drastic choices until the end so don't worry about messing up half way and needing to restart. You'll be ok. Even the ending is nice and long and it gives a semi-heartwarming "good" ending although dont expect it to last very long.
- Routes. There are SO many routes so you'd be spending hours upon hours trying to get them all (especially if you want the achievements).
- Difficulty. This visual novel is difficult to get by without a guide although I always use a guide for any visual novel I read as I like to get the best possible ending first before getting the bad endings. I did attempt this without a guide at first but alas, it wasn't easy especially with the puzzles you have to solve. Although the puzzles were still fun, even with a guide.
- No Romance. I'm a huge sucker for a good romance but amidst all the death and despair there isnt a single romance going on. We know 1 of the protagonist's friends loves him however they never go on a date, kiss, talk about it or anything. It's only implied by actions made and nothing comes of it (considering the "good" ending, I suppose I see why but still).
- Language. This story uses a lot of "big words" to put it simply, I dont consider this to be a con for me but some may consider it as such so I shall place it here for readers notice.
This was an amazing visual novel, although not a romantic one it definitely didn't fail at being a dark mystery visual novel. The sinister elements, the happy times, the twists and turns and the all out performance was fanatastic. For my first visual novel, I do highly recommend this read, you WON'T be disappointed in the slightest.

I played the free weekend only. When I write a thumbs-down review like this, it's out of genuine desire to not have people waste their money, and to not encourage the bad habits of game developers.
There's something to like about this game. The graphics and sound are top-notch. Animation is very fluid. All the heroes have excellent visual design. The combat system is also clearly quite deep and offers a lot of options.
Neutral on the single player and story. I see it as an extended tutorial, not a gripping novel.
Now to the problems.
Constant connectivity issues. I have an excellent Internet connection, play online games frequently, and routinely have low pings all across North America and even acceptable pings to Europe. Attempting to play 4v4 resulted in desynch notices or disconnections in 50% of my matches. Unacceptable for a AAA title that's been out this long.
Poor attempts at fair matchmaking. It tries to match you against equal skill level for about 10 seconds before matching you with just about anyone. You can end up in a match against an opponent or team far better than you. The game even knows it because it tells you ahead of time the relative skill level between you and the opponent(s). Matchmaking also took a long time in general.
Very, very high learning curve. It's clear to me that to truly succeed, you have to have good knowledge of all heroes' gameplay styles, not just the one you're playing. You can know your character inside and out, but it doesn't stop you from walking into a Counterattacker's game plan, or having your attacks fail to stagger a Heavy or Berserker who has some kind of invulnerability mechanic. If you're not interested in practicing for a hundred hours and reading every guide you can find just to be "decent", then move along.
The game has excellent style. But the excellent substance is buried somewhere under a mountain of problems.

I want it to be clear from the beginning – I am a Resident Evil fan. And I liked most of new Resident Evil games. Most, but not this one.
While I completed totally unfriendly RE 4 PC without mouse support mods and enjoyed the hell out of RE5 by playing both single and local co-op with my brother, this game just fatigued me after a few hours.
Its main problems is terrible controls allocation and a ton of useless commands spread throughout most of the keyboard. Don’t fool yourself – you’re not going to use even 30% of them, and if you try you get dead while you look for the correct kay. I honestly cannot imagine if the controls are easier with the gamepad, since some of commands required two keys, plus a correct direction key.
Another issue is  that it’s bloated to four separate campaigns whose structure is at least inconsistent. So is storytelling. I was disappointed when after completing the first (Leon) campaign I got through most of weird Chris Redfield campaign, and discovered, that some sequenced I did from the same perspective, instead of opposite. The pinnacle of WTF was when at the end of first campaign i reached the part already shown in prologue, and it was completely retold in different way. That’s not how you are supposed to tell viewpoint related stories.
What’s good about it? Probably graphics are okay, but they don’t impress me much after RE5, or rather introduction of X360 generation graphics. Really nothing else was better than in 5. The graphical low point for me was the new image of Ada Wong, who now looks as a china doll with much too wide cheeks, and too small mouth. Maybe it was an attempt to make the game more realistic, but I preferred the more manga-like version from RE4, and CGI movies.
The worst part is that I was genuinely interested in the story, and gave up on it near the end of second campaign. My recommendation? RE Revelations is a much better game even though it was converted from Nintendo DS. So either try this one, or wait for the upcoming sequel.

The basic gameplay of Crysis 2 take very few risks. You can carry two weapons, two explosives, and a rocket launcher. The weapon variety is very limited - most of the guns function and feel the same, and some of them are such direct upgrades that the prior versions all but vanish from later levels. The only non-humanoid enemies are the boss-types, which only show up a few times. Aliens have both gained and suffered from this - they are less of a chore to fight than they were before, but this is as a direct result of them being more similar to the regular human enemies.
A number of cues seem to have been taken from Call of Duty, Gears of War, etc. when it comes to other areas. Health is no longer shown as a bar on the HUD, but is instead represented by red splotches showing up on the sides of the screen. This is less precise and guaranteed to get in the way during critical moments by cutting off peripheral vision and blurring colors. The player can now lean out of cover by holding the right mouse button when near the edge of a barrier or wall, but the only way to find the sweet spot is by edging up against the corner until the prompt appears and risking a bullet in the arm.
The Nanosuit's operation has been streamlined, and now feels less like a vehicle and more like a passive system. Only the Stealth and Armor modes can be manually selected; Speed and Strength have been merged into a new category, Power is now activated automatically when the player uses a corresponding action. With direct access to only two modes, the Nanosuit's operation is more intuitive, but also feels less rewarding to successfully use. Minor upgrades may be unlocked, but only a few have visible effects.
Stealth mode hasn't changed much. Sneaking past enemies is still just as easy, and the majority of enemy AI is still lazy enough to simply shoot at the point at which you disappeared from sight. However, a few enemies are located at the other extreme, and have inexplicably impeccable aim no matter how visible you are.
Armor mode also performs the same, transferring damage from health to energy. However, it has suffered from the changes to other systems. When active, hexagons appear on the corners of your screen. This meansit becomes nearly impossible to tell whether you have Armor mode active when you are close to death, because the screen's contrast drops and the red splotches cover most of the screen. Worse, this is usually when it is most critical to know if you have Armor mode active.
Power mode is hard for me to get behind entirely. On the one hand, streamlining all of the extraneous suit functions into automatic actions makes for faster action and less micromanaging during combat. On the other hand, you can't sprint without suit battery left, and you throw items about as far as most regular people could. Furthermore, melee attacks are almost useless - it's far more effective to simply shoot the foe with whatever you have in your weapon.
The binoculars have gotten an upgrade this time around, and now highlight many objects of interest through walls and floors. A small number of enemies may be tagged through the visor, which will let you see their locations even when not using them. It also has a new function called "Nanovision," which provides a thermal-esque color overlay pointing out enemies and objects of interest. However, it suffers from a short range, and drains the suit's batteries while in use.
Level design has suffered. The developers have ditched the spacious, free-roaming environments of Crysis 1 in favor of much smaller areas. Although initially confusing, this decision actually meshes better with Crysis 2's gameplay than more open environments. Sprinting is slower, and vehicles are rarely placed in locations where they could be effectively used by you. Gone as well are the large turret and vehicle sections, which is only an improvement as far as I'm concerned. Additionally, most objectives are simply to reach a point behind a number of enemies, although this greatly incentivizes turning on cloak and walking past them all instead of dealing with them.
Although not a masterpiece, the story does an effective job of both moving the plot forward and maintaining player interest. Unfortunately, most of the major players have only the bare minimum of characterization, and there are several gaping plot holes. That said, I rather enjoyed it, and the story and gameplay combined to keep me interested enough to continue playing without it feeling like a slog. Unfortunately, there were several scenes where player interaction suffered to make way for the story, which left me feeling like a non-participant in the game I'd paid money to play. A few well-done scenes, however, managed to hit the sweet spot between player interaction and storytelling where I felt involved in the character's situation, instead of left out of it.
Crysis 2 suffers from a number of basic design problems. Doors are largely unopenable, except for some specific plot-necessary ones, which are usually similar to every other door in the room, and the player must check each one for a prompt. Hints given after death are almost never helpful, and after a while start feeling a little mocking. A quicktime event later on has nearly the exact same thing happen regardless of if you succeed or fail, except that if you fail it kills you. Some weapons take up one of your two slots, but can't be refilled from ammo crates, making them dead weight when they run out of ammo. Autosaves are located very far apart most of the time, meaning that dying could set you back a lot more than you might have expected.
Despite being a AAA title, this game has a remarkable number of glitches, crashes, and sloppy mistakes. I've seen every type of enemy try to shoot me through walls, over and over. Possibly my favorite example of the sheer sloppiness of the AI in this game is the number of times I have seen a humanoid yell "FRAG OUT!" and then throw a grenade at the wall he's taking cover behind, only to ignore it as it bounces back, ticks down, and explodes, killing him.
To summarize: is Crysis 2 a game you should play? Sure, if you already own it, or if a friend owns it and offers to let you play it. It is entertaining, despite its flaws. However, that isn't the real question I'm answering here: is Crysis 2 a game you should BUY? No. Crysis 2 brings very little to the table that cannot be found, and done better, in other games, for either the same price or cheaper. The game's primary mechanic, the Nanosuit, is interesting, but in the end, it doesn't stand out very much from the crowd, especially with the lengths it took to stand closer to titles like Call of Duty and Gears of War. The story is passable and gets the job done, but certainly nothing to write home about, especially with its large plot holes and how little characterization most of the characters get. Most of the weapons differ only superficially from each other, and the enemies differ even less. Crysis 2 is not the worst purchase you could make, but you could certainly do better.

A plethora of distractions stand in your way in the form of a flickering lamp, political dissidents that need to be shot, and good ol' fashion stress (remedied with vodka and pipe smoke). I've been learning to play guitar for about 7 months now and got this within the first month of picking up a guitar. My first issue with the game is that it didn't support acoustic electric which led me to buying my second guitar so it could be supported.
Usually when I improve by using Rocksmith I'm improving my skill by being overwheled with a tempo I couldn't handle chords I didn't know etc. During lessons usually I could get through the lesson just by smacking a chord rather than actually playing it. If the tempo was too fast for me and there were multiple chords that I knew but couldn't change between quickly i could basically slap my fretboard with my fingers and pass which I feel like is not a good thing to learn as a beginner. Often I would pass like this and then take a few days to practice what I had learned and then retake said lesson just so i could do it with what I was pretty sure was not as wrong as it had been before.
Another thing that sucks about lessons is sometimes it just won't pick up with what you are playing. Every once in awhile it'll tell you to play something, one that I've had recently was Barre chordes, it told me to play I think it was a G which looked like,
3 1 1 1 1 1 1
4          3
5   2 4
after it would just sit there for awhile and say "no make sure youre putting your first finger on the third fret." or "It sound's like youre on the 7th frett, move your fingers up to the 3rd frett." despite me being in the correct location, leading to me just strumming really fast and eventually having it tell me congrats on doing it right. This can be infuriating. I've just closed my laptop put my guitar on it's stand and went for a walk more times than I can count with this game.
The minigames are super fun and great pracitce, but it would kill my uncallused noob fingertips for overdoing it, which is my own fault. By far I enjoy this game the most on a regular basis while playing Mini games. They are super addicting and teach you individual skills rather than trying to combine skills for a single song, rythm etc. Theres one for sliding, where you have to slide back and forth up and down the fret board to get your character (a ninja) to spire jump onto scyscraper points, slide to far and he falls and you lose some time while it resets him, to little and the same thing. Meanwhile creeping up behind you is a wall of electricity that will shock and kill your ninja if it hits him, so it's a race against time with the utmost importance on accuracy. There are a bunch of mini games like that that emphasize different stuff, from chords to harmonics. I love them but I will shred my fingers or cramp my hands from this pretty often.
One thing that I have a lot of mixed feelings about as well is the DLC, I got some of my favorite songs which is great and all, but I'm a college student so my practice time fluxuates. There was a 2 week period where i basically practiced like three times the amount i spend working on school and I got one of the songs up to 54% completion. I felt extremely accomplished by this. HOWEVER, now every time I play the song, unless I have practiced for about an hour so I could actually get a decent score, I get incredibly let down by my lack of skill since I don't practice as often as I should.
This can be incredibly demoralzing as I see my skill spiking and then decending. Most days when I play it now, I tend to fool around with some mini games and songs to warm my fingers up then try to learn a few lessons and just turn the computer off due to self dissatisfaction then go play my acoustic instead because there's no preset instructor to tell me I'm doing everything wrong with minimal help settings. Most of the time the instructor will give like 1 tip on how to do something and then just repeat that after you failing for awhile.
All in all I would advise to get the game, it's really fun and everything but if you get demoralized easily it may not be for you. I would advise to spend like 3 times the amount of time you play the game practicing what you learned from it if you're a begginner like myself.

This probably isn't going to come as a shock to anyone who's heard of the game, for those of you out there that haven't:
This is a puzzle game - you control a variety of different characters (the exact mix of which varies from level to level), all of whom have different attributes. Some can jump higher, others can float in (the normally deadly) water, some pretty much just act as a stepping stone so that their higher-jumping buddies can reach a switch (and that's ok!) - using all of their talents together, you must move them from their starting location(s) to their goals (outlines that look like the character.)
What really brings the game together is the excellent narration and minimalist (but perfectly done) music - despite the characters being (literally) squares and rectangles, you really get a feeling for each character's personality, and (dare I say it) you even begin to care about them and their journey.
I wouldn't go so far as to say that it's a buy at its normal $10 price-point, as it's fairly short (I completed it in ~4 hours), but if you can find it either in a bundle or at a high discount, it's well worth picking up.
I enjoyed every second of playing this compelling story-driven puzzle-platformer.

Overall: It is a well done game with surprisingly interesting characters. The use of minimalism does wonders in an age filled with HD and CGI out the wahzoo.
But section 9 (last section) is frustrating. The bulk of the game is really fun and teases your brain, but section 9 suddenly feels like the game designers were trying to show off or something. It becomes a big mess rather than an interesting adventure with characters I cared about.
Sometimes the jump doesn’t work and there is this glitch that causes your characters to stick to walls mid-jump. This is very annoying considering jumping is the only thing you do in this game.
4/5. It’s good overall, but there are sprinkles of BS here and there

I'm mad that Doki Doki Literature Club got more attention in a week than Lucid 9 did in a year. This VN is a true masterpiece that deserves to outshine the majority of its competitors; DDLC just needs to be burned. But that's only a side note...
This game won't disappoint those looking for some actual effort put into their games. It's amazing that the devs put this up for free; this could easily be a paid game for the quality it was made with. Trust me, everything from the story to the music to the art is top notch; the only complaint is that the sprites for the male protagonists and the side characters aren't as polished as the female sprites, but that's a nitpick. So having played For Honor for the free weekend and putting in a good number of hours, I gotta say it's really just an OK game. The fact that they even have the gall to charge $60 for this is just... It blows my mind. Nowhere near being worth that much. On sale? Sure. $25-30 is a much more reasonable price for the game considering what you get.
There are issues with the servers, this is absolutely true. First day I had some connection errors, wasnt constant but they were there, also some crahses thrown in. Annoying, but I can deal with that. The second day? Holy jumpin' shitballs! it's like the game didnt want me to play it! After awhile I finally got to stay in matches, but you can see the other players were getting disconnected too. Luckily they were being replaced by bots but still, it's a serious issue.
Now the combat is.... well its fun, but its also tedious and a bit annoying at times. From my experience it seems to come down to who has the better defence and can get in a guardbreak or parry to open up your opponent for a series of combos and big hits since they'll be stunlocked. A lot of stuns in this game, very frustrating. I remember getting stunlocked basically to death by a lawbringer and again by a raider, literally unable to move or even defend myself I just had to sit there and wait for him to kill me... yeah VERY fun. Some classes really seem to be just better than others in terms of moveset and damage potential. Doesn't feel very balanced. But still, the combat has its moments of intense battles and fights so yeah its a mixed bag. The matchmaking is a mixed bag aswell. I've had more one-sided matches than balanced ones so, It's a bit of a mess.
Something that really bothered me is this little thing called the "revenge mode" mechanic. Apparently(according to people in game)its suppose to help "even the odds" when you're fighting mutiple people since being double-teamed is.. Over-powered... are you fookin serious? If you put yourself in a losing situation I really don't think you should be rewarded with super powers, ok? Granted you can just avoid them and let it run out or kill them before they activate it but it's still a really dumb mechanic, imo.
You really should just die in those situations or retreat if possible. This is made worse by the fact that armour and weapons all have abilities that they can buff... yes weapons and armour have stats they can increase like stamina regeneration and damage... and they can boost how quickly you can get revenge mode, how long it lasts and how much damage you can do while its on. I remember a match where this warden was getting double teamed and was about to die but then popped his revenge mode on, which knocks people down who are close to him(ffs) and proceeded to kill one of the attackers since his attacks did more damage, he had a health boost and his attacks were uninteruptable. Such skill. And what felt like 10secs later, had it up AGAIN! I personally wish all the weapon and armour customization were purely aesthetic but, whatcha gonna do?
Anyway, It's an alright game that has its moments of fun and enjoyment but there are a lot more things wrong with the game than are right. I'd reccomend picking it up on sale but DO NOT pay full-price for this. It is not worth $60. I wish there was a middle of the road recommend instead of just Yes or No becaue thats what I'd choose.

I am cutting and freezing my way through the post-apocalyptic mushroom jungle wearing my clone's face, on a quest from a race of subterranean albino ape technologists, feeling like a powerful mutant warrior wielding a surreptitiously acquired fist of the ape god. Then I suddenly come upon a group of sludge-beings that spontaneously evolve from primordial goo and lava and who are just barely able to collectively melt me to nothingness despite my psychically boosted toughness, sleeping gas spraying out and a clutch of grenades. Of course this is all typical in Qud.
Pros: huge game world, intuitive UI, incredibly unique and deep setting w/ lore contained in books, characters, descriptions and the physical environment (and the philosophy references e.g. to the logic of Russell and to Socrates are awesome for someone who knows any philosophy), huge amount of ability to customize character both at start of game and throughout play, huge amount of player agency (as there should be in any proper roguelike, but this world and its emergent gameplay feels more natural than e.g. ADOM, which I also enjoy but no where near as much as Qud), beautiful graphics (for me anyway), really truly great music (please more!), new features and bugs squashed every week, optional permadeath and saving/loading, dynamic faction allegiances, infectious diseases with procedurally generated cures, tons of items to craft and various ways to modify gear, cybernetic implants, and I'm sure a million other things I'm forgetting
Cons: main quest is not yet finished, and after countless hours in Qud starting a new character in Joppa for the umpteenth time feels a bit tedious (but still worth it)
Overall: game is amazing, up there for me with classics like Fallout 1/2, ADOM, Darklands, Ultima Underworld. If the game continues to develop to completion I'm sure it will be considered one of the all-time great RPGs by those with refined taste.

Once again a game I can neither recommend nor downrate which proves there should be a "neutral" button. It is difficult to evaluate this game considering the issues and also the good parts it has. I am in between and being offered the two extremes only is not sufficient.
The good stuff:
--- The game offers not one but four campaigns! This is pretty cool considering the 4 couples you have which means 8 characters - each with a different personality, extra attack or weapon and importance when it comes to the storyline. Also, enemies approaching you differ in each campaign. The same goes to the locales. While Leon and Helena traverse through the big city, a cemetery and a cathedral offing dozens of zombies Chris and Piers do the same but in China. They are attacked by J'avos - these are infected people with the ability to plan their attacks and can also use firearms.
--- Graphics / cutscenes / sound effects -> production value. Well, after episode 5 it was obvious the creators would take this to another level.  The game looks stunning and the atmosphere is there. The coop and action sequences once again decrease the horror elements but nobody can say they did not try! Also, there are dozens of cutscenes and in the game's menu you can rewatch all. Altogether I'm sure it will take at least 2 hours to go these in one sitting.
--- Longevity. Once again we have collectibles that come in the form of emblems. I have found many but could not find a lot either. There are no more treasures as collectibles. Instead, there is something else that is dropped by the enemies and they represents points. This amount can be used to purchase skills. These can then be levelled up. 3 skills can be active at a time and there are enemy-specific ones, too. So, you and your coop partner need to work together and decide who equips what. Multiplayer also returns in the form of Mercenaries and there is now a new game mode called Agent Hunt.
The bad stuff:
--- 4 campaigns: In terms of story and characters this is really good but there are too many intersections. In fact, there are boss battles you need to play twice. Really? Of all this it is Ada's (4th) campaign that is the worst. First of all, almost all the areas are familiar and you encounter hardly any new enemies. Throughout all the campaign you know what's going to happen and the ending is a total letdown. Not only this but Ada plays alone. Your friend assumes the role of a so-called Agent - a guy who's just there so that the creators can tell they did really make a coop game. Agent wears a mask and does not have a real name.  In the cutscenes you see Ada alone and throughout the campaign Agent cannot interact with anything. You cannot open doors or chests, you cannot solve any puzzles and no QTEs for you (which is actually good). You can pick up bullets, of course and fight with Ada but feel like an unnecessary character who does not even have a story.
--- Cheesiness: If you thought episodes 5's dialogue was bad you are in for a great surprise. Some of the conversations the protagonists have are just dumb. In fact, you can easily guess what will happen next. The script should have been reworked at least 3 times to eliminate some of the worst dialogues this franchise has ever seen.
--- Boss battles: They are waaaaaaaay toooooooooo loooooooooooooong! You battle the same guy while he assumes at least 3 different forms one after the other. The tactic is different as well as the environment. It is not necessarily a problem but the game is very difficult and also you are 100% sure you eliminated your foe when he returns once more to annoy you. I have to admit the enemies are great (each one of them poses a real threat) but you battle them for too long. This gets boring and aggravating considering the difficulty of the game.
--- Difficulty level: This game is annoyingly difficult. From time to time you get a QTE which is next to impossible to complete for the first time. Missing it will result in a death cutscene - well, I appreciate the developers wanted to show me what cutscenes they had conjured up in their mind but this is still pretty annoying. Boss battles can be a pain and the controls do not help either. It is a sad thing to say since this game enables you to do pretty much everything: you can run, do fistfight, dodge and even slide. And finally: you can walk while aiming at an enemy! The problem is with the turning and the speed. Also, the camera does not help and sometimes you get attacked because our heroes are looking at what's going on elsewhere in the distance.
For me Resident Evil 6 was annoying. I could handle 5 but the latest instalment was just too much. Campaign and firefight was good but Ada's story was a silly way to end a game and the difficulty level did not pose a real challenge (it was annoying instead).
If you are a newcomer, do not start with this one. If you liked the predecessors you can pick it up but buckle up as the ride will be long, tiresome and irritating! Of course, for hardcore RE fans the 6th instalment is a must.

Resident Evil 4 on PS2 was what brought me to the Resident Evil series, and I enjoyed it a lot. While waiting for the release of RE5, I took the time to play the previous games in the series (RE0, REmake, RE2, REVX, and Outbreak1&2). I never really thought of zombies as the main focus of the Resident Evil. I felt like the main focus should be the B.O.W.'s. Biohazard seems to be a more appropriate name for that reason. That said, Resident Evil started out as Survival Horror, and started to lean towards a more of an action game, which is perfectly fine if B.O.W.'s were the main focus.
Resident Evil 6 provides a mostly linear gameplay which provides you with a specific objective after another. I feel that it takes out the exploration, which I enjoyed from the previous games. They also have route mechanic that functions similiar to that of the Dead Space series that tells you where to go. There were no need to back track.
Ever since RE4, the melee mechanics has been evolving for resident evil. RE6 offers counter-attacks, melee without the need to stagger enemies, environmental kills and more. The counter-attacks are dependant on the enemy's attack as well as the weapon you are wielding. Meleeing on command also depends on the weapon you are wielding. The combat system just makes the game a bit more fun, especially in the mercenaries mode.
I never really got into the story into older Resident Evil games, for the exception of Veronica: X, but the Chris's story really stood out for me. Leon's story was similar to previous RE games. There were lots of cutscenes in the game, which kinda of interrupted the gameplay. Sometimes, I just wanted to play the game. That said, the cutscenes in the game were well done, loaded usually with explosions and pretty good voice acting. It almost feels like I'm watching a decent action movie.
I disliked the coop system in RE5, mainly because I mostly played with the AI, and she can die. However, in RE6 when you play offline your AI cannot die and doesn't share the same inventory with you. I was playing RE5 on the PS3, and getting matched with other people was always an issue. Playing RE6 on PC, however, coop is pretty common. There's even a matchmaking group for any multiplayer modes. It's always a better experience to play online.
Good game. Have fun.

Calm down, Stalin takes place during the cold war, and you play as. Who else? Stalin, who fends off an enemy invasion simply by menancingly holding his finger above the large red button which will launch an attack on the rest of the world. The game progressively gets harder, as you are given more and more chores to tend to, such as answering your phone, hitting your poorly working office lamp and later on assassinating people.
At first i thought this game was just a simple time waster, and to some degree it is, however there's more too it than meets the eye.
For example:
-You need to maintain the integrity of your country, which slowly but surely worsen with each 'story' mission you do, abruptly ending calls, or not answering them at all will decrease the country integrity after you've unlocked the phone
-You get stressed by things around you, smoking your pipe is a way of relieving stress but you can't do both that and hold your hand near the button so you will need to spend every second you get very wisely to avoid getting invaded, having your country colapse or accidentally launching an attack.
You shouldn't expect to get thousands of hours worth of gameplay out of this, but it is a entertaining game to boot up now and then, and it's nice seeing a game with a silly premise get released these days but actually have a bit more to it than
An average day in the Soviet Union...

It's hard to provide a generic 'Recommend' or 'Not Recommend' rating for this game.
I don't like the 3D style fretboard (I would prefer a scrolling tab display) and would also love to sacrifice some of the eye-candy for faster loading times and less CPU use. I would prefer looking at it as a learning tool rather like a game.
Menu navigation and keyboard short-cuts are hard to get used to - I couldn't get so far. It would have been lovely to manage some of basic menu navigation with guitar strings.
It has a lot of content but not organized. The 'My Path' feature is not enough to give you directions on how to advance and what to learn. A 'Career' mode with missions one after another would be much easier to use.
The lessons have a pretty steep learning curve so if you are an absolute beginner - like myself - you will not find this game as much fun and will progress slower than with classic methods.
I ended up with a 1-year subscription for
and made much more progress in a few weeks than with this.
Still, the game itself is good, it comes with solid content and the price is reasonable just don't expect quick progress if you pick up the guitar for the first time.
