Dark Void isn't a must-play game. It's somewhat buggy, it crashes from time to time, there's not a huge amount of weapon or enemy variety, and there are certain parts of the game that are pretty boring. It also has a Securom online activation that was broken for almost a year, and even though Capcom has now reached out to them and fixed it there's always the possibility of it happening again. But it's one of those games like Dark Sector where while at heart they're just third person shooters, they have unique concepts that I haven't seen anywhere else and do them just well enough to be worth trying. In this case, the concept is the jet pack, which gives the game more verticality than most cover shooters have. The controls for flying it take a bit of getting used to at first, but once you do it's a lot of fun playing in the areas where you're free to fly around. There's a disappointingly high amount of missions that mostly involve confined spaceship interiors where there isn't much room for the mechanic to shine, but there are just enough missions that are great to make up for them. The story is also somewhat interesting, though the concept is more interesting than the actual execution of it and the main characters are just bland enough to feel like they don't really deserve to be in a story concept that neat, and the side characters that you actually want to hear more from usually get benched. The game goes on sale for around $2 pretty often (I got it for $2 from the Green Man Gaming summer sale), so it's probably better to wait for one of those times since it isn't exactly an "you should urgently play this game right now"-good game, but it's certainly worth trying for the sake of playing the good parts. Dark Void isn't the best third person shooter you'll ever play, but chances are it's not the worst, either.

9/10: A truly minimalist puzzle-platformer buoyed by a delightfully succinct narrative and quadrilaterals with robust personalities.
At first glance, Thomas Was Alone appears highly abstract, with graphics limited to various four-sided figures. However, the immediate narration reveals that these aren't just shapes: they have names. While Thomas starts off alone, his journey brings him into the company of many others including the cantankerous Chris, narcissitic John, and several other colorful rectangles of unique abilities.
Deceptively simple in execution, the game is supported by a relatively deep story. These personable little characters aren't merely abstract characters, but artificial intelligences being spawned within a system. As their virtual quest for knowledge progresses, the blurbs between sections reveal that the effect of their efforts result in the AI escaping the system, causing the charming relationships between the shapes to be cast in a curiously dark context akin to Skynet or HAL rebelling against control. The result is a very intriguing yet not convoluted story of how a group of AI's set out to enlighten themselves and as a result changed the world forever.
Lengthwise, it's short and sweet. With only two collectibles per chapter, the usual grinding and frustration that lengthier platformers pad their time with is negligible here, allowing you to simply enjoy figuring out puzzles as the narrator describes the quadrilaterals innermost thoughts to you. Still, if you find yourself looking for more after finishing the story, make sure to check out the last two chapters (starting with "Target"), as they aren't part of the core story but are actually a bonus set of "prequel" stages.
Altogether, a great puzzle platformer whose simple appearance belies a depth of narrative that many AAA games could learn from.

Lucid9 was a very fun and enjoyable experience for me. Seeing that this game had impressive ratings and was for free, I instantly installed it to my computer. It is somewhat really hard to believe that something of this polish is actually for free in the market, especially when most visual novels that are for free tend to be more of low quality.
The story of Lucid9 starts rather slow, presenting its cast of characters and their dynamics. Due to this, the story has a large focus on showing each character’s personal history, life circumstances, and how they react to the mysterious murders that surround them which is the focus of the plot. It also knows how and when to give the details of its story which helps in keeping you intrigued and interested all the way to its climax. It also can get crazy and a bit dark if you aren’t prepared.
Due to the story of Lucid9 focusing more on its characters, it is quite important that the character holds up well and can keep you invested in them. Each individual character appears to have their own past and outlook in their current situation that despite being a tad bit generic was still rather enjoyable. Throughout the course of my whole experience with its characters and its story, I ended up being invested and caring for them thanks to their natural, likeable and expressive dialogue.
For a free visual novel, Lucid9 actually has some really delightful visuals. It might sometimes look a bit off in some areas of the game, but for the most part they do the job right. The music really struck accord with me. With some lively music for high school life and some suspenseful music for its darker scenes, it really did a nice job in setting the tone and mood which complemented each of its respective scenes.
Overall, Lucid9 was a cool experience. It knows what it’s trying to do and does it very well in all aspects through its story, characters, visuals, and soundtrack. Just let yourself enjoy the experience which Lucid9 is trying to offer you and maybe you’ll have a very fun and enjoyable experience.  As I stated before at the beginning, it’s for free so there really isn’t anything to lose but a few hours of your life.
I recommend that you give Lucid9: Inciting Incident a shot.

Crysis 2 Review TL;DR@bottom
There not much to be said about first-person shooters today. For the most part if something moves, you shoot it until it stops moving. Crysis 2, for the most part, is no different, but it certainly is beautiful to look at.
All cynics aside, Crysis 2 actually surprised me more than I was expecting. The game takes place after the events of the first Crysis. This time it takes place in the middle of New York. Without giving away too much of the game I can say your name is Alcatraz and you have come across a once in a life time opportunity where you get to dawn on a multi-million dollar suit. Not that you have a choice, but you are now a super soldier.
This game got a lot of flak about it not being as open as the first Crysis and there is some understanding to that but I didn't feel all that claustrophobic when playing the game and I think it was done with a mix of intelligent level design. Let me explain my perspective. In the original Crysis you were on an island. For starters you can already tell how big the game is going to be right from the get go. In Crysis 2 you're on the mainland (America). Unless you’re a flight sim you're not generating the entire continent. In this case it is some of the various cityscapes of New York. The biggest complaint, that I've seen myself, is the structured level design. I can see where the complaints are coming from. The standard "rubble" or "blocking traffic" or "barricades" are all used to direct the player but when I am playing the game I don't notice the limitation at all. Now that's not to say that it's perfect. Some places I would like to go because I feel that I would have had a tactical advantage over the enemy and let’s face it, in a combat situation (especially with the nano suit you get), there’s not going to be much that will block my way to provide myself an advantage but I digress. There are however multiple ways to handle situations and that's a plus. The ability to use the environment in a limited fashion really helps. For example, if I'm low on ammo and a Ceph solder is 14 meters from me with only a wrecked car between me and him, I can use the car as a weapon by kicking it. This sends a 1800lb car flying in the direction of the enemy. They can't really stop that if they are too close. Of course you've now just hurled your cover away so think before doing that. Regardless, it is a nice option to exploit if need be. That's a more organic example of the suits use. Others are sprinting now uses the speed of the suit. Despite the wiki's claims that the first nano suits speed was slower than the second generation suit seen in Crysis 2, it seems the other way around but either way it’s an example of a more organic suit use. Hold down the space bar allows for the super jump and the "Q" and "E" keys on the keyboard are your cloak and armor modes. I found this setup more welcoming than the first ones, probably because your relying more on tactical keys than the on-screen suit mode switching. Upgrades can be done to the suit as well such as decreased energy consumption, threat tracker, faster regen of energy. These allow for different play styles for different gamers.
The graphics are beautiful. I could spend days talking about how good the CryEngine 3 is but let’s just say they continue to set the bar. Sadly my poor machine has to turn down a couple of things to get it to run smooth but it still gorgeous to look at (cut my computer a break, it's going on 7 years old). I think the only engines that rival this engine are Frostbyte 3(Battlefield 4), Unreal 4 (tech demos), and REDengine3 (Witcher 3). An argument could be made that the Unreal 4 is better (probably is in the long run) but lets let bygones be bygones.
In the end the game is certainly not as "sandboxy" as the first one but then again the first one seems to have more of an illusion of freedom, as you get further into the levels you’re still blocked off by cliff sides or an ocean. Crysis 2 does get some things better like natural nano suit usage and the story ups the ante so in my opinion I would say if you're looking for a shooter that makes you feel tactical and smart about combat logistics I would say this game is for you. Just don't expect the freedom of a Bethesda game.

I've never felt like my death was undeserved in this game. In a mechanical sense surely; I messed up, I didn't understand an interaction, I died. But also in a meta sense; the game's horrifying world never makes me feel special enough to deserve anything more dignified or glorious than death by some horrible mutant insect I found in some slimy pit.
This makes things pretty intense, all the time. Early game is less a chore than a sort of scrabble about in the dark for supplies, hoping not to wake a sleeping monstrosity. Progress is dreamlike, a product of staying alive. I don't get attached to my characters or progress in Qud; I fear for my life. Death is a kind of release.
Also; amazing devs. Very regular updates.
Get this game.

I...... Cannot really recommend this. Which is a surprise, to myself.
I've played a good deal of MUDs and Rogue-likes (actual Rogue-likes, as in not just procedural/random generation and permadeath games), lately I've spent an embarrassing amount of time playing Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead (Which is free, by the way!). I've also played NetHack, and an assortment of other similar games. And I find them thoroughly compelling.
And this was just not very compelling. Does it look slightly fancier? Sure, yes. The animated sprites intermixed with the "tiles" does look genuinely neat - I applaud that. I'm not stuck-up about "Rogue-aesthetics". Turning off the tiles for an "ascii mode" is silly and looks bad, this is not a terminal window, and it shows. But that's not really a problem, just leave the tiles on.
However, the actual interface is .... Well, it's a lot of not-good.
So, the user interface aside, and I have to point out that it's quite hard to do worse, UI-wise, than a terminal-based Roguelike. Even games that have it down to a T, like Cataclysm DDA, are sorta clumsy and unintuitive. This is worse. Despite being a Unity game, not a literal Windows CMD or linux Terminal window.
Alright, so what about the game? I don't know about the game... I could not give it an honest try. In a game like this, the user interface IS the game, to a large extent. I don't doubt that it can generate interesting worlds and all that jazz. But it's too clunky, and feels too ... flat? Not flat in terms of elevation, just ... flat in terms of character. The fake scan-lines are cute for about 10 seconds, but says a lot about the intent of the game - the intent is to
a terminal-type oldschool game (by the way, no PC monitor ever had scanlines like that, ever. I owned many - they're clear and clean like an LCD).  It does a lot to force this upon the player - it beats you over the head with a giant club, saying I AM SO RETRO WOW HAVE YOU NOTICED IT YET SO RETRO.
That's funny sometimes, and some games take the whole "play pretend retro" theme and run with it, and succeed gloriously at it, or for that matter some games just choose to go very low-fi because they wish to, because they like to, because it lets them focus on other things, and it's fine. But here, there's just nothing to back that up. It's just a generic Roguelike (nothing wrong with that), trying to .. pretend.. like.. it's a generic roguelike? Like, I don't even.... There's some disconnect somewhere. Do tiles, or don't. Don't make tiles made out of ASCII characters. Yeah, sure, they can be minimalist and tile-esque, that's cute, I liked that part, but please, skip the silly parts. Make it a -good- minimalist theme instead, people will have much fonder memories of that.
Anyhow. I found this a frustrating experience. I'll go back to CDDA or NetHack or any other of the dozens of very well made, and free (not that I care, particularly), Rogue-Likes around.
I wished it had been a better experience.
Because; we need these games to exist in a more commercial sense - we need them on Steam, we need them to be developed by paid and excited full-time developers, so that the genre remains healthy and heck even allow the genre to advance in some areas, because there's room for that. Cataclysm is proving it with a incomprehensibly advanced world simulation, Dwarf Fortress is proving that you can generate amazing and complex and deep worlds... NetHack is being the conservative master of the classic, it does classic better than classic itself. So clearly, there's plenty to sink your teeth into if you're making a real Rogue-like in 2016 (or whatever year). Maybe Caves of Qud wanted to be the Roguelike that improved the user experience by NOT being a terminal-type game, by having a more understandable and friendly UI. But this isn't it. It's made in Unity, so clearly they can do this. In fact, as a Unity developer myself, it's evident that the amount of work put into TRYING TO BE a terminal application, must have been quite significant - rather than making an original, thought-out and friendly UI.
I hope this does well, and I hope I'm just a stingy old fart who can't appreciate it. Best wishes to the developers, I hope you find your niche and that the game works out. I hope you can finish your game, we sorely need a Roguelike that is actually complete, rather than stuck in Pre-Alpha/Alpha for the rest of our natural lives. We really do!

Jazzpunk is a single-player, first-person adventure game, focusing on exploration and comedy over puzzle-solving. Each mission has one central objective, but the player is free to explore the game world at their own pace, which is populated with a large number of interactive NPCs, each with their own action or gag. The player takes the role of Polyblank, a silent protagonist. The game begins when Polyblank is mailed to the espionage agency in a human-shaped suitcase. He is then given several missions by the head of the organization, all of which begin by ingesting a dose of prescription medicine. The missions assigned to Polyblank are almost always bizarre and nonsensical, relying heavily on free association and references to older movies and video games. Tasks include degaussing and smuggling pigeons, assassinating cowboys, cross-dressing, killing a pig with a ukulele, and photocopying Polyblank's bottom to fool a security scanner. The game was originally created as a prototype in 2007, running on a standalone engine. The project was then transferred to Torque3D before being transferred to the Unity game engine, on which the final build was created.

Jazzpunk is a unique spy game developed by Necrophones Games and published by Adult Swim Games. It was released on the 7th February 2014 and has gain a small fan base on Steam, but I believe it deserves more of a following than it has.
The game can be run on Windows, Mac or Linux and is not very demanding so you should be able to run it smoothly on any reasonably good computer. As for bugs, I have not experienced any serious bugs or glitches in which I would call important in anyway.
Jazzpunk costs £10.99 which I believe is a bit steep, but it frequently goes on offer so if you want to buy it, just wait for one of the times in which it does. Having bought it and played through the story line a number of times I can see why this game has become popular. The joke play style which stays consistent from trailer to end of game is fun and enjoyable for everyone.
The music in game suits the style well and adds to the overall enjoyment you get whilst playing the game. On top of this the storyline is engaging and light hearted, and the amount of stuff there is to explore could keep you amused for many hours.
However, the game is very short, if you play it through without fully exploring the map you would be able to complete the game in about 2 hours, which is not a lot of game time for the price. However, due to it's comical properties and cleaver design, you will be able to back to it and discover more every time.
To conclude, yes I do recommend Jazzpunk and you will enjoy playing it, but that enjoyment may not last as long as you will be hoping when you first buy it, due to it's short story length.

Every now and then I have to stop playing the games I spent $60 on with graphics that can only run on the highest quality of computers and play a free game that could run on a toaster. Somehow Princess Remedy in a World of Hurt could hold it's own against those $60 games.
Princess Remedy's gameplay is mainly found in the combat, which plays like a bullet-hell, with a bit of puzzles mixed into the mix.
You fight a cast of enemies who vary depending on the person you are healing, each with their own strategy and weakness.
The fights get more difficult as you get more powerful.
It's simple, but it works.
What I liked the most was that losing meant nothing! Every time you fail to cure someone you can just try again! This doesn't work well for every game, but it works well here.
The story in Princess Remedy is as generic as it gets and is basically all put out on the table for you before you even get to play.
You go on a quest to save a princess...
Except he's a prince...
And you use the power of modern medicine...
Fabulous.
Along the way you unlock the next areas with "hearts". "Hearts" are earned by helping out people with their troubles, which is where the real story comes in.
You find people troubled by all sorts of ailments and most of them are hilarious.
You'll find a slime who only smells a little, a flower who needs confidence to tell a tree to get out of his way so he can get sunlight, and a man who's face melted after getting to close to the sun.
This game genuinely made me laugh, multiple times, which cannot be said of many games.
I won't spoil the ending, but it also leads to many hilarious moments.
I will say though, the game's ending revealed how much of the game you beat. I was informed I had only completed 97% and, after wandering aimlessly for another 10 minutes, couldn't find any of the hearts I was missing...
Other than that the only real problem I had with the story was the length! I finished this game in just over an hour!
The graphics are charming. Everything about them screams "old school".
At one point in time I tried to learn how to create pixel art. I was told it was the art of creating beauty through limitations. This game takes it's limitations and makes it it's strength.
From the enemies, to the overworld, to your attacks, everything is simplistic yet dazzling.
My favorite bit of pixel art are the attacks made by Princess Remedy. Her attacks start off as band-aids, then pills, shots, and eventually sparkles, each wonderfully animated.
I played this game talking with a friend who was also playing Princess Remedy and one of our favorite parts was the music.
From the moment you hit the title screen to the second you beat the game, you are in for a great time. The music is spot on and matches the theme of each level perfectly.
You can listen to the soundtrack
. My favorite track was
, which will probably be my next ringtone.
There are multiple different difficulty settings and easter eggs to find, which makes the replay value decent, but unless you feel like playing the game multiple times, which isn't a problem considering it can be beaten in about an hour, there isn't much to do.

This one appears to have been abandoned mid-development.
It's got potential, but it's not fully finished.  Even in single player with graphics set low it hitches like it's struggling to keep the FPS above 10.  The game mechanics for the enemies are interesting, and in certian places the graphics shine, but unfortunately the world is just unfinished and most of the graphics are nothing beyond so-so.  Even so, the world looks damaged and destroyed, as it should, with overgrown areas where parks and other green areas were before things went South.
Sadly they went with "hold use key to do action", instead of just press the key and have a timer pop up until the action is complete.  I hate it when games do this as it's unnecessary for me to sit there holding a key down, the game knows what I want to do.  This is, however, a minor gripe.  The melee combat is passable, but it needs work.  I haven't been able to get a decent gun so I can't really comment on the gunplay.  I'm sure it's passable, too.
Scavenging is time consuming because things are very far apart, and not much happens if you're sneaky about it.  The player base is so small that you're unlikely to run into other players in PVP servers, but I'm sure you'd regret it if you did.
I don't have a whole lot more to say, it's unfinished and that's too bad because it does a few things that other games of this kind don't do, but overall it's a mediocre experience.
You can still play this in single player, or on one of about a half dozen active servers, but I'm not sure if it's worth the $10 or so it's currently going for.  I had some fun once I got the hang of it, but the game's just so rough around the edges it doesn't stand up to other, similar titles in the genre.  It really is a shame that they didn't stick around to finish this properly.

LONG REVIEW - BE PATIENT.
The best advice I can give if you are going to play RE6, is start with the Leon missions. Do missions in the order they appear; Leon, Chris, etc. I thought you chose one character and played the whole game with that person and skill set. I chose Ada, the last character, and it was incredibly difficult with hardly any ammo. Sheer desperation made me mention how hard it was in a forum, and I was told start with Leon.
The game is cram packed full of cut-scenes, either long or short. The short ones are on average about every two minutes. It constantly pulls control away from the player. It might just be that  the ground rocks, but then you lose control, the camera sways, and the character wobbles. Then you have to press your control keys again to get going. There are parts of the game where it happens less, then there parts when it's non-stop. There are even times when it takes camera angle control from you and expects you to carry on.
Over-all though it is a constant wrangle to maintain control. When you get to a ledge, you can't just jump up it. You have to wait for it to say 'space', then you can press space and jump up. Nearly everything is controlled in this way throughout. Endless, endless pressing keys.
That brings you onto the quick-time-events. Non-stop button mashing that has nothing to do with normal control. It's Ok to an extent, but even the most patient person gets annoyed. You think, "what is this for".
Then onto how difficult it can be. There is one part I recall. 3rd Chris chapter, you have to run across a load of boats and moorings. You have to make it within time, or wherever you are you die. Checkpoints make you repeat it until you get it right. I can not tell you how bad that whole event was. I was screaming. (Not the only time I was screaming in this game either.)
5/10 is generous, but I don't quite think it's a 4/10. It's strong points are that sometimes the combat is great. The sets can be OK, but mostly they are dimly lit. The cathedral chapter in the Leon campaign is epic. If only they had made the whole game like that.
The bosses are just unbelievably annoying. The Leon boss kept coming back at various latter stages of the Leon missions. I became sick of the sight of it, and sick of shooting it. Completely stupid method to kill it. I had to search online to find out how. What they have done is build up the difficulty over each character's campaign. Only it doesn't work. It feels like catastrophic insulting garbage from the developers, and you want blood as compensation. They try to make it a huge experience. However all it does is fall flat on it's face by kicking you in the teeth non-stop.
Falling over is something that happens a lot with your character. Endless boom, flat on your back. It's noisy a lot. In fact they should have called the game - 'Boom, flat on your back'. I honestly don't know if I can finish it. I have given it a good go. I sold RE5 (CD-copy) unfinished as well.

TL;DR: If you can pick it up for under 20 dollars, it is worth a purchase.  I wouldn't pay full price for it though.  6/10
I can recommend this game, with caveats.  The story is passable, but the dialog is almost universally unbearable.  Cheesy bordering on sickening in some parts.  If I hear another character say "Are you serious?" or "You gotta be kidding me!" in a Resident Evil game, I will probably close the game right then and there and throw my wireless mouse at a baby.
The gameplay is... unpolished? To say the least.  The degree to which the game starts to get annoying / hard to play / needlessly complicated varies depending on which campaign you play.  I saved Leon's story for last since I was hoping his would be the best / most entertaining / interesting.  Mistakes were made.  In order of enjoyable gamplay, I would rank the campaigns Jake > Ada > Chris > Leon.  In order of enjoyable story, I would rank the campaigns Ada > Jake > Chris > Leon.
Leon's campaign really makes me upset.  It has a different set of enemies than the other 3 campaigns and even on normal difficulty, you will die a lot.  I have played almost every Resident Evil game and consider myself to be pretty experienced in the gameplay, I still found myself dying a lot to a lot of stupid things, most of which you cannot control.  For example, there is one boss encounter where you are forced to take constant damage for a brief period.  If you are below half health before this segment starts, you will die instantly and cannot be revived by your partner.  In another section, you are attacked by concealed enemies and without prior knowledge of the encounter, there would be no feasible way to avoid incoming damage (it's a semi-submerged area).  Again, if you are attacked in this spot with low health, you will immediately die with no chance to heal or be revived by your partner (you get knocked down and then instead of triggering the "hurt" state where you can crawl away to safety, you will instantly drown).
QTE's are also a big part of my problem with this game.  They are more intrusive than RE4 or 5's, in my opinion, and very rarely add any enjoyment to the gameplay experience.  Having played RE4 somewhat recently, the QTE events in that game were never as punishing and always at least gave you a brief warning before you were expected to react.  A lot of QTE in this game expect you to know what is coming and react to it with prior knowledge.  I died a lot of times to random QTE events during cutscenes that had no warning and didn't really provide any good context or necessity for them.
The prologue would make you think that Leon's is the campaign you should start with, I would put it at second or third.  If you play it first, you might quit the game entirely before you get to the more fun campaigns.  If you save it til the end like I did, you will leave the game with a bad taste in your mouth.  Leon's campaign has some of the worst dialog and the weakest plot of the 4 main campaigns, in my opinion.  While the whole story is traversed by most of the cast, Leon's portion just feels icky.  Helena is a terrible partner and Leon himself is basically a one-liner spouting husk of his RE4 self.  Other campaigns have bad dialog, but at least I didn't actively want the characters in those stories to die so that I would not have to endure it.
I have not personally played co-op but from the single player missions, I can tell that the co-op experience here is almost identical to that of Resident Evil 5.  You and your partner will often be working together nearby, followed by sporadic sections of splitting up to help each other through obstacles while covering one another.  It lends itself to an "easy" co-operative experience, meaning there is low performance stress on you and your partner.  At most, you will find yourself running to knock an enemy off of your partner, whereas most of your co-op interactions will involve pressing buttons and spinning the stick to move a platform or open a door.
All in all, if you like Resident Evil games or third person shooters involving zombies, you'll enjoy this game.  If you're not a fan of the Resident Evil franchise or only casually looking at this game as a co-op option, I would recommend looking elsewhere.

Wow. I had this game sitting in my library for months before I decided to give it a try. I am amazed by the amount of effort that was put into this free visual novel. For a free-to-play game, this was exceptional. I would've paid maybe $10 or $15 for it, to be completely honest. It's a high school slice-of-life, mixed with mystery/suspense, and even aspects of a psychological thriller. The art is what must've made this game free, because it was unimpressive at times. The story wasn't lacking. A perfect amount of multiple endings. I didn't necessarily get the ending I desired, but that doesn't damage my enjoyment. There were puzzle elements, though they were easy enough to complete. Made it really interactive, especially since they make you type things to advance in the game at some points, so they're required. The themes are powerful and I often saw myself applying myself to them. The subjects this game addressed consists of mental disabilty/disorder, human purpose/ability/capability, and death of loved ones. The dialogue was also very intelligible. I've mentioned how I have an affinity for rather extensive vocabularies present in games. I was forced to actually think in this game, became attached to some of the characters, and was genuinely surprised when the twist happened(find out for yourself lol). The length only poses an issue when considering replayability. It's good, but not to the point where I'll go back just for completeness. Even with the skip function and save points, it would take too long. Other than that, my qualms with this game cease. Devastatingly shattered my expectations for a free-to-play visual novel. Maybe its flaws aren't too detrimental after all.

Crysis 2 was the most enjoyable of the crysis franchise for me (note* do not own crysis 3 yet).
Exciting, well paced, its campaign was reminisent of COD4's campaign, arcadey and fun.
The nanosuit integrated strength/speed in this iteration of Crysis and it was a welcomed change.
You now choose from Armor or Stealth for your suits powers.
There was an added suit powerup rpg element added, but its thin and only is there to encourage the killing of the more difficult opponents, the alien steph.
AI works well as usual for the crysis series, and is a suitable and fun challenge at the Normal difficulty (which I played through on).
Weaponry was mostly boring, although the sniper rifle was amazing and powerful.  Definitely could have used some weaponry variety as most guns felt identical or were identical.  The special x-43 was not very fun or special.  I stuck with the rifle whenever it was available.
Completed the game, took 7:30 minutes of actual in game campaign play.
Multiplayer is interesting and fun too, a sleeper hit.
Recommended at sale level, as I never buy a full priced game and neither should you (drive prices down, $60 is never reasonable for a gaming experience unless you are talking skyrim type games with 100+ hours of  atual gameplay).

So, most of the negative views for this game revolve around an issue where the SecuROM DRM failed to yield an activation.
That issue has since been fixed, so you can buy and play this game reliably.
That aside, this game was, for me, a pleasant surprise. It satisfied an itch I've had for a shooter, but also gave me something else to yearn for in the future - seamless horizontal to vertical combat.
Writing wise, the game is pretty solid. There are some thematic elements that will feel familiar - a LOST-style island, references to reptillian conspiracies, a bit of the Matrix-style Oracle-tells-Neo-To-Save-The-World kind of stuff. It's a little flat towards the end, but its engaging enough to be enjoyable.
The characters themselves are simple enough - the main character (voiced by Nolan North of Uncharted fame) is the typical male super-protagonist, pilot turned badass super soldier with a jetpack. You don't get very much A.I. help, and the friendly A.I. are just barely useful. That said, they aren't really necessary for much more than that - the majority of the game you alone are enough to handle the enemy hordes while the A.I functions nicely as cannon fodder. They _do_ deal damage though, which is nice - you can't assume they can finish an enemy off, but they certainly help a bit.
The enemy A.I. isn't half bad either. They make use of cover, attempt to flank, use grenades, and will use jetpacks in mid-to-late game to get around you and take a vertical position of fire. It's not the smartest A.I. in the world of gaming, but they certainly put up a decent challenge.
Now, with that said, the gunplay is pretty straightforward at best - cover-based combat in the beginning isn't anything special. But you'll find you don't use it very often, because you have a BLOODY JETPACK.
The jetpack transforms you into Rocketman, blasting around the landscape with mounted guns blasting the crap out of enemies. It's well balanced - in hover mode you can boost around, taking advantage of the landscape to take on enemies on lower planes of battle, or engaging mid-air enemies efficiently. Some areans allow for full-range combat, converting from hover to full jet mode. In the latter you forgo your traditional weapons for a mounted gun that does tremendous damage to ground troops and moderate damage to flying ships.
The addition of vertical combat was a very welcome change. It reminded me a bit of old Unreal tournament or Tribes in a sense - being able to descend upon the enemy was a very warm and awesome feeling. Smart use of aerial maneuvers could allow the player to zip through and lay down fire like an A-10 on enemis, swap to hover mode, and rain down from the rear while what few A.I. friendlies keep up fire from the front. It *does* work rather well in the end.
The maps are generally well done - many times there are areas to engage enemies vertically, as well as traditional horizontal cover-based advances. Your jetpack is given plenty of areas to be used, and this helps keep combat fluid and engaging. There are always ways for you to get an advantageous position on the enemy, even at the risk of being shot out of the sky.
I do have some gripes, in the end - there is an upgrade system that feels very half done. Weapons can gain up to 3 levels of linear upgrades, as does the jetpack. But it doesn't seem like there are enough upgrade orbs in the entire game to allow for more than a few fully leveled weapons. I went with the standard human weapon and a fully upgraded jetpack in the end, because the human rifle gets explosive rounds and that seemed to last well into the endgame. I will say this - endgame opponents are serious bullet-sponges, even with upgraded gear. It got a little annoying because the upgrade tree maxes out so quickly. It was an unfortunate oversight as it would have allowed for end-game units to be challenging instead of annoying. There is a dearth of instruction in the game - you can hijack enemy aircraft, but there is (to my knowledge) no guide to figure out the mixture of pressing 'E' to rip a panel off, and A/D to dodge around. There is at least one boss battle where the prompt says 'PRESS A AND D' instead of "PRESS A OR D". The latter will save you, while the former will force you into re-doing a relatively time-consuming sequence.
There are not a lot of quicktime events, thankfully, but the ones that are there do not feel very challenging or engaging. I feel that if you are going to have QTE for boss/miniboss sequences, make it something a little more involved - the final boss QTE is very underwhelming.
It is, in the end, a rather short game - expect to beat it in a sitting. I did it in about 7 hours on normal - I think hard would only yield another hour of gameplay at best. There are collectibles that may extend the gameplay experience - new game + allows them to pop up on your radar so you'll find them a bit easier (which, given the often extensive maps to fight on, its easy to miss them). Unfortunately CAPCOM didn't take the opportunity to really expand on a world that could have dived much, much deeper. I would say this title is worth it on sale for a Saturday worth of blasting lizard-robot alien scum and saving the world.

Dark Void is a mix of a lot of different games. Take the ground combat of Killswitch and Gears of War, throw in some flight combat like Crimson Skies, add a pinch of human enslavement from Prey and Half Life 2, and you have Dark Void. Now it's not as good as any of those games, but it is worth a play through. The story is an interesting take on The Bermuda Triangle but has more than a few holes in it, but i would like to see someone pick this up and continue on with it. In the right hands and a little more finesse, I think it could turn into a decent franchise. For me the vertical cover system and the ability to go from cover based firefights to hopping in the air with your rocketpack to flank and even strafe your enemies was the freshest and most interesting part of the game. It is without a doubt worth $10 in my opinion.

The story is told entirely through narration (and great narration, at that), since none of the characters can speak. This choice on the part of the developers was pure genius. The wording and the voice of the narrator really allowed me to connect with the plotline and with those lovable little shapes. That fact alone is worth repeating: This game actually gave me a personal connection with characters that were nothing more than geometrical shapes. Any game that can do that is truly worth playing. Not only that, but the ending makes me cry, every time I play it. Maybe I'm a wimp, but I think that the ending is really that good. From the beginning, when we meet Thomas (who was alone), to the breath-taking end, this game is truly a journey, one that will leave you in awe of how such a simple story with such simple characters could leave such a profound impact.

I keep meaning to write up this review, but one thing has kept getting in the way: playing more Caves of Qud.
CoQ is a turn-based roguelike sci-fi RPG with a static overland map and prodecural dungeons that is unashamedly old-school in style and presentation. It has a steep learning curve and is often very obtuse; for instance, finding out that you need to buy the Corpus Choliys from Mayor Nuntu in Kyakukya to cure diseases is not mentioned in the game text or dialogs. And then following the instructions to cure said disease can require further delving into forums and message boards.
But for all its frustration, CoQ is a very enjoyable game that keeps pulling me back. The character creation options are very broad, and the interaction of various mechanics in the game is rich and varied. The game is very much in Early Access still, there is a memory leak that pops up warnings to save and restart the game from time to time, and the main quest is not fully implemented yet. Some people have reported that patches have made their old saves unusable, although that hasn't happened to me yet.
But if you can forgive its flaws and rough edges, the charm of the game outweighs its detractions. If you don't like old-school RPGs like Wasteland, the early Ultimas (I-V) or other roguelikes like ADOM, URR, C:DDA, Dwarf Fortress, you probably won't be converted by CoQ. But if you do, you're in for a treat. Recommended.

Don't let the minimalist graphics fool you. Blueprint Tycoon has a lot of depth in the core loop of balancing multiple competing supply chains. The core gameplay involves managing labor supply, resource extraction, transportation, and refining on a two stage pattern: On the first level, buildings, roads, ships, and airships form the common elements of the genre. On the second level, each building has its own cellular automata that can be programmed to provide faster speed, more output per input, or less waste. The default blueprints are typically near the best speeds I could reach and very resilient about recoving from a temporary stoppage due to empty inputs or full outputs, but at higher levels there's room to program them for lots of improvement.
The implementation isn't what I'd demand from a major developer, and the game suffers from the lack of a few features like the ability to troubleshoot when a building's production blueprint hangs and the lack of an audio cue when losing money or reputation at the end of a day.
If you like the economic-production-line niche, it's worth the few bucks. If you don't like that niche, Blueprint Tycoon is definately not for you.

=TL;DR=
Crysis 2 - Maximum Edition is a solid, though largely unremarkable shooter that does it's fanbase a disservice by dropping the free roam and multi-optional gameplay from the original for a linear, Call of Duty like experience that obviously tries to hard to copy CoD, but never took much steam from the series and harmed the reputation of Crysis in the process. The game is fine for folks that like CoD campaigns and the Crysis theme.

=Overview=
Note: I completed this game in 10 hours within Origin. Steam probably shows no time for me.
Crysis 2 - Maximum Edition is futuristic, modern military shooter set in the Crysis universe: which means it mostly involves gunplay, combat options, well detailed environments and use of the Nanosuit, which grants Supersoldier like ehancements to the average Marine. Unlike it's Crysis 1, Crysis 2 is even more linear due to a level design that shoves players down corridors and streets with little options for exploration and a game design that provides no incentive to customize your gameplay. It's essentially a Call of Duty campaign with a Crysis theme.
=Presentation=
It looks as good or better than most games of its time. The nanosuit is beautifully detailed as usual, and character models seem to look better when you can see them close. The Ceph look great up close and would make for some excellent real world figures. World textures are generally good, but not perfect - screens and signs look great, but wall textures look console quality. Physics act as expected and rarely I've had moments where an enemy body would hilariously fly off the screen without good reason or get stuck in geometry "Bethesda game style". I played this in Origin (don't remember why), sI couldn't get screenshots. Not that it mattered, as there were only a few times I wanted one, versus the 100+ times in Crysis 1.
Sound design is as it should be. Combat sounds like guns, explosions, and melee have the expected punch that a AAA game should, though I don't specifically remember stuff like loud echoes in tight spaces or super loud bangs from sniper rifles and shotguns (which still sound good, but not so loud that you would need earmuffs or head gear in real life). The soundtrack is of great quality which should be considering much of it is composed by Hanz Zimmer, but beyond the main menu music, is good, but unmemorable. I do however really like the menu music, which really has that dramatic, epic, and dreadful feeling as seen from Modern Warfare 2.
Voice acting is good, though you probably won't remember any voices beyond Prophet and the nanosuit.
=Gameplay=
The open world gameplay has been stripped down to a bog standard corridor shooter with occasional open spots with few options. While Crysis 1 was still a very linear game. it gave you options on how to approach "objective areas" well before you got to it, unless there was only one way into it. Now, you're following a path and then you reach the objective area in which you do have a few options, by taking a slightly alternate path to flank, creeping around to perform stealth kills (or not kill at all), finding a turret, vehicle, or explosive barrel to use against packs of enemies....Honestly, the combat options are actually equal to that of Crysis 1, but it generally feels that the best option is to take care of the biggest or nearby threats, and then hustle it to the objective, as it will eventually take you to the next area for you to skip the enemies. Stealth is effective, but it's much easier to use cloak to occasionally hide from enemies after combat or get the first shot on them.
Considering that your upgrades all come from Nano Catalysts which drop from the Ceph enemies (which stupidly enough, disappear after a certain time. This aint the NES era!), there's no bonus or detriment to killing enemies a certain way - you may as well run and gun since the heavier enemies require explosives or heavy weaponry to take down. The upgrade system provides handy upgrades that slightly customizes your play, but nothing to dramatically change your playstyle - you could probably play the game successfully without even bothering with upgrades.
The gunplay is solid, though nothing new. Guns feel good to use, especially the Feline Revolver, Heavy Machine Gun (which are pretty neat to dismount), and some of the later "Power weapons" like the L-Tag grenade launcher or the XFire. The use of abilities are more streamlined than the first game, so instead of switching modes to enable every action, the suit enhances you where it makes sense. Your speed mode is enabled the moment you run, super jump (holding the Jump key to jump higher than normal), and climb (your climbing speed can be upgraded). Strength mode engages when you melee, detach HMGs, or steady yourself with Shift to shoot more accurately - however, it can be enabled manually to reduce fall damage as well as the enchancements listed earlier. Armor mode and cloak however, are much like the previous game where they need to be activated and deactivated manually unless energy is depleted. However, Armor now does drain energy over time. While I miss the RPG-esque styling of the original, this does work better, but you have to be careful when sprinting around and armoring/cloaking behind cover - you will be looking at the energy bar alot. The function that allows you to toggle different suit modes is seriously less responsive and clunky. Before in Crysis 1, I could easily roll the mouse while holding the assigned mouse key to select a mode. Now in Crysis 2, that function is still partially there, but sometimes, the game doesn't recognize where your mouse is and doesn't register a selection, requring me to move my mouse alot to get to where I need. I believe this has to due with the fact of having the game ported to console systems, so the circle could probably recognize which "zone" the player pushed the stick. While I can just as easily use assigned keyboard keys, I preferred the radial mouse key menu.
My biggest gripe about the game is it's clear "I want to be Call of Duty too!" Syndrome. Extremely linear game design, regularly scripted setpiece/cutscene moments, "slow walking can't use your gun while listening sequences", hunts for mostly pointless and tallied collectibles (there are keys for civilian vehicles, but you won't be driving much in this game. I entered a car maybe 6 times?), and on rails tank rides. Don't forget typical military jargon. I'm sure EA coerced the developers to make the game much like Call of Duty to compete with them. This means this game does pratically nothing unique for the genre or industry and made itself another CoD clone to get lost in the shuffle. You even have those typical satellite, wireframe debriefing overviews like every other modern military shooter does, but at least I personally like those.

Multiplayer community is nearly dead with about 3-6 active servers. The little I played was a decent CoD clone, but I got kicked out of every server because the game couldn't verify DLC purchases, even though, i just put in the key to unlock the Maximum Edition  "DLC". Don't buy this for multiplayer. Like all games of this type these days, you can't use custom weapons and classes until after gaining XP.
=Summary=
Crysis 2 is a decent linear shooter, but you're not missing out on much. If you're a core shooter gamer, chances are that you're playing something or could be playing something else better anyways. If you were wanting more of Crysis 1, checkout it's modding community, or maybe even Crysis Warhead and Crysis 3 (I haven't played them yet). I can't recommend this to somebody who really values their time and doesn't want to waste it on anything but the best games - it mostly a standard modern military shooter.

CRYSIS 2 MAXIMUM EDITION is a first-person shooter video game developed by Crytek, published by Electronic Arts and released in 2011 as CRYSIS 2 REGULAR EDITION before being later released as CRYSIS 2 MAXIMUM EDITION in 2012. It is the sequel to CRYSIS aka CRYSIS 1.
Set during the Great Depression of 2023, CRYSIS 2 MAXIMUM EDITION focuses on Prophet, a nanosuit-wearing mute soldier from a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, agricultural industry changes, and bank foreclosures forcing tenant farmers out of work. Due to his nearly hopeless situation, and in part because he was trapped in the alien invasion apocalypse, Prophet sets out for New York. Along with thousands of other generic gun-fodder soldiers, he sought jobs, land, dignity, big guns that can murder ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and a future.
CRYSIS 2 MAXIMUM EDITION is infrequently played in American high school and college literature classes due to its lack of historical context and nonexistent legacy, plus the fact it is a video game, not a book. A sequel, CRYSIS 3 MAXIMUMEST EDITION was released in 2013 to general lack of interest, but it's only on Origin, and who would want to use Origin? Nobody, that's who.
Anyway, CRYSIS 2 MAXIMUM EDITION is not very good.

Great roguelike! It fits the classic roguelike style in a lot of ways, but it definitely has it's own feel. The early game difficulty seems to vary, but I hear it gets extremely hard later on.
I have no idea how it would be received by a non roguelike player, as I've been playing ascii roguelikes for years, but the controls and menus are definitely more stream-lined than dcss/adom/etc. It's EA, so a lot of these elements are still being worked on and improved.
--------------------------
For roguelike players, I really feel like this game truly has a unique feel, so it's hard to explain. I'll try to relate examples I'm familiar with that express the 'feel' of the game.
It has the big open overmap style of ADOM, where you can really go wherever you want (and probably die). From the big overmap squares you can 'enter' the ground level and travel in normal turns. It's far from complicated Nethack in gameplay, but it's not quite as simplified as DCSS.
There are a lot of interactions, here's a fairly strong example; you have containers you use for carrying water for drinking and trading. But there are other uses, if you are on fire, you can pour water on yourself to put it out, you can make puddles on the ground, drop bloody weapons into them to wash it off. You can gather pretty much any liquid, afaik, including slime, tar, and use it as a (fairly ineffective, in my experience :p) trap. You can even gather blood, for whatever reason. All of these fluids you can pour on the ground, you can drink them and see what happens, you can pour them on yourself. There's a lot of fun experimenting. But I wouldn't say the item interactions are to the complex level of Nethack.
Most of the time when you are actually exploring the world or dungeons, it's more about you using your skills and mutations effectively, or running/using consumables when you're in over your head. But you won't have huge stacks of teleport scrolls or haste potions or anything like that. It's pretty common to see a really strong monster even when you're just lvl 2. You will need to use the sprint skill. Your build and play style is heavily dependant on your mutations/skills. Character building is huge. So far I haven't found any 'get out of jail free card's, like ?tele, in this game (besides the all powerful sprint skill, and some really powerful mental mutations).
Because of the fact that there's no 'clock', you are free to progress as fast as you want. Food and water is easy to get.
There's no cursed items, and the ID game is for a subset of items called artifacts (that end up being various things, like grenades, chairs, weapons) and consists of paying someone to ID it for you, or getting the intelligence/skills to id them yourself.
--------------------------
The free, outdated ascii version gives a bit of insight as to whether you might like the game, but the steam version has come a very long way; I didn't get hooked on the older version nearly as much as I have the new one.
It's EA. So far, I found one bug that caused me to lose data until my last save (that was promptly fixed about twenty minutes later, but still, save often, and turn on the auto save option). I've been having a very complete and really fun experience so far. The price is also really amazing for even the current level of content. I don't expect to make it far enough to see, but the main quest is unfinished. And there are other big upcoming changes, such as more content in the very early game (which you're likely to be seeing a lot of), and eventually different starts. I heard complaints about losing saves, but apparently you can just roll back to the last version thru steam and the save should still be there. I don't tend to like EA, but I'd probably be willing to pay more than the purchase price for the game in it's current form.

Let’s get the obvious out of the way first: CRYSIS 2 looks great. You would expect stunning visuals from Crytek and they deliver here in spades. Alien-devastated New York feels very realistic as you work your way through the dust and trash that blows in the air. Much has been said about the fact that you have to work our way through the streets rather than roam freely, as was possible in the first Crysis game, and it’s true that C2 is less open-world than the original. But it never feels as though you’re being herded and there is some room for exploration within the confines of the streets. But even though this aspect is a little disappointing C2 is an improvement on the original in most aspects. The suit controls have been made far more intuitive and it’s now possible to upgrade it as you gather points through despatching alien invaders. The story is less nebulous than in the first and the action is far more intense, with barely a moment to take a breath at times. The set-pieces are more epic in scope and there’s a real sense of urgency throughout. Sadly it’s not a long game. I took my time but still completed it in a little under 20 hours. But if you like the Crysis franchise this game is a worthy follow up to the original, even though it doesn’t quite have the same overall impact. Now onto Crysis 3 … 4/5

Have just completed it. However, it's vastly inferior to the first installment of Crysis (as is the case with many console-first games) in terms of graphics, gameplay, FOV, basically anything you can come up with. In a desperate attempt to compensate for all of this, Crysis 2 is full of special effects and movie-like scenes.

The main strength of the campaigns of Crysis is their sandbox, unrestricted nature, and Crysis 2 is a step back from Crysis 1 and Warhead in this regard, as you run through cities with closed-in walls instead of trek through jungles. However, each specific battle (and there were many times I felt like I was facing "boss" enemies) takes place in a pretty large area, so I never felt particularly restricted.
The guns and combat are as crisp and satisfying as they were in the first two Crysis games.
The suit's powers are now accessed with keyboard shortcuts, which makes their use feel more isolated, like sprinting in other games, and power jumps are accessed with a single button (holding down space), instead of requiring an activation of strength mode, making me feel less like I was operating a special suit, and more like I was just a superhero - it's less mechanical-feeling, for better or for worse, I guess.
Towards the end of the campaign, I became extremely dependent on cloaking, which is overpowered. It's much faster to sneak around the enemy strongholds, going straight for the objectives, than it is to run roughshod over every enemy one-by-one. Maybe I became so objective-oriented because I was enthralled with the campaign (wishing to finish it as soon as possible), because, in other games, I generally take the time to kill every enemy I see.
My most significant complaint about Crysis 2 is that, with the closed-in areas, specific, restricted routes are required to arrive at objectives within each mission, but there is no guide system (line on the ground) to show you where to go, which would have been appreciated at several points in the campaign, as I found myself trapped in rooms, going in circles trying to open doors that wouldn't budge. If you get stuck and resort to searching online for a level guide, you'll find many other people commenting that they were stuck at the same point as you.
Dying can set you back annoyingly far. Don't die.
The suit's upgradability is neat, but generally not integral, and unlikely to scope an individual's tactics.
There aren't a lot of people playing Crysis 2's multiplayer, although there are more than enough to have a few big games going at all times. Still, this is a game to be bought for its campaign, and I highly doubt you will be left disappointed after completing it. It's exciting, engaging, and challenging, and ranks among my favorite 10-11 hour spans of gaming

I want to like this game I really do, but it's just too flawed to really enjoy myself.
Ok, let's start with balance, or lack there of. In a coordinated group, counslers are almost impossible to stop from escaping. With multiple stunning options and the easy ability to kite for a minutes at a time. Add to that the spawning has a set pattern, it can be fast and easy to complete multiple objectives. On the flip side if you play with inexperianced or unskilled players it's a slaughter for Jason. This can lead to frustration for both sides, and ultimately a very bland and silly meta forced due to bad mechanics.
Then the glitches, oh the glitches. I could write a small novel on how buggy this game can be. Add the slower patch times to the mix, and you should get the idea.
Finally the lag issues. I have no problems with my ping. It sits a little high for my taste (70-90), but I personally rarely have issues. No the problerm lies in all the non NA regions playing with 200-400 ping on NA servers causing annoying teleporting kills. It's very frustrating to juke Jason just to teleport back and die. A region lock is desperately needed, the NA servers are flooded with Russians and it's not fun to deal with as a NA player.
While it can have fun moments, I just cannot recommend this game or give it a positve review. Maybe things will change in the future as updates and content are planned in the coming months, but for now, avoiding this game is probably the better idea.

It does use a lot of RAM, when I alt tabbed out of the game I saw I was using 8GB so if you have less then 16GB you may run into issues. The fighting style was great for single player. Basically defense is more important then offense and you have to block or you will get destroyed. You have to counter attack. The single player story was awesome and I think I just got to the last mission before the free weekend ended. All that being said I have the feeling the fighting style would be bad for a PVP game. From the reviews I've read between the fighting style and laggy servers it looks like this game fails to deliver a good PVP experience. That's why I'm on the fence. I've played enough PVP games to know if a large portion of the player base is complaining there's probably a problem. There's no way I would pay $60 for this game and I'm not sure I would pay $30 either. I'll have to research to see if there is any more single player content before I decide because that was top notch. I did get 23 hours in so there's a fair amount of story content and it does have replayability on different dificulties and to look for collectables. I'd say if you can get it on sale it's worth buying for the single player content and I imagine the devs will attempt to improve the PVP aspect.

Slender: The Arrival was a rather great game. It had a complete story line to lore you in, a beautifully building atmosphere, and the graphics where absolutely STUNNING. There are little few bugs from what I've found(And trust me, the second I get a game, I like trying to break the maps to said game.), and a nice map to free explore.
But by far, the best thing I found about Slender: The Arrival, HAD to be it's atmosphere. It had a great build up that left the player on edge, which made the jump scares all the more better. The rustling of the forest around you, the crunching of the leaves, or in the case of the generator level, the sound of footsteps running at you, all help immerse the player. The game uses rather nice functions of forcing the player to do what they don't want to, such as entering a building or going down a hall to grab a note, knowing they'll have to go back and he might be standing there.
Although, I will say, the complaint I have about this game is that the enemies themselves often get stuck on objects while coming after you. It subtracts from the game play to know if you angel yourself right or quick turn a corner, you could get them stuck there for a moment. In Slenders case, He'll become unstuck the second you move to far away and instead transport away, but in Kate/Jeff The Killer/ Whoever the one running after you is, They could get stuck there for a good while.
This game is best played in the dark, with either surround sound or headphones in for best possible outcome.
Overall, I'd give it a 8.9 of 10.

This is the definitive game for the Horror genre. Psychological horror at its finest. This is like a scream of fresh air in a dark, underground cave -- compared to the unimaginative games that claim to embody fear in the form of gore. In this game you will find almost no gore. You will be scared because you are scared of fear itself. You have no big guns to protect you, no base-building or crafting that will distance you from this inevitable horror. Thomas Was Alone is a 2D puzzle platformer created by Mike Bithell first as a flash game, and later ported to the unity engine and released in 2012. The game is also available for PS3, PS Vita, Linux and android besides Steam's PC and Mac version.
This game is about getting rectangles to the end of the level. No, seriously. These rectangles can move, jump, and some have special abilities. Also, they come in all shapes and sizes. Working together, they have to reach their corresponding exit. Sounds amazing right? No? Well, thankfully it's a bit more than that. Taking cues from the widely successful Bastion, the game's story is told by an exceptionally good narration, done by Danny Wallace (also know as Shaun from Assassin's Creed II and onward). But he is not just telling the story, he represents the thoughts and personality of the rectangles, whom by the way have their own name. How can a rectangle have personality, you might ask? They are actually A.I.s inside a computer system. A.I.s, become sentient and suddenly realizing their fate and purpose. Your job is to guide them across the hazards of the enviroment to get to their destination. Additional story bits can be seen as pieces of the programmers e-mails pop-up from time to time. So as you may have guessed, in the beginning Thomas was alone, and then came others to help him in his journey. The narration is very well written and also very humorous, frequently telling us about the A.I.s relationship with each other. As you progress through the game more and more A.I.s come, slowly introducing new personalities and abilities to the game, keeping you interested throughout the entire story. It won't be always crowded tho, the number of rectangles you have to get across are varied. But what of the hazards? Not really much to say on that regard, at first you won't have any, your goal will be to get them across walls mostly. Later comes water (which only can be traversed by one A.I.) and of course the all time favourite spikes. In the late game some of the A.I.s abilities are mixed together, so the challenge will be to maintain the use of the right one. The gameplay is solid, all movement animations are spot on and hard to find problems with them. The only thing I found hard to get hold on is the character change mechanic, I never knew which I'm going to switch to. The graphics are very minimalistic, even for a 2D platformer. All solid objects are black and every A.I. is represented by it's unique color, while the background is made of one color and a dark one at that, ocasionly having a pattern on it. Two things stood out for me in the graphics: The water looks and feels great, and the shadows also been done very well. Gravity is simulated very well, making a good jump feels satisfactory and diving into water realistic. Sadly the game comes to a short but satisfying end, lasting not much longer than six hours. Thankfully the ending is a good one, both happy and sad, and I shed a well deserved tear as the credits rolled. Achievement wise it's a fairly easy game, half of the achis are for completing the story and the other half is for finding all the hidden hollowed rectangles in the game. Some of those are a bit challenging, but nothing serious.
While Thomas Was Alone may only be a short, one time experience, it's an excellent game, achieving everything it's set out to do. The great level desing, exceptional narration will suck you in really fast and won't let you go till you finish the game. I can recommend this game to everyone, even if you don't like the genre, as the difficulty is not that high here. That may turn down some hardcore platformer fans, but even if you never come back to this game, the story still worth it alone.
Thanks for reading, and feel free to comment or contact. Good gaming to you!

*Sigh*  Where to start?
I love horror titles like this.  This, and Dead by Daylight are a couple of my favorite multiplayer horror IPs.  I definitely WANT to reccomend this game, and in the end will give it a thumbs up because it CAN be pretty damn fun, but there needs to be some serious polish done to server connectivity (which at the time of this writing I am unsure there has been much of save a couple of instances).  Second, granted these are simply my opinions, I feel like the following tweaks could be made to promote better gameplay perhaps:
-Playing as Tommy should be an additional win condition.  As the only character in the series known to "kill" Jason, having a player to luckily stumble across his CB Radio should create a new win condition with Tommy's shotgun.  One random player, one shot, one kill.  Everything rides on them, creating a new level of tension.  I know the arguement may be that Jason is SUPPOSED to kill everyone, or that a one-shot mechanic may be too powerful, but tell me honestly how many times you've seen Jason Instant Transmission dodge a surefire shot, or how many times you've seen a scared player as Tommy completely goof the shot?  You will on occasion get the one individual to respawn as Tommy who can make the play, but with the roulette on top of Jason's powers, I'd like to say its a 50/50 chance.  Jason could also get some sort of personal notification that his nemesis has entered the field, letting the Jason player know that the playing field just got serious if they really want to go for a full clear.
-Give Jason some emotes.  Whenever I play as Jason, its never my intention to murder straight away.  I like to chase players around, talk to them through voice chat while putting on silly voices or soundboards.  It would be even better I feel if Jason could get some emotes as well.  You could make them silly, serious or a mixuture in between, but I think it would bring some more fun to the playing field.
-Get rid of the handheld radio.  I've a few hours logged into the game, and of those hours I've had scarce few instances of people using the radio for its intended purpose.  It just becomes an empty item to pick up, more often than not.
-Give counselor players some kind of indicator of who picked up a Win Condition item, such as Car Keys, boat propeller and the like, as well as give players some kind of minimap indicator- perhaps lasting for a few seconds- of the WC-Holder's drop when they are killed, while keeping these indications muted from Jason, as I would think cannonically, he wouldn't really care for things that weren't able to be used to kill Campers.  Minded players can venture that way under risk so that they can continue to proceed through win conditions, rather than sputtering uselessly because Johnny No-Talk or Susan Solo-Player have picked up the Win Condition items, then died somewhere out in the woods, far, FAR away from everyone else.
I'm sure there are other things that more intelligent and more well-played players could suggest, but I'm only one man with one opinion.
I'm excited for the new Paranoia mode that they've been really tight-lipped on (AFAIK), and cannot wait to see what they have in store.  If you HAVEN'T bought the game yet, maybe wait for a sale.  If you're a Jason diehard, then this game can occasionally be a very good experience, with some muddling to occur along the way here and there.  It's not quite where it needs to be yet, I don't think.  But with some proper encouragement and funding, perhaps the experience will be even better.
3.5/5.  It's a decent game, not perfect, but not bad either.

For Honor is an original IP in an endless sea of AAA sequels and remakes. Unfortunately, For Honor is a game of caveats, which means that for everything positive there's something equally negative.
+The campaign is a fun romp which gets you familiar with the gameplay,
-But it's really short and you don't get to try every core character class.
+The game features a great soundtrack,
-But it's woefully underused.
+The gameplay is fun, deep, and plays like a 3D fighter,
-But the game just doesn't facilitate the gameplay well.
+Weapons and Armor are potrayed realistically which gives you a lot of Customization options,
-But they're locked behind grinding or microtransactions... and have useless stats tacked on.
+There's a huge multiplayer focus,
-But there's too few gamemodes and no dedicated servers.
Bottom Line:
I really wanted to be able to recommend For Honor and while it does have enjoyable aspects, it currently rests at a 6/10 and a way to high asking price. Try it during a free weekend or get it when it's REALLY cheap, but as for right now, the multiplayer is deserted and you're left with a fun, yet short campaign.

Positive - -
It's a crisis game, the gunplay is tight and responsive, when it works, and the nanosuit is still a lot of fun to play with, I appreciate the simpler control mechanics, and merging maximum speed and strength into the core functions, making combat more fluid. Instead of the old modes you are given a cloak and maximum armor toggles.

Weapon choices are varied and fun, giving you something for any engagement and some fun variations like the K-volt "Taser" SMG, a suppressed pump action shotgun and plenty of customization for each.

Negative - -
Having reached the half point of the game, I can tell you the story is just about all that keeps me going at this stage. Crysis 2 is horribly broken, the fun is getting hard to find, and the following explains why.
The AI is for the most part brain-dead, with occasional instances of brilliance, they will often completely fail to perform the simplest things, like throwing grenades and walking through doorways, sometimes letting you shoot them without a hint of reaction or even completely ignoring you.
Add to that several other mechanic breaking bugs like being unable to switch weapons / reload / aim down sights / pick up ammo at random, which got me killed more times than I care to remember. cloaking and the cover system only work partially and some enemies always manage to see you after cloaking or hiding behind cover to recharge, which makes taking the stealth route very tedious and frustrating.
Furthermore immersion is broken on a regular basis by malfunctioning AI constantly spamming their voice dialogues, sounds will also cut out for no apparent reason.
BIG disappointment, Crytek. The original game was hard on the computer, but at least it worked properly for the most part.

Has a hell of a lot more depth than I was expecting for £2, you can set up elaborate trade networks to complete contracts for the price of a pint of disgusting craft ale from Wetherspoon's.

This game is 5% plan, 5% build and 90% press the upgrade button for each building.

Blueprint Tycoon is a video game about managing supply-production chains, with tiers of workforce having requirements, as well production of goods for export from which wages are paid, setting up routes (such as own decision if one wants harvester to supply to crafter directly and/or through storage), research, buildings and routes being possible to upgrade, and as well being able to modify the "blueprints", meaning the actual production line within the building.
I enjoyed playing the six scenarios which come with the game, and it also has a classical open-end sandbox mode. But what I think makes the game really great is the in-game scenario editor, which lets not only set up just mission requirements but actually lets change most of it all.
So e.g. while the standard template says: "well, tier 1 workers require vegetables, which need to be grown on arable land from which they are taken to market and from there distributed to tier 1 worker housings", if one would actually want them to have e.g. coffee with that as well or perhaps just instead, the scenario editor lets set up coffee as resource, perhaps even add a production building before it gets to the market (if one wants to) and from there it gets distributed, while being able to import own pics for resources/products. Similarly about any production chain. Want to set up e.g. a template/scenario for detailed (heavy) industry production chains or perhaps furniture production chains or ...? Quite easy to do with the scenario-editor without any need whatsoever for classical modding, and all that easily uploadable to workshop to be shared.
Of course, one needs to keep in mind game mechanics for it all to be playable, but I find the scenario editor a great tool for creative approach about setting it up as one wants to in terms of what actually gets produced.
Visually it is alright, but in my opinion due to not plenty of visual distinction lacks an option to be able to highlight types of buildings since when there are plenty thereof and one can't be bothered to remember exactly where was what put, one needs to look for little icons, zoom in a lot or click on buildings individually. Also, being able to close a window by right clicking on it would be very nice since as far as I noticed none of the windows actually have the right-click as any functionality so playing with mouse it would be nice to not have always go for that X to close it. Besides that tho, great game.
