Ah, Rocksmith 2014 (now remastered!), the sequel to Rocksmith and a game, which is claimed to be 'the fastest way to learn guitar' (and bass). I'm here to elaborate on this statement.
First, I'd like to answer some potential questions related to the game.

Q: "What do I need and how do I start?"
A: Well, it IS in a way a guitar teacher, so you will obviously need a guitar or bass (notice: it can't be a classic or acoustic guitar) and the Real Tone Cable, so I advise the reader to buy the Rocksmith bundled WITH the cable. From what I heard, there was also a bundle with the guitar, but since I already had a guitar, I decided to buy Rocksmith for Xbox 360 with the cable. Starting is relatively simple, you plug the cable in your guitar and the computer,
and start the game.
Q:"Will I learn to play it like a super pro?"
A: I can't guarantee anything, it depends on YOU and YOUR dedication. If you want to master the guitar, you will have to train hard.
Q:"How long will it take for me to master the guitar/bass?"
A: Once again, it takes some people a couple of months to get really good, some might train for years. I learned the guitar in two years.
Now, questions aside, I should write down pros, cons, features and setbacks of the game.
Pros:
-You can play this game anytime. Unlike having scheduled lessons, choosing the perfect time is up to the player.
-This is not just a teacher. Rocksmith has many other features, which will be written down below.
-Huge amount of DLC. You can buy lots of songs you prefer, from Social Distortion to The Smashing Pumpkins.
-Cable versatility. If you, say, bought an Xbox 360 Rocksmith 1 version with the cable, like me, you can still play the PC version of Rocksmith 2014.
-
Yes, that's right, if you have a microphone, you can connect it to your computer and play the acoustic guitar! Alternatively, you could choose to play without any input, although this way most of the game's features won't be available.
Cons:
-Poor song selection. Not that I want to say there are more bad songs than good, there are just not enough free songs bundled with the original game. However, if you're willing to pay, there are lots of songs listed as DLC in the store.
Features:
-Guitar lessons, Rocksmith 2014 includes over 80 interactive lessons to help teach you almost every technique associated with guitar and bass.
-Session mode, where you can assemble and play with a virtual band.
-Mini-games. Yes, Rocksmith 2014 includes mini-games, concerning different techniques.
-The tuner. You will also be provided with a variety of guitar tunings to choose from. Not all Rocksmith 2014 songs are in E standard tuning. You can choose from several open tunings, as well as Eb, Drop D, C; D, C#, C standard and many more. And now you can even skip it!
-The chord book. It's not much of a book, but it sure has lots of different chords. Diminished, augmented, 13th, they're all there.

Setbacks:
-Uplay account requirement. Yes, unfortunately, you will have to create a Uplay account to play Rocksmith 2014. However, I somehow managed to start Rocksmith 2014 directly through steam, so I suppose it is no longer necessary. Apparently, however, now it's not a requirement. You COULD use it once or twice in order to unlock special songs and arrangements, but for the most part it's unnecessary.
Of course, I could not fit all of the things I wanted to say, but I believe it is enough to form the reader's opinion.
In conclusion, I would like to say that if you want to learn to play the guitar/bass and don't know anybody who can teach it, or just want to have fun in the game and play your favorite songs, Rocksmith 2014 would be one of the best solutions. Do get the game if you get the chance!

If you like building bridges, then this is a really good game!

This game surprised me.
Every time my bridge fails I giggle like a little girl. There's a lot of humor in these failures. There's also a lot of satisfaction to getting the little car to its destination even as the bridge under its wheels falls apart. What sort of hair-brained solution can you come up with that fits the budget?
I don't normally play games like this, but this is a good one.
Bridge building is an interesting metaphor. For civilization. For software development. For folly of man.
It's also hysterical just how fragile those things are. One wrong push and the whole card house disintegrates.
So why is it fun? This sounds like entropy, right? A very depressing affair?
It's physical humor.
1. Your bridge has a budget.
2. When you finally succeed, you will be graded based on how much money you spent.
3. There's a leaderboard for every level.
4. Can you make it cheaper?
5. Can you make it more flimsy?
6. Can you make it so pathetic that it crumbles the moment the car passes over it?
What follows is a series of ramps and accidents on a shoestring (literally) budget. Instead of a bridge, you make a swing with a ramp that grabs the car and flings it to the other side of the river, backflipping the entire time and landing on the goal post flag on its roof.
Because all that matters is that it got there. Never mind the dents on the roof or the bumpers.
Happy fishing!
But wait. Let's grade this on my 3 star scale.
1. Does it have elves? Nope.
2. Does it have swords? Nope.
3. Does it have pvp? Yes!
Those leaderboards totally count as pvp. Let the cheapest contractor win! 1 out of 3 is not bad!
P.S. You may never cross a bridge in real life again.
P.P.S. This game is an educational game. Sneakily, under the hood, it teaches you sound principles of engineering. And being a cheapskate. Those are vital life skills in today's economy.
P.P.P.S. I am recommending an educational game about crumbling infrastructure. Is this how it ends?

Not a bad game at all, so as long as you don't treat it like your typical RE game. Recommended to be played with online friends, or else it'll suck.
When I first played this on the PS3 on release, I was completely appalled with RE6's control mechanics. Trying to turn the franchise people knew and loved into a typical FPS shoot em' up, this is not what people expected after RE5.
However, as time passed, this game has found a place in my heart. Not as another RE game, but as a coop game to play with friends online, and this is where the game really shines.
When you play this game by yourself or play on split screen, the game is a chore. AI buddy is too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to be of any help, and playing split screen really can strain the eyes, especially if you don't have a monitor bigger than 27".
Honestly, I wish Capcom put the option to play offline coop on dual display, rather than being forced to just stick with two cropped rectangles on one screen, then this game would have gotten more thumbs up on my end.
But regardless, if you have a friend to play with and both of you have steam, get this game when it's on sale and play with each other online. You guys will have an awesome time.
Also a warning: If you guys are here for the story...yeah, you might want to chuck a good portion of that out the window. Most of the story is garbage, and won't be fun for either of you if you guys plan to take this game seriously. I tried playing this game both serious and both as casual fun, and I found myself loving to crack jokes at this games' story than actually being sucked into the story. And I'm all
story when it comes to games.
If you still plan to get the game, just know the controls take some time in getting used to. But if you're familiar with playing AAA fps games, then you'll get the hang of the controls faster. But if the only thing you've played is Resident Evil...you might curse the controls until the day you die.
But all in all, this is a game that people should try out for kicks. Just make sure to catch it when a sale hits.

I've been playing roguelikes since Rogue came out, though around those days I mostly played Nethack.
The genre has exploded, and the term "roguelike" has been greatly deprecated to mean something like "a fantasy or sci-game with some randomization each game." Sometimes, for extra special authenticity, the devs will include "permadeath" as a feature.
This is so far from what makes these games so fun and why they endure almost 40 years (!!!) later. Roguelikes are not only vastly different each play, the sheer number of possible combinations and the infinite dynamic terrains make each game an immersive and often hilarious experience. Caves of Qud captures everything fun about classic roguelikes, such as the seemingly infinite variability in how the game can be played, the diversity of character classes that puts Skyrim to shame, the vastness of dynamically generated landscapes, but with fascinatingly original features, factions, items, and stories. This is obviously a labor of love for the developers, who patch the game with new features EVERY WEEK.
I love coming back to this game after letting it sit for a few months and seeing all this new stuff in it. It's already a classic in the genre and it's just going to get bigger and weirder as time goes on.

After putting nearly 100 hours into this game, I can confidently say I thouroughly enjoyed this game. However, its plagued with a nasty community, and bad networking. Thankfully the devs have been hard at work tweaking the game to make it as balanced as possible, and they recently announced dedicated servers, which should fix the majority of networking problems.
The Pros:
-Deep and complex battles
-1v1's, 2v2's, and 4v4's are all nice gamemodes that really play on the games strengths
-Nice customization with emotes and effects, all purchasable with in-game credits
-Singleplayer isnt special, but its there and is a nice way to be introduced the different classes
The Cons:
-Bad Networking (being fixed)
-Toxic community
-grinding for cosmetics can be very tedious, but currency rewards have been increased since launch
-The larger scale gamemodes like dominion can be boring and frustrating.
In my opinions, the great gameplay is worth it, the smaller scale battles are deep and rewarding, and no character seems wildly overpowered against the rest. And while the community can be incredibly toxic, you can also find extremely helpful people who will give you tips on how to play better. Something I rarely see in other, less toxic communities. However, getting into the game right now might be frustrating for newcomers, as most people playing now can sweep the floor with newbies.
Overall, this is definitely a game worth checking out if you are at all interested in fighting games or Dark Souls. Currently, though, the game should only be bought while on sale, its not worth the 60$ price tag. Though as of writing this its 30$ so I would definitley recomend the game for that price point.

Art assets. There aren't many. This is obviously a direct result of the budget, and I'm personally not upset about it in the slightest. This is just fair warning for what you can expect to see. You will feel emotions. Sad emotions. This isn't something I personally dislike at all, in fact it's part of what makes this VN experience so great in my opinion. Unfortunately, some of you suck! A few reactions that I've read indicate that tragedy bothers people, but for a pseudo-mystery pseudo-slice-of-life, it's absolutely appropriate. Just be prepared to be hit with some dark stuff!
I am writing this (and played this) before the release of the second part. If you are like me, then you have to go into this knowing that although the ending will absolutely feel like the ending to a legitimate, full game, you will most likely wish you could get into the next part of the story. Unless you are late to the party (HAHA, losers!), you will have to wait. it sucks, but don't let that stop you from playing the game we have now!
This last one almost goes without saying, since this is always a risk with VNs. the MC might not always do the things you wanted him to do, or think the things that you wanted him to think. This is mostly because he isn't just an empty vessel for us to project into. Not entirely, at least.
Even though there are quirky weirdos, there is more or less a "real person" feel to your relationships with the cast. Now, I'll give you fair warning that the people themselves often have exaggerated elements, but I mean "real person" in the sense of how your character interacts with them. Even though they can be frustrating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at times, that's how people are in the real world, too. You aren't always satisfied with what they say or do to you. You aren't always treated fairly. Not every female is gonna suck your donger (Sad, I know). You might have characters you hate, even though you really wanted to love them going in. And people annoy you with their jim-jams when you don't even wannna hear it! This might just be me, but a certain topic that few characters wouldn't shut up about was something that I had no interest in. At first I was a tad salty, but it isn't something that made the experience less enjoyable. Having conflict is important, and making the player salty isn't always a bad emotion to bring out.
GOVER MECHER IS A WORK OF ABSOLUTE ♥♥♥♥ING GENIUS
This is for the people that have played multiple VNs before. You can't take anything for granted. This game doesn't adhere to the unspoken rules set by other games in the genre. I can't tell you how many times I was groaning in anticipation for a plot point that was either cliche or too boring and unimaginative. I'm not saying that you won't ever be able to predict what's coming next (although I think a few twists may get you), but there will probably be times when people who've played these types of games before will think "I know what they're going to do with this, and I'm already disappointed." There may be a couple instances where you feel let down (I can't read minds), but if you have too many preconceptions then I can guarantee that they won't be met.
You get a bit of everything. As I mentioned before, this game has some "slice-of-life" mixed in with some "mystery," and the two parts are merged in a satisfying way. You get time for a light-hearted goof, and you get time for some spooks. This game has got it all.
Look here, kiddo. I know I told you that not every anime grill is gonna suckle on your ding-dong like in your dating-sims, but you made it this far, so here's the skinny on the situation. You will find the elusive "best grill" in this game. In fact, that's the best part of the mystery. You've gotta hunt for the best grill, and it won't be easy! You'll be saying to yourself "Oh MCMECHA, why couldn't your review just TELL me who the best grill is! I'm too foolish to find her on my own!" But you see, that's the fun part! It's not easy to find out who the best one is, because you'll want to jingle your jangles with more than one, if my playthrough is any indicator! They've all got strong points and weak points. Hell, I'm almost glad that you won't be able to choose Yahiko in part 2 just because the allure of GOVER MECHER would draw me away from the ladies!
All things considered, you seriously need to play this game. It's worth every minute of your time, and this VN deserves all of the support it can get from the fine people here on steam. So play the hell out of it and tell your friends. If you don't, I'll give ya a big smack on the head, y'hear?

Actually, I am not very familiar with the genre of visual novels. I tried some so far, both free and bought ones, but none of them was slightly thrilling. When I found this VN on steam, it really catched my attention due to its tremendously high rating. However, I was sceptical in the beginning.
Free? Plain artwork? No synchronisation? That sounds like a very cheap product. Not even worth my time. But hey, it's free. At least I can try it out.
And I was proven wrong. Goddamn wrong.
What catches your eyes immediately is the way the protagonist talks with the other characters. The verbal exchange of words and the endless witty remarks are absolutely hilarious and entertaining. If you are someone, who likes to reflect on new ways to express trivial things, likes to explore the borders of the spoken word or loves absurd dialogues, then I can assure thee undoubtely, this visually animated opus of modern literature will bestow great fortune on thee, little chap. (Note: If you liked the dialogues in the anime
, you will surely love this one as well)
The main characters talks with every characters in a different way, depending on the situation and the story developed so far, thus creating a very vivid and immersive atmosphere. At some point, I really awaited conversations with specific characters eagerly, because you could rest assured, you will laugh like bloody hell with a cup of tea in your hand.
A vast cast of characters is introduced, everyone unique with their own traits and behaviour. Of course, some of them are the typical generic characters everyone knows from animes, but some had personalities I haven't seen before. But don't let the first impression fool you. Some of the characters (sadly not all) are much more complex than anticipated and reveal their depths of their character as the plot unravels (But do not expect too much depths!! You might brake your ankle!!). To my surprise, this VN also thematized psychology to an extent, that it was not ridiculously anymore and could be taken seriously. However, I must warn you again, that the theory of Sigmund Freud or Jung are not discussed in this VN, but a basic comprehension of psychology is crucial to the understanding of the protagonist's thought and behaviour.
The story itself is mainly a composition of dialogue, comedy, mystery, thriller, and a pinch of romance and masterly switches the atmosphere at any time. Last sentence was a hilarious joke and suddenly we are terrified by new informations. Additionally, the mood of the current situation is always perfectly captured by the background music. Whether a light-hearted tune or tensed melody, whether the music relaxes you or sends a chill down your spine, it amazingly fits well the whole time. As for the lenght of VN: Holy moly, it is ♥♥♥♥ing long. And I mean ♥♥♥♥ING long.
+ great dialogue humour
+ diverse story telling
+ immersive atmosphere
+ matching soundtrack
+ interesting characters
+ FREE!!
- No controversial drama
- simple animations
- No seriously, if you are still reading this review, then you don't have any excuses to NOT play this free game!
If you liked the dialogues of this VN, you should really consider watching the anime

OH MY GOSH, THIS GAME!!! WHY ARE YOU READING THIS REVIEW AND NOT PLAYING THIS AMAZING, FREE GAME?!?!
I'll admit, I never tried a visual novel before, and after a binge on downloading some free ones, I deleted three out of four pretty awful ones...then the fourth one was this... Oh my gosh. For a grammar-freak like me, this game is excellent. The whole game I think I might've caught one or two--three at the most--typos.
I thought the characters seemed stereotypical at first: the jock, the doofus, the love interest, etc., but they are SO MUCH MORE THAN THAT! About five minutes in I was laughing along and getting so caught up in Yama's (the main character) sardonic wit, how his character plays off his friends,  and the humor and brightness of his friends, contrasted with the dark undertones of the game's mystery.
This game--this NOVEL--compares even to my love of paper books, which is saying something. What may seem simple at first glance and hardly a mystery will fit in beautifully like puzzle pieces later on, and the characters, in which this game has quite a cast, will come alive, each with their own unique personality from each other and any other character you've met. While the puzzles are few, they are fun and stimulating (those who meet Shigure will know), and if you're ever having a bad day, this game will put a grin on your face  a minute in. Alongside the great cast, well-written story, and vibrant humor, there is also more than a handful of poignant moments and themes that will raise fascinating philosophical questions. At times you'll feel like crying, others laughing until your rib hurts at the HUMANESS of this novel, but you will always be left with a promise of hope and courage.
Now enough with my praise. If you want to laugh, grin like a happy fool, and think like a genius, PLAY THIS GAME!!!!

This isn't a terribly challenging game, nor is it aiming to be overly serious or cerebral, which makes it a great game in its own light for that. You're not a hero, there's no deep conspiracy they're batting over your head, and it has fun with all of these facts. It gives a dash of helium to much of the silliness of games, both in the puzzles you encounter and the mini-games you can find within, making it a great retreat from all the rote tales of other games that try to rope you into their very super serious affairs which if you'll stop for a second and look at stuff/jump around falls apart almost instantly.
In many ways, this game is arguably a deliberate satire of some beaten to death game elements, but never in a derisive way, so much as a, of course you're going to be doing this and of course we're going to have fun with it, why wouldn't we? It's such a little joy for that alone, where other games seem to blindly repeat themselves without making much of a nod to say, "We know you're familiar with this, here's a dash of self-aware shortcutting of it to let you know," this game isn't blind to that. Instead, it sometimes has you go all the way through it, taking it to absurd extremes (in a humorous way, not an overly long way), or recognizing what players would do (bull in a china shop).
If you play lots of games, and want something that pokes fun at what you've had to do a million times, I highly recommend this game. It's a little on the short side, but if it had gone any longer, you'd probably have stopped laughing by the end, like a comedy that didn't know when to quit, so it really is best at its length.

Resident Evil 6 is hands down the single worst Resident Evil game ever made by Capcom.  Basically if Resident Evil 5 and Operation Raccoon City had a deformed digital game-love-child using Call of Duty as a surrogate, RE6 is what would come out of it. The game seeks hard throughout its 30 - 40 hours of game play to find an identity, and unfortunately it finds 4 different identities, none of which are stellar and ALL of which were lifted directly from other games that unsurprisingly did it better.
Leon's campaign is a contrite, try-hard amalgamation of Resident Evil 4 and 5's Tomb Raidery, Mario-ey parts filled with nonsensical obstacles, endless holes in the earth, exploding air vehicles and cars, and poor excuses for zombie scares. - not to mention a clear disregard for the intelligence of the Biohazard fanbase when they repeatedly make Leon an unlearning single celled organism whose only display of personality is to make quips about his luck with women. Ignoring the tutorial which attempts to Tarantino the story, poorly, and introduces the main trope of Leon's game: Everything is always on fire and will always explode, you start out in what almost seems like it might be a throwback to Resident Evil 2, until the first 5 or 6 pseudo-jump-scares officially turn you off of any notion that this is a survival horror game. When you finally do meet "zombies", they are fast moving but boring engagements often composed of QTE and they don't even necessarily die from headshots. If this wasn't bad enough, there is no logical consistency whatsoever to the plot and the game tries offensively, pathetically hard to convince you that "This is just like Raccoon City." Yea, the god awful game Operation Raccoon City, maybe. Certainly nothing like RE2 and maybe a bit like RE3 considering that's where the franchise went action-centric.
Sherry's campaign (because I refuse to call it Jake's) is a mixed mess of third person shooter elements and stealth gameplay wherein a pathetic emulation of Nemesis and the Tyrant happen to be in multiple chapters. It's not even a matter of Ustanak "stalking" you like Tyrant or Nemesis did because he doesn't stalk you. You are just forced via linear progression to be in the same area he is and then occasionally run from him and try not to♥♥♥♥♥♥him off. In fact, it seems like Capcom made it their goal to copy as much of Binary Domain as possible, but the thing is....Binary Domain was so  much better and it was pure third person shooter. There is far too much stealth gameplay involved, and don't even get me started on the horrid snowmobile sequence. Did I mention Jake is complete retcon and ruins the entire game on his own? Sorry Troy baker i.e the only voice actor in gaming. My issue isn't with you, you're good - but with this awful, awful, awful storywriting.
Chris's campaign, and this is the absolutely disgusting part, is the only solid one out of the original 3. It is pure, 100% third person shooter. Not the slightest trace of "survival horror". You're in the BSAA, obviously - ignoring entirely that his partner Jill is inexplicably no where to be found at all despite the numerous times they've been in the same situations and should be working together still - and you end up chasing "Ada" around the world, with biohazard outbreaks happening to be there each time, or happening while there. Frankly, if this had been it's own separate game in which terrorists and rebel armies are using BOWs and viral weapons with some over-arching story that made sense, it would have been a solid game. Obviously not resident evil, but a solid game. But this is Resident Evil. Like I said though, Chris's campaign is the only one of the main 3 which maintains consistent game mechanics and never forces you into complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, out of place gameplay sequences like flying airplanes except for the one extremely long and ridiculous car chase scene. On top of that, the dudebro sentiment of the story is at least commiserable.
That leaves Ada's campaign. Before Capcom noob-patched the game, Ada was on her own. No partner - could not co-op. It was the only one that resembled survival horror and it was actually fun to boot. Not to mention, you HAD to play it to actually piece together the god awful story that tied the entire game together. Now it's co op and the entire allure of that campaign is gone.
Despite those massive failures, the game does have some decent non-story multiplayer, and mercenaries mode is the best it's ever been. It's just too bad the game, like all modern Capcom titles, got pounded into oblivion by oversaturated DLC.
Seriously, to hades with this game.

I remain ambivalent towards first-person shooters in general, and Crysis really does nothing to change that.  However, the graphics on offer are just so much better than anything else on offer that it's a noteworthy game.  Even now, several years after release, this is probably THE game to use when you want to see just what a new rig or GPU will do.  With loads of brightly colored outdoor environments, the game fortunately eschews the repetitive, bland and drab palettes of competitors like Metro.  The crispness of the textures, depth of shading, and wide range of color gamut still have the power to bewitch sixty times a second.

i enjoyed this game, once i found and installed the quick save mod. Without it, i would never have finished the game. It utterly disgusts me that Crysis 2 and 3 do not have their own quick save feature and that they rely on checkpoints. Checkpoint systems are why i almost didn't finish Batman Arkham Asylum (found a trainer to get past the problem area on that one). Checkpoints SUCK.
But back to Crysis 2... The game has been criticized for the lack of non-linear gameplay. It's true that the game doesn't feel as open as Crysis and Crysis Warhead, but i don't think it's as bad as some have made it out to be. Yes, you're following a path through the game, there's really only one path, and there's no way back, but that's how the previous games were too.
The engineering and art of this game are excellent. The story is thin but interesting. My only complaints with the game would be the same complaints i have with almost all FPS games, so i wont go into them here. i DO want to comment that i was very glad the final level didn't consist of the same stupid boss style objective as the first two games (Crysis 1 and Warhead both ended with monstrous bosses that required no freedom of play style whatsoever).
i liked this game enough to play it again (with the quick save mod running, of course). i'm looking forward to Crysis 3 being available on Steam, on sale, and with a quick save mod, but so far none of those conditions have been met.

Switching suit modes is a lot more fluid in Crysis 2 compared to the original and nothing beats ripping a 50cal from its mountings and going berserk.  In true CryTek fashion the scenery and effects are spectacular and the story is absolute B-grade.
Even though the gaming industry makes more than hollywood, someone will eventually realise that games need better stories.  We need to see people like Joss Whedon writing the scripts to these games.

2. CAPCOM says it's Steam's problem, because they gave you a dodgy key.
3. Two or three weeks of collecting emails, and you're now ready to open a support ticket on CAPCOM's customer support so that, another week or so later, if they feel like it, they'll get around to adding your key to the database
.
3a. Oh yeah. I'll take proof of purchase, screenshots of your steam account etc. and probably a call or three to the support line as well before they finally give you access.
4. Also, the whole time you're doing the above, remember this : This is a well-known problem that numerous people have documented (most of which has been scrubbed from forums etc.). Absolute delight of a game.
Would pay up to £4 for.
It's short and sweet, yet weirdly doesn't need to be anything more than it is.
The whole thing is controlled by basic direction keys and a single action key that acts to open the menu, sprint, interact, or throw flasks ("grenades") depending on the context of its use. 5 buttons total.
There's an Apathetic Frog who entirely lives up to its name.
Some of the battles ("healing mode") offer a decent challenge; the game itself not punishing the player for failing a battle, at least on the normal difficulty setting.
One mechanic sees flasks only deducted from your inventory if you succeed in that particular battle scenario, ensuring you never feel that they are wasted given their limited number in the game. A defeat returning you to before the battle commenced (Again, at least on normal difficulty. I can't speak for the higher difficulties, yet).

Caves of Qud is a very in depth roguelike with a unique setting.  The setting is a post-apocalyptic world that has both sci-fi and fantasy.  True-kin humans and mutated humans are the playable races, and each race has a variety of classes they can pick from.  Mutated humans differ greatly in that they can choose from various mutations, as well as empower the ones you start with, or choose new ones later through use of mutation points.  I like the graphics very much, as minimal as they are.  They're further enhanced by a wealth of descriptions and use of ansi color on items to give it a MUD-like feel, which is something I'm quite fond of in games, albeit rarely used outside of text MUDs themselves.  This is what I'd call a real roguelike, up there with ToME / Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup/ ADoM/etc.  It is hard and quite unforgiving, but you can also run across some very lucky item caches quite early.  Most of my deaths so far have been classic roguelike deaths, getting too overzealous in a deep cave after getting a good haul of loot and xp, or finding some ruins with some interesting chests and turrets only to be roasted alive by a goat-man shaman.  All in all, I look forward to seeing this game grow even more and even though it's early access, it has more to do than most games in released state and full fledged AAA $60 games.

Slender: The Arrival is one of my favorite horror games I have ever played. It is incredibly terrifying and still frightens me now, even after I have beaten it, something few horror games can claim. Here is a Pros and Cons list for this game:
PROS
-Partially made by the original creators of Slender: The Eight Pages, and even incorporates the original game into this game's story
-Terrifying antagonists. The Slenderman may be scary, but he can get a bit repetitive at times. To counteract this, two additional enemies (his proxies) exist in the game. The Chaser, and Charlie. Both of them are terrifying and nasty.
-Sound design can make or break a horror game, and this game nails it on the head. The Chaser's scream will haunt you.
-Pacing in this game is great. Most modern horror games go for the jumpscare, but Slender: The Arrival knows how to instill paranoia.
-The mines level. You will know what I mean when you play it.
-A great party horror game. You know what I mean, get a few friends together and play it, just like the original Slender.
-Graphics are pretty nice in my opinion, even on low settings.
CONS
-I am legitimately having difficulties coming up with negative things to say about this game.
RATINGS
Story: 10/10
Gameplay: 10/10
Atmosphere: 10/10
Total: 100
This game is very very very good. Buy it.

It's very hard to like this game. That's why I don't. Slender: The Arrvival is a short game which I payed £15 for. That was about £5. When I say short, I mean short. A campaign which can take under 20 minutes to complete, the game is filled with missions which all add up to about 1 hour of gameplay. Unfortunately, your given little knowledge of how to activate some of them. For example, the scariest chapter in the game, Homestead, can be played by clicking on the TV screen after playing a recording in which you play as the main charaters Mother. Most of the Chapters are pretty short as too.
If your looking for a scare then this is the game to buy. I genuinly♥♥♥♥♥♥myself playing this game. It is an excellent blend of jumpscares, atmosphere, and a truly-terrifying story. The mission where you play as Charlie as a child undoubtedly disturbed me. However, if your looking for a fun horror game, then you should probrably look for another game. The gameplay is sticky and unevenly paced, and the scares mask over any type of enjoyment for the light-hearted.
But out of all of this, the worst part of this game is each of the 3 endings. For players who bought the game without Steam, the game ends in the radio tower when you get jumped byCharlie. On the Steam version, the game advances to an old burnt down barn I had previously visited in the game. This is by for the best ending in the game.Unfortunately, it's all about waiting, but it does reveal the rest of the story. Within 5 minutes of this scary atmosphere, you die and.... game over.
However, the final ending, which is activated by playing through the game in Hardcore mode, is so bad it's hilarious. For some reason the your character jumps off the radio tower and, dies. Yep, that's it.
My personal review is a 5/10, because of how inconsistent the game actually is. It is far too overrated.

The graphics are nice, and I am a fan of the Slenderman.  I can never fully rationalize away my fears, because he strongly resembles a childhood recurring nightmare that I had.  (A long, pale figure, with empty eyes looking into the window, unmoving, unblinking.)  I think this may be some kind of universal brain-glitch that we have as human beings.  LOTS of people feared similar creatures, whether things they imagined themselves, or things from various mythologies in different parts of the world.
But having gone through the introduction, and knowing Slenderman, who is by now a meme, I was not at all frightened, when I could flick my flashlight on and off at him in the first stage, and even stare dead at him, without so much as a flicker of movement or threat.  This is a great way to yank me out of any sense of suspense and tension.  And the way you start a game really has a great deal of impact on the way the rest of it feels.  So eh, 2/10.  Good graphics, story seems like it'd be good?  But poor setup, and stage 2 is a rehash of a free game.  Shouldn't have to go through an hour of boring/ rehashed material to get to the good stuff.

I really wanted to love this game. My friends urged me not to play it. The servers were garbage they said. The gameplay mechanics are clunky and clumsy they said. Bah! I wanted Viking glory, and I dismissed their pleas to gain my seat in the golden halls of Valhalla and dine with Odin. So I installed it on this free weekend thinking that perhaps they were wrong, and I should give it the benefit of the doubt.
Boy was I wrong. So very, very wrong. I sunk some good time into War of the Vikings, expecting skirmishes that may have been just an nth of a degree as solid as those battles were, and found my jaw on the floor. This game wasn't just bad, it was epicly bad. Worse, is that this was the impression I got from just a free play weekend. I can't imagine being somebody who was so hyped for this game, that it had to be a day one purpose, only to be met with the shame that had befallen me as I gave 60 dollars or more to this company on good faith that this product would be solid. The controls are awkward as all hell, and I just couldn't get comfortable. My axe didn't feel like an extension of my hulking Viking frame. Nay, it was cumbersome and instead of a fluid transition from guard stances, I found myself fumbling over myself just trying to get a lock on a target, let alone get an accurate guard up in time.
"Maybe it's better on controller!"I had thought. Nay! This combination was clunky as well! This wasn't the way I'd get my deeds sung of in song as I gloriously drink from curved horns in golden halls. The illusion was shattered. I went to read reviews to see if maybe it was just me who was experiencing this letdown, and it was hardly the case. I still want to love this game. I still want to drink from curved horns in golden halls, with buxom valkyries smiling at me as they refill my drink. But not for $60. There may come a day when I return to this game, but it is not this day!

Princess Remedy in a World of Hurt is the story of a selfless healer's whimsical adventure through Hurtland, a place where everyone and their dog suffers from maladies ranging from the plague to hypochondria. Your job as Princess Remedy, physician extraordinaire, is to cure afflictions by navigating screens full of baddies and auto-firing them into oblivion while tossing healing flasks and avoiding damage.
The gameplay is a turbo-drive romp through pixellated forests and towns with intentionally limited color depth; the music uses every one of its eight bits to rock out to the tune of your superstar curing prowess. Your projectiles transform and multiply as you become more efficient at healing, while your hearts and regeneration increase, allowing you to take more hits from nasty germs and carcinogens.
Serious business goes out the window straight away: a jealous chest won't let you open it if you've opened other chests before it but will still accept your hand in marriage; NPCs are given colorful names such as "Some Girl" and "Moonbunny"; and years of estrangement can be righted in one fell swoop with a box of chocolates. Who need reality, anyways?
A disproportionately high number of levels can be defeated by simply standing still which is offset by the moderate level of Bullet Heck present in some of the more challenging screens. It's nothing repeated attempts won't smash down, however, and that's one of the attractive features of this relatively short game: pressing buttons until you win.
Overall, I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a quick bit of fast-paced fun.

tl;dr Exploratory roguelike with brilliant writing, a huge pool of interesting abilities, and an expansive world to explore.
Caves of Qud! One of the best roguelikes I've ever had the pleasure of playing - I have endless entertaining stories from this game, from the time I knife-fought a bear and won, to the time I set the horrifying Slog on fire and shot lasers from my eyes until he died! (And oh so many amusing deaths, such as the time I was flying over a river, fell into it, and was eaten by madpoles. It's one of those games, see!)
Before I can recommend it, however, I must offer a few caveats: first, most importantly, the learning curve is high for those who aren't used to roguelikes. The GUI is entirely keyboard driven, and having a numpad is highly recommended. There are handy dandy references on display - hit F1, read the quickstart - but you will need to actually read for a little before you're off and running.
Second, character creation will be intimidating when you first run into it. There are so many interesting mutations to take, and so many True Kin classes - don't panic. Pick whatever sounds cool, and marvel at the choices. Take a lot of Toughness, grab freezing hands or light manipulaton, get yourself into the game.
Thirdly, it's still in Early Access. There is a lot of content - there is so much content the devs could stop developing it today (and I'd weep!) but it would still be a full game in its own right, capable of entertaining for hours. The skinny: the main quest line is unfinished. As far as I know, it's roughly halfway done? But: it's difficult and long already, and unless you're really good at roguelikes you won't get to the end of what's in already. (And it will tell you when you hit the end for now.) (Note: the devs are updating it weekly! They revamped caves just recently, and there's even more stuff in the pipeline that hits every friday.)
So, with those caveats in mind, you might be asking - why would I rec this? The answer is: once you learn the ropes and get going, it's one of the best roguelikes out there, and quite possibly the king of the exploratory genre of roguelikes. Caves of Qud is well-written (flavor text abounds!) and has a lovely tileset, and poking around in its jungles and deserts and caves leads to all kinds of fun. There are bears you can talk to in this game, and even bigger, deadlier bears with jetpacks you can die to, for example. There are also actual books in there, Elder Scrolls-style with multiple pages of in-game lore, and those are honestly more exciting to me than the rest of the game, but I'm a lore hound, and I digress.
Once you've poked around the starting town and assigned hotkeys for your numerous abilities, you'll use the world map to either go north to Red Rock or east to the Rust Wells, and there you'll fight in traditional roguelike style - bump against the monster to harm it, on a turn-by-turn basis. Or use your mutant abilities to harm things from afar, or get the multiple arms mutation to dual wield greatswords against your foes. Invest in axes, dismember the limbs of your foes! There are so many interesting options, and the mutations interact in interesting ways as you fight through these distinct areas to get loot and - more importantly - more food and water. Water is the game's currency, and you need both it and food to live. It's a survival sim, in that respect, and you should be careful that you don't go into the desert without food, because you will run out and die of starvation.
Slowly you'll learn where the dangers are - use the look command always to assess your enemies - and you'll learn when to run, or use the big guns in your arsenal. Slowly, you'll forge your way to Grit Gate, and Golgotha, and beyond.
And you'll die. Over and over and over, trying new mutations every time, or just using the "replay most recent character" option until you're sick of playing espers. Caves of Qud, for all it has a learning curve and its brutal difficulty - coaxes you back in by asking you repeatedly: "what if you had this mutation instead?"
It works brilliantly. Please buy this game and enjoy it!

I would also like to mention that the game never went under 35 frames (but not over 78.)
Gameplay
For most of the singleplayer you go around shooting faceless grunts who realistically fall and bleed all over the place, but the twist here is that you get a few superpowers to help you out. For some reason in the future the nanosuit recieves a downgrade from it's original 5 powers (now chaged to 3) but in return battery usage and visible UI have a few minor upgrades that keep it worth your time to use. The suit also has a new power where you get to play ghost hunter and use your thermal camera, and now the second you grab someone in the neck they die from shock or something (idk why grabbing people makes them die.) I would also like to say that gone are the free roaming jungles of Crysis because the devs thought making the areas as small and clausterfobic as possible would really please fans of the original (not add MSAA options is enough to displease the fanbase) but if you can get pass crysis 2 was marketed to CallofHaloFutureSoldiers it can be dismissed as EA's marketing flaws, BUT that does not stop crysis 2 from being freaking awesome and a blast to play and replay. I should probably also mention the collectable items throughout the level, but due to the linearity of the gameplay you'll either miss them right under your nose (erm facemask) or they'll be staring you right in the face with blinking lights around it saying PICK ME UP I'M USELESS! I would also like to mention that they broke the physics too. I'm serious they took something perfect and said naaaaaaa console players can't handle that, now, it's very rare to be able to throw enimies into each other.
Story
This is where I feel the game excels and also ruins my expectations. You play as a marine corps guy who isn't much for words who gets a suit from Eli Vanc- I mean Prophet, and you have to save the world because Prophet just wasn't good enough? Idk it's never really explained why he gives you the suit... and doesn't tell any of his friends about it... and you start killing people because they fired first. Oh, and a nerd named Gould keeps bothering you to hurry the hell up and get to him... because... I still don't know for sure why he called, but everything is pretty so I shouldn't care should I, and after that you murder more helpless victims until you start taking orders from some other guy, and he betrays you and you learn that anything with a human face is good while you should just pump as much lead into everyone else. That is, until you get to the leader of the blue clad suicide unit, and this is where I got a little mad. Spoiler: you kill him. Don't ask for answers or try to change him just let him swear at you until your magical touch of death kicks in and you get to throw him out a window. Yay... anyway aliens happen and all the pollution and bad fire effects in New York turn their color from blue to red for no reason and what else would you do but give a little on the fly dissection. You know the more I think about it the more I feel like the games major enemies stem from when a sibling says: "well he started it!" after your younger brother is hospitolized because you touched his neck or something.

Lucid9 is a decent game. Some might not think so much of it, some might think more, but I, for the most part, enjoy the story. The first time, that is.
Although this is a positive review, I'm first going to point out one of more frustrating points of the game. To beat it and get all the achievements, you're going to have to go through it several times. Certainly, this can be shortened by saving at certain points, but you have to start from the beginning if you happen to miss anything early on. It may seem minor, but, as there are quite a few choices in the game regardless of relevance to the story, it can get rather tedious.
Now, onto the overall review.
The art was very nice, as far as I'm concerned. It fit the story at most points, though I think some of the characters were a tad plain. Yama, for instance. He's the one you play as, but nothing stands out beyond his yellow eyes. And the yellow eyes don't even really complement him. Other characters could also be seen in the same light. Beyond this, the art suited the game. The eyes did get on my nerves, though, and not just on Yama. Also, the characters look pretty... stunted? It makes them look like children, but that may just be the effect of me looking at them too long.
The characters don't just have their looks, though. A lot of them were also good in terms of character development. Some of them could have been done better, yes, but overall I think it worked out well. To name a few of the characters that fell short, there was Natsuki Tanaka, Masato Kurogane, and Rui Hayata. One of the characters, Akira Karube, did get on my nerves. Her personality has been done to hell and back in games all across the board. For a major character, however, she contributed very little to the story. Is this a negative or a positive?
Now, for the story itself... I really don't have many complaints here. I do think there should've been more hints along the way about what was really going on, and the player (reader?) ought to be able to figure out at least some of the story before it comes down to the big conclusion. It should also be worth more that the player/reader get close to certain people. At current, are there any benefits to learning about those around you? No. Is there anything relevant to the case? No. Why should you pursue other characters? Curiosity?
That being said, I did get a bit off-track there. The story is ambitious, I'll give you that, but I think it took too long to get it out there. Some scenes simply dragged on, like that carnival thing. Completely unecessary, that scene. It served no other purpose besides letting you learn some minor things about the main characters, and took too long to get past. There were other scenes like that scattered about, and it isn't very pleasant to go through them five or so times for an achievement or something of that sort.
I'm just going to slide this in since I kind of forgot about it, but the music wasn't bad. I liked the main title theme, but some of the other tracks were obviously overused. Others merely faded into the background. This aside, it wasn't terrible.
Lucid9 was one of my first visual novels, and was altogether memorable. It was altogether an enjoyable experience that I would recommend. You'll have to tolerate a few holes (maybe more than a few...), but it can be difficult to find any game without such things. Lucid9 definitely has problems, but it isn't a bad game.

Lucid9 is a free visual novel game that takes a dark turn from an otherwise seemingly-cheerful-and-cliched group of high school friends.  Many characters that take the stage will seem overdone at first; you have the dumb guy who thinks he's the most powerful and brilliant person ever; you have the rich girl who is intelligent because she has a standing to uphold; you have the quiet girl who is really good at video games; etc.  However, the characters evolve much further than that in their own, flawed ways that make them seem just as human as anyone you stand next to right now.  To give a fair warning though, if you are NOT OKAY with anything that involves detailed horror, turn away now.  The climax WILL scar you and it is meant to do that.  Lucid9 leaves a very deep and meaningful impact on each that reads to its end, and to add on it has many little bits of dialogue that can be missed on your first playthrough that might just coax you to experience it again.  Although I already finished it last year, I've been thinking of playing it again, to remember everything.

I've always been a big fan of Friday the 13th but I'm not sure ANY movie deserves the kind of tribute that's in this game!  The attention to detail is astounding.  Never mind that it's good, dumb fun to play, what really blows me away is how the developers somehow captured that 80's vibe and successfully translated it into a videogame.  The music appears to be lifted straight from the movies and it sounds so crystal clear, I'm assuming it's been remastered and I love how it plays at the most appropriate moments.  The frenzied music that kicks in during the final 2 minutes of the match is incredibly intense!  They even have Alice Cooper's dopey 'Man Behind the Mask' during the credits!  Really looking forward to future content, Vitual Cabin 2.0 sounds great being the F13 fanboy that I am.
If you're not a Friday the 13th fan I'm not sure you'll be so crazy about it, but I'm sure anyone can appreciate the asthetically pleasing level of polish.  As far as gameplay goes, the gameplay mechanics and objectives seem to have more variety than it's rival Dead by Daylight, maybe not geared as much for competitive play if you're looking for that. Also, you're kinda stuck with just one killer in Friday, whereas if you get bored playing as one of them in DbD you can just pick a different killer with vastly different abilities.  Maybe in a few months I'll be singing a different tune but honestly I think it's worth the full $40 price tag and for now I'm having a blast with it.  Just stupid, mindless fun.

I really wanted to love this game. My friends urged me not to play it. The servers were garbage they said. The gameplay mechanics are clunky and clumsy they said. Bah! I wanted Viking glory, and I dismissed their pleas to gain my seat in the golden halls of Valhalla and dine with Odin. So I installed it on this free weekend thinking that perhaps they were wrong, and I should give it the benefit of the doubt.
Boy was I wrong. So very, very wrong. I sunk some good time into War of the Vikings, expecting skirmishes that may have been just an nth of a degree as solid as those battles were, and found my jaw on the floor. This game wasn't just bad, it was epicly bad. Worse, is that this was the impression I got from just a free play weekend. I can't imagine being somebody who was so hyped for this game, that it had to be a day one purpose, only to be met with the shame that had befallen me as I gave 60 dollars or more to this company on good faith that this product would be solid. The controls are awkward as all hell, and I just couldn't get comfortable. My axe didn't feel like an extension of my hulking Viking frame. Nay, it was cumbersome and instead of a fluid transition from guard stances, I found myself fumbling over myself just trying to get a lock on a target, let alone get an accurate guard up in time.
"Maybe it's better on controller!"I had thought. Nay! This combination was clunky as well! This wasn't the way I'd get my deeds sung of in song as I gloriously drink from curved horns in golden halls. The illusion was shattered. I went to read reviews to see if maybe it was just me who was experiencing this letdown, and it was hardly the case. I still want to love this game. I still want to drink from curved horns in golden halls, with buxom valkyries smiling at me as they refill my drink. But not for $60. There may come a day when I return to this game, but it is not this day!

Jazzpunk is a comical and eccentric game.  It takes place in a very weird, 1960s style spy world with abstract characters based on electronic technology. The game is not to be taken seriously.  The challenge level is very low, and the flow is more like a series of scenes with dozens of mini-games. Some of the mini-games can be novel and fun, others are just filler.  The dedicated 1960's themed style, even in its extremely abstracted form, is pleasant and interesting.
However, Jazzpunk should only be purchased as a curiosity or novelty piece.  Players who are dedicated to all of the mini-games and side-dialogues will still only find about five hours of gameplay, and the game can easily be completed in far less than this.  For this reason, the price of $15 is completely outrageous unless you are a fan of extremely odd titles or 60s style novelties. This is going to be a quick 2 part review.  First on the game, second on the DRM.
Firstly, the game is an okay Sci-fi FPS.  There are two distinct modes in the game, the FPS part and the flying/shooter part.  I perferred the FPS to the Shooter part as the flying is a little clunky in the controlls department.  Aswell the flying shooter part also felt lackluster as there was a very limited enemy pool and the enviroments were a little dull.
The FPS was actually not bad, it was a typical cover based shooter.  However the cover mechanic was pretty decent as there was parts in the game where you had to scale or descend and the cover mechanic was used quite well in those as well.  In particular the end of the first chapter/mission had a real fun use of the scaling cover.  There is a lack of weapon variety in the game but you can upgrade your weapons to change them up slightly as well and at the beginning of each chapter/part you can switch up your weapons and there are weapon chests in the levels were you can do the same.
Story was okay, not specatular, it was a little predictable, but still a interesting enough that you are interested in the story.  As well there is lore hidden about in levels to add to the story if you so choose to read it.
Graphics were good and really enjoyed some of the level design, first level/area in particular.
Alright, on to the second part, the DRM.  The DRM for this game is terrible to be fair.  When you buy/install/launch the game you won't be able to.  For some reason the Steam Keys don't end up in the third party DRMs (securcom? I think).  Anyways, the process sucks and takes some time but the game does work in the end.  Here is the proces I followd:
1.) Launch game -> doesn't work even using Securcom directions
2.) Contact Securcom, provide them with screen shots of steam key, they will reply it's not in their database and to contact Capcom support.
3.) Contact Capcom support and provide them with screen shot of steam purchase hisotry showing purchase as well as screen shot of steam key.
4.) Capcom support will email back that the key has been added to database.
5.) Launch game.
That process is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and is not needed, especially on such an old game and if you have a stance on DRM, don't buy this game.
For me, the DRM process was stupid, but the game does work and it was an enjoyable game for me so I give it a very hesitant recommendation.  I recommend the actual game, I DO NOT recommend the crappy DRM that comes with it.

CoQ is a great Rogue-Like. The tiles are genuinely good-looking (as opposed to some other games, where the ASCII actually looks better...), the mechanics are tight, there's plenty of customisation and plenty of different playstyles. -- But that's not the main draw of CoQ, not at all. That's the excellent world that comes with it. This has some of the best lore I've seen in *any* game, let alone a rogue-like. The theme's already amazing (Dune style sword-and-planet, hell yeah!), and the writing fits the atmosphere perfectly. You genuinely feel like you're in the decaying remains of an old, old world. CoQ is definitely the game for anyone wanting to have a dash of story with their dungeon crawling.

TL;DR: 8/10. Buy it if you're into character creation.
Caves of Qud is a rogue-like RPG, but where it really shines is character creation and experimentation. The idea is that you're set in a world so far into the future that everything is unrecognizeable. The range of abilities you can have is very extensive, though hindered slightly by the constant death. If you're not into restarting the entire game every time you accidentally die, I highly recommend you turn off permadeath.
That being said, I get the feeling that Qud is meant to be extremely deep. It wants to be a deep and complex world teeming with politics and people. However, because of the permadeath, I think there's a strong need for the development to be focused on the "wide" aspect rather than the "deep" aspect. The story (as far as I know) isn't completely finished, and while the new features are very helpful and fun, there is very little attention given to the later stages of the game.
The game is still very fun though.
Pros:
-Faction system makes certain creatures friendly while others might hate you
-Very interesting world with unique lore
-In-depth character creation that makes it exciting to experiment
-Memorable story
Cons:
-Unfinished story
-Mouse input is very limited
-At times, the world feels too random
Overall, I'd recommend this game. Good value for the price and the developer is a nice guy.

Just finished the campaing today and I can safely say that it was one of the most enjoyable FPS campaings I've played in a long while. However, this game is quite expensive at full price and I finished the campaing in just under 12 hours. From what I hear the multiplayer is full of hackers these days and is pretty difficult to get into. Also a lot of people have reported problems with logging into the multiplayer myself included since I could not log in to even try it out. I recommend that you wait for a sale and pick this up at around the 15$ mark just for the singleplayer.
The graphics are impressive even without the HD texture mod and stand up to todays standards in my opinion. This game also runs reasonably well on a wide variety of setups. For example, I tried playing this with a GTX 260 and I got around 60 FPS most of the time. Lowest the framerate dropped was around 35 so it's still playable at that point, not optimal but playable.
Verdict:
+ Story (if you like alien invasion and sci-fi stories)
+ Freedom of choice regarding playstyle
+ Gun and Nanosuit modification on the fly supports versitility
+ Graphical fidelity
+ Runs well
+ Nice soundtrack
+ Sudo open levels
+ Nanosuit is COOOOL!
- Too few interesting guns (I mostly used 3 to 4 different guns during the campaing out of ~20 guns)
- Multiplayer doesn't work/full of hackers and no quarantee if there are populated servers available
- Sound assets (aside from the musical score and Nanosuit sounds)
- Plot may be confusing to some if this is your first Crysis game
- Cost at full price
- Experienced frequent crashing on a 500 series GeForce card that I tried running this game on, tho the card maybe at fault, I can't be sure so I'll add this to the negatives
- Don't like aliens? You wont like this game then
Summary:
Buy at discounted price if sci-fi and singleplayer FPS games are right up your alley. If not, give this one a pass.

is a free to play visual novel set a fictional 2018 Japan. In this game you play as Yama, a lazy good-for-nothing with quite a few mental issues. A string of disappearances are happening, all of them students from the school Yama attends which is supposed to be highly secure. You’ll have to juggle your school and social life while trying to find out what’s happening to the students and who is doing it. Can you do it before someone you care for joins the list?
Unlike many people who found this story to be touching or sad, I found myself more indifferent and bored. The story drags on for a while, this due to the fact that our protagonist doesn’t actually actively care or do anything about the disappearances until over halfway through the game. While players are fully aware that something is wrong, we experience this through Yama’s eyes. A good chunk of the first game is spent just chatting with friends, taking tests and other mundane things, which is fine if this was a slice of life title. Putting that aside, the other reason why I found the game to drag on was Yama’s pretentious nature. His inner monologues are long, drawn out and reek of someone trying to sound smart but failing miserably. That being said, the characters besides Yama and Rui are enjoyable and I enjoyed the scenes where you interact and get to know them.
Story aside, everything else about
is fine. You use your mouse to play the game, though there are two points in which you will need a keyboard. You can click to progress the text or put it on auto and relax, there is also a skip feature to zoom past text you’ve already scene while trying to achieve other endings. The user interface is simple and offers all of the options needed for a visual novel such as the ability to hide text. One thing I did not like about the gameplay is how your choices mean very little. Other than failing the final steps against the villain your choices have no impact. Passing or failing tests is meaningless, getting to know a girl or not does nothing, you can’t end up with her and in any deduction sequence choosing the wrong answer will just lead you to try and pick a different one. The ending of the story is always bad and you can’t change it which I don’t mind but it can be a downer.
I really enjoyed the music in the game, it was cheerful when it needed to be and had great sad melodies as well. The music always fit the scenario. The game also has sound effects which were fine, though I found the phone ringing one annoying since there is at least once you don’t answer the phone right away because Yama is having yet another long inner monologue. The art is fine, I enjoyed it and the character models were cute. The game has superb CG art, even of the most unpleasant thing. My only complaint is that where weren’t more CG scenes. The game is rather long and I would have enjoyed seeing more of the lovely artwork.
I may sound critical of the game but did like it on some levels. While some things dragged on for a bit it did build up the feeling that slowly but surely Yama was losing everything around him and it was satisfying when he overcame this. This satisfaction is probably why the lack of any happy endings hurt so much because in the end it seemed like it was all for naught. The game is free so you’re not losing anything by giving
a go, the developers promise more content in the future as well. For now you have Steam achievements and cards and an overall interesting experience for free.

(English is not my mother tongue, so the text below may not fit the standarts set by Jane Austin, Charles Dickens or whoever is considered as an example of good English writing. Or even the standarts set by your school teacher.)
In brief: a really enjoyable visual novel with a few "it's-bugging-me" issues.
In not so brief. While I haven't played too many visual novels and I suppose that there might be some diversity there, most of the ones I played were basically about "choose a girl, collect enough love points and get your romantic ending (or possibly see her breaking and leaving or commiting suicide if you haven't got enough points)". It was somehow refreshing to play a VN that has you do something else. The beginning seemed quite boring - while the writing style itself was (and is) good, the contents itself were not that promising, and the only thing that was saving the day for me was the humor. I have to give the writers credit for this, I laughed like crazy at the "Yama imagines his possible future jobs" sequence. Despite that, some hours in the game, somewhere around the amusement park part i though like "just how much of all this slice of life is there in shis supposedly detective story". But then the things got better, much better. I absolutely enjoyed the whole "investigation in imagination" sequence (orchestrated really well, indeed), the writers did their best to make me doubt my theories even though they seemed quite solid, and the climax really gave me chills (while, I've got to say it, some choices seemed quite counter-intuitive). I also liked the many little flashbacks about the previously foreshadowed and then totally forgotten things during the revelation (when a gun on the wall shoots, it's really nice of the author to remind a forgetful reader like me that it has been hanging there in the first place). At the same time... Well, OK, I'm not going to talk about the ending I've seen until there will be the others. Or I will, in brief (some spoilers here)... Sometimes you feel that the ending, no matter how bad, is deserved, and you make it so with your own decisions, and sometimes you don't. Here, I didn't. It was kinda uncalled for. Absolutely uncalled for. But OK, let's wait for the next part and then see.
The music. I was going to call it "passable", but, if I think twice, it is better. It is definitely doing it's job in maintaining the athmosphere, and even if I didn't like the soundtrack in general as much as I liked the music of Everlasting Summer or Katawa Shoujo, still I really liked some particular tracks, and "Process of elimination" was just great, really contributing to the scenes it played in.
Also, as we're at it, solving puzzles was enjoyable. Quite a good way to make the player involved, maybe better than all the classic "say a compliment to the girl or stay silent" VN choices.
Can't say too much the visuals as I'm not an art expert. It seemed like there is too few CGs, but I suppose the backgrounds could have taken too much resources. As for the sprites, it could have really helped if, for example, when a character is said to wear a cat suit, actually have such sptite. As rare as these occasions are, if the visuals clearly contradict the written text, it is somehow damaging the thing they called a willing suspension of disbelief.
Speaking of which, the thing that annoyed me most. Dear creators, if you read it: if you have a Japanese setting, please, be consistent with it. A line like "No, cats don't speak English" doesn't make sense because, well, the characters are not speaking English! Even if the novel itself is written in English, it is set in Japan, the signs are in Japanese, the characters are Japanese, so the language they speak in-universe must obviously be Japanese. The same goes for the units of measurement. Even if the creators are English or American, and even if the majority of the audience are English or American, if the characters are Japanese, they use neither feet nor pounds, they should use the metric units. Anything else will look, I don't know, like a Japanese novel set in the US and featuring the American characters using koku or shaku instead of gallons and yards. Not the best idea.
The special effects, like transitions, are well done, and I have to especially praise those who made the phone calls and text message effects and the VR displays "interface". Really nice. The only thing I didn't like was how a character sprite leans closer whenever the said character is speaking. It seemed to me somehow distracting and not really necessary.
ALL IN ALL: some really good job the creators did, especially for a freeware product. I totally do not regret about the 20+ hours I spent playing, would really like to see any other visual novel from this developer and, should it be commercial, would not hesitate to pay for it, provided that it is of the same level of quality.

Each counselor(and each Jason) has different strengths and weaknesses to fit different playstyles. It can be frustrating at first when you're learning how to play but as you play more and learn more, the experience becomes more rewarding and more fun. This game also does a fantastic job of recreating the movies it is based on and making you feel like you are in one. My only minor complaints would be that there are some occasional bugs every now and then (i.e. not being able to attack as Jason) and toxic players who either rage quit or assist Jason as a counselor and team kill other counselors. All the content updates for this game are free, there are no lootboxes, and the only microtransactions are cosmetic items.

I was first introduced to "Slenderman" by a co-worker back in 2010 when the original Something Awful creepy-pasta contest entry was just starting to gain some meme-level ground.  I spent a late night after closing at the drug store we were employed at looking over all of the classic photoshops of a tall, thin man holding the hands of children and appearing just out of the foreground in old black and white photos.  Browsing creepy-pastas and looking at a picture trying to find "the monster" somewhere in the trees became a bit of a spooky "Eye Spy" game.
My curiousity in the concept of Slenderman would eventually lead me, like many intrepid fans, to Marble Hornets.  This isn't the outlet to critique THAC's series, but if you're interested in the writing style employed in Slender: The Arrival (STA), I would suggest looking it up on YouTube.
About two years later, Slender: The Eight Pages (STEP) hit the scene and started blowing up online when "Let's Play" style shows and streams started to pick up steam in the gaming community.  I'll admit, STEP often lead me to facepalm when a professor would ask inquistively to the class "what's a slender man?" and a half dozen classmates would respond "its this game-", etc.  My roommates and I still ended up downloading the game and plugging a laptop into our 36" Vizio on Halloween night 2012 to properly get spooked out.  The screams eventually died out by midnight as the novelty wore off and we started to figure out how to game the AI, but I digress.
I'm offering all of this information up as I feel that my familiarity with Slenderman (the creepy-pastas, the various YouTube shows, the movie, etc.) greatly impacts my reccomendation for this game.  If you're unfamiliar with the whole concept of Slenderman this might not be the best way to start into those (sometimes super spooky) waters.
STA, while not a perfect execution, really manages to nail a few of its key components.  The levels go back and forth between variations on the original STEP gameplay with "collecting" something randomly placed around the map while avoiding a stalking, and increasingly aggressive enemy, and what some may "lovingly" refer to as a "walking simulator".  Both gameplay styles are evenly paced out so neither have enough time to grow stale in long bursts.  The exploration levels, and well, the entire game looks gorgeous.  The environments stay with you in this game, even after a week after I completed my playthrough I still remember the striking landscapes more than anything else.  Various collectable pamphlets, emails, etc. dot the maps and help build out the core cast and their history.  I would reccomend tracking these down as they provide most of the world building and really highlight the writing contributions provided by THAC for the game's script.
The player controlled character can feel kind of clunky and slow at times, and I undestand the limited endurance was a design decision to prevent constant sprinting away from enemies but in the portions without something to avoid this can feel somewhat limiting.  The graphics for props, buildings, etc. aren't anything to write home about, but the wilderness and skyboxes always manage to look gorgeous.  Finally, I think my main issue with this game is that after my first death at the hands of Slenderman (or The Operator, or whatever) the scare factor had mostly worn off.  Again, I attribute this to already being burnt out on STEP and other Slenderman series.  The model's head just doesn't seem right either, especially with the more defined cheek bones.  I prefer Slenderman to only have a human silohuette and no other details in the face, but again, that's a personal preference.
So, if you liked STEP (and speaking of which, this game contains an HD remaster of that level unlocked after beating the main story), or are just a fan of anything Slenderman I'd reccomend this.  Its no AAA horror game, but its a competent couple hour romp.

%This Review is for the readers whom may be intimidated by the textheavy / Ascii look of Caves of Qud%
If your reading this, by now you've watched the trailer, seen the screen shots and read the breif discription of this game while trying to acertaine the following question.
Is this game right for me?
Caves of Qud plays like a true Rogue-like with hints of game play akin to Nethack when inside a cave or dungeon. If you've had the oppertunity to enjoy such classic games like Nethack or Slash'um you will find yourself playing a game with a rich lore and solid game play.
For those who never played a /true/ Rogue-like, these games are built to be a challange.
You will be fooled, tricked, lured, rewarded and punished while on your adventure.
You can expect to get lost, confused or face a situation of untimely death.
And when you die, the only thing carried to the next life is a stronger grip of the game, the lesson that lead to your death.
In the beginning you will learn how to play the game, and in the end you will learn how to be a better player.
I recommend rogue-likes to people who want to invest time into learning a game, and do not mind restarting a game from the very beginning.
The games interface while intimidating in the beginning is infact clean and userfriendly to keyboard users, and while it only took me less then 30 minuites to get myself familer with the key binding, if you've not played other rogue likes things will feel out of place. Take this time now to understand you will be mapping skills, you will have a keyboard full of commands like s to search, i for inventory, g to get, c to chat.
As for the game play, Caves of Qud Delivered something that keeps me playing, It's very interesting combat system and character creation. Their are great reviews detailing both game play and character creation.
If you still need help deciding if this game is right for you, or if you've installed it and need help. Please don't let this gem sit in your library and ask some one for help. You can add me, or look for anyone nice enough to broadcast or stream it.

Technically still unfinished and in Early Access, but there is already so much content in this game that it's hard not to recommend to lovers of Roguelikes. CoQ is one of the most visually impressive ASCII-games out there, and the new tileset used in the Unity Engine improves the look while still keeping the very minimalistic genre-typical aesthetic. The game has a lot of its own weird mechanics for a roguelike, most notably the mutation system that puts a different spin on every run. I haven't gotten that far into the game yet as the early game is incredibly difficult, but I already consider this one of my favorite Roguelikes out there with ADOM and Stone Soup, so if you like those games, definitely give Caves of Qud a shot.
Worth noting, I don't normally buy into Early Access stuff anymore, but developer Freehold Games have been showing a lot of commitment to this project, with pretty substantial weekly updates every friday. It'll probably be done before I even get to the endgame...

All in all, definitely worth the $10 they usually charge for it....
