Pros:
* VERY well-written story and characters (that ending though! I want a sequel quick!)
* Dedection sections are very fun; the player gets to be the detective, unlike in Higurashi
* Free to play! This is totally a steal! Very much worth the time to go through!
* The humor is AWESOME! Written very much for a Western audience, with great puns and hilarious situational humor.
* When it's scary, it's SCARY, but no jump-scares, more like tiny little flashes of images that put you on edge. It's all the subtle things that make this game so thrilling.
* I very much appreciate that, while there is violence, it doesn't go over the top, like "999" levels of description.
* I'm probably one of the few to consider this a pro, but the lack of gratutious sexuality as is done so often in visual novels is very refreshing. I'm so glad the creators understand that we don't need sexual innuendos or panty shots to create humor and cut some tension (I'm looking at you, Corpse Party).
* My personal preference: I like stories that are more linear among the bad endings, like Ace Attorney or Danganronpa.
Considerations:
* In the style of Higurashi, where the first half is filled with a lot of "everyday" interactions and "shenanigans", as I like to call them. I understand why: to bond with the characters. But there were times when I was thinking, "C'mon! Hurry up with the mystery portions!" That being said, the "shenanigans" are very fun, and the character development is very well placed and spaced out in between. To the creators: my suggestion is to have more deduction sections, gameplay, or plot elements during these fun times. I know this is supposed to be a visual novel, but I feel that you have something going with the deduction sections that deserves more screen time.

While it lacks the open world of its prequel, this is a pretty fun game. Levels, althrough of the corridor-shooter variety, are varied and do allow for some variations in tactical approach. Typically, the shooting occurs in arena like settings with either waves of enemies to take out as they arrive, or with a large number present, but still in need of taking out. But how you choose to do so is up to you. Stealth kills work due to the suit's invisibility and weapon silencers (weapon custimization is a breeze), sniping is also an option, but the real fun is just going Rambo; sneaking up on an enemy, killing it, grabing its partner, throwing it into and explosive barrel, leaping over the flames, landing with a stunning stomp and unloading a clip, or two, or three. Sprinting for cover, cloaking and flanking, putting shields up and wading into the fray with a shotgun vomitting shells.
The downside is that it can get a little repatative. Yeah, ok, I killed the last few guys with the sniper, the gusy before that with running and gunning, the guys before that with a stealth kill.....after a while the fights do just become a slog. My remedy to that has been to simply play the game in 1-hour bursts to keep it a bit fresh.
I would recommend picking up this game to anyone who enjoys Crysis or FPS games, although I would suggest waiting for a sale.

I picked up this game on 75% sale, and so I'm not horribly dissapointed, but I'm glad I didn't pay the full price.
As for positives: Jazzpunk's unique style, somewhat surreal or even dadaist, is refreshingly unique. As advertised, the humor is a welcome step above most "comedy" games, and there were some moments while playing that actually made me laugh out loud.
However, I found these humorous moments generally far between. Jazzpunk is mostly what you make of it: if you simply follow the instructions for each level without exploring, you could easily finish this game within an hour. The game invites you to explore each level, although how rewarding this exploration will be varies greatly between somewhat ammusing mini-games to quick visual gags that fall a bit flat more often than not.
All in all, based solely on the gameplay, Jazzpunk probably would have come out slightly on the positive side, but instead I have to leave a negative review based on how many game-breaking issues I encountered. In one level, I got stuck at a loading screen for several minutes, so I tried saving my game and reentering the level. However when my save game loaded, the avatar had been placed below the visible map in free fall (below any bounding boxes), and I had to restart the level. Later, on the second hole of a golfing minigame, I hit my ball onto the playing field for the third hole, and reasoned that if the game allowed this trickery to occur, it might be an easter egg, and finished the third hole instead of the second. However, instead of supporting this behavior, the game instead removes the item required to hit the ball from inventory, but then requires you to complete the third hole again. I could not advance and was once again forced to restart the level.
I tried to fight through frustrations like these, but ultimately they made me keep losing interest in finishing the game. I applaud Jazzpunk for creating a unique aesthetic, and enjoyed bits and pieces of the humor, but overall, especially at the full price point, I have to recommend a pass on this one.

Great game with a very fun base concept. If you enjoy multi-tasking and physics-based mechanics games, I'm sure Calm Down, Stalin.
HOWEVER, the game often times feels rushed. Once you reach a point where your desk is completely filled with items, you question how often the gameplay was tested. I sincerely like this game, but there are some simple "bugs" that are nearly game breaking.
Currently I think this game would be hugely benefitted by:
-Restraining the objects from passing a certain points on the desk's axis.
If I throw an object too far down the table, I may not be able to reach that object for the remainder of the round. If I knock my phone out of my hand with my other hand (that's another bug by the way), it can also fall BELOW the table. Why not restrain it if it's never supposed to be there?
-Fixing the phone's recall leap.
It landed on the button 4 times in a row when I was starting off. Other times it just gets stuck. In this case I'd consider removing the physics aspect of this and just making it dash back into receiver if it can't be fixed otherwise.
-Creating more space for objects.

The punching bag for example, introduces another task without it DIRECTLY getting in the way of others, which is good. It's a fun little supply chain management game, but a bit short-lived.  I enjoyed setting up my production lines and making adjustments to manage efficiency.  Customizing the blueprints your production buildings use was a neat touch.  I was able to improve the efficacy of a few of the defaults; however, the defaults are still pretty good.  That being said, you will likely be done playing after going through all the scenarios.  You could try a user created scenario or try making your own, but otherwise there is not much to do other than replaying a scenario and try to finish it faster.  You are given the option to continue playing after finishing all the goals in a scenario, but there is little reason to, since there’s nothing to work towards.  Aspects of the game are repetitive, and many of the goals consist of waiting for your factory to produce something.  There is no punishment for taking longer, so often just waiting some time is easier than trying to improve efficiency.  Still, for the price, I recommend playing this game.

So engaging, so rewarding.  This feels like gaming in a futuristic society where leisure time is abundant and gaming is widespread as a form of education and stimulation, instead of just addictive.  As the game progresses your mental labels of the various rectangles stops being their color or their size, and you start to identify them by name.  The game doesn't force that anthropormophization, but it's so much richer for it.  Similarly, you couldn't just listen to the narration without the context of the game and understand the story, it's a journey you take together.  Can you imagine if Smithsonian exhibits were given as much attention to engagement?

There are some similarities to Braid in Thomas. The game is more about the experience and the journey of the characters than the gameplay aspects. I’ll admit, nothing in Thomas Was Alone is original or groundbreaking. All of the puzzle platforming elements have been seen before and the game doesn’t really bring the difficulty level. I mean, OK, there are a few levels that can be a bit frustrating but they don’t come until world 7 and there’s only a handful that had me scratching my head. I’m not the best gamer in the world, so that’s saying something. But the story that’s told about these once lonely individuals with radically different personalities and hopes and dreams and things to say, I was quickly sucked into it much like I did with Braid.
Another note I wanted to mention, especially to those aspiring game developers out there who feel they don’t have the snuff to make a great game. Graphics can be tough. We all can’t be great artists. Thomas Was Alone uses shapes… that’s it. And this game is amazing and should be experienced by all who like 2D puzzle platformers. You don’t have to be the best pixel artist, musician or programmer, and you can make an amazing game that stands out amongst the rest in storytelling and compelling characters. And that’s how you can make a game! I will buy it everytime.

So, all in all, it's a well made game with huge potential and a fun combat system. The online play is the literal worst experience I've ever had on a video game. Until they get dedicated servers, I recommend avoiding this game like a hooker  with suspicious lip sores.

This game has an issue with Securerom where if you buy it, and try to activate it will show you "activation failed" and deemed your cd-key invalid, claiming it is not in their databases.  That is because, it isn't.  You have to contact Capcom and give them a screenshot of the cdkey, and proof of purchase (A screenshot of the email steam sends when the game is bought).   After doing this, you wait a day or two and try to install it again and everything should work beautifully.
If you went to Capcom, and nothing happens, try again, over and over until it does.  It took me 3 tries but finally got the game to install.  Below are the instructions to get your copy working if you run into the invalid cd-key issue.
1) Go to

2) Click on the "Contact Us" button under the search bar.
3) Explain your issue, something like "bought Dark Void, trying to install got invalid cdkey, etc"
4) Provide screenshots of your cd-key, and proof of purchase.
5)  Wait.
If for some reason this method doesn't work, repeat until it does.  Steam support can't/won't help you and the whole secure-rom team is probably crying in a room cause everyone hates them, so no point in trying to make contact for help.

Well I spent almost 8 hours playing this game, 3 which were spent trying to install it over and over due to the cd key issue.   I don't feel like wasting more time on this so my review is short and to the point.
Graphics 8/10
It looks good for a game of 2010 (I am old, so it's weird to say it that way, but yah, for it's time the game holds up quite well)
Gameplay 2/10
You'll play the first level and that's basically it, no other elements are added to the gameplay maybe 2 or 3 different weapons and the upgrades for them and the jetpack.  Overall the game is SUPER repetitive, making this game boring as hell.   All the missions are the same "oh no, enemies, shoot them please"  once the enemies are gone, that's it.   Some levels have you running around for no reason only to trigger a "oh no, enemies again".   If you enjoy repetitive gameplay, go for it, this game is for you, but you can just watch a video of youtube in loop, hold any sort of gamepad and try to play along like a child who is being tricked by his/her parents so they can go bone in peace. You'll save the money and won't feel as stupid as I do right now.
I played this game in the hardest difficulty by the way, and it was as hard as throwing a rock into a lake.  So maybe sucking at games will raise the challenge for you.  The last boss is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  Seriously.  I don't like to use the word ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at all, and I am sorry for the last boss's relatives, but it was very disappointing, lame and just overall stupid.
Sound/Music 3/10
Umm... nothing memorable, just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ background music.  Noticeable enough that you don't hear the sound of a piece of your soul dying while playing this game past lvl 1 and forgettable enough that you can actually sleep at night after the feeling of emptiness leaves your body before bed.
Story  3/10
I was going to give it a 1, but that's mean, and I've been mean enough already.   The story is bad, just full of holes and the character development is nonexistent.  The characters have names that you won't care about, there's a cameo of a cool scientist for like 2 mins total, and even then, they don't managed to properly include him in the overall development of the story.
I feel they hired dead fish to write this story, but since fish can't hold pencils or pens, they had to just wing it and interpret the smell of slimy scales under the sun into a filler story to get this game out there and ready to sell.  If only they had hired a child capable of mumbling words this game would be entertaining enough to follow along till the end.
Replay value -1000/10
When you finish they game they give you an unlocked radar to find all the hidden treasures...  HAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA  omg.  Nice one guys.  That is the best April fools joke ever.
Overall - 3/10
This is not an average at all, I just felt like 3 is a nice number.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥ enough to be under 5 but good enough to be above 2.  At first I had the "don't buy this game cause you can't install it" review, but now I edited to say, don't buy this game cause it will make you dumb.
I mean it is entertaining for like 20 mins, so if you are ok with that, go for it.  If not, please heed my advice:
Go outside and pick up a rock, throw it in any direction as far as you can, then close your eyes, count to 10 and go look for the rock.  You'll have a lot of more fun than playing this crap, you'll play outside, you'll get some sunlight tan and who knows, you might hit a leprechaun or something and find some gold.

So, after playing through most of the game, I have to say...
...This game wasn't very good.
Storyline - 7/10
The story is alright, but not very good. Honestly it all feels rather tacky, like a kind of rushed development sort of thing. Nothing too bad or exceptional here. Here's a cop who's been betrayed, here's a guy who's lost his fellow comrades in battle, here's a dude who can save the people because he's virus immune, etc.
Gameplay - 4/10
The gameplay is fun and good at first, allowing you to go about and deck zombies in the face, shoot some j'avo, etc. But as time goes on there becomes more and more collectathons for you to do, and while I get the sense they're supposed to be a fun challenge or a puzzle, they're just designed in such a way that it feels tedious, and almost badly designed. The boss enemies like Ustanak feel very static, I.E they have very little or no reaction to your bullets, giving you a poor idea of if you're doing decent damage to them or not. And by the end of the game, I was tired of dealing with B.O.W's, as they were, just like the collectathons, tedious to deal with and not very fun half of the time.
Characters - 6/10
Not much to say here, other than it got a 6 because if you go into this not really having played R.E, you'll be confused at some points about who's who and what their importance is in the series.
Music - 1/10
I was usually too busy to hear the music at most points, but the music I did hear got really old, really fast.
Overall - 3/10
It was generally an unsavory experience. By the end of the campaign I was no longer hooked, as many of the plotlines had been solved, and I didn't particularly have an interest in how things wrapped up. I had gotten well fed up of boss fights, and the combat generally failed to impress due to the way too excessive use of quick-time events. If you're a really diehard fan I'd suggest to get this at least to know how the plot of R.E continues, if you don't get too super salty about these kinds of games. Otherwise, probably just avoid it.

Even if I'm giving it thumb down I could recommend this game to certain people. Its a decent shooter, with nice graphics, and some great moments.
However, personally, I didn't like it very much, and theres a lot of reasons for that. Comparing to its predecessor it has improved story, multiplayer, and alien design, but overall, original was a far better game (but still far from my favourite game). Original Crysis was obviously a game designed with PC in mind, and you could see that in every aspect of it - graphics, huge levels, level of destruction, and other stuff. It was ported to consoles years later, but in Crysis 2 version of engine, and with no surprise.
Instead in the jungle on islands Crysis moved to the jungle on concrete, how they call New York, and very popular thing to say during this game's advertisement period. Levels are now far more stiff. Here and there you may stumble upon some more open area, but rarely, soon after you will return to your usual corridor roam. No matter how wide its corridors are, corridor shooter is still a corridor shooter. Initially, it came with only dx9 assets. It got dx11 facelift later, but even after that you can still see a lot of hidious textures, especially on the walls. Here and there you may break some glass, TV screen or a vase, but generally environment is indistructible. You can use carboard boxes as a solid cover or even hide behind cellophane wall. Which is just ridiculous comparing to the original, where you could level down structures, or even cut down the trees with shooting. But this is just a nitpicking, mostly. Despite all of that, even without highres textures, its a pretty looking game, theres no doubt about it.
AI in this game is brain-dead, and I'm not even exaggerating. You may not notice it initially, because of the sheer numbers of opponents you'll be facing most of the time. But sooner or later you have to see how they love that cover... They love it so much that they won't move from it even if you stand right before them, or even after putting a bullet in their body. It happens that they forget about you after you run past them, you or they hide behind the cover, or ignoring the fight which happened just couple of metters behind them. Sometimes they won't acknowledge your presence until you shoot them, even if you are in the open in front of them, in their sight range. Other hilarious stuff includes your marine ally getting killed because he accidentally stopped where scripted event occured and jeep runned over him, killing their colleagues (or even themselves) with their own grenades, blowing themselves up after accidentally shooting the red barrel behind which they were hidding...
But what I hate the most is that camera movement. PC designed original had nice and smooth aiming, unlike Crysis 2. Its not that bad, but no matter how much I'm tweaking mouse sensitivity, I just can't get rid of that feeling like I'm moving controller thumbstick, and not a mouse. Like something drags me down. Lowering settings to get some extra frames doesn't help either (game runs smooth on highest settings anyways). In SP with laughtable AI its tolerable, but in MP its a killer. Yet another sign of its console design. Similar problem I had with Halo 2 PC port, or Bioshock Infinite, yet another console-infested game.
As I said, story is better this time, but again - nothing for an Oscar. You are some US Marine grunt, infiltrating New York via sub with your team. But soon hell breaks loose after alien incursion, your whole team gets killed, and you are saved by Prophet, character from the first game. You will see him just  briefly at the beginning, he is infected by the alien virus, and can't last much longer. He gives you his nano-suit, and puts a bullet in his own head to break the link with the suit. But before that gives you the order to find certain scientist, that guy who your team supposed to find anyways. For some reason, your character doesn't say a single word for the whole durration of the game, not even "I'm not Prophet, God damnit!" to all those people trying to murder him screaming "Its Prophet!", but eh.
Nano-suit went through some changes. You still have the option of modding weapons with various attachements, and armor and cloak modes are working as you used to. There's an additional option: by eliminating filthy xenos you can collect nano-catalyst points from their dead bodies (aliens are coming in several types, and how much you get depends from the type), and you can use them to upgrade your suit. Abilities are divided into 4 classes, with 3 potential upgrades for each, and only one upgrade at the time can be chosen per class, (such as improved health and energy regeneration, improvements for cloaking, bullet tracing, etc), and in that way it gives you certain amount of customisation. If you have enough patience you can easily farm catalysts on certain locations, where  you can just run around and melee alien grunts, since they are no challenge anyways.
Strenght and speed modes are now combined into one "Power" mode and its active all the time. High jumping, grabbing and kicking your opponents/items, and running is using your suit energy. While for strenght mode it makes some sense, why someone decided that simple sprinting is using your suit energy - I really have no idea. Not to mention that running in this game is on par with walking in majority of other games, and walking is painfully slow, plus when we combine that with console treated aiming... Since levels are smaller and far more linear now, designers probably thought there wasn't any need for that super-dash, or normal walking. Maybe its more realistic that way, and I'm nitpicking again, but I'm playing games for fun mostly, not for their realism (as much as the game with setting like this can relly on realism).
MP is fairly basic, and fun for a while, but nothing that kept me for too long. Btw, you are required to create a 3rd party account, since this game doesn't use Steamworks. Since MP in this game is almost dead, ranked matching is not an option if you plan to play at all, so you are stuck with the custom server browser, which often results in playing with far more leveled players than you, with far better unlocks and perks (besides regular aim-bot users). You can play either in nano-suits, or as regular troopers. Playing with nano-suits is not particulary fun, its just a bunch of ghosts shooting each other, because cloaking is far too often used, and no wonder - you are literally invisible. But even without it its hard to spot someone most of the time, because design of uniforms easily blends with the envronment. Besides several pre-determined classes, with your unlocks you can create your own custom loadout, only one is available at the beginning, and if you bother to play enough you can unlock more by leveling. EDIT: With Gamespy service shutting down Crysis 1 and 2 are losing their MP support on the PC, so you are only stuck with the SP from now on.
And lastly, I have to mention great sound assets, and fantastic soundtrack. You can unlock it completelly in extras by finishing campaign levels, so nothing costs you to give it a try. I recommend tracks "SOS New York", "Chase", "Rampage" and "One Way In".

Outstanding Visual Novel: a free dark pyschological teen highschool dating serial killer suspense novel.
First and foremost, it's the wry self-aware writing that draws me in; it is supported by the typical VN backgrounds and character drawings, and a very effective soundtrack (35 titles) and sound effects, with some sparingly used visual effects. The pacing and building of suspense is top notch; there are several times where I thought the game was nearing its end only to draw me in and push me on some more. This goes on for hours, it's that big; which is very unusual in a free VN.
The game focuses on a group of eight protagonists: we get to know them, their backstory and character, and while the game is not afraid of re-using VN and anime tropes, it is aware of that and manages to not come off as clichéd throughout. It is here that the novel really shines: I was very interested to get to know these characters, and often seemed to know more about them than the narrator does. The crime mystery plot is also executed well. At the same time, this could never be the plot of a Disney movie: while there is a lot of (well-excuted) lightness, the game gets very dark at times, too.
It is not hard to choose those gameplay options that will result in uncovering most of the story elements, except for getting past the bad climax: remember to save when you get a phone call in the subway (you can right-click to access the menu from any screen) -- and you do need to get past it, the ending that follows is not a quick one. Apart from this episode, and a small section where the narrator perspective shifts to Riu (why was that even necessary?), story progression was smooth and kept me on edge.
Technically, this renPy game is well crafted and has all the features you'd expect: it runs windowed and works well on older systems.
If you like to read a good story, I can only imagine you discarding this game if you either have no tolerance for the high school dating sim tropes that this game employs in parts, or if it is too dark for you: you will find out about the latter in the first few minutes. Very much recommended.

This is the first non-Gyakuten Saiban visual novel that I have finished. At first I did not know very well what to expect since the world of visual novels is something relatively new for me. But what I was looking for was an incredible and enthralling story through which visual novels are characteristic, and boy Lucid9 did not disappoint at all.
The plot is incredibly well written in this visual novel, I didn't expect it to be so good. The development is one of its strongest points. The story gradually becomes darker, Madoka style. Most of the characters are very well written, each has a credible personality within the story, which makes them believable. Their relationships, the dialogues, everything is natural according to their personality. I came to feel affection for them, worry, hatred, sadness. I would give it a perfect rating at this point if it weren't for some minor elements of the plot that didn't totally convince me, and because the end didn't hit me as intended because of the multiple bad endings.
As for art, in general it is fine. It is not the best thing I have seen but it fulfills its role. The character portraits are fine, in fact there are some that I quite like. However, there are some that need a little more polishing to look good. On the other hand, the lack of variety of background images is often evident. Excessive reuse of these can lead to distraction if you don't have enough imagination. Another problem is that most of the CG scenes don't look that good. This is because in all these cases, the drawings of the characters are not well proportioned.
The music in Lucid9 is gorgeous, easily one of the best video game soundtracks I've ever heard. Each theme is unique and brings tonality and emotion to the situation in which you find yourself. Sounds, on the other hand, don't stand out so much, they are simply there to add relevance to certain actions that happen in the story.
In conclusion, do I recommend Lucid9? Absolutely. If you are enthusiastic about good stories this is an assured recommendation. In fact this is a visual novel that I'd recommend to anyone who is remotely interested in visual novels. It's really worth it.

Blueprint tycoon is a management game where you set up supply chains and to produce materials and manufactured goods. The game starts off easy but very quickly ramps up the complexity. To produce basic goods, you only require workers. However, to advance, researchers must learn new blueprints, and these new goods may required specialized engineers and eventually experts, each of which have different needs that must be met in order to be fed and work. Likewise, earlier manufactured goods can be used as components for later blueprints.
The gameplay is pretty basic, to the game's benefit, but there are still a few issues. My main complaint is with blueprint system. You are given the option to rewrite the default blueprints in order to make recipes faster, produce more goods, generate less waste, etc. However, sometimes the steps will get disrupted if there are any kinks in the supply chain. When this happens, depending on how you set up the blueprint, it is possible for the building to be unable to restart. The blueprint system would be improved significantly if either (1) buildings restarted automatically whenever this happened, or (2) more information was given in order to debug where in the blueprint the issue arose.
My other issues with the game are minor. Some audio issues where some of the music would start and stop suddenly, even in the middle of a loop. The game also gives off the impression of wanting you to super-optimize everything, but there is so much available land to build on that, due to the blueprint issues I mentioned above, I got to a point where I had to force myself to build sub-optimally just so I could finish the scenario and be done with it.
On the topic of scenarios: there are 5 scenarios in the game, each with increased difficulty. They serve as both the tutorial and the main game mode. There is the option to play sandbox or user-generated levels, but by the time I finished the last scenario I was done with the game.
All that said, though, for the price I think the game is worth your money. Sure, there are a few things that could be improved still, but what's here is still solid. If you're looking for a quick management game with a pretty complex blueprint component tree, pick this one up!

Visual:

All of the missions seems like an extended tutorial, even though the needs of the tiered units change from mission to mission.

There is also a sandbox mode for those who just want to build.
Overall for the price, you can't go wrong. You'll definitely get several hours out of it.

If you'd like to spend a handful of hours playing a clumsy platformer with dull graphics, boot up Thomas Was Alone. Like most 'games' that can't quite pull of the 'game' portion of their existence, Thomas Was Alone attempts to make up for all of that by telling a story with its game, shifting weight onto that story to apologize for why the game itself is lacking. With pretension seeping from its pores, this game seeks to imprint itself as a narrative of overcoming boundaries and working as a team. While cute in its execution, it is just that--a baby's first steps, which become a dull affair after hours of watching the child fall. If you've got an afternoon to blow on what plays and feels like a college student's senior project in game design, go for it. So, I have finished Slender: The Arrival in about 200 minutes.
I am not gonna start with ratings. No, ratings are not really my favorite thing and I do not see the point why one does have to rate every single piece of ♥♥♥♥. Most of those reviews are usually very oppinion-based, therefore, how can one take those reviews seriously (with a few exceptions, of course).
So I am trying to caputre what this game actually is, following up with a conclusiong with a small insight of my own impressions.
First of all, about the overall graphics in this game. It is a game developed by an indie-studio, so you may think the visuals are not really good. They look similiar to other games, though there are a few things that make it outstanding (blurry, how your character runs, the sunrays,...), so it is not a poorly designed game. The animations are stiff though.
The atmosphere swaps from tense to relaxing quite often, giving the player a few breaks.
Tense because if you are being haunted, you feel haunted. That is something not easily accomplished in horror games (I like to relate to Cry of Fear or Outlast).
The relaxing parts are surely needed, since calming down is important - You feel your blood pumping over and over again, making this a worthy experience for someone who likes those tense experiences. I also have to mention the game gives you a few jumpscares (While I do not think they are necessairy in this game).
Controls and environment in overall are simple, while rather strict. That means you can not really interact with your environment. You can not climb outside of windows, neither can you jump, or anything else like that. What you can do is focusing your flashling + zooming it in/turning it off alongside moving around and sprinting/crouching. That works suprisingly well for this game, thus not even making one miss any acrobatic or environmental interactions with your world.
As you can see (or read) I tried to be mostly objective there. Finally, I would like to add a few own thought about this game though,
I played this game pretty much in one go. I only died twice in the end, since it was really unclear where you had to run to and that there actually is a goal there....that is about the only real complaint I have about this game. That chapter was not really necessaire in my opinion (No, not even that boy catched me off guard).
While there are few aninmations regarding the beings haunting you, the environment itself is beautifully designed. Especially the sunlight made this game unique to me, it was well implemented in this game...while the nights revealed very, very sinister feelings in me. Had me pretty hard in its grip, the atmosphere is really great.
I will surely play it another time, because I missed a few collectibles (7 I think). So it is a rather short game....paying around 10 bucks for this surely is ok, although I recommend buying this one on sale. It is pretty short, with a rather low replay-value. What is really interesting though is that you play very different parts, mostly just one chapter, with people you read about in the game itself. While the end of the game is not that interesting I would say, it all fits together in the end.

This is such an incredibly poor game it's hard to put it into words. If you want a short review, just imagine a man reduced to screaming and hurting himself because Resident Evil 6 is just that bad.
The first problem is just how dark the game is. Not 'Oh, scary grimdark shennanigans Batman!' dark, dark like you will never have any idea what the hell is going on because there are just two people floating in the middle of your screen in a pure black void. I managed to make a little progress as Leon simply by making him jump facefirst into things and picking a different direction when he went Gnugh and somehow I managed to find a cake. I'm assuming there was some sort of party going on in the level, but you will never know because it's utterly pitch black. As far as I'm concerned, that cake may as well have been the end of game boss.
The cutscenes aren't bad, and as of about halfway (I think) into the story of the first two characters and there haven't been any instadeath quicktime minigames right after any of them, which is always a plus. The cutscenes are odd in that you can skip some, but not all of them and there's no clear rhyme or reason to which ones it allows you to jump past.
The character graphics are pretty fluid and fairly seamless, which is nice, but the enemy sprites really aren't amazing. They all look pretty much the same, which can be a problem when you waste all your ammo shooting into the helmet of a hat zombie (some zombies wear helmets and the remains of armor) because you simply couldn't tell what he was. Zombies don't really react to attacks like they used to in previous games, either. You can shoot them, but unless it's a killing blow or they were winding up for a ranged attack they really don't bother telegraphing anything. This can be a problem because some of the zombies are absolute bullet sponges and it's impossible to know if you are even hurting them.
One big problem I have here is how enemy attacks take priority over player actions. I've lost count of the number of times I've been reduced to swearing out loud because a melee attack against a zombie has been cancelled halfway through the animation because the zombie attacked, the game prioritized the hostile NPC's action over the players, I take damage and oh look, time to play the little button mashing 'escape the zombie' minigame, AGAIN. I really, really do hope something quite terrible happens to the man who decided that should be added.
The single worst thing about the game (and consider the competition it has) is the inventory, and the UI in general. If it was designed for a PC, it wasn't a PC built by or for humans. Gone are the inventory management systems that featured in previous games, replaced by something that looks and works a lot like a puzzle from one, albeit a puzzle that would quickly have been patched out due to being so utterly awkward to use! The entire thing was more than likely built with a gamepad in mind, which is fine, but when you consider how utterly fluid the keyboard/mouse controls were in Resident Evil 5 you realise they really have no excuse.
What else?
I haven't talked about the story yet, mostly because I haven't seen much of it, but a womans sister did turn into Kerrigan. Spoiler alert I guess. And no, I'm not kidding. She turns into the woman from Starcraft, though I'm pretty sure Kerrigan wears some sort of alien armor and doesn't bounce around naked like ResidentKerrigan here does. You fight her in the mine cart scene from Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. After that you go to the center of the Earth. Sadly so far there have been no dinosaurs, but I remain hopeful. I'm still not kidding.
The bats**t insane Resident Evil madness we all love is there, it just feels... hollow? I guess? it's difficult to describe, but it feels like the entire thing is just Capcom phoning it in to make some cash. It's like a bored schoolkid telling you about what he did on his holidays. And then this happened and then this happened and then this happened and then this happened and then this happened and... Sure, it all sounds like it should be fun, but you just know the lil' guy wants to go ride bikes somewhere else. His heart isn't in it, and neither was Capcoms.
That might be down to the characters, who haven't really had a chance to shine. With so many player characters they had to assign a very small amount of development time to each, so what you get is very short and doesn't really help you get attached to anyone. Character wise, the series really hit its peak when Leon went on his little adventure to NotSpain. It's been downhill since then.
TL:DR - Skip it. It's bland as hell in all respects.

This game is a perfect illustration of the need to playtest early, often, thoroughly, and with fresh batches of new people. Ithas some really interesting ideas, but the interface keeps getting in my way. After an hour of playing through the tutorial and, after that, 3-4 attempts at *actually* figuring out the system by playing through the first level, my reaction was "man, I really hope this is an early access game". If this were early access, all of these issues would be perfectly understandable, and I'd recommend the game as an intersting take on the genre. But nope. It is not.
Starting with the tutorial,where about the 3rd tutorial message blocked the button it was telling me to click. I eventually figured out that (1) the button is under the tutorial message window and (2) you can move windows around. But juggling tutorial windows continued to be a problem.
The tutorial itself follows the not-so-fine "oldschool" tradition of showing you some stuff you can (and ought to) build, but not explaining how all the numbers fit together and how the systems actually work. Or, half the time, where the numbers even are. or what they mean (some of the numbers are percentage values! I could only tell after I noticed, through observation, that they vary from 0 to 100.)
The systems fit together in an intersting way, but they don't make intuitive sense, so they are really hard to figure out at first. Workers MUST have roads to travel when they are working, but they can magically teleport to their place of employment as needed, as you re-distribute workers and build new things. All transportation MUST happen via workers, over roads, with you manually specifying the path(which, of course, is different from the road.). Except when it doesn't, because a flying thing does it automatically. There are at least 3 types of flying things with 3 different sets of limitations that don't really make much sense. I had a hell of a time figuring out why I could build buildings, and *sometimes* I could build objects, but then my production was halted, all my wood-related buildings were filled with wood, but my object-building building was complaining about lack of wood. If you are confused, then welcome to my world.
All the right clicks/left clicks/mode changes/pause/unpause/ context-sensitive highlighting just do not flow together into a coherent thing, especially when building new stuff. Each time you build a (production) building, you have to do 3 separate things: roads, supply paths, blueprints. All of these are in different contexts and sub-menus. The only thing that tells you what you got wrong is a cryptic icon on the building, which has no word translation. And I hope you remembered to manually pause before you started fiddling with the bluepripts! especially if you're just starting and you're not profitable yet.
The blueprint idea is cool, but the interface makes me really, really miss and appreciate SpaceChem. Also, thus far, there's not much interesting I can do that's not already in the default blueprint. And I'm sure that by the time I'm advanced enough for the default to be sub-optimal, I'll have already developed a habit of clicking "default blueprint" (which, btw, you can't even examine easily...)
why is the storage building in its own separate box instead of in the building menus?
why does space take me to the main building instead of pausing/unpausing, like in most games that have a pause functionality that needs to be frequently used?
what is with roads altogether? why are they necessary? they don't seem to cost anything. they're just more busywork.
there seems to be a lot of busywork/challenge by annoyance stuff in the system like this: e.g. the separation between the delivery storage and the actual delivery area, and the way the workers manage that path, which is totally different from the way workers work in any other place.
Or the fact that the interface makes it super hard to have a high-level view of most of your production pipeline (except the very end, we really care about the very end of the pipeline!)
Why does 5 worker houses give me 63 workers? worker houses seem to be the one and only way to get workers. but how many do I get, and why?
do "available" workers even draw money? how am I supposed to figure this out?
Why are there two "route" buttons, and why is there so little visual feedback as to what the heck I'm making when Imake the path, and whether I succeeded in making it? why do I have to click "new route" to finalize creation - or worse, edits - to the route I am currently working on?
why are there so many clicks involved (in such arcane and counterintuitive places) in starting to make or set a blueprint, *especially* for the object crafting in the Main building?
why do *some* buildings have directed in/out doors, but others have two-way doors? what is the point of one-way doors in the first place ('dwchallenge' through annoyance?), and why is it inconsistent?
If it's called a "default" blueprint, why isn't it on by default? Do you know how many times I've set a thing into a queue in the main building, only to discover soooo much later that my queue is stopped because I forgot to click the "default" button?
why won't my automatic delivery storage-to-delivery men take the milk from the storage and deliver it right after I set up the route? why do they have to wait until the next day to figure this out?
what principle does the air baloon use to decide how many items to deliver at a time? it seems to vary quite a bit.
why don't I get any benefit out of an overflow of income? I just lose everything above what I need to pay my workers? why do I care, then, that I "missed" some income - a thing that stays up in red constantly on my screen if my efficiency in the one specific area it's measuring is not perfect. (who cares about all the other pieces of the pipeline though!)
some things make a "wrong" buzz sound, even though they are just asking me to interact with a follow-up menu(e.g. please specify the type of item to transport) and others do not, even though the game has refused to do the thing I asked for (e.g. not enough researchers for research.)
sometimes I need to get more researchers, but the game tells me to get more workers!
it's often not obvious which window I'm interacting with, and even sometimes that I'm supposed to interact with a pop-up window, because the hierarchy and the placement of windows is very strange.
What are the green numbers on the Delivery that are similar to, but not the same as, the prices for the products listed on the contracts?
I keep finding that my routes get changed or cancelled seemingly without my intervention, e.g. I finish one research, start another, and later find that it's backed up because somehow one of the trash runs along the route is just not there anymore. Or suddenly I am no longer selling any cheese or milk because my cheese/milk balloon has randomly started 'delivering' things in the opposite direction than it used to. did I do that?.. I don't know! I wish it were more clear when I did stuff and what the effects were!
... I keep finding more of these issues, but I think you get the point.

There is one famous Japanese series that Lucid9 reminds me of a little: Higurashi. Both start off light-hearted and have their fair share of
comical slice-of-life high school shenanigans, and both eventually take a much darker and more serious turn (although Lucid9 has no supernatural elements). This is not to say they are the same, but I wonder whether the creators were inspired by 07th Expansion's work.
I believe this comparison already sets the bar pretty high, and trust me, the game does not disappoint. Writing is very good and each character has a very distinct voice, filled with entertaining expressions and colourful vocabulary that get you through even the lengthiest calm/comedic moments (which I am personally not very fond of). The mystery parts are also well written and visual/sound effects work well with the narrative to convey a story that made my heart race and my eyes never deviate from the screen.
Another plus of this novel is the portrayal of mental illness. It is a central topic to the story and it is never portrayed in stereotypical or negative light, only realistic. I also enjoyed their use of dissociative disorder, which is hardly ever seen in media.
As for the cons, the main ones I'd list would be the length of comedic filler, the fact that some choices seem to serve no purpose but get achievements, and the character art. While most sprites look alright, others look strange and most CGs have issues, especially with proportions and facial angles. They are not
, but definitely need some work.
Either way, I still recommend this and am very surprised to have stumbled upon such a good free VN
. Definitely looking forward to the next arc.

I’ve always been one for visual novels. Lucid9: Inciting Incident showed up in my queue, and it instantly piqued my interest. I was surprised that it was free, but I decided to give it a try anyway. I immediately loved the game after playing through it. This visual novel is well crafted, and is definitely able to make you feel many different emotions throughout its story.
To start off, I’ll talk about the characters. Normally, I’m one to forget a character or two if there happen to be a lot of them. There are indeed many characters in Lucid9, but they are all extremely memorable for their personalities.  I won’t go into specific details because of spoilers, but every character develops over the course of the game, and it definitely is something that is important for visual novels.
The game’s overall synopsis involves a high school student named Yama Ishimoto in Japan during 2018. Later on, he is asked to be involved in an investigation regarding a chain of disappearances that have occurred at the academy. Again, I won’t spoil in case someone does read this, but the mystery definitely builds up throughout this story. Though it may seem like your choices don’t matter, don’t make this assumption. Lucid9 likes to throw some curve balls to make this visual novel more and more interesting.
It may seem like this game is only cute, that is not the case, as it transforms into something that contains purpose. It can make you feel happy or apologetic for these characters. You never fully know these characters, and that’s what makes this game different from most visual novels. You think you know everything, but in the end there are still secrets that we don’t know about the characters. The overall plot and ending prove this as you experience it first hand.
Overall, this game makes you laugh at the comical and happy moments, and at other moments, it makes you feel pain and may bring you on the verge of tears (that happened to me at least). If you plan to play the game, it is highly recommended that you play it without any spoilers to fully enjoy the experience that this visual novel offers. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’m going to continue to cry obtaining the achievements in this game.

Forget the 'bridge' part of the name. Most of what you have to build in this game has more to do with ramps, rollercoasters, elevators, and even loops. It is in effect an elaborate 'lattice structure puzzle game' that is very challenging, quite often frustrating, and yet very much addicting if you like this kind of stuff.
The challenge comes from having to build, sometimes very elaborate, structures from short pieces of wood, steel, rope, and cable on a very small budget. Sometimes you have to add in hydraulics to create drawbridges or lifts, but for the most part you have to build solid structures out of what can best be described as matches, In many ways it resembles the "build a bridge from 5 sheets of paper" challenge from school. If you do know how real bridges are built, then you will have to forget that knowledge for many of the levels since many of the solutions we'd use in the real world simply cannot be done in the game (load transfer systems are especially difficult to make due to length limitations of the available pieces).
The game has a few shortcomings in its physics model and lack of realism, but many of its puzzles are designed around this - especially the ones involving hydraulics.
You will occasionally find that some bridges will work or fail when they feel like it, suspension bridges will sway and wobble without any load, and the way hydraulics are simulated is unrealistic. The hydros are not a simulated piston in a cylinder, but simply a line than can grow shorter or longer. Since the effective length is based on the starting length, hydaulics that start contracted are effectively shorter than those that start expanded. You could say the game would be too easy if it didn't work this way. You could also say that it'd be a better game if everything worked like you'd expect.

Caves of Qud is a truly amazing roguelike, developed over a 10+ year period by two guys and a ton of love. While most people think wizards and dragons when they hear the term roguelike, CoQ instead brings the world to a post-apocalyptic setting somewhere on the planet earth.
At this point in the distant future, much of the land is a vast salt-desert, interspersed with jungles, mountains and more. The remaining humans and mutants (and even weirder creatures) struggle to survive, traversing the brutal heat and unforgiving landscape with the hope that maybe this settlement will last. Water is the currency of choice; with so much of the land arid, clean water is rare and since life depends on it, unbelivably precious as well. Yet beings have survived and thrived, and the game presents a huge amount of lore in various forms to reflect this.
Alongside the history is the present, with all the fracturing of groups and the different factions that result from a collapse of modern society. Species hate other species, religions hate other religions, and sometimes the enemy of my enemy is my friend. CoQ has a layered faction system, where the player's actions (and even equipment) can change their standing in the eyes of the denizens of the world.
And with the amount of character customization, your choices will have an impact. From the true humans, non-mutants of various castes and professions, to the mutants, with the huge amount of physical and mental positive and negative mutations, the game can be approached in a vast amount of ways. The specifics are covered elsewhere, but know that builds can go from traditional gunslingers to four-armed, two heart furry ape-like creatures that leak slime and occasionally warp in and out of existence. It's even possible to be hunted by an evil, alternate-dimension version of yourself.
What makes Caves of Qud so engrossing and keeps it from collapsing under the weight of the huge amount of features is the streamlining of the classic roguelike experience, especially in regards to the UI. Things just make sense. Very rarely will the game fight against the player, instead they're allowed to lose themselves in the world of Qud. This is even apparent in the graphics; light is cast and blocked by different things, smoke curls and acid spreads, and water will splash as the player runs through.
The game now offers tiles, though I'm personally a fan of the ASCII setting after playing it for so long. That doesn't mean the tiles are bad though; in fact it's quite the opposite. Items and enemies are easy to identify, there are various settings to tweak how it looks, and even a fair amount of performance options for players on older computers. It even has music slowly being added, though no sound effects currently. It also supports user mods, for the players who want to add their own changes to the game.
A final note: Caves of Qud is definitely following the footsteps of traditional roguelikes. The term has been diluted to mean permadeath and maybe randomly generated dungeons, so you can end up with a realtime side scrolling platformer with permadeath being labeled "roguelike". This is not one of those. It's turn-based, requires lots of reading, much trial and error to learn the mechanics, and is meant to be played on a keyboard. It does greatly expand on quite a few of the roguelike traditions, but still keeps the core gameplay of one.
You will not regret buying this game.

If you'd like to spend a handful of hours playing a clumsy platformer with dull graphics, boot up Thomas Was Alone. Like most 'games' that can't quite pull of the 'game' portion of their existence, Thomas Was Alone attempts to make up for all of that by telling a story with its game, shifting weight onto that story to apologize for why the game itself is lacking. With pretension seeping from its pores, this game seeks to imprint itself as a narrative of overcoming boundaries and working as a team. While cute in its execution, it is just that--a baby's first steps, which become a dull affair after hours of watching the child fall. If you've got an afternoon to blow on what plays and feels like a college student's senior project in game design, go for it. Otherwise, this game ranks medium--it can't be called rare and it certainly isn't well done.

Thomas Was Alone was amazing. Its a platformer focusing on writing and narrative.
Its well-designed. Witty. Deep. Emotional.
Its literally, just a bunch of shapes yet its probably one of the most emotional journeys I have had in my time as a gamer.

At times, I hesitate to even call this a game. It is more of an experience.
Playing as Thomas and his compatriots can be seen as just moving around colored blocks, and on the surface that is what you are doing. take a little time to invest yourself in the story, and you start to see the game in a light far more refined than how it seems to start.
What really helps the story along is the narrator. While not as overly tied to the allure of the game, like Rucks in Bastion or the narrator of The Stanley Parable, this narrator does a well enough job in bringing the emotion of these little blocks to the forefront. He has a dry wit, which shines through at certain points and helps break the monotony that can set in.
The plot, while nothing overly unique, is well laid out. It all comes back to the idea that you are taking squares and rectangles, moving them around, and creating a relatively complex story out of what happens.
If you are looking for a massive game to devote your time and essence to, this won't be for you. But if you are looking for something to enjoy, rather than just play, then maybe, just maybe, you have come to the right place

This game brings me back to the late 90's - early 00's style PC multiplayer games. It has a classic feel to it, and while it may be a very simple and basic game, it keeps making me laugh. You run to the cheese and run back to the hole as fast as you can, and you get scored on how fast you are. However, the maps are often treacherous and have falls, drops, obstacles and things that make you die. I find myself chuckling out loud quite often while playing this simple game. Would recommend!

The game comes with three tutorials and three scenarios, it seems. However, the thing I was looking forward to that the game lacks is a sandbox mode, leaving us to try to create our own in the scenario editor. But I likely ran into the same problem: The scenario editor is way more in depth than we were imagining. Which is okay!
The bad thing about this game is it's looking like it's made to be a tool for players to create and share scenarios of their own, but very few people are actually willing to go so far to create one.
I think that the devs should allow us to import goods/recipes/blueprints/etc. from other scenarios, the ones the game supplies, into our own scenarios. It would save us ametuars time when we want to make our own. Alternatively, the devs should create a sandbox mode... but I see how it wouldn't really be easy, considering how each scenario has different requirements for goods and workers and the like.
For the price, it's a good game, but don't expect much out of it unless you want to sit around continuing scenarios after you finished the main objectives. It's only a couple hours of fun otherwise, or however long it takes you to finish them. After that, you're stuck either dealing with the fact that you beat what little content the game provided, or start to create your own content, and be prepared to invest hours into that before it's even playable.
TL;DR You get what you pay for. If you want more, you have to create more.

Complete guitar noob here. I always wanted to play, but never knew what I was doing. I don't have much of a music / muscial instrument background to speak of either, so no shortcuts to fallback on for me. I've seen people who have taken some guitar lessons or have already mastered another instrument and they just take to Rocksmith like a duck to water (leaving me far behind...).
The Ugly:
Rocksmith won't teach you much. It won't really guide you at all. It's more self-directed than all of that. It's the classic example of what you put in to it (including from external sources) is what you get out of it. But it does have three things going for it that nothing else has.
The Good:
1) Guitarcade is where to practice techniques to build up your muscle memory and it's not boring. When has practice not been boring?!
2) From time to time, some songs you'll just get and you'll start rocking out. This positive feedback keeps me coming back. "Hmm, that's how you play that rift. Awesome! I can do that!" or "I've never seen that before... Whoa... It's not too hard. Those notes are coming so fast! But it's not too bad at all." Go ahead and headbang ;).
3) It's very difficult to put down once started (just one more song...) and I only seem to do it to give my fingertips a break.
The Bad:
1) Pricey DLC. I buy all mine on sale and frankly have too much. Learning to play guitar doesn't require a gigantic song library.
2) Let's you have very sloppy technique for a very long time. It's up to you to recognize you're not helping yourself by over struming, not palm muting / using sustains, faking hammer ons / pull offs, over fretting, etc.
3) Doesn't reinforce much of the basics: a guitar's ergonomic fit (5'6" here - A Les Paul's neck (scale length) is significantly smaller than a stratocaster's), streching / warm ups to increase reach / hand span, thumb position changes for different parts of the neck and different strings, and chord playing vs. soloing technique differences that are to be expected.
How to counter act the cons?
You want theory, technique, guidance, and best practices, so get a book, get a guitar playing friend, watch a lot of YouTube videos, and don't "play" Rocksmith like Guitar Hero / Rock Band where only the score matters. In the beginning playing for score is fine because you want to see instant progress. That's what gets you hooked. Later on you'll switch from wanting to score higher to actually wanting to play better. When that mental shift happens Rocksmith will have done it's job. You're no longer a noob... You're an ax wielding apprentice and can chart your own path using Rocksmith as a tool.

However, as the game progresses, you see that thomas, chris, john, claire, laura, james and sarah are far deeper as characters than their simple appearance may suggest. The ambitions, insecurities and aspirations of each character are told in stunning soliloquy and beautifully narrated. By the end of the game, I cared about these colored rectangles more than some people in real life.
Music direction was very good. It fits very well with the theme of the game. In the beginning it's not pushy - the music really brings about an air of exploration which ties into the story very well. When you become genuinely concerned about the well being of these rectangles, The music reflects the urgency with which you rush to the portal.

As far as free games go this is one of my all-time faves. I normally don't like novel games, because I would much rather read a manga or a physical book, but this one was really interesting, and the many different endings were quite diverse depending on how you went along in the story, and the choices you made. I loved the characters, and there were so many paths to explore. The main story, for me (I got the bad ending), turned out to be almost 9 hours-- much longer than I was expecting out of a free game. The only problems I had with it, though, was that it took so long to get to the choices, and I had a hard time choosing with no idea where that branch would take me. I didn't follow a guide, so if you want to look up a guide on how to get each achievement use it as you are playing if you want to get a certain ending. Just know it is a very long game, and the choices are far in between. Nonetheless, I recommend this game for story-lovers-- which I am. It is worth it-- especially since it is free!

This is the biggest pile of crap in gaming.  Forget that this totally abandons any last bit of suspenseful survival horror the franchise may have had left, but this crapfest doesn't even pull off being an average 3rd person shooter.   All of its game and combat mechanics  completely work against each other.    Even on the easiest level ammo is way to scarce, reloading takes way to long, and swapping weapons is nightmare.
For a game centered on action they made combat so freaking moronic that it's nearly impossible to take part in the action.  You'll spend more time running around trying to collect ammo and reloading your weapon than fighting monsters.  And these monsters are the now trademark Resident Evil bullet sponges.  You'll also fight he camera as its control is funky and unintuitive and will always do a lot of stuff not quite the way you expect it to.
The interface is god awful, and the inventory is the most insane system to navigate than any that's ever been.  And the menus, god the menus.  You will have to go through so many menus and button clicks just to do anything it's insane.  Click to start, click to check DLC, clikc to acknowledge this game uses auto saves, click to start again, clik to play, clikc to play story, click for chapter, click for game settings, finally now you can play.
Then there's the extended boss fights.  Spend 30 seconds shooting, then a minute of edgy combat cutscene, 30 more seconds of shooting, and then another minute of cutscene.  Then action sequence where you're out of ammo and have to shoot something or die, die, reload, then have the smallest amount of time to do it again, but having to collect the ammo, select the weappon that uses that ammo, then reload the weapon, and hope you can still shoot that explosive barrel before you insta die again.  No thanks.
The game has a lot for you to do, too bad it makes doing even the smallest tings a real chore.  This game completely sucks as both a Resident Evil game and even as a generic monster hunt 3rd person shooter.

Have you ever played a classic roguelike? I'm talking NetHack, ADOM, Dungeon Crawl, any of the games that started life as a nigh-incomprehensible block of ASCII characters. Old roguelikes were big on randomization but low on approachability, requiring you to know all sorts of interactions and tricks and symbols just to avoid dying to a bird or something. Caves of Qud plays like a classic roguelike that prioritizes fun over tricks, and does so with a unique setting and sense of style.
Character creation is a major highlight in Qud, allowing you to pick more than just attributes and a class (though even the classes are extremely interesting and varied). Being a post-apocalyptic sci-fi sort of game, you get to be a mutant if you want (yes, you want) and pick special powers from a hefty list of dozens. There's everything from telepathy and night vision to multiple limbs, flight, temporal clones, and mind crushing. These powers are on pretty generous cooldowns, and give you a wealth of tactical options in the game that a lot of roguelikes don't offer. My current best is a four-armed spastic teleporting rogue-thing that can emit sleeping gas or EMPs in emergencies, and I love him to the bits he will eventually be.
Once your character is made, you get dropped in the little town of Joppa with some intro quests to do and houses to loot. The quests in Qud give some much-needed direction, as the world is quite wide-open and there's plenty of places to get lost and die in. Dungeons are varied between caves, ruins, and higher-tech locales, and you can indeed get lost in the jungles and canyons between them. These places are populated with a colorful cast of creatures including rust crabs, goat men, and sentient ooze. The simple graphics are clear enough to distinguish the people and critters you encounter, and a very helpful Look function gives you all the information you need to know about approaching something new.
If it seems like I'm gushing about Qud, it's because I've never played a roguelike with so much depth and discovery that, at the same time, has so many user-friendly features. The menus are dense and busy but display everything you need to know in sensible order and with useful icons and colors. Item, skill, and attribute descriptions leave nothing to the imagination, so you'll never be left wondering where you should spend your points. And the quests really are fantastic signposts for the game, giving you more to do than the simple "descend and find the doodad" premises of the classic roguelikes.
It's not a perfect package, of course. If you've never played a classic-style roguelike there's going to be a significant learning curve, both to the interface and combat. You'll generally have enough tools to get yourself out of bad situations but learning how they work is going to take some experimentation, and it'll often be fatal. The activity log that explains what actions are being taken each turn is also too compressed to be terribly useful, and hopefully it'll be expanded into something easier to parse. There's no sound or music yet either, which makes it a good game to play while listening to music or podcasts but doesn't do any favors in terms of immersion.
These are all minor quibbles, and ones that will most likely be addressed during Early Access. Caves of Qud is already a rich and deep enough package to lose yourself in for hours on end, with plenty to see and do and try and die to and try again. It may take you some time to come to grips with the old-fashioned displays and interfaces, but the effort is well worth it. Fans of roguelikes, RPGs, sci-fi, and post-apocalyptic games will all find plenty to enjoy here.

I've often heard that when making a game with retro graphics, one must allow the graphics to fit and even enhance the gameplay. I've actually played a few old-school roguelikes before going to Caves of Qud and in all of them, I felt that a graphical update would improve the gameplay, but Caves of Qud is the first ASCII-roguelike I've ever played where I felt that the graphics did not need an update.
The reason for this is that it shares a huge similarity with older roguelikes in that much of the equipment needs to be identified before you know what it is, but there is a major difference in that when said equipment actually is identified, it immediately becomes apparent that any graphical representation whatsoever would have made it obvious what said object really is to the player. For example, the carbine, a very powerful mid-game rifle. Before identification, the description says, "A strange artifact" but afterwards, it says "A composite carbine with a banana-shaped magazine." If anyone here can make a Fallout game where the average joe could not understand what an assault rifle is without giving the player an unfair and/or non-immersive advantage in identifying it, I would love to see it.
There's also the fact that the lack of linearity and graphical fidelity, and yes, I did just say graphical fidelity, gives you more freedom and better immersion as well as lowering frustation. Very, very few ASCII roguelikes actually have blood splattering on the ground and on many occasions, death can really just creep up on you for no reason. In fact, these graphics hold a special place in my heart for actually being very unnerving in one specific instance, WITH NUMBERS AND LETTERS!!! There's also a major advantage in that if you run into an enemy that you can't fight, you not only get a clear indication of that, you also get options. There are actually other places to grind for XP, which can not be said of most other roguelikes and if a really dangerous enemy won't let up, there are numerous escape options. There is no telling how many times Warden Indrix has saved my characters' life.
Another major difference is how character-building is based less on power-gaming and more on building a character that suits you. Character building for True Men is bog standard but the system really comes alive with mutants. There are various Mental Mutations that give you a great sense of power and Physical Mutations that make your character more likely to end up on DeviantArt. I wish I were kidding, it takes only one mutation point to make your character a f***ing furry. Given that I main as a character with Heightened Hearing, Night Vision, Thick Fur, and has four arms, four legs, and two heads (as well as being amphibious), seeing him as some kind of froggy cattaur with double arms and heads would only be natural.
Lastly, identifying objects is based a lot more on skill and a lot less on luck. On many of the older ASCII roguelikes, dying without knowing what half of your equipment does is just part of the experience and there are many occasions where you can find out that your unidentified equipment could have saved your life. In CoQ however, there is no equipment that is necessary for straightforward identification and no need for sneaksy little tricks for said identification that often left me with 2 dozen tabs open in Firefox just to not be lost. I can not stress the importance of the "Examine" feature enough, it separates this game from all of its peers. Even then, it's not overpowered, you can't "Examine" equipment in merchants' inventories and without the right skillset, "Examine"ing something stands a good chance of breaking it. This can lead to some moments where you really have to gamble on getting something powerful or practically useless to you.
Final Verdict: 10/10 Would accidentally blow most of my fresh water reserves on a box of crayons again.

An amzing roguelike, holds up very well against old and modern classics.
Pros
Super indepth character creation.
Awesome graphics that balance the clarity of ascii and ease of viewing.
Nice difficulty curve, starts hard stays hard. Does not spike after clearing first area.
Amazing lore.
Deep, yet (somewhat) simple combat that feels weighty and meaningful.
Amazing UI and controls, clearly states whats happening and navigating the menus is easy.
More then one way to skin a snapjaw: many different methods to play: crafting, hunting, exploring, salvaging, trading, diplomating? and more.
Early variety: a serious failing of most roguelikes is that the begining is slow, repetitive and boring (Im looking at you ToME), Caves of Qud provides a quick, and fairly randomized begining.
Weekly? updates.
Cons:
Most of these are only problems to those new to roguelikes.
No tutorial: throws you right into a difficult roguelike, those new to the genre should look up how to play, not go in blind.  Maybe watch a letsplay and read the steam guides.
Overwhelming amount of options: Its often hard to decide what would be an effective character build, course of action or level progression, as so many options are present.
No music or sounds :(
(go make your own playlists)
Verdict 8.5/10

Jazzpunk is quite unique.  It's really fun to look at, it's odd and absurd, which is great, but for me it goes nowhere with it.
I am going to give it a thumbs down because: 1) It takes no effort or thought to play.  I have clicked everything, played all the mini games, searched every corner, gotten all the achievements and feel like I didn't do anything worthwhile when all is said and done.  2) The humor was not my kind of humor and it's unrelenting.  That's a problem since humor seems to be half the game content (the other half are the visuals).  For the most part, it is a continuous stream of computer-geek puns. IE: You go into a restaurant and the waitress says "I will be your dedicated server."  Lots and LOTS of that. There is almost no dialogue per se, just a lot of word play.  3) The game made me feel ill which really surprised me.  If you play for more than 30 minutes in a go, especially after the first chapter, most likely you will end up with a degree of motion sickness no matter how rarely you get it in real life.  This game could probably be weaponized for that ability.  4) The game is very very short, though given everything else, that is sort of a plus.
I kept expecting something in the game to wow me, to grab me mentally at least once, but nothing ever did.  It's colorful fluff.  If you like computer puns and pure silliness -- you'll probably have a great time.  If you want more from a game than just being taken on a ride, or if puns make you roll your eyes and sigh in annoyance -- then you probably want to give the game a miss.

If you want a funny, rediculous game, this is it.

I've played just about every survival MMO out there. Nether, initially, had its own style an offered a form of gameplay that none of the others offered. Where all the other survival MMOs feel like walking simulators for long stretches of time, Nether was made with a small, arena sized map based on post-apocalyptic urban decay. You could team up with your friend immediately and see them on the map so grouping up was easy. The gameplay was extremely suspenseful because the next encounter was right around the corner. It wasn't perfect, but so much fun when it worked that the imperfections could be brushed over.
So what happened?
Hackers. All survival MMOs have them but this game was riddled with them. The devs didn't have the resources and/or knowledge or maybe even the desire to fight this problem. It ruined the experience.
Nether. I thought they should just remove Nether completely. They were buggy AF and never really added to the enjoyment of the game. The good times were had in PvP encounters with other players. In such a small map, the encounters were frequent enough to warrant removing the Nether as they were more of an annoyance than anything.
I would like for a dev team to take the idea of a survival MMO, like Nether.. Small urban decayed map, easy to team up with friends, PvP focused, and run with just that. I think it would do well on Steam. This, unfortunately, did not.
