This review was originally negative, reflecting the game as it was back late 2015. Most of the complaints in the original review below below have been addressed.
-------
As someone who plays a lot of Dungeon Crawl: Stone Soup, I came to this game with high expectations. There is a lot of depth of gameplay here, but you're constantly fighting against the User Interface and the way the map works more than the monsters themselves.
You will constantly find yourself bumping into walls you can't see because rather than keeping the game world centered on the player, you're going from screen to screen. It feels very clunky and it constantly takes me out of the experience. There is a giant box of information to one side of the screen that blocks a huge portion of the map, but for how big it is, it really doesn't tell you a whole lot.
Another annoyance is the auto-explore AI. It is extremely poor. It skips over items you have on auto-pickup, and it's constantly getting stuck on nothing when the screen is nowhere near fully explored.
The game also seemed to discourage exploring too deep into any given cave - there are dead ends everywhere, and no easy way to backtrack like in most roguelikes. I was very disappointed that there didn't seem to be any way to get back to the surface other than the way I came, forcing me to try to retrace my steps over an hour and a half.
Another issue I had with the game is the performance - you would think such a simple looking game would run smooth as silk, but this game has to stop and think an awful lot. I didn't get far into the game and the files it generated on my computer total up to 385MB - 60MB for the save file, 60MB for a backup of that save file, and an enormous amount of cache. Like many early access titles, this game really needs some optimization done to it, but it's just surprising to see it from a game like this.
I feel like the entire engine needs to be rebuilt from the ground up, getting rid of the per-screen nonsense and keeping the world centered on the player, and with a much better User Interface. I really wanted to like this game, but I just don't. It needs to be better.

This game is the first roguelike I've really gotten into, and it may very well be the last. It blends fantasy and sci-fi in a way that I've never seen before, and I doubt I'll ever see something like this again. It's cringe-worthy, rage-inducingly hard, but I just cannot. Stop. Playing. I've never played a game that gave me as many character creation options as this one does. A lot of the lore is randomly generated and yet still manages to be intriguing and entertaining. This game is so good, I'm worried it'll overshadow all the other sci-fi RPGs I know and love. But not too worried, because if I had to pick a single game to play for the rest of my life, I'd pick CoQ, no question.

Played this a lot pre-steam and despite technically being in a Beta state this is tied for my favorite roguelike with ADOM.  If you like ASCII this game is a masterpiece.  I highly recommend buying this, turning off the tiles and basking in the amazing pixels and DnD style gameplay.  Like loot?  Like post-apocalyptic RPGs like Fallout, Wasteland or Borderlands?  Need a lesson in patience (you can turn off permadeath if you're lame)?  Just want an amazing game that you can pick up and put down anytime?
Buy CoQ.  Seriously, buy it.

Honestly this is my favorite roguelike. (Maybe my favorite game???) The setting is absolutely inspired, and riddled with atmosphere and lore (Books!! So many books!). There's new lore, features, items, abilities, and quests coming out on a weekly basis, the developers really care about this project and it shows. The tiles are gorgeous, and the smoke, fire, flowing water, etc, is a really nice touch. The mechanics go soooo deep, and there's so many options at character creation and a TON of different ways to play the game, and most builds are actually pretty viable if you play your cards right, some just take a lot more awareness and more than a little luck. The faction system is a really nice touch, and can actually be really funny sometimes (Baboons revere you, and consider you one of their own. You are welcomed into their holy places.). I've played hours of this game (More than it shows on steam!! This game has been around for years as a free roguelike.) and it still captures my imagination in the same way. There's no sound yet, unfortunately, but it goes great with something ethereal (Geidi Primes by Grimes mayhap?), because it's, to me at least, got that kind of dreamlike, up-five-hours-past-bedtime-playing-games feeling from when you're a kid.
Another thing I really like about this game is that you really get into your characters, because of the intense customization, and because of that it feels like this game has a sort of emergent storytelling quality of it. It's really deceptively immersive, and I don't really foresee myself putting this game down anytime soon.

This game is trully a masterpiece of narration. The sounds blend perfectly with this eerie first-steps curiousity soaked atmosphere of the game. A prime example that one does not need flashy graphics to have an emersive experience. It's very short and that only contributes to the feel of the game, ending right after the climax, with no unnecessary repetitive ordeals. 100 levels of fairly clever mechanics, but while the mechanics can carry the game on their own it is the narration that trully shines. By the end you'll find yourself smiling at the curiosity of Thomas, or rooting for the love affair of a certain two socially awkward geometric shapes while they traverse the new world they find themselves in. To top it all off you'll be given a different perspective on the events adding yet another layer to the story itself.
In short, if you want an experience that will leave you wondering where the past few hours went this game is for you. I never thought I'd feel an emotional connection to rectangles but this game does it so well, it seems like the most natural thing in the world.

Let's paint a beautiful picture for the people.  You're 1987 Volvo is driving down a wooded road on the Appalachian Trail (Or somewhere along the lines of that), when all of the sudden your car loses control and slides into a tree.  Your phone isn't getting any reception and there's no other cars or buildings in sight.  You know your friend Kate's house is right down the road and so you make your way down the dusty pebbled pathway. Down this longwinded path you notice a long brick fence, and contemplate: just who exactly can afford such a fence, and who exactly are they trying to block out? For there is no other houses or population for that matter in sight.  Regardless, you wonder down this road and find a 1998 Range Rover abandoned on the path and make nothing of it whatsoever, because the only people that own Range Rover's are divorcees who ran off with their lawyers. I'm getting carried away now.
You reach the end of the path and see Kate's house (Her mother's in reality) and in a remarkable 5 seconds it goes from day to night and you nonchalantly carry on with your way into her house.  It's dark, the bass is heavy and there are scribbles of trees and Slender himself on the wall.  You wonder around this dark and lustrous house in search of clues and wonder just where your friend Kate is.  Among further investigation you notice a pamphlet from Kate's mother's funeral service, as well as a letter (clue 2) talking about how weird things have been happening around the house lately and they aren't really explainable.
From there, you head outback after covering everything in the house and you'll find another clue (not disclosing its location) and off you are into the woods to help find Kate.

Day 1: Arrived in forest, full of optimism. I'll just find my friend and everything will be fine.
Day 1: *screams*
Day 1: Makes emergency trip to clothes store to buy new underwear.
Day 2: Plays Slender again with friend controlling mouse, and I controlling movement keys. What can go wrong?
Day 2: *screams*
Day 2: We make emergency trip to clothes store to buy new underwear.
11/10 - Would brown pants wth friend again.

Ok, For Honor has been out for quite a while now so everybody probably knows about the unbalanced MP.
But furthermore let me elaborate on why I don't recommend this game:
1.) Forced online connection (*pukes*)
WHY on ♥♥♥♥ing earth do so many games in the recent years require an internet conncetion to play a SINGLE PLAYER campaign? WHY? There is ZERO justification for that. All it does is to make you dependant on some servers when you want to use an aspect of the game that would work perfectly fine on your computer. And even better: If Ubisoft decides at some point in the future to shut down the servers you can no longer play the game. You'd then have a product that you paid for, but you're no longer able to use it. I now decided to give it a thumbs down because I was kicked out of a mission because the servers didn't respond. If I would have payed for that game I wouldn't be able to use a product I payed for simply because of a completely unneccessary "feature". Plus it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥anyway to start a mission again. Just quit this BS.
2.) The combat system.
It is slow and very simple. You block in of 3 directions, break the defense of your opponent and you have a weaker (and faster) or stronger (and therefore slower) attack. Really annyoing: the auto focus on enemies. I fight against a bull of a viking who stands right in front of me but the game rather chooses to focus on the enemy 10 meters away, causing me to receive a hit. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Also you can't change enemies while focusing on one. You have to stop focusing and then re-focus to fight the other enemy. This takes way to long and can be very disadvantageous when you have to fight 3 or 4 enemies at once because you can't quickly change the focus. You can get into a situation where you can't fight one enemy because 3 others are standing behind you, ramming their axes into your spine. Instead you're focused on one as if the others don't exist.
3.) The story.
I chose to play as a viking. But for some reason I started the story as a knight. The ♥♥♥♥? You also switch between characters. There is not this one character that you play with all the time. And overall the story feels rather...put together with exchangable pieces.
"Ohhh, now you're at castle X where you play a character that was barely introduced with 3 sentences"
*3 missions later* "Hey look. A new mission with no real connection to the last one. Also you no longer play the character that you played before...for three whole missions. Have fun getting used to the new combat style of your new char with his new weapon"

Your Fps will drop from 80 to 27Fps and the VRAM usage will skyrocket from ~1950Mb to ~3660Mb. Just leave it turned off and use that auto enabled AA mode. When I first saw this game, I got a bit excited. I love cute things, and I love cute cartoony mice. A cute, cartoony mouse multiplayer? Sure! Sounds great! I downloaded it right away to begin playing it.
I was so disappointed.
The overall concept of the game isn't bad. In fact, it's rather interesting. But the execution kinda sucks and the players of this game don't seem to know the meaning of working together.
In this game, you're a mouse, and you must work with other mice to gather cheese. Each level, one mouse as chosen as a "shaman" and is supposed to help all the other mice with this goal by moving or places objects to make getting to the cheese possible.
I've been the shaman several times, and it's hard to figure out. Overall, what you need to do isn't the problem, but rather, how to get it to actually work. I clicked on the objects to place them but they didn't appear for the other mice. It seems like figuring out how to properly shaman for other mice can be rather difficult.
An unfair aspect of being a shaman, is that some shamans have powers that others don't. As you level up your mouse, you fill out a skill tree. That skill tree seems (to me) to be restricted ONLY to shaman mice. There are some levels that seem like they can only be beaten if your shaman has a specific power, and if your shaman doesn't, no one can advance.
Some movements that your mouse is supposed to be able to do easily aren't easy, or on certain levels, your mouse's movement seems to turn sluggish, and it doesn't appear to be a DESIGN of the game. It appears to just be something crappy that happens, not a designed challenge.
You can customize your mouse, changing fur color and giving them clothes to wear that make them even more adorable. However, items are overpriced. You have to play a LOT to get any of the items most people seem to want, and the alternative is using in-game transactions. Which, though countless games do the very same thing, is still a pretty lousy way of trying to make money off your game. Especially a game that feels as unfinished and unfair as this game.
Now, let's talk about this whole "working together" thing.
Each game can have quite a few mice playing. There are many levels where you have to carefully balance things so the wooden board you're on doesn't fall, etc. The majority of users have no regard at all for that. The moment the level starts, they all run off to get to the cheese and cause the board to collapse and almost (if not) everyone falls off the screen and can no longer participate in attempting to get the cheese for the rest of the level.
Other than the couple of competent shamans I was lucky enough to play with, it's pretty difficult to work together because the players want to finish the level as quickly as possible, even if it means collapsing delicate structures and screwing over everyone else trying to play with them.
There does NOT appear to be a way to kick anyone from a game. Which means that if everyone else is working hard together, but there are two or three players that are rushing everything and ruining the chances of completing the level for everyone else, there's no way to get rid of those specific players. Instead, you have to quit playing the game, then hope that you get into another game full of patient players and no more jerks. Which is pretty impossible. Often, you'll just get thrown back in the game you were just part of, with the same jerks that were ruining it for everyone still there and still ruining it for everyone.
Don't get me wrong, the game itself has an interesting and even appealing concept. But it is poorly executed and it's just way too easy for only a couple players to completely ruin the game for everyone else.
The mice are adorable, but not nearly enough to make putting up with this game worth it.
I believe that if the game were cleaned up and smoothed out, it could be a very fun game to play. But in its current state, it really, really sucks. It's sad that so much potential was thrown away like this.
Even though this game costs the low low price of free, I just can't bring myself to recommend it to anyone.
Edit: Oh, another aspect that I forgot to mention is how vulgar and offensive a great deal of the community is. I'm not shy about cusing or vulgarity, but the amount in the community is excessive. There's a time and a place for everything, but playing a cute mouse game that may appeal to children and their parents is certainly NOT the time or place for such extreme vulgarity.
So even for the super cuteness of the game, I have to warn parents not to let children that can read -- even beginning readers -- to play this game. The amount of profanity and vulgarity in the game chats is so excessive that it really counters even the more positive aspects of gameplay. And this is coming from a guy that often cuses enough to make sailors blush.

Lucid9 is a visual novel. There are not many decisions to be made in this game, and most of them do not really do a lot. Many just let you learn more about other characters, but the romance angle is basically not developed and even the girl you choose will end up rejecting you per se. Most of the choices have to do with certain mystery cases that you need to solve, where there will be one "correct" answer and you will trial and error through all of them before you find it.
I found the art quite charming and the story was interesting. I don't know the developer's fixation with death though. Parents die, siblings die, friends die, friends of friends die, etc. In most cases, I think a murder/death should be a strong element that invokes emotion; but in this case, it happens so often, and it affects so many people that you get desensitized to it.
I found the character development very good, with the game spanning 13 hours so far for me. The archetypes are fairly typical, but with enough individual flair to keep the reader engaged. The mystery/action sequences are also well done, although I do wish there was a way to skip past them on subsequent playthroughs as it does get rather repetitive.
I did some research and apparently the developers will be putting out the rest of the story (for free!) at some point. The amount of free content here is simply amazing. Well done and can't wait to continue the journey (and to figure out what the name of the game means)!
As a sidebar, if you liked this game, you should check out "One Thousand Lies" - similar art direction and goofy type of dialogue. Also has one of those neat plots where everything comes together at the end too. Free.

I came across this thinking it was just some lame free game that couldn't compare to other visual novels that actually cost money. Boy was I wrong. Though there is no voice acting(I believe it is being added), the dialogue is great, all the characters are genuine, interesting and unique. The story was fun, it kept me going. I haven't played many VN's but this is my favourite so far. The animation is cute, repetitive at times but the game isn't long enough for it to be noticeable. Some people don't like the ending but I don't mind. The choices are of little value but they add a little flavour to the game. All in all it's a pretty good game, and it's free! I hadn't expected that a free game would be as fun as this was for me so it was a pleasant surprise.  It won't cost you anything to try it if you're interested in this sort of game.

If this is your "starter VN" - enjoy! It's cute and quite easy to read. Be sure to check out other visual novels at
after you're done, and welcome to the community!
On the other hand, if you're a VN veteran or simply just played a few of the notorious VNs, you're bound to be annoyed or offended. To say this game borrows from other VNs would be a terrific understatement.
The entire character types and personalities, plot points and even some of the character designs are almost straight out copied out of Devil on G-String with some heavy Kara no Shoujo "inspirations" along the way. I am struggling to find something in this visual novel that is not a complete VN\anime cliche or trope.
Generally, the overall feel of the novel could be described as amateurish, both in writing and art department. I have a constant feeling that the different assets of the novel just don't really work together, with character sprites not really mixing with BGs and struggling to show what the text wants them to. They did nail the UI and fonts perfectly, though, by hiring an outside UI designer, which was a good choice.
Overall, if you can get past all the cliches and "inspirations", you're going to have a pleasant experience, so go ahead, it's not like you're going to lose money trying it out.
I admit I'm being a little too hard on it, for an amateur free project. It is certainly a pretty nice step forward for the English VNs and I'm looking forward to seeing more ambitious EVNs in the future.

While I can understand the hype behind the Slender myth as a social phenomenon I can't say the same for the game. Sure, Slender : The Arrival looks and plays better than its freeware counterparts but overall it's a disappointing game, especially if you put it next to Amnesia : The Dark Descent, a game that helped the renewal of the horror genre.
The first chapter managed to set up effectively a scary mood. Exploring the house and its surrounding was really stressful and made me felt really vulnerable. I always expected the worse. The second chapter is more like a remake of Slender : The Eight Pages. While the scare factor was still there the experience felt repetitive. The third chapter is certainly where the game went downhill. The little child is creepy the first time he jumps at you but after a while it gets repetitive and at the end we don't care anymore. The chapter where the events unravel from someone's else perspective was really surprising but at the same time it was too short. At the end of Chapter 6, we are left with an unexpected but disappointing conclusion. The game just lasted 1h 30min.
To summarize, the lack of work on the game design is what hurt Slender the most. Playing the game feels more like walking on an alley of jumpscare than facing dangerous threats.
Don't get me wrong. I'm not against the idea of a commercial Slender game. I just wish the game could be more polished since it has so much potential.
Hopefully, the next commercial Slender game on PC will get everything right.

Without the narration, this would be a horrifically boring story about colored rectangles jumping on unforgiving black platforms. I wouldn't have made it through the two hour playthrough, except that the story was well executed. Each block has its own personality, and the way they think and interact makes you want to finish levels to hear more. As you progress through chapters, you get little plot interstitials that sound like after-the-fact interviews about what happens in the game, and ties the story together with a sense of something larger - that you're playing the prequel to something that changes the world.
All that, and you're just jumping little blocks around.
This game's definitely one that shows the power of storytelling, and it's definitely worth the experience.

This game is an aberration.
As a Resident Evil game, it fails completely. There is almost no horror or tension at all in the game. Some inklings of it in Leon's campaign is all you will get.
Story wise, it's completely non-nonsensical and doesn't really advance anything. On the other hand, it's a fully self contained story with almost no references to other games in the series.
It also falls completely flat as a third person action shooter. The pacing is terrible, there is a tiny amount of enemy variety. Getting shot instantly knocks you on your back. You will have to drop stuff from your inventory every few minutes even on higher difficulties.
The game is also plagued with a constant stream of Quick Time Events. All of them different, and all of them extremely tightly timed, to the point where you'll have to take your hand off your mouse to mash your keyboard with both hands to beat them. It's absurd.
The camera is used to increase the difficulty of certain boss fights for no clear reason. It'll switch from over the shoulder to fixed angle with no warning, sometimes making you about-face right into instant death.
Even the COOP is messed up. Ada's campaign gives you a token faceless companion who can't even interact with doors or the environment, unlike in the other 3 campaigns. It was obviously meant to be a single player experience.
The characters look nice, have a good amount of detail to them, but the environment textures are terrible. You will constantly get closeups of textures so blurry you can't even identify what they're supposed to represent.
Avoid this game at all costs. It manages to be worst in every way than Resident Evil 5. It fails as survival horror, 3rd person shooter action and even COOP. Do not touch this turd.

(TL;DR; at the bottom)
+===+ Developer +===+
This review has changed over time as some of the things I mentioned previously as holding the game back have been fixed/improved. For that reason I rate the developer of this game highly as an alpha-developer.
All in all, this is one of the better alphas I have played - and it is now in full release with many of the issues I highlighted in a previous review have been fixed:
+ Right click menu implemented as a simple radial (in keeping with simple UI)
+ All islands show the "fertility" graphic when a building is selected to be built instead of just the hovered island
+ Some fine tuning of buildings/workers/research seems to have been done, making population easier to manage (along with pathing improvments)
+ You can now specify which pathing routes can take which materials (this stops any material being taken on any defined path)
+===+ UI +===+
I quite enjoy the somewhat simplified world graphics (although this can start to get busy when you have little people legging around with parts) and the UI is also quite simple.  I started off playing this game with Steam controller and I have to say, even though controllers are not supported, this game made it easy to use (almose entirely point + click with WASD camera movement mapped to joystick).
Buildings are only 1 level deep in the build menu and are organised in a sensible manner, (houses, raw resources, combining buildings/factories, research buildings).  One of the things that is not immediately obvious, (but boy is it helpful when you discover it!) is the sales graphic in the top right.  This little display shows you quantaties that you are currently selling, any special orders you have going and (crucially!) if you are bottle-necking your deliveries building by not supplying it with enough product!
+===+ GAMEPLAY +===+
As with the Settlers/Cultures/Factorio this game is mostly about building production chains and managing them.  The tutorial is a simple guide to get you going and then you get to dive straight in and crack on building.  As with the Settlers, there are many layers to how you build, what you build when and how you manage your resource chains.
In addition to the production chains of buildings, there is a sub-production element within each building.  This element allows you to manipulate the chain of production within each production building.  Each building starts off with a default (which is pretty efficient), but there are ways you can tweak the chains to make them more efficient (sometimes doubling/tripling building output).  This is a novel idea and one I quite like to get lost fiddling around in just trying to eek that little extra from my buildings - but the default blueprints are pretty effective as they are.
With the Settlers you could eventually get yourself in a position where a thriving city could fall and crumble because of space resrictions and having to force that poor little settler to walk from one side of the city and back again with his cargo.  Eventually the roads would upgrade (if travelled enough) and finally your settler would gain a donkey to help speed him on his way.  In Blueprint Tycoon you get hot air balloons and trade ships instead.  Trade ships allow you to transfer large amounts of cargo between islands (but are restricted to a start island and an end island - building circular routes is helpful, and perhaps the developer could implement a return cargo slot) whereas hot air balloons are pretty good for doing cross-island hops from storehouse to storehouse.  This allows you to spread out your production over larger areas.
+===+ SCENARIO EDITOR +===+
As promised by the developer, there is a scenario editor in the game.  The editor is pretty powerful allowing you to modify just about all of the aspects of the gameplay (resources, research, buildings) and with some good Steam Workshop integration to boot.
+===+ TL;DR; +===+
+ Simple UI with useful graphics
+ Easy to map a Steam controller to the UI interactions
+ 1 layer deep build menu, sensibly organised by building type
+ Plenty of building chains already implemented
+ 5 research tiers to work through
+ Easy to transfer goods long-(ish) distances and thus spread out production
+ Easy to spend hours playing with the sub-mechanics of the game
+ Great scenario editing capabilities
All in all, I would recommend!

It's not very expensive, and it's definitely worth a few dollars, but I'm pretty mixed on it, overall.   I'm right on the cusp between 'positive' and 'negative' on this one.
Basically, if you're familiar with them, this is a variant on the Anno series games.  That is, it's about building complex supply chains, and dealing with the logistics involved in moving lots of stuff around.   Like Anno, it's split up among uslands, with different islands being good at different resources.  Unlike Anno, the islands are TINY.
The fundamental engine is pretty interesting, but the space problem is so overwhelming that I end up not having very much fun with the game.   It's just.... it becomes such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to try to work around yet ANOTHER space problem.  There's never enough room for stuff, so you can never build what you really want.  Getting through a level of Blueprint Tycoon ends up feeling like work, because it's just this endless hassle trying to figure out where to squeeze something else in.   The way the buildings all have fixed entry and exit points only exacerbates the problem, making it fairly impossible to use space very efficiently, when using space efficiently is THE thing you have to do.  It's very frustrating.
Anno has similar complexity in their economic model, but you've got like ten times as much space to work with, and you don't have the facing/spacing issues.  I find those games a LOT more fun.
I'd enjoy BT more if the islands weren't so tiny.  But, as is, I got a few hours out of it (it says 19.6 right now, but I actively played it about eight), and I'm done.  I just can't face the tedium of trying to build up yet another economy on five or six postage stamps.

As a fan of the original Konung: Legend of the North, buying this game was an easy decision for me to make. That said, I believe that this game can be a fun and engaging RPG experience for all fans of the Genre.
Konung 3: Ties of the Dynasty doesn't stray far from its predecessor in overall game execution. It is an RPG that requires the player to do a bit of thinking for themselves, as your path is not clearly laid out for you, and there isn't a flashing marker on your map showing you where your next quest objective is located. You will often be required to fully search the game map in certain areas. That said, the area maps are not extremely large, and I haven't found this to be tedious, especially as the experience gained from finding foes around the map is neccesary in this challenging RPG.
Rather than following one long storyline, the character falls into many short stories during the progression of the long campaign to find the champion sword. I find the quests and stories to be witty and in many cases comical, often earning a chuckle or laugh while I play along. That said, you will tend to follow a somewhat linear progression from place to place, especially early in the game. However, you can go back and forth from place to place, and in certain cases, will be required to. This is easily accomplished through the use of jump stones (portals) which are located in every settlement I have seen thus far.
The primary difference between Konung 3 and earlier titles, is an entirely revamped character creation system that includes 4 primary attributes (Intellect, Agiliity, Strength, Stamina), a variety of weapon skills, combat skills, defensive skills, magic skills, and several general skills (Alchemy, Healing, Bartering, etc) which causes the player to have to specialize different characters in their party with different skills in order to be effective. Your starting character will be limited by having to invest points in the "Leadership" skill in order to be able to have more party members.
Overall I have found this game to be fun and engaging and would reccomend it to any RPG gamers who enjoy having to do a bit of problem solving (thinking for themselves), and who can sacrifice modern graphics for a better RPG experience.  This game didn't receive rave reviews from critics around its release date, but its easily worth $4.99.

I like Caves of Qud quite a lot, and it deserves the positive ratings it has gotten.  However, it is not quite ready for a consumer audience and is quirky enough that it would turn a lot of people off.  I'm writing this "negative" review so that you can understand its shortcomings before buying it.
Caves of Qud is actively in development, with all that entails.  By "development" I do not mean "polish".  There are almost daily updates which sometimes break old savegames.  Mob combat AI is still getting major improvements, items are still being added, large balance changes are made regularly.  The main quest is not finished, some major locations (the kind you can see from the world map) are not finished, and some of the few named unique NPCs have no dialogue.
This is a true early access game, not a beta.  If you are passionate about roguelikes and/or science fiction to the extent that you'd like to help develop the game by finding bugs through hilarious death, you might want in on this.
Beyond its incomplete status, this game is a roguelike.  By genre convention it lacks a great many of the conveniences most gamers are accustomed to.  Input is keyboard-only.  The default keybinds for laptop are both horrible and incomprehensible.  Permadeath is on by default and the disable-permadeath option is somewhat cryptically hidden.  Many enemies can and will destroy you even in starter zones and a "fair fight" is a myth.  You will not always get warnings when steering your character towards certain death.  You will have absurd runs of bad luck that are not your fault and you will die of them.  CoQ makes excellent use of its tile art system, but it's not what most modern gamers will expect.
If you are not comfortable reading books at least a chapter at a time, you will probably not be comfortable playing.  If you cannot occasionally relinquish control and adapt to chance circumstances, you will find this game infuriating.  If you cannot sometimes let go of a good thing, this game might break your heart when your character dies.
This game, overall, has a high barrier to entry.  If you overcome it, though, the world beyond is rich and lovely, as a hundred other reviews will attest.
Caves of Qud is a lovely roguelike with beautiful tile art, a piece of far-future fiction that sci fi fans will immensely enjoy.

I had never actually seen a madpole before. Even the best hunters in Kyakukya would talk about them as merciless killing machines.
The thing looked as mean as they said. Rows of jagged teeth flashed between frantic snapping as it splashed about. I watched from the banks of the river a few feet away, peering down my carbine's scope to get a closer look. It was ugly.
I pulled the trigger; the madpole tried to flee, but another pull and the water turned red around its corpse. Three more madpoles swam over. I shot another and they scattered. I emptied my carbine, reloaded, and saw that only one was still moving.
Feeling sporting, I shouldered my rifle and drew my daggers. I waded into the river and charged the last madpole, landing both blades in either side.
You can imagine my surprise when this madpole ignored the blades I planted, latched onto my shell, and I could feel its teeth through my carapace. The very same carapace had, just last moon, merely sizzled as laser fire hit me.
Even more surprising was watching my right arm come off in the madpole's mouth, then fall into the water as the madpole took another attempt at ripping my shell from my body.
I stabbed as hard as I could with my remaining arm to try to dislodge the madpole. This worked, in a way; the madpole released in order to gnaw at my feet, shearing them off with such speed that my terror obscured my pain. My remaining forearm was taken off at the elbow.
Rolling myself onto the bank of the river, the madpole released me to fall back into the water lest he suffocate on land. I rummaged through my now thoroughly-bloody pack with a stump and my face; I found it: My last shot of Ubernostrum.
Held in my teeth, I shot my bicep-stump full of superdrugs and watched as my arm sprouted back, as painfully as it did quickly.
I dug out my revolver, shot the remaining madpole to death, and collapsed. I decided to wait and wash my bag as I waited for my natural mutant regeneration to generate bones and sinew to regrow my limbs, and to reseal my carapace where the madpole had bitten through.
I dined on my severed feet while I waited.

Caves of Qud is a "science-fantasy" roguelike by Freehold Games. It's currently in Early Access, but I've already gotten a lot of hours of enjoyment out of the beta. It has a lot to offer for those who enjoy exploratory dungeon crawling, tense strategic situations, varied playstyles, and a good deal of mystery in their games. Here are some of the highlights, in my opinion:
Character creation: Your character can be created with a huge number of physical and mental mutations, and gain more as you level up. These act as your spells and passive bonuses, and come in a really wide variety of forms. Physically control your adrenal glands for a quick boost of speed in combat, release an EMP to disable enemy grenades and robots, or even manipulate time to produce several clones of yourself. Trying out new combinations of mutations really keeps me coming back to the game. My only real complaint is that, at the time of this review, physical mutations seem less powerful and interesting than mental mutations overall. Rebalancing is sure to come in the future.
If you're looking for an alternate playstyle, you can also choose for your character to be a "true kin," a non-mutant human who lacks special powers but starts with useful artifacts and higher stats.
The gameplay: True to its genre, Qud has randomly generated levels, randomized loot, and permadeath. If the latter is really a dealbreaker for you, it is possible to turn it off in the "debug" option category. Graphics are either ASCII or a clean, if simple, set of tile icons.
Unlike other staples of the genre such as Nethack, there is not one ultimate goal (fetch the amulet) but a series of main quests with other objectives you can find on the side. There are also various ways to complete the quests, from what I've seen. Another feature of Qud is the world map, which can be used to quickly travel between locations in the game at the cost of running down your hunger and thirst quicker.
Enemy balance is pretty good, in my experience: you may run into a really strong monster, but as long as you stop to think, there is usually a way for you to escape and return later.
The world: Caves of Qud takes place in a setting where it seems as if almost anything goes - yet, it's very good at hitting its own specific tone. The weird world of Qud, while putatively post-apocalyptic, has a lot more in common with The Dark Tower than Fallout. The dead civilizations you ransack are
, and the artifacts you dig up range from your everyday hand grenade to more exotic types such as the "shade oil injector," which will cause you to phase out of reality for a little while. I admit I am a bit of a sucker for the trope of forgotten technology aging and turning into artifacts of myth, and Qud does pull it off well. Lore is tantalizingly doled out in item descriptions and NPC dialogue.
Overall, I'm very excited to watch Caves of Qud develop. It's already quite large in scope, and should only be getting better. As another plus, the devs seem to take player feedback very seriously and are active in the forums.

I've been playing guitar for about 15 years now. I'm not too bad but I should be better for that amount of time.
One of the things I've always lost patience with is learning to play other bands songs. I'll learn the main riff or a certain cool part but when it comes to trying to learn any solos, I get bored and start messing around writing/recording my own little ideas instead - which is fun, but doesn't improve any aspects of my playing. Lead guitar has always been my weakness but since I started playing the original Rocksmith, it improved a little. Then I got bored of it because the lag issue bothered me too much.
Bring on Rocksmith 2014, with no lag at all! Brilliant.
The riff repeater is so much better in this version. I remember the first one only gave you a certain amount of "lives" on the riff repeater, which wasn't cool. This one is easier to use and I can happily spend hours trying to learn a solo; something that I've never had any patience for with any other learning tool. You can choose a section to loop and slow it right down till you've mastered each note at tortoise speed, then gradually knock up the tempo till you're shredding like Dimebag. For the first time in a long time, my fingers are frigging killing me!
Being put right into the song and having your guitar tone change for each part without having to mess around with any pedals is nice too. Your playing blends right into the song.
Another thing to note is that there are some decent lessons on here for beginners. It teaches you all the basic techniques, chords and scales. For complete beginners I'd still recommend a guitar teacher (as well as this game, obviously!) as they can point out things that you might be doing wrong. Rocksmith can't see if you're holding your guitar in a funny position, holding your plectrum like an idiot, cheating using your thumb on certain chords, using bad a fingering technique (ooohhhh), etc... It's good to have a human there to fix these problems early before they become bad habits (like me, I hold my pick like an idiot and my fingering technique is abysmal - according to my girlfriend).
I was talking to a friend about how I've hardly been playing guitar since I got hooked on Steam, because all I do is play games on here (Risk of Rain anyone!?), and I said that something needs to come along to tear me away from Steam so I can get back into playing guitar again. It's funny that a game on Steam has done that for me...
In all, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who's either new to guitar, or people like me who need a little push to polish up on your skills.

This is a decent Resident Evil title. And no, RE is not a horror game anymore, just get used to horror themed action already. RE6 improves drastically on gameplay and mechanics, finally giving us typical TPS controls with dedicated attacking/shooting on a trigger rather than using the action/confirm button for that.
Health now is measured by a bar composed of 6 sub-bars (?) which will regenerate
if one is not completely depleted, and the complete depletion of one results in the character being knocked out. Herbs now are turned into pills which recover one sub-bar each. That health system makes harder for the player to die against huge hordes of enemies, but doesn't allow them to abuse of it as in other games, making a good system if you hone your skills properly.
The player now has a stamina bar which depletes whenever they make a physical attack. Opposed to the previous titles in which you could only attack physically an enemy with knives or something in similat fashion. This broadens the possibilities of damaging enemies in many aspects since physical attacks deal a considerable damage, but punishes players who overuse it, since guns are there, as always.
Each campaign is themed around a type of gameplay, with Leon and Helena on a more classic take, hacing zombies and other type of monsters as enemies, Chris and Piers with a more modern take with Ganado-like enemies (J'avos) that resemble more a third person shooting game and Sherrie and Jake's which focus on a smaller combat/shooter aspect with some stealth and exploration sections. There's also another campaign which combines aspects of each, but that will be available only after completing the game.
The new skill system is much simpler than the weapon customization, but doesn't feels quite as glamurous, specially since how the customization worked on RE4 (which only went backwards in my opinion, REvelations is the only one that has a custom system that feels nearly as satisfying).
In terms of story RE6 is horrible. Is like they had ideas for the story, decided to scrap them and, for some reason, decided to made it apparent on the final version. Although it can be enjoyed, the story of the game is just plain bad.
I recommend this game if you're a more open-minded fan of the series or someoen who enjoy shooters in general. If you're a fan of the classic series I'd recommend on a sale or just to skip it altogether.

Reminds me of that catapult simulator game, Beseige.
All-in-all, it's decent sandboxy/puzzle fun for a while.
Building bridges does give you some room to be creative. I was enjoying creating minimalistic bridges rather than stable ones - the lowest cost possible, basically. Which means my bridges were often... unstable :P I got a lot of satisfaction trying to make bridges that wobbled like the Tacoma Narrows Bridge. When you complete a level (the vehicles get across the bridge), it gives you graphs showing how you compare to others for stability, material cost, etc.
Three complaints:
1) the vertices system is kinda obnoxious. Why should the joint for a wooden support have to line up with an arbitrary segment of road? This does make you do some more careful planning, but it's pretty obnoxious at times. This could be fixed easily enough; just make the maximum length of segments a hair longer.
2) the hydraulics are really poorly explained in the tutorial, and ultimately I ended up building a jump to bypass the first level with hydraulics. That was sorta entertaining, but it's really unclear what is going on when you place a hydraulic piece, and how that interacts with split joints. This is the main reason I lost interest in the game after 2 hours or so.
3) you don't get any real feedback on what pieces are helping vs unnecessary. ultimately this isn't really needed, but it would reduce a lot of trial and error. the closest is a stress-color-coding during the simulation run - things about to break change color. this works fine, but it'd be nice to have this outside the "running" mode. Truth be told, finding out exactly why a bridge broke is my least favorite part of this game. Maybe that means I'd like an easy mode for just messing around.

+ The gameplay is surprisingly fun, relaxing, and very addicting. If you are a fan of physics games, puzzle games, or bridge builders you absolutely MUST try Poly Bridge. You will love it.
+ One of the most relaxing soundtracks I've heard from any game
+ Great physics and all the stress points can be clearly seen making it easy to go back and fix your bridge after multiple trial runs.
+ One thing that's incredibly neat about this game compared to other bridge building games is the "hydraulics" which will allow you to expand, retract, and move your bridge to create things like drawbridges to let boats pass.
+ Loads of content with 100+ levels. (Each level can take anywhere from 5mins to an hour to complete)
+ Very challenging without being overbearing. This creates a large sense of encitement when completing a level or finally making a working drawbridge. (There's also leaderboards which rank you based on how little you spend)
+ Each level is unique. Multiple sized cars, boats, ramps, all sorts of objectives that keeps the game interesting.
- Hydraulics can be painstaking to learn, and the tutorial doesn't do a good enough job explaining the hydraulic mechanics.

I was actually a little surprised at how much I enjoyed this game.
It has a lot of things in its favour.  The story, while not exactly the next Great American Novel, served adequately as backdrop for the action and most of the characters have enough personality without being obnoxious.  The visual style fits the concept very well, clearly influenced by the same alternate history comic the main premise is based on.  The air combat and cover based shooting mesh surprisingly well and I found switching between them to be fairly smooth and intuitive.
I did read some other reviews mentioning that the air game was hard to control, however I believe this is because the game was designed to be played with a controller.  By realising that fairly early, I had no problems at all.  In fact I found that the whole air game felt particularly "good".  You can buzz around with your jetpack, take over enemy aircraft, hop into friendly AA turrets and seamlessly move between flying and hovering.  Note that the game doesn't really tell you to do these things though, I didn't even realise I could take over enemy ships until halfway through.  Still, it is small optional elements like this that sold the game to me.  In fact, I was impressed enough that if someone told me these developers made an open world game using the mechanics demonstrated here, I would probably throw some money its way.
Naturally, it has its flaws.  Chief among which that the game is rather short and a bit random at times, most likely because the developer was more ambitious than its wallet allowed.  There are some signs of separate segments of the storyline being Frankensteined together in an attempt to keep things coherent after money ran out, but all in all this won't bother you much and I felt that a good job was done all things considered.  At least not until the very end.  There the game ran out of steam and threw in two bossfights in quick succession that obviously were only thrown in because it is what was finished.  Oh well.  Bigger titles have done the same with less excuse.
Another issue I had was the placement of the checkpoints, which were not always properly spaced.  There was a defend section I had to do over a few times because I failed a quicktime event and died instantly.  Yes, the game has quicktime events.  That's another minus.  A minor saving grace there is that they are short, sometimes optional and, in the case of one particular hostile, even allow you to choose which quicktime sequence you want to do by picking between two different prompts.
My final grievance is the upgrade system.  The game has you collect points to upgrade your weaponry of choice with, allowing you to hold 2 weapons at a time.  Upgraded weapons are vastly superior to non-upgraded ones, meaning you'll often stick with the ones you upgraded instead of picking whatever would objectively be a better weapon for the situation.  It is here that the game is also a little bit schizophrenic.  On the one hand, it allows you to steal the weapons your enemies use if you run out of ammo.  However, ammo packs and chests are plentiful and dying resets you to your last checkpoint with full ammo regardless of how much you had when you passed that point.  In addition to that, you'll only find enough points to upgrade 2 or 3 weapons properly, further encouraging you to really just use whatever you picked as your first upgrade choices for the entirity of the game and killing off what could have been a good way to add challenge to the game.
Still, maybe it was because was I going through a backlog of generic shooters at the time and had low standards going in, but I really am glad I picked this one up.  It impressed me enough to write a review at least and I really only do that for games that leave a mark in some way.

This game is executed very WELL! Simplistic graphics, with somewhat simple gameplay elements works so well for this game. It leaves a heap of creativity and efficeint planning up to you to deal with.
The only downside about this game, which could easily be fixed in a soon to come patch, is that the 'end game' becomes extremely easy. After you have researched everything you need, you can essentially allow your economy to tank, hire workers without feeding them, and essentially freely build anything you wish.
If they fix the glaring issue with the ease of play, and non-punishing element in the later stages of play, this game could be fun forever with user created levels and even extend the amount of fun in the regular campaign.
On a side note, I was unable to get the map editor to work easily, it was slightly confusing, and seemed to be missing some basic functionality or was unclear on how to go about doing basic things such as shaping land.
All in all this game was an amazing experience for the price, and I managed to get all 45 achievements completed within the 15 hours I have played.
If you like city-builders, base planning, resource micromanagement, and just being rewarded overall for your o.c.d. and efficiency, then simply click BUY!!

Maximum edition? More like maximum bugged port.
I don't know what happened during development of this game. My best guess is they wanted to focus on a console market, and that's what all PC gamers got: A terrible port which has been downgraded in all departments compared to the first game. This is how Crytek wants to deal with high amount of piracy from their first Crysis: "You're interested in our IP? Have a bag of♥♥♥♥♥♥with Crysis 2 tagged onto it, since you're just going to pirate it anyway."
I feel like the PC audience has been alienated here.
There's just so many things that went wrong with developing this game. The game doesn't even want me to beat it cause like I wrote in my first paragraph, you will encounter both in-game bugs and technical bugs that  can result in crash to desktop. This edition of the game somehow manages to have more bugs than the leaked beta test. It controls like the first Crysis, however, your nano suit has been casualized only to carry OP mode, stealth, binoculars which are only used as a waypoint system to find ammo, and nightvision, which is only viable to use in like freaking 3 parts of the whole game. Gotta have something to support that console controller! The checkpoint system WILL drive you nuts. It rarely logs down your progress on your map and just seem to live breathe its own life. If you get a CTD during a map, enjoy being thrown all the way back to the beginning of the map.
Avoid this, even if you liked the first game. It's not a PC game, it's a quick money grab to make up for all the cash they didn't earn with their first game. I hope you got this through the cheap EA bundle like me. I feel bad for anyone actually getting this for full price.

I will try to keep spoilers to minimum or even not write any.
I expected this game to be long (in terms of story) and this was the case. As you can see by my playtime it took me over 20 hours to get all the endings and achievements. This is the main reason why this
game had been sitting on my wishlist for over 5 months. The other reason is that I am not into visual novels lately but once I start reading them I don't stop till I reach the end. Well, I can say I've no regrets.
As I already mentioned for a
visual novel the story is really long. Not only that but it's really well written. There's variety of words, inversion, puns, no grammar or whatsoever mistakes(?). Not wanting to spoil the story for you I will say that there were moments when I laughed out loud (10+ times?) and other when I cried. The funny thing is I haven't done the latter in years. Literally. You can only guess how touching the story actually was. There are a few plot twists, some of which are really unexpected and I won't be surprised if your jaw drops with your mouth wide open. I will just say that this is not your average they-lived-happily-ever-after novel so prepare to turn into an emotional wreck after reading it (if you're the emotional type that is).
There are a lot of them. I liked some more than others but I didn't hate/despise any of them. I'd like to mention that they were all very well-drawn (which is truly praiseworthy given the fact that the game is
)
. Since the story was so interesting, as if I was part of it, I felt some of the characters really close - like people who you could spend time with or share anything with. Sometimes one of them would say something stupid or odd, or both and that would make me chuckle or even laugh out loud.
As a muzical addict I've paid attention to the music. If I've said it was great that would be an understatement. Well, it sounded familiar for a moment or two (maybe because the dev(s) have other visual novels that I'd played) but other than that I really enjoyed it. At some parts you will hear the same music that you've heard earlier but it's no surpise since the novel is long. I don't say this as a bad thing, mind you. I want to donate somehow and adding a paid soundtrack DLC seems like a good idea (at least to me).
I would have written a longer review if I wanted to add spoilers but decided not to. I appologize if I did, if so - it was unintentional. I am glad this game has achievements otherwise I'd have probably skipped it. I am puzzled at how is it even
given the fact that it takes a good 10+ hours to read the whole story. I've played a lot shorter novels and I'd paid money for them. That's why (as I said) I want to donate if that is possible. I'd already done the same with 3(?) other visual novels that were free. I can't help it. I am a simple man - I read a good
visual novel, I donate. So do NOT hesitate and give "Lucid9" a try. I assure you that if you're a visual novel fan (not the pls-boobs type) you will have a great time with this one. Since it's
(did I mention this?) you won't lose anything except maybe some of your time.

I can't believe this is Free To Play. It's absolutely full-blooded (sorry) with more story and character development than you'll get in many VNs you've spent too much on. The story is a slow build - maybe too slow - but it's a consistent build that kept me going. And in what you *think* is the last third, there's some really meaty psychological stuff that'll have you thinking. It's almost as if the actual whodunit is beside the point. Then, if you're lucky, a climax...then some useless stuff...then absolute gut punches. If I was to be super-picky, there could be some more gallery CGs and more different backgrounds and there is some silly chaff, but considering this was kind of a co-op project AND OH YEAH DID WE MENTION FREE, it's a terrific achievement and highly recommended.

Caves of Qud is a "science-fantasy" roguelike by Freehold Games. It's currently in Early Access, but I've already gotten a lot of hours of enjoyment out of the beta. It has a lot to offer for those who enjoy exploratory dungeon crawling, tense strategic situations, varied playstyles, and a good deal of mystery in their games. Here are some of the highlights, in my opinion:
Character creation: Your character can be created with a huge number of physical and mental mutations, and gain more as you level up. These act as your spells and passive bonuses, and come in a really wide variety of forms. Physically control your adrenal glands for a quick boost of speed in combat, release an EMP to disable enemy grenades and robots, or even manipulate time to produce several clones of yourself. Trying out new combinations of mutations really keeps me coming back to the game. My only real complaint is that, at the time of this review, physical mutations seem less powerful and interesting than mental mutations overall. Rebalancing is sure to come in the future.
If you're looking for an alternate playstyle, you can also choose for your character to be a "true kin," a non-mutant human who lacks special powers but starts with useful artifacts and higher stats.
The gameplay: True to its genre, Qud has randomly generated levels, randomized loot, and permadeath. If the latter is really a dealbreaker for you, it is possible to turn it off in the "debug" option category. Graphics are either ASCII or a clean, if simple, set of tile icons.
Unlike other staples of the genre such as Nethack, there is not one ultimate goal (fetch the amulet) but a series of main quests with other objectives you can find on the side. There are also various ways to complete the quests, from what I've seen. Another feature of Qud is the world map, which can be used to quickly travel between locations in the game at the cost of running down your hunger and thirst quicker.
Enemy balance is pretty good, in my experience: you may run into a really strong monster, but as long as you stop to think, there is usually a way for you to escape and return later.
The world: Caves of Qud takes place in a setting where it seems as if almost anything goes - yet, it's very good at hitting its own specific tone. The weird world of Qud, while putatively post-apocalyptic, has a lot more in common with The Dark Tower than Fallout. The dead civilizations you ransack are
, and the artifacts you dig up range from your everyday hand grenade to more exotic types such as the "shade oil injector," which will cause you to phase out of reality for a little while. I admit I am a bit of a sucker for the trope of forgotten technology aging and turning into artifacts of myth, and Qud does pull it off well. Lore is tantalizingly doled out in item descriptions and NPC dialogue.
Overall, I'm very excited to watch Caves of Qud develop. It's already quite large in scope, and should only be getting better. As another plus, the devs seem to take player feedback very seriously and are active in the forums.

Of all the rogue likes ive played, Caves of Qud is by far one of the best of the Classic/tradition styles. only really topped by Dwarf Fortress in depth in both story and similation. while you may not be able to throw a rabbit with enough force to decaptitate a cyclops, you can freeze it solid and shoot it with a rocket launcher.
Of course the only real flaw with the game for the genre, is being of the classic style, it has archaic controls, being pretty much completely keyboard based. (part of the charm in my book, but it can get annoying at times)
Another issue you may come across (besides the genre specific issues such as difficulty) would be figuring out whats going on at times. the tiles are amazing and make things significantly easier, but they still dont stop the age old issue of too much clutter. I've had many a character die because i didnt realize that an enemy aproached me, or was even on screen, though a simple fix for this would be to highlight hostile NPCs.
the only other issue new players may run into, would be the simple lack of ingame information. some of it can be obtained through books and such ingame, but many things such as mutations developed after starting a character, have no info to them, thus having the wiki or google up is a must for all but the most veteran of players.
In summary, if you love classic rogue likes, like dwarf fort, this game is a must have, however it has the same issues and complexity that plagues that part of the genre. if you are on the fence still, or are new to the genre, i'd highly recomend watching some youtube videos before purchase, the genre isnt for everyone.

I bought a guitar when I was 16 and it sat in the corner of my room collecting dust for 7 years. I found myself bored of the initial stages of learning guitar which can be very slow and unrewarding. Then I found Rocksmith last September.
When I found Rocksmith, everything changed. Suddenly, the initial, usually slow process of learning guitar became fun. That, to me, is the best thing about this game. It reduces the harsh learning curve of playing a musical instrument by using fun minigames or allowing you to play along with songs even though you aren't good enough to hit all of the notes yet.
Today, only 9 months after picking up a guitar, I can play fairly well because of Rocksmith. I can play a good amount of songs from multiple genres including classic rock, country, modern rock, and metal. I still have trouble with fast guitar solos, but it's something I'll get down eventually.
However, Rocksmith is not a game that is going to entirely teach you the correct way to play from the basics up to being a master. It works best as a supplemental learning device and you should still be reading and watching videos and even getting lessons outside of Rocksmith if you're serious about learning the instrument.
For most people, Rocksmith will do what it says it's going to do: teach you to play guitar. And it does that well. I'd give it a 10/10 as a supplement to regular practice and lessons (even video lessons on youtube). I'd still give it a 7.5/10 if you are only interested in the game itself and aren't going to be playing guitar outside of the game. All in all a great way to pass some time and learn an instrument.

First and foremost, based on reviews, the Rocksmith Real Tone Cable is very fragile so take extra care of it! Over at my place the cable is not easy to find and is rather expensive so you don't want to go through hassle of getting another one or modding a guitar usb cable.
Rocksmith is a fine tool for beginners and pros alike. There are plenty video lessons that would be helpful for beginners, even when you are playing a guitar for the very first time. In Rocksmith, you don't do readings, unlike reading tabs, chords, music notes or using Guitar Pro software. Rather you learn through videos, visual graphics and repetitive motions.
All you really need is an electric guitar, and the game will handle the rest. The tones, amps, and all the tools that will mod & filter the sounds that are available in real world are all installed in the game and it sounds really, really awesome. *Branded, expensive stuffs, mind you*. Jamming in real life won't get you the exact sound without these proper tools thus in this game you will play the songs as it is meant to be played. *Thank god the tones are not DLC's* *No, I'm not giving any idea, Ubisoft*
The game has a mode called Riff Repeater where it allows you to learn sections by sections of the songs. It also have difficulty setting whereby you can control your pace of learning so it really caters to beginners very well. *Imagine learning the solo's without this mode, oh god*. Practicing would be boring, if you're not interested in the song in the first place. So song choice matters! Start immediately with the songs you like and don't just play at random! Also, it has a build-in tuner so you won't get your tuning wrong for all the songs. Having said that, outside of the game, you gonna have to learn how to tune the guitar to suit the songs perfectly and that would depend on your own initiatives.
Ultimately, with or without Rocksmith, you have to be passionate and dedicated enough to be able to enjoy playing the guitar. Rocksmith is just a tool, and it's not a game where you will have fun without practicing a song over and over again. I see that many started this game but stopped after a short while because they seem to lost interest. So take this into consideration if you are going to start this game as you don't only have to buy the game, but also the guitar and its cable and almost everything that accompanies it which by then you will find out this hobby is as costly as any other.
Points doesn't matter, as long as you enjoy playing & I do, I enjoy playing. So if you are looking to play a guitar, whether beginning or restarting the musical journey, I wish you good luck and have fun!

Thomas Was Alone. A simple game on the surface. Yet a story with an involved storyline, narrated beautifully by Danny Wallace. The game follows the exploits of various AIs (represented as different coloured rectangles), and their journey to reach the 'fountain of wisdom' and help future AIs escape into the real world.
The game itself is fundamentally a platform game, with a number of simple puzzle elements. Having to switch between the different characters and use their abilities to reach the 'portals' at the end of each stage. All whilst avoiding pools of toxic water, spikes and the mysterious pixel cloud.
The recent update brought along two additional levels, that act as the prologue to the main game. Overall, some nice puzzle mechanics, brilliant narration and great soundtrack, along with some nice visuals (however basic on first glance). Definitely worth your time; Thomas Was Awesome.

Don't put too much stock in all the bad press this game got. RE6 is a fun action game with tight shooting mechanics and a slight over-reliance on QTE segments. Examples include having to drive a vehicle while your partner mans a mounted machine gun, holding off zombies while your partner hacks a terminal, and providing sniper support as she navigates through another section of the map.

Dark Void™ is a sci-fi action-adventure game that combines an adrenaline-fueled blend of aerial and ground-pounding combat. Set in a parallel universe called "The Void", players take on the role of Will, a pilot dropped into incredible circumstances within the mysterious Void. This unlikely hero soon finds himself swept into a desperate struggle for survival, joining forces with a rebel human group called The Survivors. Trapped in the Void, these resistance fighters are battling to hold off a mysterious alien race that plans to threaten Earth.
Dark Void’s unique combination of jet pack-booster aerial dog fighting and third-person combat brings a thrilling new gameplay dynamic to the third-person shooter experience. Taking 3D action to a whole new level, Dark Void’s unique vertical combat system allows players to dangle from thousand foot drops as they take cover and hurl enemies to their doom, bringing a whole new sense of tension and thrill to the player. Will is also equipped with a powerful rocket pack which allows for fierce in-air combat, hurtling through the Void at blistering speeds while shooting down anything that gets in his path.

Game has no way to adjust keybindings that I'm aware of and the controls themselves feel messy and clunky. The overall lighting is aweful and it takes forever to find a toy plane hiden in an obscure spot. Way too dark with no way to adjust the lighting.  Keybinds where c for crouch, e for action, and w-a-s-d for movement. Mouse for looking/ view. Although it sounds simple enough, it bothered me enough to mention it.
The overall design of the levels/ areas seem laughable. You start out with an oddly designed, but rather nice looking house and then from there it just goes downhill. I say this because you seem to spend the vast majority of the game wandering the house and the house is just so ridiuclous. The basement desgin is so ridiculous that if it was real I would first facepalm, and then suggest moving in homeless people to live there because of how unecessarily large and maze like it is. This house designer is cray-cray no joke.
As for Krampus the monster, he feels uneventful and not scarey. I'll get bored wandering around lost in the dark before he shows up and then when he'll show up randomly its just like "oh, hi there Krampy". First few times felt jump-scare like, but its only jump scares and those lose effect after a few times of it being repeated. His image itself was not at all scarey, in real life maybe, but a game? Nope. I've had better jumpscares from Slendy (SlenderMan) to be quite honest, and he's super underated.
Lots of run around pick up a key then run around some more to find another key and then another and so on. This gameplay got repetitive and boring very fast. Theres a few other puzzle types, but the bit with the keys felt very heavy. I stayed playing for the story.
Story seems to be alright, but I only just made it to the attic stairs when my entire game crashed. Which was a bit of a buzzkill, even after being frustrated with the very poor lighting and annoying key binds. I'm now stuck in the attic, mkay.
TLDR:
No tutorial, so good luck learning the keys and what to do.
Poor key bindings and no options or way to adjust any part of the game be it lighting or key binds.
The lighting is terrible and theres no way to brighten the game to look for objects/ objectives, which are, by the way hidden in obscure and dark little nooks and cranies.
The gameplay is repetative. Its basically find a key and find a lock for said key, then continue to find more keys and more locks after some point. Lots of find said object and goto said location with said object.
Areas are designed in weird and crazy ways which don't make any sense to me.
Cheap jumpscares that even Slenderman can do better.
Maybe worth a shot if on sale or cheap in general, but the lighting and key binds need improvement, as for the jumpscares, well have you ever played Spooky's House of JumpScares? Not that great of a successor to the original Crysis. The game shipped out with only dx9 capabilities, missing a dx11 patch, high res textures, and came with a badly optimized way of rendering water underneath the level thus requiring further resources than necessary for the level. The game is much more closed in level design than Crysis 1, so as to appeal to a more broad basic FPS market, and also ops for a mute, personality-less main character that you play as. While Cryengine 3 does look impressive, you can tell this was rushed in order to be released soon and to consoles. While some suit functions are nicely streamlined like running, and power punching, the drain rate on the suit and amount of enemies you encounter bring a rather pretty but somewhat boring FPS experience. Still, the soundtrack, modding support, graphics, gun recoil and level design is worth at least playing to see how you feel.
Multiplayer is nothing to write home about and the running makes the game crawl to an incredible low pace.

I recently acquired this game through humble monthly, which is great because I had wanted to pick it up in the past but couldn't justify the price tag. Here are my thoughts.
The short of it: I like it a lot. I enjoyed it at least as much as I expected to, and maybe a little more. If you're interested, I'd say buy it.
The long of it: Within 10 to 15 seconds of launching this game, you'll already be building your first bridge. You'll be admiring the simple but cute graphics, and the charming soundtrack. Within a few minutes, you'll be thinking, "Hey, this is pretty easy! I hope it gets harder!" - and it will. Levels get progressively harder in a way that really is tantalizing to anyone who enjoys a good physics puzzle. However, roughly 6-7 hours in, I'm finding the difficulty curve has spiked right up. The game is producing challenges for me to solve that I feel I've not been adequately equipped to tackle. As another reviewer said, it feels like in some of these levels there really is only one particular solution and you'd just better figure it out because at that point it's no longer about creativity and more about trying to get into the dev's head and trying to understand what they were thinking when they were designing said level. This is not a bad thing necessarily, but I am feeling a bit mystified, and to be fair, that's why I've decided to pause and write this review.
Having finally gotten to try this game, I've been at it all day and it has made for a great deal of amusement. I recommend it just so long as you know going in that eventually you might find yourself looking up guide videos on youtube or something - but that's okay, cause Poly Bridge is still cool... and there's also like 90 levels, and that's quite a lot for a game like this. Thumbs up from me!!! :)

Deplorable execution of a great concept.  Really wanted to like it but left me dissatisfied and frustrated.
I was very excited to try this game.  The style and concept is right up my alley.  It had good graphics and lots of different playing modes.  It included a limited but sufficiently interesting and supportive storyline for story mode that you could complete individually or with a group of friends, a short required basic practice with a long advanced practice option that is highly helpful before pvp that you could repeat as much as needed, and a great concept for multiple pvp lvl based matches with personal loot and points for the banner you fought under with 3 factions to choose from.  Sounds like a great game idea, however I think the concept is wasted on this game.  The basic blocking and attacking controls are OK but advanced maneuvers or working with multiple enemies are extremely frustrating.  It needs tweaking and makes me think none of the developers actually tried playing through the whole story mode.
I love the combos and that you actually have to think about attack strategy based on your opponent's current action, however, the game couldn’t deal with quick command inputs to have effective gameplay.  Keep in mind that I am not a quick player.  I’m a decent weekend player but certainly we’re not talking legendary skill here.  Even though I died the least of my friends that tried it this weekend and got the furthest through the story mode, I got so frustrated with the game ignoring inputs that I quit before completing the story mode for protection of my keyboard from my frustrated fists.  Even in practice mode it is almost impossible to accurately time combos because of missed commands.  However, my greatest frustration would have to be with the targeting.  If you enter guard mode to target, spar with, and defeat an opponent, most gamers assume the game should change to the next target in range and then exit guard mode if no remaining targets are found in range.  This is not what happens.  Instead you can use either Ctrl or Alt (pretty sure we could remove Ctrl from this string of code all together but moving on) to enter guard mode and use Alt to change targets, but when you run out of targets you stay in guard mode facing the last target’s location, unable to pan back out to the rest of the field, turn, or move effectively until you hit the Ctrl key again.  Hitting Alt gets you nowhere as you keep retargeting the same invisible foe that has already faded after death and hitting Alt or Ctrl when there are no targets has you in the same situation of zooming in on a random location with no target.  This is troublesome when attacking in a crowd, especially when you have to be in guard mode to attack one and out guard mode to attack all the little guys that don’t look all that different.  This is just one example of the types of poor planning and execution that plagues this poor game.  I may try it in the future after several GBs of updates but sadly I am uninstalling as I am not optimistic it is worth the space on my drives.  Sorry for any grammar errors but it is late, I am frustrated, and I am done ranting so I'm not checking.
