Free. And worth recommending even if it wasn't.
Want a free introduction into the visual novel format that justifies the genre?
It's like getting a really nice eBook or manga for free.
What has been penned by Fallen Snow's writers is a interesting murder mystery wrapped up in a familiar high school setting in Japan. It starts off in typical tropervile scenarios, but begins to throw things upside down within a few in-story days, with a climatic choice-filled encounter serving as the peak.
Unlike some other VNs, I have never quite felt a need to skip through unread portions of Lucid9 - most of it is engaging. Story has always been a integral part of VNs, and Lucid9 doesn't disappoint.
Writing wise, there are aspects that bug me. Firstly, you can tell that the writing is westernized and English based, despite the setting being in Japan. That's not surprising; Lucid9 is a VN of non-Japanese, international origins.
But when you consider suggestions that the characters are actually conversing in Japanese (strongest hint is that only half-English Elizabeth is billingual), some of the phrases, rhymes, and so on just don't seem like they'll fly in Japanese. But it's not a dealbreaker.
There are also current pop culture references that seem out of place in Japan.
That said, the story takes some meta jokes that might be silly but are good for laughs anyway. General writing is not overly flowery - it's at a level that is just nice for visual novels.
Then there are all the characters. Each, archetypal at first glance, has at least a decent amount of depth and don't beg you to forget them with their colorful personalities, all lovable.
Choices-wise, Lucid9 is not a kinetic, but
is the first arc, the "common route", of the story. The ultimate outcome is almost singular, despite your choices, and during the aforementioned climax, there is only one way to succeed (but many variations to failure, ala
)
What else I can respect is a lack of fan servicey writing or situations throughout Lucid9:II. Perhaps those are reserved for the heroine arcs of the second part, but for now it is nice to see a VN that doesn't need to prop itself up in this way. But bear in mind that this is VN with some dark themes and graphic descriptions of violence. Tread carefully.
Content length? Easily seven hours at minimum, and engaging enough to keep you there nonstop.
Lucid9's artwork has a vaguely amateur feel to it. It's not bad, per se, it just feels a bit below the expectations you might harbor if you've seen some of the more famous 'big' works. But then, fate/stay night's original artwork wasn't that professional at the time either, look how that stopped it.
You can sort of see that the girls, drawn in softer, moe styles, contrast with those of the guys' who are prominently sharper and more defined. There are some mild clashes in art style for the drawn characters, but it's not at all as unnerving as say, Driftwood, another recent free visual novel up here on Steam.
Being more picky, I feel a need to complain about Misaki's alternate poses (where she is facing straight on or holding her phone). Proportionately, they look odd. And her face more so.
Elizabeth's sprites also look awkward from my point of view.
Backgrounds on the other hand, are consistently done well and are not sources of complaint.
As with the story writing, fan service in the artwork is also non-existent. Whether that is a downer or not is up to you, okay? But then, fan disservice is. Bloody scenes are present. You're warned.
First, I want to sound off that Lucid9 has a pleasantly surprising range of sound effects through out, including the good choice in interface blips. This is a department that some VNs are lacking in these days, especially free ones.
What else is pleasantly surprising, especially for a free-to-play project, is the upcoming inclusion of voice acting (in English).
The music, like the artwork, has a sense of amateurism, but not in the same way as the art. To explain, most if not all the tracks sound like they were made on a home software suite. Which I expect they were. To elaborate, they are not bad compositionally (there are several composers involved here) - some tracks just sound like they were made with rather low end instrument libraries. None sound like they were made with live instruments, and that's not really a surprise, given Lucid9's origins. No, no, it's not a dealbreaker, it's just something I want to point out.
That said, I'd like to hear Miki's theme produced with some new libraries - I like hers particularly.
Which brings me on to the fact that just about every major character appears to have a leitmotif accompanying them, linking to their personalities. Elizabeth has a slightly jazzy piano number with her and Airi has a distinctively music-box like theme.
At first glance I didn't think Lucid9 was built on RenPy, though closer examination (and finally a look at the files) confirmed it was. The interface is pretty and the main menu is foreboding, but you can still tell this is RenPy when you notice the "Skip Mode" prompt on the top left and familiar options in the menus.
Unlike other RenPy games though, there is an actual backlog, rather than 'rewinding' when you scroll back, which means you cannot change your mind about a choice you've made unless you've made a save. Which isn't too bad, given the decently large number of save slots (64). I'd appreciate a "return to last choice" function, but again it's not a experience breaker.
Lucid9 also leverages some effects such as 'character zoom' where a currently speaking character's sprite 'moves forward', which is a nice touch. There are also clever manipulations of the interface at critical moments such as flickering text and one of my favorite small touches is the change in color of the interface at the 'darkest' moments.
There are also a couple of moments where you have to enter text to answer a question.
FSS has made a visual novel that can definitely stand on its own along other western-origin entries. It's gotten all the necessities right with above average production value among its kind. Which would be true even if it was $10. But it's not - it's free!

Lucid9: Inciting Incident was quite a surprise for me since it was one of my very first VNs. It starts with the Highschool-Story you might expect, likable characters, some funny and romantic parts spiced with a nice appearance and a good soundtrack - but thats just the start... The story soon gets more thrilling and you get very curious what happens next. Different aspects of the story such as highschool, romance, drama or crime provide a great diversity, but in my opinion, the story is most influenced by the heartbreaking drama part. The story heats up step by step and gets extremely intense (wich is perfectly rounded by the music). In my opinion, it has one of the most gripping stories I've ever experienced in a game. If you've never played a VN and doubt that it might be as much fun as a "normal" game - forget it, it's awesome! :D But you should prepare for the end (I know, it was mentioned in other reviews before :D), I mean seriously, the end is brutal, in all the different ways you can experience it. You probably won't believe what happened... Although it's really hard, the end makes the story even more intense and remarkable. I can't wait for the next part to come, you probably won't too! ;-) My recommendation: PLAY IT! PLAY IT! PLAY IT! It's really worth it, every minute you enjoy Lucid9: Inciting Incident! Just in case you've reached the part in the end, where you try to save your best friend and the hostages... There are several possible endings, but only one where you and your best friend get out of this school. Don't resign too fast!

While it was initially the ratings/reviews and the description (as well as the unbeatable price tag of free) that drew me in, once I started playing there was no turning back. For a variety of reasons.
First though I think it makes sense to give a few reasons to stay away from the game. As of now there is no sequel, and for some that is a major drawback. Later on this will be remedied though. It also lacks diverse, multiple routes and instead has a common route with a variety of potential Bad Endings. Anything else really would be spoiler territory.
For a free game made by developers that created it in their free time, the production value is impressive. Most of the background art and character art is really good, and there are some select examples of really great artwork. Despite a large number of music contributors, the soundtrack feels unified and though the songs range from average to great, their use in creating mood (as well as a lack of music) within the game is tasteful and adds a lot to each scene and every interaction. Its UI is standard and everything works, so no faults to speak of there.
In terms of the actual canon content, the pacing is questionable at times and the characters are a little bit tropey but they all still exhibit their own distinct personalities. Some more than others. Though I understand the reasoning for the balance choice between slice of life and mystery/thriller/horror elements I think that it can be a bit skewed and at times works to the story's disadvantage, but it also makes for some great build-ups and climaxes. Maybe I'm stupid, but the mystery remained a mystery to me up until its reveal, and that was very satisfying to me. Each scene and every "chapter" so to speak flowed well but there are bits that feel like they drag on.
From a more critical perspective the characters are fairly shallow but the plot writing is done well; everything feels like it adds up which isn't easy to do. Thematically it feels hackneyed, processed, and clunky, but despite all of these it never actively took away any notable amount of enjoyment for me. It just didn't add anything. I didn't walk away from it thinking that I had really learned anything, but I did walk away from it knowing that I was looking forward to the next release by Fallen Snow Studios in this series.
is a fun and solidly written story boasting impressive audio/visual production and sets up what could be a really interesting story. It still ends very satisfyingly, and I hope that it gets more recognition and that Fallen Snow Studios can follow it up with an equally good or even better product.

Probably the worst game I've ever played. Making a walking simulator is no excuse for lack of content. You're basically walking in the same flat, boring and poorly optimised enviroment the entire game. I'd say that's alright seeing as the game is so short, if only that single view was even mildly well made. Even with everything on ultra the graphics seem outdated at best. With flowers appearing out of thin air as you walk by them, flat plants and repeating trees, animals frozen in the same movement and completely ignoring your pressence,  rocks that make plastic seem realistic etc. The map is tiny and you'll find hidden walls whenever you try to step away from the road (which is often unclear, making you bang your head against the hidden walls repeatedly).
Seeing as there is no gameplay whatsoever, only a single piece of music repeating itself the whole game long, the controls feels cluncky and the movement feels extremely slow (probably to make the game seem longer than its content's worth) I fail to see where the devs actually put their time.
The game may be very cheap, but it offers pretty much nothing in return. Whereas some games in the same price range manage to make the best out of minimalism, this one clearly does not.

is one of Tonguç Bodur's earlier games, presented to the community sometime last year. He has been kind enough to present me a copy of its sequel,
to review, but I felt that I needed to play its predecessor first, in purpose of treating the story progression and presentation fairly. So, here we go!
Here in this short little exploration game, we take the role of a lonesome man, who lives alone in an island. As the game begins, we take a long, yearning gulp from a bottle of wine and take a glance at a note left for us. It is a cold winter day, and the woman that we loved abandoned us recently. Maybe with the effect of alcohol, or thanks to plain melancholy, we decide to take a walk outside. As we grab our coat and take a couple of steps, we encounter her... her visage stoic, her gaze ever fixated on us. As we approach, she disappears; and the only thing left is another note. For the remainder of the game, we are to take a long walk through this winter island, following her trail and her notes, in hopes of shedding some light into the mystery of her appearance.
Well, as a walking simulation, this one is breath-taking, I must give you that straight. The environment is a majestic nature trail, during a snow-covered winter, giving you a genuine sense of desolateness. The color white dominates the landscape ferociously, and the constant snow keeps shining under the sun to present you the illusion of something being, or happening around momentarily. Yet, as you take a walk towards that direction, you discover nothing but the light, shining upon trees and rock formations to play a game on your senses. The soft vail of the winter wind persists, and you keep hearing the crackling of a branch or the crushing of some snow under your very boots. There is nothing - no one - but you, in the end.
It sure is wondrously pretty, but you cannot help yourself feeling sad. Sad in a forlorn, aching, beautiful way... the very definition of melancholy, is depicted for you in this game. As you keep walking through the white coated landscape, you start acknowledging the sharp difference between solitude and isolation. There is no horror, or even thriller element in the game. Don't expect any kind of action either. It presents you a common story of "the woman, leaving the man", and that is the beauty of it all. That man can very well be you. This island can be the topography of your state of mind. You are left alone, and there is little for you to do in hopes of mending it.
The game takes half an hour to complete in your first playthrough. Once you complete it, you are given the option to replay it in "walk noir", a feature that would present the game in black and white, which harbors a different kind of ending for the same story. Overall, I can safely recommend this beauty to whomever favors the genre, and whomever would like to witness the portrayal of a feeling, rather than actually playing a game. But for others, it could be declared unsatisfactory, since there is nothing in this game to actively participate. For me, it was a gentle work of art. Enjoy!

This is probably one of the best examples of "mixed bags" that I can think of. Resident Evil 6 is both great and horrible in so many ways I won't be able to go over them all but for that reason alone I feel it's a game for anyone who considers themselves a "gamer" should play at least once to see what I mean.
RE6 is an action title with the occasional horror aesthetic thrown in to tie itself in whith its lineage. While best played with a friend it's very much playable solo. Players will take control one of 3 pairs of characters (or possibly an additional duo or a single character for the fourth campaign) as they experience the story of the game from three different perspectives and this is where the idea of the mixed bag begins. Instead of a single cohearent script, its divided amoungst three different stories that constantly leaves the player confused and in a stupor. Even with all the campaigns completed I had to read some of the in-game lore from the easily missed extras menu once I shot enough blue emblems in the game. While the Resident Evil series isn't known for its story, previous entries were at least easy to understand, not the case with this title, often throwing characters at the player that even veterans have no idea as to who they are.
Controling the characters is another issue for this game. In many games designed with a controller in mind, often times a button is used as a modifier for every other button. In previous games, what would be holding down the left trigger would then make the character aim at which point the right will fire. While that is a simple method, RE6 has layers of these that are poorly explained if at all. New players should take their time figuring out the controls as even into my second campaign I was still learning what certain combinations of buttons and motions did. However once learned, the complex control scheme actually makes for excellent stylish feats but not everyone will get used to them.
Probably one of the best things about the title is how it can incorporate multiplayer into the campaign. With certain options selected, a player can allow others online to join the game as a co op partner, random players to take control of basic enemies for a little extra challange, and even run into other players who are in other campaigns in overlapping story sections where up to four players can take on a segment of their campaigns together. The only problem with this is that due to the small playerbase many of these things wont happen without coordination with other players such as through Steam groups.
While there is definitly more to say I feel that these are some of the biggest issues. I do enjoy the game despite all its faults, however I will say that it may be my least favorite of the RE series that I have experienced. Many others damn this game as complete garbage, and while not all of their complaints are invalid or wrong, it does have entertainment value and some excellent points. If you are looking for a coop third-person action title, there are not many on the market but you should not settle for this unless you are already played through better titles. Give it a look but be aware it is flawed.

Friday The 13th: The Game; a loveletter to the horror-community.
First of all...
This game is amazing. You can tell I think so because of the amount of hours I've spent in this game with just basic multiplayer. Don't get me wrong, by now there's really no "groundbreaking" story (well at the moment there's no story), but it is so much more than I ever expected it to be. There's a reason I've spent so many hours in this game, one of the biggest reasons is because of the countless people I've talked with in this game that has made me both annoyed and amazed at how a community can be surrounding one particular game made by indie-developers. Of course, as any game, it's release state was buggy but not "game breaking", and even the bugs (that mostly now are fixed) were funny as hell. The game still has an amount of bugs in it, but those bugs that are left are minor and happen much more rare now than they did before. The game is also very fun to play with friends in a closed lobby.
The second reason you should buy this game..
Now, some people may say that the price is too high for this game, and to them I say that it really isn't if you think about it. The graphics are very good, the frame rates are also almost always above 80 online on a decent build (well, for the PC version at least). And not to speak of that the game is filled with content and is releasing more all the time as time passes. Examples of things coming to this game is Singleplayer, new game modes to the already amazing multiplayer, more Jasons, more maps, more clothes and emotes and more kill-animations. All this for free, now let me ask you, is the price really that high now that I've mentioned some of these things compared to the normal 60dollar price tag on games these days?
The third reason...
The atmosphere is just brilliant. The music composed by Harry Manfredini really set the stage of how Jason's theme should sound. For example, Jason from F13: Part IV gives an entirely other sence of fear than Jason from part 9 does, all because of the horror Icon Kane Hodder doing the animations for Jason and the music combined with the darkness of some maps and the weather effects. All from when It's quiet, to when you see a dead body to when Jason shows up. The music is perfect and really sets a creepy atmosphere and is a perfect resemblance if you have seen the movies. Now they've also added rain effects that changes the game's atmosphere almost on it's own. As I mentioned previously, Kane Hodder is doing the animations for Jason, and for that reason, combined with how they nailed how Jason is supposed to look for each different part, you really do sense some fear when Jason's around you or chasing you. Even better, when you play as Jason it really makes you feel like Jason Vorhees with his different abilities and kill-animations. The counselors also have different perks that you can unlock which makes it easier for you in matches, and there's a ton of unlockables and badges in the game. The achievements for this game, I know not everyone cares about achievements, but the achievements in the game are also a challenging aspect of the game in a good way, especially if you're a completionist like I am.
Fourth and final reason...
There's a lot of hidden easter eggs in this game, and if you're a fan of the series you'll really notice them and you'll notice how much attention to detail they put in when they made this game. Even if you haven't seen any of the movies, you can still admire how it makes you feel, all from the atmosphere to the people you meet in-game. You have to play it for yourself to really know what I'm talking about. There's more content on the way so be sure to look out for that.
I could go on for days, but why read this boring text when you can play the game yourself and have a blast for many, many hours? All this that I've mentioned, it really is a love-letter to horror fans and for that I would strongly recommend you pick this up and play it. With or without friends, this game is awesome! :)

So, you want to get Rocksmith 2014 do you? Well, in this review I will try and help you and decide if you should!
First of all, guitars. Already have one? Or do you even know how to play around a bit? Skip this part.
Now, when getting a guitar, especially your first one, you should really think through your descision, since it will pretty much be your best friend until, well, you get a new one!
When I bought mine, I made the mistake of buying the cheapest thing I found. Now I have a rather crappy guitar when I can play a bit, and that is not that fun.
Instead, look around a bit. Second-hand guitars can be a real deal! I have heard that Gibson studio guitars can be found really cheap second-hand and has a real nice quality (don't take my word for it though, I have never tried one myself.)
Rather get a new one? Nice! Check out some videos or reviews, and stay miles away from anything under 100€ since that is bound to be crap if new. If we look at budget guitars, Squier guitars can be found from all ranges from 200-450€. If your budget can take it, you may look at real Fenders or why not something like a Chapman? Of course it's going to be YOUR guitar, so take one that feels nice in the hand and is pleasing for the eye.
Nice videos to look at might be just the creator of Chapman guitars,
, where he reviews a lot of different guitars while having a laugh aswell.
Now, to the actual game. The game is fun. At times that is, Sometimes I just want to throw my guitar out the window. Here's why.
Positive: The games comes with lessons, helping you with all teqnices you'll encounter in the game, everything from basic chords to two-handed tapping. These lessons is pretty much a must, so don't just play the 'Learn a song' mode and learn teqnices too!
The game comes with the guitarcade, full of minigames that will help you learn all the teqnices!
Riff repeater, well look it up. It's pretty awesome.
You can download custom songs, check out the
for more help on this!
Now to the negative: This game was made for musicians, not gamers in that sense. This means that the gameplay aspect, such as in the guitarcade games, are REALLY poorly designed at parts. Not to mention the bugs, also very present in the guitarcade. These never seem to be fixed, and some are so annoying you'll want to chew your headstock off.
The menus. What can I say, they are what gamers would call "the worst pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥porting I have seen since the Big Bang". They are appaling and every game designers worst nightmare. Especially prominent in Riff repeater. This might be the only deal-breaker, it's a really big problem.
Now, should you get this game? Well, if you can handle menus that take ♥♥♥♥♥on of time to get used to and don't mind some bugs, then yes. A really nice way to stay motivated is to take the
. Just don't stare yourself blind at the promotion-videos and make sure to have fun while learning! I would also like to recommend playing around a bit outside Rocksmith

First and foremost, based on reviews, the Rocksmith Real Tone Cable is very fragile so take extra care of it! Over at my place the cable is not easy to find and is rather expensive so you don't want to go through hassle of getting another one or modding a guitar usb cable.
Rocksmith is a fine tool for beginners and pros alike. There are plenty video lessons that would be helpful for beginners, even when you are playing a guitar for the very first time. In Rocksmith, you don't do readings, unlike reading tabs, chords, music notes or using Guitar Pro software. Rather you learn through videos, visual graphics and repetitive motions.
All you really need is an electric guitar, and the game will handle the rest. The tones, amps, and all the tools that will mod & filter the sounds that are available in real world are all installed in the game and it sounds really, really awesome. *Branded, expensive stuffs, mind you*. Jamming in real life won't get you the exact sound without these proper tools thus in this game you will play the songs as it is meant to be played. *Thank god the tones are not DLC's* *No, I'm not giving any idea, Ubisoft*
The game has a mode called Riff Repeater where it allows you to learn sections by sections of the songs. It also have difficulty setting whereby you can control your pace of learning so it really caters to beginners very well. *Imagine learning the solo's without this mode, oh god*. Practicing would be boring, if you're not interested in the song in the first place. So song choice matters! Start immediately with the songs you like and don't just play at random! Also, it has a build-in tuner so you won't get your tuning wrong for all the songs. Having said that, outside of the game, you gonna have to learn how to tune the guitar to suit the songs perfectly and that would depend on your own initiatives.
Ultimately, with or without Rocksmith, you have to be passionate and dedicated enough to be able to enjoy playing the guitar. Rocksmith is just a tool, and it's not a game where you will have fun without practicing a song over and over again. I see that many started this game but stopped after a short while because they seem to lost interest. So take this into consideration if you are going to start this game as you don't only have to buy the game, but also the guitar and its cable and almost everything that accompanies it which by then you will find out this hobby is as costly as any other.
Points doesn't matter, as long as you enjoy playing & I do, I enjoy playing. So if you are looking to play a guitar, whether beginning or restarting the musical journey, I wish you good luck and have fun!

If you're into Rogue-likes check this one out. It's done in that strange 70's sci-fi style that is post-apocalypse and bordering on fantasy. You play a mutant or a pure human from a closed arcology and go rampaging through the wasteland.

Have you ever wanted to play a computer RPG inspired by Gamma World? Have you ever wanted to load up a character creation screen and see pages upon pages of mutations to choose from for your character - everything from shooting fire from your hands, talking to machines, making psychic copies of yourself, multiple limbs and organs, and more than I could possibly summarize here? This is your game.
What to do with all this power? This is an old school, hardcore roguelike, so after picking up your amazing powers there's still a good chance you'll die on the first screen to a salthopper and find yourself back at the character creation screen. Doesn't sound fun? It is. If you manage to survive past the first screen, you will discover a world of ruins and remnants of an ancient, advanced civilization. You will fight with sword, bow, musket, and wild mutations, while trying to dechiper and deploy strange high tech artifacts from the past: grenades, shotguns, rifles, chemical injectors, turrets, and electronics.
The writing in this game is wonderful, describing the exotic, alien world in perfect detail. The plot is superb. Too bad you'll die before you get to enjoy it. Trading is a big feature of this game as well, and the currency is fresh water, which leads to an interesting balancing act of upgrading your gear and saving enough "money" to drink.
If you have Pandora, I recommend cranking Persian Traditional music while playing this game. Live and drink, friend.

Caves of Qud to break it down simply is a HD ASCII Roguelike. It's odd placing the acronyms "HD" and "ASCII" next to each other, but there really isn't a better way to describe the game. it keeps true to it's heritage of Dos based roguelikes, from it's HD ASCII visuals, to it's keyboard command scheme. Even the mechanics and visuals are redesigned versions of what you may find in games like Rogue or Dwarf Fortress.
If you've never played an ASCII Roguelike game before, getting into Caves of Qud, could prove challenging. It won't control like modern games, forgoing mouse and gamepad, and sticking strictly to keyboard commands. There is a help menu which I highly recommend any new player to check before proceeding. But once you get over the learning curve, you'll find an expansive randomly generated world to explore, with a ton of replay and experimentation potential. You'll be able to create your own class, and tackle the game's quest and world as you see fit. It's wide, expansive, and deep.
Visually it may look unimpressive at first glance, but when you compare it to it's original ASCII version you can clearly see where all the work went into. Instead of actual ASCIIs as representation of the characters and the world, the game uses low-fi sprites that carry a similar visual feel of ASCIIs. Even the font choice and spacing is carefully designed to remind us of older times, while keeping things modern and easily read. There is no sound to speak of, no music, no midis. The game is in early access so it could be something to be added later, however, I suspect the omission is done intentionally, as the original Caves of Qud featured no sounds as well.
The game is fantastic, even as a player who've never played a whole lot of ASCII games in the past, but with that said, it's not perfect. Though the lack of sound could of been done deliberately, I'd still prefer if it featured some midi sounds to go with it. Also the initial area is consistent and always the same, with areas outside of the starting point being RNG. This coupled with the high learning curve of Caves of Qud will make the initial few tries at the game feel more tedious than if it was also randomly generated as well.
Overall Caves of Qud is what I'd like to consider "The Pillars of Eternity of Roguelikes". Much like Pillars of Eternity, Caves of Qud keeps true to both the gameplay and visuals of it's inspired genre, without sacrificing the original's spirit, all while being an immensely enjoyable experience.
Pros:
- Great looking "HD" ASCII sprites and design
- Keeps true to it's heritage
- Deep and engrossing
- Endless experimentation and replayability
Cons:
- Might not be for every one
- No sounds

Caves of Qud is by most, if not all, definition a traditional rogue-like which features plenty of untimely deaths and tons of quirky living and non-living things. There are light elements of survival with some needs for food and water, and you are also able to make new stuffs if you happen to come across the 'data disk' for you and if you have the necessary skills. Being a traditional rogue-like also means graphics is restricted to ASCII or tiles (static icons effectively) so kindly do not expect to see the fringe of your character’s hair flowing in the breeze.
Rogue-likes us]ed to exist at a time which requires people to use their imagination, and so it is only as fun as you imagine it to be. That said, the lack of graphics also mean more effort can be put into crafting deeper lore, additional content and balancing game mechanics instead of having to fiddle around with body proportions and rag-doll physics. Considering that you can choose to play a mutant with multiple hands, legs and heads (just two), perhaps it’s better not to fiddle around with the rag-doll physics too. Fun is when you actually make an effort to overcome an in-game obstacle and take pleasure in doing so, or when you prevent your next character’s death by learning from his/her predecessor’s demise. Fun is also when you are able to get randomized loot, crappy or otherwise, and make the most out of them. Fun too, is when you beat bad RNG odds to survive. Fun is all of the above; everything else is merely enjoyable at best.
It looks as good-looking as alphabets and sentences can be. There’s quite a bit of reading to do, mostly flavor text and background lore and whether you might be dying or not, or did you lose a limb or two. Other than these, graphically-representative icons are all that you have to feed your imagination with.
There is a free ASCII version on the developer’s website
which you may wish to download and check out for yourself on the content and gameplay. I would also advise watching a few Let’s Play episodes somewhere to gauge if you can dedicate the hours needed to enjoy the game. There are still some issues which needs to be ironed out, and the developer has been pretty hardworking so far to get these sorted out. All in all, still playable as it is, and the more hours you are willing to pour in, the more value for money the game is going to be.

If I could take one game with me to a desert island, it'd be Caves of Qud.
**DIFFICULTY**
Is it hard? Yes.
Is it too hard? No.
Even for somebody who's never played a roguelike before? Totally do-able.
You will die. A lot. The game is designed to be hard, but not tear-your-hair-out frustrating. The way that it manages to be very difficult and yet wholly enjoyable despite death after death is a masterpiece of gaming.
**INTRIGUE**
There is deep political simulation, effecting every last mob in the game. Gain enough reputation with certain types of creatures or people (arachnids, farmers, tortoises) and they will rush to your aid in battle. Lose enough, and they'll attack you on sight. The landmarks in the game--like the starting village, Joppa--are always the same, but the wilderness and caves are procedurally-generated. That means that as you try to reach the deepest depths of, say, Red Rock, you could find the next staircase down mere feet away or on the other side of the map. What's more, there are very in-depth and extremely interesting crafting and trade systems that you can master in time.
**COMBAT**
Deceptively simple. Like any proper roguelike, you have to come up with creative ways to deal with certain situations. Choosing whether to shoot your rifle or swing your sword could be a life or death decision. It's easy to learn, hard to master.
**CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION**
Oh, boy. Wanna be a beguilin', time-dilatin', flame-throwin', photosynthesizin', gunslingin' cowboy-snake called Grassy Jones? You got it.
Want to be one of just a few remaining true men, an aristocrat as well versed in ways of the trigger as he is in the way of the blade? You got it.
Wanna get a few more points to put into useful mutations by taking a debuff that puts an evil twin somewhere in the world, an exact clone of your character who may one day find you and kill you? Yep. You can do that too.
**LORE**
Just play it, man. It's awesome.
**CONS**
Sometimes, you get attached to your beguilin', time-dilatin', flame-throwin', photosynthesizin', gunslingin' cowboy-snake called Grassy Jones. While after he dies you can click 'replay most recent character' on the new game screen and get Grassy Jones back, you won't get his successes back. Half the time, that's fine and it's just as fun to do it all over again. There's actually a disable permadeath button, but for now it doesn't work. There are other little cons, but they're too small to mention.
**THE BEST PART**
It ain't even finished yet, cowboy.

Well, I'm going back to the classics today with Tonguc Bodur's Bottle. I've played this now a total of four times (two normal run-throughs and two Noir mode playthroughs), for a total of less than an hour and a half.
If that doesn't tell you all you need to know about this game, no need to fear. I've got the scoop: Bottle is yet another TB walking simulator with nonsense poetry, caves, and stock assets, but this time we've got a new twist--an even more trite metaphor than usual.
You see, you play as a man that was left by a woman, so he's lonely, and as many lonely men do, he replaces the companionship of his partner with--you guessed it--a bottle of wine. You start out in an exorbitantly decorated wooden shack with a bottle of wine in front of you, then you walk down a patch reading some random notes you find as you chase the mirage of your ex-lover. Eventually (and it feels like it takes half your life) you reach a wooden shack near a lake where you find one of two endings, depending on whether you are playing in Noir mode or not. Protip: you're a sad drunk either way, like in a few other TB games I can recall.
And just in case those turns of events don't drive the point home, Tonguc has made it even clearer by making your menu cursor in the shape of a wine bottle, and flat-out telling you in the last memo you pick up. So, you know, that way you know you're a deep, intellectual soul when you understand the deep moral message.
Also, as in most TB games, you're surrounded by insipidly beautiful scenery. I will say this game really tones down the scenery compared to games like Drizzlepath. It also tones down the characteristic voiceovers that we know and love. There is only one line of monologue in the main game, which occurs if you try to leave your house without your coat. Interestingly, this is the only TB game I've played thus far (note: I have not yet played The Hunting God) with a male narrator. In Noir mode, you get a fourth wall-breaking joke hidden in the game.
For those of you not familiar with this genre of game, let me break it down just a little bit: you hold the W key. You look around. In this particular iteration, you open two doors and pick up 4-5 notes. You get three speed boost pickups. There is one completely skippable jumping section that lasts 10 seconds. The whole thing lasts 20 minutes. AKA a complete non-game.
My main question for the developer is: If you are going to make a game this close to just being a short film, why not just cut out the tedium of the interactions and make it completely non-interactive? It would be more fun. I see "relaxing" tagged up there in the description, but there is a fine line between relaxing and infuriatingly boring which has been firmly crossed in this instance. You just hold W and wait for something, anything to happen, and that wish is not granted.
So, in a nutshell, what I like about this game is that it is much shorter than other TB games like Drizzlepatch: Genie, and that there's no faux intellectual babble so you can talk through the whole run and not miss anything. What I don't like is the boring music, no button that automatically walks without holding W, and that nothing happens. Oh, and that there's some shameless self-referential advertising thrown in, which just makes TB's hard-translated-from-Turkish kindergarten metaphors even shallower. Therefore, I find myself unable to recommend this game.
Tonguc: If you're reading this, man, I swear I will recommend Drizzlepath when I replay it. That is a jolly good time. I promise I don't just write these vitriolic reviews out of some personal spite in my heart against you. It's just that these games are neither relaxing or fun or illuminating in any way. Drizzlepath was honest-to-goodness fun, so one of these days I'm going to play it again and review it positively because I like it. Promise.

Have you ever played a game, and by the time you finish, you're asking yourself, What was the point? That's basically what Bottle did to me.
Once I completed the game, I didn't really feel like I achieved anything. I mean, there are several achievements you can acquire in this game, but when the summary tells you this is a short game, it truly means it's a short game.
You can wander around off the beaten path.
There are a few miscellaneous things to come across.
There's even a second version you can play after you beat the normal mode.
Like with Drizzlepath, the soundtrack isn't consistent, but there doesn't seem to be a trigger that I can notice. Maybe there is though. But if not, it's odd they'd make the game go completely quiet while you're in the middle of walking around with nothing but random rustlings nearby.
Which is weird, because there's no wildlife. Whenever there's a rustling sound, don't worry. You're not actually being stalked by an animal.
But unlike with Drizzlepath, the graphics in this game are repetitive. You see the same trees, the same boulders, the same flowers, the same textures. Worst of all, it's noticeable.
The sunlight reflecting off the snow can be a bit too bright at times. And as one of my viewers on my Twitch streaming channel had said, "This game tops the charts for visual glitches per second." I can't exactly disagree with that statement. The graphics really aren't that great for this not being a first try at a game.
There's a woman you come across on occasion, and the only way you'll be able to figure out what she says is if you replay her audio backwards. She's speaking backwards, but multiple times overlapping one another, so...it's gibberish. I don't know why they did this, but it seems pointless.
Maybe you as the character are confused on why she said certain things to you in the past and this is him reflecting on it.
Who knows.
I certainly don't.
As a walking simulator, there’s not much in the ways of gameplay. You can interact with an axe! But you can’t kill anyone with it, unfortunately. There’s a couple other interactions with objects, but the main point of the game is to take in the sights.
Even if you just saw them five seconds ago.
I don’t think there’s any good tidbits that would allow me to even bribe someone to play this game, let alone recommend it. I suppose if you’re a game creator, you can play the game and understand what not to do if you’re going to walking simulator route. But aside from that?
No.
Just no.

Resident evil 6,  was by the time of the original console release, a massive blunder thanks to a lot of problems within the game, such as terrible camera, too much focus on action, sloppy controls, bad level design and inbalanced difficulty. Now updated to fix some of those problems and with the benefits of being in pc....its still a letdown; but an interesting, entretaining one.
The game has a massive amount of content: 4 different campaings, each one of 5 plus hours alongside with various difficulty levels, the now classic mercenaries mode, including all eight main characters along with an extra outfit, which changes their weapon setup and the flawled but interesting agent hunt, in which you go online and control the enemies other players fight during the campaing mode. However it feels obvious that there was not enough communication between the 600 hundred people(!) who worked in this game. During campaing mode (all of them) there is an obvious dissconect between the gameplay and the level design, for not mentioning the dissapointing musical score and the cheesy, hilariously over-the-top cinematics, full of bombastic action, unnecesary explosions and idiocy in general.
Now to elaborate on the gameplay... its simply awesome. You have your standar 3rd person shoter fare and control settup, but with new features and actions, such as dedicated inputs for elaborated melee attacks, (there are over 8 different of them, for each character) counterattacks, quickshots, manual evassive inputs (No qtes) slides, and more. Mowing down hordes of undead was never this fun in this kind of games.
However the level desing is against this awesomely tunned gameplay. Its constricted, dark and filled with corridors when in reality what you need are open spaces with lots of movility to enjoy all the actions you can do. There are times where entire leves are just a big, giant hallway with some dead ends and a good deal of "cinematic cutscenes" that makes playing through the campaing a total hassle, as if the stupid story and horrible character interaction was not bad enough....
Im giving this game a possitive review in the end, just because of the Mercenaries minigame, in which you have to mow down hordes of enemies in limited time, scoring points for sucessive kills and dealing with lots of high level enemies IN OPEN SPACES, WITH LOTS OF OPTIONS, WEAPONS AND TACTICS TO USE. Its obvious that this game was made with high speed action shotouts in mind, but they ♥♥♥♥ed up hard with the level design and tone of the game...for gods sake the first thing you do in the game is to shot a zombified president of the US in the head; somehow the game still takes itself seriously after that right throught the end.
Long story short: Recommended...for ten bucks or less, not 30 bucks, let alone 60

As some someone who just cleared it recently completely on No Hope difficulty. I thought it was a 5/5 game. Completely awesome and I'll even explain why.
I've completed just about mainline RE game with the exception of RE3 which I dropped. Including 0. The earlier ones I never considered "survival horror" games. But rather cinematic action games with a focus on exploration and ammo conserving. The reason for this is generally every camera angle in the early games was set up like a film angle. Along with the generally good animations and visuals they had at the time.
Now for RE6 actually being good. It greatly expands on what RE4 and 5 established. With greater enemy variety, a need for precision still (As context sensitive attacks are still the best way to kill generic enemies), now with a surprisingly complex dodge system that is actually meaningful, and added manual melee moves that balances ranged combat and melee too.
For the dodge system. You have a crouching dodge that allows for extremely fast recovery. A generic roll which is self explanatory. A roll that puts you in a prone position which is adequate for fast recovery and repositioning to pull off a shot. While having a knife equipped. You character performs side dodges instead of rolls. Which is basically a curve instead of a straight line. Allowing you to dodge attacks to perform a quick stun and perform a quick melee of some kind.
The much bloated upgrade system from RE4 and 5 was removed. Now you'll find yourself using all weapons equally. Along with melee attacks to generally conserve ammo. Now shooting at first feels weird since there's an actual need for recoil compensation this time. But enemies are just reactive as ever just like in 4. Shooting zombies will leave bulletholes inside them. Shooting Ja'vos in the skull makes it partially cave in. Enemies get stunned, knocked down, and etc.
There's variation in weapons for each character. So, you won't have to deal with obsolete weapons by midgame like RE4 and 5.
As for the campaigns. They do actually capture some variety between them. Hell, the weakest one is Ada Wong's. Which I would have marked the game off a for a few points if Mercs wasn't better than ever.
If I ranked them it would be like this
Chris>Leon>Jake>Ada
Chris's campaign not only gives some of the biggest environments to fight in. But also shows off the mechanics the best. Piers is a ♥♥♥♥ing bro too.
Leon did have some cool levels. Like the graveyard and the crypt. Which were very challenging. Helena had a very nice♥♥♥♥♥
Ada's however is fairly weak. Featuring tons of recycling and some pretty weak level design. I wouldn't call it the worst in the series though. That goes to the intro of 5. Some of the levels actually required some navigation. Like encountering the grinches while playing in Leon's campaign and again in Chris's. With them being unkillable, you are forced to disable them temperorially or avoid them while searching for items in a complex environment.
Another thing is that though the controls are a bit clunky still. The UI and inventory is massively improved. They finally removed inventory tetris from 4 and the god awful inventory from 5. A good number of things however are poorly explained, either not all or too late. Like melee combos or dodge variations.

One of the biggest failings on consumer's part in a long time, this game, while criticized justly, is really unique and deserved better reception/sales.  The game revolves around the use of a Jetpack and it does so in such a beautiful way it is like playing a air combat game like Ace Combat one moment, then with the press of a button you switch to hover mode and its like the jetpack parts of San Andreas but with nice and responsive controls.  And finally once you hit the ground, it becomes a competent third person shooter with standard cover mechanics.  Except if you are by a ledge where you take vertical cover and fire down or up on enemies.  The vertical cover moments really feel like those crazy moments in the Time Crisis arcade games where your character uses something really rediculous for cover, like in Time Crisis 3 where you take cover by a ledge then hang upsidedown to return fire.  And then at any time you get bored of the ground you hit a few buttons and you are flying away like you just hijacked an airplane in Just Cause 2, which you can actually do using your jetpack incase you want some extra protection.
The criticism leveled at the game isn't wrong, although for me I had no issues with controls or framerate, but I think that was console criticism.  There was 1 part early on that caused a CTD but running the game in windowed mode got me past it and afterwards the game only had 1 more crash which is pretty good considering Triple A titles everyone owns crash more frequently.
The game sadly suffers from being either too ambitious or being rushed, there are a few rapid jumps through time where it feels like the developers had an extra hour of gameplay planned and skipped it, and this really does make the game in the end sort of disappointing, however once you get your rocketpack addition to the jetpack, you will want to just fly around and never stop.  But the game does stop, and it stops very abruptly and the poor reception the game got probably means we won't see a game with this type of unique gameplay for a long time.
If you enjoyed using the grappling hook in Just Cause 2, the Sky-Rails in Bioshock Infinite, the VTOL vehicles from Saints Row, or just the idea of freeroaming huge areas with a jetpack, you won't regret buying this game at it's current price, and if its on sale you are doing yourself a disservice by not getting it, its not an epic, but it is something anyone who wants to be able to fly around a series of huge battlefields should at least give a try.

I've been playing guitar since October of 2007, and I got this game not too long ago, so it didn't teach me really anything more than I already knew. That will not be a factor, since I simply bought this to learn more songs accurately and not have to rely on false guitar tabs. The game is great, especially for a learning tool, but I do have some complaints about some technical features that made me rarely ever want to play it.
It's 2015 at the time of typing this, however, Ubisoft must think we're back in the early 1980's where the dreadfully inaccurate needle tuner was mostly present, and that is what is used in this game. Granted it's a digital emulation of one, but that thing couldn't figure out exact pitch if you wanted it to. For instance, I have a couple tuners from BOSS and Delta Lab that work great and have sniper-like accuracy. If I tuned to what Rocksmith defines as "exact pitch" on that A-string, for example, my tuners will say I'm about 10-15 cents below what it should be, and they're correct because I do guitar covers like crazy, and I'm NEVER out of tune. They need to completely redesign this in the next game, or at least have BOSS or Delta Lab create the new tuner.
My only other issue is that this game really likes to fail to register notes/chords that are played in some songs ("Wasteland" by Earlyrise is prime example), even though you KNOW the note would be loud enough and clear enough to be album worth, lol. I've turned the cable gain option up about 2db, but that isn't really helping. And my guitars are quite loud, so this makes little sense to me. Also, I DO know about setting up guitars for specific tunings and play styles, so don't think I'm some idiot who doesn't know about something as easy as intonation, lol. :P
In all, this game is perfect as a learning tool and a way for already seasoned guitar/bass players, but it has its fatal flaws. If you can get past the wonky tuner, the chances of your notes not registering, and the weak custom tones, you should have a good time.

If I could take one game with me to a desert island, it'd be Caves of Qud.
**DIFFICULTY**
Is it hard? Yes.
Is it too hard? No.
Even for somebody who's never played a roguelike before? Totally do-able.
You will die. A lot. The game is designed to be hard, but not tear-your-hair-out frustrating. The way that it manages to be very difficult and yet wholly enjoyable despite death after death is a masterpiece of gaming.
**INTRIGUE**
There is deep political simulation, effecting every last mob in the game. Gain enough reputation with certain types of creatures or people (arachnids, farmers, tortoises) and they will rush to your aid in battle. Lose enough, and they'll attack you on sight. The landmarks in the game--like the starting village, Joppa--are always the same, but the wilderness and caves are procedurally-generated. That means that as you try to reach the deepest depths of, say, Red Rock, you could find the next staircase down mere feet away or on the other side of the map. What's more, there are very in-depth and extremely interesting crafting and trade systems that you can master in time.
**COMBAT**
Deceptively simple. Like any proper roguelike, you have to come up with creative ways to deal with certain situations. Choosing whether to shoot your rifle or swing your sword could be a life or death decision. It's easy to learn, hard to master.
**CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION**
Oh, boy. Wanna be a beguilin', time-dilatin', flame-throwin', photosynthesizin', gunslingin' cowboy-snake called Grassy Jones? You got it.
Want to be one of just a few remaining true men, an aristocrat as well versed in ways of the trigger as he is in the way of the blade? You got it.
Wanna get a few more points to put into useful mutations by taking a debuff that puts an evil twin somewhere in the world, an exact clone of your character who may one day find you and kill you? Yep. You can do that too.
**LORE**
Just play it, man. It's awesome.
**CONS**
Sometimes, you get attached to your beguilin', time-dilatin', flame-throwin', photosynthesizin', gunslingin' cowboy-snake called Grassy Jones. While after he dies you can click 'replay most recent character' on the new game screen and get Grassy Jones back, you won't get his successes back. Half the time, that's fine and it's just as fun to do it all over again. There's actually a disable permadeath button, but for now it doesn't work. There are other little cons, but they're too small to mention.
**THE BEST PART**
It ain't even finished yet, cowboy.

A visual treat of a follow-up to Crysis, the sequel completely changes direction and almost suffers from it, if not for its otherwise excellent game-play.
Whilst Crysis and Warhead did very little truly interesting in the narrative department (with Warhead at least trying to do something about addressing that) the sequel quickly puts you into an entirely new environment and situation with very little explanation into a world that is a mess. Being ferried from one set-piece to the next on a strictly linear and far narrower path, I quickly realised that I was losing focus on what was going on with a conflict that seemed to spring out of nowhere and whilst there are obviously connections to the original, they seem tenuous at best. Crysis 2's narrative is a mess and whilst Crysis got away with its minimalist approach as it didn't shove it right up your face, it's hard to ignore the silliness going on in 2 as it, unfortunately, does shove it in your face.
The plus of all of this is that the core game is still very fun, if not severely reduced in scope and potential variation. Replacing open objectives are checkpoints along a trail that mostly replaces the how you approach an encounter with where you approach it from; the game does at least provide different routes for you to approach fights from that can give eager travellers an upper hand. This is particularly important given that the nature of your enemies have changed and whilst you're still fighting a lot of humans, you also have various alien enemies to take out, from foot soldier equivalents to large walking annoying bosses.
The removal of island openness does at least make way for some truly fun set-pieces though as the further you get into the game, the more interesting they become culminating in an extremely fun final level. As memorable as some of them may be though, there is an inherent reduction in the replayability in the game; you can only approach encounters in so many ways, set-pieces are only unique the first time and weapon variation (both in what's available and how many you can carry) limit the empowering craziness of the original and Warhead.
Ultimately, 2 feels very much like an extension of the ideas in Warhead, but at double the length and losing what made Warhead a fun in-between point of Crysis' openness and general FPS linearity. By the end of this game though, whilst I had felt satisfied, I was in no rush to play it again, nor even consider how I would attempt to go back to
particular set-piece and try completing it in a different manner. Essentially, there's one good run here before the game feels like it has expired.
Whilst Crysis 2 does look fantastic and has a great sound-track to boot, it lacks much of the uniqueness that its predecessors had whilst only providing minor boosts to the things that already made it a great shooter. Fun overall, but a greatly reduced experience overall.
Multiplayer: There's a greater push for the MP component in 2, but it essentially plays out like many small map-based shooters. A few interesting quirks here and there, particularly in your suit-enabled movement, but otherwise an extended feeling from the main game, that of competency and not much else.

When the game was first announced It didn't fall under my radar, therefore I had no hype for it. Medieval battles, this time between samurai, vikings and knights... I can't say that it's a ground breaking, and absolute stunning concept, unlike something that Star Citizen promises. But still, ubisoft do make visually stunning games, and this one is no exception to that. With that said, I've collected my thoughts on experience from 20+ hours of open beta & Several hours from the August 2017 Free Weekend.
The Good:
- Character movement and how he interacts with everything is nearly perfect.
- The visual battle choreography is absolutely stunning.
- In battle, being locked in a duel puts you on the edge of the seat and puts a lot of stress on your reflexes. (Now this is probably something that a Dark Souls player like me would appreciate a lot since, the feeling is highly remeniscent to what I've used to experience).
- Good overall character customization*
The Bad:
- It's pure focus is Multiplayer, Singleplayer can be disregarded in general, just an excuse to add value to the game.
- It lacks game mode variations terribly, the multiplayer maps are small, I think they might be even way too small to entertain your for more than 20-40 hours of multiplayer experience. It would be actually really awesome to have a Rush mode with a bigger map.
For instance: Break through the gates >>> Battle in the inner yards or streets >>> Break through the inner wall >>> Make your way to the final area.
- Back to character customization. While i like it, I don't think there are a whole lot of items to customize your character with. Then the type of color/material of the armor look stunning on the Knights, since... well... Golden plate on a Warden makes you equal to a Golden Ak74... But golden leather makes you look like an filthy casual who decided to add some cheap golden dye to your rags.
- The sheer existence of power ups.
- P2P... we all know and heard that, it's just disgusting. There are plans for Dedicated Servers, however, I wouldn't trust Ubisoft in advance, untill they actually get that done.
The Ugly:
- Doesn't feel like a $60 game. More then that, it feels that I might have been a great Multiplayer only but high quality game that would have micro-transactions like the most popular Moba's and Warframe.
- Long Livability. I've predicted this during Open-Beta but the online will be dead in a couple of months, so it happened. Free Weekend is something that will get people in but will not keep them, so expect a drop again.
- Season Pass. It's a $60 game that most likely it might have a perfect amount of multiplayer content for a Free-to-Play. But for putting in perspective other nowadays giants, i don't think For Honor has that much to offer, and still asking for a season pass is just madness.
Conclusion:
I don't want to be an ******* and Yes, I know that game development is a very hard and ungrateful industry to work in, Plus in addition the ROI is constantly at peril especially when Developed AAA games don't break the expected sales mark. Ubisoft's development team creates eye candies, but when it comes to running a game it just kills me and many other players, yes, my fellow the division community, i feel your pain after the first major patch in The Division.
With that said, even though I wasn't hyped before, open beta got me really hiped, and Free Weekend kept me interested, but the reality is that this game will never ever live up to it's true potential. I think it's a lost opportunity and the game could have been so much better if only there was more time, and resources may be it's the management who disregarded many things due to budget costs and cuts.

Bottle is the third Steam project from lone developer Tonguç Bodur has worked on and you may consider this title, as his return to roots. All the way to Drizzlepath perhaps, even if Bottle clearly continues some of Drizzlepath: Genie's ideas. So why compare the third game with the very first one he released? The game I’m reviewing today is as short and to the point as Tonguç's first foray into game development. And no, I don’t consider it a full step backwards.
If you played Bodur’s previous two releases, you know by now not to expect a storyline at face value. Bottle is as abstract as all this developer’s creations and that is wholeheartedly beneficial onto a Steam library that holds so few such niche titles. You wouldn’t play this particular type of walking simulators because of their action or adventure genre features. Stay informed and always read the game’s description and reviews before a purchase. Elementary tips that shall shield you from any potential disappointment. I do hope that games such as Bottle don’t disappoint their player base though, whether we’re talking of subgenre veterans or newcomers.
In any case, despite not making any direct references, it was clear to me that Bottle is a game about personal loss and how people should cope with that. Unlike the original Drizzlepath or the Genie sequel, Bottle skips the “drizzle” part (a light type of rain) and goes straight to snow, a feature reserved when players would be near the end of the previously mentioned titles. It might be a symbol for a shorter journey or for something more deep. Don’t expect me to spoil the experience for you. One thing I can reveal to you: no Mountain of Fire in this game and far fewer symbols or metaphors, yet the title is just as relaxing as its predecessors and has a personality of its own.
Same as with Drizzlepath: Genie, the developer continued working on Unreal Engine 4 assets. Why fix something that’s clearly not broken? Unlike the unstable frame rate from 2015’s Drizzlepath (thanks to CryEngine 3), Genie and Bottle both offered me 4K screenshots at 40 frames per second or more. Running the game maxed out, naturaly. I would rather have “taken down a notch” to 2K res, than sacrifice visual details or play below 30fps. I did find the perfect conditions for nearly 50 new screenshots to capture through the Steam Overlay. So in that regard, no matter how brief the gameplay itself might be, you will still have a lot to see and admire if it’s eye candy you’re after.

Bottle has a handful of piano songs playing in the background and that’s about it. The voice acting is limited to a single line spoken by the protagonist in the first 5 minutes of starting a new game and some indistinct chatter from a female character, placed near several locations you pass through. No narrator in this game, or abstract poetry recited along guitar riffs. That is a “break from tradition” if you take into consideration the first two Drizzlepath games that came before Bottle. I didn’t really miss the poetry, but the female narrator was a nice touch in the previous titles.
A walking simulator through and through, Bottle allows sprinting only on two occasions throughout its entire gameplay duration. This isn't bothering me in the slightest, since the game can be completed in about an hour and a half. That’s about 3 hours for both the Normal and Noir modes. The only differences between these two is mainly related to the visual style and barely noticeable ending alterations. Noir features a more pronounced skyline, while Normal has the best scenery details thanks to vivid colors. You’ll be excused if you settle just for the Normal mode and never play Noir, since that one gets unlocked after you’ve already completed Bottle once. At least keep Noir Mode in mind, if you ever wish to replay the title at a future date.
In Bottle you get to explore tranquil surroundings in a winter forest environment. That’s about it. A meditative journey that looks close to Skyrim’s own snow covered woodlands, minus the constant attacks from bandits or wildlife. As in all of Tonguç Bodur creations, you stick to a clearly defined dirt path that takes you from point A to B and along the way you may stop and take in the sights, anytime you wish. No one is rushing or forcing you in any way. The game map is designed with few invisible walls in mind, so you can leave the road and travel in some directions that may not further the story, but will still reveal certain interactive symbols which reward players with new Steam Achievements.
If one thing can be agreed upon, Bottle is priced decently for what it offers. The sheer amount of hard work and details that went into it, already place it above many similarly priced Steam games. The screenshots don’t lie, folks. Neither the official Store Page ones or my own. It’s ultimately up to you to decide, if you’re interested in a brief but beautiful journey from one winter cottage to another. Of course, if you’re already fans of the abstract genre and arthouse games in general, feel free to hit that Bottle. No headaches or regrets are included.

Bottle is the third game by Tonguc Bodur, the lead designer of Drizzlepath and Drizzlepath: Genie. Since I enjoyed both of those games, I thought I'd try his third game, Bottle...and since I own the rest of his repertoire I'll probably skip to the next one shortly after that. Heck, they're short enough, and it's not often one gets to review six games in a row by a single developer who, while sticking to one persistent genre ("walking simulators"), tends to mix things up a little from game to game (and apparently works with slightly different supporting artists, like writers and voice actors, from project to project).
So what do you get with Bottle? Well, you get gorgeous semi-open snowscapes and a slightly surreal lack of footstep sound effects, as well as the occasional item to interact with, the occasional note to read, and the occasional eerie female character who persistently shows up and appears to be possessed, considering that when she speaks, she is Legion. The music is also very pretty and conducive to a contemplative mood, but I did kind of miss the voice narration element so common to this genre (though the sound of just the cold wind blowing, animal noises, and the occasional rustling of foliage below your feet does still evoke quite an atmosphere). The developer does in any case appear to have learned a lesson from his previous game, Drizzlepath: Genie, by returning the game's length to one more suitable for what is, ultimately, a leisurely stroll through a lovely landscape (that said, this one could easily have been a bit longer, given its thirty to sixty minute duration).
"Waitaminute...THIRTY TO SIXTY MINUTES?" I hear you cry. Hey - it's two bucks, with cards, less in a bundle or a sale. Get over yourself. Indie devs have to eat too.
My biggest complaint about the game would be that it ultimately all feels a bit directionless, unlike the dev's previous two games in which there was a genuine sense of a journey, created by a generally clear path to follow and the vague narrative flow of the voice-over narrations. I suspect the game might last even LESS than thirty minutes, if you don't have as much of a propensity for getting lost and running into invisible walls as I do. (I was oddly grateful for the invisible walls, though, 'cause they were about the only thing which stopped me from walking several MILES in the wrong direction before realising I'd given myself a bum steer. It also didn't help that I plum walked past a cave I was meant to enter, and didn't find it again 'til ten minutes later.)
I'm not afraid to declare this my least favourite of Tonguc's games so far, but I have three more to go and have reason to believe they will only get better. If you're in the market for an abundance of either gameplay or story, this probably isn't the product for you. If, on the other hand, you genuinely enjoy going for a very relaxing, casual wander through beautifully-rendered digital landscapes, you may well love this, and get as much as hours of enjoyment from exploring its every inch and attaining every Achievement. It really does come down to individual taste. Me, I'm a little more into the story-oriented end of things, and can take or leave Achievements at the best of times, but if you suspect there's even the smallest chance you'll get some joy from this, that low, low price really is a bit of a no-brainer.
Verdict: 6.5/10.

After some dabbling with the character creation, my half-man and half-plant wanderer named Leaf Licker arrives in the peaceful hamlet of Joppa.  A community of watervine farmers, I ask around for some poor saps in need of my skills.  I eventually find a young man by the name of Mehmet, who claims that the community's water vines have been ravaged by unknown critters north in Red Rock.  I traveled along too the destination in question and delved down into the depths of Red Rock itself.  After many hardships, I discover the creatures responsible for it, slaying one quickly and taking it's carcass back to Joppa where I'd present it to Mehmet for verification.  When I had arrived back at the village, everything was normal as ever.  As I took steps back toward Mehmet though, things took a turn for the worst.  A lightning bolt of cosmic proportions decended upon the poor, unsuspecting soul as if summoned by Thor himself.  Within a split second, Mehmet had died before my eyes, his body blown to nothingness making my effort all for naught.  Stricken with sorrow for the poor farmer, I wandered too the salt flats to the west, where the only thing I had to look forward too was death by dehydration which came quickly, ending Leaf Licker's life in moments.

Resident Evil 6 (RE6) is the third Resident Evil game I’ve played (only played 4, 5, and 6 since I don’t have a Playstation). The game has a relatively low metacritic rating (69 last I checked) but I found it to be exactly what I expected after playing RE5 a year earlier. If you’ve only seen the Resident Evil movies then you may not be aware that the games have a completely different storyline and I think they’ve been retconned a few times as well.  You would probably recognize a bunch of the characters though since almost every Resident Evil character I know appears in RE6.
The game is a third person “over the shoulder” game played in coop with another person. Just like Resident Evil 5, if you don’t have a friend playing with you, the computer controls the other guy. There are 4 campaigns for you to play and in each of them you can play one of the 2 characters. The campaigns all intersect multiple times so you might be playing the Leon campaign and run in to Chris Redfield. Then when you’re playing the Chris campaign you run into Leon and play as the other side of the encounter. It’s a great way to see the plot from various viewpoints and you’ll understand why characters are acting in a certain way. After you’ve completed the game you can go back and play as the second character in each campaign as well. There’s over 50 hours of gameplay to be had in single player alone. Each campaign is divided into chapters and each chapter into sections, for example Leon Campaign Chapter 1-1, 1-2, 1-3, etc. The game saves at checkpoints during each section, so if you’re knocked out and your partner doesn’t revive you in time, you restart at the checkpoint. Your inventory is saved between sections and you can replay previous sections freely. There is no more “inventory screen,” now it’s just a quick menu where you hold a button to display and scroll through your items. There is no level up system, but you can gather “exp” points to unlock perks such as improved damage or better aim stability. Then you can pick which 3 perks you want equipped between missions. So you can replay levels over and over for more exp or replay some of the bosses a few times for fun.
I believe the complaint that a lot of Resident Evil purists had was that beginning with RE5, the games aren’t really “survival horror” anymore. Now the focus is on action and shooting. I remember in RE4 that conserving ammunition was a big challenge so you use melee attacks as much as possible. The melee system has been enhanced a great deal since then and ammunition has become a lot more plentiful (you can also replay levels to grab ammo and then just save + quit). You’ll definitely do a lot of shooting, but you should definitely master the hand to hand (or knife fighting depending on which character you’re playing).
Storywise, the game picks up a few years after Resident Evil 5. The world is continuing to circle the drain as various warlords around the world use biological weapons to create zombies and other super powered monsters. Each campaign has its own antagonist though they cross over a lot, as mentioned earlier. If you haven’t played the previous games you might not understand a few “peculiarities” of the playable characters. I certainly didn’t know who some of the people were and the ways that their backstories drive the game’s plot.  It is mostly understandable though if you play the whole game through. Just accept that everyone knows each other from previous games.
Pros:
+Excellent built in co-op play for the campaign, and for different game modes like Mercenaries. Steam sells the “complete pack” that includes everything, kind of like a Game of the Year edition.
+Very long game (at least 35 hours even if you rush), you’ll get your money’s worth.
+A lot of replay value (you can unlock “perks” by grinding for exp).
+You can play as a monster! Join someone’s game and ♥♥♥♥ them up. A few people tried dropping into my brother and my games, but since we were on levels with only normal zombie enemies (so they spawned as normal zombies), we blew them away easily lol.
Cons:
-Multi player is kind of dead now. Hard to find a game to join unless it’s a friend inviting you or vice versa.
-According to Resident Evil “purists” the game is more action than “survival horror.” If you’re new to Resident Evil games and just looking for a co-op shooter, this won’t bother you.
-There are a few times when you need to run through an area in a short amount of time (like escaping a giant enemy) and the camera keeps subtly shifting so you slightly change running directions and hit a wall or something, then you die. This is VERY annoying but only happens in a few areas. Most of the time you can play leisurely.
Overall I would definitely recommend Resident Evil 6 if you like action games and / or zombie bashing games. The visuals are disturbing and the monsters are grotesque, as expected in a Resident Evil game. The game is 100% better if you have a friend to join your game for coop play. And once you’re done with the campaigns you can spend a lot of time on the various game modes that are included, most especially the Mercenaries mode, which returns from Resident Evil 5. It’s kind of like a survival mode where you try to live to the end of the timer killing as many enemies as you can. The enemy types keep changing until you’re fighting mini bosses.

Game Review: ★★★ (3/5 Stars)
What we have here is an indie game with extraordinarily good graphics. I played this game on the highest settings and it was a journey through heaven. The landscape was absolutely beautiful and the background music very relaxing. Bottle is a Walking Simulator - and it takes that title very seriously. The gameplay consists of one main thing: Walking!
Apart from a few notes we can find and pick up, and a short sequence in the beginning and the end of the game, there is nothing but a very linear, almost non-existing storyline. A few implications are made, but there is no consistent story or setting that I could find. I've tried exploring a little bit and got lost with no pointers as to where to get back to the path I had to go, which means that while the game is somewhat open world, it's potentially very frustrating when you decide to use that feature.
To me, for the purposes of a "bedtime story" type of game to calm down before going to sleep, it definitely does its job, but as a game in general, it's at most acceptable even though beautiful.
