I don't recommend this game for most people, however for the few that will accept it in it's current state, I do.
This was probably the most ambitious game of 2013. Everything was going great for a while. It seemed promising and offered a unique atmosphere that no games have come close to matching (Closest are S.T.A.L.K.E.R and the Metro series). It was possibly the most unique and fun MMOFPS Survival game and pioneered that genre even competing with DayZ for some time (That's died down too now, and the genre is currently dominated by mediocre generic survival "build a base and raid" games that offer nearly the same atmosphere. The game met it's downfall by slowing updates and rising cheaters, later to even lower in popularity and rating when a new dev team was introduced. This team put more effort into microtransactions and DLC (Although that DLC pack was decently fun while it was available). Then the team left (I don't remember why) After a long while the first team came back and introduced the "Resurrected" edition. Removing all microtransactions and DLCs, bringing the game back to the state were the original team left off, however it did take time to get back because (If I remember correctly) the 2nd team had corrupted the map files and it took a while to work around. It did bring some players back and introduced many new community based features. We could finally host our own servers and kick the cheaters. Still the playerbase declined again due to slow updates and (I believe) the publishers removing the 1st dev team again from the game. **Progress has since halted. See below for a follow up.**
If you're looking into the game now, I'd recommend staying away unless you'd like to contribute to our community's last efforts to keep the game alive. There is talk that a new dev team might take over. If they do, it could be a bright light in dim water.
For playerbase, the peaks recently for 24 hours have been near 30 at a time. 2,000 unique players a week, so the community is not completely dead. Many of these reviews left currently on this page are sort of on a weird "hate on Nether bandwagon" although there are a few good negative ones.
tl;dr The game is solid, but doesn't feel complete, it needs work, lots of it, but it still holds the potential it once had. It's still fun sometimes with friends, and it provides a great atmosphere. It's a unique game that attempts to (and partially does) bring an experience like no other, even with that the atmosphere is unmatched, and I still consider it my favorite MMOFPS Survival Title there is. Community is moderately dead nowadays, 30~ish peaks.Though there is hope in the game with talks of a new dev coming in. (Progress currently halted) I'd recommend for some but not for most. It has an interesting history of course, and has provided some with great memories.
**If any of this information is incorrect in this review please correct me by commenting or contacting me.

Short version: This game takes you back to the good old SSB-brawling-with-your-friends times. The rule changing mechanics are a really nice idea. Recommended specially if you have firends/family to play locally with.
TLDR: Keep in mind that this is an early review. There are many things the devs are working on.
Controls: Controller works GREAT. It feels fluid and intuitive, you won't catch yourself having a hard time switching cards, jumping and hitting someone at the same time. On the other hand, keyboard controls feel plain out weird, specially on the card-controlling part (controlled using u, i, o, j, k, l). My first games were played using this imput method and it could sometimes get frustrating. This point is further aggravated by the fact that there are no remapping options at this point.
Gameplay: This is the strongest point of this game. It is a 2D brawler with constantly changing rules (tag, king of the hill, racing, FFA and more), which are twisted further by players constantly playing their cards to, for example, double the points given or disable melee attacks for some time. 4 player games can get insanely fun, specially (as I already mentioned) in local games.
Community: Right now the community is pretty small, and it can take some time to find a match to play in online. This can get frustrating at times, especially if you experience the "UPNP router bug" which won't let you create a lobby (which the game will automatically will do if it can't find a situable match, forcing you to lose even more time as it can't be cancelled until the error shows up).
Overall: The game is fun, but does not feel complete yet. If the genre draws you in and you don't mind encountering a few bugs along the way, you will surely have a nice time playing. The devs are active in the forums and the community seems to be growing in a by-day basis, so even with its current flaws, I recommend this game.

Overruled has more twists than your favorite reality television show, and more strategy too!
Overruled is everything you could possibly enjoy in a madcap multiplayer game. There are cards that change the rules at any time, which could help with timing in respawning, timing for your projectile weapon, or the amount of points possible, or the very game themselves.
The rule is simple - get as much points as possible, but how you get those points (and how much) depends entirely on the rules randomized every 30 seconds (or presented by a fellow player)
But at one point during the game, you have an "OVERRULED" card which negates any card presented on the table, so it's a game of juggling not only the platforming and combat, but the very rules and scoring themselves.
Play according to your skill set, or hinder your opponents on their best skill set. It's a very addictive game, and can't wait to see new levels, new characters and possibly more "twists" as the game continues.

Resident evil 6 does exceedingly well at making most of the characters likable and actually makes you feel like you are playing in a party during the game. Again, the models in the game are really good, If you are the kind of gamer who doesn't care as long as it looks good, just buy it, because it does pull off all of its good ends without a hitch, and so well it's as tolerable as repititiveness in a sandbox game with good graphics and open spaces.
But in my opinion, that's where it ends, If you were screening this game off to a friend or group of followers they'd almost be permitted to bring glasses and popcorn, because from the screen to the viewer, it is magnificent.
As a player, however, the gameplay makes me upset out of the health system and the general mechanics of the game itself. Bosses will stab and pretty much kill animate you for the same damage that a legless zombie can get out of your ankles. One unit. The units do not always empty completely so there's no real excuse. I don't understand how getting stabbed 6 times or taking about 6 shots of damage allows for the unit of damage to still recover but god forbid my ankles get slapped... Please, jump in the river Styx completely before you come back. Also... staggers... Where are they when you need them? I can stagger in monster hunter with No effort mid attack, whatever, But here, shooting a shotgun shell at a zombie in mid leap does nothing unless they will die from it. I don't get how that works, and in that sense, George Bush would have gotten hit by both of those shoes. Now, I know not all games work as well with mechanics but capcom has already had working systems in games like lost planet and the earlier mentioned monster hunter.
Also, the game rarely mentions how they want you to do things, Zombie epedemic survivors like leon should want to shoot dead bodies on the floor or sever anything even remotely close to intact or infected, but they do not, and act surprised when they finally come to life after they tripped over them just to get to the key. again... movie experience. Meanwhile they let loose on zombies they can almost be sure still have some sort of consciousness. I don't get it. Other times they tell you you need to do something and have a feild set to almost show you you're going to be doing area defense. hey, sever that! okay! Let me waste all of my ammo when you really want me to jump on his back. How was I supposed to know that when you're respawning 9mm ammo from cases I destroyed 10 minutes ago? It just makes zero sense. And I feel like someone screaming at the movies because they just make really poor decisions overall. You see a zombie with a machine gun? a sniper? You cannot have their gun. And if you see a sniper sight you? You better hope there's a wall nearby because he's not going to miss. Hey look, lockers, let me hide in one hopefully they will have to actually look before finding me or giving up, found instantly. If you're playing next to someone who played and mastered resident evil 5, They're probably going to give you the look of grief until it finally happens to them.
Quickshot... how about an aim mode that doesn't obligate me to use it if they're too close. The aim and controls are akin to being in sniper mode. Someone leaps behind you, you either sprint away, hope you can turn and aim fast enough to make the shot, and if it does not kill or stun fast enough you will get hit, or quickshot. In my opinion, It's just bad news, even online players aren't as blatant about noscope as this game is. Capcom can do better. Because quickshot should not cost stamina when you're trying to simulate relatively close shots. The cover system Is very workable, but sprinting around in circles is more effective currently for me, as sniper enemies seem to never exist when you can actually dodge the shot. That being said, quickshot has a multitude of uses that can be good or bad, they ultimately open some characters up to empty their clips on enemies with guns, or they just miss and give a better more closer opportunity to aim properly. Quickshot is necessary, but not a need, in my opinion the quickshot system is a clear call that they expect you to never have an opportunity to sit still. It's probably the biggest mixed bag in the game, because It takes a lot of load off of the developers for making a shooting system that pretty much lacks in terms of the situation at hand. But hey, resident evil does feature an intricate targeting system where certain areas do more damage, they've been doing it forever, so maybe I'm just doing it wrong, I am okay with that.
The inventory system is another thing that makes me cringe. you cant hold two herbs but you can hold 200 9mm bullets. I have no first aid spray but it's forever bonded to an icon in my selection. You can carry every gun in the game but you can't carry the ammo stack.
I know this is supposed to be survival horror, But failing to organize their inventory or not even saying, wow player, this is not going to work, at all. Your partner is telling you good job when you just mutated 3 enemies and they're going rogue while your partner is firing a pistol. A PISTOL. Even dynasty warriors will slap you with variants of you're too far out when you are clearly making the game harder than it has to be, Not this game. Hey, push a huge dumpster to move along the game. Oh an umbrella token is under the table? BLOW UP THE WHOLE TABLE THERES NO OTHER WAY! Why capcom?
I enjoy the game when I can ignore these things, and don't mind getting killed from an ankle slap occasionally. But even at the end of a story, It just feels like you're a witness and not really playing the game. Alright I shook off that zombie, who cares, just got smacked by a train. I have to open that hatch before we all die, My partner is being ignored because he's using one pistol... LEON YOU HAVE TWO PISTOLS WHAT ARE YOU EVEN DOING. Like I said, as a movie this thing gets a million out of 10. But as a game, by developers who clearly know how to do things they've pretty much missed, no. I think everyone I personally would try to recommend this game to will think I am either a monster at games for not seeing how easy it is to die constantly, or rude enough to make people pay for a badly executed gaming experience. Listen to what everyone is saying, It is very arcade oriented, Being scared because you didn't reload or out of not having a clear idea of how the game wants you to defeat the enemy is not survival horror, It's having opinionated multiple choice answers and you slightly disagree with all of them.
I enjoy it because I have it, But unless you're up for some really bad turns. Or think the online experience may be different. (I do admit my online intersection was laughably easy save for the fact we were stuck mashing x for 5 minutes because of reasons I am not aware of) I am not mean enough to tell you to buy the game.

The combat is fun and frantic, while easy at first it takes some time to learn how to properly prioritize and dispose of enemies on screen. There's also a fair amount of inventory management, with you keeping track of items for each member of your party as well as breaking down junk to upgrade your gear.
There's also a bit of party management with different characters to swap in and out of your party when the situation calls for it. On top of that each seperate character has their own unique abilities and skill trees to upgrade, allowing for different styles of play.
The art and animation are very well done and add to the cute and goofy humor of the game.

I can’t help but feel that the title of this game is more than a bit apt to describe the experience I had with this game. This game makes no sense from a story perspective. If this is what tripping on drugs is even remotely like, I don’t think I want to ever experience the real thing. I’m not even going to try and describe the story or the purpose you play in this game because even I’m not certain what the purpose of this game is supposed to serve. Oh right, a comedy adventure.
Reviewing a game's comedy is a very dangerous road to walk on. What I find funny isn't what you'll find funny and vice versa. I stay away from talking about a game's humor and generalize what it's like. You may find this incredibly hilarious while it's all completely lost on me. So, I’ll just break it down to its parts. What you’re essentially getting is a collection of unremarkable (or boring) mini-games with walking sequences between them. During the entire time you will be subjected to a multitude of references and jokes from various forms of media that you may or may not get. (Prepare to not get a lot of them). This style of game has been rising in popularity of late and frankly, it hasn't been my favorite to play. Which this entry has only further cemented my dislike of it.

Let me make one thing perfectly clear before a few of my sentences are taken wrong: I absolutely love this game. I was terrified all the way through, even that first walk to the house in the beginning scared me quite a bit because this game has ATMOSPHERE. If there's anything that the entirety of video game writing has difficulty with, it's characterization. One-dimensional, unrelatable, unsympathetic casts are no stranger to a vast majority of the gaming industry, and most of the time the dilemmas of the characters don't really matter to the player at all. Rarely do we actually care about the thoughts and feelings of our adventurers. Thomas Was Alone is the antithesis to that tendency, it is a game where you play primarily in interest of your characters', the most simplest of characters, internal discussions. This game has more personality and relatability in its characters than perhaps any game I've played before, and proves that all you need to do to inspire sympathy and concern in the player is some frantastic writing worked beautifully into some simple puzzle gameplay.
The actual puzzle aspect of the game is decent, but not much. It has a interesting twist as you control various shapes with their own distinct properties and personality told through the third person around a level with a specific exit. Towards the end it's a tad repetitive, and it's never difficult. If you're really looking for just a puzzle game, you'll find an average one at best here. It works, it carries you along, but that's it. Yet, if you're playing this game just as a puzzle game, you're missing the point entirely.
That is not to say that the gameplay is just average. The puzzle aspect, which one may understandably but wrongly assume is the primary aspect of the gameplay, is just average. However, the way the narrative and story works into the dynamic between the shapes solving puzzles together is extremely clever and charming. As I previously stated, there is a large cast of different shapes, each with a certain property that distinguishes themselves as puzzle solving agents. Each character has a unique personality that goes along with their personal ability, and moreover, they each have interactions and opinions of each other that work into their relations and teamwork required to solve their various challenges. It's fantastically done, it really is, all told through a charming third person narrative, further emphasizing how the qualities and gameplay of the characters define their personalities, leaving it open that their personalities is just a natural projection of the player and narrator. It's remarkably impressive how well Mike Bithell was able to incorporate the characters gameplay interactions with their own personal relations between one another, and it creates this sense of charming companionship rarely seen in any video games today, a sense of companionship that forces the player to love and follow the characters to the very end. Needless to say, I beat the game in one sitting. It's a short game, but it's certainly one of those games that you think about a while after beating it, and I still think about it as guideline to how characterization should be in video games, and as a benchmark for writing. You're certainly paying for quality over quantity, just like how you don't buy a book or a movie based on their length for more bang for your buck.
Lastly, David Housden's soundtrack is amazing as well, definately pick that up. The crescendoing at times really helps pull at the heart strings. Also, as previously stated, the narration is no less enjoyable, and the game would not at all be the same without it. So yeah, buy this game.

Here's the deal with RE6:
I LOVE this game. I love it for the same reason I love transformers, John Woo films, and all the Die Hards: It's entertaining, and it's always trying to one-up itself in terms of special effects and nasty biological warfare weapon crap. A work of art or a masterpiece, it is not. A adrenaline-fueled ride against zombies, T-Rex's, giant bosses, and an ridiculously long and frustrating scene in the snow trying to find little microchips? Absolutely.
I'm not afraid to admit that this game has flaws, and there are many, but it does NOT make this game complete garbage, like many critics claim. Here are the biggest ones:
1) During Leon's campaign, cars will come out of nowhere and kill you instantly, which is VERY frustrating.
2) QTE's are EVERYWHERE, but with the exception of a few, they're not particularly difficult.
3) The snow level. Just saying. I've played through this game in it's entirety on the xbox multiple times and every time I just have to force myself through this terrible, horrible, God awful level. Everything about it is what's wrong with games.
4) Leon looks weird.
5) Villain is dumb, writing is mostly bad, and parts where enemies are shooting guns really aren't very fun. The game just wasn't built to be Gears of War, but sometimes it tries to be.
6) Local co-op makes you share items, but online doesn't? This makes the game EXTREMELY difficult when playing locally.
7) Not scary, except for a few parts, which are very scary.
Now for the good, which totally outweighs the bad, by the way.
1) The John Woo action style controls are AMAZING. People will hate on them, but they just take a long time to master. Once you've got it down, you can basically Matrix your way through the whole game. Honestly, sliding away from zombies and shooting the crap out of them still is satisfying hundreds of hours later.
2) TONS of campaign. Seriously though, this game takes forever. When you finally beat all three of the six or so hour long campaigns, ANOTHER one opens up that's single player only, and it's pretty awesome (though also very confusing and a little dumb as far as the story is concerned.)
3) Amazing boss fights, and it can be truly terrifying when some of those zombies leap across buildings to get at you (but with a side-roll you can dodge them, which feels truly epic.)
4) BIG awesome bosses. This game does 'em right. Except for that naked chick...that was weird. Like, why is she touching herself? I was playing this game in my living room, guys. Come on.
5) All the campaigns have their ups and downs, but each of them have at least one section that is mind-blowingly good. Leon at the school, Chris at the underwater place, and Sherri when you lose all your weapons and have to punch your way out. Great stuff.
Anyway, yeah, play this game. If you don't like it, you don't like it. But I'd recommend at least beating ONE of the campaigns before tossing it so you can get a feel for how everything works, and you'll probably want to start with Leon. Anyway, I love all the resident evil games, but I felt I needed to write this since people might avoid their new favorite game, based on nasty reviews.

"Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥" I think to myself as crocodile bites into my flesh. I assumed that I could beat the glorified lizard like I could in so many other games. I was wrong. This was just the first of many deaths I would experience in my first couple of hours with the game.
TL;DR at the bottom.
I'm an unabashed fan of roguelikes. The focus on character building and death meaning something have always been a huge draw to me. If you look at my library, I have a lot of these suckers. You may wonder if there's still games in the genre that can still surprise me. The answer is HELL YES. Caves of Qud is one such game.
Throw out the typical fantasy setting you probably picture when you think of a roguelike. This is the post-apocalypse and your two choices are to play as a pure or mutated human. I've tried both and the latter seems to be way more fun. It kind of reminds me of the episodes of Futurama with the mutants in the sewer. You can turn yourself into all kinds of monstrosities, and I suspect the number of options will only grow over time. My most recent playthrough I decided to take a mutation which gave me flaming hands. I didn't realize it meant I would never be able to wear gloves. This is a great illustration of the mutation system: most of the time it involves trade offs, especially for the really fun powers, like being made up of quills like a porcupine (a personal favorite).
The graphics are ASC, but put through a filter that makes it look like you're playing on a much older computer. One that may or may not be from before your time. I personally love the look of it, but the result makes it deceptively system intensive.
The controls will be divisive to the say the least. Some will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that the controls are so obtuse, though once you play with them for a while they do start to feel natural. They can all be rebound though, and if you're willing to put in the effort to do so you can bind them in any way that your heart desires!
I haven't even explored a fraction of the world yet, nor have I managed to complete the first quest I was given. There are still enemies that would seem menial in other games that can kill me if I'm not careful. Call me a masochist but this is more than a little bit exciting to me. Two hours into a game I generally feel like I get what's going on, but here I'm still trying to figure out what exactly I'm supposed to do. The procedurally generated, fully destructable world is huge, and I get the feeling that even without permadeath (that is an option for those who are turned off by having to reroll all the time) the game would be collosal.
If you're into that kind of thing, there's tons of lore here too. More than I'll ever manage to sift through realistically. It's a world of mutants and sentient bears; the writing ain't half bad either.
Negatives are that the game uses far more system resources than it needs to. It looks pretty, but functionality trumps graphics, especially in a roguelike. Also, the game isn't friendly to those who aren't willing to be patient with it. You'll die a lot before you start to see successes. Then you'll continue to die frequently. That can be disheartening and will certainly put off some players. This game is harder than Nethack in my opinion, and that's not something I would say lightly. Tutorials would be a welcome feature, more than just a series of paragraphs to read in the help section.
TL;DR: This is the roguelike for the true hardcore roguelike player. It's tough, it's massive, and inventive enough that I feel like telling my friends about the porcupine-beetle-man hybrid that I rolled last time. For an early access title its chock full of content. Check it out, but just be ready to die.

.

The audio is very well done. The soundtrack was definitely my favourite aspect of the game; all of the music, ranging from catchy, upbeat tunes to dark and foreboding ambient tracks really pull you into the protagonist's head, making the immersion all that much better. [10/10]

After finishing my playthrough, there's only one aspect of the game I remember disliking. The main character (Yama) is initially built up to be quite perceptive
, but afterwards it becomes quite clear to the player that outside of this he's almost... unbearably dense
. I feel that when the player becomes more knowledgable than the character they play as, it breaks the immersion. It's an obviously necessary mechanism for setting up a sequel, but I feel that just in this one situation the writing could have been better.
TL;DR, give this VN a look, it definitely won't disappoint! Overall I place it at an 8/10, although as stated I don't have a lot of experience with the genre so take it as you will.

Before I begin to discuss Rocksmith or Rocksmith 2014, I first feel the need to clarify that I wouldn't personally classify this as a video game. I only say this to help understand the points I'm making. I consider Rocksmith/Rocksmith 2014 more of a learning tool(s) than an actual game. However, if you enjoy playing guitar as I do, then it certainly feels like a fun game at times.
There are a lot of changes from the original Rocksmith to the 2014 version. I would highly recommend the 2014 version over the original format, just because there are far more tools available, more music, more capability for learning. Personally, I wouldn't recommend this to those that do not have experience playing a guitar. My advise would be to seek a teacher or you may find Rocksmith to be a bit frustrating.
Also, if you're wondering if this tool/game will be good as a replacement for a good guitar/music teacher...then I will say NO. It's a great tool, but it's one of many tools that you need to be a solid rhythm, lead, or bass guitarist. It's not going to teach you how to read music as it's tab only, (kinda in it's own tab format, but if you can read tab you'll understand. If you can't read tab, Rocksmith's way isn't that hard to understand, but some notations will take some getting used to).
For new guitar players, there's a bit of a learning curve that the developers assumed that you already have. By this I mean, understanding how to make a chord and some hand positions or having bends down.  You'll be given a video demonstration and you'll be told if you played the chord/bend/or technique correctly or not. You won't be told what you're doing wrong, or if you're fretting too hard or have some incorrect positioning. Getting bends to be recognized can also be a real pain if you're new to guitar and aren't certain what is wrong, be it you or calibration of your instrument, (or possibly other issues resulting in your bends not being counted as correct). There are arcade games, (called Guitarcade within Rocksmith 2014), that are mean't to help you practice specific techniques. However, there is not a "no fail" mode so that you can just keep strumming and/or trying without having your game ended for incorrect patterns/chords/notes. I personally feel that due to this, the game is better suited to intermediate to advanced players rather than new players. I warn about this as I would hate for someone to give up on learning guitar after becoming frustrated from the game. Learning music and/or an instrument is hard. Having a teacher to give you advice prevents you from learning bad habits that you may have to unlearn later, (thus increasing how long it takes you to get better with your instrument).
If you try to save money, or time by using rocksmith instead of investing the time & money into a "good" guitar teacher as well as books or the internet to read about learning music, music theory, composition, etc... then most people may instead frustrate themselves from what they are not learning. If you're only goal is to learn how to play a song you love, one paticular way, then yes this will be perfect. I say one paticular way since there are many different ways to play the same note or chord, depending on pitch, range or your own expression rather than who wrote that piece of music.
So if you're funds are limited like many of us, and you're wondering if you should invest that money into Rocksmith 2014 or pay monthly for a teacher...I would advise you to take the instructor and learn. You can always get Rocksmith 2014 later or some even newer version of it down the line. What you'll gain from a teacher will benefit your playing for the rest of your life. Rocksmith, while great and fun, will only benefit you're understanding of individual songs, but you may not understand how they were written and other fundamentals.
If you want to understand music and be able to express "yourself" and the way you interprete that song and how it makes you feel as well as any piece of music, definately use Rocksmith 2014 as well as practicing without Rocksmith 2014, and read all about music and learn from a tutor/teacher that is good at teaching the style of music you're interested in. Feel free to search the internet on tips to find a good music/guitar teacher as well.
-----------------------------------------
For those that have decided to use Rocksmith 2014, my advice would be to find a song you like and keep working on getting down a section at a time. Using Riff Repeater and selecting small sections to practice at a low speed, perhaps 50% or lower if you need. Give yourself plenty of time to get comfortable with it and don't get frustrated if you have bad days. The muscles in your hand build over time just as they do in the rest of your body. Your muscle memory of remembering where each note and chord is takes time to develop too. Give yourself a few months to get the entire song down, (longer if needed). If you feel that you can't get past a certain speed, try speeding it up 5% higher and take a few mintues at the higher speed. Then go back down to the lower speed you were already having trouble with before. That sometimes helps with those sticky points.
Feel free to use guitar forums and other internet sources if you find trouble with a paticular technique, chord, or even a song phrase. You may even wish to read how other musicians divide their practice time since many people become frustrated because they try to practice too much. If you find a section of a song giving you trouble, watch how another person plays that song and see their hand position(s), which could help with your own progres.  Keep in mind that missions can help with your overall progress. Don't forget to work on them as well.
The best advice that was given to me about learning guitars was, "If playing guitar was easy, then all the pawn shops in town wouldn't be filled with guitars."
Best of luck with your music endeavors. I hope this review has helped you.

After a lifelong career as an air guitarist, and several instances of complete failure trying to teach myself guitar, I decided to try Rocksmith.  A couple of years later I'm actually a passable guitar player.
What the game will not do:
It won't make you Joe Satriani, Steve Vai, Guthrie Govan, or guitar hero x.
It won't hold your hand or answer every minor question you have when you first start playing.
It won't teach you all the theory behind the songs you're playing.
What the game will do:
It will teach you enough theory to get by (via some pretty generic lessons and mini games).
It will introduce you to improvisation (session mode).
It will probably introduce you to some pretty cool music you haven't heard before.
Possibly trigger a mid-life crisis.
Probably turn you into a guitar gear junky.
But most importantly it will get you past those first HUGE humps to learning guitar - building callouses, finger dexterity, and getting in some effective practice.  The biggest roadblock for me on my previous attempts to learn was wondering WTF to play when I did sit down to practice.  This game helped me personally with that a lot since you can just flip on a great song and play along without turning the pages in some book or trying to decipher a tab.  The dynamic difficulty has some quirks no doubt, but in the end you can always manually adjust what level you want the song at (for those wondering how to do this, just put the whole song in riff repeater). In the end, I would call this an extremely effective introduction for brand new guitar players, and a very good practice tool for beginners and intermediate players.  If you can't get into playing using this software, then playing guitar may not be for you.

Many fear Crysis 2 to be the franchise’s turn from an open-ended objective-based shooter into a linear shooter that parrots the gameplay trends of all the other AAA shooters these days. For the most part it is, but that doesn’t stop it from being better than almost all those games. It’s very different from the original Crysis and Crysis Warhead, but Crysis 2’s level design still has a certain quality that’s rare these days.
If you can find my user reviews of Crysis and Warhead, I described those games as possibly the last examples of sandbox-style mission design where you’re free to tackle objectives how you want in absolutely massive maps. Crysis 2 chucks that whole approach for something more similar to Call of Duty or better yet Halo. Crysis 2 has obvious chest-high walls for cover everywhere, quick-time events, a storyline about aliens and mercenaries that’s generic despite having been written by a published sci-fi author, upgrades bought with experience points, and generally gives players fewer options than its predecessors. It doesn’t however shove you down straight corridors, but maintains some semblance of the franchise’s open-ended nature.
Where in the original Crysis players would get a full map of an area and multiple objectives at a time, Crysis 2 will display a single waypoint at a time at the other end of a medium-sized area with maybe three or four routes through it. You might see a sky bridge flanking around some enemies, a hole in a barricade, or a small tunnel underneath the area. And the game will directly tell you all this by highlighting weapons and routes on your tactical visor, assuming you’re used to more linear shooters.
For what they’re worth Crysis 2’s levels are pretty well-designed. It’s still possible to sneak through most areas of the game and play the whole thing stealthily. When firefights do break out, instead of just popping in and out of cover you have a lot of room with which to employ some positional strategy on enemies. Effectively it’s like fighting in a Halo game’s combat arenas but with fewer vehicles.
The nanosuit’s powers have been adjusted a bit from the earlier games but the same general strategies apply: use cloak to sneak by or flank enemies (prone is gone by the way), throw objects and leap around with strength, etc. The main change is that armor mode is no longer the default but must now be switched on manually, so you have to factor it in when managing the suit’s energy. Speed mode is pretty much just the sprint which automatically consumes suit energy. Strength is actually just a super jump and a melee attack.
The aliens in Crysis 2 are simultaneously a bit more interesting to fight and more boring in how they work. In the earlier game Crytek tried to make them feel more “alien” by having them float around in the air with vague shield abilities, which could often make combat with them feel odd. In Crysis 2 they behave a lot more like humans as they walk on land, use what look like guns, and generally behave like your human enemies. Because they have different weak points and can sometimes disable your suit energy though, you still have to approach them differently. There’s one interesting new boss-type enemy that appears a few times throughout the game, and Crysis 2’s final combat sequence manages to be an unusually interesting and challenging fight.
One area in which Crysis 2 is unquestionably an improvement over the original is its visuals and its strain on your hardware. The sequel both looks and runs better than the first game, especially in DirectX 11. I guess being released on consoles meant Crytek had to actually optimize the game this time. Crysis 2’s use of lighting, post-processing, bokeh depth of field, and tessellation put it above all but a handful of games released since 2011 in terms of tech. It’s probably one of the earliest games to reach the threshold we’re seeing on PS4 and Xbox One now.
On my i5 and GTX 760, on maximum DX11 settings in 1080p the game runs at 60 frames per second almost all the time, occasionally dipping down to 50, and never going below 40. However, like its predecessors Crysis 2 does suffer the problem of locking to 24Hz when played in fullscreen on a TV. Forcing a borderless windowed mode with external software can fix this.
To compare, in my earlier reviews I called Crysis and Warhead simulations of 80’s action movie tropes where you can manipulate the mechanics of Predator and First Blood Part II however you want. Instead of a simulation, Crysis 2 feels like a game -- everything about its levels and mechanics has been transformed into a smaller set of rules Crytek wants you to follow, but within those rules it’s still one of the better games on the market.

Having played again since the new control changes the devs recently implemented, can happily say the game feels and plays vastly superior to the drag&drop system they had previously. The option is still there for anyone who desires it, but theres now also the choice to use a more common rts style of having selected characters and clicking to do actions such as moving/attacking.
The gameplay itself is fun and challenging enough that even in the early stage of the game im at, it's keeping me at least slightly on my toes. The abilities are fun to use and plentiful with their relatively low cooldowns and the number of them you will have available to you over the course of the game. Having a fair amount of simple exploring to do in the overworld is nice, it's certainly not going to keep you searching for long, but I think it's a nicer choice that just selecting the next battle/area to attack. Here you can avoid combat if you like, or go looking for it in the form of monsters seen in the overworld, and it brings you to a combat area where you will engage whatever it is you ran into.
The loot system is simple and easy to use, and it's enjoyable to gradually upgrade all your characters gear along with finding more interesting pieces. If anything I feel like the gear comes a little too easy? But I've not yet played long enough to really understand just how powerful the early game legendaries are.
If you've heard of Battleheart for mobile, then you'll feel right at home with this. Fun to play, and the story so far, albiet a little generic, is engaging enough to keep me reading. The different difficulty levels are a nice feature to encompass all gamers, and I believe if you like the sound of a party based rts game, this is enjoyable on several levels.
Lastly but not least, the developers for this are very vocal, friendly and seem geuninly careing about the furthering of their game; great to see.

Don't let the bobble heads and big ol' eyes fool you... behind Sentry Knight Tactics' cute exterior beats the heart of a monster, and we wouldn't have it any other way.

In a word: Beautiful.
Don't think of Thomas Was Alone as a puzzle game, because it's really not. Sure, the point is to use your characters to solve platforming puzzles, but the real key here is the way the story is presented. Every single character has a recognizable personality that you will recognize in somebody you know. The ensemble cast in this game leap out of their minimalist 2D confines to become something so real you can almost touch them.
The soundtrack and voiceover is what really sets this game apart. The video game aspect is almost inconsequential, but it does its part to fill in the necessary gaps within the rather minimal narrative of the story. This is a game of mood and emotion, rather than challenge and action.

Let me start off by saying that this is a bad resident evil, but I think it is a good game.
It is a bad resident evil as there is no survival aspect. Sure, they brought back real zombies for a campaign, but that's about it. Even then, most of them jump around and♥♥♥♥♥♥and swing weapons all over the place. No. Thats not how they should work. Inventory management is GONE. Once you pick up a weapon, thats it, you can keep it forever and not worry about switching them out. All you gotta worry about is inventory for ammo, herbs and grenades which doesn't come up much. The other campaigns are the same, but its more like gears of war as enemies are just infected people again with guns. Where's Marcus' dad?
Gonna be honest, even for RE the stories are horrible. Jake's Ending? AHAHAHAHAHAHHA no.
As a game, I did have fun. The movement is really neat, and melee combat is quite nifty. You get a LOT of playtime for every campaign, as there is a lot of story to go through. Agent Hunt is a really neat idea, where you are a zombie and attack players as they do the story, but it's not executed too well, I remember hating it. The stamina mechanic doesn't fit in with the game, but it's quite neat for the mercenaries mode.
Mercenaries is what makes this game for me. I've spent hundreds of hours in this gamemode and never get bored of it. It's just fun at its best. If you enjoyed RE5's mercenaries, you're gonna enjoy this just as much. Only complaint about it on PC is that there doesn't seem to be as many levels as on console. I remember buying several map packs for it, and I'm not sure if they're in here, but I doubt it. I'll update this part if I get confirmation.
It runs really well for me so far, but the FOV seems low and the FOV option didnt seem to change much. It's a solid port.
All in all, if you're expecting classic resident evil (not likely) turn away. If you loved the mercenaries in RE5, for the love of god buy it. If you like gears of war and stuff, try it out, you might like it.
